Carrick has overseen a disastrous start to their season which has United in 18th and in the relegation zone. The 45-year-old has won only one game in the league, against Ipswich in August, and three in all competitions. United were knocked out of the Carabao Cup by Brighton in September.

Sports.title: Danny Kelly, football broadcaster and renowned editor, dies aged 69
Sports.content:
Danny Kelly, the renowned sport and music journalist, has died at the age of 69.

A statement from TalkSport, who he joined in 2007 and for whom he broadcast regularly until stepping away in March after being diagnosed with throat cancer, read: “We are heartbroken to share that our much-loved friend and colleague Danny Kelly has died, aged 69. A cherished part of talkSPORT for so many years, Danny brought extraordinary wit, warmth and knowledge to our airwaves. His passion for football, music and life was infectious, and his kindness touched everyone around him.

“We’ll miss you dearly. Our thoughts are with Danny’s family, friends and everyone who loved listening to him.”

Kelly, a former NME and Q Magazine editor, supported Tottenham, with the Premier League club paying tribute to “one of our own”. A club statement read: “The entire Tottenham family mourns the loss of one of our own, broadcasting legend Danny Kelly. Our thoughts and love are with his family and friends at this incredibly sad time. Rest in peace, Danny.”

His former broadcasting colleague Danny Baker also paid tribute. “My great friend, supreme broadcaster and funniest man I ever knew, Danny Kelly, died yesterday afternoon,” he said in a post on social media. “I cannot believe I will never hear his voice again.”

View image in fullscreen Danny Kelly at the launch of the Football365 website in 1998. Photograph: Patrick Barth/Shutterstock

Kelly also co-founded the 365 Corporation internet company in 1997.

Sports.title: League One clubs aim for further curbs on spending as budgets continue to spiral
Sports.content:
League One clubs want to introduce new spending restrictions to reduce losses by limiting investment from owners.

Clubs in the division voted to tighten the rules last summer by reducing spending limits from 60% to 50% of turnover, and removed a staggered approach to owner investment, so that only 50% of equity injections can be spent on squad costs, with the rest assigned to infrastructure projects. Less than six months later many want to go further.

The Guardian has learned that two proposed models are being considered: a cap on the amount clubs can lose over three years, and the introduction of a luxury tax by which 50% of owner investment above a capped threshold would be redistributed to their rivals – with the former proposal seen as the favoured outcome.

The move to introduce more spending curbs comes despite a legal challenge to the existing rules from the Professional Footballers’ Association, which launched proceedings in August on the grounds that the clubs had failed to abide by the terms of their membership of the professional negotiating and consultative committee.

An attempt by League One and League Two to introduce salary caps of £2.5m and £1.5m respectively was withdrawn in 2021 after the PFA took them to an independent arbitration panel.

Discussions over stricter controls have been taking place for some time, but have been given fresh impetus by last month’s publication of the State of the Game report. The first piece of work by the Independent Football Regulator showed that 94% of clubs in the EFL and National League are loss-making, and that 32 of the 96 would not survive for a month without owner funding.

Last summer’s changes reduced the percentage of clubs’ income that can be spent on wages, with managers’ salaries included for the first time, but there is a renewed move to reduce losses, which averaged £7.5m per club in League One last season, up from £5.3m the previous season.

One owner told the Guardian further regulation was necessary because the clubs had repeatedly shown they could not restrain themselves, pointing out that League One wage bills have increased by 15% this season, and that a top-six budget in the division five years ago would now rank in the bottom three.

Reading and Peterborough have long campaigned for tighter spending controls, but face opposition from clubs such as MK Dons and Wycombe, and it is unclear whether any proposal would gain the two-thirds majority required to be introduced.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

A source at another League One club warned that an unintended consequence would be to create a cliff edge in terms of financial resources with the Championship, which loosened its regulations last season by permitting owners an inject up to £33m over three years, an equity allowance that does not count towards the 85% wage spending/revenue limit.

League Two clubs are not formally involved in the discussions at this stage, but sources have indicated they would probably follow the direction of League One.

The EFL declined to comment.

Sports.title: Bone broth, sweets ban and acupuncture: Harry Kane’s road to record England cap
Sports.content:
It was Harry Kane’s dirty little secret. Something the England captain got up to after matches. He felt he deserved the indulgence. Yes, it can be revealed, Kane loved to reward himself after a gruelling 90 minutes with a bag of sweets. “I do like a Haribo,” he said with a smile after the Nations League win against Czechia in Prague at the end of September.

No more. At the beginning of last season, Kane took the decision to cut out the naughty treats. After a while, he noticed a difference. He felt sharper; able to sprint more, make a greater number of accelerations. Was it down to this latest entry on the list of personal sacrifices? Or was it a consequence of his broader health regime, the scope of which is mind-blowing?

The bottom line was that there was a gain. So Kane did what he has always done – he leaned into it. Strongly. As the goals flowed as never before, he said it became “addictive”. The 33-year-old striker finished the season with 61 goals for Bayern Munich and 12 for England. According to data from Gradient Sports, his sprints and accelerations per 90 minutes for Bayern were up significantly on 2024-25. This season, he has 10 goals for Bayern and six for England. Again, his sprint and acceleration statistics have improved.

It is a window into Kane’s mentality, the insatiable quest for self‑improvement, the fixation with details large and small, which was the basis for his Ballon d’Or coronation two weeks ago. It is why, as he prepares to make his 126th England appearance against Croatia at Wembley on Thursday night and overtake Peter Shilton as the nation’s most capped men’s player, it is hard to argue that he is not getting better with age.

Kane is the ultimate modern‑day professional, who controls everything he can control. The no‑sweets choice is the most recent on a dietary journey that started more than 10 years ago when he began to work with the nutritional specialist Dan Sargeant.

Kane had his meals prepared by Sargeant, who believes that everyone has a different reaction to food and analyses everything from bone broths to the white bits on oranges to tailor individual plans. Kane has not worked directly with Sargeant since his transfer from Tottenham to Bayern in 2023 – he has a different chef in Munich – but he continues to follow his advice.

It is common knowledge that Kane is teetotal during the season, albeit he had a few drinks as he celebrated his Ballon d’Or triumph. It was the first and almost certainly the last time he broke his rule. Similarly, everyone is aware of Kane’s obsession with recovery after games; his use of ice baths and infrared saunas. He also places great store in the quality of his sleep.

Less well-known is the depth of his relationship with his private doctor, Alejandro Elorriaga Claraco, who specialises in electrical neurofunctional acupuncture. Kane started seeing the Spaniard on a recommendation from the golfer Justin Rose after sustaining a severe hamstring tear playing for Spurs in 2020.

View image in fullscreen Harry Kane celebrates after scoring 79 seconds into his England debut against Lithuania. Photograph: Joe Toth/BPI/Rex

Claraco is based in Canada but travels to see Kane and spends at least a week every month with him. During that time, he will treat Kane on a table for four to five hours each day, getting his muscles pumping with acupuncture needles hooked up to a small battery. Claraco has been fundamental in helping Kane to understand his body; what he can and cannot do, plus how he gets over injuries.

Kane is hurtling towards his record-breaking England cap. He is in better shape than ever; mentally, as well, because he has grown so much as a leader and public speaker, particularly over the past few years of his England captaincy. He was given the armband on a full-time basis by Gareth Southgate in 2018, the fulfilment of a boyhood dream.

Kane has never hidden the fact that England is his priority, mainly because he was such a fan of the national team as a boy. It will be an emotional occasion for him against Croatia and his journey will flash before him. It began with the goal on his debut against Lithuania in 2015, 79 seconds after he came on as a substitute for Wayne Rooney, and it is worth dwelling on the numbers.

Of Kane’s 91 goals – an England record – 21 have come at major tournaments: 14 at World Cups, seven at European Championships. Only two European players have more combined goals at World Cup tournaments and European Championships: Cristiano Ronaldo (25) and Kylian Mbappé (23). Kane has scored 12 times in the knockout rounds. As an aside, he has 21 assists for England, which puts him joint‑second on the all-time men’s list with Steven Gerrard, behind David Beckham (39).

The best moments? Kane is very fond of the Lithuania goal, not to mention the last-gasp winner against Tunisia in the 2018 World Cup group stage and the clincher against Germany in the last 16 at Euro 2020. He always says that one of his best England performances was against Ukraine in the quarter-final of that tournament, when he scored twice. More recently, there were the two goals that saved the day against the Democratic Republic of the Congo in the last 32 of the World Cup last summer.

Kane’s penalties are a major part of his England story. His record shows 26 successes and five misses, although he scored on the rebound against Denmark in the Euro 2020 semi-final. His conversion against the Netherlands in the Euro 2024 semi-final involved withstanding incredible pressure. Ditto the one against Mexico in the last 16 of this past World Cup. The scar that will never heal was the miss in the 2-1 World Cup quarter-final defeat by France in Qatar in 2022. Was it the low point of his career? Kane is on record as saying the World Cup semi-final exit against Argentina in the summer was worse.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

He was never supposed to make it this far; to reach the Hollywood moment of winning the Ballon d’Or, receiving the trophy from the Brazilian Ronaldo and giving an acceptance speech that tugged hard on the heartstrings. His voice wobbled as he paid tribute to his mother, Kim, who had tears in her eyes, and his father, Pat.

View image in fullscreen Harry Kane scored 31 goals in his first full Spurs campaign and has proved wrong those who considered him a one-season wonder. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Kane was never a wonderkid at Spurs; he had difficult loans at Norwich and Leicester. He was doubted. It is true to say he has wrung every last drop from his talent; the dedication has underpinned everything. And yet the raw ability was always there, something often overlooked.

Harry Redknapp, the manager who gave Kane his Spurs debut in 2011, tells a story from the player’s formative days. It involved a behind-closed-doors game at the training ground against Birmingham, whose centre‑half Scott Dann was on the verge of a move to Arsenal. Birmingham included Dann in their team as he returned from a minor injury and Arsenal asked Redknapp whether they could come along to watch.

“I got a call from Pat Rice [the Arsenal assistant manager] and Steve Rowley [the chief scout] and I said: ‘Of course, no problem, come over,’” Redknapp said. “Arsenal were signing Scott Dann, they just wanted to check his fitness. So they came to watch and I think Harry scored four goals that day and Arsenal didn’t sign Scott Dann. Harry absolutely ran amok that day.

View image in fullscreen Harry Kane saved the day for England – again – when they faced DR Congo at the World Cup. Photograph: Chris Brunskill/Fantasista/Getty Images

“We always felt Harry was going to be a player. No one could come here now and say we knew he was going to be England’s all-time record caps holder, record scorer and Ballon d’Or winner. Anyone who says that is talking rubbish. But we did think there was a player there. How good he would be, no one was ever sure.”

Kane was breathtaking when he broke through for Spurs and England in 2014-15 and there were people who thought that would be it; he was tagged as a one-season wonder. He has been a wonder in every season since, the dynamics finessed, perhaps, by the sense that nothing has been given to him; his humility, too.

There has never been the hint of scandal about Kane and it is perfectly possible that Haribos may be his biggest vice. The Ballon d’Or is the Boy Next d’Or and there was genuine happiness in all quarters when he won the award – not only among his friends in the game. That said, the reaction of his former Spurs teammate Son Heung‑min, who is at Los Angeles FC, was gold. He tore off on a goal celebration‑style run at his club’s training ground when he heard the news.

Where can Kane take this? When will it end? Nobody knows but two things are clear. He is equipped to keep pushing for a good number of years and it has long since passed the point where it is reasonable to doubt him.

Sports.title: Is No 10 still the best, or No 41? The myths and maths of Premier League shirt numbers
Sports.content:
How much is a shirt number worth? It costs £8 if you want two digits added to the back of Arsenal’s 2026-27 home shirt, whereas Manchester City add on £16 for customisation, whether you want a name as well as a number or not.

That is cheap compared to what baseball players decide among themselves. Juan Soto bought Brett Baty a $92,000 (£69,000) car in exchange for getting his preferred number (22) when he joined the New York Mets last year. But that’s baseball, where they allow players to wear ‘0’. Anything goes.

There’s a lot of choice in football, even if nobody has worn zero. According to Transfermarkt’s data, every number from one to 99 has been used at some point by at least one of the current Premier League clubs. Not until we go above 45 do we find a number that has been omitted by any of them. And it highlights how random these things can be once you reach the upper reaches of what is permitted, as Brentford and Manchester City have never had a No 46 but have issued a No 99 and No 98 respectively.

The weirdest anomaly is Chelsea not having had a player wear higher than No 81 when it seemed like they were making that many signings every summer. Or maybe the strangest state of affairs is at Everton, who are on to their second No 10 of the 2026-27 season when they haven’t got a No 7 or a No 9. Riddle me that, Toffees.

Fixed squad numbers are a relatively recent development within the history of football. Numbered shirts were first introduced in 1911, with the starting players normally wearing No 1 to No 11 until the 1990s. Iconic footballers have always gravitated towards the key numbers; Kenny Dalglish wore No 7 for Liverpool, bestowing immense value upon that shirt. But if he was unavailable, then someone else would wear it. These days, numbers may be more important to a given player than the club they represent. They become part of their brand.

Opta have data on Premier League goals scored by different shirts since 1993, when the competition introduced squad numbers. The top five are between seven and 11. Traditional numbers still carry the most weight. The standings thereafter are less obvious. Thierry Henry did some heavy lifting for No 14 but there have still been almost 1,300 goals from others who have worn the number. Thinking of players who contributed even a decent chunk towards the 1,100-plus goal tallies for the shirts between 17 and 20 is not easy.

Far more than goals determine player worth. Transfermarkt use the wisdom of crowds to establish a theoretical market value for every player based on numerous factors. It’s a guide, rather than definitively what a footballer would cost to buy from their current club.

With this data we can see which shirt numbers are the most valuable in the 2026-27 Premier League. There is no real pattern on an individual level. The 13 footballers who are believed to be worth at least €100m share 10 different numbers between them, with No 11 the most notable omission from the group. This wouldn’t have happened during Mohamed Salah’s peak.

There is also only one No 9 in the top eight, though Erling Haaland is the most valuable player in the Premier League. Despite João Pedro also being in the €100m club, the highest cumulative total market value (€766m) across the division belongs to No 10, ahead of No 9 (€752m) and No 7 (€683.5m). None of these shirts has the highest average, though. When it comes to valuing a number, take quality over quantity.

If you don’t support Chelsea, Manchester United or Newcastle, you probably can’t name the player who wears their number No 41 shirt. You might struggle even if you are a fan. But with Arsenal’s Declan Rice on hand to accompany Estêvão, Harry Amass and Jacob Ramsey respectively, No 41 has the highest average market value in the Premier League.

These standings would have been different in seasons past, with likely more than four of the traditional 1-11 in the top 10. At various points in 2018 or 2019, N’Golo Kanté and Raheem Sterling were estimated to be worth at least €100m while wearing No 7 shirts, with Eden Hazard, Harry Kane and Sadio Mané of similarly high value when sporting No 10. But No 41 is the shirt number that is worth the most on average today, thanks largely to Rice.

Sports.title: Which football club has had most international captains in the same team? | The Knowledge
Sports.content:
“Which club team has had the most international captains playing together at one time?” asks MH Zahid. “Conversely, which international team has had the most club captains in its starting lineup at one time?”

A quick web search finds a fuss being made in various corners of the internet of Chelsea’s 2009-10 squad because it contained six national team captains in Michael Ballack (Germany), Petr Cech (Czech Republic), Didier Drogba (Côte d’Ivoire), Branislav Ivanovic (Serbia), Mikel John Obi (Nigeria) and John Terry (England). These are, indeed, six people who captained their countries, playing together at one time, but crucially they were not all international captains at that time, which because we like to have our hands bound as tight as possible – no questions please – mean they are disqualified from this particular tournament. Ivanovic, you see, was not named Serbia captain until 2012 and Mikel, who was but a whippersnapper at 22 when the 2009-10 season started, was still seven years from getting his hands on the Nigeria armband.

But if that Chelsea team are not themselves the best answer that Knowledge has come up with, they are at least associated with them, having been knocked out of the Champions League by José Mourinho’s captain-strewn Inter. Inter ended up beating Bayern Munich 2-0 in the final, with a team that included the then full-time captains of Brazil (Lúcio), Romania (Cristian Chivu), Cameroon (Samuel Eto’o) and Macedonia (Goran Pandev), while the captain of Serbia (Dejan Stankovic) came off the bench to replace Chivu in the second half and Pandev was replaced by Sulley Muntari, who while not Ghana’s full-time captain had led the side in their most recent game, a 2-1 defeat at Bosnia and Herzegovina that March.

View image in fullscreen Inter pose before the 2010 Champions League final. Back row, from left to right: Goran Pandev, Júlio César, Maicon, Cristian Chivu, Lúcio, Walter Samuel. Front row: Javier Zanetti, Esteban Cambiasso, Samuel Eto’o, Diego Milito, Wesley Sneijder. Photograph: Stefano Rellandini/Reuters

But that’s not all! Among the unused substitutes was Iván Córdoba, who at this point in his career had lost Colombia’s armband to Mario Yepes but been given it back for their previous game, against Paraguay, in the absence of his fellow centre-back. Also in the team and worthy of note, if not of inclusion in our tally of then captains, were Wesley Sneijder, occasional Netherlands skipper and still their all-time record appearance maker, and Javier Zanetti, who regularly captained Argentina and is No 4 on their list of all-time appearance makers (he would be higher had he not been frozen out by their then manager, Diego Maradona, before the 2010 World Cup), with occasional Kenya captain McDonald Mariga also among the subs.

By our count that’s seven players in one matchday squad who could boast of being their country’s current captain at kick-off, and none of whom captained their club side – that honour went to Zanetti. Our searches have not found another team to match that one, but readers have suggested a couple who came close, in the shape of Tottenham in 2020-21 (who boasted five international captains at the time in Hugo Lloris of France; Serge Aurier of Côte d’Ivoire; South Korea’s Son Heung-min; Gareth Bale of Wales; and England’s own Harry Kane, suggested by John Curry) and Liverpool just last year, when in Conor Bradley, Andy Robertson, Virgil van Dijk, Wataru Endo, Mo Salah and Dominik Szoboszlai they had six – though they never played together while they were all incumbent international captains. Any more for any more?

The fastest former footballer we found in time for last week’s instalment was Alexei Smertin, the former Russia and Chelsea midfielder, who screamed around the Kazan Marathon course in 2020 in just two hours, 48 minutes and 17 seconds. But as Richard Askham emailed to point out, that has since been bettered by Joe Skarz, formerly of Bury, Rotherham and Oxford United, and current manager of Golcar United of the Northern Counties East League Premier Division, who in 2025 finished the Yorkshire Marathon with a chip time of 2hr 47min 33sec.

The next question is what level of football do you need to reach to qualify as a footballer? Because Stig Lindmark tipped us off about the former AIK academy player Andreas Almgren, whose dreams of football glory were derailed by injury in his teens and eventually shifted his focus towards distance running. In New York at the start of this month – while the retired cyclist Tom Dumoulin was putting most former footballers to shame with a time of 2:27:12 – he ran his first ever marathon and only went and won the thing, in 2hr 6min 1sec. With no senior competitive appearances he probably does not count, but it’s a good enough effort to get a mention.

Heads up

“Has a headed goal ever been awarded goal of the season,” wonders Rupert Sheard. “I can think of a few belters, but awards tend to go to ones kicked in.”

“The closest I could get was Robin van Persie’s flying header at the 2014 World Cup in Brazil, for the Netherlands against Spain,” writes Sinan Eccles. “He was pipped to the official goal of the tournament by James Rodríguez’s iconic volley, but did make it to third in that year’s Puskas Award – behind Rodríguez and Stephanie Roche.”

Peter Tomlin writes: “Having researched the goal of the season awards in many countries, the only header I could find that won was Keith Houchen’s fantastic one in the 1986-87 FA Cup Final for Coventry v Tottenham. However, Alisson’s dramatic 95th-minute headed winner v West Brom was voted Liverpool’s goal of the season for the 2020-21 season.”

And Mark Johnson points out that Basile Boli’s ridiculous bullet header for Marseille against PSG at the end of the 1993 season would surely have won the Ligue 1 goal of the season award but for the inconvenient fact that no such award existed at the time.

Surf’s up (2)

Martyn Amos has responded to last week’s scepticism about the possibility of an Ipswich fan website existing in 1990, the year before the first known website went online. “Just to clarify, the original page was set up by Phil Clarke, who was working at BT Labs in Martlesham (near Ipswich), in 1990,” he writes. “At the time, as I said, the web was still experimental, and I think the page was only available internally. Your correspondent is correct in saying that the first public website appeared in August 1991. But the ITFC page still existed, in some recognisable form, using the standard web technology, in 1990, so I think it counts. That’s my understanding, anyway.”

Knowledge archive

With Lee Power taking charge of Swindon Town, in last week’s Knowledge archive we dug up our piece from 2006 on chairs acting as managers, we wrote in October 2015. Neil Bellis, the director of communications at Chester FC, writes to point out we missed Terry Smith off our list.

“He took over four games into the season despite not really knowing much about ‘soccer’,” writes Neil. “He was a former American Football coach but for some reason ending up buying our club. Not only did we end up getting relegated from the Football League for the first time in 1999-2000 we also saw a few very strange ideas from him including having a team talk as the Lord’s prayer and appointing a captain in defence, midfield and attack. Thankfully we are now fan owned so this level of insanity shouldn’t happen again.”

One of Smith’s first games as manager was against Aston Villa in the League Cup, a fixture that prompted a visit from ITV to see what was going on. The result of that visit can be seen here:

“There’s nothing magical about being a coach,’ said Smith not long after his arrival. “It’s like being the general manager of a business, the coaching principles are the same in any sport.” That doesn’t sound too promising but things didn’t really go horribly wrong until the end of November, when Chester began a run of 11 defeats in 12 matches. There’s some footage here of the aftermath of the 5-1 home defeat by Leyton Orient just after Christmas – “I want to thank you guys,” says Smith in the dressing room. “That’s the most pitiful, pitiful effort I’ve ever damn seen.”

Smith stepped down as manager and brought in Ian Atkins in January 2000, then sold the club in October 2001.

Can you help?

“What’s the highest score by a team or in a match where no player scored more than one goal?” writes Paul Gage.

“Manchester United have 20 league titles, won by three managers. Liverpool have 20 league titles won by 10. Which teams have the most and fewest titles won by the most and fewest managers?” asks Will Marquand.

“Djed Spence (shirt No 99) set up Pio Esposito (No 94) in Inter’s 2-0 win over Como at the weekend. Has there ever been a combination for a goal (assist and scorer) with a higher combined shirt number than 193?” writes Joe Strawson.

“Did the Fenerbahce side have more combined Premier League appearances than Liverpool in the teams’ recent Champions League match? If so was this the first instance of a club in Europe playing opposition who had more game appearances in their own league than they had themselves?” ponders Josh Wolff-Martin.

Sports.title: McTominay reveals he had heart ‘shocked’ two days before World Cup opener
Sports.content:
Scott McTominay has revealed he was in hospital under sedation to have a “shock on my heart” just 48 hours before Scotland began their World Cup campaign against Haiti in June.

At the time McTominay’s absence from training was put down to a stomach complaint. It emerged in August that the Napoli midfielder needed surgery to remedy an irregular heartbeat. The operation took place in September, causing McTominay to miss Scotland’s first four Nations League matches. The player has now said the matter arose in the US as Scotland prepared for their World Cup opener at Boston Stadium.

McTominay is back in the international fold for Scotland’s fixtures against North Macedonia and Switzerland. Talking to media in Glasgow the 29-year-old said: “The World Cup was difficult for me to be honest. I had to go and get the shock on my heart. It was two days before the Haiti game and you have prepared so well. I was in such good condition and then something like that happens. And you think: ‘How is this happening to me?’ But then you have to get on with it.

“These are cards you are dealt in football. Sometimes things don’t go your way and you have to continue to do your best. It’s nowhere near an excuse but it’s something you have to look back on and say it’s part of the process.

“Whenever you are sitting in a hospital bed two days before the first game at the World Cup, about to get put to sleep it’s not ideal is it? When things like that happen it is what it is, there’s nothing you can do about it. After the World Cup I reflected on it and it’s probably the most disappointed I have been in my career.”

View image in fullscreen Scott McTominay has been in goalscoring form since returning to action in October. Photograph: Franco Romano/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

Scotland were knocked out in the group stage, with McTominay’s performances among those criticised. A poor campaign also led to the resignation of Steve Clarke as manager. Sébastien Pocognoli, Clarke’s successor, will call on McTominay for the first time when North Macedonia visit Hampden Park on Friday. McTom­inay returned to the Napoli team in early October. He has since scored five goals, including doubles against Bodø/Glimt and Roma. He sought to play down the significance of his heart problem.

“I’m feeling much, much better than what I was,” said McTominay. “It [the operation] was something that needed to be done. In your career you have moments like that, where things can take you by surprise. It looks a lot worse to people in the media and family or friends who reach out to you when they see news relating to a heart issue, but it was a relatively straightforward procedure which went really, really well in Manchester. I’m really happy to be back and playing football again.

“It was explained to me really well by the doctors at Napoli and my cardiologist in Manchester so the process was really straightforward. The doctor with Scotland when we were away at the World Cup explained, if that was going to be the case how it would look. All the staff members made me feel so relaxed about the situation.”

Sports.title: Crystal Palace could avoid significant compensation if Pierre Sage rejoins Lens
Sports.content:
Crystal Palace could avoid paying Pierre Sage significant compensation if he is reappointed by his former club, Lens, with the manager’s departure from Selhurst Park yet to be confirmed.

The decision to sack Sage was made on Sunday evening after Palace slumped to a 3-1 defeat against Liverpool. It was their fourth successive loss in the Premier League and left them bottom of the table for the first time since 2017.

Despite reports on Monday that the Frenchman had been dismissed, there has been no announcement, and it is understood negotiations are continuing over compensation for his three-year contract. However, Yannick Cahuzac’s sacking by Lens on Tuesday after they were embarrassed 9-1 by Como in a record-equalling Champions League defeat last week, before losing 2-1 against Marseille in Ligue 1, has opened the possibility of a swift return across the Channel.

The Lens owner and president, Joseph Oughourlian, has remained in close contact with Sage since he left to pursue what the 47-year-old described as his dream move to the Premier League. After winning the French Cup and finishing as runners-up in Ligue 1 under Sage, Oughourlian is thought to favour reappointing him in an attempt to get their season back on track. That would mean Palace could avoid paying compensation, having already spent more than £4m to buy Sage out of his contract when he replaced Oliver Glasner in the summer.

Cahuzac was promoted from his role as assistant to replace Dino Toppmöller when the German was sacked in mid-September after just four matches. But he has been under growing pressure, with supporters unfurling a banner before the defeat by Marseille that called the players a “disgrace”.

Sage remained hopeful that he would be given more time to turn things around at Palace but there have been few signs of improvement since a 5-0 thrashing by arch-rivals Brighton last month. Some players are understood to have questioned his training methods, although several others are said to have sent him messages of support since the Liverpool defeat.

Thomas Frank is the leading contender to take over, with the former Tottenham and Brentford manager having indicated that he is looking for a new challenge. He held talks with Palace in the summer before they turned to Sage. Sean Dyche and Vítor Pereira are potential alternatives, while Eddie Howe is believed to have rejected an initial approach in recent weeks.

Sports.title: Danny Kelly dead at 69: Broadcasting legend passes away after oesophagus cancer treatment 'did not go to plan' just eight months after stepping back from radio work
Sports.content:
talkSPORT presenter Danny Kelly has died at the age of 69, the broadcaster has announced.

Kelly had been undergoing treatment after being diagnosed with cancer of the oesophagus, which led to him stepping away from his talkSPORT role in March.

In an update to fans in August, Kelly informed fans his cancer treatment had 'definitely not gone to plan' after revealing he had been hospitalised on seven occasions, including spending time in intensive care.

talkSPORT confirmed Kelly's death in a statement on Wednesday morning.

'We are heartbroken to share that our much-loved friend and colleague Danny Kelly has died, aged 69,' the broadcaster said.

'A cherished part of talkSPORT for so many years, Danny brought extraordinary wit, warmth and knowledge to our airwaves.

talkSPORT presenter Danny Kelly has died at the age of 69, the broadcaster announced on Wednesday

Kelly had updated fans throughout his treatment, which he admitted in August had 'not gone to plan'. Source: X/dannykellywords

'His passion for football, music and life was infectious, and his kindness touched everyone around him.

“I love football, Stan. I love it.” We loved you, Danny.

'We’ll miss you dearly. Our thoughts are with Danny’s family, friends and everyone who loved listening to him.'

Kelly had provided updates following his diagnosis and thanked fans for their support during his treatment.

'KELLY CANCER KRONIKLES. Cos so many of you kindly asked for an update... My treatment has most definitely NOT gone to plan. SEVEN hospitalisations have turned an already tough journey into a messy stagger. I spent last week in the Intensive Care Unit. Scary stuff,' Kelly shared in August.

'Some of this is just terrible luck. The syndrome that had me in ICU is SO rare that nobody in ireland is an expert. My tests were sent to LONDON. Several brain scans, multiple infusions and a lumbar puncture later, I’m a bit “better”. Maybe even going home (again) today..

'One medic commented that I’ve “the constitution of an ox.” Which made me feel very sad for an ox, alone and weedy in a field somewhere, with MY constitution...

'I have to say this, cos it’s true. The ICU nurses - half locals, half from the south Indian seaside state of Kerala - are amazing. Their diligence, compassion and humour pulled me through. I have a list of their names; I will never forget them.

Kelly joined talkSPORT permanently in 2008 and presented the Tottenham focused 'View From The Lane' podcast for The Athletic

Kelly previously edited NME and Q magazine, while he also launched the Football365 website

'As always, I thank you all for your support. Especially from bands I haven’t worked with for years. Members of Dexys, the Waterboys, The Fall, Primal Scream, The Loft, The Coral and the mighty Manics, among others, have all wished me luck. Note; only great bands; im humbled.

'Onward…'

Kelly had been part of talkSPORT since 2007, joining the broadcaster permanently the following year.

In a famous moment, the ardent Tottenham fan was heard shouting in delight when they rescued a 4-4 draw with a last gasp equaliser in the North London derby against Arsenal in 2008, telling co-host Stan Collymore 'I love football, Stan, I love it.'

Kelly hosted the Trans Europe Express show on talkSPORT, as well as appearing as a regular on Hawksbee & Jacobs.

He also presented the Tottenham focused 'View From The Lane' podcast for The Athletic, while he previously edited NME and Q magazine.

'The entire Tottenham family mourns the loss of one of our own, broadcasting legend Danny Kelly,' a Tottenham statement read on social media following the news.

'Our thoughts and love are with his family and friends at this incredibly sad time. Rest in peace, Danny.'

Kelly's close friend and long-time broadcast collaborator Danny Baker was among those to offer a tribute, writing: 'My great friend, supreme broadcaster and funniest man I ever knew, Danny Kelly, died yesterday afternoon.

'I cannot believe I will never hear his voice again.'

talkSPORT reporter Ian Abrahams wrote: 'Absolutely heartbroken to hear Danny Kelly has passed away. One of the best broadcasters I’ve worked with.

'One of the most amazing, kindest, funny, passionate people I knew. Danny, we’ll always have “I love Football”. I will miss you my friend, sleep well.'

'We are absolutely devastated at the death of our host, our leader, the great Danny Kelly,' the View From The Lane' podcast shared.

'We all loved him as much as he loved Spurs.'

Sports.title: Taking instructions from a schoolboy and showing class at half-pace... William Saliba made impressive injury comeback for Arsenal Under-21s - now he faces fight to take Ezri Konsa's spot, writes ISAAN KHAN
Sports.content:
Taking instructions from a schoolboy and showing class at half-pace... William Saliba made impressive injury comeback for Arsenal Under-21s - now he faces fight to take Ezri Konsa's spot, writes ISAAN KHAN

It was a scene straight out of Will Ferrell's Elf. In the middle of Arsenal's Under-21 team huddle stood William Saliba, all 6ft 4in of him, towering over his teenage team-mates as 17-year-old captain Marli Salmon delivered his pre-match rallying cry.

One of the world's finest defenders was taking instructions from a schoolboy.

For the hundreds of Arsenal supporters who had descended on Boreham Wood's Meadow Park on Sunday, it was an extraordinary sight. Four months after suffering a back injury in France's World Cup semi-final defeat by Spain, Saliba was finally back on a football pitch.

But his carefully managed 45-minute appearance in a 5-2 victory over Aston Villa's Under-21s marked the beginning of another challenge. Saliba must now win back a place in an Arsenal defence which, remarkably, has barely missed him.

That is largely down to Ezri Konsa, the £55million summer signing from Aston Villa who has been so impressive in Saliba's absence that Mikel Arteta faces a genuine selection dilemma.

Saliba and Gabriel have been Arsenal's established central defensive partnership since the opening day of the 2022-23 season. But Konsa, arguably Arsenal's outstanding defender this term, has made a compelling case to keep his place.

William Saliba towered over his teenage team-mates and played 45 minutes on Sunday

His performance in the 1-0 victory at Liverpool, Arsenal's first win at Anfield in 14 years, was particularly impressive. He won every ground duel, made 14 defensive contributions and completed eight clearances, leading the match statistics in all three categories. Liverpool failed to register a shot on target.

It was precisely the sort of performance that has given Arteta something to think about. And the Arsenal manager is understood to have challenged Konsa to fight for his place rather than simply make way for the returning Frenchman.

There is another solution. Konsa can operate at right back, a position he has occupied for both Villa and England, including during the summer's World Cup. That would allow Arteta to restore the Saliba-Gabriel partnership without sacrificing a player who has become such an important part of Arsenal's defence. For now, however, there will be no rush.

Saliba's injury history explains why Arsenal have been so careful. In 2022-23, another back problem kept him out for 97 days and contributed significantly to the collapse of a title challenge that had seen the club spend 248 days at the top of the Premier League.

Arsenal have since finished runners-up again and finally claimed the title last summer, but the lessons of that earlier setback have not been forgotten.

Leading back specialists were consulted over Saliba's latest injury before the club settled on a conservative rehabilitation programme, deliberately extending his recovery rather than risking another setback.

He returned to full first-team training last Tuesday, ahead of Arsenal's 2-1 victory over Slavia Prague, but Sunday's appearance represented his first competitive action since July. His absence from France's squad during the international break should allow Arsenal to continue building his fitness without interruption.

And there was plenty to suggest that the long wait has done little to diminish his quality.

The Frenchman is building up his fitness after four months on the sidelines

Saliba faces a tough test to try and break up the partnership formed by Gabriel and Ezri Konsa

Playing comfortably within himself, Saliba repeatedly strolled past opponents before threading passes through the Villa midfield. At times he ventured so far forward after set-pieces that supporters began joking about whether he fancied himself as a centre-forward.

Even at half-pace, the gulf between a world-class defender and academy football was obvious.

Yet it was Saliba's interaction with his young team-mates that provided some of the afternoon's most revealing moments.

Throughout the first half he could be heard directing Salmon, shouting 'man on,' 'high, high' and 'well done, Marli' as he guided his teenage defensive partner through the game.

When Arsenal scored their opening goal, Salmon initially stayed back rather than joining the celebrations. Saliba promptly ordered him forward to enjoy the moment.

Marli Salmon, pictured laying a wreath for Remembrance Day, was the one barking out instructions and seeing Saliba (left) among the youngsters was an extraordinary sight

It was a small gesture but typical of the interest Saliba has taken in Arsenal's younger players during his rehabilitation.

He is understood to have spent time asking about their families and offering advice about life in professional football.

One particular message has been the importance of looking after their parents if they are fortunate enough to make a successful career in the game. The affection is clearly mutual.

Children clamoured for autographs as Saliba arrived and departed, while Arsenal had prepared for the unusual attention surrounding an Under 21 fixture.

Large QR codes directing spectators to the team line-up had been displayed around the ground and a member of the first-team security staff accompanied Saliba between the dressing room and the pitch.

His afternoon was meticulously choreographed. At half-time, his work completed, he disappeared into the changing rooms before leaving through a side exit.

Saliba made his comeback for Arsenal's Under 21 side after a long injury absence

The 45 minutes will have provided reassurance to Arteta and Arsenal's medical staff, as well as a memorable afternoon for the teenagers who shared the pitch with him. For Saliba, though, the real work is only beginning.

Few would have imagined when he suffered his injury in July that he might return to find his place under threat. Konsa's performances have changed that calculation.

Arsenal have their defensive cornerstone back. Now Arteta must decide what to do with him.

Sports.title: Crystal Palace will sack Pierre Sage after disastrous 16-game spell - this is how his reign fell apart over late, intense sessions, dinner at the training ground and an unpopular assistant manager
Sports.content:
Crystal Palace will sack Pierre Sage after disastrous 16-game spell - this is how his reign fell apart over late, intense sessions, dinner at the training ground and an unpopular assistant manager

Crystal Palace players and club chiefs have grown frustrated over Pierre Sage's training methods, Daily Mail Sport can reveal - and the 47-year-old will be sacked having won just two of his first ten Premier League matches.

A 3-1 defeat by Liverpool on Sunday saw Palace drop to bottom of the Premier League for the first time in nine years and proved to be the final straw for club bosses, who will tell the Frenchman his time is up.

Daily Mail Sport understands that while the Palace players got on well with Sage, they were frustrated by his late training sessions – with some not starting until 4pm. The regimented routine required players to stay at the training ground for dinner on the night before matches, with some not returning home until 8pm ahead of a 2pm kick-off the following day.

The club's hierarchy, meanwhile, expressed concerns early in the Frenchman's tenure that he was not doing enough defensive work on the training pitch.

Sage's philosophy was that the best way to defend was having the ball, meaning training sessions focused on running, pressing and possession rather than defensive structure.

But the lack of focus led to a poor defensive record, with Palace conceding 30 goals in 16 matches across all competitions. Defending set-pieces and counter-attacks has been a persistent problem for Sage’s side.

Pierre Sage will become the first Premier League manager to be sacked this season after a dismal spell at Crystal Palace

Palace sit rock bottom of the Premier League after winning just two of their first 10 games

Daily Mail Sport understands many players voiced fears they were being pushed too hard in training, with sessions the day before a game particularly intense. There were also significant concerns about the quality of Sage's backroom staff, with his assistant Jamal Alioui proving especially unpopular among the players.

There has also been considerable turnover among senior executives, with six departures over the past 18 months. Chief financial officer Mitesh Velani is set to add to that number in the coming months. One well-placed source told Daily Mail Sport that the disruption to the club’s business operations has the hallmarks of a club heading for relegation.

As Palace look to bail themselves out of trouble, Daily Mail Sport understands former Brentford and Tottenham boss Thomas Frank is in pole position to replace Sage, with six-pointers against Hull City and Coventry City following the international break. Sean Dyche also has admirers at Selhurst Park.

Palace chairman Steve Parish first contemplated sacking Sage over his lack of defensive nous in September, but gave him a stay of execution after Palace kept a clean sheet in a spirited performance away at Leeds on the eve of the international break. However, that display proved an anomaly as Palace shipped 19 goals in the following nine games.

Palace have won just once in their last eight matches in all competitions, beating Fulham 1-0 in the fourth round of the Carabao Cup.

In September, Daily Mail Sport revealed tensions had emerged between Sage and Parish when the latter took a dim view of the decision to drop teenage defender Jaydee Canvot in their defeat by Ipswich Town.

Palace paid French club RC Lens £4million in compensation to appoint Sage in June after he won the French Cup, finished second in Ligue 1 behind Paris Saint-Germain and was named manager of the season last term. It was the first time in 10 years that Palace had paid compensation to appoint a manager.

Palace chairman Steve Parish (right) first contemplated dismissing Sage in September over a lack of defensive nous

Palace players found Sage’s training sessions too intense and struggled to adapt to the late schedule

Succeeding Oliver Glasner, Palace's greatest manager, proved too big a task for the 47-year-old.

Following Palace's loss to Liverpool, Sage insisted the Eagles have been playing better than their league position suggests and pleaded for more time.

'A lot of times I’ve said we deserved better and it was the case again (on Sunday),' said Sage. 'My job is not the most important thing, as I always said from the beginning. The most important thing is to find an efficient solution for the team and for the club.

‘I know how important it is for the club to stay in the Premier League. The club just have to believe in (me), and if it's not the case, they will take a decision. I always have confidence in myself because it's a big, big mistake to not be 100 per cent involved in what I have to do.

‘We have to adjust some positions during the winter transfer window to give more solutions and more efficiency and I think it will be OK.’

Sports.title: Joe Root shuts down Usman Khawaja's claim that 'the whole world' was ball tampering after Australian's explosive Sandpapergate confession... and Jacob Bethell flies home from tour with knee flare-up
Sports.content:
Joe Root has played down Usman Khawaja’s claim that ‘the whole world’ was tampering with the ball after the former Australia opener revealed his team had picked the seam during the 2017-18 Ashes.

Khawaja, whose autobiography, Sabr, has reignited the sandpaper controversy of eight years ago, wrote that the Australians had discovered during their 4-0 win that winter that ‘if we raised the flaps up on the quarter seam on that ball, it was almost like it had a rudder on it and it’d start reverse swinging’.

He added: ‘And before you start going at me, calm down. The whole world was doing whatever little they could to try and reverse swing the ball.’

Asked whether that was the case, Root replied: ‘I can only speak from my own experiences. That’s not how I feel.’

With emotions running high in Australia following Khawaja’s claim that the whole team knew about the sandpaper plot at Cape Town in 2018, and not just the three players who took the blame – Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft – Root repeatedly sidestepped questions on the subject.

‘We obviously have no idea,’ he said. ‘It’s all speculation. Our focus, our concerns are on this three-match series.’

Joe Root (left) insists it is not the case that the 'whole world' was ball tampering as Usman Khawaja (right) has claimed in his new book

Pressed on how Khawaja’s allegations made him feel about the 2017-18 series, when Root was captain, he replied: ‘I wasn’t in that dressing-room. I don’t know what went on. I don’t want to speculate, as I said. My focus is with this team right now and what we’ve got coming up.’

Meanwhile, Khawaja has pulled out of TV and radio interviews to publicise his book after he was grilled on its contents on the Australian Broadcasting Corporation’s high-profile 7.30 programme on Tuesday evening.

Khawaja was repeatedly asked by host Sarah Ferguson to elaborate on his claims that the whole team knew about the sandpaper plot, including Pat Cummins, now Australia’s captain.

But Khawaja declined to add more details, insisting: ‘I’m not here to inflame the situation any more.

'I was here to tell my truth, what I saw, what I felt, and to stick with those three guys that were made out to be the only people who have taken [the blame].’

BETHELL TO FLY HOME

Jacob Bethell’s part in England’s eight-match white-ball tour is over before it has begun after he suffered swelling in his troublesome right knee – casting doubt on his fitness for next month’s Test series in South Africa.

Bethell, who will fly back to the UK from Perth on Saturday, has not played any cricket since July 19, when he injured the knee during the Lord’s ODI against India.

Friday’s first ODI against Australia at the Optus Stadium was supposed to mark his comeback, but instead he will see a specialist back home to ascertain the extent of the problem. The first Test against the South Africans begins on December 17 at Centurion.

With fast bowler Josh Tongue already ruled out of the three-match 50-over series and the five T20s to follow because of a toe injury, England have called up two uncapped players as cover: Sussex’s spin-bowling all-rounder James Coles and Hampshire quick Eddie Jack.

The loss of Bethell is a blow as England look to build a settled side capable of competing in next year’s one-day World Cup in southern Africa, though it resolves one question: the path is now clear for Tom Banton to continue the opening partnership with Ben Duckett that flourished during the recent tri-series in Pakistan.

Sports.title: 'I feel betrayed, misled, in shock. It was a stupid thing for them to do': ANDY WOODMAN relives the moment he was 'brutally' sacked by Bromley - and how his best mate Sir Gareth Southgate helped him cope
Sports.content:
Every sacked manager has a sob story – but few dismissals have felt as harsh as Bromley’s recent decision to part ways with Andy Woodman.

Pound for pound, no club has outperformed their history, budget and expectations in English football across the last decade as much as Bromley. But after an understandably tricky start in League One – two wins from their first 10 games – Woodman was shown the door.

In his first interview since that decision last month, the 55-year-old tells Daily Mail Sport about feelings of 'betrayal' and 'shock' before making his pitch to future employers. But the most eye-opening part of our candid conversation comes when I ask the man with more than four decades of experience to recall the club he took over in 2021.

‘Look, Bromley is your classic non-League club,’ says Woodman. ‘I mean that with the greatest respect to all non-League clubs and I hate the word “non-League” as I think it should be “League Three”, as they are all professional.

‘But the facilities are non-League, the mentality is non-League. Everything is done day-to-day, hand-to-mouth, every penny counts, every decision that costs money counts, it is run by people’s personal money.

‘It was tough when I started: we had no turnstiles, no club shop, we trained on the pitch because it was astroturf, we had no gym.’

Andy Woodman was sacked as Bromley boss last month despite leading the club to the FA Trophy in 2022, promotion to the Football League in 2024 and then another promotion to League One last season

Woodman with the FA Trophy in 2022. 'Every manager who gets sacked, we all have a story of hardship to tell and all feel it is unfair,' says the former Bromley boss

Under chairman Robin Stanton-Gleaves, Woodman and Co, Bromley changed this mentality and shot up the pyramid, winning the FA Trophy in 2022, promotion to the Football League in 2024 and then another promotion to League One last season. Two months later, it was all over.

Asked how he feels about the decision, Woodman, who used to coach in the Arsenal academy system, says: ‘Yeah, I feel betrayed. Every manager who gets sacked, we all have a story of hardship to tell and all feel it is unfair. That’s fine, I get how the football business works.

‘But the bit that didn't sit comfortably with me was the conversations I was having with people at the club or owners, everyone above me… there was no inkling of any of this. I feel misled. I was surprised.

‘One day, we were talking about plans and the way forward and how to get through this sticky little period with players out injured, then the next minute it was a change of direction. Nothing like, “Right, you’ve got three games to turn it round”, none of that, nothing.

‘My record was good there, the owner always said if anyone can churn out results it was myself. Football has no patience. In football, people always forget where they come from. I understand wanting to move forward. It’s disappointing really, that’s the best word I can use. I feel let down.

‘It was just a normal day when they told me. I was going into training, popped across to where the chairman’s office was and then was just told, “We are going to take a change of direction”. It was no more than that, I didn’t try to change the decision or ask why.

‘It was a two-minute conversation, it didn’t need more than that really. I went to tell the staff and went home! It sounds brutal and it is… I am sure people will read this and think, “You deserve this” and “You deserve that” but what else can you do? There’s no easy way of doing it.

'When you have been told you are sacked, you don’t really want to stick around and have a long conversation. They didn’t give an explanation. They needed results, they said. We lost to Leicester which was not a great result, obviously. But realistically they are Leicester… and we are Bromley.’

'It was a two-minute conversation, it didn’t need more than that really. I went to tell the staff and went home! It sounds brutal and it is'

Woodman, who used to be the Arsenal youth team goalkeeping coach, says: 'When I left Bromley that day, I just felt in shock to be really honest'

To hammer home that last point: Woodman’s first game was against Wealdstone in April 2021 in the National League at Hayes Lane. On that same weekend, Leicester were hosting soon-to-be champions Manchester City. Oh, and the Foxes won the FA Cup a month later.

‘When I left that day, I just felt in shock to be honest,’ continues Woodman. ‘I felt the next three games were winnable. I had played seven of the top 10 teams, beaten the top team Huddersfield, my goalie was just coming back from injury and some others were coming back.

‘We had two teams in the bottom four and one just outside so I felt it was my best opportunity to get some much-needed results.

‘To take someone out who has been in football 40 years and been in coaching 25 years and then to put (his former assistant) Byron Webster in charge who had just been fresh out of playing and has never done a coaching session… with every respect, it feels unfair to him. It was a stupid thing to do. I found that really strange, they took one point from those three games. It fascinates me.’

Now, with Bromley bottom of League One, Karl Robinson, the former Salford and MK Dons boss, has taken over. Woodman, though, is keen not to sound bitter and will remember his five-and-a-half years at the club with fondness. He says his best memories are taking Bromley into the Football League, playing at Newcastle in the FA Cup and beating ‘Hollywood Netflix club Wrexham’ in the FA Trophy final.

Sir Gareth Southgate remains his best friend, the pair having met as teenagers in the Crystal Palace academy. They took turns in being best man at each other’s wedding and Southgate is godfather of goalkeeper Andy’s son Freddie, who is on Liverpool’s books.

They also co-authored the 2004 book Woody and Nord which chronicles two polar opposite career paths that started at the same level, one going on to play (and later manage) England, the other a journeyman in the lower leagues.

‘Nothing surprises Gareth and I,’ adds Woodman. ‘We have been in the game for 40 years now. You can argue that in his tenure at England, he got them as high as they have ever been in 60 years and it still was not enough. So it doesn’t surprise us. People have to make decisions and they are business-related, only time will tell if it is the right decision but that’s not my problem any more.

Woodman and lifelong friend Sir Gareth Southgate at the release of their 2004 book 'Woody and Nord' which charts two very different careers in football

Southgate is godfather to Woodman's son Freddie, a goalkeeper on Liverpool's books

‘Gareth was very supportive, so was Alan Pardew and the support from the Premier League right down to the National League, there has been no end of messages I have had, which is comforting.

‘That first Saturday after being out, I didn’t want to be watching or listening to the game, I just wanted to get away because that is the worst. I have had two clubs ring me, there are ongoing conversations and I am just making sure it is the right vehicle for me. What I mean by that is I want an owner that is aligned and who thinks they can compete to get out of their league.

‘My record speaks for itself. If you ask most managers how many promotions and trophies they have won, I bet over long careers, they haven’t got many. For me, with the smallest budget in the leagues, we maximised the team and maximised success.

‘To get two promotions and an FA Trophy win against Wrexham, hitting the play-offs four times in five years, that is something I am really proud of. If nothing else, the Bromley supporters and town are grateful.’

Sports.title: Man United advance in talks with Mauricio Pochettino as club chiefs jet to Monaco to make final call over sacking manager Michael Carrick - with bookies suspending betting on the 54-year-old taking over
Sports.content:
Manchester United are advancing in talks with Mauricio Pochettino as they prepare to appoint the Argentine as Michael Carrick’s replacement as head coach. United chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox are in Monaco for a meeting with minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe that is expected to lead to Carrick being sacked after 10 months in charge. United insist that no final decision has been made, but it is understood that the club are now finalising a deal with Pochettino for the 54-year-old to leave his role with the US national team and take over at Old Trafford. Bookmakers Betfair have suspended betting on the next United manager. Pochettino’s contract with the US Soccer Federation, which was renewed after the World Cup in the summer, means that United will have to pay £7million in compensation. The former Tottenham, Chelsea and Southampton boss is currently busy at the US national team base south of Atlanta preparing for a CONCACAF Nations League quarter-final double header against Haiti, but it is known that he would like to return to the Premier League. Pochettino was strongly linked with the United job before the club appointed Erik ten Hag in 2022 and again when he was under pressure two years later. US men's coach Mauricio Pochettino is United's choice to take over at Old Trafford Michael Carrick is pictured arriving at Manchester United's training ground this morning Carrick checked in at Carrington at 7.45am on Wednesday with his fate in the balance Pochettino is pictured working on United States national team duty on Tuesday (Source: X/USMNT) Berrada and Wilcox flew to the south of France on Tuesday to attend a scheduled summit of Ineos executives. They will make their recommendation to Ratcliffe today, with all the indications pointing to Carrick paying the price for his team’s alarming descent into the Premier League relegation zone. Co-chairmen Joel and Avram Glazer would still need to give their approval for the sacking. It’s understood that the Old Trafford hierarchy would want to inform Carrick of their decision face to face, so there may not be any official confirmation from the club until Thursday. The 45-year-old turned up for work at Carrington at 7.45am on Wednesday morning to oversee training with the players who are not away on international duty amid increasing uncertainty. Sacking Carrick would leave United searching for their third permanent head coach this year after he replaced Ruben Amorim in January, and push the compensation paid out to coaching staff and executives over the last three years under minority owner Ratcliffe and Ineos close to £30m. Sir Jim Ratcliffe, Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox are meeting in Monaco for talks today The United execs meet in Monaco today (Pictured is the Casino Monte-Carlo in Monaco)

Your browser does not support iframes.

Carrick was only handed a two-year contract in May and would be due a pay-off from United who have already spent £22.7m in compensation since 2024. It includes £10.4m to Ten Hag and his staff when the Dutchman was sacked four months after being given a contract extension, £4.1m to Dan Ashworth who lasted just 159 days as sporting director, and £8.2m to Amorim and his backroom team when they left after 14 months. It would have been as high as £16.7m but United saved half of that figure when the Portuguese coach returned to work at AC Milan. It’s unclear what would happen to Carrick’s backroom staff. Goalkeeper coach Craig Mawson was already at the club when Carrick arrived and would be likely to stay, along with Travis Binnion who moved up to first-team coach after working with United’s age-group teams. Jonny Evans had just left his role as loans manager, but returned to work alongside his old United teammate as part of a new coaching team that includes Steve Holland and Jonathan Woodgate. Yesterday, United legend Teddy Sheringham placed the blame on two players for Carrick's seemingly imminent exit after their chaotic 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on Sunday. 'I feel like this Manchester United team doesn't know whether they are supposed to be pressing or dropping off,' he told BOYLE Sports. 'I don't think they know what they're supposed to be doing from the first minute because even the little things are missing, for me. 'When the ball was played out to Harry Magurie against Aston Villa, who is a senior pro, he heads it but doesn't really head it out or head it to a teammate and it goes out of play and from there they take a quick throw. It's such a weird way to start a game. 'The goalkeeper, Senne Lammens, looks nervous to me as well. He makes mistake after mistake after it puts you on the backfoot straight away. The way they reacted after going behind is good, it shows they're still fighting, but you can't carry on like this as Manchester United.'

Sports.title: A Yeboah back in the Premier League? Leeds legend Tony's nephew Kelvin wanted by several clubs in January transfer window after scoring 18 goals in MLS for Minnesota United this term
Sports.content:
Another goal-packed season for Kelvin Yeboah in Major League Soccer (MLS) is expected to spark interest among Premier League and Championship clubs in January. Yeboah has ended the campaign with 18 goals and made five assists for Minnesota United who finished 10th of 15 teams in the Western Conference, just one point outside and one place outside the play-offs. It means the season is over for the 26-year-old nephew of Leeds legend Tony Yeboah. Yeboah describes himself as 'more of a modern nine' than his uncle Tony, who was famed for his muscular physique and his ability to strike with ferocious volleys from distance. He is sharp and mobile with a goal instinct. Premier League and Championship clubs have been monitoring his progress this season. Everton and Crystal Palace, both in search of firepower and options up front, are among those who have been linked to a move. Free-spending Ipswich are another. Kelvin Yeboah is wanted by many Premier League goals after a fine goalscoring season in MLS Yeboah scored 18 goals for Minnesota United - with Everton, Crystal Palace and Ipswich keen The striker is the 26-year-old nephew of Tony Yeboah, a Leeds United legend of the mid-1990s There is interest also from Europe. Hoffenheim boss Christian Ilzer signed Yeboah when in charge of Sturm Graz, after the young forward had scored four goals against his Austria Vienna team in a cup tie in the previous season. Yeboah has been in Minnesota since the summer of 2024. There is another season on his contract and the option of one more after that. But he remains keen to test himself at the top of the European game and there is a growing feeling that he could be on the move in the next window. 'As a footballer, you want to play on the biggest stages and express who you are as a person,' he told Daily Mail Sport in an interview on the eve of the MLS season. 'I just want to keep scoring goals and give myself the best chance of that happening.' He grew up in Italy from the age of three to 15 and represented the Azzurri at Under-21 level. He is also eligible for Ghana where he was born. At 15, he moved to London where he played non-league football for AC London and had trials at several clubs including West Ham before joining WSG Tirol in Austria at the age of 18. Yeboah scored 20 goals in a year at Sturm Graz before returning to Italy. He was 21 when Genoa signed him for £6million. It should have been the perfect homecoming but the club then owned by 777 Partners plunged into financial chaos. Relegated from Serie A they were unable to pay wages and Yeboah was loaned to three different clubs in three different countries before finding stability in Minnesota. He has 36 MLS goals in 79 appearances. READ: 'I'd watch his Leeds goals on video and try to recreate them!' Meet the Premier League cult hero's nephew you could be seeing at the World Cup
