Sports.title: 'I miss the children we would have had': Heartbreaking tribute of husband of Olympian Ciara Mageean, who died aged just 34 after bowel cancer battle, after carrying her coffin at funeral just weeks after their wedding
Sports.content:
Ciara Mageean's widower Thomas Moran has written a heartbreaking tribute to his wife following her death at the start of this month.

The Irish Olympian died aged 34 due to bowel cancer - revealing her stage four diagnosis in May 2025.

The Northern Irish athlete, who represented Ireland at two Olympic Games and claimed European gold in 2024, died surrounded by her loved ones.

Mageean's death came just weeks after she married her long-term partner Moran in an intimate civil ceremony in Belfast. Just days before her death, the couple celebrated their marriage with family and friends at Darver Castle in County Louth too.

And taking to Instagram on Tuesday night, Moran wrote a lengthy and heartfelt statement in memory of Mageean - declaring his devotion to her and pride since they met 12 years ago.

'Twelve years ago, I was lucky enough to meet a girl. I knew immediately that she was special: kind, caring, generous, infectious and beautiful beyond words. I did not just fall in love; I became entirely devoted. Her joy became my joy, her fears my fears, and her dreams my dreams. My purpose in life shifted to helping make those dreams come true, in any way that I could,' his captioned post begins alongside the Instagram carousel of memories of their relationship.

Thomas Moran has written a heartbreaking tribute to his wife Ciara Mageean after her death. The 34-year-old Irish Olympian died at the start of the month due to stage four bowel cancer

He took to Instagram to reflect on his time with Mageean since first meeting her 12 years ago

Mageean and Moran married last month in an intimate civil ceremony in Belfast and then celebrated their marriage with family and friends at Darver Castle in County Louth another date

'In the years that followed, we chased those dreams wholeheartedly. We built our own little world, a home with two cats and a dog, and filled every space with a love that’s only ours. We travelled and raced and won and lost, lived a life with all its flaws, but we did it together.

'I’ve tried to think of how best to describe my feelings in this moment, and how to capture a life with Ciara in just a few short words. So rather than a message filled with sorrow or sadness, I want this to be one of pride.

'I’m proud of every second I got to spend alongside Ciara in this world.

'Proud to have grown into adulthood together.

'Proud to have supported her as she chased her dizzying dreams.

'Proud to have carried her across the threshold of our first home.

'Proud to have seen the joy on her face the day she first held her puppy, Sam.

'Proud to have held her hand through the worst of her cancer treatment.

'Proud to have seen the tear in her eye as she walked down the aisle on her dream wedding day.

'And proud to have lain by her side in her final moments of life, there with her family until the very end.'

The love for Mageean was evident at her funeral as hundreds of mourners were present in her hometown of Portaferry at St Patrick’s Church.

As an athlete she competed at the Rio 2016 and Tokyo 2020 Olympics, missing out on Paris 2024 due to injury.

However, earlier that year she made history in 2024 by winning European 1500m gold in Rome, becoming just the second athlete after Sonia O’Sullivan to secure an individual European title for Ireland.

Hundreds of mourners paid tribute to Mageean at her funeral earlier this month in Portaferry

Mageean represented Ireland in athletics and won European 1,500m gold in Rome in 2024

'Ciara meant so much to so many people. She became, in a way, Ireland’s daughter. Immensely proud, immensely loyal and immensely fierce, she was the epitome of the Irish warrior spirit,' Moran's Instagram tribute continues.

'Before the Rio Olympics, I gifted her a small necklace with the word "Invictus" inscribed on it, taken from the famous poem by William Ernest Henley.

"In the fell clutch of circumstance,

"I have not winced nor cried aloud.

"Under the bludgeonings of chance

"My head is bloody, but unbowed."

'I wanted it to serve as a symbol of strength and resilience, but in an almost prophetic way, she went on to embody those qualities in ways I could never have imagined.'

Moran concludes his tribute by envisaging what the future could have been with Mageean.

'I will miss Ciara forever. The miles we would have run, the homes we would have made, the children we would have had, and the long future we had planned together. But she will forever be in my heart, that flame of hope and inspiration, reminding us to fight on, no matter how fierce the battle, just as she did.

'For years, Ciara would stand at the top of Windmill Hill, behind her home in Portaferry, and tell me how it was her favourite place in the whole world. I stood up there numerous times over the days of her funeral, taking it in. The weather was clearer than I had ever seen, the sky bluer, the grass greener, the trees all the colours of autumn. You could see further than ever before, tens of miles in every direction, from the top of Strangford Lough, to the Mournes in the south, to the Isle of Man across the Irish Sea, all with perfect clarity.

'I've never seen it quite so beautiful. I don't normally believe in superstition, but someone was showing off.

'I knew in those moments that Ciara is in the real heaven now, because she is back home in Portaferry.'

Sports.title: Danny Kelly dies aged 69 as tributes paid to legendary sports presenter
Sports.content:
Danny Kelly dies aged 69 as tributes paid to legendary sports presenter

Danny Kelly, a long-time presenter on talkSPORT, has passed away aged 69 following a battle with throat cancer

View 4 Images Danny Kelly had throat cancer

Sports presenter Danny Kelly has died aged 69 following a battle with cancer.

‌



Kelly is a sports broadcasting legend and had spent 20 years working for talkSPORT, where he presented Trans-Europe Express. He was diagnosed with throat cancer in March and had been receiving treatment at his home in Ireland.

talkSPORT said in a statement: "We are heartbroken to share that our much-loved friend and colleague Danny Kelly has died, aged 69.

"A cherished part of talkSPORT for so many years, Danny brought extraordinary wit, warmth and knowledge to our airwaves. His passion for football, music and life was infectious, and his kindness touched everyone around him.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

“'I love football, Stan. I love it.' We loved you, Danny. We’ll miss you dearly. Our thoughts are with Danny’s family, friends and everyone who loved listening to him."

Kelly was a lifelong Tottenham fan and the club wrote on social media: "The entire Tottenham family mourns the loss of one of our own, broadcasting legend Danny Kelly. Our thoughts and love are with his family and friends at this incredibly sad time. Rest in peace, Danny."

Long-time collaborator Danny Baker wrote: "My great friend, supreme broadcaster and funniest man I ever knew, Danny Kelly, died yesterday afternoon. I cannot believe I will never hear his voice again."

Kelly's talkSPORT colleague Ian Abrahams wrote: "Absolutely heartbroken to hear Danny Kelly has passed away. One of the best broadcasters I’ve worked with. One of the most amazing, kindest, funny, passionate people I knew. Danny, we’ll always have 'I love Football'. I will miss you my friend, sleep well."

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

View 4 Images Danny Kelly shared his battle with cancer on social media

Reporter Alex Crook added: "This is so sad. Danny was a great broadcaster and a brilliant colleague and friend. Had a wonderful day with him watching Spurs' last game at White Hart Lane. talkSPORT will never be quite the same again."

Speaking on Trans-Europe Express in June, Kelly explained his diagnosis: "I don't intend to mince my words here. I'm going to tell you that I am a sick man. Six weeks ago, I went to the doctor, hat on the side of my head, something going on with my eating.

"I thought it was probably acid reflux and he would give me a big bag of Gaviscon. Other tablets are available. Instead, it turns out that I have cancer.

View 4 Images Danny Kelly was a much-loved voice on talkSPORT (Image: talkSPORT)

"To be specific, I have cancer of the oesophagus, a really dangerous thing. Now look, that's the bad news. The less bad news, because it isn't really good news, is that after another long series of tests, after a very tense three or four weeks waiting for results, the medics say that the thing hasn't spread inside my body and that they can and they will help me.

"What I'm facing, to be truthful with you all again, is a tough and lengthy programme of treatment. There will be chemicals, there will be surgery, and there will be chemicals again. It is a hard road, but one that the doctors are hopeful that will see me emerge recovered and healthy at the far end."

View 4 Images Danny Kelly was a sports broadcasting veteran (Image: talkSPORT)

He added: "This isn't just about me. I've learned something really incredibly important in the last few weeks. I think I knew it, but it's been nailed home to me.

"If you feel something just isn't right in your body, I don't mean you've got a hangnail or a bit of earwax or something, but if you know something is not quite right in your body, for God's sake, go to the doctor. Get yourself checked out.

"99 per cent of the time, it will be nothing. But if it is something, the sooner it's caught, the better the chance of getting it sorted out. Get yourself checked out."

Sports.title: Cheltenham Festival-winning jockey Tom O’Brien dies aged 39 as tributes pour in
Sports.content:
Cheltenham Festival-winning jockey Tom O’Brien dies aged 39 as tributes pour in

The world of horseracing has entered a period of mourning after Cheltenham Festival winning jockey Tom O'Brien passed away

View 3 Images Tom O'Brien celebrates winning the Pertemps Network Final Handicap Hurdle on Third Wind (Image: PA Archive/PA Images)

Cheltenham Festival champion Tom O'Brien has passed away aged 39 after a long and brave fight against cancer. O'Brien was victorious at Cheltenham on two occasions, before retiring from horseracing in 2023.

‌



‌



He rode Silk Affair to victory in the 2009 Fred Winter Juvenile Hurdle and then repeated the feat in 2022 while atop of Third Wind in the Pertemps Network Hurdle Final. He also came second in the Grand National during a fantastic career.

‌



Elsewhere, he also retired with five Grade One triumphs and two Welsh Grand National successes while also being crowned champion amateur and champion conditional throughout his time in the sport.

‌



Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources

O'Brien's list of victories is endless. His notable winners include riding Souffleur in the 2007 Challow Hurdle, while his Welsh Grand National triumph in 2009 took place while riding Dream Alliance, before winning again on Elegant Escape in 2018.

He leaves behind his partner Hayley and two sons Archie and Toby. The racing world has come out in numbers to pay tribute to O'Brien.

‌



TalkSPORT reporter Alex Crook wrote on X: "Heartbreaking news that jockey Tom O’Brien, two time Cheltenham festival winner and rider of 1000 winners, died last night aged 39 after a long battle with cancer. Met him and his lovely family at Chepstow a couple of years ago. Thoughts with everyone close to him. RIP Tom."

View 3 Images O'Brien enjoyed a successful career in horseracing (Image: PA Archive/PA Images)

‌



Crooks' talkSPORT colleague Ian Abrahams also posted: "Some incredibly sad news, Tom O'Brien, who rode more than a thousand winners, has passed away aged just 39, after a battle with Cancer. I was lucky enough to meet Tom a few times, what a great, humble man, he’ll be greatly missed - thoughts with all his family & many friends."

Racing broadcaster Alan Marron also tweeted: "That is so sad. What a jockey Tom was and remember his wind on Third Wind for the Hughie Morrison team in the Pertemps at Cheltenham so well.

‌



"Got some run out of him up the hill. Another young person gone too soon. Thoughts with family & friends. RIP Tom."

View 3 Images O'Brien while riding Garden for All Seasons to victory in the Handicapn Hurdle at Ascot Racecourse in 2022 (Image: PA Archive/PA Images)

‌



At the weekend, jockey Ciaran Gethings dedicated his triumph at Aintree to O'Brien after riding Javert Allen to victory in the 2m handicap chase.

He said to ITV racing: "A very special friend of ours and mine and in the weighing room, Tom O'Brien, is going through a tough time at the minute.

Article continues below

"I said if I won today, I would mention him. Hopefully he's sat at home with the fire, looking at that win, and it's brought a smile to his face."

Sports.title: Mauricio Pochettino, Eddie Howe and more - the pros and cons of the Man Utd candidates
Sports.content:
It's becoming common practice for Manchester United to appoint a new manager every other year. After Erik ten Hag in 2022 and Ruben Amorim in 2024, it will soon be someone else's turn to take on what is rapidly being framed as the Impossible Job.

United chiefs have already appointed one manager this year, of course, but Michael Carrick's arrival in January was supposed to be temporary, only for the caretaker to do such a good job that he had to be handed a longer contract.

Carrick's shortcomings are now set to cost him that job with United in crisis, languishing in the relegation zone with more than a quarter of the Premier League season gone.

And unlike in 2022 and 2024, the market for potential replacements suddenly doesn't seem quite as vast. Part of the reason for handing Carrick a lifeline two weeks ago was that the club's decision-makers were unconvinced by the pool of potential replacements.

‌



Man Utd and Ineos' five shocking decisions as constant failure set to cost Michael Carrick READ MORE :

Michael Carrick's Man Utd future to be decided in Monaco meeting with Sir Jim Ratcliffe READ MORE :

Four years ago it was a long process that was only ever about Erik ten Hag or Mauricio Pochettino. It didn't feel like there was a wrong answer and Ten Hag got the job off the back of a hugely successful stint at Ajax.

In 2024, United quickly honed in on Ruben Amorim, the hot young thing of European coaching. Again, it felt like an obvious decision with plenty of upside.

Now, there are as many pitfalls as there are positives with the list of candidates, and the leading contender has come from nowhere to suddenly be in the frame for a job he has already come close to landing twice previously.

Mauricio Pochettino

View 6 Images Mauricio Pochettino is currently the head coach of the United States (Image: Robin Alam/Getty Images)

‌



Make sure you don't miss the best Man Utd coverage by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

Pros: As well as 2022, Pochettino was in the frame for the United job in 2019, after Jose Mourinho was sacked, only for Ole Gunnar Solskjaer to nail his audition. Pochettino has always had an interest in managing United, has Premier League experience, has worked in elite environments before and has a clear, distinguishable style of play.

Cons: Stock has fallen since his days at Tottenham and spells at Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea weren't a resounding success. Has been out of the club game for two-and-a-half years and a feeling his best days may have passed.

Eddie Howe

View 6 Images Eddie Howe is interested in the job (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Pros: Has plenty of Premier League experience and is available to start quickly after he left Newcastle United in the summer. Twice got the Magpies into the Champions League and delivered success at Bournemouth. Has a high-intensity style of play that United seem to need at the moment.

Cons: Time at Newcastle ended badly and doesn't really have a CV that would make you think he is a United manager-in-waiting under normal circumstances. Newcastle regressed in both seasons in which they were in the Champions League, which has to be a red flag.

Julian Nagelsmann

View 6 Images Julian Nagelsmann's time at Bayern Munich raises concerns for Manchester United (Image: Alexander Hassenstein/Getty Images)

Pros: Has worked with a very high standard of players, is a modern coach from the German school of pressing and would bring a real identity to the team. His spell at Bayern Munich means he has the experience of working at a club where the spotlight is always bright.

‌



Cons: Wasn't particularly popular at Bayern, where he had a habit of rubbing up people the wrong way, and his habit of skateboarding around the training ground raised eyebrows. Failed as Germany boss during this summer's World Cup.

Antonio Conte

View 6 Images Antonio Conte has been linked with the Manchester United job (Image: Francesco Pecoraro, Getty Images)

Pros: The candidate with the strongest CV and a serial winner capable of delivering success when it isn't necessarily expected. Has won league titles with Juventus, Chelsea, Inter and Napoli. Is available after leaving Napoli at the end of last season.

Cons: Combustible is probably understating a personality that has seen him fall out with his bosses at plenty of clubs and his time in charge of Tottenham ended in acrimony. Might deliver an uptick in results, but unlikely to last any real length of time.

‌



Unai Emery

View 6 Images Unai Emery is about to sign a new deal with Aston Villa (Image: Javier Borrego/Getty Images)

Pros: Has built a reputation as a manager capable of diligently building a club up through methodical planning and clever tactical tweaks and that is arguably what United need at the moment. Has been very successful in charge of Aston Villa.

Cons: Has had two spells at the elite level, at PSG and Arsenal, and neither went well. Isn't a great communicator and perhaps lacks the force of personality to drag United to where they need to go.

Sports.title: Scott McTominay opens up on heart scare and reveals shock treatment before World Cup match
Sports.content:
Scott McTominay opens up on heart scare and reveals shock treatment before World Cup match

Scott McTominay noticed an irregular heartbeat in the build-up to Scotland's first World Cup match against Haiti in the summer and underwent shock treatment in Boston

View 3 Images Scott McTominay underwent routine heart surgery (Image: Giuseppe Maffia/Getty Images)

Scott McTominay has explained how his heart scare struck on the eve of Scotland's World Cup campaign.

‌



‌



It was first revealed in September that McTominay had been diagnosed with a mild benign arrhythmia, an irregular heart rhythm. It is considered non-serious but required surgery and saw him sidelined for Napoli and Scotland.

‌



The midfielder first noticed the symptoms a few days before Scotland's first match at this summer's World Cup, against Haiti. He knew it wasn't just nerves and told manager Steve Clarke, who took the concerns seriously.

‌



McTominay was given a police escort to hospital in Boston, where doctors used anaesthetic to put him to sleep before resetting his heart with shock treatment. The 29-year-old has now spoken about what he went through for the first time.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



“Atrial fibrillation is a fairly normal routine thing for people in general," he said at a press conference ahead of Scotland's Nations League match against North Macedonia on Friday.

“They might not know that they have it. But when you're an elite athlete across football or sport, you know if you've got something that's different. Whenever you're running, you check your pulse and it's got a slight irregular beat there.

‌



“It feels like your heart's coming out of your chest. That's the sensation that you have. That it's pumping, but not a regular heartbeat, like bum, bum, bum, bum. Mine was going bum, bu-bu-bum, bum, bu-bu-bum. So you know the difference.

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



View 3 Images Scott McTominay played against Haiti after undergoing shock treatment on his heart (Image: Fred Kfoury III/Getty Images)

“Was it on my mind in the games? No, I put it to bed. I tried my best, anyway. Whenever you go under anaesthetic and you have to get put to sleep, it decreases the athletic performance a little bit, as well as your sleep and stuff like that.

‌



“But you have to get back round to doing it again. It was far from ideal but those are the cards you're dealt, there's nothing you can do about it.”

Scotland opened their World Cup campaign with a 1-0 win over Haiti in Boston, but McTominay was understandably not at his best. Clarke's side were then beaten by Brazil and Morocco to exit at the group stage, prompting criticism of their talismanic midfielder.

‌



He says he would never have missed those games and didn't let the criticism get to him.

View 3 Images Scotland had a disappointing World Cup campaign (Image: Megan Briggs/Getty Images)

‌



“You know yourself as a professional footballer if you’re not quite where you should be," McTominay said. “You just try to block it out. Were there concerns from my family about playing? No, I wouldn’t have listened to it. They had just flown 10 hours for the first game of the World Cup.

“I didn’t sit there thinking I might not play. That would never be the case. I was always going to play in that game. Maybe selfishly, I don’t know.

‌



“I’d worked for 20 years as a young footballer and as a professional to get to that point. To try and play well at a World Cup. Players play with injuries all the time when they’re not quite right. But I was fully functional.

“It wasn’t easy after the World Cup. I probably had two or three weeks of putting my head in the sand, thinking we let one slip. That was the bottom line.

"It took me longer than it normally would to get over disappointment in football. The reason why I felt like that was because we could have done more. It was probably one of the worst moments of my career."

Sports.title: Man Utd's 'final two' to become new manager before dramatic sack U-turn
Sports.content:
Man Utd's 'final two' to become new manager before dramatic sack U-turn

Manchester United were ready to axe Erik ten Hag back in 2024 with Thomas Tuchel on their radar, only to change their stance following their FA Cup success

View 2 Images Man Utd's FA Cup victory in 2024 kept Erik ten Hag in a job (Image: Tom Jenkins/Getty Images)

Manchester United's trajectory could look very different had they opted to sack Erik ten Hag in 2024, with two men lined up to replace the Dutchman.

‌



Ten Hag would ultimately retain his job despite leading the Red Devils to an eighth place finish in the Premier League - at that point their lowest ever showing. A victory in the FA Cup final at Wembley proved crucial in him remaining in his post.

Sir Jim Ratcliffe and Ineos were newly on the scene and had scoured the market for a new boss with the decision to sack Ten Hag all but taken, only to change their minds late on.

Prior to that FA Cup success over Manchester City United had looked elsewhere and settled on Thomas Tuchel and Roberto de Zerbi as their two main candidates, reports the Athletic, with both men out of a job at that point.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

Tuchel had been moved on by Bayern Munich, but had huge pedigree having led them, PSG and Chelsea - leading the Blues to Champions League glory. United's decision to opt out would be England's gain, with the German now leading the Three Lions.

De Zerbi meanwhile had seen his stock continue to rise at Brighton but chose to bring his tenure to an end. He had long been tipped to make the step up but sticking with Ten Hag meant the Italian moved to Marseille, and is now in charge of Tottenham.

Earlier this season he took his Tottenham team to Old Trafford and, even though they escaped with a point thanks to a late header, Tottenham dominated Carrick's side but were hugely wasteful in front of goal.

View 2 Images Thomas Tuchel is now in charge of England (Image: Eddie Keogh - The FA/The FA via Getty Images)

Mauricio Pochettino, who is in the frame if Michael Carrick is sacked this time around, did interview for the position, but was ranked behind the likes of De Zerbi and Tuchel.

United's decision to stick by Ten Hag proved short lived and the Dutchman was sacked after just nine Premier League games the following season. It shone a light on the decisions taken by Ineos, who have continued to make calls that have only set the club back.

Ten Hag was allowed to sign the likes of Joshua Zirkzee and Manuel Ugarte, two men who are now deemed surplus to requirements. And following his sacking Ruben Amorim was hired, lasting just 14 months before he was given his marching orders. Carrick's interim spell saw him handed the job on a permanent basis, but he too is now poised for the chop.

Sports.title: Liverpool wonderkid Rio Ngumoha sets his sights on winning the Ballon d'Or
Sports.content:
Liverpool wonderkid Rio Ngumoha sets his sights on winning the Ballon d'Or

Liverpool wonderkid Rio Ngumoha could be in line to start for England against Croatia on Thursday - and is already setting lofty ambitions for his fledgling career

View 2 Images Liverpool's Rio Ngumoha during training with England

England wonderkid Rio Ngumoha says he is desperate to follow in the footsteps of Harry Kane and win the Ballon d’Or.

‌



‌



Teenager Ngumoha, 18, says Kane is an inspiration for every young England player after the Bayern Munich superstar was crowned as the best in the world.

‌



Liverpool winger Ngumoha says Kane’s achievement is a huge boost for English football and it has made him dream of also winning the prestigious honour.

‌



Ngumoha said: “Yeah, 100%, Harry Kane winning the Ballon d'Or is definitely a big, big thing, being known as the best player in the world.

“It's also helped English football now because everyone's seen one of us win the Ballon d’Or, it is definitely encouraging many more people to wanting to definitely be known as the best player in the world. For me, I would like to achieve it and I think I can do it.”

That is a bold claim but Ngumoha says Three Lions captain Kane - who is set to become England’s most capped player at Wembley on Thursday - is already helping the young players and sets an example every day in training.

‌



Ngumoha said: “I haven't spoken to him much, really. When I first came, I was a bit shy, so I was keeping myself to myself, but then they got me in the group, and just watching him train, watching all the players train, but especially him, like the finishing drills that you see.

“You can see why he won it and why he's known as the best striker, best player in the world. Definitely an inspiration to me, but just to every young player and probably every England player as well. He's a top guy.”

‌



View 2 Images Ngumoha is taking inspiration from his Ballon d'Or winning skipper Harry Kane

Ngumoha has won three senior caps for England but with Bukayo Saka out injured there could be a chance for him to start against Croatia on Thursday.

‌



He added: “Hopefully. I think you know I'm competing with the best players in the world, so it's not going to be easy.

“But yeah, just if I can show myself in training and if the manager gives like faith and believes in me, then yeah, I'd love to start. But obviously, it's difficult, and yeah, I just keep just keep going really.”

Sports.title: Rio Ngumoha on ‘no brainer’ Liverpool transfer call and living out his England dream
Sports.content:
Rio Ngumoha used football as a “top escape route” to put him on the path to glory.

Liverpool winger Ngumoha, 18, is one of English football’s best prospects and he says he owes a huge debt of gratitude to his brother James and mum Liz.

James is his mentor, agent and best friend while Liz has given up her job at a school to move to Liverpool to help him reach his full potential in what has become a family affair.

Ngumoha’s talent and single-minded attitude is the reason he has already broken into England’s senior set-up, went to the United States as part of their pre-tournament training camp and caught Thomas Tuchel’s eye.

‌



Liverpool wonderkid Rio Ngumoha sets his sights on winning the Ballon d'Or READ MORE :

Ben White reveals heartbreaking reaction to missing World Cup and response to England boos READ MORE :

Make sure you don't miss the best England coverage by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

London-born Ngumoha admits that even as a kid he visualised himself playing for England and now all of his dreams are coming true.

Ngumoha said: “Yeah, 100 percent because I feel like if you don't visualise anything or you don't dream big enough, then you might not ever achieve it. So I think just having the belief and the force in your mind thinking, one day I can play for England.

“I think you definitely need to have that so you can drive to achieve it. So yeah, I've definitely always believed in it.

‌



“My brother has been a massive part of my journey. He saw the talent in me from when I was like five years old, which is crazy to say. But yeah, he's my agent as well now. He just wants the best for me, and he's really supportive.”

View 4 Images Rio Ngumoha is taking his England opportunity with both hands

His brother was a “tough” taskmaster but that hard work - and endless training sessions - have paid off now. It also meant that Ngumoha just focused on his football even though he grew up in tough part of East London.

“Yeah, growing up in Manor Park, everyone knows it's a tough it's a tough area,” said Ngumoha. “Newham, especially.

‌



“But to be fair, I think the people around me and all my friends and family made sure I wasn't a part of anything that was too rough, or just to keep me on my toes really. And I had football, which is a top, top escape route for any things such as like crime and stuff.

“My brother is tough, sometimes. I definitely needed that when I was younger. My mum has done a lot for me. The hardest thing for her has been moving up to Liverpool. She left her job to come move up. She does everything for me and my brother. She’s just amazing.”

Ngumoha had spells at West Ham and Arsenal before joining Chelsea aged just eight but then took the really brave decision to sign for Liverpool in 2024 because he could see a clearer pathway to the first team.

View 4 Images Ngumoha's decision to swap Chelsea for Liverpool is already paying off

‌



That choice is now paying off as he has become a firm favourite with the Liverpool fans who he describes as “the best in the world.”

“I feel like I needed a new challenge. I feel like if I stayed at Chelsea... not saying that I wouldn't have got to the first team as quick, because I believe in my ability, but I feel like Liverpool just gave me a new pathway. The plan that they set for me was straightforward really,” he said.

“For me, it was a no-brainer going to Liverpool, and they just said if I prove myself, because they know how much ability I had, then they know that I would definitely be a first-team player and definitely a star for them in the making. I think going to Liverpool so far has been the right choice.”

Ngumoha went to the United States in the summer and scored a “worldie” in a behind-closed-doors game and also played against New Zealand in a friendly.

‌



He was not on England’s long list so could not get promoted to the World Cup squad and, in a way, he says that took the pressure off him and he just played his natural game.

View 4 Images Ngumoha made a big impression after being called up to England's pre-World Cup camp

Ngumoha added: “I feel like I'm quite fearless. I feel like if there's an opportunity to beat my man, I'll always do it. I feel like it was the way I came up really, playing in cages near my house.

“To be fair, I knew before going to the camp that I couldn't go to the World Cup anyway, which obviously as a young player you would want to go to these tournaments.

‌



“But it is difficult because I only started really playing towards the end of last year at Liverpool, but I just chose the pre-camp at the World Cup to just prove myself and just to be free and play with some expression.

“I did that and I made a good impression, so I just want to keep up the impression.”

Sports.title: Man Utd and Ineos' five shocking decisions as constant failure set to cost Michael Carrick
Sports.content:
Since Ineos came on board at Manchester United back in 2024 they have made bad call after bad call and, even if results have been poor, Michael Carrick is poised to pay the price for those continued failings.

A summit in Monaco involving all of the Red Devils' senior figures on Wednesday is likely to conclude with Carrick being relieved of his duties at Old Trafford.

The club sit in the bottom three having won just one of their 10 Premier League games with the club sinking to new lows. Carrick has been unable to find the winning formula but, as many continue to point out, he has not been set-up to succeed in Manchester.

A lot of the issues that are rearing their head long pre-date Carrick's arrival and, even if Ineos arrived with a glimmer of hopes following the longstanding Glazer issues, the direction of travel in Manchester has not changed.

‌



Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

Sir Jim Ratcliffe is now being viewed much the same as the club's majority owners over in America. His lieutenants are also hugely unpopular with their number of poor decisions stacking up and up.

We take a look at the calls made by Ratcliffe, Ineos and co that have ultimately done nothing to make United the force they hope they can be, instead landing them in a possible relegation battle.

‌



Backing - and then sacking - Ten Hag

This was the first sign of the United hierarchy not sticking to their guns. Before the FA Cup final of 2024 they were looking at their options with Erik ten Hag presiding over a poor domestic campaign. All the signs pointed to him getting the sack. Yet a shock win over Manchester City caused a u-turn.

View 4 Images Ten Hag was sacked by United in 2024 (Image: Justin Setterfield, Getty Images)

In reality that result at Wembley should not have caused such a shift and, after handing Ten Hag a new deal, he lasted just nine games of the following season before he was sacked. Ratcliffe and those alongside him should've had more conviction come the end of 2023/24.

The Amorim saga

I mean this felt doomed from the start and the fact it went on so long seems purely down to the fact Ineos didn't want to admit they got their first managerial appointment wrong. Ruben Amorim won just 24 of his 63 games in charge, all whilst playing a style that was never going to suit United.

‌



His tenure come with a series of entertaining soundbites, which included him calling his side the worst Manchester United team ever and telling the board they need to sack him if they want to see a different playing style. He would ultimately get his wish 14 months after being appointed.

View 4 Images Ruben Amorim presided over Man Utd's worst ever Premier League finish (Image: Carl Recine/Getty Images)

Poor PR moves

Ratcliffe previously claimed that United were in danger of going out of business before his cost cutting measures were undertaken, not sure anyone particularly agreed with him there. But he and Ineos have excelled in PR disasters, which has bought them no goodwill from supporters.

From the cutting of hundreds of jobs to the removal of concession ticket prices to threatening to remove season tickets from those they wrongly accused of reselling their tickets. If Ratcliffe and Ineos are unpopular, then it is largely a situation of their own making.

‌



Neglecting the defence

You can say United's results from the New Year onwards were impressive, and they were, but it is the club's job to take a closer look at things. Had they done that they would've seen that Carrick's United conceded more than a goal a game across his 17 outings.

That was with a defence that hadn't seen a major signing since Leny Yoro, and even then he is seen as a player for the future. Otherwise it is made up of signings from several years ago and the club opted to plough £155m into their midfield in the summer.

View 4 Images Man Utd's defence has not been bolstered for several years

So few can be surprised that United have now conceded more goals than any top flight team in a major European league this season with a backline that includes the likes of Harry Maguire, Lisandro Martinez, Diogo Dalot and Luke Shaw - the latter being signed when Louis van Gaal was at the club.

‌



Ignoring Carrick's red flags

It was mentioned earlier about the club's bosses sticking to their guns - or not. Well ultimately hiring Carrick was never part of the plan, he was a makeshift solution until the end of a troubled season. But wins over Arsenal, Manchester City, Aston Villa and Liverpool made the man hard to ignore.

What wasn't hard to ignore was the fact United had no European football and no domestic competitions to worry about. That meant Carrick was working with a fresh squad and had ample time to prepare for games. That was ultimately unrealistic and not a fair reflection of what was to come.

If Carrick wasn't the man long-term in January, then a few statement wins shouldn't have changed that. But it did, and we find ourselves where we are today.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson urges UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in a behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; there were allegations of spitting by an Israeli player at half-time, while the Israeli government criticised the Irish players for bowing their heads during the national anthem

Republic of Ireland: Heimir Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future after tense draw

Ireland's head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson has called for UEFA to keep his team and Israel separate in future

Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

The Ireland boss was speaking following his side's 1-1 UEFA Nations League draw with Israel behind closed doors in Serbia.

The games between the two nations this international break were overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

This continued in Serbia, as Ireland fitness coach Damien Doyle was allegedly spat on by an Israeli player at half-time, according to reports in the stadium.

Irish media reported that the incident took place as the teams went down the tunnel. Ireland boss Hallgrimsson confirmed there was an allegation, but he admitted he didn't see it and declined to comment further on it.

However, when asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Israeli Government accuses ROI of 'moral blindness'

The Israeli Government have accused the Ireland football team of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during their national anthem.

For the second time in a week, the Irish players, coaching team and FAI all bowed their heads while the Israeli national anthem was played pre-match.

Image: Republic of Ireland players bowed their heads during the national anthem

The official Israeli Government X account posted: "While some use the football field as their political theatre, for us this is personal.

"1939: Irish players raised their arms in salute to Nazi Germany.

"2026: Irish players bowed their heads during Israel's anthem.

"Different generations. The same moral blindness.

"Today, Israel's players wear black armbands to remember those brutally massacred by Hamas on October 7 - including former professional footballer Lior Asulin.

"Some of us have skin in the game. Others just make a show of it."

Sky Sports News has contacted the FAI for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged that a derogatory term had been used, which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. The term is not associated with antisemitic or anti-Israeli abuse.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying: "That's completely untrue," before bringing the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called following an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist, who said a microphone had been taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands that no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland draw with Israel in second Nations League meeting
Sports.content:
Match report and reaction as Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out after the break; sides clashed at half-time

Republic of Ireland 1-1 Israel: Troy Parrott scores again as sides draw second controversial Nations League meeting

The Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in the second controversial Nations League fixture between the sides.

Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out by Dor Peretz after the break in the behind-closed-doors game in Serbia.

The Republic's 'home' fixture was held on neutral territory at the 4,500-seat TSC arena in Backa Topola, due to "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil" according to a June Football Association of Ireland (FAI) statement.

Both sides wore black armbands. The Republic's, the same as in Hungary to acknowledge - as the Football Association of Ireland chief David Courrell explained before that contest - "all lives lost" in the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict.

Israel's armbands - which read "7.10" - were to commemorate the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on southern Israel, their official X account confirmed.

The pitch featured no sponsored content or branding, just UEFA graphics with slogans like "football for all", a decision taken by the FAI.

Image: The referee pleads with the benches in Serbia

Tensions rose at half-time after a fracas broke out in front of the tunnel and players from both sides engaged in a heated argument, with the Israeli Government later accusing Irish players of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during Israel's national anthem, as they did in Monday's first match.

Officials broke up a second altercation in three minutes of added time, and there were more heated words exchanged after the final whistle.

On the pitch Parrott, who has now scored 10 times in his last seven competitive internationals, fired the Republic in front from the spot in the 39th minute before Dor Peretz drew the sides level two minutes after the restart.

The result puts Ireland third in Nations League Group B3, level on points with second-placed Kosovo.

Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future

Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

Speaking after the 1-1 draw, Hallgrimsson also declined to comment on the half-time fracas between the two sides.

When asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

On the half-time incident, he said in his post-match press conference: "I was there. I'm not going to comment on it. It's something that a disciplinary committee is probably going to look at."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called due to an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist who had the microphone taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there was no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Ireland news conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland vs Israel is being played in Serbia as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott; protests briefly halted Ireland's draw with Austria on Thursday over opposition to Sunday's Israel fixture

Republic of Ireland vs Israel: Heimir Hallgrimsson's press conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media

Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson's pre-match press conference ahead of Sunday's match against Israel in Serbia ended abruptly after a tense exchange with Israeli media.

The media access was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed they were racially abused by Irish players during their match in Hungary last Sunday.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close as one of his colleagues remonstrated with the reporter.

Image: Ireland's players bowed their heads before facing Israel in the reverse fixture last week

Hallgrimsson later labelled the accusation a "verbal attack" during a separate briefing for members of the Irish press.

The exchange in the main press conference took place after Hallgrimsson was also asked a question about a co-pilot who attacked a pilot and tried to hijack a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv earlier this week.

The reporter's question was shut down by the FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there are no open UEFA investigations at this stage from the previous meeting between Israel and Ireland last weekend.

The FAI are conducting their own investigation into whether striker Adam Idah was racially abused by Israeli supporters during their 3-0 UEFA Nations League win but have yet to make an official complaint to UEFA.

Image: Protesters interrupted Ireland's draw with Austria by throwing tennis balls onto the pitch with Palestine flags on them

Despite the high-profile nature of the fixture, members of the Irish media later reported that there was no UEFA delegate present at the news conference.

Sky Sports News was told a UEFA match delegate does not have to attend press conferences. The duty is left to the venue media manager, whose job it is to report anything if there is an incident.

Sunday's match is being played in Backa Topola, Serbia, as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott.

Sky Sports News has approached the FAI for comment.

Sports.title: Ireland held by Austria despite Parrott double as protests interrupt game
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott scored twice but the Republic of Ireland were forced to settle for a 2-2 draw after Austria came back in the second half of their Nations League encounter at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

The contest was twice interrupted in the opening 45 minutes, first due to what campaign group Stop the Game later referred to in a statement as a "limited tennis ball protest", when - around the 20th minute - tennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text '#StopTheGame' were launched onto the pitch.

The match paused a second time when an invader carrying what appeared to be a Palestine flag entered the pitch and was promptly tackled and carried off by security.

The protests came after Ireland's decision not to boycott their game against Israel last week - although goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu did make himself unavailable.

Ireland are due to face Israel again on Sunday.

Image: Tennis balls with Palestine flags were throw onto the pitch

Before the protests, Parrott scored a sensational 12th-minute opener, and then added a penalty on the stroke of half-time.

A pair of substitutes proved Ireland's undoing after Alexander Prass halved the deficit in the 71st minute and Michael Gregoritsch drew the sides level six minutes later.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had a chance to top Group B3 with a victory, but they sit third behind Austria and Kosovo at the halfway point of the group stage.

Hallgrimsson made three changes, including the reintroduction of Finn Azaz, who was greeted warmly when his name was announced over the PA system before the match.

Bazunu was back in the squad, while Liam Scales and John Egan were awarded starts.

There was a significant security and police presence outside the stadium, where a small group of protesters also gathered before kick-off.

There was an audacious early effort from Sasa Kalajdzic, who tried to catch Caoimhin Kelleher off his line with a lob from midfield, before Ireland enjoyed a couple of attacking spells deep in the visitors' half.

Image: Parrott is congratulated after scoring his second goal against Austria

It was a brilliant opener from Parrott, who realised he was on his own after bringing down Adam Idah's glanced-on header from a goal kick.

The Real Betis striker was sandwiched in a triangle of white shirts, before nutmegging Philipp Lienhardt and evading every other challenger with a mazy run before planting the ball past Florian Wiegele and into the bottom corner.

Image: A protestor was carried off the pitch during the game

Kelleher denied Patrick Wimmer and there were a few more promising spells for Austria before Parrott doubled their lead.

Ryan Manning won the penalty after he was clipped in the box by Nicolas Seiwald. Parrott stepped up after a VAR check and blasted it past the Austria 'keeper.

Austria cut the deficit after Liam Kitching was caught out and Austria worked the ball to the unmarked Prass, who blasted the ball beyond Kelleher. The offside flag was initially raised, but the decision was reversed after a VAR check.

The Brentford goalkeeper then failed to stop Gregoritsch's free-kick as Ralf Rangnick's side fought back for a point.

Ireland captain Dara O'Shea was denied by an excellent leaping Wiegele save, Gregoritsch directed a shot over the crossbar and both sides fended off attempts at a late winner.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson admits 'toughest days' of career after Ireland beat Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Hallgrimsson: I couldn't be more proud of the players

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"It has been some of the toughest days of my coaching career, but its not about me.

"The game, the desire the players showed to make a statement on the pitch - they are football players, they wanted to show on the pitch, make that talking with their feet.

"What they did was impressive. In tough times that's when you find your leaders, there were so many players that stepped up in these tough times. The energy levels they showed was impressive.

"The performance was good given all the preparation, the lack of training, all of our meetings were about something other than football.

"I couldn't be more proud of the players.

"By playing I know we are making some people unhappy. By playing we are making others happy. Winning probably pleases everyone, but there will still be people angry that we played the game.

"I hope we can settle that slowly down and stay together as a team. I wish people in Ireland continue supporting these boys, because they certainly deserve it."

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: Why have the Republic of Ireland's two games against Israel become so controversial?
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will face Israel in a men’s football fixture for the first time since 2005 in this international break, but there have been calls for the two UEFA Nations League games not to be played at all.

Both meetings - the first played in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday and the second scheduled for the Serbian town of Backa Topola on October 4 - have been overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

Uncertainty over the games going ahead might have subsided, but the tensions between the two nations have not.

Heimir Hallgrimsson, the Republic of Ireland head coach, has been accused of "stupidity and hypocrisy" by the Israel Football Association after last week suggesting his team would be "playing against genocide" when facing Israel, while his players are not ruling out their own protests ahead of the games.

The Athletic examines the key issues ahead of the first meeting this weekend.

Why have these games caused controversy?

This has been a contentious issue rolling down the tracks ever since the 2026-27 Nations League draw was made in February. Group B3 saw the Republic of Ireland pitted against Kosovo, their opening opponents this evening, and Austria, but it was the prospect of facing Israel which created immediate unease.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) had overwhelmingly approved a motion that called on UEFA to ban Israel from its competitions just four months earlier due to violations of the governing body's statutes, including "the organisation of clubs in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank without the consent of the Palestinian Football Association".

The Nations League draw duly reignited the row. Irish politicians, including the FAI member Joanna Byrne, were quick to call for a boycott of the Israel games in the following days and protests ensued when Qatar visited Dublin's Aviva Stadium for a friendly in May. Tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag were thrown on the pitch by supporters, twice causing brief interruptions.

Image: Tennis balls with a Palestinian flag on were thrown onto the pitch in Dublin during protests in May 2026

The FAI had already confirmed its plans to go ahead with the Israel games by then, and that decision was formally approved at an EGM in July.

That saw only 32 votes in favour of a boycott, with 75 members voting for the games to be played. The FAI had argued that boycotting games would cause "significant and lasting harm to Irish football" due to the likely disciplinary sanctions from UEFA.

A measure of the opposition to the Republic of Ireland facing Israel also came with the acceptance that the "home" fixture would not be played in Dublin. The FAI cited "operational challenges (that) could impact the delivery of the game on home soil" and the decision was eventually made in late June, with the support of UEFA, to move the game to Backa Topola, a small town in northern Serbia, on Sunday week.

No tickets for the game will be made available to Ireland fans.

The FAI has subsequently revealed that a request to see the two nations kept apart in future competition draws has been rejected by UEFA.

"The answer I got was very clear," FAI chief executive David Courell told reporters on September 18. "That would not be possible because Ireland and Israel have never been in direct conflict."

What is the political backdrop?

The Republic of Ireland has consistently outlined its backing for the Palestinian people since the conflict with Israel began almost three years ago, joining Norway and Spain when officially recognising a Palestinian state in 2024. Taoiseach Micheal Martin has also made his stance clear, accusing Israel of committing "genocide" last year in comments reported by the Irish Mirror.

The conflict in Gaza began after Israel responded to attacks by Hamas militants on October 7, 2023, which saw around 1,200 people, mostly civilians, killed in Israel and 250 taken hostage. The war has subsequently seen 73,000 people killed, according to figures from the Gaza Health Ministry and used by the UN.

Strained relations between the Republic of Ireland and Israel have continued this year. Two Israeli government ministers were the subject of travel bans in June, while foreign minister Helen McEntee also confirmed Ireland's intent to limit goods trading with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank this summer.

Image: Taoiseach Micheal Martin

A meeting between the Republic of Ireland and Israel on a football field this weekend has subsequently taken on enormous significance against such a backdrop.

There are similarities in Ireland's political stance with those of Norway, who faced similar calls for a boycott when Israel travelled to Oslo last October. The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) had aligned itself with its government and said in a statement leading up to Israel's visit that the "tragic humanitarian suffering in Gaza" had made the fixture challenging.

That World Cup qualifier, won 5-0 by Norway, saw thousands take part in a protest march to the stadium.

Who has opposed the games taking place?

Moving a home game 1,500 miles away has not stopped the objections building ahead of the two teams meeting on Sunday. More than 160 Irish sportspeople signed an open letter asking their national team to boycott the Israel games under the banner of the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, who have also run the "Stop the Game" campaign that protested outside of the Irish team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter said.

Kevin Kilbane, the former Republic of Ireland international who holds 110 caps, has also been unequivocal in his views. "The Republic of Ireland should not be playing Israel… not while Israeli forces are committing genocide," he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.">he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.

Amnesty International also issued a fresh statement on Tuesday that said UEFA risked letting football "rubber-stamp apartheid" by allowing Israel's continued participation in its club and international competitions. A spokesperson for the Israeli FA responded to that by saying: "Their obsession with the idea of Israel as a state is incurable, as is their need of attention."

The Irish media, meanwhile, has faced its own dilemmas in the coverage of the Israel games. RTE, the public broadcaster behind Ireland's boycott of the Eurovision Song Contest in the last two years due to Israel's continued involvement, has stripped back its coverage. Contractual obligations will be met, RTE confirmed in a statement, but there would be no studio coverage or commentators sent to either fixture.

Image: Kevin Kilbane, former Ireland international, has spoken out

What have the key stakeholders said ahead of this weekend?

Relations between the two nations have grown increasingly hostile in the last week. Hallgrimsson appeared in front of the media to announce his squad for the upcoming friendlies and made pointed remarks when asked how his players would focus on football.

"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," the former Iceland head coach told reporters. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

The reaction to those words, in a social media post from the Israel FA account, raised temperatures further still. "We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way," it read. "Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach. We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we're playing against the coach who embodies them."

Martin, who was among the world leaders attending the UN General Assembly in New York, was then drawn back into debate on Tuesday. "I think those are unacceptable remarks. They should be withdrawn. Israel can't keep denying what the world knows and what the world understands."

The FAI has not addressed Hallgrimsson's comments publicly, but the Republic of Ireland's head coach said on Wednesday that he had been "grateful for the support" he had received.

"Maybe from a leadership point of view, it was not clever from me to take the attention (away) like this. It's a tricky time for us," Hallgrimsson said in his pre-match press conference ahead of facing Kosovo.

The same extends to his players, too. Dara O'Shea, the Ipswich Town defender, said, according to the BBC, that he and the rest of the players would come together on Friday to "openly discuss" the prospect of a protest ahead of the first Israel game in Debrecen on Sunday.

Image: Dara O’Shea, left, and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson during Wednesday’s press conference

Why are the games being played in Hungary and Serbia?

Hungary has acted as an adopted home for Israel since the start of the conflict. They first played there in November 2023, when resuming their attempts to qualify for Euro 2024 when hosting Switzerland at the Pancho Arena in Felcsut, a small village 26 miles west of Budapest.

Victor Orban, who lost his position as Hungary's prime minister this year, had been a long-standing ally of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and claimed Hungary to be the "safest country in Europe" for Jews.

The World Cup 2026 qualifiers against Estonia, Norway and Italy were all held in Debrecen, which has also previously hosted European games for Israeli sides Maccabi Haifa and Maccabi Tel Aviv.

The Republic of Ireland's choice of Backa Topola, Serbia, is less clear. Dublin ceased to become an option, even behind closed doors, as the opposition to Israel visiting became clear, which left limited options for relocation.

It needed to be a nation sympathetic to Israel to avoid further protests and Serbia, neighbouring Hungary to the south, has forged strong diplomatic relations. According to the Associated Press, Serbia's president Aleksandar Vucic inaugurated an assembly factory for Israel-made drones last week, with plans for three more production sites.

A switch to Serbia was reliant on UEFA approval and it will be Backa Topola's home of the TSC Arena where this story ends on October 4.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"
