Sports.title: F1 2026 calendar update: Imola off the table, no plan B if Iran war escalates
Sports.content:
The Qatar and Abu Dhabi grands prix which will conclude Formula 1’s 2026 season are set to proceed as planned, provided there is no dramatic escalation of the Iran war.

The Middle Eastern conflict, which started in late February as the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran, has destabilised the region. The calendars of many motorsport championships have been impacted – not least F1’s, whose Saudi Arabian race was cancelled while Bahrain’s round was postponed and hosted in Malaysia.

F1 has been monitoring the situation closely, with a chilly Imola as an alternative season finale on the first weekend of December if Qatar and Abu Dhabi were unable to host their respective events.

Lusail did run its MotoGP round without major issues last weekend, though both Yamaha teams withdrew from the competition due to the geopolitical situation.

10 November was F1’s deadline to provide Imola with a final answer as to whether the Italian track would have to prepare for a grand prix in the next three weeks; it will not.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, Isack Hadjar, Racing Bulls Photo by: Zak Mauger / Motorsport Images

So the 2026 season will end with the planned Las Vegas-Qatar-Abu Dhabi triple-header, with travel insurance and governments’ travel advice currently allowing it.

However, there’s a caveat: F1 is aware it cannot guarantee the situation won’t change by early December and insists it will prioritise safety if the conflict escalates.

Team bosses have been maintaining a straightforward stance on the matter – they trust F1 and the FIA to make the right calls.

“I trust them to take the best decision for all of us,” Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur commented in Mexico. “Me, personally, I want to race. It doesn't matter where, but I want to race. Now, I will go where they will tell us to go.”

“Stefano and Mohammed have been pretty clear about the situation that Formula 1 follows what the international guidelines are, whether there are travel restrictions, airlines not flying, any warnings in the region, the kind of feedback that local governments are making,” his Mercedes counterpart Toto Wolff added in Friday’s press conference at Interlagos. “So not only the promoters, but what the local governments are making. And this is what you need to rely on, in my opinion, and I'm fully with that.

Toto Wolff, Mercedes Photo by: Mark Sutton / Formula 1 via Getty Images

“I think that if riders stand up, who know nothing geopolitically about what's going on, but have an audience that listens, I think that is something that creates media value. But I would have done the same as MotoGP management has done. You want to ride or drive, go. If you don't want to, don't go. It's as simple as that, and everybody can take their personal decisions on that, and I respect that.

“Of course, you've got to be wary of what's happening in the next few days, a few weeks, and Stefano has his finger on the pulse to monitor that. If things were to get more dangerous and we would get that feedback, then he's going to be the first one, together with Mohammed, to protect the people that were meant to travel. So that's why I'm following their guidance.

“From what I'm hearing internally, it hasn't been raised. It hasn't been a topic. But also there, if someone feels they don't feel comfortable, he or she doesn't feel comfortable travelling, then it's something that I would always respect. And maybe that's an opportunity to give somebody else a chance. It wouldn't change anything for the relationship. I've always respected that some people didn't want to go to certain grands prix, and that's how I see it at the moment.”

Additional reporting by Ronald Vording

Sports.title: FIA reveals ADUO results in final review of 2026 F1 season
Sports.content:
The FIA has announced its final Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities (ADUO) results for the 2026 Formula 1 season, with no changes granted for any of the power unit manufacturers.

From this season, the FIA installed a mechanism in the F1 regulations which allowed power unit manufacturers the ability to make updates, if they fell behind the leading engine, in the form of tokens permitted under a performance scale.

After the first period in 2026, which ran from the Australian Grand Prix to the Canadian GP, it was announced that Red Bull Ford Powertrains emerged as the benchmark, while Mercedes’ internal combustion engine trails by between 2-4%, which gave the German manufacturer to one additional upgrade this year and one more next season.

Ferrari, Audi and Honda fell into the category of being more than 4% behind on ICE power, which grants them two upgrades during the current campaign and two more in 2027.

Red Bull Ford Powertrains asked for a review of the ADUO analysis, which delayed the official publication of the first results, as it disputed the results and being considered the manufacturer with the strongest engine.

As agreed before the start of the season by the teams, the FIA only measures the internal combustion engine, but once a manufacturer qualifies for ADUO, it is also allowed to modify electrical components such as the battery and MGU-K.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Colin McMaster / LAT Images via Getty Images

So while Red Bull’s rivals have been able to install power unit upgrades across this season, the Milton Keynes-based effort has effectively faced an engine freeze.

In the third and final FIA analysis of ADUO – which took engine data from the Dutch GP up to and including the US GP – there has been no change and therefore no manufacturer will gain or lose its current concessions.

There was also no change in the second ADUO period over the summer.

“For the third period, the relative performance gaps to the leading ICE evolved, but these changes did not result in any additional homologations being granted to the Power Unit Manufacturers,” an FIA report stated.

Given the dispute over how ADUO is measured, the FIA is open to changes in the system in the future, subject to approval from the power unit manufacturers, while FIA single-seater director Nikolas Tombazis is confident the concept is working as desired.

“The FIA has undertaken extensive analysis as part of the review of ADUO this year. Based on the quality of the data and the robustness of the assessment process, we are confident in our findings and the conclusions reached,” Tombazis said.

Nikolas Tombazis, FIA Photo by: Kym Illman / Getty Images

“The first year of implementation has also reinforced our belief that the ADUO concept is the right one for Formula 1.

“However, it is important that the system continues to evolve to ensure it remains efficient, relevant and fit for purpose. To that end, we have been working closely with the power unit manufacturers and teams to explore refinements to the methodology that will support the continued effectiveness of ADUO in future seasons.”

The next ADUO period will start in 2027, covering the opening six races of the F1 season from the Bahrain GP to the Miami GP.

Sports.title: What's behind Piastri's split with Webber – and what it means for his F1 career
Sports.content:
On the Monday after the Formula 1 Brazilian Grand Prix, Oscar Piastri and Mark Webber announced in a joint statement that the latter and Ann Neal would no longer manage the 25-year-old McLaren driver. The timing may come as a surprise – now rather than at the end of the season – but the news itself had been on the cards for some time.

The clearest hint came from Piastri during pre-season testing in Bahrain. While this writer was mainly interested in his opinion of the 2026 cars – which immediately brought a telling smile to Piastri's face – an Australian colleague raised the subject of Webber's changing role.

Read Also: Formula 1 Piastri and Webber terminate management agreement

"There wasn't anything specific, we just made a decision for things to look a bit different," Piastri said on that unusually cold February evening in the Bahrain paddock. "Mark is still very much involved and I've been in contact with him a lot over the last few weeks. He just won't be trackside as much anymore. So that's really the extent of it. There was nothing specific that triggered it."

Although that last point is essentially true, it is clear that the 2025 season was intense on several fronts – including behind the scenes, at least from Webber’s perspective. That was naturally closely linked to the 'papaya rules' through which McLaren tried to treat both drivers as fairly as possible, but which also made life difficult for the team at certain moments, as Andrea Stella frankly admitted at the beginning of this year.

It is no secret that Webber was not always happy with how McLaren handled certain moments on track, nor with the explanation for Piastri's dip in form during the final quarter of the season, which ultimately cost him the world title. It is important to emphasise, however, that a manager's role is also to defend the interests of his own driver, even though there are multiple ways of doing so.

Webber naturally had the experiences from his own Red Bull years in mind and wanted to prevent Piastri from ever being labelled a number two driver in the F1 paddock. In a recent interview with Autosport, former Red Bull team principal Christian Horner even described this as a key part of Webber's mentality, a worldview that Horner believes he brought into the cockpit.

"I think probably the difficulty with Mark was, he motivated himself through adversity. He always drove better when he felt that the world was against him," Horner said. "He could see this talent emerging in Sebastian [Vettel], and he was using everything in his locker to try and destabilise that, or to cause any tension in a way that would then fall back in his favour. I think as a team we were learning how to handle these dynamics."

Watch: Christian Horner on Toto, Abu Dhabi 2021 and Life After Red Bull.

The differences between Red Bull back then and McLaren today are considerable, however. Red Bull was led at the time by Horner and Helmut Marko, two men who were certainly no strangers to the political side of F1, whereas McLaren is now much more engineering-led under Andrea Stella, who constantly emphasises the principles by which he wants to go racing – including fairness. This brings a different dynamic and also means that any attempts to avoid being pushed into a number two role are viewed in a completely different light.

It must be emphasised that McLaren has never formally asked Piastri to change his management, but Autosport understands that the driver himself, with some input from those around him, has formed his own view of what he needs going forward.

In any case, the decision had already been made at the beginning of this year for Webber to take a step back and operate primarily 'behind the scenes' rather than being in the spotlight during race weekends. With hindsight, that was a first step towards this split, which, according to the statement, has come about by mutual agreement. "Following our reduced trackside involvement this season, we have collectively agreed that now is an appropriate time to bring our management agreement to a close," Webber said.

Piastri's development and a new reality in the F1 driver market

Aside from all that, it must also be said that Piastri's situation is very different now from what it was at the beginning of his career. Consequently, what he needs from the people around him has changed as well. This applies in two areas: his experience as a driver and the current situation in the F1 driver market.

In his younger years, Piastri needed Webber's experience as a racing driver more than he does now. When the Australian made his F1 debut at the age of 21 – and was, as Toto Wolff tends to describe young drivers, still a "deer in the headlights" – it helped to have a trusted figure by his side who had already experienced it all. Someone outside the team who was concerned solely with his interests and could help him avoid potential pitfalls.

When Autosport spoke to Piastri in Barcelona during his debut season, that was precisely the added value he highlighted: "Mark’s advice was to not underestimate the challenge of F1 and how big of a step up it is, not just from the cars but from everything: the amount of people you need to interact with, the media commitments, and the sponsor commitments. It's all much higher than before. I think having him reminding me of that before the season started was nice, not to be shocked when I arrived. That's probably been the biggest thing.

Oscar Piastri, McLaren F1 Team, 2nd position, is congratulated by Mark Webber in Parc Ferme Photo by: Steven Tee / Motorsport Images

"But he's very helpful with small driving tips here and there as well, and sometimes thinking of questions for the engineers that don't even come to my head at the moment.

"He's still very sharp. He thinks like a racing driver still and is always trying to get the best out of me."

More than three years later, Piastri has experienced all of this himself and therefore needs that hands-on guidance as a driver less than he did during his rookie season. Logically, this means that a different type of management can now suffice, with different priorities in that respect as well.

Moreover, the situation in the driver market has changed. Piastri is committed to McLaren for the longer term, with a contract running until the end of 2028. Yes, an extraordinary amount has been said and written about Piastri's seat this summer, particularly in light of the Max Verstappen rumours, which have been blown considerably out of proportion by certain publications. In reality, however, the Dutchman indicated that he had come much closer to retiring from F1 than to moving to another team, meaning Piastri has not seriously been looking elsewhere either.

He did describe it as 'flattering' that his name was linked with Red Bull during the summer months, but the reality is that this route appears to be closed for the coming years. After all, Verstappen has extended his contract, meaning Red Bull – provided it gives him a competitive car – has its lead driver in place. And with talents such as Isack Hadjar, Arvid Lindblad and perhaps Nikola Tsolov in the longer term, Red Bull appears perfectly capable of filling its second seat from within its own talent pool.

Add to that the fact that Mercedes and Ferrari also still have long-term lead drivers in Kimi Antonelli and Charles Leclerc, and maintaining and further strengthening his relationship with McLaren seems far more important for Piastri than having contacts elsewhere, for example through Webber at Red Bull. These two factors may still make the timing surprising, but not so much the decision itself to end the partnership after Webber had already taken a step back.

Oscar Piastri, McLaren with Mark Webber Photo by: Getty Images

Finally, it must be said that Webber did play a key role in the early years of Piastri's career, one that should not be forgotten at a moment like this. Indeed, Piastri himself has not forgotten it either, as his quote in the joint statement demonstrates: "I'd like to thank Mark and Ann for all their support and advice over the years. Their guidance has been invaluable, particularly in navigating the beginning of my F1 career. I wish them all the best going forward."

The most important move, of course, was leaving Alpine for McLaren, including Piastri's now-famous tweet. That was a period in which Webber's 'us against the world' mentality, as Horner described it, proved particularly useful. The move also saved Piastri from the quicksand that Alpine was, especially at that time. It is a decision for which he remains grateful, but this phase of his career calls for something different, and that explains why the partnership between two of the four most recent Australian F1 drivers has come to an end.

Webber played an important role in getting Piastri to where he is today, and the current seventh-placed driver in the championship has not forgotten that. But he feels that something different is needed for the next phase of his career, ideally one of harmony within McLaren – and, given all of the above, that is understandable.

Sports.title: How the Racing Bulls pendulum is swinging back towards Lawson
Sports.content:
When job security is in short supply, there's one solution for an Formula 1 driver. Be so good they can't ignore you.

That's easier said than done, but it certainly seems to be what Liam Lawson has taken to heart as he battled for his future over the recent Americas triple-header. Having been an integral part of Racing Bulls' rise to fifth in the constructors' championship, which will be the Anglo-Italian team's best-ever result, Lawson took ninth in Austin before bagging a pair of seventh-place finishes in Mexico and Brazil.

Following his challenger Nikola Tsolov's strong FP1 debut in Mexico, and Lawson's unfortunate run-in with Red Bull's stalwart Max Verstappen, signs are now pointing towards the pendulum having swung back in Lawson's favour with a decision expected over the Las Vegas Grand Prix weekend next week. A report from The Race, which Autosport understands is accurate, says Lawson is now set to stay put after all with Tsolov coming on board as a reserve in 2027. Sources have indicated a final decision is close but not signed off yet.

Driving for his future has been exhausting for Lawson, even if it's not a new situation for the 24-year-old. Ever since he arrived as a deputy for the injured Daniel Ricciardo in 2023, Lawson has effectively been fighting for his seat, first from the sidelines and then as Ricciardo's full-time replacement with little to no job security beyond the next race weekend.



It all came to a head over the past triple-header as Racing Bulls and the wider Red Bull organisation kept delaying a final call between Lawson and Tsolov.



If Racing Bulls had been a standalone team, the decision to retain Lawson and Arvid Lindblad would have been a no-brainer. Rookie Lindblad is still seen as potential Red Bull material in the future. And while that window appears to have come and gone for Lawson, he has amassed 89 points as the highest point scorer outside the top four teams.



With Racing Bulls tasked to train young drivers for the Red Bull senior team though, it is understood Red Bull's Austrian parent company is particularly excited by F2 frontrunner Tsolov's promise. However, a decision to keep Lawson wouldn't necessarily work against Racing Bull's objective, as having such a solid benchmark in the other car has been useful to gauge Lindblad's performances this year too. Meanwhile, 19-year-old Tsolov would still benefit from a full year as a reserve driver, which includes more FP1s, private testing and simulator work.

Liam Lawson, Racing Bulls Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images

Racing Bulls qualifying head-to-head

Arvid Lindblad 7-14 (6-11 without sprints) Liam Lawson 9 (+1.253s in Q3) Australia 8 15 (+0.334s in SQ2) China (sprint) 13 15 (+0.019s in Q2) China 14 10 Japan 14 (+0.386s in Q2) 16 Miami (sprint) 17 (+0.171s in SQ1) 17 (+0.538s in Q1) Miami 12 9 Canada (sprint) DNS 9 Canada 12 (+0.349s in Q2) 15 (+0.777s in Q2) Monaco 10 11 (+0.255s in Q2) Barcelona 8 10 (+0.052s in Q3) Austria 9 10 (+0.440s in SQ3) Britain (sprint) 9 9 Britain 10 (+0.411s in Q3) 8 Belgium 11 (+0.491s in Q2) 9 Hungary 11 (+0.405s in Q2) 15 (+0.246s in Q2) Azerbaijan 12 16 (no time - grid penalty) Bahrain in Malaysia 11 17 (+0.281s in SQ1) Singapore (sprint) 8 10 (+0.412s in Q3) Singapore 9 9 United States 10 (No lap time in Q3) 9 (+0.088s in Q3) Mexico 8 14 (+4.638s in Q2 - rain) Brazil 5

Racing Bulls has also been explicitly asked by Austria to stand on its own feet both in terms of identity and performance, so that's why a dyed-in-the-wool F1 veteran like team principal Alan Permane would have been keen to maximise performance and stick with Lawson.



"The main factors are, as always, pace and speed. That's the very first thing we look for," Permane said when grilled on the topic on Friday in Sao Paulo. "But we're not just a team that exists solely to compete. We are here to bring young talent through, so we have to keep an eye on that. And that doesn't necessarily mean that we just keep churning young talent through the car. We need to maybe have some experience as well to measure that talent."

The clearest hint that a difference in opinion between the various stakeholders is what has really been holding up the decision came from Lawson himself. "I feel like Alan's been extremely supportive to me and I appreciate that a lot," he said. "I've enjoyed working closely with him and with the team this year. Obviously, it's a big organisation so..."



Permane recently inked a fresh deal until 2031 as Racing Bulls team principal and co-CEO, so it's obvious that his opinion carries plenty of weight. And it would stand to reason that Permane has wanted some assurances about his share in the decision-making before committing.

"Alan is doing a tremendous job, and the progress the team has made is a direct reflection of his experience, commitment and competitive mindset," said Permane's boss Oliver Mintzlaff, CEO Corporate Projects and Investments Red Bull. "He brings clarity, composure, and a deep understanding of what it takes to perform in Formula 1, while creating an environment where people can consistently deliver at their best."

Meanwhile, fans of Lawson and the team have been flooding the squad's social media channels urging it to re-sign the Kiwi. He said: "I appreciate all the support. I've seen it over the last few weeks. It's honestly really nice to see.

A treacherous Brazil weekend was one of Liam Lawson's finest. Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

"Obviously, I would love it if it was more from a team. But at the moment I'm just trying to enjoy driving the car because with everything else going on I don't really know what else I'm meant to do. I don't really know what else I'm meant to say to you guys. So, at the moment I'm just going to keep driving and see what happens."

When it mattered the most, Brazil was perhaps Lawson's finest weekend yet. In treacherous conditions, Lawson took fifth on the grid, starting from third after grid penalties for George Russell and Charles Leclerc.

In the rain, he picked off McLaren's Lando Norris for second at the start, only to fall back to his natural position once drivers got their intermediate tyres back in the right operating window. Lawson battled to claim eighth on the road, being promoted to seventh after Leclerc was penalised for barging his way past in the closing laps.



Permane was obviously appreciative of how tough the past few weeks and months have been on one of F1 2026's standout performers, but said the team is nearly there.



"I realise it's frustrating for our drivers," he added. "I realise it's frustrating for everyone else, but we want to get it right, and we will get it right. I'm sure when we announce it in the coming weeks, everyone will be happy..."

Sports.title: Piastri and Webber terminate management agreement
Sports.content:
Oscar Piastri and Mark Webber have mutually agreed to terminate their management agreement, the pair have announced.

Webber and his wife Ann – who ran Mark’s career herself back in the day – became Piastri’s managers in 2019, the year the youngster narrowly beat Victor Martins to the Formula Renault Eurocup title and a spot on Renault’s F1 academy.

Piastri’s rise was meteoric from then on, as he clinched the Formula 3 title the following year – again marginally, with Theo Pourchaire and Logan Sargeant just a few points adrift – and won Formula 2 in 2021, also as a rookie, and with little competition that time.

Under Webber, Piastri made the career-defining move to leave the Alpine fold and sign a McLaren race deal for the 2023 Formula 1 season, which paved the way for his 2025 title bid. Across 88 career starts so far, the Australian has taken six pole positions and nine victories.

“We are proud to have played a pivotal role in the formative years of Oscar's career and to have placed him in F1 so that he could compete at the front so early on,” Webber said.

“Following our reduced trackside involvement this season, we have collectively agreed that now is an appropriate time to bring our management agreement to a close. This will allow Oscar to build on his achievements under a new management structure, and for us to embark on our new ventures. We wish Oscar all the very best for a long and successful career.”

Oscar Piastri, McLaren Photo by: James Sutton / Formula 1 / Formula Motorsport Ltd via Getty Images

Piastri added: “I'd like to thank Mark and Ann for all their support and advice over the years. Their guidance has been invaluable, particularly in navigating the beginning of my F1 career. I wish them all the best going forward.”

Webber had taken a step back at the start of the 2026 season and no longer supported Piastri trackside, with a couple of new figures assisting the McLaren driver – Pedro Matos, his race engineer at Prema in Formula 2, and mental coach Emma Murray.

“There wasn't anything specific, just we made a decision for things to look a bit different,” Piastri said back in February. “Mark is still very much involved and I've been in contact with him a lot over the last few weeks. He just won't be trackside as much anymore. So that's really the extent of it.

“There was nothing specific that triggered it.”

Appearing on the High Performance Podcast in May, the 25-year-old added: “The relationship's good. Very thorough, is Mark. When I first got into F1, Mark was coming up with questions and ideas that literally hadn't even entered my brain. I would hear him say it and go like, 'How the hell did he think of that?' Or like, 'How am I ever going to think of that?'

Oscar Piastri, McLaren with Mark Webber Photo by: Getty Images

“And I think just with experience, we're always learning every day, but now starting my fourth year, I have either the answers to a lot of those kinds of questions that I wouldn't have had in the first couple of years, or I know the questions to keep asking, which just comes with experience.

“There's naturally less and less for Mark to do on the racing side of things the more experienced I become. But especially in the first couple of years, there are some lessons you have to learn the hard way, and there's no other way of doing it, but I'm sure there could have been plenty of other slightly annoying, tougher lessons to learn that I was probably spared because of Mark's experience and Mark's guidance.

“There's probably always going to be situations or things that have gone smoothly or almost problems that weren't problems that I'm never going to know about because Mark managed them for me. That's probably how it's changed in the last few years.”

Sports.title: Leclerc penalised for Lawson clash; Antonelli and Oliver Bearman also punished after F1 Brazilian GP
Sports.content:
Charles Leclerc was handed a five-second penalty after the Formula 1 Brazilian Grand Prix for his clash with Liam Lawson, dropping the Ferrari driver down to eighth place in the final results.

The Monegasque was battling the Racing Bulls driver for seventh place on lap 69 of the Sao Paulo race when the pair made contact into Juncao, Turn 12, but both were able to continue and finish the race.

The clash did enable Leclerc to take seventh place from Lawson but the incident was placed under investigation for a post-race hearing.

After speaking to both drivers and assessing the video and data, the FIA stewards determined Leclerc was to blame and duly gave him a five-second penalty, dropping the Ferrari driver behind his rival and into eighth place in the final results.

The FIA stewards accepted that the contact was minor and in wet conditions, which was enough mitigation to keep the penalty to 5s and not a potential 10s punishment.

The FIA stewards report read: “While the contact was minor and Car 30 was able to maintain the lead thereafter, the driver of Car 30 claimed that the contact damaged the rear left rim of his car and also enabled Car 16 to get closer to him on track and then eventually overtake him 5 corners later. Furthermore, under the Driving Standard Guidelines, Car 30 had the right to the corner and it was for Car 16 to take the necessary steps to avoid a collision.

Liam Lawson, Racing Bulls Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

“The driver of Car 16 claimed that it was a minor contact with no obvious sporting consequence.

“While we acknowledge that the contact was minor, having examined the fight on track between the two cars, we conclude that Car 16 was able to get closer to and thereafter overtake Car 30 because of the contact. The contact clearly disrupted Car 30 and allowed Car 16 to pull up alongside when it was further away before the contact. This was an obvious sporting consequence.

“In mitigation, the wet conditions coupled with the nature of the contact (i.e. minor) was taken into account in imposing a 5 second time penalty as opposed to a 10 second time penalty.”

Antonelli and Bearman also penalised for unsafe releases from pitstops

New F1 world champion Kimi Antonelli was also given a five-second penalty after the Brazilian GP for an unsafe pitstop release.

The Italian was released from his final pitstop of the race into the path of the oncoming Franco Colapinto and despite attempting to take avoiding action it was judged unsafe and a five-second penalty was duly handed out.

But because Antonelli finished over 20s ahead of Oscar Piastri, who was directly behind him on the road, it does not change his final finishing position of fifth place – as Mercedes secured this year’s F1 constructors’ championship.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

In a separate incident also involving Leclerc, Oliver Bearman was given a post-race five-second penalty for an unsafe release from a pitstop. The Haas F1 driver was released into the path of the Ferrari driver, which forced Leclerc to check-up in the pitlane.

The penalty has no consequence to Bearman either given he finished in 17th and one lap up on Sergio Perez in 18th place.

Sports.title: Antonelli explains "weird" spin and car instability which cost F1 Brazilian GP win
Sports.content:
Kimi Antonelli vowed to put aside his Brazilian Grand Prix anger to celebrate Mercedes winning the Formula 1 constructors' title, as he rued the balance issues and the spin that took him out of victory contention.

The new world champion had picked up the lead from polesitter Lando Norris at the start, and was building a pretty healthy lead over the Briton in the opening laps of the race. He held the lead either side of the first round of pitstops, as the circuit was dry enough for slicks, although Norris' undercut had taken a considerable chunk of time out of Antonelli's advantage.

At the start of lap 20, Antonelli then lost the car and this precipitated a spin at the opening corner. He was able to recover, but Norris had long since bolted past for the lead - and it left the Italian in the clutches of Isack Hadjar.

Antonelli had reported before his spin that he was worried he'd picked up a suspension issue, and that the car was pulling to one side under acceleration - and his difficulty with balance cost further positions to Hadjar and Max Verstappen. However, no clear cause had emerged during the race.

"I'm very disappointed for the race. I'm very angry to be fair, but I'm going to put all this aside for now because the team clinched the title," Antonelli said.

"We clinched the title for the team, and they all deserve it and I'm very proud to be part of this group and this team who has done and still does so much for me and I'm very happy for them. But talking about the race specifically, yeah, very disappointing.

Lando Norris, McLaren, Liam Lawson, Racing Bulls, Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

"We were on for the win up to that point. Also in the lead, once I was able to get some temperature I was getting to the rhythm. But yeah, the spin came which still is something I need to look at because I don't know why I lost the rear so quickly as well.

"Like no warning, nothing. But already to be fair when I put the soft, I felt something weird with the car. So, we need to check what happened but on the other hand yeah, shame because we lost the race there."

When speaking to Sky Sports, Antonelli expanded on the issue and noted that it was only occurring in the left-hand corners, particularly in higher-speed sections - which, around Interlagos, would account for much of the first and third sectors.

The tyre flat spots sustained in the spin made his life much harder; when he'd taken a second set of soft tyres, his improvement in lap time was demonstrable and this afforded an opportunity to challenge Hadjar late on.

"We need to check something with the geometry of the car, of the rear, because I had this issue only in left corners. So especially at the high speed was when I was feeling it the most," he told Sky.

"And the rear felt very unstable, even in coming into the finish line in the left kink, the rear was very loose, which was weird.

"We need to check something in the car to see if anything happened. But it was a very odd feeling. And then when I spun, the tyres were gone; all four wheels flat spotted. Only when then I put on the second set, we got back to pace. It was a shame."

Sports.title: On This Day: F1’s first female racer, Maria Teresa de Filiipis, born 100 years ago | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Maria Theresa de Filippis, the first woman to start a round of the Formula 1 world championship, was born 100 years ago to this day.

She started 19th on the grid for the Belgian Grand Prix in 1958 (above) in a privately-entered Maserati 250F. She took the chequered flag in 10th place, but unlike today, only the top five finishers scored points.

De Filippis started two other races that year, but retired from both with engine trouble, and made two unsuccessful attempts to qualify for the Monaco Grand Prix. She died 10 years ago.

Sports.title: Lawson made sure Red Bull saw he helped Verstappen in Brazil after Mexico incident | Formula 1
Sports.content:
“When you’re fighting for your seat, it’s not very smart behaviour,” remarked Max Verstappen after Liam Lawson refused to get out of his way during practice in Mexico last week.

A week later during the grand prix at Interlagos, Lawson was far more obliging. He dived out of Verstappen’s way when the Red Bull driver appeared in his mirrors. Lawson then made sure his Racing Bulls team – and perhaps more importantly its senior sibling Red Bull – did not overlook how helpful he’d been.

It’s not uncommon to see drivers make way for their team mates when ordered to on the radio. In the same race Isack Hadjar slowed significantly to let Verstappen in the other Red Bull past.

Lawson, in theory at least, drives for a rival team and has no need to be helpful at all. But while a midfield team driver such as Lawson would likely see no benefit from wasting time and tyre life fighting one of the front-running cars, nor would they be expected to cost themselves time by slowing down. “Don’t lose time with him” is typical advice from race engineers.

Yet that is precisely what Lawson did. Racing Bulls made sure he was aware how quickly Verstappen was gaining on him. Then Lawson dived out of the way on the Reta Oposta back straight, slowing so sharply he dropped down two gears and lost over one-and-a-half seconds.

Job done, he pointed out to race engineer Alexandre Iliopoulos he had not cost Verstappen any time:

Lap: 9/71 LAW: 1’28.088 Iliopoulos Copy. The car behind is now Max. Iliopoulos Some cars around are struggling with tyres. Iliopoulos Car behind is Max, two seconds. Iliopoulos Feedback on balance when you can Lawson Well, it’s just graining, so I have no fronts, and the traction is really, really bad. Do you want me to try clear it? Lap: 10/71 LAW: 1’27.900 Iliopoulos Yes. Yes, we think that’s the best option. Iliopoulos Engine braking eight if you want. Engine nine position three. Lap: 11/71 LAW: 1’29.516 Iliopoulos Push toggle last corner if you want. Iliopoulos Lawson pulls over, slows down and lets Verstappen pass him

Car behind, Piastri, one second, and Hulkenberg is six behind you. Lawson Yep, I let him go. Iliopoulos Copy.

Lawson is still waiting to learn if he will remain at Red Bull’s junior team next year. He clearly wanted to demonstrate he is ready to help Racing Bulls’ sister team.

He was much more prepared to fight his corner in Miami earlier this year, when he challenged Racing Bulls’ order that he let Verstappen past.

But Lawson’s eagerness to show his worth to Red Bull also highlights how unusual their arrangement with their junior team is. One driver pulling over and slowing down so blatantly to let a driver from a rival team overtake him – and then drawing attention to it – would be astonishing if it involved any other pair of teams on the grid.

Sports.title: Social Media: Hamilton witnesses humanitarian relief effort in Gaza Strip | Brief
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton travelled to the Gaza Strip today to see the work being done to bring humanitarian relief to those in the region.

He visited the Rafah land crossing between Egypt and the territory, plus a logistics facility where aid being sent to Gaza is processed.

The Ferrari driver has repeatedly called for peace in the region and criticised the lack of action from other countries. Over 74,000 people are estimated to have died in the war in Gaza which followed the Hamas attack in Israel on October 7th 2023, in which 1,195 were killed.

The North Sinai Governorate shared further details of Hamilton’s visit.

Sports.title: F1 scraps back-up plan to race at Imola if Middle East GPs are cancelled – reports | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Formula 1 has committed to holding the final two rounds of the 2026 world championship in the Middle East or not at all.

The series had made contingency arrangements to relocate the final round it Imola in Italy if it decided the risks posed by the war in Iran meant it should not proceed with its races in the Middle East. Multiple reports now claim F1 has told Imola it will not be required to hold a race.

The world championship will resume at Las Vegas in the USA next week. Following that it is due to race at the Losail International Circuit in Qatar and Yas Marina in the United Arab Emirates on the following weekends.

The series cancelled its grands prix in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia earlier this year due to the war between Iran and the USA. It later held an event using the ‘Bahrain Grand Prix’ title at Malaysia’s Sepang International Circuit.

The political situation in the Middle East remains uncertain. US president Donald Trump this week suggested he would not escalate its military campaign in the region, but has made similar comments since beginning his war in February, only to subsequently launch further strikes. The US retains a significant military presences in the region and moved more troops there last month.

However Moto GP, which like F1 is owned by Liberty Media, raced in Losail on Sunday. It postponed its Qatar round in April due to the war.

Four bikes were missing from the field as Yamaha did not participate. Most of the series’ riders expressed concerns over visiting the country and asked the championship to provide extra guarantees for their security.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff defended Moto GP’s decision to race in Qatar. He criticised riders who expressed concerns about racing there, saying they “know nothing” about the situation.

Many television broadcasters also opted not to send their staff to the region.

The 2027 F1 season is due to begin in the Middle East with races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia next March. F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali told investors last week “the disruption we experienced in the Middle East this year does not change our long-term regional strategy and ongoing partnership with our promoters.”

“This year, we currently remain scheduled to complete our calendar season and at this stage, continue to plan to finish the season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi,” he added. “We will continue to monitor the situation. As always, the safety and security of everyone in the sport will remain our first and foremost priority.”

Many other series have cancelled events in the region due to the war in the Middle East. The World Endurance Championship called off its planned rounds in Qatar and Bahrain, replacing them with races in Italy and Spain. The 2027 Dakar Rally, previously held in Saudi Arabia, will take place in Africa. The 2026-27 Asian Le Mans series, which previously raced at Dubai Autodrome and Yas Marina, will take place in Europe under the name ‘Winter Le Mans Series’.

This article will be updated.

Sports.title: No F1 engine manufacturers to get extra upgrades after FIA’s third ADUO evaluation | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The FIA will not to offer any engine manufacturers the chance to perform extra power unit upgrades following its latest Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities (ADUO) evaluation.

Under new rules introduced as part of Formula 1’s 2026 power unit regulations the sport’s governing body controls how often manufacturers can upgrade their internal combustion engines.

The evaluations take place periodically throughout the season. The FIA has completed its third such evaluation and, as was the case during the second, determined no further engine homologation opportunities should be offered.

The third evaluation period concluded after the United States Grand Prix last month. The second followed the Hungarian Grand Prix.

The first evaluation period, which ran from the start of the season to the Canadian Grand Prix, remains the only time any additional upgrade opportunities were awarded. On that occasion Red Bull-Ford were found to have the top-performing power unit.

Audi, Ferrari and Honda’s units were found to be more than 4% less powerful. They were permitted two extra homologation opportunities this year and two more next year. Mercedes were found to be within 2% and 4% of the leading power unit and therefore received one extra upgrade this year and next.

Separately, in May the FIA changed the ADUO rules to allow any manufacturer which was 10% off the leading design to spend more money. The revision was expected to assist Honda following their poor start to the season.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Some have likened F1’s ADUO to the World Endurance Championship’s heavily-criticised Balance of Performance regulations. The FIA’s single-seater director Nikolas Tombazis defended the regulations but indicated they may be revised in coming seasons.

“Based on the quality of the data and the robustness of the assessment process, we are confident in our findings and the conclusions reached,” he said.

“The first year of implementation has also reinforced our belief that the ADUO concept is the right one for Formula 1. However, it is important that the system continues to evolve to ensure it remains efficient, relevant and fit for purpose.

“To that end, we have been working closely with the power unit manufacturers and teams to explore refinements to the methodology that will support the continued effectiveness of ADUO in future seasons.”

Sports.title: “The car is steering by itself, don’t you see it?”: How handling trouble baffled Antonelli | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli looked on course to win his first race as the new world champion as he pulled out an eight-second lead over his pursuers over the opening 12 laps at Interlagos.

But he reported something felt wrong with his Mercedes’ handling soon after switching to slick tyres and spun off, allowing Lando Norris through into the lead. The two Red Bull drivers passed him and by lap 34 Antonelli was 17 seconds off the lead.

Antonelli’s exchanges with race engineer Peter Bonnington underline how he was mystified by his car’s handling. Bonnington kept him supplied with notes on where he could find more time but it was only after he swapped his flat-spotted set of slicks for a fresh set that he began to show more competitive pace.

Unfortunately for Antonelli, the rain returned soon afterwards. He pitted for intermediates again – collecting a penalty for an unsafe release as he did – and the early leader had to settle for a fifth-place finish.

Selected messages from Antonelli in the Brazilian GP

Most drivers switched from intermediates to slicks on lap 16 but Mercedes kept the race leader out a lap longer.

Watch the white line on entry. Lap: 18/71 ANT: 1’47.139 Bonnington So caution on the pit exit, George spun in the pit exit, it is still very greasy there. Bonnington Push and hold on exit. You are all clear. Bonnington So Norris at two behind. Turns one, two, three are still slippy. Gap at 0.7 behind.

Sports.title: Jai Opetaia Gets WBC No. 2, Awaits Benavidez vs. Cieslak
Sports.content:
Jai Opetaia landing at No. 2 in the latest WBC cruiserweight rankings changes little about his immediate path. The Australian already holds a guaranteed crack at the winner between David Benavidez and Michal Cieslak courtesy of the WBC’s ruling in September.

The real drama scheduled for December 5 in Glendale is scale: whether Opetaia walks into a three-belt unification blockbuster against Benavidez over Cinco de Mayo weekend, or finds himself facing Cieslak solely for the WBC green strap.

Opetaia locked down official mandatory status by halting Noel Mikaelian in September. WBC bylaws dictate that occupying the top spot in the rankings does not automatically confer mandatory rights; the governing body must issue an explicit order. Opetaia holds that formal mandate in hand, giving him ironclad leverage regardless of who emerges victorious in Arizona.

“The fight that I got to honor first is the fight with Opetaia because I told him I’d fight him Cinco de Mayo next year,” Benavidez revealed on Brian Custer’s show.

Clinging to that No. 2 WBC ranking like a life raft looks completely neurotic when you look at the reality of the situation. Benavidez has not been playing coy. He got right into the ring with Opetaia in September, looked him dead in the eye, and told him they were doing this on Cinco de Mayo.

Fighters do not commit to a date on a holiday weekend in front of a live broadcast unless they genuinely want the scalp. He’s eager for this matchup because he looks at Opetaia and sees someone who is fundamentally vulnerable around the whiskers. He watched Opetaia get hurt by Huseyin Cinkara and Noel Mikaelian

To a volume puncher like Benavidez, who drowns people under relentless flurries and body punches, a guy with a suspect chin and an aggressive offensive style is tailor-made target practice. Benavidez does not fear Opetaia’s power; he thinks he can walk him down, clip him, and turn his lights out.

Yet Team Opetaia is acting like they need Mauricio Sulaiman and a WBC paper trail to save them from being bypassed. If Benavidez is practically begging to fight you because he thinks you have a glass jaw waiting to be cracked, you do not need to hide behind WBC bylaws or celebrate a No. 2 ranking. You just show up, let him sign the contract, and try to prove him wrong. Right now, all the anxiety coming out of Opetaia’s corner makes them look terrified that the cash-out might evaporate if Benavidez decides to look elsewhere.

All the holiday talk creates an ideal spoiler scenario for Cieslak. An upset in Glendale hands him the unified crown while shifting the WBC mandatory obligation directly onto his shoulders. Even with three belts on the line in December, Opetaia’s contractual entitlement applies strictly to the WBC belt under sanctioning bylaws, leaving any full unification terms subject to fresh administrative approvals.

A Benavidez triumph fulfills the public pact struck between the two fighters following the Mikaelian clash. Finalizing that Cinco de Mayo showdown would still require both promotional outfits to hammer out broadcast splits and purse distributions, with the looming threat of a WBC purse bid deadline if talks drag out. Before any contracts can be printed for May, Cieslak gets the first opportunity to tear up the script.

Sports.title: Ryan Garcia’s $100M Bluff to Lure Floyd Mayweather Out of Retirement
Sports.content:
Ryan Garcia is daring Floyd Mayweather Jr. to put his spotless 50–0 record on the line for a theoretical nine-figure payday.

The reigning WBC welterweight champion insists he will put the 49-year-old icon to sleep, claiming Mayweather will wake up $100 million richer for his trouble. The catch is simple: nobody has stepped forward with that kind of capital.

Garcia laid out his pitch on Kick with signature bravado: “Then, you wake up, and you’ve got $100 million. That’s good. You’re just going to get knocked out real quick. You love money, right? I’m going to test that theory on how much you love money.”

The math makes that purse an enormous stretch. At $80 per purchase, 1.5 million pay-per-view buys yield roughly $120 million in gross revenue. Once cable platforms, satellite providers, and streaming distributors take their cuts, production overhead gets covered, and Garcia secures his own check, a $100 million guarantee for Floyd evaporates.

Live ticket sales and brand sponsorships bridge some of the divide, but any backer writing that guarantee is gambling heavily. They must bet that modern audiences will shell out premium cash to see an aging Mayweather enter a real contest after a decade of theatrical exhibitions. Garcia generated massive numbers against Gervonta Davis, yet that blockbuster relied on Davis bringing an equally rabid audience.

Mayweather built an empire around being untouchable, an aura he preserves through low-risk exhibition tours. An authentic 12-round championship scrap completely shatters that protective bubble.

Ryan’s signature left hook poses immediate physical danger to a fighter turning 50, testing whether Mayweather’s legendary shoulder roll and counter instincts can outrun Father Time. Floyd stepped into a pro ring last in 2017 to dispatch Conor McGregor. He has not fought an elite, active professional boxer since outpointing Andre Berto in 2015.

Sanctioning politics complicate the picture just as much. WBC president Mauricio Sulaiman signaled that Mayweather could challenge for the title pending medical clearance and standard licensing. Even so, the WBC would face intense scrutiny for greenlighting a 49-year-old on a nine-year professional layoff ahead of deserving, active welterweight contenders.

With a broadcast partner, host city, and signed contracts entirely absent, Garcia’s February 6 target date looks increasingly like theater. Pointing toward Mayweather keeps Garcia dominating headlines while he entertains a practical matchup against Teofimo Lopez. Mayweather loses nothing by ignoring the noise. Garcia is the fighter with a date to fill, and finding a partner to share the stage matters far less than finding someone willing to fund it.

Mayweather isn’t 39; he turns 50 in February. At nearly half a century old, the physical drop-off is a complete biological cliff. In his exhibitions over the last couple of years, the reflexes, the spring in his legs, and the twitch speed that defined his prime are simply gone. What remains is muscle memory, shell defense, and pacing himself against novices, YouTubers, and MMA fighters who do not know how to cut off a ring or throw punches with real professional malice.

Putting that version of Mayweather in a sanctioned 12-round fight against Ryan Garcia, who is 28 and carries genuine, explosive power in his left hook, is not a competitive sporting event. A shell defense only works when you have the hand speed and counter-threat to keep a puncher honest. If you cannot deter a prime fighter from walking you down, the shell just turns you into a static target along the ropes. At 147, Garcia would walk through anything Floyd threw back, find the gaps, and the fight would likely be over as soon as Garcia committed to an exchange.

The financial reality makes it an even bigger non-starter. Riyadh Season and the Saudi backers have shown that while they will pay astronomical figures, they are spending with a purpose: legacy unifications, undisputed clashes, and top-tier matchups that build sports authority. The era of writing blank, nine-figure checks for absurd circus acts has dried up, especially with tighter watch on returns.

Paying $100 million to a 49-year-old fighter to take a severe beating in a sanctioned professional bout offers zero prestige and terrible optics. Nobody with that kind of capital is going to underwrite a one-sided blowout, and Floyd’s business instincts are still sharp enough to know that 50–0 is worth far more intact than whatever embarrassment awaits him in a real ring.

Sports.title: Jake Paul Calls Cédric Doumbé a Tune-Up
Sports.content:
Jake Paul plans to let his jab dictate terms when he meets Cédric Doumbé in Dubai on Christmas Eve. During their press conference in Paris, Paul labeled the former GLORY kickboxing standout an easy tune-up, projecting a stoppage inside four rounds. In his breakdown, Doumbé relies on wide, winging hooks that carry obvious warnings and operates behind a porous guard.

“Yeah, a lot of wild looping shots, no straight shots; everything he throws is predictable. He telegraphs his shots. He doesn’t set anything up. But he does have power, you know, behind them sometimes. Doesn’t have a good jab, not so good defense, and his chin is in the air. The body is open. There’s a lot, there’s a lot,” Paul said.

That critique points out real technical gaps, but it glosses over how kickboxers control space. In kickboxing, the threat of low kicks forces an opponent to stay light on their lead leg, preventing them from sitting down comfortably on a straight left. In a pure boxing ring, Paul steps forward without that hesitation. That lets him establish lead-foot dominance, pin Doumbé to the ropes, and lean on his cruiserweight bulk to tie up the smaller man whenever exchanges get chaotic. Doumbé spent the bulk of his combat career competing near 170 pounds, meaning Paul holds a clear frame advantage to grind on him along the perimeter.

Doumbé cannot afford to stand at mid-range waiting to time a home-run shot, because Paul will simply bank rounds behind the jab. His genuine opportunity comes from exploiting Paul’s habitual flaw: dropping the rear hand to chest level when stepping out of a combination. If Doumbé utilizes twitchy shoulder feints to draw Paul’s jab into the same rhythm, he can slip inside the line and fire his overhand right while Paul’s lead shoulder is fully extended. That requires disciplined ring cutting rather than the sudden forward blitzes Doumbé often used in GLORY.

Doumbé made no secret of his primary motive, pointing out the odd dynamic of facing an executive who signs the paychecks. “My boss will pay me to knock him the fuck out,” Doumbé stated. He gets eight rounds to prove his explosive power carries into a 200-pound cruiserweight ring on December 24 at Coca-Cola Arena.

Sports.title: Alycia Baumgardner Becomes A Two-Division Champion
Sports.content:
Arlington, Texas – On Sunday night, Alycia “The Bomb” Baumgardner became a two-division world champion by defeating the “Golden Turkish Warrior” Elif Turhan for the IBF world lightweight title. She may have put on the best performance of her career by showing her technical skills, being defensively sound and offensively great. She utilized her jab effectively, landing more jabs (92) than Turhan did total punches (50).

Elif (14-1, 8 KOs) was viewed as a dangerous power puncher with true knockout power, which, according to Alycia, the WBC/WBO/Ring Magazine lightweight champion Caroline Dubois avoided. Baumgardner was able to neutralize the Golden Turkish Warrior’s power, holding her to career lows in total punches landed – – 50 punches and held her in single digits of landed punches in all 10 rounds. Alycia was masterful offensively, landing 51 percent of her power punches, a career high for her. (Compubox).

At the post-fight press conference, Alycia (19-1, 7 KOs) told the media about the fight, “Tonight, we became a two-division world champion against a tough…tough opponent. This was someone I was very humble to fight, and I needed this fight to keep me humble, to keep me hungry, and again being the best fighter that I can be.”

With the win Baumgardner is one step closer to the undisputed super fight set to happen next year. First, she must await the winner of the unification match between Caroline Dubois (14-0-1, 5 KOs) and Stephanie Han (13-0, 3 KOs) scheduled to take place February 20 in El Paso, Texas. Both were present for the Turhan-Baumgardner match and want to be the opponent whom she’ll fight for the undisputed clash.

Caroline appears to be the favorite to win the unification match against Stephanie Han, and she’s been the most vocal, stating she wants to fight Alycia and become undisputed champion. When asked if she declined a fight with Turhan, she said it was not true, calling it absolute BS. After the fight, Baumgardner and Dubois exchanged stares and words. With Caroline asking Alycia multiple times, “Are we going to fight?” Dubois appears determined to be undisputed and may get her opportunity soon; she mustn’t overlook Han, who is fighting in her hometown in El Paso. The undisputed lightweight championship match will be one of the biggest in women’s boxing, setting up two potential superstars in the sport.

Sports.title: WBC Moves Pacheco Toward Canelo Despite Thin Record
Sports.content:
Diego Pacheco has inched toward a massive Canelo Alvarez payday without taking the fights that would prove he earned it. His ascent to the WBC No. 1 spot at super middleweight comes after he passed on opportunities against Christian Mbilli and Hamzah Sheeraz.

The WBC confirmed the ranking during its annual convention, per EverythingBoxing. Because Lester Martinez still holds the interim title, Pacheco’s top spot does not make him Canelo’s immediate mandatory challenger or secure the next championship crack. Instead, he meets Darius Fulghum on Saturday, November 14, in Carson, California.

That reality forces a hard question on the sanctioning body: what has Pacheco done against prime opposition to merit the highest numeric spot?

His resume features victories over Steven Nelson, Trevor McCumby, and Kevin Lele Sadjo. None of those names proves he belongs above the division’s true elite. Sadjo even scored a knockdown before dropping the decision. Pacheco has stacked up wins, yet he has bypassed the tests that would reveal his actual ceiling.

The Mbilli episode stands out because the sanctioning body was directly involved. After turning away from an IBF final eliminator to fight Nelson, Pacheco’s side pulled out of a WBC interim title matchup against Mbilli in 2025. Two distinct paths toward an elite opponent evaporated before he ever stepped through the ropes.

Pacheco justified that second move through business logic. He argued the money didn’t warrant heading to Quebec and taking a smaller financial split for a hometown draw.

“Honestly, the purse wasn’t that great,” Pacheco told The Ring.

Boxers have every right to reject offers that undervalue them. Sanctioning bodies, however, must evaluate real in-ring achievements. Turning away from a formidable foe may preserve a fighter’s bankroll, but it does not prove he could win the fight.

The missed clash with Sheeraz is tougher to excuse as routine positioning. That matchup was ordered for the vacant WBO world championship, offering Pacheco a direct shot at a legitimate belt. He walked away in January after talks entered purse bids.

Legitimate backstory accompanied the withdrawal. Eddie Hearn pointed to coaching and managerial friction, while Pacheco stated he felt unsettled with his camp. Those reasons carry weight, but declining a world title bout does not count as a victory.

Fulghum now arrives with a chance to wreck the design. Pacheco defends his WBC Silver strap at Dignity Health Sports Park, carrying extra risk thanks to his new position. A loss would shatter his argument for a Canelo date before he has even tested himself against a top-tier contender.

Martinez holding the interim belt also clouds the pathway. The WBC boosted Pacheco up the ladder while another fighter sits on the secondary championship.

Pacheco can validate his position by handling Fulghum and signing to fight a premier super middleweight next. For now, the top spot credits him for potential while overlooking the caliber of fighters he has actually shared the ring with.

WBC ordering Pacheco against Lester Martinez would force total clarity on the 168-pound picture. Either Pacheco proves he can handle an aggressive, heavy-handed puncher who can back him up, or Lester eliminates him and removes any lingering question about who deserves Canelo.

The sanctioning body will never mandate it, though. By giving Pacheco the No. 1 ranking while Lester holds the interim belt, Mauricio Sulaiman gives himself maximum room to maneuver. If Canelo decides he wants a clean, recognizable name with a major promoter behind him, they can trot out Pacheco. If Canelo prefers a mandatory with a regional belt to check a box, they have Lester.

If you looked at Christian Mbilli and decided the purse wasn’t worth the beating, and you backed out of a WBO world title shot against Hamzah Sheeraz during purse bids, Lester is the last guy you’re volunteering to fight.

Lester is high risk with zero casual crossover. He works behind heavy pressure, punches with power, and does not give you room to breathe. Kevin Lele Sadjo gave Pacheco absolute fits just by winging shots on the inside and dropping him. Lester brings that same kind of heavy, physical pressure, except he is bigger and hits harder.

Matchroom is not about to put Pacheco in with an avoided, heavy-handed Guatemalan who brings no pay-per-view juice when they can just feed him fighters like Darius Fulghum, sit on that No. 1 ranking, and pray Canelo calls their number before someone forces Pacheco to take a real test.

Sports.title: Devin Haney Wants Ryan Garcia After Paro
Sports.content:
Devin Haney is talking about Ryan Garcia and undisputed crowns at 147, but public wish lists rarely match promotional reality. Haney insists Garcia is his primary target after Liam Paro, presenting a four-belt unification as the ultimate prize. If Garcia falls short against Teofimo Lopez in their proposed clash, Haney claims he will gladly face Lopez instead.

Haney has to deal with Paro on December 19 at the Chase Center in San Francisco before any of those grand scenarios can materialize. Paro is not a prop. He is a tough, natural junior welterweight titleholder stepping up in weight, possessing the physical strength to test Haney inside. Haney enjoyed a distinct frame advantage at lightweight, but welterweight erases those physical cushions. Overlooking a durable southpaw to game-plan a dream tournament is a familiar trap in boxing.

“The Ryan Garcia fight is the fight that I want the most,” Haney said to the media. “It starts with Liam Paro, but, yeah, for sure. Once I win this fight, you guys know who I got my eyes on.”

Haney wants to believe that collecting straps automatically grants him control over Garcia. That is a tactical miscalculation. Belts do not dictate commercial power in modern boxing, pay-per-view draws do. Garcia demonstrated in their first meeting that he can generate massive gates and pay-per-view numbers on his own terms. Even if Garcia beats Lopez to capture the WBC and WBA belts, he does not need Haney to command enormous paydays. Haney needs Garcia to attempt to erase the most damaging night of his career.

Devin and Bill Haney have spent years operating under the purist boxing currency: belts equate to leverage. In their minds, capturing the WBO and IBF straps against Liam Paro gives them undisputed collateral, and in the traditional sanctioning body system, two champions meeting for all four belts automatically calls for an even split.

In the modern commercial landscape, belts do not sell pay-per-views. Garcia proved in April 2024 that his platform dwarfs the hardware. He brings millions of casual eyeballs, viral reach, and ticket sales that Haney simply cannot generate as an A-side. Ryan knows who drove the commercial engine of their first fight, and he knows who held the psychological upper hand by the final bell. Demanding parity from a fighter who views himself as the sole economic driver of the promotion is an immediate non-starter.

Without third-party intervention, Ryan has zero incentive to capitulate. He holds the win that damaged Haney’s commercial aura, meaning Haney is the one chasing closure, redemption, and a career-defining check. Ryan can fight Rolly Romero, Conor Benn, Gervonta Davis, or even pursue exhibition routes and generate massive purses without ever having to accommodate the Haney camp’s contractual demands.

The single wildcard that alters the math is His Excellency Turki Alalshikh. Riyadh Season has repeatedly shown a willingness to distort traditional pay-per-view economics by simply overpaying both sides to eliminate negotiating hurdles. If Saudi backing arrives with an astronomical flat guarantee that makes Ryan indifferent to the split, the fight happens.

If the bout has to survive on standard domestic pay-per-view metrics, Haney’s 50-50 stance is a poison pill. Unless Haney swallows his pride and accepts the reality of being the B-side on the financial sheet, the rematch remains trapped behind a wall of commercial delusion.

Haney addressed the possibility of facing either man, attempting to maintain an air of indifference while clearly favoring the grudge match.

“If Ryan is victorious, still got to beat Teo … or even if Teo is victorious, it doesn’t matter. I would take either-or for undisputed,” Haney said. “But obviously I want Ryan Garcia to win so that I could right that wrong.”

Garcia wandering into exhibition talks with Floyd Mayweather illustrates the fundamental problem with Haney’s strategy. Garcia moves wherever the maximum money and spectacle lie. Haney, meanwhile, is betting his trajectory on the sanctioning bodies and conventional promotional pathways.

When asked about the Mayweather rumors, Haney took a reserved stance. He pointed out that Mayweather’s name routinely circulates around potential bouts that never reach the ring, treating the talk as typical posturing until contracts get signed.

The promotional terrain presents an even larger hurdle than fighter preferences. Haney points to his DAZN deal as the vehicle that will deliver these mega-fights, but DAZN does not control the entire board.

“Other people were offering me crazy money,” Haney said. “Of course, DAZN gave me a great deal, but most importantly, if you don’t have the opponents, how can I become a great in the sport?”

Cross-platform negotiations between competing networks and rival promoters routinely swallow undisputed fights whole. Landing belts at 147 might look clean on paper, but turning a regional fight in San Francisco into a massive multi-network blockbuster against Garcia requires solving promotional gridlock that sanctioning body hardware cannot fix on its own.

Sports.title: William Zepeda vs. Jadier Herrera Announcement Expected Soon From Golden Boy
Sports.content:
Jadier Herrera is set to challenge WBC lightweight champion William Zepeda after the WBC passed him over when the full title was vacant. The fight will settle who holds the WBC’s only belt at 135 pounds.

Golden Boy is expected to announce the bout soon, according to Darshan Desai. From a pure business perspective, taking on Jadier Herrera is a terrible risk-reward calculation for Zepeda. Herrera brings almost zero casual name recognition, practically no box office draw, and zero commercial upside. What he does bring is slick Cuban pedigree, southpaw counter-punching skills, and enough technical ability to make Zepeda look ordinary.

If Zepeda dominates him, casual fans will shrug and dismiss Herrera as an obscure mandatory. If Zepeda struggles or gets outboxed, his entire commercial standing evaporates overnight. Meanwhile, the alternative landscape offers massive paydays and legitimate star-making opportunities. A unification clash against WBO champion Abdullah Mason is by far the biggest pure boxing event at 135 pounds right now.

Mason carries immense promotional backing and serious buzz. Unifying the belts against him would instantly establish the winner as the true king of the lightweight division. An in-house Golden Boy matchup with Floyd Schofield delivers pure domestic pay-per-view numbers and massive promotional traction. Schofield talks, sells tickets, and brings a built-in fanbase that turns any clash into an event.

A blockbuster showdown against Gervonta Davis remains the ultimate lottery ticket in the weight class, offering career-defining money and mainstream reach. Compared to those blockbusters, defending the WBC belt against Herrera is pure sanctioning body tax. It does nothing for Zepeda’s bank account, nothing for his profile, and risks everything he built by winning the title from Roach.

The only reason Zepeda is entertaining it is that the WBC forced his hand with a mandatory order to clean up its interim title mess. Outside of keeping the green belt, the matchup is all downside.

Herrera has held the interim title since January, when he stopped Ricardo Núñez. That same month, Shakur Stevenson moved up to light welterweight and beat Teofimo Lopez. The WBC subsequently stripped Stevenson of its lightweight title, citing unpaid sanctioning fees.

The WBC could have elevated Herrera or put him in a fight for the vacant championship. Instead, it approved a deal the promoters had already put together for Zepeda to fight Lamont Roach Jr. The winner was expected to face Herrera, and Zepeda took the belt by unanimous decision on August 1.

Zepeda had a case for the opportunity. He had held the interim belt himself before losing to Stevenson, and both he and Roach were highly ranked. Their promoters also had a fight ready to go. The WBC could fill the vacancy by sanctioning a bout that had already been agreed, leaving Herrera to wait for the winner.

The wait cost Herrera a chance to be one of the two fighters chosen for the vacant title. When the belt opened up, the WBC could have made Zepeda or Roach fight Herrera to win it. Its decision gave Zepeda a chance to become champion before he had to face Herrera. The interim belt secured Herrera the next fight. A deal between two promoters secured the first one.

Sports.title: Ramon Cardenas Tests Junto Nakatani After Inoue Loss
Sports.content:
Ramon Cardenas provides an immediate measuring stick for Junto Nakatani following his first career defeat. The veteran counterpuncher possesses the exact timing required to test Nakatani’s willingness to commit after taking a solid hit.

Promoter Sampson Lewkowicz confirmed at the WBC convention that Cardenas reached a deal with Nakatani’s promoter, Akihiko Honda, via reporting from Darshan Desai of EverythingBoxing.

Cardenas proved his danger by dropping Naoya Inoue with a sharp counter left hook in the second round of their May 2025 meeting before Inoue halted him in the eighth. Facing a southpaw like Nakatani presents a distinct target profile.

The orthodox overhand right carries lethal potential, particularly because Nakatani tends to finish straight lefts in an upright stance and retreat along a direct line. That straight exit negates his reach advantage, leaving a clear path for Cardenas to press forward while Nakatani carries his guard low.

The technical tell will surface in subsequent exchanges. Nakatani must establish his right jab to unlock sustained punch combinations. That constant offensive pressure forces Cardenas into a shell, taking away his counter opportunities.

Firing isolated straight lefts gives Cardenas a predictable timing read on Nakatani’s backward retreat. Protracted lulls between combinations only grant Cardenas extra seconds to plant his feet and set traps.

Discipline inside the pocket will prove decisive. Absorbing a heavy punch requires Nakatani to tie up immediately. Pivoting out to open canvas gives him room to re-establish distance without trading out of pride. Firing back instantly without set feet hands Cardenas a clean opening to string punches together.

A wide points victory will not reveal the entire picture. The critical details lie in Nakatani’s punch selection the minute after Cardenas lands flush, alongside his defensive movement once combinations conclude. Those exact sequences will expose whether lingering hesitation from the Inoue loss remains.

Ghana News.title: Agbodza gives contractor one week to resume Bolgatanga-Bawku bridge works or risk termination
Ghana News.content:
Minister of Roads and Highways, Kwame Governs Agbodza, has given Rango Construction one week to mobilise and resume work on a bridge along the Bolgatanga-Bawku-Pulmakom Road, warning that the government will terminate the contract if the contractor abandons the site again.

Mr Agbodza issued the ultimatum during a monitoring tour of the road project, following growing public frustration over delays and the deteriorating condition of the road.

Residents along the stretch have recently staged protests over the lack of progress, citing severe dust pollution, numerous potholes and difficulties faced by commuters.

They have also accused the contractor of returning to work only when there are indications that government officials, particularly the Roads Minister, are expected to visit the project site.

The Minister expressed disappointment with the contractor's performance, insisting that there was no justification for abandoning the project, especially after President John Dramani Mahama had made it a priority.

Addressing the contractor during the inspection, Mr Agbodza said the government would no longer tolerate a situation where work resumed only when officials visited the site.

“Rango, I would say we are not happy. Because when we came here with the President, you were seen on site doing some work. You have absolutely no reason to pull back at any time,” he said.

He added that the contractor should not need constant pressure from the Ministry to fulfil its obligations.

“It shouldn't take the Minister to tell you to stay on site and work because, behind the scenes, we've worked out the strategy to complete this work,” he said.

Contractor given one-week ultimatum

Mr Agbodza said he was particularly disappointed that construction had slowed despite an earlier unannounced visit during which residents had indicated that the contractor was making progress.

He expressed confidence in Rango Construction's ability to complete the project but insisted that the company must demonstrate its commitment through consistent work.

“I have no doubt that you have the capability of completing this project,” he said.

The Minister disclosed that the contractor had undertaken to complete a temporary section of the road within one and a half weeks to allow traffic to be diverted.

However, he questioned why work had not commenced on the bridge itself, arguing that construction of the bridge and the temporary section could proceed simultaneously.

He consequently directed the contractor to mobilise within one week, adding that the government expected to see active construction within two weeks.

He warned that any further abandonment of the project would result in the engagement of another contractor.

“When I leave here, and you and your team leave the site, don't come back. Because you'll come back to see another contractor here,” he warned.

Mr Agbodza said the project had received high-level government attention and was being funded under the Big Push infrastructure programme.

He dismissed suggestions that financial constraints or engineering design challenges were responsible for the delays.

“It's not because of money; it's not because of lack of engineering design that this project is delayed,” he said.

He also expressed support for residents who had been demanding the completion of the road, noting that the project had been outstanding since 2015.

“And I agree 100% with the communities pushing that this be done. Because it's far too long since 2015,” he added.

Minister appeals to motorists

Mr Agbodza also appealed to motorists to exercise caution while using the road, stressing that road safety was a shared responsibility between the government and road users.

He warned against excessive speeding, particularly when driving through communities and residential areas.

“I always ask people if I don't know any driver who drives through his own hometown at 120km because you might kill your cousin. But when we are in somebody else's town, we think that it's normal,” he said.

He cautioned that even careful motorists could become victims of crashes caused by other drivers who disregard speed limits.

“You might be a victim not necessarily because you are overspeeding, but somebody overspeeding might crash into you,” he warned.
