Ghana News.title: ‘It’s very worrying’ – Selassie Ibrahim raises concerns about AI in filmmaking
Ghana News.content:
Ghanaian filmmaker Selassie Ibrahim has expressed concern about artificial intelligence (AI) in filmmaking, warning that it could push many industry professionals out of business.

Speaking to Kwame Dadzie on Joy FM’s Showbiz A-Z, she acknowledged the benefits of technology but said the growing use of AI could have adverse effects on the film industry, particularly for people who lack the technical skills to use it.

“For me it’s very alarming. It’s very worrying because it might throw a lot of people out of business. It’s not everybody who is technologically inclined to use AI. So if you don’t have what it takes to use AI it means you are gonna be out of business, which is very worrying. It breaks my heart but that is what technology has brought to us. So we just have to up our game. But we still have people who ant to watch the content we create so like I said we have to up our game,” she told Kwame Dadzie.

Selassie, who is the founder of the Regal Film Festival and Awards (REFFA), also ruled out the possibility of accepting AI-generated films for the festival for now.

Asked whether such productions had a place at REFFA, she said existing AI platforms were not yet capable of producing content that adequately represented African stories.

“No. Not yet. We will get there. I don’t think AI platforms have enough to fill the space of African content yet. When you watch their lip, it doesn’t coordinate with the dialogue. And then the movement, you see someone, the same person standing here, the same person moving, by the time you release he’s gone to the left. No. Not yet,” she said.

She added that improvements could come with time as education and knowledge about the technology increased, allowing developers to identify and correct some of its shortcomings.

Her comments come amid growing conversations in Ghana about the use of artificial intelligence in music, filmmaking and other creative fields. Musicians, filmmakers and other industry stakeholders have been weighing the technology’s potential to support creativity and production against concerns about job losses, copyright, ownership of creative works and the possible displacement of human talent.

The debate also extends beyond Ghana. AI-generated and AI-assisted films have attracted attention in international cinema, including discussions about the eligibility of productions using the technology for consideration at the Academy Awards, popularly known as the Oscars. In the international music industry, AI-generated songs, cloned voices and questions surrounding artists’ rights have also sparked debate, with industry stakeholders calling for clearer safeguards as the technology develops.

Ghana News.title: UG’s Communication Studies Department to host maiden Chambas Memorial Lecture
Ghana News.content:
Front Entrance of University of Ghana

The Department of Communication Studies at the University of Ghana (UG) is set to host the maiden edition of the Dr Mohamed Ibn Chambas Memorial Lecture on Thursday, December 10, as part of efforts to promote discussions on the role of the media in diplomacy, regional integration and peacebuilding.

The lecture, scheduled for 3:00 p.m. at the University's Great Hall, Legon, will honour the distinguished career and contributions of Dr Mohamed Ibn Chambas, a renowned Ghanaian diplomat and statesman who has served in several key regional and international positions.

The event will bring together members of the diplomatic corps, government officials, security and peacebuilding professionals, academics, media practitioners, students and civil society organisations to reflect on Ghana's contribution to regional stability, African diplomacy and the promotion of peaceful coexistence.

A major focus of the lecture will be the media's role in diplomacy and peacebuilding, particularly its influence on public understanding, conflict prevention and efforts to strengthen relations between countries.

The choice of theme highlights the importance of responsible communication in addressing conflicts, promoting dialogue and building trust among communities and nations. It also provides an opportunity for media professionals and other stakeholders to examine how journalism and strategic communication can support diplomatic efforts and contribute to lasting peace.

Dr Chambas, whose career spans diplomacy, regional governance and international peacebuilding, is widely recognised for his contributions to African integration and conflict resolution.

Among his notable positions, he served as President of the ECOWAS Commission and as a United Nations Special Representative. His experience in regional and international affairs makes his career a fitting subject for a memorial lecture that seeks to encourage reflection on the future of African diplomacy and peacebuilding.

The maiden lecture is expected to provide a platform for meaningful engagement among practitioners, policymakers, academics and students on the challenges and opportunities facing Ghana and the wider African continent in an increasingly complex global environment.

It will also offer participants an opportunity to examine how the media can contribute to democratic governance, peaceful conflict resolution and stronger regional cooperation.

The Department of Communication Studies is inviting members of the public and interested stakeholders to participate in the event.

Attendance is free, although registration is compulsory due to limited seating capacity.

Interested participants can register online through the following link: https://forms.gle/ntUcjmyh71TBp7x26.

Ghana News.title: Motorists must adapt driving to road conditions to prevent crashes – Former DVLA Boss urges motorists
Ghana News.content:
Former Chief Executive of the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Authority (DVLA), Justice Yaw Amegashie

Former Chief Executive of the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Authority (DVLA), Justice Yaw Amegashie, has urged motorists to adjust their driving to prevailing road conditions to reduce crashes and fatalities.

He said road users must prioritise their lives and exercise caution regardless of the state of roads across the country.

According to him, "You have to drive according to the road conditions. If you say that the roads are not car-worthy, it helps you, it provides the opportunity for you to move from one direction to the other. And for that reason, your attitude will determine how safely you can arrive at the next destination," he said while discussing the TraffiTech-GH initiative and the state of roads in the country with veteran television personality Kafui Dey on his recent YouTube vlog,

He argued that even when roads are in a deplorable state and unsuitable for vehicles, drivers have a responsibility to protect themselves and other road users by driving cautiously. "So if you say the roads are not car-worthy and therefore you will drive anyhow, you are risking your life; life is only one."

The retired road safety expert and lawyer stressed that placing greater value on human life should guide motorists' decisions on the road, particularly when navigating dangerous stretches.

"So if you put more value on the road condition and the driving that you are undertaking instead of your life, you will not survive," he said.

Ghana News.title: Mahama breaks ground for $98.41m project to expand Takoradi Port’s cargo handling capacity
Ghana News.content:
President John Mahama has broken ground for the construction of the 300-metre-long Berth 19 facility at the Takoradi Port, a project expected to expand the port's capacity to handle larger vessels and increased volumes of cargo.

The $98.41 million project is expected to improve the handling of bulk cargo, particularly mineral ores for export and clinker imported for cement production.

Speaking at the groundbreaking ceremony, President Mahama said the expansion has become necessary because of increasing demand and capacity constraints at the port's dry bulk terminal.

He explained that the facility would allow the port to handle more mineral exports and imported bulk products.

"BERTH-19 is very important," he said, adding that the project would increase the port's capacity for bulk cargo handling.

President Mahama said significant investments had been made in expanding the Takoradi Port since 2012, including dredging works to allow larger vessels to dock.

He noted that the port, which was originally established during the colonial era mainly to facilitate the export of commodities such as timber, cocoa, bauxite and manganese, has evolved into both an import and export hub.

The President also disclosed that the construction of the Berth 19 facility is expected to take 26 months, expressing hope that the government would return to commission the project within that period.

The groundbreaking ceremony also marked the commencement of work on a floating dry dock project, which President Mahama said was the first project under Ghana's Growth Partnership with the United Kingdom.

He described the commencement of the two projects as an important step towards strengthening Ghana's logistics and transport infrastructure.

"In today's world, the logistics value chain is very important, so expanding your ports, building your railways, and reconstructing your roads are all things that are necessary to give the economy that oomph so that it can take off," he said.

Ghana News.title: ‘We don’t place value on human lives’ – Former DVLA boss on road deaths
Ghana News.content:
Former Chief Executive of the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Authority (DVLA), Justice Yaw Amegashie

Former Chief Executive of the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Authority (DVLA), Justice Yaw Amegashie, says road crashes and fatalities in the country can only be significantly reduced when people begin to place greater value on their lives.

He believes many road crashes are preventable but occur because road users fail to prioritise their safety over the vehicles, motorbikes and roads they use.

"For us to reduce road deaths through road crashes, we should place value on human lives. Because I have a strong belief that we don't place value on human lives," he said, speaking in an interview with veteran television personality Kafui Dey on his recent YouTube vlog.

The retired road safety expert and lawyer expressed concern about dangerous behaviours among road users.

He cited the practice of motorbike riders carrying more than two passengers, pedestrians using mobile phones while walking or crossing roads, and drivers failing to exercise caution as some of the behaviours contributing to road crashes.

"A non-negotiable requirement is that every vehicle must have a pair of warning triangles. But on our roads, one thing that annoys me is when I see vehicles break down and some of them put a gallon behind them. A motorcycle is meant for the rider only and a pillion rider, but we see three people, at times, our wives, sisters and aunties carrying their children, one in front of the rider, another behind the pillion rider."

"So it appears we don't place value on human lives.... people don't look at it that way, every little mistake you make can lead to death. When you go out now, you will see pedestrians when crossing the road; they are on their phones, so they put value on the phone. We also take unnecessary risks, people are dying as a result of playing with their motorcycles, and people know that people are killed in such acts, but they continue to do it," he said.

Justice Amegashie said that addressing these safety lapses requires a change in attitude and greater personal responsibility among road users.

He argued that when Ghanaians recognise these dangers and take deliberate steps to avoid them, road crashes and fatalities in the country will reduce significantly, if not end altogether.

Ghana News.title: Kow Essuman threatens to sue government over unpaid salary arrears and terminal benefits
Ghana News.content:
Former legal counsel to President Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo, Kow Essuman, has threatened legal action against the government over unpaid salary arrears and terminal benefits, saying efforts to resolve the matter through correspondence have yielded no response.

The dispute follows a letter from his lawyers, Vint & Aletheia, to the Finance Minister, Dr Cassiel Ato Forson, demanding payment of Mr Essuman’s outstanding salary arrears and terminal benefits by Friday, September 11, 2026.

The lawyers warned that failure to settle the claims by the deadline could result in legal action.

According to the letter, the entitlements being claimed include four months’ consolidated salary for every completed year of service, an installation grant equivalent to one month’s salary, and a resettlement grant equivalent to one month’s salary for each year or fraction of a year served.

The lawyers described the continued withholding of the payments as “arbitrary, discriminatory, unfair and unlawful”, arguing that other public officeholders had received their entitlements.

In an interview with JoyNews’ Gemma Appiah, Mr Essuman said he was prepared to take the matter to court if the outstanding payments were not settled, although he hoped an agreement could be reached before then.

“I’m ready because this is contractual. I hope that we can resolve it before then. Honestly, but the attitude of the Finance Minister and the Attorney-General of not responding, not paying any heed to a former government official who’s written regarding salary arrears and terminal benefits is something that we really as a country need to look at,” he said.

Mr Essuman described the situation as unfortunate, arguing that he should not have to pursue the government repeatedly to receive benefits he believes are contractually due to him.

“It’s quite unfortunate. It shouldn’t get to this. It shouldn’t get to it. And I was not just a government official – I was legal counsel to the President and subsequently acting Secretary to the President. You know, that’s not how this country should act. It shouldn’t be me that should be writing to a Finance Minister to demand this. It’s completely on principle and unfair,” he said.

Mr Essuman says he remains willing to resolve the matter without litigation but is prepared to pursue legal action if the government does not address his claims.

Ghana News.title: Ghana’s economy expands by 6.8% in August 2026, driven by the services sector
Ghana News.content:
Ghana’s economy recorded a 6.8 per cent growth in August 2026, up from 5.3 per cent in the same period last year, driven largely by strong performance in the services sector.

Data from the Ghana Statistical Service’s (GSS) August 2026 Monthly Indicator of Economic Growth (MIEG) shows that the services sector remained the biggest contributor to economic expansion, accounting for 69.9 per cent of total growth.

The sector expanded by 10.7 per cent during the period, compared with 7.1 per cent in August 2025, with information and communication activities leading the growth.

Industry also recorded an improvement, growing by 4.5 per cent, up from 0.8 per cent a year earlier. The performance was largely supported by manufacturing, alongside mining and quarrying activities.

However, growth in agriculture slowed significantly to 2.6 per cent in August, compared with 8.6 per cent in the same period last year and 3.7 per cent in July 2026.

The latest figures indicate that services contributed 4.8 percentage points to the overall 6.8 per cent growth, while industry accounted for 1.4 percentage points. Agriculture contributed 0.5 percentage points, with net taxes accounting for the remaining 0.1 percentage point.

The Government Statistician, Alhassan Iddrisu, said the monthly indicator provides an early assessment of economic performance ahead of the publication of quarterly Gross Domestic Product (GDP) figures.

The MIEG data further shows that economic activity grew by 7 per cent in July 2026, although the figure was revised downward from an earlier estimate of 7.4 per cent following the availability of additional data.

The August performance brings the average growth recorded in July and August to 6.9 per cent, providing an early indication of economic activity in the third quarter of 2026.

The Ghana Statistical Service says the monthly indicator has consistently tracked quarterly GDP performance, with both measures recording 6 per cent growth in the second quarter of 2026.

The August figures are provisional and subject to revision as additional data become available.

The next MIEG release, covering September 2026, is expected in the second week of December.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.title: Russian authorities detain suspect over St. Petersburg cafe blast
World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: Rights group raises concerns about jailed Dr Abu Safia amid strikes on Gaza
World.content:
An Israeli rights group has accused Israeli authorities of ignoring the deteriorating health of Dr Hussam Abu Safia, the jailed director of Gaza’s Kamal Adwan Hospital, as the Israeli army continues to launch attacks on the Strip.

It comes as two Israeli courts rejected petitions on Wednesday seeking to release 14 doctors from Gaza imprisoned without charge, and to allow Abu Safia to receive an independent medical examination.

The Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI) said it obtained an independent medical review of Abu Safia’s records showing a weight loss of 14kg (31lb) in four months, a significant drop in haemoglobin levels and chest pain that was not properly investigated.

The reviewer, Amit Tirosh, was not permitted to examine Abu Safia in person. He disputed an Israeli court’s finding that high blood pressure was his only medical problem, writing that the ruling “does not line up with the data”.

PHRI says the Israel Prison Service has refused to release Abu Safia’s latest medical file.

“Not only has he been deprived of his freedom without trial, but he is also being denied his basic right to an independent medical examination,” PHRI’s Naji Abbas said.

The Israeli army captured the doctor in December 2024 during a raid on Kamal Adwan Hospital in northern Gaza.

PHRI said on Wednesday the Supreme Court dismissed a petition seeking the release of 14 doctors, including hospital directors and specialists in essential medical fields, who are being held in Israeli prisons without being charged or brought to trial.



PHRI argued that the prolonged arbitrary detentions – in some cases for more than two years – constitute a violation of their individual rights and further undermine Gaza’s healthcare system, which faces a severe shortage of medical professionals.

The Supreme Court dismissed the petition, finding no grounds to intervene in the Chief of Staff’s decision not to release the doctors. It maintained that their cases had been reviewed in light of changing circumstances and the shortage of doctors in Gaza, but that no exceptional grounds had been found to justify their release.

Gaza’s health sector has been largely destroyed during Israel’s genocidal war in the enclave since October 2023. Almost 90 percent of its overall infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed.

Meanwhile, sources at al-Shifa Hospital told Al Jazeera that an Israeli drone attack in the western part of Gaza City killed a Palestinian and injured others. Another Palestinian died from injuries caused by an Israeli attack on a family home in Gaza City on Tuesday.

Gaza continues to face regular Israeli attacks despite last year’s “ceasefire”. More than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed by Israel in the besieged enclave since the United States-brokered agreement, according to the territory’s ‌Ministry of Health.

World.title: Passenger train derails in India, leaving several injured
World.content:
NewsFeed Passenger train derails in India, leaving several injured

Video from inside the driver’s cabin captured the moment a train derailed in India’s Assam state after a reported braking problem. Authorities said several minor injuries were sustained, but that all of the passengers were safe.

World.title: Man City whistleblower Rui Pinto could help UK uncover more sporting crime
World.content:
Rui Pinto is ‘in talks’ with UK authorities to help uncover more crime in exchange for police protection, reports say.

Football whistleblower Rui Pinto, whose leaks triggered an investigation into Manchester City’s financial misconduct, has held discussions with authorities in the United Kingdom over a new role in helping uncover financial and sporting crime in the country, reports in British media say.

Pinto’s lawyers have been contacted by the Serious Fraud Office (SFO) after he stated he would be willing to assist UK authorities with investigations in exchange for police protection, British newspaper The Guardian reported on Wednesday.

Al Jazeera sought confirmation of Pinto’s reported contact with the authorities, but the SFO did not confirm whether the whistleblower was in talks.

“In line with long-established practice to avoid prejudice to law enforcement activity, we can neither confirm nor deny any investigation into this matter,” the SFO said in an emailed statement to Al Jazeera.

Pinto appeared to confirm the reports of his discussions with the Serious Fraud Office (SFO) by reposting an article on his social media account.

The 38-year-old is the founder of the website Football Leaks, which obtained private documents that showed City broke league rules from 2009 to 2018, leading to a probe by the Premier League’s independent commission.

City were found guilty of all but one of 115 charges brought against them over breaches of Premier League financial rules.

Pinto’s lawyer, William Bourdon, who has represented other high-profile whistleblowers including Julian Assange and Edward Snowden, was quoted by the Guardian as saying: “I can confirm that the process is under way.”

Pinto said last month that he feared for his life after being told his witness protection programme would end on October 10 and launched a crowdfunding initiative to help him establish an anonymous new life.



“The Commission responsible for Portugal’s witness protection programme informed me of its decision to terminate my participation in the programme and withdraw my police protection, thereby knowingly placing me in a life-threatening situation,” he wrote in a social media post.

“Given these circumstances, I have no alternative but to relocate, within the next few days, to an undisclosed location for an indefinite period of time, due to the multiple death threats I have received and the serious risk of an assassination attempt against me.

“For this reason, I have just set up a GoFundMe campaign and I am asking for everyone’s support to help me survive this serious situation created by the Portuguese State, which, as I have already stated, has knowingly decided to place my life at risk.”

However, the Portuguese Ministry of Justice said it would extend his protection pending a new hearing, after Pinto’s lawyers challenged the decision.

Reports last month said Pinto had reached out to UK authorities to offer cooperation in ongoing investigations in exchange for security measures being placed around him.

Pinto said at the start of his trial in April 2020 that he was “proud” to be a whistleblower on European football clubs’ big-money dealings.

The former history student and self-taught computer expert faced 90 charges – from unauthorised access to data and violation of correspondence to attempted extortion – in the case heard at Lisbon’s Central Criminal Court.

“I don’t consider myself a hacker. I am a whistleblower,” he said at the time. “The revelations are serious and I’m proud; there’s no shame. I haven’t done anything for money,” added Pinto, who acknowledges releasing 70 million documents on football’s backroom workings.

He was given a four-year suspended sentence in September 2023 for illegally obtaining documents, committing other cybercrimes and attempted extortion. He was later acquitted on 241 separate counts in a second trial in April 2026 after the court ruled the charges were ­­“invalid”.

Pinto has been a protected witness since August 2020 after agreeing to grant Portuguese authorities access to millions of files gathered before his arrest. His first trial in Portugal began a month later.

World.title: Israel kills Gaza goalkeeper days after playing in cup for slain athletes
World.content:
Israel kills Gaza goalkeeper days after playing in cup for slain athletes

NewsFeed Israel kills Gaza goalkeeper days after playing in cup for slain athletes

Mahmoud Abdel-Malek, a 20-year-old goalkeeper for Gaza Sports Club, was killed in an Israeli airstrike on Gaza city days after playing in a tournament honouring 1,017 Palestinian athletes killed since October 2023.

World.title: Did Democrats save Pete Hegseth from impeachment?
World.content:
Eleven Democrats are absent from a procedural vote that narrowly shelves a House impeachment vote against US defence secretary.

The United States House ⁠of Representatives has blocked an attempt to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in a surprise reprieve for President Donald Trump’s administration as Republicans reel from their midterm election defeat.

The impeachment articles were introduced by Republican Congressman Thomas Massie, but the effort was backed primarily by Democrats. They accuse Hegseth of abuses of power and conducting illegal military operations.

The Republican-led House voted 211-204 on Tuesday to refer the articles back to the House Judiciary Committee, where they could remain indefinitely. The procedural move in effect killed the impeachment drive for the duration of the current Congress’s term, which ends in eight weeks. On January 3, Democrats will take control of the House and Senate.

In a twist, the absence of 11 Democratic lawmakers during the vote proved decisive.

Here’s what to know about the vote to block Hegseth’s impeachment and what could happen next:

What was Tuesday’s vote about?

The vote was not on whether to impeach Hegseth. It was on whether to refer the articles of impeachment to the Judiciary Committee, where they may be further investigated or amended.

Such procedural moves are often used as stalling tactics. With the current Congress due to conclude soon, the resolution is unlikely to return to the House floor before its term ends.

Massie called the vote “a procedural motion to kill the resolution”.

What was the result of the vote?

It narrowly passed 211-204.



Massie was the sole Republican to oppose the measure. The remaining votes fell along party lines with Republicans supporting the measure and Democrats opposing it.

Eighteen representatives were absent from the vote – 11 Democrats and seven Republicans. Had the Democrats shown up and voted with their colleagues, they would have had the numbers to defeat the procedural move, forcing a full House vote on whether to impeach Hegseth as early as this week.

Trump cheered the result of Tuesday’s vote in a social media post, saying the Democrats’ impeachment effort had “miserably FAILED!”

Who were the 11 absent Democrats, and why did they miss the vote?

The Democrats absent from the vote were:

Julia Brownley (California)

Lou Correa (California)

Nancy Pelosi (California)

Laura Gillen (New York)

Steven Horsford (Nevada)

Jonathan Jackson (Illinois)

Brittany Pettersen (Colorado)

Melanie Stansbury (New Mexico)

Haley Stevens (Michigan)

Marilyn Strickland (Washington)

Frederica Wilson (Florida)

The representatives have given varying explanations for why they did not show up.

Strickland, Jackson, Stansbury and Gillen all blamed a traffic delay in Washington, DC.

Pelosi said she was in her home state for a veterans event while Correa said he was in California before undergoing a health procedure. Horsford’s office cited a personal emergency.

Pettersen, who said she helped introduce articles of impeachment against Hegseth in April, said she had been “denied the ability to vote on this motion” without elaborating.

Jackson, Stansbury, Gillen, Strickland, Horsford, Pelosi and Pettersen all said they would have joined their Democratic colleagues in opposing the measure. Jackson and Stansbury also said they had formally recorded their opposition in the Congressional Record although this does not change the official vote count.

There was no immediate comment from Stevens, Brownley or Wilson on their absences.

Stevens previously criticised the Trump administration for launching the war on Iran with Israel and sought more congressional oversight. But days before the US midterm elections on November 3, the Michigan congresswoman, who had lost the Democratic primary for the state’s open Senate seat earlier to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed Republican candidate Mike Rogers against her own party’s nominee.

Wilson, 83, on Monday attended the groundbreaking for a housing project in Miami-Dade County. Wilson and Brownley, like Stevens, previously opposed Trump’s handling of the war on Iran and demanded the administration seek congressional approval for the fighting.

What has been the reaction?

Democratic politicians and progressive commentators have expressed outrage that poor attendance from Democrats impacted the outcome of the vote.



Congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove from California said: “We knew that this vote was coming, so people should have gotten their raggedy selves up these steps to vote.”

“There is no reason why we should have lost this vote because of attendance issues,” she added.

Senator-elect El-Sayed, responding to a question about the absent Democrats, said: “You should show up and do your job.”

Some pundits pointed the finger at Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become the new speaker of the House in January. They accused him of failing to exert sufficient pressure on party members to defeat the measure.

Political commentator Krystal Ball called the vote “a major Hakeem Jeffries fail”.

“You could have impeached the war criminal Pete Hegseth but Dems didn’t show up to vote,” she said.

Progressive writer Laura Bassett said: “Jeffries didn’t even whip the vote. He told people to ‘vote their conscience’, and 11 members of his caucus didn’t show up. This is why people want a stronger leader.”

Could Hegseth still be impeached?

Yes. When the new Democratic-controlled Congress convenes in January, they could begin the process again and will be in a stronger position to advance impeachment articles.

Jeffries has said he will consult members about another potential bid to impeach Hegseth next year. “We’ll have that conversation at the appropriate time,” he said.

However, a vote to impeach Hegseth does not necessarily mean he will be removed from office. Impeachment itself means the House has formally brought charges against a federal official, similar to a criminal indictment.

A successful impeachment vote triggers a trial in Congress’s upper chamber, the Senate, on whether to convict.

A conviction, which immediately removes the official from office, requires at least two-thirds support in the Senate. That means Democrats, even with their incoming majority in the chamber next year, would likely need about a dozen Republicans to join them to secure Hegseth’s removal.

Only eight officials – all federal judges – have ever been convicted by the Senate. Trump has been impeached twice – in December ⁠2019 and January 2021 – but the Senate acquitted him on both occasions.

World.title: AI boom or bubble?
World.content:
A tech sell-off has raised questions about AI spending and the risks to jobs and growth across the global economy.

Great inventions have often brought a rush of investment. Sometimes, it ends in a crash.

Some experts fear artificial intelligence is heading the same way.

Hundreds of billions of dollars are pouring into AI, far ahead of the profits it can deliver.

Last week, investors blinked.

The Democratic Party swept the US midterm elections, and some of its candidates had called for tighter rules on data centres that power AI.

Fears of a slower buildout wiped trillions of dollars off stock markets. They have only partly recovered.

The stakes reach far beyond Wall Street. Pensions and growth are riding on the AI boom.

World.title: What’s the Falklands oil project at the heart of latest UK-Argentina spat?
World.content:
The UK says it will defend its interests at the Law of the Sea Tribunal hearing, as Argentina seeks measures to block the offshore project.

Share What’s the Falklands oil project at the heart of latest UK-Argentina spat? on social media

The United Kingdom has pledged to defend its interests in the Sea Lion project to develop an oilfield near the Falkland Islands, as Argentina has brought a legal challenge before a tribunal over the offshore oil exploration, citing environmental concerns.

Attorney General Ellie Reeves, representing the UK government at the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS), said billions of pounds crucial to the future of the Falkland Islands will be lost if Argentina is successful in getting the project blocked.

The Hamburg-based tribunal is sitting for two days as Argentina seeks a provisional ruling to suspend oil drilling.

Reeves also said Argentina’s objection to the development was rooted in its territorial claims. “The hearing is not about the sovereignty of the Falklands,” the UK prime minister’s official spokesman said on Monday, echoing his country’s position that the island’s sovereignty is not up for negotiation.

The dispute is the latest in rising tensions between the UK and Argentina over the British overseas territory in the South Atlantic Ocean.

Here’s what we know:

What is it about?

The Sea Lion development is a UK-Israeli venture to drill for oil in waters administered by the Falklands.

The UK’s Rockhopper Exploration and Israel’s Navitas Petroleum, operator of the Sea Lion oilfield, located about 220km (137 miles) from the islands, are expected to start the project in March 2027, with oil production to begin in 2028.

According to Rockhopper Exploration, the Sea Lion exploration field holds an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil in place, of which 500 million barrels are recoverable resources.



However, Argentina’s President Javier Milei announced measures to block the development in September and said in a post on X that he had instructed the Foreign Ministry and the country’s legal teams to initiate arbitration proceedings against the UK.

“If in 2 weeks the United Kingdom does not halt the illegitimate exploitation, we will go to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea. THE MALVINAS ARE ARGENTINA’s, and they are defended with facts, not words,” he wrote, using the Argentinian name for the Falkland Islands.

Argentina formally filed a complaint at the Tribunal seeking provisional measures against the UK on October 13.

The UK has administered the Falkland Islands since 1833. However, as the territory lies off Argentina’s shores, Buenos Aires claims sovereignty over what it calls Las Malvinas.

Milei has also threatened tougher sanctions on companies involved in the oil exploration project, preventing them from operating in Argentina’s oil and mining sectors.

Milei’s government argues the project violates a United Nations resolution calling on both sides to refrain from unilateral actions in the islands until their dispute over the territory’s sovereignty is resolved.

What was said at the Tribunal?

On Tuesday, Reeves told the Law of the Sea Tribunal, which issues legally binding rulings on maritime disputes, that Argentina wanted to “take control of those resources for itself”.

“The provisional measures sought by Argentina would prevent the people of the Falkland Islands from developing their natural resources as they are entitled to do so, pursuant to their fundamental right to self-determination,” she said, according to The Guardian.

“The measures sought would have devastating consequences for the Falklands people. They risk losing billions of pounds in money, which is essential for the islands’ economic development.”

But Argentina’s lawyer, Mario Oyarzabal, argued that action was needed to block the project.

“[Argentina] respects the interests of the inhabitants of the islands and their way of life as enshrined in the Argentine constitution…What these British citizens do not have is a right to decide to which state the islands belong,” he said during the hearing, The Guardian reported.

“These resources belong to the Argentine people. Some 46 million of them, including the 1,247 inhabitants born on the islands, whose interests will be duly taken into account,” he added.



In 2013, Falkland islanders voted overwhelmingly to remain with the United Kingdom, despite Argentina’s claims.

What has the UK government said?

On Monday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s official spokesperson told the Independent news outlet that the UK was “fully engaged in the UNCLOS [UN Convention on the Law of the Sea] process, and we’ll clearly set out our position on Argentina’s request for provisional measures before the Tribunal”.

“We’ll continue to robustly defend our interests and those of the Falkland Islanders,” the spokesperson added.

Last month, Burnham also discussed the bid to block the oil project during a call with United States President Donald Trump.

“The prime minister raised the economic consequences of Argentina’s coercive measures for the UK and US and reiterated the importance of respecting the islanders’ right to develop their natural resources,” Burnham’s office said.

What are the latest developments?

The fraught relationship between the UK and Argentina remains tense and heavily focused on the Falkland Islands.

Milei has capitalised on Trump’s refusal to say whether Washington would support the UK in a future conflict over the Falklands after the US president criticised London for not doing more to support the US during its attacks on Iran.

In September, Milei said the “winds of change” were blowing in Argentina’s favour when it comes to its claims of sovereignty.

“The United States is considering this change in position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with Western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come,” Milei said.

At the same time, Argentina is set for an election next year, where the Sea Lion project’s halt could help Milei’s polling position.

World.title: Workers across Spain stage first general strike in 14 years
World.content:
Share Workers across Spain stage first general strike in 14 years on social media

Millions of workers across Spain are striking to demand government action over the country’s housing crisis, less than three weeks before a national election that could bring the far right to power.

The 24-hour walkout, which began at midnight on Wednesday, disrupted public transport and forced businesses, factories and shops to scale back operations or close entirely across the eurozone’s fourth-largest economy. It’s Spain’s first general strike in 14 years.

Minor incidents were reported in the first hours, including roadblocks with burning tyres in Barcelona, the second-largest city in the country. There were also scuffles between picketers and police near the country’s main wholesale market on the outskirts of the capital, Madrid.

The two main unions that called the strike, UGT and CCOO, reported widespread participation in the early hours “with significant work stoppages in strategic sectors”, including 90 percent in the automotive and port sectors, according to a statement posted on social media.

The CEOE organisation, which represents business leaders, said in a statement that the impact varied by region and area of work, with a “low participation” in most sectors.

The UGT and CCOO unions called the strike following a wave of nationwide protests over access to housing, sparked by the eviction in September of Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old Madrid pensioner who died several days later.



The demonstrations included a five-week occupation of Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square, where hundreds of tents were pitched, sparking imitations in other cities.

The average rent in Spain has almost doubled over the past 10 years, eating into household budgets and angering voters.

Spain’s socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called a snap election for November 29 after his minority government failed to secure parliamentary approval for a package of housing measures proposed in response to the protests.

“This is not a strike against anyone, but rather one in favour of a common response from all levels of government to a real problem, which is access to housing,” he said in an interview published Sunday in the daily newspaper La Vanguardia.

‘Serious mistake’

The strike has been rejected by business groups, which have described it as an election-related protest, and criticised by the conservative opposition Popular Party (PP) and far-right Vox.

PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo warned that unions risked being linked to Sanchez “forever” if they went ahead with the strike in the run-up to the election.

Feijoo, whose party leads opinion polls, said going ahead with the strike was a “serious mistake” following a high-speed train collision last month in central Spain that killed 69 people.

Spain’s average gross monthly salary is about 2,460 euros, while renting a 50-square-metre apartment in Madrid cost an average of 1,170 euros a month in October, according to property portal Idealista.

That amounts to nearly half the average gross salary, and 98.7 percent of the average young person’s income, according to the Youth Council of Spain. It’s well above the 30 percent share commonly recommended by housing experts and public institutions.

World.title: Three Iran-backed suspects plotted attacks including RAF Fairford incident, US says
World.content:
The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has announced charges against three Iran-backed operatives that it alleges were involved in a string of plots in the US and Europe.

The DOJ said Iranian agents most recently "orchestrated a terrorist plot at an air force base in the United Kingdom", saying they were involved in the major incident in September near RAF Fairford in the UK, where US armed forces were stationed.

One man, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national, is accused of communicating with contacts in the UK from a prison in New York where he is awaiting trial on previous charges. The other two are accused of doing the same from Iran.

Iran has strongly denied any involvement in the RAF Fairford incident.

Seven men have been arrested in the UK over the incident, which came to light when suspicious vans were reported near the RAF base.

Iranian Mohsen Mohajeri, Iraqi national Mohammad Ali al-Hassani and dual Iranian-Iraqi citizen Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi were charged in an indictment unsealed on Tuesday, the DOJ said.

It accuses the trio of planning attacks in Europe that were carried out under the name of a purportedly new group with the pseudonym Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (The Islamic Movement of the People of the Right Hand - HAYI).

"Of the 18 terrorist attacks in the spring of 2026 for which HAYI claimed responsibility in Europe, seven took place in the UK," the DOJ statement said. It added that the attacks involved "arsons, explosives, and in one instance, a near-fatal stabbing in London of two Jewish men, including a dual US-British citizen".

Two Jewish men were stabbed in Golders Green, north London, in April. A suspect is due to stand trial next year.

"This eight-count indictment shows the determination of Iran to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the US," FBI Director Kash Patel said.

He added that one of the three "allegedly sent coded messages to assist in future acts of violence" from detention.

Patel said the accused were involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks in support of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Iran-backed Iraqi militia Kataib Hezbollah.

World.title: US House blocks bid to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, for now
World.content:
An effort to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war on Iran without congressional authorisation, has failed on Capitol Hill.

A majority of the House of Representatives voted to refer impeachment articles to a committee - essentially killing the effort introduced by dissident Republican congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky, for now.

In his first news briefing from the Pentagon in six months, Hegseth called the impeachment effort a "farce" and "sabotage".

The bid to find the cabinet secretary guilty of misconduct and ultimately remove him from office was seen as a long shot as it could have required a number of other Republicans to defy President Donald Trump.

However, that calculation could change in January when the Democratic Party assumes control of both chambers of Congress, following its successes in the US midterm elections. For now, Trump's Republican Party remains in control.

After Tuesday's vote, the most senior Democrat in the House, Hakeem Jeffries, said: "This is not the end of it. It's just the beginning."

The question on which lawmakers were voting on Tuesday was whether or not to refer the resolution to the House Judiciary Committee, which is led by Republicans. The alternative would have been to allow the resolution to proceed in the House itself.

All Republicans other than Massie voted to refer the resolution to the committee, meaning that the congressman's effort failed in a 211-204 vote.

The move to send the measure to the panel effectively kills the effort, as there is only a short period of time left in this Congress.

More than a dozen members missed the ballot. They included 11 Democrats, several of whom blamed traffic issues for their absences.

Several members of the party criticised their fellow lawmakers for missing the vote.

"You should show up and do your job," said Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed during an interview with CNN, making a direct address to those who did not vote. The Michigan lawmaker recently won a US Senate race in Michigan, having criticised US ties to Israel and the war in Iran on the campaign trail.

World.title: Meghan's father Thomas Markle back in federal custody after allegedly removing ankle monitor
World.content:
Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, is back in federal custody in Florida after allegedly removing his ankle monitor, according to court documents.

Markle appeared before a federal magistrate judge in the Florida city of Tampa on Tuesday and was denied bond. Prosecutors say he removed the monitor early that morning.

US Judge Lindsay S Griffin found on Tuesday that Markle had violated the conditions of his pretrial release, court documents show.

Markle, who has denied possessing images of child sex abuse, was arrested in Florida last week and placed under house detention. He was also ordered to wear a location monitoring device.

The BBC has contacted his representatives.

Griffin described Markle's housing situation as "untenable", writing in the order revoking his pretrial release that "based on the lack of suitable housing, no condition or combination of conditions would reasonably assure the safety of any other person or the community and the defendant's appearance in court".

He also ordered a medical evaluation for Markle and said he "must receive all necessary and prescribed medication unless discontinued by a physician".

"Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions," Bill Essayli, the US attorney for Central California, wrote on X on Tuesday.

"We will continue to prosecute this case to the fullest extent of the law," he added.

Markle, 82, was first arrested last week after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in Los Angeles registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year, the DoJ said.

Inside the units the FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.

Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.

In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades as Markle is currently 82 years old.

Markle appeared in court last week following his arrest. No plea was taken during the appearance, which set several conditions for his pretrial release, including that he be kept in home detention.

He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, according to the DoJ.

FBI director Kash Patel said last week that Markle "allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions".

Markle has called the allegations "sick lies".

He moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was reportedly learning to walk again in Florida after having his leg amputated.

The duchess has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.

In a previously shared statement, Meghan confirmed the existence of the letter and wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."

She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

World.title: Vinícius Jr sends message to Sudan boy who received prosthetic legs after BBC report sparks appeal
World.content:
The boy we remember as shy and withdrawn is almost unrecognisable. He is confident, cheeky and full of smiles. And he is standing tall on two new prosthetic legs.

For almost a year, Cairo has been his home. Here, he has undergone surgery and months of rehabilitation, and is now able to walk and kick a ball again.

When we met in 2025, he had told us his favourite footballer was VinÃ­cius JÃºnior. We were able to pass this on to the Real Madrid star, who said he wanted to send a personal video message of support. Reunited in Cairo, we gather round to watch it together.

"I was made aware of your story. I know how difficult the last few months must have been for you," the Brazilian footballer begins.

VinÃ­cius has become a leading voice challenging racism in football and supporting black people, and a smile spreads across Zaher's face as the player tells him: "You are a hard-working black man. I really hope you will make good use of your new prosthetic legs, that you return to playing football and that you find happiness. You deserve it."

Then comes an invitation: "I would like to invite you to attend a Madrid match. We can spend the day together."

Overwhelmed, Zaher gets up and leaves the room. A few moments later, he returns wearing his new VinÃ­cius Jr football shirt. He hopes that one day he will be able to get a visa and accept the offer.

"Tell VinÃ­cius, I love him," he says. "His message has really uplifted me." His mother Habibah says she feels "like the whole world is cheering Zaher on, wanting him to succeed".

World.title: Haitian PM praises El Salvador after joint strike on alleged home of gang leader
World.content:
Haiti's Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-AimÃ© has praised "the commitment of the Salvadorean forces in the fight against gangs" after a joint strike on a house allegedly used by the leader of the 400 Mawozo gang.

El Salvador's President, Nayib Bukele, had earlier announced that a joint task force had "destroyed" what he described as "the house of LanmÃ² San Jou and the 400 Mawozo gang's headquarters".

A small contingent of Salvadorean troops has been in Haiti since January 2025 as part of a multinational force deployed to suppress gang violence.

Last month, Bukele sent an extra 2,000 soldiers to rescue four Salvadoreans who have been missing since they were ambushed on 18 October.

Bukele's post on X, external was accompanied by video of several helicopters firing on a large complex.

As the helicopters circle above, dozens of people can be seen running out of the property, fleeing the strikes.

Writing in Creole, Bukele said "we kept our promise", adding that the alleged gang members "ran away without even trying to fight".

Local media reported that as many as 20 people were killed in the strike, which they said was carried out in the early hours of Sunday.

They also reported that LanmÃ² San Jou, whose real name is Wilson Joseph, was not at the property at the time of the attack.

Posting on X on Monday, Fils-AimÃ© thanked the Salvadorean military's commitment "in the fight against gangs" and said the two nations would keep working together, along with the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), to "regain control of the territory and restore state authority".

"THE GANGS WILL GET NO SLEEP!" he added.

While he did not provide any further details about the joint operation or the number of casualties, Fils-AimÃ© posted a still from the video shared by Bukele showing a helicopter firing a projectile at the compound.

The BBC has not been able to verify the video posted by Bukele, nor whether the property is indeed the headquarters of the 400 Mawozo, Haiti's largest criminal gang, which is infamous for carrying out kidnappings for ransom.

World.title: Kennedys sue to block Trump's arch, arguing it would cast shadow on JFK's grave
World.content:
The family of former US President John F Kennedy has sued to block construction of a triumphal arch that President Donald Trump plans to build in the nation's capital.

Nine members of the political dynasty argue the 250ft (76m) structure would block the view of Kennedy's grave, as well as the graves of thousands of veterans buried at Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia.

Last week, a US judge temporarily halted the project on the heels of a vote allowing construction to proceed.

The White House said it was "unfortunate" to see that some members of the Kennedy family had joined litigation against an arch "intended to honor our heroes who rest in Arlington Cemetery".

"The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation," White House spokesman Davis R Ingle said in a statement to the BBC.

"We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds," he added.

World.title: Judge allows Trump's $10bn defamation case against BBC to proceed
World.content:
A federal judge in Florida has allowed US President Donald Trump's defamation case against the BBC to go ahead after the broadcaster sought to dismiss it.

But Judge Jeffrey Kuntz dismissed a second claim in the $10bn (Â£7.5bn) lawsuit under the state's unfair trade practices law.

The US president is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol in 2021.

Trump called the judge's ruling a "huge victory" in a Truth Social post on Tuesday. A BBC spokesperson said: "We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court's authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage."

The BBC spokesperson added: "We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process."

Judge Kuntz found Trump's defamation allegations against the BBC sufficient for the case to continue, although he did not make a ruling on the merits of the case.

"Whether President Trump can prove these claims and establish he sustained damages at summary judgment or trial is left for another day," he wrote in Tuesday's order.

Trump's lawsuit - filed in Florida - accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021.

The BBC apologised and said that the broadcast had given "the mistaken impression that Trump made a direct call for violent action".

The broadcaster has since asked that the court dismiss the lawsuit, arguing the programme does not meet the legal criteria for defamation and was not available in the US.

Along with defamation, Trump claimed in the lawsuit that the broadcaster had violated Florida law, specifically the Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.

Kuntz on Tuesday dismissed that part of the lawsuit, ruling that the documentary did not constitute commercial speech.

World.title: US warns Madagascar over growing military ties with Russia
World.content:
The US has warned Madagascar against strengthening its ties with Russia, saying similar partnerships with military-led governments in West Africa have failed to improve security.

US Africa Command deputy head Lt Gen John Brennan said Madagascar's strategic location in the Indian Ocean made it important to global trade.

He warned against what he called the "Sahel model", which he said risked fuelling instability across the continent.

Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, all under military rule, have reduced ties with the Western partners and turned to Russia to support their fight against jihadist groups.

Russia has expanded its co-operation with Madagascar since the army seized power in 2025, supplying weapons and military instructors.

"We are concerned about Russia wanting to proliferate [the Sahel model] elsewhere across the continent," Brennan told reporters in an online briefing.

"Madagascar sits in a location that is extremely important, as is Mozambique, and we don't want to see those models be applied in those two locations," he said.

The three Sahel countries had blamed their former Western partners for failing to contain jihadist violence before turning to Moscow.

However, Islamist militant attacks have continued despite their closer military ties with Russia.

Brennan also raised concerns about security in the Mozambique Channel, which separates Mozambique and Madagascar from mainland Africa and is an important route for international shipping and trade.

He said it was vital to prevent militants linked to the Islamist State group in northern Mozambique and other hostile actors from threatening maritime activity.

Citing recent piracy-related incidents along the coast, Brennan said they were adapting their tactics, including developing greater maritime capabilities.

He said US partners were "free to partner with whom they wish" but urged them to understand the potential risks.

Madagascar has not publicly responded to Brennan's comments.

However, President MichaÃ«l Randrianirina has recently reiterated his support for stronger ties between Russia and African countries.

During the Russia-Africa summit last month, Madagascar and Russia signed several co-operation agreements covering defence, tourism and trade.

In February, a few months after seizing power, Randrianirina visited to Moscow. It was the first official visit to Russia by a Malagasy leader in nearly 50 years.

World.title: Winners emerge in Abia tertiary education sports fiesta
World.content:
Michael Okpara University of Agriculture, Umudike (MOUAU), has emerged overall champion of the 2026 Abia State Tertiary Education Sports Fiesta (ABTESF), winning 136 medals in the competition involving 18 tertiary institutions.

MOUAU secured 47 gold, 47 silver and 42 bronze medals to finish top of the medals table at the second edition of the competition, which featured 24 sporting events.

Ogbonnaya Onu Polytechnic, Aba, finished second with 98 medals (47 gold, 31 silver and 20 bronze), while Abia State University, Uturu, came third with 87 medals.

Gregory University, Uturu, occupied the fourth position with 68 medals (37 gold, 15 silver and 16 bronze).

The competition ended on Friday with a closing ceremony at the Umuahia Township Stadium.

Speaking at the event, Governor Alex Otti said sports were essential to the overall development of students, arguing that education should not be limited to the acquisition of academic qualifications.

Mr Otti, represented by the Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice, Ikechukwu Uwanna, said physical, mental and social development are important components of education.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Having 18 institutions compete in about 24 sporting competitions is a hit. And we know that this will contribute greatly to the all-round development of our students,” he said.

The governor added that investments in educational infrastructure would have limited impact if students’ mental development was neglected.

“If the brick and mortar are overhauled and the mind remains the same, we have achieved little. So we know that what is happening today will overhaul the minds of our children and make us ready for the outside world,” he said.

The governor’s remarks were contained in a statement posted on Facebook on Sunday by Ferdinand Ekeoma, his special adviser on media and publicity.

Sports and talent development

The Commissioner for Tertiary Education in Abia, Uche Eme Uche, said the competition was introduced to promote physical fitness as part of the state’s broader educational objectives.

She said the second edition recorded improved organisation, increased participation and stronger commitment from participating institutions.
