“Building on experiences and lessons from the inaugural edition, we have witnessed improved organisation, broader participation and stronger institutional commitment to making ABTESF a sustainable feature of our tertiary education calendar,” she said.

Ms Uche expressed appreciation to Mr Otti for approving and funding the competition.

Also speaking, the Chairperson of the Central Working Committee and Special Adviser to the Governor on Tertiary Education, Emeka Enyiazu, said the fiesta provided an opportunity for students from federal, state and privately owned institutions to compete on a common platform.

He described the competition as an avenue for identifying young sporting talents, promoting unity and developing discipline, teamwork and resilience among students.

According to him, the initiative would help prepare promising athletes for national and international competitions.

The 2026 edition brought together 18 tertiary institutions across Abia State, with organisers expressing optimism that the competition would become a permanent feature of the state’s tertiary education calendar.

World.title: Court rejects police request for arrest warrant against FIJ founder Soyombo
World.content:
The Federal High Court in Abuja on Tuesday rejected a police request for a bench warrant against ‘Fisayo Soyombo, founder of the Foundation for Investigative Journalism (FIJ), over a case in which he and another journalist are charged with cyberstalking and criminal defamation.

The prosecution asked the court to issue the warrant, telling Justice Joyce Abdulmalik that it had been unable to serve Mr Soyombo with court processes.

But the judge declined, saying Mr Soyombo, charged alongside an FIJ journalist Daniel Ojukwu, had yet to be produced before her to be able to exercise such powers over him.

PREMIUM TIMES reported Tuesday that Mr Ojukwu, who had been detained on honouring police invitation, was produced before the judge for arraignment.

The judge remanded Mr Ojukwu at the Kuje Correctional Centre in Abuja after the journalist pleaded not guilty to the charges in which he and Mr Soyombo were jointly named as co-accused.

The police accused the journalists of publishing reports that defamed Adejoke Orelope-Adefulire, a former senior special assistant on Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) to late President Muhammadu Buhari. The 12 counts include allegations of cyberstalking and criminal defamation.

At Tuesday’s proceedings, prosecutors Kunle Lawal, Tolulope Osho, Grace Baiyeshea and Marvellous Orji told the court that efforts to serve Mr Soyombo had been unsuccessful.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Opposing the application, Oluseye Moore, lawyer to the defendants, said both journalists had been granted administrative bail by the police during investigations.

He argued that the police were responsible for ensuring their appearance in court until they were formally charged and their bail conditions determined by the court.

Mr Moore also told the court that the prosecution had filed an ex parte application seeking permission to serve Mr Soyombo electronically.

The court rejected the request for a warrant against Mr Soyombo.

For Mr Ojukwu, his lawyer, Atanda Kayode, raised futile objection to the request for his remand.

Mr Kayode informed the court that a bail application had already been filed on behalf of the journalist.

But the judge, Ms Abdulmalik, declined to hear the application, saying it was not ripe for consideration because it had only been filed on Monday.

The defence also asked the court to allow Mr Ojukwu to continue on the administrative bail earlier granted by the police, arguing that he had not breached its conditions.

The judge rejected the request and ordered his remand until 1 December, when the bail application is expected to be heard.

Background

The charges relate to four FIJ reports published between November 2023 and January 2024 about the activities of the Office of the Senior Special Assistant to the President on SDGs.

One of the reports, published on 7 November 2023, questioned a payment of N147.1 million to a restaurant for the construction of classrooms at Ajeromi Primary School in Lagos.

Another, published on 3 December 2023, raised questions about a N47.5 million classroom construction contract awarded to Tru3 Nigeria Limited.

The other reports examined the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission’s forfeiture of N241 million linked to the SDGs office and the failure of solar panels installed at classroom blocks in Ogun State shortly after installation.

The police alleged that the journalists conspired to commit cyberstalking and criminal defamation and knowingly published false reports about Ms Orelope-Adefulire.

Mr Ojukwu was previously arrested over the reports in May 2024. He was reported missing on 1 May after his phones became unreachable. His family and employer later discovered that he was being held by the Inspector-General of Police’s Intelligence Response Team.

He was detained at the State Criminal Investigation Department in Panti, Lagos, before being transferred to the Nigeria Police Force National Cybercrime Centre in Abuja.

He was released on 10 May 2024 after 10 days in custody, following public protests and pressure over his detention.

Mr Soyombo is expected to appear before the court on 1 December.

World.title: NDC accuses Benue govt of plotting to disrupt Obi’s visit
World.content:
The Benue State governorship candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Terhemba Shija, has accused the state government of planning to disrupt the visit of the party’s presidential candidate, Peter Obi, to the state.

Mr Shija made the allegation on Tuesday at a press conference in Makurdi ahead of Mr Obi’s scheduled visit on Wednesday.

He said Mr Obi would visit Yelewata, a community in Guma Local Government Area, where hundreds of people were killed in an attack in June 2025, to pay tribute to the victims and console their families.

Mr Shija said the former Anambra governor would lay a wreath at a cenotaph erected in memory of the victims along Lafia Road. He added that Mr Obi would not visit any government facility or internally displaced persons’ camp during the trip.

According to him, the presidential candidate would also hold a town hall meeting with residents at the multi-purpose hall of the Mission House, behind the Benue Links head office in Wurukum, Makurdi.

Mr Shija alleged that the state government had threatened to stop Mr Obi from visiting Yelewata, recalling an earlier incident in which the presidential candidate’s visit to the community was disrupted.

“This very government sent thugs of the infamous No Alia, No Benue to waylay, throw stones and stop President Peter Obi’s planned visit to Yelewata town two months ago,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He called on security agencies to protect Mr Obi and his supporters during the visit, while urging the government not to interfere with the party’s activities.

The NDC candidate also accused the government of tolerating armed groups allegedly targeting supporters of opposition politicians. He, however, said his party would not take the law into its own hands.

Government denies allegation

But the Benue State Government has described Mr Shija’s allegation as false and politically motivated.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, the Commissioner for Information and Orientation, Solomon Iorpev, said the government had no reason to prevent the presidential candidate from visiting the state.

“Benue is a land of hospitality, and every Nigerian is free to move within it, including those who seek our votes,” Mr Iorpev said.

He urged the NDC to ensure that its supporters conducted themselves peacefully, adding that the government was responsible for the safety of visitors to the state.

The commissioner also cautioned against using the 2025 Yelewata killings for political purposes.

“We mourn with the families of the victims every day. No one should turn that grief into a political stage, and no one should use a visit meant to console the bereaved as material for a publicity campaign,” he said.

Mr Iorpev warned that security agencies would deal with anyone attempting to cause disorder, regardless of their political affiliation.

Previous disruption

The latest disagreement follows a reported incident on 8 September, when Mr Obi’s convoy was forced to turn back after suspected thugs and security operatives confronted it along Gboko Road in Makurdi.

PREMIUM TIMES reported that the convoy was stopped near the Air Force Base shortly after arriving in the state. Videos obtained by the newspaper showed men carrying sticks, stones and other objects pursuing the vehicles as they turned back.

Mr Obi’s campaign photographer, Esther Umoh, alleged that the men were sponsored to prevent the presidential candidate from entering Benue.

Mr Shija also accused the state government of being behind the incident. The allegations had not been independently verified.

Mr Obi said he had intended to visit the state to show solidarity with communities affected by the Yelewata killings.

The September incident followed an earlier disagreement in April 2025, when Governor Hyacinth Alia warned Mr Obi against making what he described as an unscheduled visit to internally displaced persons in the state.

In a statement issued on 14 April 2025, the governor’s spokesperson, Tersoo Kula, said people planning to visit IDP camps were required to obtain approval from the Benue State Emergency Management Agency.

Mr Alia later defended the decision in an interview on TVC on 24 April 2025, saying high-profile visitors needed to inform the state government and comply with security protocols.

The latest exchange comes as political parties begin preparations for the 2027 general elections and amid continuing security challenges in parts of Benue State.

World.title: Nigeria’s solid minerals revenue hits N101bn in nine months — Minister
World.content:
Nigeria’s solid minerals sector generated more than N101 billion in revenue January through September, up from N6 billion in 2023, the Minister of Solid Minerals Development, Dele Alake, has said.

Mr Alake attributed the improvement to the reforms introduced by President Bola Tinubu’s administration, saying revenue from the sector rose to N38 billion in 2024 and N70 billion in 2025 before topping N101 billion in the first nine months of 2026.

He disclosed the figures on Tuesday in Abuja at the unveiling of the All Progressives Congress 2027–2031 manifesto.

According to the minister, figures from the Central Bank of Nigeria showed that revenue from the sector continued to rise in 2026.

“When I resumed there in 2023, the total revenue that the sector generated was N6 billion. With the introduction of creative policies and reforms, within one year, in 2024, it rose to N38 billion. By 2025, it rose to N70 billion,” he said.

Mr Alake said the increase demonstrates the impact of the administration’s economic policies and efforts to restructure the mining sector.

The minister defended the removal of petrol subsidy and the unification of multiple exchange rates, arguing that President Tinubu has prioritised national interest over political considerations ahead of the 2027 general election.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Ordinary politicians will think of the next election and avoid contentious policies that probably could mar their political aspirations. But not President Bola Tinubu. He puts the nation ahead of self,” he noted.

Mr Alake asserted that no civilian government since Nigeria’s independence in 1960 has undertaken structural reforms on the scale of the current administration.

He said the new manifesto will consolidate the reforms and extend their benefits to security, healthcare, agriculture, industrialisation, manufacturing and solid minerals.

The minister added that the administration’s objective is to translate macroeconomic improvements into better living conditions for Nigerians.

Mining sector’s economic potential

Nigeria has deposits of several commercially valuable minerals, including lithium, gold, iron ore, limestone, barite, coal and lead-zinc, but the sector has historically contributed relatively little to the country’s overall economic output.

The government has repeatedly identified mining as an alternative source of revenue and foreign exchange earnings, particularly as it seeks to reduce dependence on crude oil.

However, the sector continues to face challenges, including illegal mining, weak regulation, insecurity in mining communities, limited processing capacity and inadequate geological data.

The government has also been stepping up efforts to expand local processing and value addition rather than the exportation of raw mineral resources, with the aim of creating jobs and scaling up industrial activity.

Also speaking at the event, the Minister of Information and National Orientation, Mohammed Idris, urged Nigerians to support the administration’s economic reforms, saying their benefits are becoming evident across different sectors.

READ ALSO: FG grants drug manufacturers N24bn tax waivers to boost local production

Mr Idris cited improved security on the Abuja-Kaduna and Abuja-Kano highways, 1.6 million beneficiaries of the student loan scheme, declining inflation and rising gross domestic product as evidence of progress.

He also said Nigeria’s removal from the Financial Action Task Force grey list and improved international credit ratings have strengthened investor confidence.

Minister of Budget and Economic Planning Atiku Bagudu said the president believes Nigeria can attain the level of economic development recorded by countries such as Brazil.

He stated that Nigerians have begun to experience the benefits of having a leader willing to take difficult decisions, particularly in implementing economic reforms.

World.title: United Nigeria Airlines apologises after expert questions six-hour flight delay
World.content:
United Nigeria Airlines has apologised to governance expert Joe Abah over a six-hour delay to his flight from Enugu to Abuja, acknowledging that its communication with affected passengers fell below expectations.

Mr Abah, who was scheduled to travel from Enugu to Abuja at 8:30 a.m. on Tuesday, said the flight was eventually delayed until 3 p.m., prompting him to question the airline’s explanation and demand an immediate refund.

In a post on X on Tuesday, Mr Abah tagged United Nigeria Airlines and the Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA), demanding an explanation for the disruption and asking the regulator to outline how affected passengers would be compensated.

He said ground staff in Enugu and Abuja could not explain the delay, while a customer service representative who promised to investigate and call him back failed to do so.

Mr Abah also questioned the airline’s explanation regarding the weather, noting that Enugu Air and Air Peace operated flights from Enugu around the scheduled time.

He further said United Nigeria Airlines’ staff told him the aircraft had been diverted to Anambra because of weather conditions but subsequently operated flights between Anambra and Abuja.

“Having delayed the flight for more than six hours, it would be an absolute disgrace if the refund is not immediate,” he wrote.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

United Nigeria Airlines responded to Mr Abah on Wednesday, apologising for the disruption and acknowledging that its communication and follow-up with passengers were inadequate.

The airline said the aircraft scheduled to operate the Enugu flight had begun its operations in Lagos, where it was fourth in the departure queue because of runway congestion.

It said other aircraft departed ahead of it and arrived in Enugu before weather conditions deteriorated.

By the time its aircraft approached Akanu Ibiam International Airport, Enugu, conditions had worsened, making landing difficult, it said.

The aircraft consequently diverted to Anambra in line with aviation safety procedures.

The airline said weather conditions could vary across routes and airports, as well as change within short periods, explaining why other airlines might have landed in Enugu while its aircraft could not.

“At United Nigeria Airlines, safety is non-negotiable,” it said, adding that decisions are guided by flight crew judgement, prevailing meteorological information and safety protocols.

“We would rather inconvenience our passengers than expose them to an avoidable safety risk,” the airline said.

“While weather-related disruptions may sometimes be beyond an airline’s control, keeping passengers adequately informed remains our responsibility, and we acknowledge the need to improve in this regard,” it added.

United Nigeria Airlines said Mr Abah does not need to wait for seven working days until his refund to be processed.

It asked him to complete a refund request form on its official website, saying the request will be treated for immediate processing once submitted.

The airline also expressed regret over his decision never to fly with it again, saying it recognised that passengers’ trust depends on consistent service and accountability.

Mr Abah is a public policy and governance expert who previously served as the director-general of the Bureau of Public Service Reforms. He is known for his advocacy on public sector accountability and service delivery.

The incident has again drawn attention to passengers’ concerns over prolonged flight delays, inadequate communication and the handling of refunds by domestic airlines.

Nigeria’s Civil Aviation Regulations provide consumer protection provisions covering flight delays, cancellations, passenger assistance and compensation in qualifying circumstances.

The NCAA advises passengers to first lodge complaints with airlines and escalate unresolved cases to its Consumer Protection Department.

While weather and operational challenges may disrupt flight schedules, the incident raises questions about how airlines communicate delays, explain operational decisions and ensure passengers receive remedies in accordance with aviation regulations.

PREMIUM TIMES contacted Mr Abah to confirm whether he has received a response from the airline, but is yet to receive a response from him.

World.title: FG grants drug manufacturers N24bn tax waivers to boost local production
World.content:
The Nigerian government said it has granted N24 billion in tax waivers to pharmaceutical manufacturers between 2025 and 2026 as part of efforts to increase local production of medicines and reduce dependence on imported healthcare products.

The Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Muhammad Pate, disclosed this on Tuesday at the 2026 Nigeria Health Sector Joint Annual Review (JAR) in Abuja.

Mr Pate said the incentives were introduced under the presidential executive order signed in 2024 to support domestic manufacturing of medicines, medical equipment and other essential healthcare products.

He also disclosed that the government had secured 12 technology-transfer agreements and was pursuing prospective investments exceeding $5 billion in the healthcare manufacturing sector.

According to him, the government is working to ensure that the proposed investments translate into operational businesses capable of producing affordable healthcare products and creating employment opportunities.

“The Executive Order signed by Mr President in 2024 has supported N24 billion in tax waivers for pharmaceutical manufacturers in 2025–2026,” he said.

“We have 12 technology-transfer agreements and a prospective investment pipeline exceeding $5 billion.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Pate said the government’s priority was to translate the prospective investments into actual manufacturing activities.

“Our task is to help those prospective investments become operating businesses that supply safe, effective and affordable products and create opportunities for Nigerians,” he said.

Expansion of local manufacturing

Mr Pate said 10 factories or manufacturing lines had been commissioned under the government’s healthcare industrialisation programme, including six in 2026.

He explained that the facilities cover the production of pharmaceuticals, rapid diagnostic tests, long-lasting insecticidal nets and medical oxygen.

The minister acknowledged the contribution of the Presidential Initiative for Unlocking the Healthcare Value Chain (PVAC), coordinated by Abdu Mukhtar, to the government’s efforts to expand domestic manufacturing.

Also speaking at the review, the Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare, Iziaq Salako, reported an increase in local pharmaceutical production.

Mr Salako said locally manufactured medicines accounted for 50 per cent of Nigeria’s pharmaceutical market in 2026, compared with 30 per cent in 2023.

He said figures from the Pharmaceutical Group of the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria and the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) also showed an approximately 10 per cent increase in the number of active local pharmaceutical companies.

He said the improvements reflected ongoing efforts to strengthen domestic manufacturing and reduce Nigeria’s dependence on imported healthcare products.

Meanwhile, Mr Pate said NAFDAC was strengthening regulatory measures against falsified medicines to support the development of the pharmaceutical industry.

He also disclosed that the government was working to operationalise Medipool, a group purchasing organisation designed to consolidate demand for medicines and other healthcare commodities.

According to him, the initiative would help organise government procurement while allowing other supply channels to continue operating.

The arrangement is intended to create more predictable demand for healthcare products and support local manufacturers.

Background

Nigeria has been working to expand domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing amid concerns about dependence on imported medicines and disruptions to international supply chains.

In July 2024, President Bola Tinubu signed an executive order introducing fiscal incentives to encourage local production of medicines and other healthcare products.

The order provided relief from tariffs, excise duties and Value Added Tax (VAT) on specified pharmaceutical machinery, equipment and raw materials used in manufacturing.

In May 2025, PREMIUM TIMES reported that the presidency had identified the executive order as one of the government’s major health sector reforms aimed at attracting investment and reducing the cost of pharmaceutical products.

The government said the incentives were designed to make local manufacturers more competitive and encourage increased production of essential healthcare products.

In September 2026, PREMIUM TIMES also reported that the federal government was targeting at least 70 per cent local production of essential healthcare products by 2030.

Speaking at the 8th Nigeria Pharma Manufacturers Expo in Lagos, Mr Salako said the government was using financing and tax incentives to strengthen domestic manufacturing.

He disclosed that 87 local manufacturers were benefiting from the presidential executive order granting zero tariffs on pharmaceutical machinery, active pharmaceutical ingredients and other production materials.

Mr Salako also said PVAC had secured about $2 billion in financing commitments at single-digit interest rates, with approximately 50 Nigerian healthcare companies in advanced discussions for funding.

He explained that increasing local production would help strengthen medicine security and reduce the country’s vulnerability to disruptions in international supply chains.

Sustaining local production

Despite the reported progress, Nigeria’s ambition to expand local pharmaceutical manufacturing will depend on sustained investment, access to financing and the ability of manufacturers to produce medicines that meet required quality standards.

At the September 2026 pharmaceutical manufacturers’ expo, Mr Salako emphasised the importance of expanding production beyond finished medicines to include active pharmaceutical ingredients, vaccines, diagnostics and other essential health commodities.

He also identified research, innovation, regulatory cooperation and access to regional markets as important areas for developing the industry.

The 2026 Joint Annual Review, held under the theme “Make the Data Count”, brings together federal and state government officials, development partners and other stakeholders to assess progress under the Nigeria Health Sector Renewal Investment Initiative.

The initiative is being implemented through the Sector-Wide Approach, which seeks to improve coordination, financing and accountability in healthcare delivery.

World.title: Keyamo flags off Kogi airport construction, says project will attract investment
World.content:
Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development Festus Keyamo on Tuesday flagged off the construction of Kogi International Airport in Zariagi, saying the project could attract investment and expand economic opportunities in the state.

Mr Keyamo, who performed the groundbreaking ceremony alongside Governor Ahmed Ododo of Kogi State, attributed the project to the federal government’s economic reforms and the state government’s infrastructure development priorities.

He said the removal of petrol subsidies and reforms in the foreign exchange market have increased revenue allocations to state governments, giving them greater financial capacity to undertake infrastructure projects.

In a statement issued on Tuesday by his Special Adviser on Media and Communications, Tunde Moshood, the minister said the airport project reflects a combination of federal economic policies and the governor’s commitment to development.

“However, it takes two to tango. One, the positive policies of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and the vision of the Governor. These are the two things that combined to make this thing possible today,” Mr Keyamo said.

He noted that increased revenue alone could not guarantee development without a leadership willing to channel public resources into infrastructure.

Mr Keyamo described the commencement of the project as a major milestone for Zariagi, saying it would give the community greater visibility in the aviation industry.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“What is happening here today, what the Governor has done today, will resonate many, many years, centuries after today, 500 years from today. Do you understand the significance of what is happening here today? Let me tell you the significance. Today, as from today, this village called Zariagi will be on the Global Aviation Map,” Mr Keyamo said.

He defended the economic rationale for establishing an airport in a state where major international commercial activities are still developing.

“If you are waiting for the best international companies to be here, the best international hotels to be here before you put an airport, you wait for the next one million years, it will not come,” he said.

“It is the airport that attracts these developments. The airport is the precursor. The airport is the forerunner. The airport is the indicator of development,” he added.

He expressed confidence that the facility will encourage businesses to establish operations in Kogi State, improve accessibility and strengthen the state’s participation in domestic and international trade.

READ ALSO: NDLEA arrests Ugandan woman with 87 cocaine wraps at Lagos airport

Governor Ododo said the airport is a strategic investment intended to unlock the state’s agricultural and mineral resources potential by improving access to markets and attracting investors.

Kogi is endowed with mineral deposits, including iron ore, limestone, coal and marble, as well as agricultural produce such as cassava, rice, maize, cashew and palm oil.

The governor said improved transportation infrastructure will ease the movement of agricultural produce and mineral resources, create employment opportunities and support commercial activities.

The state government also expects the airport to contribute to tourism and the development of logistics services, including potential cargo operations.

World.title: Amnesty urges oil firms to fund Niger Delta environmental cleanup
World.content:
Amnesty International Nigeria has urged oil companies operating in Nigeria to contribute to a well-funded environmental restoration fund to finance the comprehensive cleanup of the Niger Delta.

Isa Sanusi, the director of Amnesty International Nigeria, made the call on Tuesday in Port Harcourt during the presentation of a report titled “Nigeria: Lifting the Lid”.

The report examined what the organisations described as 60 years of negligent oil operations by an oil firm in the Niger Delta.

Mr Sanusi said oil companies must take responsibility for the environmental damage caused by their operations and support restoration efforts in affected communities.

He called on the federal government to ensure that oil firms contributed to a well-funded restoration fund to facilitate the cleanup of polluted sites to international standards.

“The contribution of a super-fund must be sufficient to fully clean up the Niger Delta to the highest international standards.

“We are urgently calling for the initiation of a clean-up programme to restore the Niger Delta environment,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The Amnesty director also urged the government to conduct comprehensive audits of operational and decommissioned oil infrastructure belonging to fossil fuel companies.

He said the findings of such audits should be made accessible to affected communities to promote transparency and accountability.

Mr Sanusi further called for studies into human rights impacts of decades of oil pollution, particularly on the health of residents, water quality, fisheries and agriculture.

According to him, the report documents alleged failures to protect communities and the environment, which he attributed to the prioritisation of corporate profits over human lives.

He urged residents, particularly those in oil-producing communities, to read, discuss and share the report to raise awareness and demand accountability.

“Those responsible for oil pollution and environmental degradation must be held accountable for their actions and comply with the rule of law,” he said.

Mr Sanusi also rejected attempts to place responsibility for oil pollution and environmental degradation solely on host communities.

He said Amnesty International would continue to challenge such narratives and demand accountability from companies and relevant authorities.

The Amnesty director disclosed that the organisation would write to President Bola Tinubu, forward a copy of the report, and urge the federal government to implement its recommendations.

Ogoni leaders withhold consent for oil resumption

Meanwhile, the Ogoni Dialogue Committee (ODC) has ruled out signing an agreement with the federal government on the resumption of oil exploration in Ogoniland until the people of the oil-rich area have been given an opportunity to decide on the proposed return of oil companies through credible community congresses.

The decision raises a fresh hurdle for the federal government’s efforts to restart oil production in Ogoniland, decades after oil exploration was halted amid protests over environmental devastation, economic marginalisation and the killing of environmental activist Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other Ogoni leaders in 1995.

PREMIUM TIMES reported in August that 51 civil society organisations opposed the planned resumption of oil production in Ogoniland, arguing that the government should prioritise environmental restoration over reopening oil wells.

The organisations cited unresolved pollution, including the 2025 oil spill in Kpean community, and warned that renewed extraction without adequate remediation could expose residents to further environmental and health risks.

(NAN)

World.title: Mbappe misses France training ahead of Italy clash
World.content:
France’s forward #10 Kylian Mbappe reacts to his team’s defeat at the end of the 2026 World Cup football tournament semi-final match between France and Spain at the Dallas Stadium in Arlington on July 14, 2026. (Photo by RONALDO SCHEMIDT / AFP)

France captain Kylian Mbappe did not take part in team training on Wednesday and remained “under treatment” ahead of his country’s Nations League match against Italy, Les Bleus’ coaching staff said.

The French coaching staff did not provide any further details regarding the 27-year-old’s physical condition.

The Real Madrid forward is back in the France squad for this camp after missing their last three matches through injury.

Mbappe scored the winning goal in Zinedine Zidane’s first match as coach against Turkey in September in the Nations League, but had to leave the pitch shortly afterwards due to pain in his left knee.

After three wins and a draw in four matches, France top Group A1 of the Nations League and are well on course to qualify for the quarter-finals ahead of their final two pool-stage fixtures against Italy on Thursday in Milan, and Turkey on Sunday in Bordeaux.

World.title: Xenophobic attacks: Help South Africans, don’t punish them — OAU don
World.content:
A man holds a stick as Zulu protesters demonstrate in front of their hostel in the Jeppestown district of Johannesburg on April 17, 2015, against foreign nationals in South Africa. Twelve people were arrested overnight as anti-foreigner attacks in South Africa spread to parts of downtown Johannesburg, police said on April 17. According to local reports, the protesters from a local hostel demanded foreign nationals leave South Africa, setting cars alight and clashing with police. AFP PHOTO / STEFAN HEUNIS

…As varsity’s International Relations Department marks 50th anniversary

By Shina Abubakar, Osogbo

The Federal Government has been urged to adopt a sympathetic approach towards South Africa over the recent xenophobic attacks, rather than resort to punitive measures, with a don at the Obafemi Awolowo University (OAU), Ile-Ife, saying South Africans need help at a difficult time.

A Professor of International Relations at OAU, Charles Ukeje, said the xenophobic violence was regrettable, particularly given Nigeria’s significant contributions, alongside other African countries, to the struggle against apartheid in South Africa.

Ukeje spoke during a press conference organised to herald the 50th anniversary of the university’s Department of International Relations at the campus.

He blamed the attacks partly on the failure of successive South African governments to adequately educate their citizens about the sacrifices made by Nigeria and other African countries towards ending apartheid.

According to him, proper education about the contributions of other African nations could have helped foster a stronger sense of brotherhood among South Africans and other Africans.

He said: “I believe that the xenophobic violence in South Africa is very regrettable. It is regrettable because this is a country which the rest of the continent, particularly Nigeria, helped to midwife in the context of apartheid.

“So, in the post-apartheid era, you would expect that the South Africans will be more and better disposed to the rest of Africans, given the amount of sacrifice that Nigerians and other African countries have made in the bid to end apartheid in that country.

“It is regrettable that generations of South African leaders, upon achieving an end to apartheid, really did not adequately educate their citizens on the role the whole of Africa played.

“Perhaps, if they had done that, things would have been different. Perhaps, the ordinary South African citizens on the street would treat and see other Africans as brothers.”

On Nigeria’s response, the don said the country should maintain its longstanding commitment to Africa as the centrepiece of its foreign policy.

He urged the Federal Government to demonstrate leadership by showing understanding towards South Africa, despite the hostility some of its citizens might harbour towards Nigerians.

“In terms of how Nigeria should respond, Africa has always been the centrepiece of Nigeria’s foreign policy. I don’t think that is going to change.

“I think Nigeria has the responsibility to continue to see itself as a leader on the continent. I think that role for Nigeria is perhaps more important today than it was anytime.

“And I’m looking forward to the Nigerian government not really wielding the big stick against South Africa, but to actually acknowledge that the country and its citizens are facing very difficult circumstances at this time and we need to be more sympathetic to them, even with the amount of disdain that the ordinary citizens harbour towards Nigeria,” he said.

Department marks 50 years

Earlier, the Head of the Department of International Relations, Professor Victoria Akinyemi, said the department had contributed significantly to the development of manpower for Nigeria’s foreign policy over its five decades of existence.

She said the anniversary was not only an opportunity to celebrate the department’s achievements but also to reposition it to meet the demands of the 21st-century international system.

Akinyemi noted that the contemporary global environment had changed significantly from the Cold War era of the 1960s and 1970s when the department was established.

“As we celebrate our past, we must also not forget to grasp, appreciate, and proactively confront the realities of a changing world.

“It is instructive to note that the 21st-century international system is different from the Cold War environment of the 1960s and 1970s into which the department was born.

“We now live in a very fluid world that is marked by complex interdependence, unending geopolitical realignments, climate and environmental politics, social disruptions caused by new technologies, democratic backsliding, civilisational clashes, the resurgence of populism and nationalism, and emerging security challenges,” she said.

The department head said the institution would continue to adapt through innovation, curriculum development and research to remain relevant in the changing global environment.

She added that the department would leverage modern technology, particularly Information and Communication Technology, alongside strategic socio-economic frameworks, to deliver effective, cost-efficient and globally competitive academic programmes.

World.title: Lagos govt warns PSPs over refuse crisis, demands results
World.content:
…..As Solus, Olusosun dumpsites resume operations

…PSPs to deploy over 700 trucks

By Olasunkanmi Akoni

The Lagos State Government has warned Private Sector Participation (PSP) waste operators to deliver immediate results or face enforcement measures, following the reopening of the Solus and Olusosun dumpsites after months of closure.

The government said it had fulfilled its responsibility by rehabilitating the facilities and their access roads, leaving waste operators with no further excuses for the persistent refuse crisis across the state.

Commissioner for the Environment and Water Resources, Tokunbo Wahab, gave the warning on Wednesday during an inspection of the previously closed Solus dumpsite in Alimosho Local Government Area.

Wahab said the government expected PSP operators to improve waste collection and evacuation across their areas of operation, stressing that residents deserved value for the services they paid for.

“Too much is given, so much more is expected. There are no more excuses,” the commissioner said, recounting his message to the leadership of the PSP operators.

“The state government has done its own bit; let your PSP members also put their skin in it and see how they can achieve what we set out jointly to achieve because they suggested we put this into play and now we’ve done it for them.”

According to him, the decision to reopen Solus followed proposals by waste operators to rehabilitate the facility rather than wait for the development of new dumpsites around Badagry and Epe.

He explained that Solus, located within Lagos West, serves several local government areas, including Alimosho, Ajeromi-Ifelodun, Mushin, Badagry, Ikeja, Ojo and Apapa.

The commissioner said the contractor handling the rehabilitation had assured the government that the repaired access road would last at least one year, subject to quarterly maintenance.

He added that the facility was expected to accommodate at least 100 trucks daily, significantly improving waste evacuation in the affected areas.

“100 trucks from this axis coming here to discharge gives us the comfort that our streets, our homes will not be littered with waste,” Wahab said.

Addressing complaints by residents over the failure of some PSP operators to collect refuse regularly, the commissioner said the state government would enforce its polluter-pays policy to ensure operators delivered the services for which residents paid.

He warned that the government would take necessary measures to hold defaulting operators accountable.

LAWMA restructuring

Wahab also confirmed a major restructuring of the Lagos Waste Management Authority (LAWMA), ordered by the state governor, as part of efforts to improve waste management operations.

He announced the appointment of Juwon Akinyemi as Acting Managing Director, Dr Tjani Olorunwa as Acting Executive Director of Operations, and Kunle Adebiyi as substantive Executive Director of Finance.

The commissioner further disclosed that senior LAWMA staff on Grade Levels 13 to 17, with a few exceptions, had been redeployed to the mainstream civil service.

He said the changes were intended to inject fresh energy into the agency as the state transitions from a conventional waste management system to resource recovery.

PSPs promise improved service

Meanwhile, the National President of the Association of Waste Managers of Nigeria (AWAMN), Olugbenga Adebola, welcomed the reopening of Solus, describing it as a major relief for operators who collectively manage a fleet of more than 700 trucks.

Adebola said the prolonged closure of accessible disposal facilities had forced waste operators to travel more than 120 kilometres outside Lagos to dispose of refuse at Shagamu, describing the situation as horrendous.

“As an operator, we are the happiest people today,” he said.

He pledged that operators would work with the government to ensure the facility was properly managed.

“We have told the commissioner and his team and the LAWMA team that we are going to co-own this place and ensure that we use this place as a model,” he added.

Adebola also commended the government for providing new bulldozers at the Solus facility, noting that the equipment would improve operations, reduce turnaround time and prevent queues of waste trucks.

He assured residents in the Alimosho axis, extending towards Iba, Festac, Badagry and parts of Agege, that waste evacuation would improve significantly within the next two weeks.

Echoing the commissioner’s warning, the AWAMN president issued a marching order to operators in the affected areas to intensify their efforts.

“Everybody needs to double their hustles. If you cannot fly, please be running. If you can’t run, please be working. If you can’t work, then crawl.

“But no more crawling, we are saying, no more crawling,” he warned.

While expressing optimism over the reopening of Solus, Adebola appealed to the state government to expedite the rehabilitation of four other outstanding disposal facilities, including those at Ewu-Elepe, Ikorodu, Oke-Aro and Badagry.

He said communities in Ikorodu, where the dumpsite had reportedly remained shut for nearly two months, would continue to experience waste disposal challenges until the facility was restored.

World.title: ADC protesters take Mark judgment dispute to NJC, UN, EU, UK, US embassies
World.content:
By Luminous Jannamike

ABUJA — Members of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) on Wednesday staged a protest at the Federal High Court in Abuja, demanding the release of the Certified True Copy (CTC) of the judgment nullifying the party’s National Working Committee led by former Senate President, David Mark.

The protesters accused the trial judge, Justice Peter Lifu, of withholding the November 5 judgment despite an application by the party’s lawyers and payment of the prescribed fees, arguing that the delay was frustrating their efforts to challenge the ruling at the Court of Appeal.

The protesters also extended their campaign beyond the court premises, storming the headquarters of the United Nations (UN), as well as the European Union (EU), United Kingdom and United States embassies in Abuja, where they submitted letters seeking diplomatic attention and support for what they described as due process, the right of appeal and credible elections in Nigeria.

The letters bore the subject: “Urgent Appeal for Diplomatic Attention and Support for Due Process, the Right of Appeal and Credible Elections in Nigeria – Re: Judgment Delivered on 5th November, 2026 in Suit No: FHC/ABJ/CS/1819/2025 (Nafiu Bala Gombe Vs. ADC & Ors).”

Speaking during the protest, a former Acting Chairman of the ADC in the Federal Capital Territory, Yusuf Shehu Tijani, described the judgment as a sham and called on the National Judicial Council (NJC) to intervene.

“Our reason for coming here today is what Justice Lifu is doing. He is holding on to the sham judgment he said he passed. He should send the CTC, so that we can get it and appeal the judgment.

“Moreover, the Supreme Court already affirmed the leadership of Senator David Mark as the National Chairman of the African Democratic Congress. So why is the High Court going against that recognition, saying he’s passing a judgment?

“Now the judgment you passed, give us the Certified True Copy so that we can appeal. He is refusing to do that. That is why we are here,” Tijani said.

He said the protest was intended to draw the NJC’s attention to the alleged delay and compel the judge to release the document.

“So the protest is to call on the NJC to pressure this man, let him do what is right, because justice must prevail in Nigeria. This is not a jungle. This is a country that has laws, that has rules, and we have to follow the Constitution of the country.

“The stated law is that he should send the CTC so that we can appeal the judgment, which is a sham judgment in the first place,” he added.

The protest followed a November 10 petition addressed to the Chief Judge of the Federal High Court, Justice John Tsoho, by members of the ADC candidates’ forum, demanding the immediate release of the judgment.

In the petition signed by Audu Aliyu on behalf of the candidates, the group said its lawyers applied for the CTC immediately after Justice Lifu delivered the judgment on November 5 and paid the prescribed fees, but had yet to receive the document despite repeated visits to the court registry.

The candidates said the delay was undermining their constitutional right to appeal, warning that the expiration of relevant election deadlines could render the right meaningless.

“We disagree with the judgment. We have a constitutional right to appeal it. But we cannot appeal what we do not have.

“As at today, 10th November, 2026, five (5) days after judgment, the CTC has NOT been released to us. Our lawyers have visited the Registry daily to no avail without any lawful explanation,” the petition stated.

The petitioners also alleged that they had credible information that the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) was pressuring the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to implement the judgment despite their inability to obtain its certified copy.

Citing Sections 241 and 242 of the 1999 Constitution, which provide for appeals from decisions of the Federal High Court to the Court of Appeal, as well as Section 294(1), they argued that withholding the judgment could effectively deny them access to appellate justice.

In a warning about the implications of the alleged delay, the candidates stated: “If a party can obtain a judgment against the opposition on Thursday, and the CTC is withheld until the election timetable closes, then the right of appeal becomes a mere illusion. Democracy dies not by coup, but by Registry delay.”

They urged the Chief Judge to direct the Registrar to release the CTC within 24 hours of receiving the petition, setting Wednesday, November 11, as the deadline.

The petitioners also notified the Chief Judge that ADC members, candidates and support groups would converge on the court premises by 10am on Wednesday to demand the document, insisting that the gathering was not intended as a protest against the judiciary but a demand for access to the judgment.

Copies of the petition were sent to the President of the Court of Appeal, the Chief Justice of Nigeria, the NJC, the INEC Chairman, the Nigerian Bar Association, Abuja branch, and the Inspector-General of Police.

The November 5 judgment nullified Mark’s emergence as ADC National Chairman and invalidated decisions taken by the party under his leadership, including the process that produced former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar as its presidential candidate for the 2027 general elections.

Justice Lifu also directed INEC not to recognise or act on decisions taken at the party’s 99th National Executive Committee meeting held on July 27, 2025.

The judgment followed a suit filed by Nafiu Bala Gombe, a former Deputy National Chairman of the ADC (North-East), who argued that he was constitutionally entitled to assume the party’s leadership following the resignation of its former National Chairman, Ralph Nwosu.

The ADC filed a notice of appeal on November 6 and also applied for a stay of execution, urging INEC not to take any action capable of prejudicing the outcome of the appeal.

Vanguard Newspaper

World.title: Police probe Blord over armed officers’ escort
World.content:
The Nigeria Police Force has launched an investigation into a viral video showing armed police officers escorting businessman Linus Williams, popularly known as Blord, at the Akanu Ibiam International Airport, Enugu.

The Force Public Relations Officer, CSP Ani Iniedu, described the deployment of the officers as “unlawful and illegal”, saying an investigation had commenced into the incident.

Iniedu disclosed this in a statement posted on his official X account on Wednesday while reacting to the video.

“Unlawful and illegal. Investigation has commenced into this incident please. We say #notoimpunity,” he wrote.

The video, which Blord shared on his Instagram page on Tuesday, showed him arriving at the Akanu Ibiam International Airport in Enugu, accompanied by armed police officers dressed in camouflage uniforms and tactical gear.

The businessman was seen wearing a red-and-white striped traditional cap associated with the Kwankwaso political brand.

He was also seen arriving in a black Cadillac with the personalised number plate, “B-LORD”.

Other scenes in the footage showed Blord walking alongside the armed officers at the airport and at other locations, including what appeared to be his business premises.

The officers were seen providing him with an escort and opening the vehicle door for him.

Captioning the video, Blord wrote: “Back to base, business as usual. From the airport to a brief stop at BlordGroup Enugu branch, then back to Awka. Every move has its purpose, and the vision never takes a break. Blord is home!”

In another Instagram post, the businessman said he had been in Sabon Gari, Kano State, where he met his “brothers” before returning to Enugu.

The development comes months after President Bola Tinubu ordered the withdrawal of police officers attached to Very Important Persons (VIPs) across the country and their redeployment to core policing duties.

Tinubu gave the directive at a security meeting with service chiefs and the Director-General of the Department of State Services in Abuja on November 23, 2025.

According to a statement by the President’s Special Adviser on Information and Strategy, Bayo Onanuga, VIPs requiring protection would henceforth be assigned armed operatives of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps instead of police officers.

The President said the measure was aimed at strengthening police presence in communities, particularly those facing security challenges.

On December 6, 2025, the police also deployed a Special Enforcement Team to monitor compliance with the directive, beginning with an operation in Lagos.

The then Force Public Relations Officer, CSP Benjamin Hundeyin, said the exercise recorded no cases of unauthorised deployment of police escorts.

World.title: Troops ​‌‍‍‍‍⁠⁠‍‍​⁠‍‍‌​‌‌​apprehend father, son for alleged terrorism in Sokoto forest
World.content:
Photo Credit: NAN

Troops of the Nigerian Army have apprehended two suspected terrorists (father and son) in Sokoto State.

The suspects, identified as Muhammadu Ali and his son, Umaru Ali, were arrested at Bauni Forest in Tangaza Local Government Area.

The operational report made available to the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) on Wednesday said the operation was conducted by troops of 248 Battalion, supported by the French Special Forces and the NCTC-Office of the National Security Adviser tactical team.

The report said the suspects were apprehended at about 10:00 a.m. on Wednesday and were believed to be from the Bauni village area.

According to the report, items recovered during the operation included one AK-47 rifle, one magazine containing three rounds of 7.62mm special ammunition, ₦9,760 and three motorcycle tubes.

The report said the suspects were in the custody of 8 Military Intelligence Battalions for further investigation. (NAN)

World.title: Oil resumption agreement must benefit Ogonis, be enforceable — KAGOTE
World.content:
File image

…Recommends Ogoni development plan, seeks stronger HYPREP

By Daniel Abia

P/HARCOURT — The leadership of KAGOTE, the apex socio-cultural organisation of the Ogoni people, has said any memorandum of understanding (MoU) between the Federal Government and the Ogoni people on the resumption of oil exploration must be comprehensive, credible, enforceable and beneficial to the people.

The organisation said the agreement must enjoy the confidence and support of the Ogoni people and remain beneficial to generations yet unborn.

KAGOTE stated this on Tuesday during this year’s remembrance of the Ogoni Nine in Port Harcourt.

In his address at the event, the President of KAGOTE, Chief Lesi Maol, said the proposed agreement should be a historic document that future generations would read with pride and gratitude.

He said it should have the enduring significance of the Ogoni Bill of Rights and reflect the wisdom and commitment of those negotiating on behalf of the people.

Maol said: “We should aspire to produce an agreement whose significance and enduring value can stand alongside the Ogoni Bill of Rights as another defining milestone in our history.

“An agreement of such historic significance must not be judged by the speed with which it is concluded, the prominence of those who sign it or the ceremonies that accompany it. It must be judged by its content, its fairness, its enforceability and the measurable benefits it secures for our people.

“We must move beyond promises that are difficult to measure and commitments that future generations may struggle to enforce. Let us negotiate an agreement that will outlive its signatories, survive changes in leadership and remain beneficial to Ogoniland long after those of us gathered here today have departed. That is the standard our history demands of us.”

He acknowledged progress in the ongoing dialogue with the Federal Government but stressed that the credibility of the negotiation process was as important as its outcome.

While welcoming the government’s recognition of confidence-building measures, Maol said such measures should be substantially implemented with visible and verifiable results before any final MoU was concluded.

He said the measures should address the concerns of the Ogoni people, demonstrate good faith and provide the necessary assurance for meaningful negotiations.

To achieve this, he called for credible, transparent and inclusive congresses across the four Ogoni local government areas of Khana, Gokana, Tai and Eleme.

According to him, the congresses should provide opportunities for communities, traditional institutions, women, youths, professionals and other recognised stakeholders to express their expectations and determine priorities for the negotiations.

He further proposed that a competent and representative negotiating team, backed by independent legal, environmental, technical and financial experts, should conduct the negotiations based on the mandate emerging from the congresses.

Maol said the process would strengthen the legitimacy of any agreement and assure the Federal Government and prospective investors that the commitments enjoyed genuine community ownership and support.

He stressed that the position should not be interpreted as hostility towards the Federal Government, the Ogoni Dialogue Committee or any individual, but as a commitment to protecting the future of the Ogoni people.

“We believe that a little more patience today can prevent many years of disagreement tomorrow,” he said.

The KAGOTE president also called for the proposed Field Development Plan of any prospective oil operator to be made available to the Ogoni people through appropriate channels for independent technical assessment and informed community engagement before operations commence.

He said the disclosure should include relevant environmental and social impact assessments, remediation safeguards, emergency response arrangements, decommissioning obligations and community development commitments, subject to legitimate legal and commercial confidentiality requirements.

Maol said the objective was to promote transparency, informed participation and mutual confidence among host communities, government and prospective operators without usurping the statutory responsibilities of regulatory authorities or interfering with legitimate commercial operations.

On environmental protection, he warned that the resumption of oil activities must not undermine ongoing remediation efforts or expose Ogoniland to another cycle of ecological damage.

He called for stronger coordination among relevant regulatory institutions, the Hydrocarbon Pollution Remediation Project (HYPREP), host communities and prospective operators to ensure that environmental restoration, public health protection and responsible resource development remained complementary priorities.

Maol also proposed the establishment of an Ogoni Development Partnership Forum to bring together relevant stakeholders to identify priority interventions, coordinate voluntary contributions, encourage partnerships and periodically assess progress.

He said the proposed platform would help advance sustainable development and ensure that the benefits of any eventual oil resumption agreement translated into measurable improvements in the lives of the Ogoni people.

World.title: Abia first in S’East to implement CONLESS for Assembly workers
World.content:
. Otti approves 25% salary increase, implementation begins January

By Steve Oko

Abia State has become the first state in the South-East to adopt the Consolidated Legislative Salary Structure (CONLESS) for parliamentary workers, with Governor Alex Otti approving a 25 per cent salary increase for eligible staff.

The new salary structure, which covers employees of the Abia State House of Assembly and the House of Assembly Service Commission, will take effect from January 2027.

The Chief Press Secretary to the Governor, Njoku Ukoha, disclosed this in a statement on Wednesday, saying the approval followed recommendations by the committee set up to work out the implementation of CONLESS.

CONLESS is the approved remuneration structure for legislative workers in the National Assembly, state Houses of Assembly and their respective service commissions.

Its implementation has remained outstanding in several states despite persistent demands by parliamentary workers.

The approval is expected to address disparities in the remuneration of legislative staff, improve their welfare and strengthen the institutional capacity of the legislature.

The development also marks a significant step in Abia’s efforts to improve public sector remuneration and promote fairness in the state’s workforce.

World.title: THE KOH MANIFESTO SERIES…
World.content:
sponsor : Tokunbo Wahab

PEOPLE FIRST

Hamzat’s PROMISE: Putting the Lagosian at the Centre of Governance

This is an examination of the People First agenda and its 15 pledges on healthcare, education, community safety and citizen services

Every political manifesto comes with an assortment of promises, but their importance is ultimately determined by how closely they address the needs of the people for whom government exists.

For a state such as Lagos, where rapid population growth continually stretches public infrastructure and services, the relationship between government and the ordinary resident is particularly important.

A parent concerned about the cost of medical treatment, a young graduate struggling to find employment, a trader confronted by harassment on the streets and a resident spending an entire day pursuing a government document may have different immediate concerns.

Yet, all four experiences raise a common question: how effectively does government respond to the needs of its citizens?

This is the question at the heart of the People First component of the Lagos PROMISE, the manifesto unveiled by the All Progressives Congress governorship candidate, Dr. Kadri Obafemi Hamzat, ahead of the 2027 election.

Structured around four thematic areas and 15 distinct pledges, People First addresses healthcare, education and human capital, community safety, and the relationship between citizens and public institutions.

Of the 15 pledges, 11 are classified as firm commitments and four as aspirations. The distinction is significant because it separates proposed obligations from broader objectives whose achievement may depend on additional resources, external partnerships or conditions yet to be established.

Together, the pledges offer a framework for examining what people-centred governance would mean in practical terms.

Healthcare: From Building Hospitals to Improving Access

Healthcare occupies a central position in the People First agenda, with five pledges covering medical infrastructure, personnel, insurance, vulnerable populations and specialist treatment.

Among the proposed targets are a workforce of 9,000 doctors, two additional general hospitals, 120 flagship primary healthcare centres and 15 maternal and child centres by 2031. The manifesto also proposes expanding selected general hospitals, including those in Alimosho, Odan and Ikorodu.

These commitments address an enduring challenge of urban development: the tendency for population growth to outpace the availability of public services.

For Lagos, however, the issue extends beyond the number of healthcare buildings. A hospital is useful only to the extent that it has qualified personnel, functional equipment, essential medicines and the capacity to attend promptly to patients.

Consequently, the proposed expansion of healthcare facilities would need to proceed alongside effective staffing, maintenance and financing arrangements.

This is where the Pledge of Systems connects with the Pledge of the Healthcare Economy, which proposes extending Ilera Eko health insurance coverage to 30 per cent and strengthening the state’s medicine supply and healthcare financing systems.

The significance of insurance cannot be overstated. For many households, a serious illness is simultaneously a medical emergency and a financial crisis.

Wider insurance participation could help reduce the immediate pressure of paying for treatment, although the eventual benefit would depend on the services covered, participating facilities and affordability of premiums.

Another dimension is the Pledge of the Vulnerable, which sets targets for reducing malaria, maternal mortality and the burden of noncommunicable diseases, while expanding community mental healthcare across the five administrative divisions of Lagos.

Here, the distinction between inputs and outcomes becomes especially relevant.

The number of hospitals constructed can be counted. So can the number of doctors recruited. But the more consequential questions concern whether fewer mothers die during childbirth, whether more diseases are detected early and whether patients receive timely treatment.

These are the measures by which healthcare expansion would acquire meaning beyond physical infrastructure.

The fifth undertaking, the Pledge of Care on Lagos Soil, addresses specialist medical services and the ambition to reduce outbound medical tourism through facilities such as the Lagos Cancer Diagnosis Centre, Medipark and other specialist institutions.

Classified as an aspiration, it reflects a broader economic consideration: the possibility of retaining healthcare expenditure, professional expertise and medical investment within Lagos.

Its realisation would nevertheless require sustained investment in specialist personnel, equipment, quality assurance and the confidence of patients, who currently seek treatment elsewhere.

Education: Preparing the Lagos Mind for a Changing Economy

Education constitutes the second component of People First, with four pledges directed at learning outcomes, vocational training, tertiary education and access.

The Pledge of Foundations proposes strengthening the EKOEXCEL programme across public primary schools and extending its approach into secondary education.

This is particularly relevant because improvements at the primary level can be diminished if students enter secondary schools without adequate teaching support, continuity or a curriculum responsive to their needs.

But educational reform must also confront a question that has become increasingly important: what happens after students leave school?

Lagos operates in an economy where technology, logistics, construction, creative enterprise and other sectors are changing the nature of employment. Qualifications alone do not necessarily guarantee that young people possess the practical skills demanded by employers.

The manifesto therefore links its Pledge of Skills to technical and vocational education, including the proposed completion of Meiran Technical College, additional colleges in Ibeju-Lekki and Badagry, and an artificial intelligence workforce programme.

The policy implication is that education would be judged increasingly by its ability to connect learning with productive participation in the economy.

That connection, however, must be demonstrated rather than assumed.The number of students admitted into training programmes would tell only part of the story.

The more revealing measures would include completion rates, professional certification, apprenticeships, job placements and the extent to which employers recognise the skills acquired.

The Pledge of the Lagos Mind extends the reform agenda to universities, research institutions, teachers, lecturers and trainers.

Its inclusion acknowledges that expanding access to schooling without improving the quality of instruction would leave a major part of the education challenge unresolved.

Meanwhile, the Pledge of Equity seeks to improve educational opportunities for children irrespective of household income or personal circumstances, including reducing the number of out-of-school children.

Unlike some other undertakings in the manifesto, the proposed reduction is not accompanied by a precise numerical target.

That leaves room for a clearer implementation framework identifying the existing number of affected children, the annual reduction being pursued and the mechanisms for bringing them into and retaining them within the education system.

These questions matter because access, quality and employability are interconnected. A child excluded from education today becomes an adult with diminished economic opportunities tomorrow.

Community Safety: Beyond Conventional Crime Fighting

The third People First component deals with the experience of security at the neighbourhood level. Its four pledges cover local safety arrangements, crime prevention, complaints and protection for survivors of sexual violence.

The Pledge of the Neighbourhood proposes extending the reach of the Lagos Neighbourhood Safety Agency across the state’s 20 local government areas and 37 local council development areas.

The Pledge of Prevention seeks to strengthen community-based interventions involving schools, markets, motor parks and faith-based institutions.

Together, they reflect an approach in which public safety is not restricted to responding after crimes have been committed.

For residents, insecurity can manifest in relatively ordinary but persistent experiences: harassment in traffic, extortion at commercial locations, threats around markets or the absence of effective intervention when disputes escalate.

These experiences have economic as well as social consequences. They influence business operating costs, commuting patterns and public confidence in government.

The emphasis on prevention is therefore relevant, provided community participation translates into genuine intelligence-sharing, conflict resolution and accountable enforcement.

There is also an important institutional limitation. Policing remains principally a federal responsibility under Nigeria’s existing constitutional framework. The proposed state-level interventions would consequently require coordination with federal law enforcement authorities.

That makes clarity of responsibility essential. Residents should be able to distinguish between agencies responsible for receiving complaints, preventing disorder, investigating crimes and prosecuting offenders.

The Pledge of the Citizen Voice introduces specific response standards: acknowledgment of safety complaints within 24 hours, an initial response within seven days and resolution within 30 days.

Such targets provide a potentially useful basis for accountability. They would be more meaningful, especially if accompanied by publicly available data on complaints received, cases resolved and matters referred for further investigation.

The fourth undertaking, the Pledge of the Survivor, proposes expanding sexual-assault referral support across all five administrative divisions.

Beyond the availability of centres, effective protection would require confidential reporting, trained personnel, medical and psychological support, and reliable links to the justice system.

The essential issue is whether a person seeking protection can access it promptly and safely, regardless of location or financial circumstances.

Citizen Service: Making Government Easier to Reach

Perhaps the most immediately relatable aspect of People First is its final component: the way residents encounter government offices and public services. Two pledges define this agenda.

The Pledge of the Front Door proposes satellite government secretariats in Badagry, Ikorodu, Lagos Island and Epe, complementing the central secretariat at Alausa.

The underlying challenge is straightforward. A resident should not necessarily have to undertake a lengthy journey across Lagos merely to obtain information, submit an application or resolve an administrative problem.

Decentralising selected services could reduce transportation costs, time lost in transit and the concentration of administrative activities in Ikeja. Yet, the location of an office is only one part of accessibility.

The offices would need appropriately trained staff, functioning digital systems, clearly defined services and sufficient authority to resolve matters without repeatedly referring residents back to Alausa.

Otherwise, decentralisation could simply reproduce existing bureaucratic difficulties in additional locations.

The second undertaking, also described as the Pledge of the Citizen Voice, establishes standards for responding to public complaints.

Under the published manifesto, complaints are to be acknowledged within 24 hours, receive an initial response within seven days and, in routine cases, be resolved within 30 days. More complex matters are assigned a longer period in the accompanying implementation narrative.

These provisions provide clearer opportunities for measuring public-service performance.

For residents, the practical test would be whether applications are processed within advertised periods, complaints are assigned to identifiable officials and unresolved cases can be escalated without unnecessary difficulty.

The proposed integration of resident identification and government services could further simplify public administration, but it would also require dependable safeguards for personal information and effective alternatives for residents who lack smartphones or reliable internet access.

A government service is not genuinely accessible if the process excludes the people most in need of it.

2

…THE KOH MANIFESTO SERIES…

RENEWAL

Hamzat’s PROMISE: Rebuilding the Foundations of Greater Lagos

Beyond roads, bridges and rail lines, the Renewal agenda proposes a new relationship between infrastructure investment, economic productivity and the quality of everyday life.

Infrastructure has become one of the defining questions of governance in Lagos. Not necessarily because the state has failed to invest in it, but because the scale and speed of its growth continually place fresh demands on facilities that are already under pressure.

A road constructed today may struggle with traffic volumes in a few years. A drainage channel designed for an existing community may become inadequate as new estates emerge. Water infrastructure installed decades ago must contend with changing population patterns, while electricity supply remains an expensive uncertainty for households and businesses.

This is the context in which Dr. Kadri Obafemi Hamzat, has situated the second pillar of his 2027 governorship manifesto, The Lagos PROMISE.

Known simply as Renewal, the agenda contains 12 pledges distributed across four areas: roads and transport infrastructure, electricity, water supply, and waste management and flood resilience.

Taken together, they raise a larger question about the future of Lagos: can infrastructure development move beyond the construction of new facilities to the creation of systems that are dependable, properly maintained and capable of supporting a growing megacity?

Roads and Bridges: The Importance of What Already Exists

The first three pledges, contained under Building Greater Lagos, address roads and bridges, traffic junctions and rail development.

The Pledge of Roads and Bridges proposes rehabilitating the state road network and restoring bridges to publicly defined standards.

Its significance lies partly in its recognition that maintenance should be treated as an essential component of infrastructure policy rather than an occasional intervention.

Lagos has invested in major roads, bridges and transport corridors under successive administrations. Yet, the experience of commuters demonstrates that the condition of smaller connecting roads can be just as consequential as the existence of major highways.

A journey shortened by a new expressway may still be frustrated by badly maintained feeder roads, damaged intersections or inadequate drainage.

The challenge, therefore, is not only how many kilometres of road are constructed, but how effectively the entire network operates. The Pledge of the Junction addresses a particularly familiar Lagos experience: traffic congestion at critical intersections.

Hamzat proposes a continuous junction-improvement programme beginning with ten identified priority locations, alongside the restoration of traffic signals across the state within the first year.

The importance of this proposal is that congestion is not always caused by an absolute shortage of roads. Inefficient junction designs, poor signal coordination, roadside trading, indiscriminate parking and weak enforcement can reduce the capacity of existing infrastructure.

A comparatively modest junction intervention can sometimes improve traffic flow without the financial and environmental implications of constructing an entirely new road.

But the effectiveness of such measures must be tested through average travel times, traffic speeds and commuter experience, rather than the mere commissioning of redesigned intersections.

Rail Development and the Question of Connectivity

The Pledge of Rail commits to completing the Blue Line extension to Okokomaiko and linking the Red and Blue lines at the National Theatre, Iganmu. This is an important distinction in the development of Lagos mass transit.

A rail line does not derive its full value simply from the distance it covers. Its wider significance emerges when passengers can transfer conveniently between services and complete journeys without unnecessary delays or additional costs.

The proposed connection between the two lines would therefore represent more than a construction milestone. It would address a fundamental problem in urban mobility: fragmentation.

For Lagos to realise the potential of its rail investments, stations must connect effectively with buses, ferries, taxis and other transport services.

The manifesto also discusses the Fourth Mainland Bridge and major federal transport corridors. These, however, involve approvals, financing and institutional arrangements beyond the direct authority of the state government.

The distinction matters because a state administration may control the maintenance of its roads while having a more limited ability to determine the completion of federally controlled or jointly financed infrastructure.

Electricity: The Search for Reliable Power

The second component of Renewal, named IMOLE, addresses electricity through three pledges. Its most ambitious target is the Pledge of Light, an aspiration to increase grid electricity reaching households from approximately 1,000 megawatts to 3,500 megawatts by 2031.

The manifesto acknowledges that Lagos requires substantially more electricity than it currently receives. The proposed increase is therefore a contribution towards addressing an identified deficit, rather than a guarantee that the state’s entire electricity requirement would be met.

The distinction between an aspiration and a firm commitment is particularly relevant here.

Electricity delivery depends on generation, transmission, distribution, financing and regulation.

Although the Electricity Act 2023 and subsequent state legislation have expanded the opportunities for subnational electricity markets, the state cannot independently guarantee every part of the supply chain.

The Pledge of the Market proposes strengthening the Lagos State Electricity Regulatory Commission and establishing a phased state electricity market in partnership with the major distribution companies.

The Pledge of the Renewable Pathway complements this with embedded generation for industrial parks and wider deployment of renewable energy and mini-grid solutions.
