INCLUSION

Hamzat’s PROMISE: Bringing the Margins into the Mainstream of Lagos Development

The Inclusion agenda places women, young people, children, persons with disabilities, older residents and informal-sector workers within the wider conversation about economic opportunity, social protection and equitable governance.

In a city as large and diverse as Lagos, development cannot be measured solely by the scale of public investment or the sophistication of its infrastructure.

A modern transport system may exist without being accessible to persons with disabilities. An expanding economy may generate impressive investment figures while leaving thousands of informal traders unable to obtain affordable credit.

New public facilities may be concentrated in developed neighbourhoods while underserved communities continue to struggle with basic services.

These contradictions illustrate one of the central challenges of governing a rapidly expanding megacity: ensuring that the benefits of development extend beyond those already well-positioned to receive them.

This is the concern addressed by Inclusion, the fifth pillar of Dr. Hamzat’s governorship manifesto.

Containing 16 pledges across six thematic areas, the agenda deals with women’s economic participation and safety, youth development, disability rights, the welfare of older residents, child protection, informal enterprise and social diversity.

Its underlying proposition is that economic growth and public investment must be accompanied by deliberate measures to reduce exclusion.

Women’s Economic Participation and Safety

The first component, Obìnrin Èkó, contains two pledges. The Pledge of Safety proposes strengthening the Lagos State Domestic and Sexual Violence Agency and Family Support Units to improve protection for women.

The Pledge of Agency seeks to expand women-led enterprise through existing financing programmes, including the N10 billion LASMECO facility and the Employment Trust Fund, with at least half of beneficiaries in relevant enterprise programmes reserved for women-led businesses.

These undertakings address two different but related dimensions of women’s participation in society. Economic opportunity can improve independence and household welfare, but women must also have access to safe environments in which to live, work and participate in public life.

For women operating small businesses, access to finance remains an important concern. Yet, the provision of credit alone does not guarantee sustainable economic empowerment.

Loan conditions, business training, market access and the ability to manage repayment obligations all influence the usefulness of financial assistance. Similarly, support for survivors of domestic and sexual violence requires more than institutional visibility.

Effective intervention depends on confidential reporting, prompt medical assistance, legal support, survivor protection and coordination between relevant agencies.

The significance of Obìnrin Èkó would therefore be reflected in improved safety, genuine access to opportunities and measurable economic participation, rather than programme enrolment alone.

Youth: Converting Population into Productive Capacity

The second component, Ọmọ Èkó, concerns youth employment and sports development. Its Pledge of Work proposes expanding employment and enterprise opportunities through the Graduate Internship Placement Programme and the Lagos State Employment Trust Fund.

The Pledge of the Field addresses sports facilities, stadium renewal and grassroots sports development across the five divisions. These commitments recognise that young people represent a substantial part of the state’s population and productive potential.

But a large youth population becomes an economic advantage only when education, skills and employment opportunities keep pace with demographic change. The relationship between training and employment is particularly important.

Young people may complete vocational or professional programmes without securing sustainable work if the training does not correspond to market demand.

For this reason, the employment component should be evaluated through actual placements, job retention, earnings and enterprise survival.

The inclusion of sports development introduces another dimension. Sports can create professional opportunities, support physical wellbeing and provide constructive recreational spaces for communities.

However, grassroots development requires more than renovated stadiums.

Neighbourhood playing fields, qualified coaches, organised competitions and clear pathways for talented athletes are essential if sporting opportunities are to reach young people outside established professional structures.

The wider question is whether a young person in Badagry, Epe or Ikorodu would enjoy meaningful access to opportunities comparable to those available in more developed parts of the state.

Disability Rights and the Dignity of Ageing

Three pledges address persons with disabilities and older residents under the Iyì Èkó and Àgbà Èkó programmes. The Pledge of Rights proposes strengthening the Lagos State Office for Disability Affairs and relevant legal protections.

The Pledge of Universal Design seeks to incorporate accessibility into public buildings, infrastructure and transport systems. The Pledge of the Elder addresses healthy ageing, pension delivery and welfare services for older citizens.

The importance of these undertakings becomes clearer when accessibility is understood as a basic condition for participating in society. A person with mobility challenges may be unable to use a public transport terminal without ramps or appropriate boarding facilities.

A resident with impaired vision may encounter difficulties navigating buildings without suitable signage and guidance systems.

An older person may be unable to access essential government services when the process requires prolonged standing, repeated journeys or complicated digital applications.

Universal design attempts to anticipate these needs from the planning stage rather than treating accessibility as an afterthought. This approach can be more effective than attempting costly modifications after infrastructure has been completed.

The proposed strengthening of disability-rights institutions would also require meaningful enforcement. Standards are of limited value if public agencies and private service providers can disregard them without consequences.

For older residents, the concerns extend to healthcare, social protection, mobility and financial security.

The manifesto’s focus on pensions and welfare services consequently raises questions about timely payments, administrative efficiency and access for people who may find conventional service procedures difficult.

Child Protection: Making Responsibility Clear

One of the more institutionally specific components of Inclusion concerns the protection of children. Its three pledges propose a system in which responsibilities are clearly assigned and safeguarding procedures coordinated.

The Pledge of the Named Owner seeks to establish a dedicated legal institution with an identifiable executive responsible for child protection.

The Pledge of the Single Front Door proposes a multi-agency safeguarding centre with a 24-hour reporting mechanism and joint assessment of cases within 48 hours.

The Pledge of the Safe Institution provides for annual audits of schools and childcare institutions, alongside criminal background checks. These proposals respond to a persistent difficulty in child protection: fragmentation.

A child experiencing abuse, neglect or exploitation may encounter separate institutions responsible for health, welfare, law enforcement and legal intervention. When these institutions do not communicate effectively, cases may be delayed or mishandled.

A coordinated safeguarding framework could improve the identification of risks, reduce duplication and establish clearer responsibility.

However, creating a new agency would not automatically resolve the problem.

Its powers would need to be defined by law, its relationship with existing institutions clarified and its personnel equipped with specialist training.

The proposed background checks and institutional audits would also require appropriate safeguards to protect children, ensure confidentiality and prevent arbitrary treatment.

For the public, the most meaningful outcomes would be faster intervention, safer institutions and effective support for children and families at risk.

The Informal Economy: Recognising Those Who Already Work

Three pledges address informal traders, artisans, market operators and micro-enterprises. The Pledge of Formalisation proposes making business registration more attractive through incentives and simplified procedures.

The Pledge of the Fair Levy seeks to address charges that disproportionately burden petty traders and small enterprises. The Pledge of the Modern Market focuses on improving market infrastructure, sanitation and safety.

These commitments are important because the informal economy is not a peripheral feature of Lagos. It is central to the everyday functioning of the city.

Market traders distribute food and household goods. Artisans provide essential technical services. Small transport operators, service providers and neighbourhood businesses sustain commercial activity across communities.

Yet, many operate under conditions characterised by inadequate infrastructure, limited financing and unpredictable regulatory demands. Formalisation could help improve access to finance, public contracts, insurance and business support. But it must be accompanied by incentives.

If registration merely increases the number of agencies collecting charges from small businesses, the policy could become counterproductive.

Similarly, market modernisation should not be measured only by the construction of new buildings. It should consider affordability of stalls, adequate sanitation, fire safety, accessibility and the protection of existing traders from unnecessary displacement.

An upgraded market that becomes too expensive for its original occupants may improve the physical environment while worsening economic exclusion.

One Lagos: Development Across Communities

The final three Inclusion pledges appear under One Lagos. The Pledge of Pluralism, classified as an aspiration, addresses the protection of cultural, ethnic and religious diversity.

The Pledge of the Margin proposes extending public services and development programmes to riverine, lagoon-side and informal-settlement communities.

The Pledge of the Diaspora seeks to strengthen engagement with Lagos residents and communities living abroad. These proposals reflect the social complexity of Lagos.

The state is both historically rooted in distinct indigenous communities and shaped by continuous migration from other parts of Nigeria and beyond. Its diversity contributes substantially to its commercial and cultural character.

However, protecting pluralism requires institutions and policies that apply public rules fairly, safeguard lawful participation and reduce discrimination.

The emphasis on underserved communities is equally consequential. Geographical exclusion can persist even when state-wide development figures appear impressive.

An increase in the number of healthcare facilities, for example, does not necessarily demonstrate improved access for residents of difficult-to-reach riverine communities.

The manifesto proposes publishing performance data across the five administrative divisions. Such reporting could improve accountability, although more detailed community-level information would be needed to expose inequalities within individual divisions.

Diaspora engagement, meanwhile, could support investment, professional partnerships, knowledge exchange and cultural connections.

For the arrangement to become productive, its objectives and outcomes would need to be clearly defined.

6

…THE KOH MANIFESTO SERIES…

SECURITY AND RESILIENCE

Hamzat’s PROMISE: Securing Lagos Against Crime, Disaster & Climate Threats

The Security and Resilience agenda extends the meaning of public safety beyond crime prevention to include coastal protection, emergency preparedness, cybersecurity and the management of risks confronting a growing megacity.

Security is one of the most fundamental responsibilities of government. Yet, the threats confronting a major urban centre such as Lagos have become considerably more complex than conventional criminal activity.

A city may experience relatively low levels of organised violence and still remain vulnerable to devastating floods, building collapses, industrial accidents, market fires, cyberattacks and other emergencies capable of disrupting lives and economic activities.

For Lagos, the concentration of people, businesses, infrastructure and valuable assets makes effective risk management an increasingly important feature of public administration.

This is the broader context of the Security and Resilience component of Dr. Hamzat’s governorship manifesto.

Containing 13 pledges distributed across four thematic areas, the agenda combines community safety, climate adaptation, emergency response and smart-city technology.

Its underlying proposition is that a safer Lagos must be capable not only of preventing crime but also of anticipating threats, responding quickly to emergencies and recovering effectively when disruptions occur.

Community Safety and the Limits of State Authority

The first three pledges concern community safety, technology-supported policing and the welfare of security personnel. The Pledge of Community Safety proposes strengthening the Lagos Neighbourhood Safety Agency and deepening citizen participation in public safety.

The Pledge of Smart Policing addresses the deployment of CCTV systems, drones, command facilities and predictive-policing technology.

The Pledge of the Officer seeks to improve welfare, accommodation and professional training across security and emergency services.

These undertakings recognise the importance of prevention and intelligence in managing urban security. But they also encounter an important constitutional reality.

Policing remains principally a federal responsibility under Nigeria’s existing constitutional arrangements. Consequently, the state cannot independently determine all operational aspects of law enforcement.

The manifesto acknowledges this limitation and proposes continued cooperation with federal security institutions.

Lagos already operates institutions such as the Lagos State Security Trust Fund and the Neighbourhood Safety Agency, which provide different forms of support within the security architecture.

The proposed expansion of their activities would require clear coordination with the Nigeria Police Force and other relevant authorities.

Community participation could improve early identification of security risks, particularly when residents have confidence that information will be handled responsibly.

However, public safety interventions must also guard against arbitrary enforcement, profiling and abuse of authority. Technology presents similar opportunities and challenges.

CCTV cameras and other monitoring systems can assist investigations and emergency response. But their effectiveness depends on reliable operation, trained personnel and appropriate legal safeguards.

Predictive-policing systems require particular scrutiny because inaccurate or biased data can produce unfair outcomes.

The challenge is therefore to improve security capabilities without compromising the rights and freedoms that public safety institutions are expected to protect.

Coastal Protection: Preparing for Environmental Risks

The second thematic area, Resilient Lagos, contains two pledges. The Pledge of the Coast proposes strengthening coastal defences and flood protection along the state’s approximately 180-kilometre Atlantic frontage, with particular attention to lagoon-side and low-lying communities.

The Pledge of Clean Air, classified as an aspiration, addresses air-quality improvement, urban greenery and tree planting across the five administrative divisions. These interventions reflect the environmental conditions confronting Lagos as a coastal megacity.

Flooding, shoreline erosion, sea-level changes and increasingly intense rainfall present risks to housing, roads, businesses and essential services.

The challenge is compounded by development patterns that place growing numbers of people and physical assets in areas exposed to environmental hazards.

Coastal protection is therefore an issue of economic security as well as environmental management. Damage to critical infrastructure can disrupt transport, trade, education and healthcare, while repeated flooding imposes substantial financial costs on households.

Yet, coastal engineering projects must be carefully planned. Defences that protect one location may alter water movement or erosion patterns elsewhere. Large-scale interventions consequently require credible environmental assessments and coordinated planning.

The emphasis on cleaner air and urban greenery also raises issues beyond aesthetics. Air pollution affects public health, while green spaces can contribute to urban cooling, recreation and environmental quality.

However, tree-planting targets should be measured through survival rates, maintenance and actual environmental improvement, not merely the number of seedlings distributed.

Similarly, improving air quality requires attention to transport emissions, industrial activity, waste burning and other significant pollution sources.

Emergency Preparedness: From Reaction to Anticipation

Four pledges address disaster preparedness and emergency response. The Pledge of Readiness proposes strengthening the Lagos State Emergency Management Agency and the Emergency Operations Centre as coordinating institutions for multiple categories of hazards.

The Pledge of the First Responder seeks to improve fire, rescue, ambulance and pre-hospital emergency services. The Pledge of Early Warning proposes risk mapping, hazard registers and systems for anticipating emergencies.

The Pledge of the Community addresses public education, preparedness exercises and local emergency-response arrangements. The importance of this framework becomes clearer when viewed against the range of incidents that Lagos has experienced.

Building collapses, road accidents involving petroleum tankers, market fires and flooding have repeatedly demonstrated the consequences of inadequate prevention or delayed intervention.

A major emergency can overwhelm individual agencies unless their responsibilities and communications are clearly coordinated.

Consequently, emergency management should begin before an incident occurs.

Structural inspections, fire-safety enforcement, evacuation planning and emergency drills can reduce the likelihood or severity of disasters.

Early-warning systems can help communities prepare for flood risks, while regularly updated hazard maps can identify locations requiring particular attention.

But warnings are only useful when residents understand them and have realistic options for responding. A flood alert may be ineffective for a household without a safe evacuation route or access to temporary shelter.

Similarly, ambulance services cannot deliver their full potential if emergency vehicles are routinely delayed by congestion or if hospitals lack the capacity to receive patients.

The effectiveness of the proposed emergency framework would therefore depend on coordination across transport, healthcare, urban planning and public safety institutions.

Smart Lagos: Technology as an Instrument of Public Safety

The fourth component, Smart Lagos, contains four pledges. The Pledge of the Command Centre proposes strengthening the existing 767 and 112 emergency systems while creating a separate mechanism for tracking non-emergency complaints.

The Pledge of the Sensor City seeks to expand sensor-based monitoring across transport, energy, the environment, public safety and health. The Pledge of Cyber-Resilience proposes a Lagos State Cybersecurity Centre and improved protection of public data.

The Pledge of the Inclusive Smart City addresses the need for citizen-facing systems accessible even to residents without smartphones.

Together, these proposals reflect an increasingly important approach to urban administration: using timely information to identify problems and coordinate responses.

A smart-city system can potentially detect changes in traffic conditions, monitor environmental risks, support emergency services and improve the management of public infrastructure.

But collecting information is not the same as using it effectively. The institutions receiving data must possess the authority, technical competence and resources required to respond.

A sensor identifying a flooded road has limited public value if the relevant agency cannot act on the information.

Likewise, a complaint-management platform will achieve little if reports remain unresolved despite being properly recorded.

Cybersecurity is another essential consideration. As government services become more interconnected, the consequences of data breaches and system failures can become more extensive.

The proposed cybersecurity framework would therefore need to address prevention, incident response, independent oversight and protection of citizens’ information.

The decision to accommodate residents without smartphones is particularly relevant in a society where access to digital technology remains uneven. A smart city should not become a system available only to the digitally connected.







7

…THE KOH MANIFESTO SERIES…

EVERYDAY DIGNITY

Hamzat’s PROMISE: Taking Development to the Lagos Household

The final pillar of the 100-pledge manifesto examines the relationship between economic growth and the daily realities of housing, transportation, household income and the cost of living.

For the average Lagos resident, the success or failure of public policy is often determined far removed from government offices, economic conferences and official ceremonies.

It is evident in the cost of renting an apartment, the time required to travel to work, the price of food in the market and the proportion of monthly earnings consumed by essential services.

These everyday considerations may not always attract the political attention reserved for major infrastructure projects, but they frequently determine how people experience development.

A state can record impressive economic growth while many households struggle with rising living expenses. It can construct new roads and rail lines without adequately reducing the financial burden of commuting.

It can expand housing developments without bringing home ownership within the reach of ordinary workers. This distinction between economic performance and household welfare provides the context for Everyday Dignity, the seventh and final pillar of Dr. Hamzat’s manifesto, The Lagos PROMISE.

Containing 12 pledges across three thematic areas, Everyday Dignity addresses housing, public transportation and the cost of living.

Its significance lies in attempting to connect the broader promises of development with the economic circumstances of individuals and families.

Housing: The Challenge of Affordability

The first component, Home for Lagos, contains five pledges. The Pledge of the Roof proposes expanding affordable housing through the Ministry of Housing, the Lagos State Development and Property Corporation, the Lagos Building Investment Company and other arrangements.

The manifesto specifically identifies opportunities for additional LagosHOMS developments in Badagry, Epe and Ikorodu, alongside further housing investment in Ikeja and Lagos Island.

The Pledge of the Mortgage proposes a home-ownership financing pathway requiring a 10 per cent initial deposit and single-digit interest rates.

The Pledge of the Plan addresses orderly and climate-resilient urban development. The Pledge of the Long-Resident seeks to protect established communities during urban renewal. The Pledge of the Fair Rent proposes working with private developers to increase the supply of more affordable housing.

Together, these undertakings address one of Lagos’ most persistent structural problems: the difficulty of securing adequate accommodation at a cost consistent with household income.

The challenge is not simply the availability of residential buildings. It also concerns land prices, construction costs, access to finance, infrastructure provision and the relationship between housing locations and employment centres.

A residential development may offer relatively affordable accommodation but become less attractive if occupants must spend substantial sums travelling to work. Consequently, housing policy cannot be separated from transport planning.

The proposed expansion into Badagry, Epe and Ikorodu isw definitely considering employment opportunities, transport connections, schools, healthcare and other services. Without these complementary facilities, the cost of living in a supposedly affordable housing estate may remain high.

The Mortgage Question

The proposal for mortgages requiring 10 per cent equity and single-digit interest deserves particular attention. For many prospective homeowners, the initial deposit represents a substantial obstacle.

Reducing the deposit requirement could potentially make home ownership more accessible. But lower initial deposits must be accompanied by repayment terms that borrowers can realistically sustain.

Mortgage affordability depends on the purchase price, interest rate, repayment duration and the borrower’s income.

Single-digit interest rates may improve affordability, but such financing does not arise automatically in an economy where commercial lending rates can be substantially higher.

The manifesto acknowledges the importance of cooperation with the Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria and the Nigeria Mortgage Refinance Company. This dependence makes implementation more complicated than the wording of the pledge might initially suggest.

A credible financing structure would need to explain how concessionary interest rates would be achieved, whether government subsidies or guarantees would be required, and which income categories would qualify.

The published manifesto does not establish a definitive numerical target for the total number of affordable homes to be delivered. That is an important omission from the standpoint of measuring results.

Without a clear housing-output target, it would be difficult to determine whether expanded financing arrangements were sufficient to make a meaningful contribution to the state’s housing needs.

Urban Renewal Without Displacement

The Pledge of the Long-Resident introduces a different dimension to the housing discussion.

Urban renewal can improve infrastructure, eliminate unsafe structures and support more efficient land use.

Yet, it can also disrupt established communities. As land values increase, long-standing residents may face rising rents or displacement from neighbourhoods they have occupied for generations.

The manifesto’s emphasis on consultation therefore raises important questions about the social consequences of redevelopment. Consultation should be meaningful rather than ceremonial.

Affected residents need clear information about proposed developments, their legal rights, possible relocation arrangements and mechanisms for addressing grievances.

Where displacement is unavoidable and lawful, appropriate safeguards and compensation arrangements become essential. The objective should be to improve urban conditions without unnecessarily transferring the social costs of redevelopment to vulnerable households.

Lagos in Motion: Making Transport Work as One System

The second component of Everyday Dignity contains five pledges addressing rail, buses, ferries, integrated ticketing and transport terminals.

The Pledge of Rail, classified as an aspiration within this component, refers to completing the Blue Line to Okokomaiko, linking the Blue and Red lines at the National Theatre and pursuing financing for the proposed Green Line.

The Pledge of the Bus proposes expanding and reforming Bus Rapid Transit and wider bus services across the five divisions.

The Pledge of the Ferry specifically provides for 11 additional electric ferries within the OMI EKO programme. The Pledge of One Ticket seeks to integrate rail, bus and ferry services under a common payment arrangement.

The Pledge of Terminals proposes additional bus terminals across the administrative divisions. These commitments address a major economic burden experienced by residents: the cost of moving around Lagos.

Transport expenses influence household budgets directly. But the economic consequences of commuting extend beyond fares. Time spent in traffic has an opportunity cost. Long journeys reduce the time available for productive work, family responsibilities, education and rest.

For businesses, congestion affects delivery schedules, labour availability and operating expenses.

The manifesto’s emphasis on integrated transportation therefore represents an attempt to improve the performance of the overall network rather than treating each mode as an isolated project.



Cost of Living: When Economic Growth Must Reflect in Household Welfare

Perhaps the most consequential aspect of the Everyday Dignity agenda is its treatment of the cost of living, an issue that has increasingly defined the economic circumstances of ordinary Nigerians.

For Lagos residents, the question is especially significant. The state may be Nigeria’s principal commercial centre, with expanding infrastructure, substantial investment and a growing economy, but these advantages do not necessarily translate into improved purchasing power for the average household.

A family’s economic wellbeing is not determined by the size of the state’s budget or the volume of investment attracted into its economy.

It is determined, more immediately, by what remains of its income after paying for accommodation, food, transportation, electricity, healthcare and children’s education.

This distinction provides the foundation for the cost-of-living component of Hamzat’s manifesto.

The document acknowledges that the expansion of the Lagos economy has not automatically translated into corresponding improvements in household incomes.

It cites an increase in the state’s gross domestic product from N54.77 trillion in 2024 to N66.47 trillion in 2025, while recognising the continuing pressure of essential expenses on family budgets.

The policy challenge, therefore, is how to connect economic growth with the financial wellbeing of the people whose activities sustain that growth.

To address this, the manifesto proposes a coordinated household affordability framework built around three objectives: increasing earning capacity, reducing the cost of essential services and providing protection for vulnerable households.

Rather than treating these objectives as unrelated government programmes, the proposal seeks to establish connections among housing, transportation, food distribution, electricity, healthcare, education and social protection.

It is an approach that recognises the multidimensional nature of household economic pressure.

The central consideration is therefore not simply whether individual services improve, but whether those improvements collectively reduce the financial burden on households.



Income: Strengthening Household Earning Capacity

The first of the two specific undertakings under this component is the Pledge of Income, classified in the manifesto as an aspiration.

It proposes expanding household earning capacity through micro, small and medium enterprises, entrepreneurship programmes and cooperative institutions.

The emphasis on earning capacity is particularly relevant because government cannot sustainably address the cost of living through subsidies and temporary relief alone.

Households require productive opportunities that allow incomes to grow in response to economic conditions.

For Lagos, this makes the development of small businesses and informal enterprises especially important.

A substantial part of the state’s economic activity is driven by traders, artisans, transport operators, service providers and entrepreneurs whose earnings depend on their ability to operate businesses efficiently.

When these enterprises encounter excessive regulatory charges, unreliable electricity, expensive credit or limited market access, their capacity to expand and employ additional workers is constrained.

The manifesto proposes using existing institutions, particularly the Lagos State Employment Trust Fund, cooperative structures and enterprise development programmes, to improve access to financing, training and business opportunities.

These proposals also connect with the Opportunity pillar, where Hamzat outlines initiatives for expanding formal businesses, supporting women-led enterprises and creating technology-related employment.

However, increasing access to financing does not automatically guarantee higher household incomes.

The effectiveness of such programmes would depend on the affordability of credit, repayment conditions, business survival rates and the ability of supported enterprises to generate sustainable profits.

There is also the challenge of ensuring that economic opportunities reach people outside established commercial networks.

Young graduates, women operating informal businesses, artisans and residents of underserved communities may require different forms of support.

For some, access to credit may be the principal challenge. For others, the more immediate need may be vocational certification, access to commercial premises or reduced regulatory obstacles.

A carefully designed income-support programme would therefore need to recognise these differences. The classification of the Pledge of Income as an aspiration is also significant.

Although government can create enabling conditions, the actual growth of household earnings depends on broader economic factors, including inflation, demand for goods and services, productivity and employment conditions.

Consequently, the pledge would be more meaningful if accompanied by specific indicators measuring improvements in earnings, job retention, business profitability and the purchasing power of beneficiaries.

Fair Tax: Reducing the Burden on Small Businesses

The second undertaking is the Pledge of the Fair Tax, which Hamzat presents as a firm commitment. Its objective is to harmonise the levies, taxes and fees paid by small businesses.

For thousands of small-scale entrepreneurs across Lagos, the issue is both familiar and consequential.

Traders and artisans may be required to make payments to different government institutions or authorised agents, while also confronting demands from persons whose authority to collect such payments is unclear.

The resulting uncertainty complicates business planning and can increase operating costs.

For a large corporation, multiple administrative charges may represent a relatively small proportion of expenditure. For a petty trader or artisan, however, repeated payments can significantly diminish already modest earnings.

The proposed harmonisation could therefore improve the business environment by establishing clearer obligations and reducing unnecessary duplication.

But the effectiveness of the reform would depend on its design and enforcement.

Businesses would need to know which charges are lawful, how much they are required to pay, the institutions authorised to collect them and the available procedures for challenging improper demands.

Digital payment systems could improve transparency, accessible alternatives would remain necessary for operators with limited digital capabilities.

The reform would also require coordination between state institutions and local authorities, whose revenue responsibilities must be respected within the applicable legal framework.

Beyond its administrative implications, fairer taxation has a direct relationship with consumer prices.

Businesses ordinarily incorporate their operating expenses into the prices charged for goods and services. Reducing avoidable costs could create opportunities for greater competitiveness and price stability.

Nevertheless, lower business charges would not automatically result in lower retail prices. Competition, supply conditions and other operating costs would influence how much of the savings reaches consumers.

The policy’s success would therefore need to be assessed through both improved compliance and actual reductions in the regulatory costs borne by small enterprises.

Social Protection: A Safety Net for Vulnerable Households

Beyond the two formally designated cost-of-living pledges, the manifesto proposes strengthening social protection through existing cash-transfer and welfare programmes.

It also discusses establishing a Lagos Social Protection Trust Fund, subject to the necessary legal and financial arrangements.

The proposed framework identifies persons with disabilities, older residents lacking adequate support, vulnerable young people, women-headed households and underserved communities as priority groups.

This dimension is important because not every household can immediately benefit from employment or entrepreneurship initiatives.

Some residents are unable to work because of age, disability or other circumstances. Others may experience temporary economic shocks that overwhelm their capacity to meet essential expenses.

Social protection can help prevent such difficulties from developing into deeper and more persistent deprivation. Yet, the design of support programmes presents its own challenges.

Accurate identification of beneficiaries, transparent selection procedures, reliable payments and safeguards against duplication or political interference are essential.

The manifesto proposes drawing on resident data to improve targeting.

Such an arrangement could strengthen administration, provided personal information is appropriately protected and residents who are not adequately represented in existing databases are not excluded. The proposed fund would also require a sustainable financing framework.

Temporary assistance can provide relief during economic hardship, but a credible social-protection system must be capable of functioning beyond emergency interventions. And this is one of such policies.

World.title: Ogun 2027: Adeola Pledges to Prioritise Rural Development
World.content:
James Sowole in Abeokuta

The Ogun State All Progressives Congress (APC) governorship candidate, Senator Solomon Adeola, popularly known as Yayi, has pledged to prioritise rural development across Ogun State if elected governor, assuring residents of sustained efforts to improve road infrastructure, address electricity, and other challenges in communities across the state.

Adeola gave the assurance while addressing stakeholders at a strategic town hall meeting held at the Ado-Odo/Ota Local Government Area of Ogun State.

At the event, he also announced plans to distribute 150 transformers across the local government areas as part of an empowerment programme scheduled to happen in the coming weeks.

The senator identified several roads and community infrastructure projects in Ado-Odo/Ota that require attention, including Captain Davies Road, Ejila Awori Community; Paramole Road; Alapoti/Isaga-Oluwo/Adie Owe axis; Ben Pako Adefarati Road; Dagboro Phase 2 Road; Obasanjo–Eledi–Ijagba Road; Owode–Ado Road; Igbodogun Road; Atan Market Road; Ere Road Phase 2; Gasline; Esuyago; Isalu Road; Ejila Awori Leadership Road; Adelemo Tarmac Road; Ayinde Isikilu Street and Ultra-modern Market, and Oja Ota Market.

Adeola noted that rural development would receive his full attention, noting that deliberate and coordinated efforts were needed to address the infrastructure gaps affecting communities across the state.

He urged residents and stakeholders to support his vision for the state, assuring them of his commitment to delivering development that responds to the needs of communities across Ogun State.

He further assured residents that if elected governor, he would work towards ensuring that access to electric transformers would no longer remain a recurring challenge for any local government area in the state.

“I am going to give 100 per cent attention to rural development across the length and breadth of the state. This issue will continue to come up for discussion, but we must make a conscious and concerted effort to address the challenges of rural development. I give you that assurance as your representative,” he said.

His latest commitments are built on previous infrastructure interventions facilitated by the Senator across Ogun State, including the inauguration of 23 constituency projects in Ado-Odo/Ota LGA in January 2025.

The projects included road construction, three blocks of 24 classrooms, and an ICT centre at Sango Ota High School, primary healthcare centres in Iyesi and Itele, and market facilities in Ota and Ado.

World.title: Nigerians Urged to Challenge Bad Governance, Corruption, Insecurity
World.content:
Folalumi Alaran in Abuja

Nigerians have been urged to speak out against bad governance, corruption, insecurity and poverty, with citizens warned that silence and indifference could further deepen the country’s challenges.

The Chairman of the Open Africa Foundation, Tunji Aworinde, said citizens must actively demand accountability from public officials and insist on transparency, justice and respect for the rule of law to achieve national development.

He made the call at the 11th International Conference on Financial Crimes, Governance and Electoral Integrity, organised by Inspired Citizens of Africa and Nigeria and the Police Force Reform Secretariat in Abuja.

Speaking on the theme, ‘Our Voice Must Be Heard,’ Aworinde described the rule of law, transparency and accountability as indispensable foundations for national unity, peace and economic prosperity.

“Rule of law, transparency and accountability. This is the only foundation of unity, peace, and prosperity. No country that thrives on impunity and lawlessness prospers,” he said.

He expressed concern over poor conditions in public schools, citing inadequate learning facilities and unsafe classrooms, despite government budgetary allocations to the education sector.

Aworinde urged Nigerians to use their voices to demand urgent improvements, insisting that children should not be subjected to learning environments that compromise their safety and development.

“Our voice must express our outrage at the appalling learning conditions for our children. We must express our outrage and tell those people who have the power to change things around that this is no longer acceptable,” he said.

He also condemned persistent insecurity affecting schoolchildren, particularly cases of abduction and attacks on schools, arguing that the protection of children’s lives should take precedence over expensive government projects and political interests.

“The Lagos-Calabar Coastal Road could wait. The countless fleets of imported vehicles could wait. The presidential jet could wait. The campaign for our votes could wait. The safety and security of our children could not wait and must never wait,” he said.

The foundation chairman further urged Nigerians to reject political indifference and speak out against unemployment, poor electricity supply, corruption and other governance failures.

“Indifference is not a response to our national problems. Misrule, public and political corruption, arrogance, poverty, unemployment, epileptic power supply and insecurity are issues we must speak against. Indifference to human suffering makes our humanity inhuman,” he said.

Also speaking, Cardinal John Onaiyekan, Cardinal Emeritus of Abuja, called on religious leaders and Nigerians to uphold shared moral values, including justice, honesty, compassion and respect for human life, as essential ingredients of good governance.

He maintained that religion should serve as a unifying force and contribute positively to national development rather than deepen divisions.

“In the pursuit of good governance in Nigeria, religion and its values should not be an obstacle at all, but rather a positive asset that we should all jointly enjoy,” he said.

Onaiyekan also criticised the political elite for prioritising the acquisition and retention of power over citizens’ welfare, warning against attempts to manipulate the electoral process ahead of the 2027 general election.

He called for free, fair and peaceful elections, expressing concern over the growing influence of money in politics and the use of public institutions to advance personal political interests.

The cleric urged Nigerians to collectively demand their rights and hold political leaders accountable, arguing that ordinary citizens could peacefully challenge the dominance of a small political elite.

“If our 240 million ordinary Nigerians, respectable Nigerian citizens, insist on our rights against the no more than 5,000 political elite that have captured the system, then we shall overcome this peacefully, in a win-win situation for all Nigerians,” he said.

On police reform, Assistant Inspector-General of Police, Dr Stanley Ude (rtd), Deputy Head of the Nigeria Police Reform Secretariat, called for increased investment in intelligence gathering, modern surveillance technology and community policing to strengthen the country’s security architecture.

He also advocated greater involvement of state and local governments in police funding, training and welfare, arguing that the responsibility should not rest predominantly on the Federal Government.

“In the past, it has been majorly the Federal Government that has been carrying that burden. Currently, they are carrying virtually 90 per cent, but the state government should also take part of that, and then the local government should also take part of that,” he said.

Ude expressed concern that the police remained largely reactive rather than proactive in addressing security threats, particularly kidnapping, and called for improved intelligence analysis and adequate operational logistics.

“You may have intelligence available, but you don’t have the logistics to react to that intelligence. A lot of times, we have intelligence that is not properly analysed, or that is not even available, and we need to invest in intelligence gathering and intelligence analysis,” he said.

He further advocated the proper screening and training of community vigilantes to enable them to work with formal security agencies in identifying and reporting suspicious activities.

Addressing preparations for the 2027 general election, Ude disclosed that police officers were undergoing specialised training and orientation on electoral laws to ensure professionalism and neutrality during election duties.

“Our role is to support INEC to ensure that we have free, fair and credible elections and that voters feel confident to safely go and vote, observe their votes being counted and returns made accordingly,” he added.

Also speaking, Group Director, Policy Advisory, Nigeria Revenue Service, Sunday Okeowo, identified inadequate revenue generation and the country’s debt-servicing burden as major constraints on the government’s ability to finance development.

He disclosed that debt servicing, which consumed about 97 to 98 per cent of government revenue in 2023, had declined to approximately 50 per cent but remained a significant fiscal challenge.

“As of today, the debt servicing has reduced to about 50 per cent of revenue. And that is where the problem still lies,” he said.

Okeowo called for aggressive revenue mobilisation and improved tax compliance to reduce the country’s dependence on borrowing and increase funds available for infrastructure and essential public services.

“Aggressive revenue mobilisation becomes our option. We need tax, and it is human beings that pay the tax,” he said.

He described tax payment as a civic responsibility, adding that Nigeria’s new tax laws were designed to capture emerging economic activities, including digital businesses and cryptocurrency transactions, while addressing tax evasion and illicit financial flows.

World.title: Stallion Group,  Access Bank Partner on Vehicle Ownership
World.content:
Sunday Okobi

The Stallion Group has partnered with Access Bank, part of Access Holdings, to make vehicle ownership more accessible. The partnership, according to both parties, brings 10 exclusive automotive brands and 72 models within reach of customers.

They said, in a statement, that through Access Bank’s AutoFest initiative, eligible buyers can access financing of up to 90 per cent of their chosen vehicle’s value, with a minimum 10 per cent equity contribution for individuals and 20 to 30 per cent for Fleet Financing.

The statement added that delivery may be possible within 72 hours after Equity Contribution, subject to credit approval and completion of documentation.

“With more than 50 years in the automotive industry, Stallion Group brings an established portfolio of international brands, exclusive manufacturer relationships and extensive customer support capabilities to the partnership.

The offering extends beyond vehicle sales. Customers can access professional servicing, optimised cost of ownership, genuine spare parts, dedicated body shop facilities, manufacturer warranties of up to six years on eligible vehicles, and electric vehicle battery warranties of up to eight years, subject to manufacturer terms and conditions,” the statement added.

It stated further that its flexible repayment options extending beyond four years have given individuals and businesses the opportunity to acquire vehicles without paying the full purchase price upfront.

“The partnership combines Stallion Group’s automotive heritage and after-sales infrastructure with the financial strength and reach of one of Africa’s largest banking groups. Ten brands, 72 models of up to 90 percent financing with potential delivery in 72 hours,” it added.

World.title: 2027 Elections: ‘Wole Oke ‘ll Not be Distracted, Intimidated in Osun’
World.content:
Yinka Kolawole in Osogbo



The Media Team of the House of Representatives Member representing Obokun/ Oriade Federal Constituency of Osun State and Chairman, House Committee on Foreign Affairs, Hon. Wole Oke, has reacted to spate of political attacks on its principal, saying such attacks only exposes the paucity of ideas and substantive issues available for discussion on the part of the detractors.

The Pelumi Olajengbesi Campaign Organisation (POCO) has accused the member representing Obokun/Oriade Federal Constituency, Hon. Wole Oke, of allegedly using his ambition to become Speaker of the House of Representatives as a political tool to deceive constituents ahead of the 2027 general election.

The campaign group also questioned how Oke, who recently joined the All Progressives Congress (APC), intends to succeed the incumbent Speaker, Rt. Hon. Tajudeen Abbas, while President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, an APC leader from the South-west, remains in office.

However, Wole Oke Media Team said that its principal will not be distracted, intimidated or drawn into an unnecessary war of words with anyone irrespective of their political leanings.

Oke’s Media Team in a statement said its principal remained focused on his political responsibilities, constituency engagements, and the collective electoral success of his great party, APC.

“Let those who wish to trade in mudslinging continue. We will trade in mobilisation, engagement, strategic organisation and electoral victory.

“By God’s grace, we remain committed to delivering our five political priorities in the forthcoming 2027 election cycle in Obokun/Oriade Federal Constituency.

“After all, the ultimate verdict in a democracy does not belong to campaign spokespersons, social media commentators, cynics, political hecklers, purveyors of falsehood, or merchants of propaganda. It belongs to the electorate”, Omolebi-Sunday said in the statement.

He said Oke is firmly on course, remains committed, and that he remains a prominent and committed member of the APC both local, state and national.

“In Obokun/Oriade, we have five candidates on our political priority list, and our commitment to their electoral success is unequivocal – Asiwaju Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s re-election as President; Senator Francis Fadaunsi re-election as Senator; Hon Wole Oke re-election as Member House of Representatives; Prof Ifemidayo Akinmoladun election as Member House of Assembly representing Oriade State Constituency in the Osun House of Assembly and Folahan Adebiyi Samuel election as Member representing Obokun State Constituency in the House of Assembly

“These are our candidates. These are our brands. These are our political priorities,” the statement said.

The statement also noted that Pelumi Olajengbesi is a political toddler looking for relevance by attacking his personality

It posited that despite the fact that he will not want to dignify him with any response, it remarked that Obokun/ Oriade Federal Constituency will massively vote for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and all APC candidates in the forthcoming Presidential and National Assembly elections.

World.title: Mohammed Confirms Former Bauchi NUJ Chairman, Sambo,  Substantive MD of BATV
World.content:
Segun Awofadeji in Bauchi



The Bauchi State Governor, Senator Bala Mohammed, has confirmed former state NUJ Chairman, Alhaji Idris Usman Sambo, as the substantive managing director of the Bauchi State Television Authority (BATV).

The confirmation of the appointment was conveyed in an official letter signed by the Secretary to the Bauchi State Government (SSG), Alhaji Aminu Hammayo, and made available to journalists yesterday.

The statement said it was based on the recognition of Sambo’s impressive educational qualifications, wealth of professional experience, meritorious record of service, and profound understanding of media operations in Bauchi State.

According to the statement, “Alhaji Idris Usman Sambo is an accomplished media professional with considerable experience in the state’s media industry.

He previously served as the managing director of the Bauchi Radio Corporation (BRC) and also as the chairman of the Nigeria Union of Journalists (NUJ), positions through which he demonstrated professional competence and commitment to the development of journalism in the state and Nigeria in general.

Governor Mohammed expressed confidence that his wealth of experience, administrative expertise and intimate knowledge of the state media landscape would contribute significantly to repositioning BATV for greater efficiency, professionalism, and improved service delivery.

He charged the new managing director to bring his wealth of experience to bear in strengthening the institution’s operational capacity, promoting responsible journalism, embracing innovation, and ensuring that BATV continues to serve as a credible platform for information dissemination, public enlightenment, and education.

The governor further called on the management and staff of the Bauchi State Television Authority, as well as other stakeholders in the media industry, to extend their full cooperation and support to the new managing director to enable him to discharge his responsibilities effectively.

Governor Mohammed congratulated Sambo on his well-deserved appointment and wished him a successful and rewarding tenure.

World.title: Ejiogu, Emeruem, Okoye Optimistic as  PDP Flags Off Okigwe Zone Campaign
World.content:
Amby Uneze in Owerri

The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) last Sunday formally flagged off its campaign for the Imo North senatorial district, also known as Okigwe Zone, with the party’s National Secretary, Senator Samuel Anyanwu, declaring the area fertile ground for the party regardless of how the 2027 elections turn out.

The event doubled as a show of endorsement by party faithful for the PDP’s candidates, led by the senatorial candidate, Chief Mike Ejiogu, and House of Representatives candidates, Ikenna Emeruem (Okigwe South) and Chief Chris Onye (Okigwe North).

Anyanwu, who is also the party’s leader in the Southeast, urged residents to turn out in large numbers for the PDP. He described the three candidates as a formidable team capable of “liberating” the zone, citing their pedigree and credentials as setting them apart from rivals and making the party the favourite in the zone.

Addressing a large crowd of supporters, Ejiogu said he was seeking office to drive the zone’s transformation through legislation, focusing on job creation, infrastructure, human capital development and welfare support for vulnerable households.

He expressed concern over hunger, poverty and deprivation in the area, and pledged to ensure that opportunities attracted through government channels reach the grassroots.

Ejiogu, a real estate developer, industrialist and philanthropist, said his election would allow him to expand his long-running community development work, including youth and women empowerment, support for vulnerable families, and youth mentorship.

Emeruem, a lawyer, expressed confidence that the party would win in Okigwe South and across the zone. He said his candidacy was driven by a desire to serve, and urged residents not to miss the opportunity to support him and the PDP.

Onye said he was ready to give Okigwe North a quality of representation it had not previously enjoyed, promising to be accessible and responsive to constituents’ needs.

Candidates for the Imo State House of Assembly also flagged off their campaigns. They are Hon. Uchenna Anyanwu (Ehime Mbano), Chinonyerem Ajaelu (Ihitte-Uboma), Hon. Godson Anyaeze (Obowo), Hon. Chima Iwundu (Isiala Mbano), Hon. Jude Obidiaku (Onuimo), and Hon. Anayo Offor (Okigwe).

The highlight of the event was the presentation of party flags to the candidates by Anyanwu.

Party leaders at the national, zonal, and state levels who attended the event included the National Youth Leader, Bala Aboki; Imo West senatorial candidate, Rt. Hon. Jones Onyereri; Imo East senatorial candidate, Prince Eze Madumere; Southeast Zonal Secretary, Hon. Mike Ahumibe; and state Chairman, Hon. Austine Nwachukwu.

Also present were the Southeast Zonal Ex-Officio, Mrs. Esther Aguwamba; state Secretary, Gerry Ogoko; state Auditor, Hon. Damian Ogu; state Vice Chairman (Owerri Zone), Hon. Geoffrey Ihentuge; state Financial Secretary, High Chief Osondu; state Publicity Secretary, Mr. Lancelot Obiaku; state Youth Leader, Hon. Eburuaja Ndubueze; state Organising Secretary, Felix Nwosu; state Woman Leader, Mrs. Edith Nwachi; and state Vice Chairman (Okigwe Zone) and Chairman of the Campaign Council, Hon. Emeka Ubenwunne.

World.title: Chappal Energies Dispute: Court Authorises Service of Contempt Notice on EFCC over Alleged Disobedience
World.content:
Wale Igbintade



The Federal High Court in Lagos has authorised the service of a contempt notice on the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) at its Abuja headquarters over alleged disobedience of a subsisting court order in the protracted ownership dispute involving Chappal Energies.

Justice D.I. Dipeolu, in an order made on November 6, 2026, granted an application by the Founder and Managing Director of Chappal Energies, Mr. Ufoma Joseph Immanuel, seeking permission to serve the commission with a Form 48 notice through an officer in charge of its legal department at its headquarters in Jabi, Abuja.

The Form 48, titled Notice of Consequences of Disobedience to Order of Court, is a procedural step towards initiating contempt proceedings against a party alleged to have disobeyed a subsisting court order.

Immanuel, through his counsel, C.U. Wogu of Tunji Braithwaite Law Partners, had approached the court through an ex parte motion dated September 16, 2026, seeking leave to serve the notice on the EFCC through its legal department or by conspicuously pasting it at the main entrance of the commission’s headquarters.

He also sought an order deeming service through the approved mode as good and sufficient for the contemplated contempt proceedings.

However, Justice Dipeolu granted only the first prayer, directing that the notice be delivered to the officer in charge of the EFCC’s Legal Department at Plot 301/302, Institutions and Research Cadastral District, Jabi, Abuja.

The Judge declined the second prayer seeking an order deeming such service automatically good and sufficient for the contemplated contempt proceedings.

In granting the application, Justice Dipeolu held that he had considered the motion and found merit in it, particularly in view of paragraphs 7 to 14 of the supporting affidavit.

The court subsequently adjourned the matter until December 1, 2026, for a report of service.

The latest development is connected to the protracted dispute between Immanuel and his business partner, Adebisi Adebutu of R28 Limited, over the ownership and control of Chappal Energies.

The dispute, which has generated several legal proceedings in Nigeria and overseas, reportedly involves contested shareholder rights, a disputed $100 million rights issue, questions surrounding an alleged $15 million payment, and proceedings in Nigeria, Mauritius, and international arbitration.

At the centre of the latest legal confrontation is the EFCC’s November 19, 2025 publication declaring Immanuel wanted over allegations of obtaining money by false pretenses and forgery.

Immanuel has consistently maintained that the disagreement with Adebutu is fundamentally commercial and relates to the parties’ shareholding arrangements, contractual obligations, and control of Chappal Energies.

The EFCC’s publication came despite an earlier order made on September 11, 2025, by Justice Josephine Obanor of the High Court of the Federal Capital Territory, restraining the commission and other respondents from arresting, detaining or prosecuting Immanuel over issues arising from the parties’ shareholding arrangements, cross-shareholding agreements, subscription rights and contractual obligations.

The FCT High Court had, among other things, considered the dispute to be civil in nature.

Following the EFCC’s publication, Immanuel approached the Federal High Court in Lagos to challenge the commission’s action and seek the enforcement of his fundamental rights.

On February 10, 2026, Justice Dipeolu ruled that the EFCC’s publication declaring Immanuel wanted amounted to an infringement of his constitutional rights to personal liberty and freedom of movement.

The Judge also held that the commission lacked the statutory power to restrain the applicant’s fundamental rights through the publication of November 19, 2025, particularly in the face of a subsisting court order.

Consequently, the court directed the EFCC to retract and withdraw all publications declaring Immanuel wanted and replace them with a public notice retracting the declaration.

Justice Dipeolu further awarded N5 million in damages against the commission as compensation for the infringement of Immanuel’s rights to personal liberty, freedom of movement and dignity.

However, Immanuel’s lawyers maintain that the EFCC has failed to comply with the judgment and the earlier restraining order.

They also contend that the commission proceeded with criminal charges against their client despite the subsisting judicial directives.

On March 11, 2026, the EFCC arraigned Immanuel and his company, IIHL, before Justice Mojisola Dada of the Lagos State High Court, Ikeja Division, on a two-count charge bordering on forgery and obtaining $1.5 million by false pretenses.

The applicant’s legal team maintains that the criminal proceedings arose from the same commercial disagreement that formed the subject of the earlier FCT High Court order.

In October 2026, Justice Obanor reportedly issued a further restrictive injunction reaffirming her earlier order and restraining the commission from continuing with the criminal proceedings at the Ikeja High Court.

According to Immanuel’s lawyers, the judge held that the September 11, 2025 order remained binding on the EFCC and other defendants, having neither been set aside nor lawfully discharged.

Addressing the Federal High Court on November 6, Wogu reportedly argued that the commission’s continued failure to comply with the subsisting judgment raised fundamental questions about respect for judicial authority and the rule of law.

The lawyer maintained that the EFCC’s conduct amounted to a continuing disregard for the authority of the courts, insisting that a law enforcement institution could not demand obedience to the law from citizens while treating adverse judicial decisions as optional.

The applicant’s legal team also raised concerns over a recorded conversation allegedly involving Adebutu, a media commentator, and a member of Immanuel’s family.

According to the lawyers, the recording contained statements suggesting that pressure from law enforcement proceedings could be reduced if Immanuel relinquished his position in Chappal Energies.

The lawyers disclosed that the recording had been tendered in the ongoing judicial proceedings. However, the allegations arising from it have not been independently established by a court.

They also cited the Supreme Court’s decision in Ojukwu v. Military Governor of Lagos State, which established an important principle against executive disregard for the authority of the courts. The matter has been adjourned to December 1 for report of service.

World.title: Orlando Pirates midfielder makes decision on his future
World.content:
Makhehleni Makhaula has zero plans of quitting professional football when his contract with Orlando Pirates ends at the end of the season.

The 37-year-old midfielder from Randfontein is said to be planning to play football on the green grass next season.

Makhaula is set to become a free agent when his contract with the Sea Robbers ends in June 2027.



The former AmaZulu midfielder has struggled for regular game time during the 2026/27 Betway Premiership season. The Buccaneers’ Moroccan head coach Abdeslam Ouaddou has opted for the likes of Simphiwe Selepe and Mtheleleli Mthiyane in the number six role.

Makhaula had initially considered retiring at the end of last season. However, Orlando Pirates chairman Irvin Khoza famously persuaded him to extend his stay by another year to provide leadership and experience within the squad.

There had also been speculation that the veteran could move into a non-playing position at the club once his contract expires.

His representative, Sizwe Ntshangase, has now dismissed those suggestions, insisting that his client wants to continue playing.

“Yes, his contract ends in June. Makhehleni is definitely playing next season,” Ntshangase told KickOff.

“His body feels great, his hunger for the game hasn’t faded, and he still has plenty to offer at the highest level.” He added: “He will continue playing next season.”



37-YEAR-OLD STILL HAS MORE TO OFFER

His next destination remains uncertain. Makhaula’s recent achievements could make him an attractive option for clubs looking for experience ahead of the 2027/28 campaign.

The midfielder played 17 matches across all competitions during Pirates’ historic 2025/26 domestic treble-winning campaign.

That success included ending the club’s 14-year wait for another league title. It came a season after Makhaula was named the 2024/25 Premiership Midfielder of the Season.

Before joining the Buccaneers in January 2023, the experienced campaigner had represented Free State Stars, Highlands Park and AmaZulu.

Whether Orlando Pirates offer him another playing contract or he pursues an opportunity elsewhere remains to be seen.

World.title: FIVE Kaizer Chiefs stars who could force their way into Bafana squad in 2027
World.content:
Kaizer Chiefs players have once again been left out of the Bafana Bafana squad, with head coach Pitso Mosimane announcing his 27-man selection without an Amakhosi representative.

Lebohang Maboe, who was included in the preliminary squad, failed to make the final cut.

With Bafana set to face Kenya in back-to-back matches, these will be their final fixtures of the year. However, there could be opportunities for some Chiefs players to force their way into the national team next year.



Here are five Kaizer stars who could earn Bafana Bafana call-ups in 2027.

Wandile Duba

The 22-year-old has been one of Chiefs’ standout performers this season, scoring seven goals in 11 appearances.

His impressive form has put him firmly in the conversation for a Bafana Bafana call-up. If he maintains his scoring touch and consistency, Duba could finally get his opportunity to represent the senior national team.

Bradley Cross

Cross was the only Kaizer Chiefs player included in the Bafana Bafana squad for the World Cup.



Having already been part of the national team setup, the defender has an advantage over some of his teammates. Regular game time and avoiding injuries could put him in a strong position to earn another call-up next year.

Bafana squad without Kaizer Chiefs stars

Lebohang Maboe

Maboe has already earned several Bafana Bafana call-ups and remains a player with international experience.

However, injuries have disrupted his progress and prevented him from making his official return to the national team. If he stays fit and gets regular minutes at Chiefs, he could be back in Mosimane’s plans next year.

Rushwin Dortley

Dortley has looked solid since returning from injury and could once again attract the attention of the national team selectors.

Much will depend on his consistency and Mosimane’s plans for the defence. A potential friendly against Lesotho, for example, could provide an opportunity for the Bafana coach to experiment with different defensive options.

5. Mfundo Vilakazi

The 20-year-old Kaizer Chiefs youngster has shown encouraging form this season and could emerge as another option for Bafana Bafana.

Vilakazi’s creativity and ability to operate in attacking midfield could make him an interesting prospect, particularly if Mosimane looks to manage Relebohile Mofokeng’s workload or explore alternative options in the number 10 role.

For now, it remains to be seen whether any Kaizer Chiefs player can force their way into the Bafana Bafana setup.

World.title: Qantas’ new Cape Town to Sydney non-stop flight: Here’s how much it costs
World.content:
Qantas will fly non-stop between Sydney and Cape Town three times a week from 19 October 2027. Image: Pexels

Qantas’ Cape Town flights are officially on sale, giving the Mother City its first-ever non-stop route to Australia.

The airline opened bookings last week for a new seasonal route between Sydney and Cape Town.

The first flight takes off on 19 October 2027.



Until now, Australians heading to Cape Town have had to change planes in cities such as Johannesburg, Dubai or Doha.

From next October, passengers will be able to fly direct in under 12 hours (from Cape Town to Sydney) and 14 hours 40 minutes on the way back.

When the Qantas Cape Town flights will operate

The seasonal service will run from 19 October 2027 to 24 March 2028, covering Cape Town’s peak summer months.

Flights will operate three times a week, on Tuesdays, Fridays and Sundays.

According to Qantas’ published schedule:

QF89 departs Sydney at 09:15 and lands in Cape Town at 14:40 the same day

departs Sydney at and lands in Cape Town at the same day QF90 departs Cape Town at 17:55 and arrives in Sydney at 14:50 the next day

The route will use Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners and add almost 30 000 seats between Australia and South Africa.



Why Qantas chose Cape Town

Qantas already flies non-stop from Sydney and Perth to Johannesburg.

Many of those passengers then connect to Cape Town on flights run by its partner airline, Airlink.

“Every year, tens of thousands of customers use our services to Johannesburg to connect to Cape Town through our partner Airlink, so we know there is strong demand for a non-stop service,” said Qantas International CEO Cam Wallace.

The announcement also comes 75 years after Qantas began scheduled passenger services to South Africa.

What it means for Cape Town tourism

Wesgro, the Western Cape’s official tourism, trade and investment agency, has welcomed the new route.

Wesgro CEO Wrenelle Stander highlighted the importance of direct flights for tourism, trade and investment.

Return fares start from R19 327 for no bells and whistles at all from Cape Town to Sydney.

World.title: Springboks: Recent record against France under threat?
World.content:
Although France have established themselves as one of the most dangerous teams in international rugby in recent times, their record against the Springboks certainly doesn’t reflect that.

Between 2011 and 2009, France managed to beat the Springboks on six occasions in nine Test matches, while one game was drawn.

However, there has been a complete reversal in fortunes since then, with South Africa emerging victorious in nine out of the last 10 Tests, including the thrilling 2023 World Cup quarter-final win by one point.



There are currently 5.60 rankings points between the No 1-ranked Springboks and fourth-placed France, but an extremely competitive battle is expected at the Stade de France on Friday.

Springboks not buying into favourites tag against France

Earlier this week, Rassie Erasmus said both teams were having to contend with injury absentees, and that there was no clear difference on who should be seen as favourites.

“We’re at the back end of our season, and we’ve got a maximum of three games left,” Erasmus continued. “I think June is their window where they’re really match-fit, energetic and they’re not punch drunk.

“We feel at the end of the season we really have to graft – us, New Zealand, Australia, maybe Japan, Argentina. And they are building up to these matches, and then they have the Six Nations in two months’ time.

“But I sometimes struggle to understand why, if we’re clear favourites, it doesn’t make a difference, or when they’re clear favourites, it doesn’t make a difference.

“So, when it comes to being the favourites, they might think they are, and we might think we are. The only bad thing about thinking you’re the favourites is you might become complacent, and we are definitely not complacent for this game.”



Kick off is at 22:10 (SA time).

World.title: France shock by picking Antoine Dupont at flyhalf against Springboks
World.content:
Antoine Dupont will start at flyhalf against South Africa in their Nations Championship match in Paris on Friday, 13 November. Image: JEFF PACHOUD / AFP

France coach Fabien Galthie announced on Wednesday that captain Antoine Dupont would play at flyhalf against South Africa in their Nations Championship match on Friday, 13 November.

Kick-off at the Stade de France in Paris is at 22:10 (SA time).

READ | How the Springboks looked the last time they played France



Missing key players

Les Bleus are missing their four first-choice number 10s in Romain Ntamack, Matthieu Jalibert, Antoine Hastoy and Thomas Ramos, who usually plays at fullback but is also a top-class flyhalf.

Dupont and Maxime Lucu had been widely expected to line up in the half-back positions, but with the captain retaining his scrumhalf spot.

Lucu had come on at flyhalf outside Dupont against Fiji last week to replace Ntamack, who suffered a shoulder injury just past the half-hour mark.



But against the Springboks, their roles will be reversed.

South Africa boast a good record in Paris

Galthie has opted to beef up his pack against the fearsome Springbok forwards on Friday night at the Stade de France, with Julien Marchand picked in place of Maxime Lamothe at hooker.

Former captain Gregory Alldritt makes his return to the team for the first time in a year at No 8 with fellow back-rower Paul Boudehent injured.



France have lost nine of their last 10 encounters against the Springboks, including the last five meetings at the Stade de France.
