World.title: Heatwave and water demand: Could hot weather strain SA’s water supply?
World.content:
Cracked, dry ground highlights concerns over water availability as South Africa's heatwave drives up demand. Image: Pexels

South Africa’s prolonged heatwave is driving up water demand and putting additional pressure on already strained water supply systems.

A strong El Niño could prolong warmer-than-normal conditions into 2027, raising further concerns about water availability.

The Department of Water and Sanitation (DWS) has urged residents, especially in Gauteng, to save water as demand rises ahead of the 2026/27 summer season.



Department spokesperson Wisane Mavasa said the current heatwave, which has entered its third consecutive week, is increasing water demand across Gauteng.

“This is compounding existing challenges, particularly substantial water losses through leaking municipal distribution infrastructure and high average consumption per capita in certain areas,” Mavasa said.

The department warned that excessive water use in areas with reliable supplies could worsen shortages in communities already experiencing water supply disruptions.

Gauteng residents use more water

DWS figures show that Gauteng residents consume approximately 250 litres of water per person daily, well above the international average of 173 litres.

The province also loses significant volumes of water through its supply system.

Non-revenue water stands at an estimated 47%, with physical water losses accounting for about 27%.



These figures highlight the pressure on water resources as households increase consumption during prolonged hot conditions.

El Niño raises concerns about prolonged heat

The heatwave comes as the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) warns that a very strong El Niño could intensify global heat and extreme weather risks well into 2027.

The anticipated El Niño could also influence rainfall patterns, increasing the risk of below-normal rainfall in parts of southern Africa.

For South Africa, reduced rainfall could limit dam inflows, while higher temperatures could increase evaporation and household water consumption.

DWS cannot provide additional water to Rand Water

DWS has stressed that it cannot simply increase water allocations to meet rising demand.

The department allocates Rand Water an annual abstraction volume from the Integrated Vaal River System (IVRS).

It only adjusts allocations when severe drought conditions or long-term assessments justify a change.

Mavasa said the department could not provide Rand Water with additional water beyond its authorised allocation.

She urged residents to reduce consumption by taking shorter showers, repairing leaking taps and pipes.

Turning off taps when brushing their teeth and limiting garden watering to between 6pm and 6am.

Residents must also follow municipal water-use restrictions. This includes limits on hosepipes, vehicle washing and swimming pool maintenance.

World.title: How much you need to earn to afford Princess Diana’s R150 million Constantia retreat
World.content:
The former Cape Town retreat associated with the late Princess Diana comes with a R150 million price tag - but what would a buyer need to earn to afford the property? Image: Dogon Group

A piece of Cape Town property history could change hands for an eye-watering R150 million, but prospective buyers will need considerably more than a taste for luxury to afford it.

Tarrystone Estate, in the exclusive suburb of Upper Constantia, is reportedly being offered for sale off-market, with an expected price of around R150 million.

READ | How much you need to earn to live in SA’s 10 most expensive suburbs



The estate is associated with the late Princess Diana, who stayed there during visits to South Africa.

Its appeal goes beyond its royal connection, however, with an expansive property, private leisure facilities and a collection of African art.

For anyone considering a purchase at the reported price, the financial commitment would be enormous.



A R150 million property with a remarkable past

Set on 8 040m², Tarrystone is a substantial private estate featuring a main residence, guest cottages, two vineyards, a swimming pool, tennis court and private cinema.

One of its most distinctive features is a secluded thatched cottage where Princess Diana reportedly stayed. Her bedroom is said to have been preserved, adding to the property’s historical significance.

The estate was previously owned by Princess Diana’s brother, Earl Charles Spencer, who sold it in 2012.



The financial reality of buying the estate

At a reported price of R150 million, financing the purchase through a home loan would come with eye-watering monthly repayments.

Based on a prime lending rate of 10.75%, a hypothetical 100% bond would cost approximately R1.52 million per month over 20 years.

Extending the repayment period to 30 years would bring the instalment down to around R1.4 million.



Using an illustrative affordability guideline that limits bond repayments to 30% of gross monthly income, a buyer would need to earn approximately:

R5.1 million per month for a 20-year bond

for a 20-year bond R4.7 million per month for a 30-year bond

Bond affordability Estimate Property price R150 million Deposit R0 Bond amount R150 million Interest rate 10.75% Repayment term 20 years Monthly bond repayment R1 522 843 Required gross monthly income R5 076 145

These estimates assume no deposit and an unchanged interest rate throughout the loan term. They are not a guarantee of finance approval, particularly for a property at this price level.

Banks would assess a buyer’s overall financial position, including existing debt, expenses, credit history and income.



The price of maintaining a luxury estate

The bond would be only one part of the cost of owning Tarrystone.

A buyer would also need to budget for transfer duty, legal and bond registration costs, insurance, municipal rates, security and the upkeep of an estate of this size.

Maintaining vineyards, guest accommodation, extensive grounds and private facilities would add to the ongoing expense.



The reported R150 million price therefore represents the starting point of a significant financial commitment.

For the eventual buyer, Tarrystone offers more than a luxury home in one of Cape Town’s most sought-after residential areas. It offers a property with a distinctive history and a connection to one of the world’s most recognisable royal figures.

Whether the estate achieves its reported asking price remains to be seen.

World.title: Swimming away! Tatjana's Dutch switch is not South Africa's only loss
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Tatjana Smith's decision to swim under the Netherlands flag has shocked many South Africans.

However, she is not the only swimmer to take their talents elsewhere.

South Africa's sporting administration is in shambles, with no end in sight.

Smith has been involved in a legal dispute with Swimming South Africa over $35,000 (R578,000) in prize money from the World Aquatic Championships that the federation withheld.

A year after it was supposed to be paid to her, saying she wore a personal sponsor's costume (Speedo) instead of the federation's sponsor (Arena).

Swimming SA has since apologised after facing legal demands and parliamentary scrutiny and paid the prize money plus R75,000 in interest, after they had previously claimed the interest was a "management fee".

They are also embroiled in a legal battle with athletes, including a R7.2-million lawsuit threat from artistic swimmers Laura Strugnell and Jessica Hayes-Hill over sanctions and a disciplinary process, as well as an ongoing tit-for-tat friction with Water Polo South Africa.

Tired of the administrative nightmare.

World.title: Seamer Duffy back in New Zealand squad for India Tests
World.content:
WELLINGTON - Seamer Jacob Duffy is in line for his first Test appearance in 11 months after being named Wednesday in a 14-man New Zealand squad to face India in a two-match series this month.

Duffy starred with 23 wickets in the 2-0 series win over the West Indies almost a year ago but sat out the tour of England this year because of the birth of his first child.

Duffy will compete for a place with pace options Matt Henry, who has recovered from a quadricep injury suffered last month, Kyle Jamieson, Nathan Smith and Blair Tickner.

The batting line-up will depend on the fitness of several players.

"Tom Blundell (quadricep), Devon Conway (concussion) and Rachin Ravindra (shoulder) are working through their respective injuries and aiming to be available for the first Test," said a New Zealand Cricket statement announcing the squad.

The series will see the two nations meet in red ball cricket for the first time since New Zealand's historic 3-0 Test series win in India in 2024.

"This series marks the start of an exciting summer of Test cricket," said head coach Rob Walter, whose team will begin a four-Test series in Australia next month and then host Sri Lanka for two Tests in February.

"The squad is largely consistent with the team that competed in England earlier this year, so it'll be great to be back together to try and recreate some of that success on home soil."

The first Test against India begins in Wellington on November 19 with the second in Christchurch on November 27.

World.title: EU to make addictive app features easier to switch off
World.content:
BRUSSELS - The European Union will on Wednesday unveil new rules to crack down on influencer marketing, ban online features that trick Europeans and force platforms to give users the right to turn off "addictive" features.

The EU already has a raft of laws covering data protection, artificial intelligence and online content but Brussels and campaigners argue there are gaps that leave consumers exposed to harmful digital practices.

The bloc's executive will unveil a much-needed update of consumer rules dubbed the "Digital Fairness Act" (DFA) that will give it the power to slap fines on companies of up to six percent of their annual turnover in large-scale cases.

The financial harms to European consumers are vast: official data showed "problematic" digital practices led to losses for individuals reaching 10.3 billion euros ($11.5 billion) a year.

Based on draft documents seen by AFP, the proposal will include:

-- a ban on "dark patterns", the practice of tricking users into making unwanted purchases or opting in to certain settings without their knowledge

-- stricter rules on how brands promote content through influencers, demanding clear labels such as "" on posts

-- a ban on offering minors "pay-to-win" or "pay-to-progress" features, and a requirement for in-game virtual currencies to show their real-world value

-- platforms must remind consumers when a free trial period ends with details about the end date and how much it will cost to continue

-- access to human customer service operators when users demand it.

EU consumer protection chief Michael McGrath has previously said the new rules aim to "step up our fight against unfair commercial practices", pointing to data that shows 97 percent of popular platforms use dark patterns.

The European Consumer Organisation's Agustin Reyna said the proposal is a "much-needed tool to give consumers back control of how much time and money they spend online".

- 'Safety net' -

Questions have been raised over the EU's expanding digital rulebook after Brussels unveiled plans to ban children under 13 from social media, and force companies to make platforms safe for use by minors -- in addition to sweeping rules already in place under the Digital Services Act.

But Spanish EU lawmaker Laura Ballarin Cereza said the proposal aimed to make a "safer online space for everyone, children and adults alike", adding it will "fill the gaps" as "consumer law is meant to act as a safety net".

The EU also wants users to know the full price of an order before checkout, banning a practice known as "drip pricing" where fees are hidden until the end.

The European Commission, the bloc's digital watchdog, has faced pressure from EU lawmakers and consumer advocates who accuse it of failing to enforce its online content and competition rules.

"Strong rules only matter if they are properly enforced," said the Euroconsumers group, which represents users' rights across several EU countries.

NGO Finance Watch said the proposal on dark patterns goes "in the right direction, but they lack ambition to sufficiently protect consumers in financial services".

The group also warned there were "significant holes" in the draft plans. "Firms could still pay influencers to promote risky investments," it said.

Finance Watch in September raised concerns about financial influencers and the risks to consumers posed by "misleading" information.

World.title: Many AI companies will adopt advertising: ad chief Criteo
World.content:
LISBON - Many AI platforms will end up eventually adopting advertising, the head of the online advertising agency Criteo told AFP Tuesday, as investors are focused on whether the technology will ever be profitable.

"I believe that a lot of AI platforms will find their way to advertising models over time," said the group's chief executive Michael Komasinski on the sidelines of the Web Summit in Lisbon.

"Advertising is the most scalable business model in the world. It has paid for most of the large platforms that we all use and enjoy today, whether it's Google, Meta, Snapchat.

"The ad formats will continue to become more interesting, more innovative, and certainly more native to that conversational experience," he added.

Pressure to boost revenue to cover its colossal spending pushed OpenAI to begin testing advertising in ChatGPT in February in the United States for free and low-cost tier subscriptions.

It has subsequently begun to progressively roll out ads worldwide, in cooperation with Criteo.

OpenAI's rival Anthropic, which is set to go public with a stock listing, has said it doesn't plan to integrate advertising in its AI tools due to data protection concerns as well as to protect the interests of its users.

Microsoft has used ads in its public version of Copilot AI since 2023.

Perplexity has experimented with ads in the United States since 2024.

Google is considering integrating ads in Gemini.

Developing AI models and rolling them out requires massive investments.

The rally in AI-related stocks that has buoyed markets this year was testament to investor confidence, but both equity and bond investors have recently grown more wary as inflation and high interest rates are making the endeavour even more expensive.

Criteo works with OpenAI in 89 countries to develop advertising campaigns on AI chatbots.

Komasinski said some 3,600 brands have trialled AI advertising campaigns and they have noted a modest increase in their spending on ChatGPT.

He remains sceptical about AI agents being able to autonomously make purchases.

"It's actually really easy to order unimportant things, and things that are very important you would tend to not delegate to a bot," he said.

World.title: Central America grapples with footballing decline
World.content:
SAN SALVADOR - On a patch of overgrown, yellowing grass in a crowded San Salvador neighbourhood, 12-year-old Bryan Oliva dreams of becoming a professional footballer.

Hundreds of kilometres away, in a remote Honduran village, 11-year-old Darixon Rivas harbours the same ambition, training on a muddy pitch after finishing his chores on the family farm.

For both boys, the odds are stacked against them in a region where football is struggling to escape the past, starved of investment and increasingly left behind by its rivals.

"You can earn a lot of money (as a soccer player), but I don't feel like it's possible for me," Oliva told AFP in Zacamil, a densely populated neighbourhood of apartment blocks in the Salvadoran capital.

He dreams of using football to provide for his family, but fears youngsters from humble backgrounds like his have little chance of being spotted by scouts, with the few opportunities available concentrated in wealthier areas.

Poverty affects roughly half of Central America's population, but the malaise gripping its football runs deeper.

With few exceptions, investment in infrastructure and youth development is woefully inadequate, leaving a once-competitive footballing region struggling to produce new generations of talent.

"We have a long way to go," Yamil Bukele, president of the Salvadoran Football Federation, recently acknowledged as he spearheaded a plan to strengthen the country's youth football.

- Regression -

World.title: LIVE | Matlala back at Madlanga Commission for more questioning
World.content:
PRETORIA - Alleged crime boss Vusimuzi ‘Cat’ Matlala is back at the Madlanga Commission.

He has spent the past two days answering questions about his statement to IDAC investigators.

However, he has refused to answer some questions, repeatedly invoking his right against self-incrimination.

Matlala has admitted paying former deputy police commissioner Shadrack Sibiya R500,000, which he claims was intended for a family wedding.

He is expected to face further questions about his alleged links to senior police officers.

World.title: Gauteng braces for second heatwave of the year
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Gauteng residents can expect a few more days of scorching temperatures.

The province is set to experience its second heatwave of the year.

It is expected to start on Wednesday afternoon and last until Friday.

The South African Weather Service says temperatures could reach 36 degrees in some areas.

Johannesburg Emergency Services is urging residents to drink plenty of water and avoid direct sunlight between 11am and 3pm.

There could be some relief from Friday, with showers and thunderstorms forecast.

World.title: Malema faces legal challenge over his JSC membership
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The Helen Suzman Foundation has approached the Western Cape High Court in a bid to have Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) leader Julius Malema removed from the Judicial Service Commission (JSC).

Malema is accused of repeatedly attacking judges who rule against his party, raising concerns that his conduct could undermine judicial independence.

Judges Matter’s Alison Tilley says the JSC has finally issued a draft code of conduct, something the organisation has been calling for over a long period.

She says while political parties and organisations that nominate representatives to the JSC are generally responsible for holding them accountable, the draft code could be a step in the right direction.

World.title: Where are they? Senators missing in action as CSs appear for questioning
World.content:
Senate Speaker Amazon Kingi welcomes Energy CS Opiyo Wandayi to his office at Parliament buildings. [Edwin Nyarangi, Standard]

Senators are on the spot for failing to turn up for Cabinet Secretaries' question time two weeks in a row, raising concerns over their commitment to their legislative duties.

Senate Speaker Amason Kingi was forced to adjourn the House on Wednesday morning, something that also happened on Wednesday last week, despite the relevant Cabinet Secretaries turning up.

World.title: Sakaja defends Sh43.7b drop in Nairobi County's pending bills before Senate
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja tells Senate that the Sh118 billion in pending bills was inherited from his predecessors. [File, Standard]

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja has told the Senate that pending bills in the city have been reduced from Sh118.79 billion to Sh75.07 billion through verification and payment.

Sakaja revealed that internal verification established that the Sh43.73 billion reduction was not achieved solely through payments but also involved legal assessments, court-ordered adjustments and the verification of disputed claims.

The governor, who appeared before the Senate County Public Accounts Committee at Parliament Buildings in Nairobi on Monday, said addressing the inherited debt required establishment of a verification committee to scrutinise the entire outstanding amount and establish the validity of the claims.

“The reduction of Nairobi County pending bills by Sh 43.73 billion was not achieved entirely through cash payments but also involved adjustments arising from legal assessments, suspended government-guaranteed loans, court-ordered reductions and disputed claims,” said Sakaja.

He told the Senate Committee chaired by Homa Bay Senator Moses Kajwang that the Sh118 billion in pending bills was inherited from his predecessors and that he had constituted a committee to undertake an internal verification of the entire amount before payments were done.

Sakaja explained that the verification established that the reduction was not solely through payments but also involved adjustments arising from legal assessments, suspended government-guaranteed loans, court decisions and disputed claims.

“I would like to inform Senators that my administration has provided a detailed schedule accounting for the Sh43.73 billion pending bills reduction through adjustments and reconciliations,” he said.

The governor said that of this amount Sh1.63 billion related to legal assessments, while Sh19.14 billion represented government-guaranteed loans whose servicing had been suspended due to a lack of supporting documentation and loan schedules.

Sakaja told Senators that Sh19.2 billion related to LAPFUND interest and penalties which the County said had been reduced following a court consent that brought the claim down to approximately Sh8.2 billion.

He said that they had provided a signed indemnity form, in accordance with County Treasury rules governing misplaced payment documents, alongside a financial memo confirming that the works had been undertaken and payment made.

“The audit further raised concerns over Sh16.04 million in receivables from non-exchange transactions, which lacked sufficient supporting documentation,” said Sakaja.

The governor told senators that beyond the verification of pending bills his administration had also strengthened the county’s legal department to reduce expenditure on external legal services and protect public resources.

Sakaja noted that through the reforms, Nairobi saved approximately Sh8.48 billion in legal costs over two financial years by expanding its in-house legal capacity, handling more litigation internally and negotiating reductions in legal fees claimed by private advocates.

According to the County Assembly’s Justice and Legal Affairs Committee, of the 174 court cases concluded during the period under review, 84 were handled by the County’s in-house legal team, with 47 determined in Nairobi’s favour, representing a 56 per cent success rate.

Kajwang, commended the County for reducing its pending bills but asked the Governor to provide additional documentation supporting the payments and processes undertaken to account for the Sh43.73 billion reductions.

“The Senate County Public Accounts Committee requires further clarification on the verification exercise and the adjustments made to the outstanding debt,” said Kajwang.

World.title: Gachagua dismisses opposition divisions as 'polygamous family' rivalry
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua during a church service in Isinya, Kajiado County on November 8, 2026. [Peterson Githaiga, Standard]

Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua has dismissed claims of divisions within the Opposition, describing the disagreements among its leaders as normal sibling rivalry in a polygamous family, while insisting that the coalition remains united behind plans to field a single presidential candidate in the 2027 General Election.

Gachagua said the Opposition leaders were committed to working together to challenge President William Ruto, despite their differing opinions on the timing of selecting a joint presidential flagbearer and occasional disagreements among their political camps.

Speaking during a church service in Isinya, Kajiado County, the former Deputy President likened the political differences to children from the same father competing for attention but eventually uniting whenever an external threat emerges.

“The Opposition is united to a man, and we have agreed that we will have a single presidential candidate. Everybody is committed, and we talk on a daily basis. The only challenge is normal petty problems,” he said.

He added that the disagreements should not be interpreted as a breakdown of the coalition, maintaining that such differences were healthy and expected in a broad political alliance.

“Ile shida kidogo ni ya boma, watoto wengi wa baba mmoja. Watoto huko ndani, oh, baba anakupenda kuliko mimi. Mbona ulinunua kiatu kabla mimi? Si hiyo ni kawaida kwa polygamous family?” he posed.

Gachagua said the bigger threat to Opposition unity was not necessarily disagreements among its principals but the conduct of their supporters, social media influencers and political bloggers, whom he accused of fuelling unnecessary tensions through insults and online confrontations.

He cautioned Opposition leaders against allowing overzealous supporters to dictate their political relationships, warning that unchecked political attacks could eventually weaken the coalition and undermine its common objective.

“If there is anything to separate us, it is our supporters and social media bloggers. Wanawakisha moto hakuna, watu wangu na wa Matiang'i wanatukanana na sisi tunakula breakfast pamoja,” he said.

He further claimed that some political influencers associated with his DCP party had been recruited and allegedly paid by individuals opposed to him to attack his leadership and the party.

Gachagua urged coalition principals to exercise restraint and avoid reacting to every provocation from supporters, insisting that political leaders must remain focused on the bigger picture.

“I want to ask leaders in the Opposition, be careful. Don't listen to overzealous supporters and influencers; they will lead you astray. Remain focused,” he warned.

On the question of selecting a joint presidential candidate, Gachagua revealed that differences remained over the appropriate timing, with Wiper leader Kalonzo Musyoka proposing that the flagbearer be identified before December, while Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna favoured February and Narc Kenya leader Martha Karua suggested May.

Gachagua, however, argued that selecting a candidate too early could expose the individual to political pressure and possible frustration from the government.

He proposed April next year as a more suitable time, maintaining that the coalition was united on the principle of having one candidate even if its leaders differed on the timing.

The DCP leader also dismissed arguments that academic qualifications, experience or political credentials should determine who becomes the coalition's presidential candidate, insisting that electoral numbers and the support of ordinary Kenyans would ultimately decide.

“As others say they have experience and an agenda in the Opposition, the deciding factor is the numbers. I'm with the people. You say you have capacity, but the person to decide is the voter,” he said.

He added: “Akili nyingi ni nzuri, but bila kura unaweza kaa nayo nyumbani.”

World.title: Mudavadi urges Western Kenya to unite, says region cannot remain on sidelines
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Prime CS Musalia Mudavadi. [File, Standard]

Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi has urged Western Kenya to unite ahead of the 2027 General Election, saying the region must strengthen its political representation to have a greater say in national decision-making.

Speaking during a UDA delegates' meeting in Shitoto village, Mumias East, Kakamega County, he said Western Kenya could not afford to remain on the sidelines while decisions affecting the country were being made.

"2027 is the moment we must change the narrative. We must make sure that we are at the table where decisions are made. We cannot afford to remain spectators when the future of our country and our region is being determined," he said.

Mudavadi said parliamentary influence depended on numbers, arguing that electing more MPs would give the region a stronger voice in key parliamentary committees, including the Budget Committee.

"Parliament exercises authority in its own right. We want more MPs so that we can have a say in the Budget Committee and other important committees. These positions are secured through numbers, and numbers matter when decisions affecting the country are being made," he said.

Turning to the opposition, Mudavadi described its leaders as divided and challenged them to present clear manifestos outlining what they would offer Kenyans.

He said the divisions within the opposition would work in President William Ruto's favour as he seeks re-election in 2027, expressing confidence that he would win in the first round.

"We want Ruto to win without a petition. We want to thrash them in the first round," he said.

World.title: Family identifies two security officers involved in Abshir Abdi abduction
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

LSK president Charles Kanjama leads members in a protest over the disappearance of lawyer Abshir Abdi. [Benard Orwongo Standard]

The family of Nairobi lawyer Abshir Ahmedsadak Abdi has identified two security officers alleged to have taken part in their kin's abduction, even as his colleagues threatened mass protests to push for his release.

The Law Society of Kenya (LSK) said the two names have been forwarded to the police to aid in investigations and demanded that the office of the Inspector General of Police, Douglas Kanja, speed up the probe into the abduction.

"One is named Siad and the other is Hussein, and we want them released for investigation, arrest, prosecution, conviction, sentencing and imprisonment," said LSK.

The revelation came during a demonstration led by (LSK outside the office of the Deputy Inspector General of Police and other towns yesterday .

Abshir was forcibly taken on November 1 along Muchai Road, his vehicle was pursued and intercepted by armed individuals in two vehicles before he was seized.

While state security agencies have denied holding him in custody, court filings and colleagues suggest his abduction may be connected to his professional work representing clients in high-profile cases involving senior police officers.

Furthermore, the LSK presented additional names of security personnel linked to the incident, demanding immediate legal action against Chief Inspector Vitalis Kibet, Inspector Kennedy Kimani Karanja, Siad Mohammed, Abdurahman of the Anti-Terrorism Police Unit (ATPU), and KDF officer Ali Hussein.

The leadership voiced their frustration over the state's inaction and the alarming pattern of extrajudicial actions targeting officers of the court. Representatives insisted that lawyers must be allowed to execute their duties without fear of intimidation, torture, or abduction.

"We demand that the officers involved be handed over, arrested, prosecuted, and convicted. We will stand in the courts, in the streets, and in the boardrooms until abductions come to an end," they said in a statement.

The LSK has issued a stern ultimatum to the police command, including the president, DIG Gilbert Masengeli, Inspector General Douglas Kanja, and senior commanders. If Abshir is not released safely and the identified suspects are not formally charged in court by Monday, the LSK warned it will initiate private prosecutions itself.

Furthermore, the society threatened to bring activities to a complete shutdown and demand the immediate resignation of Kanja, Masingeli and Minister for Security Kipchumba Murkomen, carrying their demonstrations to Parliament and State House if necessary.

As court proceedings continue under a habeas corpus application at the Milimani High Court, the legal fraternity remains resolute: the protest at Jogoo House is merely the beginning of an unyielding campaign for justice and the rule of law.

In Nakuru, lawyers protested within the Law Courts, calling for his production.

“It is shocking that one of our colleagues was picked and today we do not know where he is. Unless we voice our concern, there will be complete lawlessness in the country,” said LSK member Ekaterina Handa. “Our lives matter and silencing lawyers is silencing justice. we will not relent until we get justice.”

Rift Valley LSK Chair Wangari Mwangi said it was shocking that the alleged abduction was captured on CCTV.

She rubbished the narrative that the missing lawyer was involved in a crime syndicate, maintaining that he should have been arrested and charged in court. [Additional reporting by Daniel Chege]

World.title: Goon financiers should be cursed and sent to hell, Chief Justice Koome says
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Chief Justice Martha Koome said goonism falls under serious organised crimes that goes against the Rome Statute and humanity. [Phares Mutembei, Standard]

Chief Justice Martha Koome now says those mobilising and financing goons should be cursed and thrown to hell.

Koome on Thursday said goonism falls under organised serious crimes that go against the Rome Statute and humanity.

She spoke at Kieganguru, Maara constituency, where she presided over the opening of the Maara law courts.

While calling on police to focus more on arresting the mobilisers and financiers, Koome said a time has come for the country to plead with God to protect the country and rescue the youth who are being misused and misled into organised gangs and goonism.

“Nobody gives birth to a child to be called a goon. Those organisers will go to hell, we curse them,” Koome said, adding, “If they will not go to hell they will meet God's justice. These are our children, and we reclaim them in the name of our Lord Jesus.”

According to her, the last time she checked, people are charged at the International Criminal Court with Organised crime.

She maintained that the best solution to the current goonism that wreaked havoc, especially in political meetings, is to arrest the organisers.

Koome said the courts cannot hold arrested goons without bail, yet the constitution grants them the right to bail or bond.

“When we arrest small people with petty crimes of causing disorder, the law allows us to release them on bail and bond, but when you bring the organisers, we will charge them under the Serious Crimes Act,” she said.

Koome said currently, the judiciary has gazetted a serious crimes division at the High Court to support Magistrates handling the cases.

“Let us look at the root cause of goonism across the country and rehabilitate those involved by getting them gainful employment,” she said.

Her sentiments, however, differ from those of Interior Cabinet Secretary Kipchumba Murkomen, who on Wednesday told the National Assembly that the judiciary was the weakest link in the fight against the menace.

Tharaka Nithi Governor Muthomi Njuki, in his remarks, supported Koome’s view of arresting the planners.

Njuki, who doubles up as the Council of Governors Chairperson, said politicians have had their time and organising goons against their opponents should not be condoned.

Using the analogy of a dog, Njuki said ‘every barking dog has an owner ’, and it is time serious action was taken against such characters at whatever level they are.

The county boss said CoG will work closely with county security teams to arrest the fast-rising menace and report all cases.

Security agencies have been under scrutiny regarding goons, with calls for their arrest and prosecution.

Earlier on, Koome and DCI boss Mohammed Amin differed on how to handle the goons during a National Council for Administrative Justice meeting as with the DCI boss also accusing the Judiciary of laxity and granting minor bail to arrested goons.

But Koome maintained the issue must be addressed lest it becomes a thorn in the flesh ahead of the 2027 elections.

World.title: IEBC warns UDA SG Hassan Omar over remarks on deceased voters
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

UDA Secretary General Hassan Omar meets Village Elders and Mabalozi wa Nyumba Kumi from Jomvu Sub-County’ on September 10, 2026. [Nehemiah Okwemba, Standard]

The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) has issued a stern warning to Senator Hassan Omar after finding him in breach of the Electoral Code of Conduct over remarks he made at a political rally in Mombasa, cautioning that any repeat offence could attract tougher sanctions.

In a determination released on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, the Electoral Code of Conduct Enforcement Committee (ECCEC) found Omar guilty of breaching paragraphs 6(k)(i) and 6(l) of the Electoral Code of Conduct.

The committee consequently issued the senator with a formal and strict warning and severe caution, directing him to comply with the electoral regulations for the remainder of the applicable election period.

Omar was further instructed to refrain from language or conduct that could reasonably be understood as encouraging or normalising electoral malpractice or undermining public confidence in the integrity of the ballot.

The decision follows investigations into remarks the senator allegedly made during a public rally in Mombasa on September 11, 2026, which raised concerns over the possibility of encouraging electoral malpractice.

According to the commission, Omar was summoned to appear before the committee on October 21, 2026, to respond to the allegations. He honoured the summons and appeared in person, accompanied by his lawyer, where he was given an opportunity to explain his remarks and present his defence.

In reaching its determination, the committee considered the context in which the statements were made, Omar's explanation that his words were intended figuratively to encourage voter registration and participation, his subsequent clarification and the absence of evidence linking the remarks to an actual electoral incident.

However, the committee maintained that the language used could not be excused by the explanation offered.

It observed that the impugned words, considered in their original Kiswahili form and ordinary meaning, invoked the use of biometric identification details belonging to a deceased person to facilitate voting in that individual's name.

The committee consequently found the remarks inconsistent with the obligation under paragraph 6(l) of the Electoral Code to reassure voters about the integrity of the ballot.

The warning places Omar on clear notice that any recurrence of similar conduct could attract more severe sanctions under the Electoral Code of Conduct and applicable laws.

“The determination places Hon. Hassan Omar on clear and unequivocal notice that the warning issued by the Committee is intended to mark a firm boundary against any recurrence of similar conduct,” IEBC stated.

The commission further emphasised that political leaders and other electoral stakeholders have a constitutional right to campaign, criticise, debate, persuade and participate in political discourse.

However, it cautioned that political expression must be exercised responsibly, warning that statements perceived as advocating, encouraging or normalising electoral malpractice could undermine public confidence in the electoral process.

“As Kenya prepares for the 2027 General Election, the Commission calls upon all political leaders, candidates, political parties, supporters and other electoral stakeholders to exercise responsibility, restraint and vigilance in their public utterances and conduct,” the commission said.

The determination comes as political activities gradually intensify ahead of the 2027 General Election, with the electoral body seeking to strengthen compliance with regulations governing political campaigns and public conduct.

IEBC maintained that enforcement of the Electoral Code should not be interpreted as an attempt to suppress legitimate political competition or freedom of expression.

Instead, it said the measures were intended to safeguard democratic participation and ensure that every Kenyan could exercise their right to vote without intimidation, manipulation or interference.

The commission reiterated its commitment to protecting the sanctity of the ballot, assuring Kenyans that every vote must be protected and counted in accordance with the law.

It warned that it would continue enforcing electoral regulations firmly, fairly and without fear or favour, as preparations for the 2027 elections gather momentum.

World.title: Death rumours made me stronger, says ODM leader Oburu
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Speakers Moses Wetang’ula and Amason Kingi when they paid a visit to ODM leader Oburu Oginga at his Nairobi residence on November 4, 2026. [Speaker’s Press Unit]

ODM leader and Siaya Senator Oburu Oginga has said rumours about his death while he was admitted to hospital only strengthened his determination to overcome his illness.

Dr Oburu who is recovering after being discharged from hospital, assured his supporters that he was making remarkable improvement and would return to active politics soon.

Speaking at his Nairobi residence on Wednesday when Speakers Moses Wetang’ula and Amason Kingi paid him a visit, the ODM leader said the rumours only strengthened his resolve to come out of the hospital bed.

“Those who wrote me off while I was in hospital by declaring me dead only made me stronger and more determined to fight my sickness. Here I am, recovering and growing stronger by the day,” he said.

He said that his recovery was a testimony to God's protection, saying those who had spread the false reports had been put to shame.

Oburu admitted that the illness had slowed down him down but he was looking forward to returning to the political arena.

“The sickness slowed my political activities. Very soon, I will be back roaring in the best way I know how,” he said.

The senator thanked the National Assembly Speaker Wetang’ula, his Senate counterpart Kingi and other legislators for taking time to visit him following his discharge from hospital.

He said the visit had lifted his spirit and revealed that he missed participating in parliamentary debates and engaging in national political affairs.

“I have no words to explain my feelings after the Speakers of both Houses and fellow legislators created time to come and check on me,” he said.

“I miss being on the floor of the House debating and roaring in the political arena. I urge my supporters to pray for me and be patient because soon I will be back,” he added.

Despite his recent health challenges, Oburu kept his visitors entertained with his trademark humour while expressing confidence that he would soon resume his political duties.

The two Speakers condemned the spread of false information on social media, particularly rumours that the senator had died while undergoing treatment.

Wetang’ula said they were encouraged by the senator's recovery and wished him a full and speedy return to good health.

He, however, cautioned Oburu against rushing back into politics before fully recovering, urging him to give his health priority.

“Prioritise your health and avoid rushing back into political engagements before making a full recovery,” he said.

The National Assembly Speaker also praised the senator for his courage and determination in facing his health challenges.

Kingi said the Senate missed Dr Oburu's contribution to debates, parliamentary proceedings and national politics.

“As the Senate, we miss your contributions to proceedings and debates as well as your guidance in national politics. We pray that you get better and resume your political duties as soon as possible,” he said.

Those who accompanied the two Speakers included Senate Chief Whip David Wakoli, Senate Minority Leader Stewart Madzayo, Senators William Kisang and Daniel Maanzo.

Others were National Assembly Minority Whip Millie Odhiambo, Parliamentary Commissioner Mishi Mboko and MP Eve Obara.

World.title: Egyptian Tax authority collects LE 14 billion through tax risk-assessment system: Official
World.content:
The Head of the Egyptian Tax Authority (ETA), Rasha Abdel-Aal, announced that the tax risk-assessment system has generated approximately LE 14 billion, noting that the ETA received around 750,000 voluntary disclosures, which contributed to a total tax yield of LE97 billion.

Speaking at a seminar organized by the Journalists Syndicate, Abdel-Aal added that the Tax Authority is undergoing a shift in its operational philosophy and approach to tax-related challenges.

This transition moves the focus beyond mere revenue maximization toward achieving a balance between increasing public treasury resources, safeguarding the interests of the business community, and streamlining its interactions with the tax system, she said.

The tax risk-assessment system stands as a cornerstone of the development and digital transformation plan currently being implemented by the ETA to modernize tax administration and enhance collection efficiency.

An effective system

The system leverages big data analytics and artificial intelligence systems to electronically screen taxpayer files, classifying them based on their level of tax compliance—all without human intervention.

This represents a significant paradigm shift, effectively ending the era of random, comprehensive audits for every single file.

The system operates through network connectivity and data integration, linking the Tax Authority’s own databases—most notably the e-invoicing and e-receipt systems—with those of other government entities, including the Customs Authority, the Commercial Register, banks, and investment authorities.

Through this integration, the system compares the actual transaction volumes of companies and individuals against the data provided in their tax returns, automatically flagging any unexplained gaps or discrepancies that may indicate potential tax evasion or undisclosed business activities.

Based on the findings of this analysis, field inspection and tax audit teams are directed exclusively toward high-risk files.

This has proven highly effective in identifying thousands of instances of non-compliance and ensuring the accurate and prompt collection of state treasury revenues.

Conversely, this mechanism offers a significant advantage to compliant taxpayers by sparing them from burdensome, routine audit procedures and fostering a stable, fair business environment.

These measures coincide with a package of tax facilitations introduced by the Finance Ministry and Tax Authority, aimed at building trust with the business community.

This policy seeks to encourage taxpayers—including those operating in the informal sector—to proactively file their tax returns and voluntarily regularize their tax status in order to benefit from the offered facilitations.

Furthermore, it aims to integrate the informal economy into the state’s formal system, thereby ensuring tax equity and bolstering the resources of the national economy.

World.title: Health Minister discusses training of Palestinian medical staff in Egyptian hospitals
World.content:
Health and Population Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar discussed with his Palestinian counterpart Majed Abu Ramadan ways to strengthen cooperation across all healthcare sectors and agreed on a plan to transfer Egypt’s expertise and experience to the Palestinian health sector, while continuing to provide humanitarian support to the Palestinian people.

During the meeting, Abdel Ghaffar underscored the deep-rooted fraternal ties between Egypt and Palestine, reaffirming Egypt’s commitment to providing all forms of support to help the Palestinian people through their current crisis.

For his part, the Palestinian health minister praised Egypt’s efforts and its humanitarian stance toward Palestine.

Health Ministry Spokesperson Hossam Abdel Ghaffar said the meeting saw an agreement on establishing a mechanism to receive Palestinian doctors from various specialties for training at Egyptian hospitals. The two sides also discussed the possibility of supplying the Palestinian side with ambulances equipped with the latest medical equipment.

The meeting also addressed telemedicine, describing it as an increasingly urgent technology for the Gaza Strip to speed up patient diagnoses and determine appropriate treatment, in addition to supporting cancer care and pharmaceutical supplies.

World.title: FM highlights food security as pillar of international peace, stability at G7 meeting
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty said food security is a fundamental pillar of international peace and stability, warning that conflicts, geopolitical tensions, climate change and disruptions to global supply chains are driving up food prices and placing mounting pressure on developing countries.

He outlined Egypt’s national efforts to strengthen food security by boosting agricultural production, diversifying import sources and upgrading storage and distribution systems.

Abdelatty made the remarks on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, while delivering a keynote address at a session on food security under the theme “Stability in the Middle East,” held as part of the G7 ministerial meeting in Paris.

The session brought together the foreign ministers of France, the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, Germany, Italy and Japan, as well as the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy and the foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia, Brazil and South Korea.

Abdelatty said the region was beset by multiple conflicts and stressed that political solutions, dialogue and diplomacy were the only way forward, ruling out military solutions to these disputes.

He pointed to the catastrophic situation in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, Israel’s restrictions on the entry of aid into Gaza and settler violence in the West Bank.

He stressed the need to ensure the regular flow of food commodities and agricultural production inputs, while safeguarding freedom of navigation through vital maritime routes. He also rejected the use of food as a means of political pressure or as a weapon in conflicts, underscoring the need to protect civilians and agricultural facilities and ensure the delivery of humanitarian assistance.

Abdelatty said Egypt’s hosting of the 18th Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD COP18) in 2028 would offer an opportunity to strengthen international cooperation in addressing drought and promoting the water-food nexus and land restoration, particularly in Africa.

He also stressed the importance of providing developing countries with the financing needed to adapt to climate change without imposing additional debt burdens on them.

The foreign minister warned that food security challenges were worsening in developing food-importing countries, particularly in Africa and the Arab region, as a result of conflicts, displacement and water scarcity.

Citing the situations in Gaza and Sudan, he said these crises were having severe repercussions for food supplies and livelihoods. He called for safe, adequate, regular and unhindered access for humanitarian aid, alongside efforts to restore domestic production capacity and rehabilitate infrastructure.

Abdelatty affirmed Egypt’s readiness to contribute to strengthening regional food security, drawing on its strategic location, infrastructure, ports, transport and logistics networks, grain storage facilities and food-processing capabilities. These assets, he said, could support global trade flows and the distribution of food commodities.

World.title: Suez Canal Marina receives first cruise ship in Ismailia
World.content:
Suez Canal Authority Chairman Osama Rabie announced, Tuesday, November 10, 2026, that the Suez Canal Yacht Marina in Ismailia has received passengers aboard the cruise ship ASTORIA GRANDE during its voyage to several Egyptian ports, as part of the authority’s efforts to promote maritime tourism.

In a statement, the authority said the visit marks the cruise ship’s first stop and berthing in Ismailia. The vessel transited the Suez Canal in the early hours of the day as part of the northbound convoy.

The ship is 193 meters long, 27.6 meters wide, has a draft of six meters and can accommodate up to 1,300 passengers. The visit is significant as the marina is being used for the first time as a tourist berth in Ismailia, providing a facility for receiving visitors and completing the necessary procedures in coordination with all relevant authorities.

Rabie said the Suez Canal Authority is seeking to strengthen the canal’s position as a key hub for maritime tourism and logistics services by developing its yacht marinas, equipping waiting areas and providing the infrastructure needed to berth cruise ships, while coordinating with the relevant authorities to facilitate procedures.

He added that the Suez Canal Yacht Marina represents a promising addition to the authority’s efforts to promote maritime and yacht tourism in the region. It offers an integrated package of services designed to boost tourism through organized domestic tour programs in Ismailia and outbound excursions to various governorates across Egypt.

The ship is scheduled to remain in Ismailia for 24 hours. During the stop, 335 tourists will visit local attractions, including the Suez Canal Museum, Ismailia Gardens, Abu Bakr Al-Siddiq Mosque and the Evangelical Church, among other landmarks.

Another 327 tourists will take part in an organized tour of Cairo, visiting major attractions including the Grand Egyptian Museum, the Giza Pyramids, Khan el-Khalili bazaar and Al-Muizz Street, as well as taking a Nile cruise.

Rabie said the ship’s itinerary includes several Egyptian ports. Its next stop will be Sharm El Sheikh, followed by Aqaba in Jordan and then Hurghada, before it transits the Suez Canal again on its return journey.

World.title: Up to $13 billion in remittances from Egyptians abroad over 9 months: CBE
World.content:
The Central Bank of Egypt (CBE) announced on Tuesday that remittances from Egyptians working abroad rose by 20.4 percent during the first quarter of the 2026/2027 fiscal year (the period from July to September 2026), reaching approximately US$ 13 billion, compared to about $ 10.8 billion during the same period the previous year.

CBE said in a statement that total inflows for the first nine months of 2026 reached a record $ 38.2 billion, up from approximately $ 30.2 billion during the corresponding period of the previous year.

Banking expert Tarek Metwally explained that this record increase in remittances reflects growing confidence in the Egyptian economy and the banking sector.

He attributed this to the success of measures taken by the CBE to stabilize the foreign exchange market and eliminate the currency rate gap between the official and parallel markets.

He added that the growth of remittances at this rate represents a positive and significant development for foreign currency resources.

Importance of remittances

Remittances are among the most important and sustainable sources of hard currency—alongside tourism revenues, exports, and foreign direct investment—and they have contributed to bolstering dollar liquidity, enhancing the state’s ability to meet its external obligations, and covering import requirements.

Metwally further explained that the reach of remittances to approximately $38.2 billion during the first nine months of 2026 confirms the continued upward trend of these inflows.

This reflects an increasing reliance by Egyptians abroad on official banking channels to transfer their savings, following the restoration of confidence in foreign exchange pricing mechanisms and the availability of foreign currency within the banking system.

He noted that maintaining this pace of growth would support stability in the foreign exchange market and alleviate pressure on the local currency.

Furthermore, it would strengthen the economy’s capacity to build robust foreign currency reserves and provide the banking sector with greater flexibility to address the needs of clients and importers.

Metwally emphasized the importance of continuing policies that preserve the flexibility of the foreign exchange market, while also offering competitive banking services to Egyptians living abroad.

This would therefore encourage them to continue sending remittances through official channels, effectively transforming these inflows into a sustainable source of support for the economy.

World.title: Egypt, Saudi Arabia join G7 talks on ME stability in Paris
World.content:
A session on Middle East stability opened in Paris on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, bringing together the foreign ministers of Egypt, Saudi Arabia and the Group of Seven (G7) countries on the second and final day of the bloc’s ministerial meeting.

Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and his Saudi counterpart Prince Faisal bin Farhan are attending the talks, which focus on energy security, supply stability, freedom of navigation through strategic waterways, particularly the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb, and Iran.

Discussions also cover regional developments in Syria, Lebanon, Yemen, and Palestine, as well as food security.

France has invited Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Brazil, South Korea and Ukraine to take part in the expanded G7+ meetings, chaired by French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot.

The meeting is the fourth and final G7 foreign ministers’ gathering under France’s 2026 presidency. The United States will assume the rotating presidency on Jan. 1, 2027.

World.title: When is Ramadan 2027 and Eid al-Fitr? All you need to know
World.content:
As 2026 draws to a close, Muslims are now eagerly looking forward to the arrival of the Ramadan holy month for 2027.

According to astronomical calculations, the first day of Ramadan is expected to fall on Monday, February 8, 2027, while Eid al-Fitr is projected to fall on Wednesday, March 10, 2027.

These dates are based on astronomical calculations; the official start of the holy month and the date of Eid al-Fitr will be confirmed following the traditional sighting of the crescent moon.

What is the Hijri calendar?

The Hijri calendar is based on the moon’s orbit around the Earth; the beginning and end of each month are determined by the moon’s movement. The time it takes for the moon to complete one full orbit around the Earth is known as a lunar month.

The Hijri calendar consists of 12 months, beginning with Muharram and ending with Dhu al-Hijjah. These months are: Muharram, Safar, Rabi’ al-Awwal, Rabi’ al-Thani, Jumada al-Ula, Jumada al-Akhirah, Rajab, Sha’ban, Ramadan, Shawwal, Dhu al-Qi’dah, and Dhu al-Hijjah.

The Hijri calendar—also known as the Islamic or lunar calendar—is associated with the Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab.

He designated the migration (hijra) of the Prophet Muhammad from Mecca to Medina as the starting point for the Islamic dating system, which took place in the year 622 CE.

It is from this event that the calendar derives its name, the “Hijri calendar.”

World.title: Will gold prices rebound after its decline in Egypt?
World.content:
Gold prices in the Egyptian market saw a decline during Tuesday’s trading, influenced by US inflation data that came in higher than market expectations.

The price of a gram of 21-karat gold fell to approximately LE 6,180, down from LE 6,250.

The Vice Chairman of the Gold and Jewelry Division at the Federation of Egyptian Chambers of Commerce (FEDCOC), Lotfi al-Moneeb, said that the US inflation data has strengthened the likelihood that the Federal Reserve will continue to tighten monetary policy and raise interest rates.

This, in turn, bolsters the US dollar and bond yields, placing downward pressure on gold globally.

Moneeb added that these expectations have led to a decline in global gold prices by approximately three percent, bringing them closer to the US$ 4,000-per-ounce level.

He explained that the Egyptian market has been influenced both by a decline in global gold prices and a notable improvement in the Egyptian pound’s exchange rate against the US dollar.

The dollar has retreated from levels exceeding LE56 in late October to approximately LE 53.4 currently, which has amplified the impact of the global price decline on the domestic market, Moneeb said.

Outlook for late 2026 into 2027

Regarding the outlook through the end of 2026 and into 2027, he indicated that price volatility is likely to persist, driven by the ongoing interplay between the escalation and de-escalation of global geopolitical tensions.

Moneeb noted that demand for gold jewelry has softened due to rising prices and diminished purchasing power—a consequence of the pound’s depreciation against the dollar—whereas gold bars and gold coins remain the most attractive options for those looking to save.

The market is not experiencing a cessation of buying, he assured,but rather a shift in consumer behavior – some are choosing to purchase during price dips, while others are waiting for greater stability.

Additionally, there are instances of individual selling—driven by the need to secure liquidity and cover living expenses—as a result of rising prices.

US inflation

The CEO of the platform iSagha, Said Imbaby, explained that US inflation exceeding market expectations exerts short-term pressure on gold and silver.

This is because it diminishes the likelihood of the Federal Reserve cutting interest rates, he said, while increasing the probability that a hawkish monetary policy will persist—or that interest rates may even be raised—in the near term.

Imbaby added that such a scenario could bolster the US dollar and bond yields, thereby reducing the appeal of gold and silver, both of which are assets that do not generate periodic returns.

He further emphasized the need to distinguish between short-term impacts and long-term fundamentals, noting that gold continues to benefit from central banks purchases, concerns regarding debt, and geopolitical tensions.

The iSagha CEO added that global projections for gold prices in 2027 vary; some forecasts place the average price per ounce at around $ 4,250, while others estimate it to be closer to $ 4,650.

According to Imbaby, the Egyptian market is influenced by several factors—not just the global price per ounce, but also the dollar-to-Egyptian-pound exchange rate and the dynamics of supply and demand.

Consequently, any projections for local prices in Egyptian pounds must be based on clear assumptions regarding the exchange rate.

Imbaby added that the Egyptian market is witnessing a shift in consumer behavior, with a segment of consumers moving toward saving and investing in gold bars and gold coins. These are preferred because they incur lower making charges and are relatively easier to resell compared to gold jewelry.

This was reflected in the growth of investment demand for gold during the third quarter of 2026, even as demand for gold jewelry declined, he added.

Imbaby noted that gold remains an important tool for hedging and diversifying savings; however, he advised approaching the current phase with caution, staggering purchases over time, and avoiding buying or selling decisions based on a single day’s market movement or an isolated economic report.

He further explained that market trends are shaped by the interplay of various economic and financial factors—particularly US interest rates, the performance of the dollar, inflation, investment and industrial demand, and geopolitical tensions.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Liberia: Monrovia City Mayor Siafa Dismissed, James Mulbah In
World.content:
Monrovia City Mayor Siafa Dismissed, James Mulbah In

Monrovia– President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has dismissed Monrovia City Mayor, John-Charuk Saah Siafa, nominating the General Manager of the Roberts International Airport (RIA) James K. Mulbah, has his replacement as new Mayor.

By Jaheim T. Tumu- [email protected]

His replacement, Mulbah joined the ruling Unity Party (UP) last December, declaring his confidence in the leadership and direction of President Boakai. Mulbah made the announcement during the Unity Party’s Homecoming Program, where he arrived at the party’s national headquarters accompanied by a large group of supporters.



In a endorsement said, he said, “My joining Unity Party today is not a political game.” He added that the UP was the first political party he had ever joined and that President Boakai’s stance against corruption was a major reason for his decision.

Asked then whether he harbored ambitions for elected office, he said he could not predict the future and that his focus was on joining the party. Mulbah would require confirmation by the Liberian Senate.

FrontPageAfrica reported early Monday that a prestigious source has informed the Siafa was out of favor with the Unity Party hierarchy after persistent complaints that the his institution was being starved.

However, Siafa has been axed after nearly three years of persistent public criticism of his handling of the capital — over piling garbage, unpaid workers and contractors, and allegations of financial irregularities — even as the mayor and his supporters have argued that the national government has never given the MCC the money it needs to do its job.

Siafa was nominated by President Boakai on January 27, 2024, and commissioned in March that year as Monrovia’s 28th mayor, succeeded Jefferson Tamba Koijee with promises to clean the city, restore transparency and depoliticize the MCC. He has been widely reported to be a close relative of the President.

But his tenure has been dogged by controversy. In June 2025, allegations of financial and procurement irregularities at the MCC surfaced in the press, including claims about the rapid elevation of staff to senior paid positions.

Earlier that year, MCC contractors protested in front of City Hall on UN Drive over unpaid wages, and the mayor and the Civil Service Agency came under fire from civil society over the dismissal of civil servants that critics described as political retaliation.

Some of the sharpest attacks have come from within the ruling party itself. In September 2025, Queen Johnson, Deputy Director for Records at the National Port Authority and a staunch UP member, publicly called for Siafa’s dismissal, labeling him corrupt and incompetent. Days later, MCC employees planned a protest demanding his resignation over the city’s persistent sanitation problems. In March 2026, another UP loyalist publicly branded the mayor a criminal amid allegations tied to an audit of the MCC.

World.title: Washington’s Blunt Verdict on Liberia’s Investment Climate
World.content:
MONROVIA — On paper, Liberia has rarely looked better. The economy grew 5.1 percent in 2025, mining and panning expanded by 17 percent, export volumes jumped 31.5 percent, and headline inflation eased to an average of 8.5 percent by December, down from a peak of 11.6 percent. The International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, the African Development Bank and the European Union are all underwriting the recovery.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Yet the United States government’s newest assessment of Liberia as a place to put money, published in early November in the State Department’s 2026 Investment Climate Statements, reads less like a sales brochure than a warning label.



Strip away the diplomatic packaging and the message to American companies is plain: the opportunities are real, the minerals are in the ground, the coastline is strategic — but bring patience, bring lawyers, and bring a plan for dealing with officials who expect to be paid.

Corruption as the “primary brake”.

The report’s harshest language is reserved for governance. It describes corruption as the main obstacle to both Liberia’s democratic consolidation and its economic growth, saying it raises costs, causes delays and exposes investors to legal and reputational risk.

Citing business surveys and U.S. Embassy reporting, the statement says some officials put short-term personal gain ahead of the investment climate, and that political cronyism often shapes decisions that should rest on merit. In one of its most striking passages, it says businesses can find it easy to operate illegally if the right political interests are paid — while companies that follow the rules get little help at best and, at worst, become targets for bribe demands.

Multinational firms, the report adds, frequently say they are charged fees that appear nowhere in their investment agreements, and accounts of extortion “at multiple levels of government” are common. The worst areas, it says, are procurement, contract and concession awards, customs and tax administration, regulatory approvals and government payment systems.

Liberia has signed the relevant regional, continental and United Nations anti-corruption conventions. The State Department’s assessment is that membership “has not produced measurable reductions in corruption.” Enforcement of domestic anti-graft laws, it says, is inconsistent, and even-handed application is “the exception rather than the rule.”

The report does give President Joseph Boakai’s administration some credit: asset declaration requirements, investigations into irregularly awarded contracts, a push by the Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission for a specialized criminal court for corruption cases, and a proposed amendment that would remove the statute of limitations on corruption prosecutions. But it labels these “nascent” efforts — a polite way of saying the results are not yet visible.

Courts that cannot keep up

For investors, a corruption problem becomes a courtroom problem the moment a contract goes wrong. Here the report is equally blunt.

The Commercial Court, which handles disputes of $15,000 and above, is described as severely backlogged, with cases taking two to five years. Judgments — especially against government entities — are hard to enforce. The report notes regular media accounts of executive interference in judicial and legislative matters, and widespread reports that court officials solicit bribes to act on cases. Appeals land at a five-member Supreme Court that is buckling under the volume.

The consequences ripple into the wider economy. Because collateral is so hard to recover through the courts, banks demand more of it and lend less, which feeds high rates of bad loans. Unsurprisingly, the report says, investment contracts with the government often specify arbitration outside Liberia, and investors prefer not to rely on local courts at all.

Liberia does belong to the ICSID and New York conventions, which oblige its courts to recognize foreign and international arbitration awards. But even there, enforcement can take years.

Land: the oldest fault line

No issue in Liberia is more combustible than land, and the report treats it as a core investment risk.

The constitution limits land ownership to citizens of “Negro descent,” so foreign investors lease — typically for 25 to 50 years. The difficulty is knowing who actually owns what.

According to the Liberia Land Authority, less than a quarter of the country’s land is formally registered, and conflicting records are common.

The report also states that much land has been allocated to commercial companies through agriculture, forestry and mining concessions, often without local communities’ knowledge or consent. Investors, it warns, can face costly disputes even after signing agreements with the government — or after years in operation. The 2018 Land Rights Act was meant to settle historical claims, but public awareness of it remains limited.

A thin, expensive financial system

Liberia has no stock exchange. It has nine commercial banks, mostly foreign-owned, and four deposit-taking microfinance institutions. The Central Bank reports a comfortable liquidity ratio of 50 percent, well above the 15 percent minimum, and calls the sector resilient.

But the State Department notes that bad loans account for about 16 percent of total lending, that commercial interest rates run between 18 and 25 percent, and that lenders often demand collateral worth 150 to 200 percent of a loan. Some Liberian banks struggle to keep correspondent relationships with international banks. The banking system, the report concludes, is adequately capitalized but “not well positioned to withstand shocks.”

There are bright spots. The Central Bank switched on a national instant-payment system in December 2025 that lets money move in real time between mobile networks, and all government-to-person payments now run through the new national electronic payment platform, which is due to be fully operational by December 2026. Investors can also repatriate 100 percent of their funds, with no exchange controls, in a country where the U.S. dollar is legal tender.

State firms in the shadows

Liberia’s 46 state-owned enterprises employ more than 10,000 people in ports, power, water, petroleum, fisheries, forestry and telecommunications. The report describes them as politically governed, financially weak, inefficient and opaque.

It says senior officials, including some who sit on SOE boards, reportedly steer these companies in ways inconsistent with sound corporate governance; that not all of them pay taxes, or do so transparently; and that their revenues and debts are not always properly reflected in national budgets. There is no formal privatization program, despite public calls to privatize the Liberia Electricity Corporation, the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation, Roberts International Airport and the Liberia Petroleum Refining Company.

The welcome mat, with conditions

The report does not suggest Liberia is closed. Its corporate law, modeled in part on Delaware’s, allows 100 percent foreign ownership with no residency requirements for directors. Tax incentives — duty and GST exemptions, tax holidays and deductions of up to 30 percent on qualifying equipment — are on offer in sectors from agriculture and energy to tourism, health and waste management. Extra incentives apply to projects in poorer regions, those creating more than 100 jobs, and those using at least 60 percent local materials.

Infrastructure is moving, too. APM Terminals is pushing the Freeport of Monrovia toward round-the-clock operations and aims to raise activity by 40 percent. A $40 million World Bank trade project is building a single window for customs. Special economic zones are planned, including a 94-acre free zone beside the Monrovia port and a 200-hectare agro-processing zone at Buchanan funded by the African Development Bank.

But the doors are not open everywhere. Sixteen lines of business — from sand supply and block making to taxis, gas stations, used clothing and used cars — are reserved for Liberians. Fully foreign-owned firms in other sectors must invest at least $500,000; joint ventures need $300,000 and at least 25 percent Liberian ownership. In September 2025, the Labour Ministry tripled work permit fees for foreigners from $1,000 to $3,000 to push companies toward local hiring.

That local hiring is not easy. The report puts the population at 5.3 million and the labor force at 2.1 million, with functional literacy just under 50 percent and as many as nine in ten people working in the informal economy. Employers, it says, should expect to invest heavily in training.

The American angle

For a country with Liberia’s historic ties to the United States, the commercial relationship is strikingly small. Central Bank data cited in the report show $57 million in exports to the United States against $63 million in imports. There is no bilateral tax treaty, meaning U.S. companies may face double taxation, and the report notes there has been no recorded investment dispute involving a U.S. investor in a decade — a sign, perhaps, of how few have tried.

Washington’s advice to American firms is cautious: do thorough due diligence, find strong local partners, stay close to the U.S. Embassy, and expect licenses and projects to take longer than planned. Mining and energy are flagged as the most promising sectors.

What it means

The 2026 statement captures the paradox at the heart of Liberia’s economy. The headline numbers show a country recovering; the fine print shows a state whose institutions have not caught up with its resources.

None of the individual criticisms will surprise Liberians — they are the stuff of daily headlines. What gives this report weight is its source and its audience. It is read by boardrooms, development financiers and risk analysts deciding where capital goes. When the U.S. government tells its own companies that rule-breakers can thrive if they pay the right people, and that rule-followers risk being shaken down, that sentence travels further than any investment conference speech.

For the Boakai administration, which has staked its reputation on fighting corruption and reviving the economy, the report is both a mirror and a test. The reforms it cites — asset declarations, contract probes, a proposed anti-corruption court — are the right ones. The question investors will ask is whether they become convictions, cleaner concessions and faster courts before the next edition of this report is written.
