World.title: Five Years, $25.6M Pledged: West Point Still at the Mercy of the Atlantic
World.content:
Monrovia – At West Point, the sea works to its own timetable, and it is not waiting for anyone.

The crowded fishing township sits on a narrow spit of sand where the Mesurado River meets the Atlantic Ocean, on the edge of Liberia’s capital. For years its residents have watched the shoreline move inland, taking homes, walkways and the beaches where fishermen pull up their canoes. Each rainy season brings the same worry: which houses will still be standing when the season ends.

By Rodney D. Sieh



In 2021 an international climate fund made the township a promise. A sloping wall of heavy rock would be built along its exposed shore to break the waves before they reached the houses, with landing points so the fishing fleet could still get to sea.

Five years and four months later, that wall exists in drawings, approvals and contract talks, but not yet on the beach.

A promise made in 2021

The Monrovia Metropolitan Climate Resilience Project (MMCRP) was approved in March 2021 and took effect that July. It is a Government of Liberia initiative funded mainly by the Green Climate Fund (GCF), the world’s largest dedicated climate fund. The GCF pools money mostly from wealthy nations to help poorer countries adapt to a warming planet. The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) manages the grant money. Liberia’s Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) runs the project day to day, working with the Ministries of Finance, Mines and Energy, and Public Works.

The ambitions are large. The project aims to reach about 250,000 people directly, and about one million more through better management of Liberia’s coastline.

It has three parts. The centrepiece is the West Point sea defence, known as a rock revetment. The second is a national plan for managing the coast, which includes mapping the areas most at risk and training government staff to use that information.

The third supports communities: protecting mangrove forests, helping people earn a living through clean-cookstove manufacturing and cold storage for fish processors, and building an Education and Innovation Center in West Point.

In total, US$25.6 million has been committed. Of that, US$21.4 million is cash and US$4.27 million is the estimated value of rock the government has pledged from the Mount Coffee quarry.

Five years of preparation

In its public update, dated November 8, 2026, the EPA says much of the groundwork has been done.

Engineers studied West Point’s currents, coastline and the ground beneath the planned wall in 2023. The GCF approved the detailed design in 2024, and stakeholders validated the construction plan in 2025. The Environmental and Social Impact Assessment, which sets out how the works may affect fishing, trading and access, won GCF approval in the last quarter of 2025.

An agreement covering the rock has been signed by the EPA, the Ministry of Mines and Energy and the Liberia Electricity Corporation, which operates Mount Coffee. Mangrove mapping is finished. Ten community stewards have been hired, six of them women. Twelve billboards on coastal risk now stand in four communities, and livelihood surveys have begun in Topoe Village, Jacob Town, Fiamah and Plunkor. Renovation of the West Point Education and Innovation Center is under way, supervised by the Ministry of Public Works, and is expected to be finished around the start of 2027.

The agency puts it plainly: “The main protection works had not yet begun.”

Following the money

The financial figures show how slowly the project has moved.

By the end of October 2026, US$5.35 million of the US$21.4 million in committed cash had been released to the project.

That is about one dollar in four. Of the money released, US$2.07 million had been spent, or 9.68 per cent of all cash committed.

The GCF grant, the largest single source of money, shows the gap most clearly. The fund has committed US$17.26 million but has sent only US$2.78 million so far, in two transfers: US$523,932 in November 2021 and US$2.26 million in August 2025. Just over US$1 million of that has been spent, which is 6 per cent of the full grant. UNDP is holding the remaining US$1.74 million to start the West Point construction.

The EPA stresses that an approved grant is not money sitting in a bank account. The GCF pays in stages, and only after agreed conditions and milestones are met. Most of the money, the agency notes, is budgeted for the sea wall itself, so spending will stay low until construction starts.

Liberia’s own contribution

One of those conditions involves Liberia’s own money, and here the statement points to a long gap.

The government promised

US$2.54 million in cash. The EPA says that by the time the Boakai-Koung administration took office in early 2024, only US$50,000 had arrived, in a single payment in 2022. The new government paid US$500,000 in December 2024 and another US$800,000 in 2026, bringing the total to US$1.35 million, or 53 per cent of what was promised.

The agency links the delay directly to the project’s slow pace. Larger GCF payments depend on government co-financing and on completing early engineering milestones. “Limited co-financing before 2024 had constrained the pace of work,” the statement says.

Even so, most of the government’s money has not yet been used. Of the US$1.35 million received, about US$253,500 had been spent by the end of October, leaving almost US$1.1 million in the EPA’s project account. A further US$1.19 million of the government’s cash pledge is still to be paid.

The 20 per cent problem

The newest obstacle is the price of the wall itself.

The EPA says the prospective contractor for the West Point revetment has asked for a one-time 20 per cent increase in its price before signing. It cites inflation and higher fuel and material costs since it submitted its financial proposal in December 2025.

The statement does not name the contractor or give the contract value, so it is not yet possible to say how much the increase would cost in dollars. It does say that no adjustment has been approved. The EPA and UNDP are reviewing the contractor’s calculations and talking to the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning about how any extra cost might be covered, along with the government’s outstanding co-financing.

The agency warns that the request “could further delay contract finalization and mobilization,” and that any price change must be “adequately justified, funded and processed” under procurement rules.

Why it has taken so long

The EPA lists a familiar set of reasons: slow early hiring and work planning, COVID-19 restrictions, later staffing gaps, complicated procurement, long technical reviews, rising construction costs and late government co-financing, especially between 2021 and 2024.

Other steps are also still waiting. A Livelihood Restoration Plan, meant to protect traders and fishing families whose income could be disrupted during construction even if they do not have to move, has been prepared but had not yet been submitted to or cleared by the GCF. Bids for the national coastal management plan and risk mapping closed only in October 2026. A request to extend the project and a catch-up plan are awaiting the GCF’s decision.

“Implementation has taken longer than anticipated,” the agency acknowledges. It adds that it “recognizes the urgency for residents and the importance of reporting physical progress alongside expenditure.”

A wider pattern

West Point’s experience reflects a common pattern in climate finance. Pledges are announced in large round numbers. The money then moves in small, conditional amounts through layers of accredited agencies, safeguards and procurement rules. Those rules exist to protect communities and public funds, but each step takes time, and the coastline keeps eroding throughout.

The EPA says the immediate tasks are to finalise the construction contract, complete the outstanding safeguards, begin the coastal planning work and turn livelihood surveys into real support for families.

For West Point, the measure of success will be visible on the beach. The design is approved, the rock is pledged and much of the money has been promised. The township is still waiting for the first truckload of stone.

World.title: Liberia: CDC Supporters Push for Former Chairman’s Return
World.content:
MONROVIA – Three years before Liberians return to the polls to elect a new president and members of the Legislature, a conversation is emerging within the opposition Congress for Democratic Change (CDC), with supporters of its former National Chairman, Mulbah K. Morlu Jr., increasingly making the case for his return to the party’s highest administrative position.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

Across several counties, including Bong, Margibi, Grand Bassa and Montserrado, individuals identifying with Morlu’s political leadership are said to be organizing themselves around a common demand that the former chairman return to the position he resigned from in February 2024.



Their campaign is expected to take a more visible form on November 14, when supporters say they intend to present a petition urging Morlu to reconsider his departure and return to the chairmanship.

Although the proposed mobilization is being described by its organizers as a grassroots initiative, its broader political significance lies in what it reveals about the internal conversations taking place within the CDC as the party considers its future.

For a political movement that rose from opposition politics to the presidency in 2017, the challenge is not merely to remain politically relevant. It is to demonstrate that it can reorganize itself after losing power and convince Liberians that it has the leadership, structure and national appeal to return to government.

Morlu’s supporters believe he is among the few figures within the party capable of undertaking that assignment. They point to his years of involvement in the CDC, his experience coordinating nationwide political structures, his role in the party’s 2017 electoral campaign and his ability to mobilize supporters beyond traditional party boundaries.

But beyond the arguments about his political résumé, the campaign also appears to be driven by a sentiment among some partisans that the CDC needs to rediscover the organizational energy that characterized its years in opposition.

A political movement looking for direction

The CDC’s defeat in the 2023 presidential runoff remains a defining moment in the party’s recent political history. Former President George Manneh Weah received 793,914 votes against 814,481 for Joseph Nyuma Boakai, who contested on the ticket of the Unity Party. The difference of 20,567 votes delivered the presidency to Boakai after a closely contested election.

While the CDC lost the presidency, it retained considerable political influence, emerging as the largest single party in the House of Representatives with 25 of the 73 seats.

For Morlu’s supporters, those figures demonstrate that the party’s political foundation was not destroyed by the electoral defeat. Instead, they argue that the CDC possesses a substantial electoral constituency that needs to be reorganized, motivated and expanded.

Their argument is that the party should not approach 2029 as a political organization starting from nothing. Rather, it should build upon the support it accumulated during its years in government and opposition.

That process, they believe, requires leadership capable of understanding the party from the grassroots to its national executive level. Morlu’s supporters say his experience in different positions within the CDC gives him an institutional understanding that would be difficult to replace.

They also argue that his return would provide an opportunity to reconcile members who may have become politically distant following the party’s loss of power and his eventual resignation.

Bong County: A call for organizational experience

In Bong County, where the CDC has maintained a considerable political presence over the years, supporters say the party needs a chairman who understands the importance of building its structures beyond Monrovia.

Samuel K. Nyumah, representing the Bong County constituency, argues that the CDC’s political strength has historically depended on its ability to maintain relationships with ordinary partisans in towns, villages and communities.

According to Nyumah, the party cannot prepare for another presidential election by concentrating its political activities around national headquarters while grassroots supporters remain disconnected from the leadership.

He believes Morlu’s experience in rebuilding the party’s structures following the 2011 elections makes him a suitable candidate to lead another organizational exercise. “Mulbah Morlu understands how the CDC is built. He understands the people who sacrificed their time and resources to make the party what it became. We are not saying that other members do not have leadership qualities, but we believe that, at this particular moment, the party needs someone who understands its structures and knows how to bring people together. We want him to return because the work ahead

requires experience, commitment and a clear understanding of the grassroots,” Nyumah said in an illustrative statement.

Margibi County: The question of political mobilization

In Margibi County, supporters are placing particular emphasis on Morlu’s reputation as a political mobilizer and his ability to organize people around issues that extend beyond party politics.

Patricia W. Kollie argues that the CDC needs a chairman who can transform political dissatisfaction into organized participation and give younger partisans a meaningful role in the party’s future. Kollie believes that the political environment leading to the 2029 elections will require more than speeches, press conferences and occasional rallies.

She argues that the party must begin preparing its supporters through sustained community engagement, political education, recruitment and the establishment of functional county and district structures.

“Politics is not only about having a popular presidential candidate. It is also about having people who can take the party’s message to the communities, listen to ordinary Liberians and organize supporters around a common vision. We believe Morlu has demonstrated that capacity over the years. His ability to mobilize people and communicate political issues is something the CDC should not take for granted. We want him back because we believe he can help restore the energy that made the party a formidable political force,” Kollie said in an illustrative statement.

Grand Bassa County: Rebuilding unity after political disagreements

In Grand Bassa County, the argument for Morlu’s return is being framed around reconciliation and the need to prevent internal disagreements from weakening the party ahead of the next electoral cycle.

James T. Wleh believes that the CDC must find a way to bring together members whose relationships may have been affected by disagreements over leadership, political direction and the management of party affairs.

Morlu resigned from the chairmanship in February 2024, citing disagreements and concerns about constraints on his ability to perform his responsibilities.

Although his departure was voluntary, supporters now argue that political differences should not permanently separate individuals who contributed to building the party. Wleh believes that Morlu’s return could provide an opportunity for the party to open a new chapter in its internal relations.

“We cannot continue to allow disagreements to determine the future of a party that so many Liberians worked hard to build. People have their differences, and political organizations will always experience disagreements, but those differences should not become permanent divisions. We believe Morlu has a role to play in bringing people together again. His return would send a message that the CDC is prepared to put personal interests aside and focus on the bigger responsibility of rebuilding the party,” Wleh said in an illustrative statement.

Montserrado County: Beyond party politics

In Montserrado County, where the CDC maintains its most visible political presence, supporters are highlighting Morlu’s activities since leaving the party’s chairmanship.

They argue that his leadership of Solidarity and Trust for a New Day (STAND) demonstrates that he has retained the ability to organize people and engage in national political conversations even outside the CDC’s formal leadership structure.

Michael B. Dolo believes the former chairman’s political activities since 2024 show that his influence is not limited to the traditional CDC membership.

Dolo points particularly to the July 17, 2026, “Lead or Leave” demonstration, which was organized amid growing public demands for accountability and concerns about governance. The Independent National Commission on Human Rights reported that the demonstration attracted more than 1,500 participants and was largely peaceful.

Supporters also point to the participation of student organizations, including the Student Unification Party, the Progressive Students Alliance and the Student Integration Movement, as evidence of the potential for broader political cooperation.

For Dolo, these developments demonstrate that Morlu can engage people from different backgrounds around issues of national interest. “One of the things the CDC needs going into 2029 is a chairman who can communicate beyond the party’s traditional supporters. We need somebody who can bring young people, students, community leaders and ordinary citizens into national conversations. What Morlu has demonstrated through STAND is that he can mobilize people around issues that concern the country, even when they do not necessarily belong to the CDC. We believe that experience can be useful to the party as it prepares for the next elections,” Dolo said in an illustrative statement.

A record supporters say should not be overlooked

Much of the campaign for Morlu’s return rests on his history within the CDC. Supporters trace his involvement to 2005, when he served as chairman of the Progressive Action for Change, a CDC-aligned auxiliary.

They say he subsequently served as assistant public relations director before becoming director of public relations that same year. Over the years, he occupied several positions, including chairman of the Policy Response Committee in 2009, chairman of the Mobilization and Recruitment Committee in 2010 and chairman of the Nationwide Restructuring Committee in 2012.

He later served as vice chairman for operations from 2012 to 2018 and chaired the party’s convention committee in 2014. Supporters consider his role in the 2012 restructuring exercise particularly important.

Following the CDC’s defeat in the 2011 elections, the party faced the challenge of reorganizing its county structures after widespread resignations among county-level leadership. According to supporters, Morlu’s restructuring committee worked to rebuild those structures and restore the party’s organizational presence across the country.

They contend that the exercise provided the foundation for the political machinery that subsequently supported the CDC’s successful 2017 presidential campaign. Morlu later became National Chairman and served for approximately six years, including during the period when the CDC controlled the Executive Branch.

For his supporters, that experience provides an important basis for their argument that he understands the demands of leading a political organization through both opposition and government. They also cite vocational training initiatives reportedly organized for ordinary partisans at the party’s headquarters as evidence that his leadership sought to provide opportunities beyond political mobilization.

Whether those experiences would translate into another successful period at the helm of the CDC remains a question that only the party’s political process and Morlu himself can ultimately answer.

The STAND factor

Morlu’s supporters also believe his work outside the CDC has added another dimension to his political profile. Through STAND, he has continued to participate in national political discussions, particularly those involving governance, accountability and public institutions.

The July 17 demonstration remains one of the events frequently cited by his backers. The “Lead or Leave” protest brought together different categories of participants and attracted attention because of its demands for accountability amid concerns surrounding governance and the country’s response to a major narcotics investigation.

For Morlu’s supporters, the demonstration illustrated the importance of political organization in shaping public discourse. They argue that a party preparing for 2029 must be capable of connecting its political objectives with the concerns of ordinary citizens.

However, they also acknowledge that leading a civic movement and managing a political party are different responsibilities. While STAND can mobilize around particular national issues, the CDC must manage internal elections, membership disputes, candidate selection, legislative coordination and the broader responsibilities associated with electoral politics.

Supporters believe Morlu’s previous experience as chairman gives him an advantage in understanding those institutional demands.

They say the combination of his experience within the CDC and his continued engagement in national affairs could help the party strengthen its political relevance.

Will Morlu accept the call?

Despite the growing enthusiasm among his supporters, the biggest question surrounding the proposed November 14 petition is whether Morlu himself is prepared to return. His resignation in February 2024 came amid disagreements over the direction and management of the party.

Those circumstances remain relevant to any discussion about his possible return, particularly because supporters acknowledge that reconciliation would require more than a public petition.

It would require engagement between Morlu and the party’s current leadership, an understanding of the concerns that contributed to his departure and a willingness among different factions to find common ground.

There is also the question of the CDC’s constitution and the procedures governing the selection of its national chairman. A petition from supporters, regardless of its size, cannot by itself confer the chairmanship. Any leadership change must follow the party’s established constitutional and electoral processes.

The position of the current national leadership will therefore be important in determining whether the proposed initiative develops into a broader internal discussion about the party’s future.

Morlu’s response will also matter. If he accepts the appeal, the party could be confronted with a renewed debate about its leadership direction and the possibility of an internal contest.

If he declines, supporters will have to decide whether to continue pressing for his return or channel their efforts into another form of political engagement.

As of November 8, no confirmed response from Morlu concerning the proposed petition has been provided in the information available for this report.

World.title: Liberia: Cuttington, Bong County University Graduates’ Clean Cities Experience Exposes Liberia’s Unemployment Challenge
World.content:
Ultimately, the country’s development will not be measured only by how many graduates its universities produce or how fast its economy grows. It will depend on whether educated young people can find decent work, support their families, and put their knowledge to use for their country. Until that happens more consistently, the stories of graduates like Tokpah and Kien will remain a stark reminder that in Liberia, earning a degree and finding a job are still two very different achievements

MONROVIA – Every morning, young men and women across Liberia’s towns and cities pick up cutlasses, brooms and wheelbarrows to clear roadsides and drains. Among them are two university graduates who once pictured themselves in offices, laboratories and farms, applying what they learned in lecture halls. Instead, they are part of a government sanitation program that offers short-term work to unemployed youth.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

Their names are Aloysius Tokpah and Jonathan Kien. Their paths to the program differ in detail, but they share a common thread: both did what Liberian families have long told their children to do. They went to university, finished their studies, and waited for the doors that a degree is supposed to open.



A degree in public service, a job on the roadside

When Tokpah enrolled at Cuttington University, the plan seemed straightforward. He would study hard, graduate, and move into a professional career where his knowledge could serve both his own future and his country’s development.

He majored in Public Administration, with a minor in Economics, and graduated in the 2024/2025 academic year. It is a combination suited to work in government institutions, public service, policy planning and economic development, the very fields in which Liberia says it needs capable people.

But the months after graduation did not unfold as he had hoped. Instead of landing a role in his field, Tokpah found himself doing roadside brushing under the Government of Liberia’s Presidential Clean Cities Initiative, a program designed to improve urban sanitation while giving young people temporary income. On November 10, he shared his feelings on Facebook. He wrote about the sacrifices behind his education, the hope that came with it, and the strangeness of finding himself doing roadside work simply to survive. Life, he reflected, sometimes takes people in directions they never imagined.

The post struck a chord because it spoke for many. It offered a glimpse of the distance between academic ambition and the realities of Liberia’s job market. There is an irony in his situation that is hard to miss. A graduate trained in public administration and economics could, in principle, contribute to planning, managing and evaluating public programs, including the sort of initiative in which he now works with his hands. Rather than sitting in an administrative office, he is helping to clean public spaces.

Supporting a family after graduation

Kien’s story is rooted in a different, equally pressing concern. A 2024/2025 graduate of Bong County University, he studied Agriculture, a field with obvious relevance for a country that wants to raise food production and strengthen rural livelihoods.

Yet since completing his studies, Kien has not found a job. With no income and a mother and other relatives depending on him, he said he accepted a place in the sanitation programme because he needed a way to support them.

For Kien, the decision was less about career than about responsibility. Waiting for the perfect opportunity in his field might mean months more without earnings, and family needs do not wait. Taking available work, however modest, became the practical choice.

His situation reflects a reality confronting many young Liberians: graduating does not automatically lead to employment, and a certificate does not guarantee economic independence.

These stories also point to something less often discussed, the sacrifices families make to educate their children. Tuition, transport, books and daily upkeep are often paid for through great effort. When graduation does not bring a job, the disappointment is felt well beyond the graduate.

What the numbers say

The experiences of Tokpah and Kien arrive at a moment when the World Bank is urging Liberia to look beyond headline growth. In the seventh edition of its Liberia Economic Update, titled Beyond Growth: Addressing Structural Constraints to Job-Rich Growth in Liberia, launched in Monrovia on November 3, 2026, the Bank reported that the economy grew by 5.1 percent in 2025.

That growth was driven largely by a strong rebound in mining, which expanded by 17 percent, and by continued gains in services, which grew by 4.6 percent. Agriculture, the sector where Kien trained, lagged behind at 2.6 percent.

The Bank’s message was that good growth figures are not enough. For expansion to improve ordinary lives, it said, the economy must generate more and better jobs. It pointed to constraints that hold businesses back and limit hiring: high production costs, unreliable infrastructure, limited access to financing, and weak links to markets. Its recommendations included sustained macroeconomic stability, stronger private-sector development, better governance, and policies that widen productive opportunities.

World Bank Country Manager for Liberia Georgia Wallen stressed that the central challenge is converting economic gains into opportunities that improve people’s lives. For graduates, that challenge is concrete. A country can post solid growth while sectors that create the most visible wealth employ relatively few people.

A labour market dominated by informal work

The problem is not only how many people lack jobs, but what kind of work is available. In a May 2026 analysis of the private sector, the World Bank found that about 87 percent of Liberian workers were in informal employment, including smallholder farming and unregistered micro-enterprises. It also reported that roughly 14.8 percent of people aged 15 to 24 were neither in education, employment nor training, and cautioned that, given the scale of informality, youth underemployment may be far larger than conventional unemployment figures suggest.

A different picture comes from Liberia’s 2024 Labour Force Survey, cited in an International Monetary Fund assessment. It recorded an unemployment rate of 12.6 percent and found that 44.2 percent of young people aged 15 to 24 were neither in education, employment nor training.

The figures differ because the datasets and measurements differ, but they tell the same story: the labour market offers too few stable, productive opportunities for young people entering it.

For graduates like Tokpah and Kien, then, the obstacle is not unwillingness to work. It is the difficulty of finding work that pays enough and makes use of what they studied. How a sanitation drive became a lifeline

The Presidential Clean Cities Initiative is a Government of Liberia intervention championed by President Joseph Nyuma Boakai Sr. It aims to improve sanitation in urban communities while providing structured, short-term jobs for young Liberians. It also seeks to encourage community ownership of public spaces and deepen cooperation among citizens, youth groups, community-based organisations and local authorities.

The first phase began on November 10, covering eight counties, 14 cities and one township. Participating locations include Monrovia and Paynesville in Montserrado County; Ganta, Sanniquellie and Tappita in Nimba; Gbarnga and Totota in Bong; Foya and Voinjama in Lofa; Buchanan in Grand Bassa; Kakata City, Unification City and Schieffelin Township in Margibi; Tubmanburg in Bomi; and Zwedru in Grand Gedeh.

The targets are specific. Government plans to engage 1,250 young people and 30 community-based organisations, with at least 40 percent of participants expected to be women. The programme aims to clean and maintain at least 120 public spaces and 100 drainage systems, support the disposal of at least 2,000 metric tonnes of solid waste, and reach at least 500,000 citizens through sanitation and awareness activities.

The first phase is expected to last three months, with participants reportedly receiving US$100 a month, or US$300 in total if those terms hold. The programme is fully funded by the Ministry of State for Presidential Affairs. Its implementing partners include the Ministries of Local Government, Information, and Youth and Sports; the Environmental Protection Agency; county and city authorities; community-based organisations; and the President Delivery Unit, which is expected to independently track progress.

For participants, the stipend may bring genuine if temporary relief. For Kien, it can help meet family needs. For Zlatan, it is a way to earn while his professional path remains uncertain.

After the three months

The harder question is what happens when the programme ends. Three months of work, and a modest stipend, cannot by themselves solve a structural jobs shortage. Participants will return to the same labour market, with the same competition and the same limited openings.

None of this diminishes the work itself. There is dignity in honest labour, and clean public spaces and clear drains protect communities from environmental hazards and support public health. No one should look down on the young people doing it.

The real issue is why graduates who invested years in higher education must so often rely on temporary work far from their fields to meet basic needs. Producing graduates is only half of a development strategy. The other half is building an economy that can absorb them.

Liberia needs trained public administrators to strengthen state institutions, economists to guide development planning, and agricultural professionals to raise food production and productivity. These are exactly the areas where Tokpah and Kien studied, and where they could contribute if the right openings existed.

That points back to the World Bank’s argument. Businesses need cheaper operating conditions, dependable infrastructure, access to finance and stronger market connections if they are to expand and hire. A healthier private sector, supported by stable macroeconomic policy and good governance, is where lasting jobs for graduates are most likely to come from.

For the Boakai-Koung administration, the Clean Cities Initiative offers a chance to tackle immediate sanitation problems while giving young people temporary support. The test will be whether such programmes sit within an employment strategy that creates sustainable opportunities rather than standing alone.

Behind every broom

As the first phase continues, Tokpah and Kien remind the country that behind every sanitation worker is a person with ambitions, responsibilities and, sometimes, years of university study.

For Tokpah, the road from Cuttington’s classrooms to roadside brushing is not the one he planned. For Kien, accepting the work was about supporting his mother and family after months without a job. Both made a choice that many young graduates face when survival becomes more urgent than professional expectations.

Ultimately, Liberia’s development will not be measured only by how many graduates its universities produce or how fast its economy grows. It will depend on whether educated young people can find decent work, support their families, and put their knowledge to use for their country.

Until that happens more consistently, the stories of graduates like Tokpah and Kien will remain a stark reminder that in Liberia, earning a degree and finding a job are still two very different achievements.

World.title: Liberia: Concerned UL Alumni Challenge Pennie’s Five-Year Acting Presidency, Demand Independent Elections AS Pennie Defends Leadership
World.content:
Concerned graduates challenge his prolonged tenure and demand independent electoral oversight, while Pennie cites constitutional succession provisions and poor meeting attendance in defending the December polls.

Monrovia — A growing dispute within the University of Liberia Alumni Association (AAUL) has intensified, with concerned alumni challenging Martin Wleh Pennie’s more than five-year tenure as acting president, while Pennie maintains that his continued leadership is supported by the association’s constitution and circumstances that prevented elections.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

In a November 4, 2026 position statement, the Concerned Alumni of the University of Liberia accused the association’s leadership of violating constitutional provisions governing elections, tenure and accountability.



Pennie, who assumed acting leadership following the death of then-President James S. Davis in January 2021, is being challenged over his continued stay in office without a fresh electoral mandate.

However, in a nine-count response to FrontPage Africa, Pennie defended the National Executive Committee’s (NEC) decisions, arguing that the constitution allows the vice president to serve as acting president until a successor is elected.

He attributed the electoral delay to poor meeting attendance, failure to achieve quorum and inadequate financial contributions from members. He maintained that the December 4–5, 2026 Annual General Assembly (AGA) and elections were constitutionally declared.

Dispute Over Pennie’s Tenure

At the center of the disagreement is Article VIII of the AAUL Constitution, which provides for a two-year tenure for elected officers, with eligibility for one additional term.

The concerned alumni said the last officers, including Davis and Pennie, were elected in 2019, meaning their mandate expired in 2021. They argued that subsequent elections should have been held in 2023 and 2025, making 2027 the next regular election year.

Although acknowledging Pennie’s right to assume acting leadership following Davis’s death on January 3, 2021, the group cited Article V, Section II, arguing that the arrangement was intended to last only until a new president was elected.

“An acting arrangement is a bridge to legitimate leadership, not a substitute for it,” the group argued.

Pennie, however, offered a different interpretation of the provision, which states that the vice president shall serve as acting president in the event of the president’s sickness, absence, resignation, removal, death or other inability to serve until a new president is elected.

He said the framers included the provision to prevent a leadership vacuum and ensure institutional continuity, particularly when poor membership participation makes elections difficult.

Pennie said the NEC repeatedly attempted to mobilize members for meetings and AGAs but encountered poor attendance and a lack of quorum. He added that meetings that achieved quorum resulted in members mandating the leadership to continue managing the association until broader participation could be secured.

He said attendance records and meeting minutes were available to support the NEC’s position.

Pennie said the NEC repeatedly attempted to mobilize members for meetings and AGAs but encountered poor attendance and a lack of quorum.

Poor Attendance or Leadership Failure?

The concerned alumni rejected the argument that poor attendance and COVID-19 justified the prolonged failure to conduct elections.

They noted that Liberia’s State of Emergency, declared in April 2020, ended on July 21, 2020, months before Davis’s death and the 2021 election cycle.

The group demanded meeting notices, minutes and attendance records to demonstrate that the leadership made genuine efforts to convene constitutionally required meetings.

Pennie countered that members also have constitutional responsibilities, including attending meetings and paying dues.

Citing Article XII, he said members are required to pay dues determined by the AGA, with the constitution specifying a minimum monthly contribution of L$100.

He argued that inconsistent dues payments and the absence of members from meetings had weakened the association’s ability to function effectively.

University President’s Intervention

The disagreement intensified following a stakeholder meeting convened by University of Liberia President Dr. Layli Maparyan on October 20, 2026.

According to the concerned alumni, Maparyan proposed an independent body to oversee the elections and invited stakeholders to recommend credible individuals for the Election Commission.

The group said Pennie rejected the proposal and subsequently reported Maparyan to the University’s Board of Trustees.

Pennie argued that the Office of Alumni Affairs has no constitutional authority to convene assemblies, appoint an Election Commission, audit the association or take custody of its assets.

He maintained that the AAUL is an independent membership organization governed by its constitution, which vests authority in the NEC and identifies the AGA as its highest decision-making organ.

Pennie said the NEC attended the October 20 meeting out of respect for the University administration but insisted that the University’s involvement must remain within the limits established by the constitution.

He also questioned why the concerned alumni submitted their complaints to the Office of Alumni Affairs rather than directly to the NEC.

He invited the signatories to submit their names, dues status and grievances to the NEC for consideration at the December AGA.

Pennie Defends December Elections

The concerned alumni questioned the December election schedule, arguing that the association’s ordinary two-year electoral cycle points to 2027.

They also argued that Article VIII requires the election venue and timetable to be announced three months before the election month. They noted that the AGA resolution was issued on September 27, while the election timetable was released on October 20.

They similarly questioned the timing of the Election Commission’s establishment.

Pennie maintained that the NEC properly declared the elections under the constitution, which provides for a five-member ad hoc Election Commission appointed by the president with the Executive Committee’s consent.

He said the NEC would consent only to commissioners who are not candidates for any position and maintained that the commission is required to invite observers, including representatives of the Advisory Council, the National Elections Commission and civil society institutions.

Financial Accountability and Eligibility Concerns

The concerned alumni also demanded financial statements, budgets and an independent audit of the association’s accounts.

Pennie rejected suggestions of financial mismanagement, saying the NEC had operated under different budgeting frameworks despite difficulties securing quorum and consistent dues payments.

He cited constitutional safeguards requiring joint signatures for bank withdrawals, prior NEC approval for expenditures exceeding US$1,000 and semi-annual financial reporting.

Although he said the constitution does not expressly provide for an external audit, Pennie stated that the NEC has no objection to one.

He said financial reports would be presented at the December AGA, allowing the assembly to decide whether to appoint an independent auditor.

The group also questioned the eligibility of the Secretary General, citing a constitutional restriction preventing university employees who are alumni from contesting the offices of president and secretary general.

Pennie said the allegation was unsupported by evidence and that no formal complaint had previously been submitted to the NEC. He added that the matter could be placed on the December AGA agenda for consideration under the appropriate constitutional procedures.

Questions Over Election Commission’s Independence

The concerned alumni also raised concerns about the perceived impartiality of the current Election Commission, citing alleged personal and social relationships between its chairperson and Pennie, including their reported association with a social club known as “The Shrine” on the Capitol Hill Campus.

The group acknowledged that such relationships do not establish wrongdoing but argued that the appearance of independence is important in a contested election.

It called for the commission’s reconstitution through stakeholder consultations, involvement of the Advisory Council and observation by the National Elections Commission.

Pennie maintained that the commission should be constituted according to the AAUL Constitution. However, he requested that the University administration nominate two observers to work alongside the Election Committee to ensure a credible, free, fair and transparent process.

He also cited constitutional provisions allowing at least 75 dues-paying members to request an extraordinary AGA and encouraged the concerned alumni to use established procedures to submit their grievances.

A Test of Institutional Governance

The dispute places the AAUL before a critical test of institutional governance, with both sides invoking the same constitution to defend their positions.

While the concerned alumni argue that the prolonged acting presidency undermines electoral provisions, Pennie maintains that the succession clause and repeated failures to achieve quorum justify the NEC’s actions.

Both sides say they support credible elections but remain divided over the legitimacy of the current leadership and the appropriate arrangements for overseeing the process.

The December 4–5 AGA is expected to provide an opportunity to address the outstanding constitutional and governance concerns.

For the concerned alumni, the objective is to restore constitutional governance and public confidence. For Pennie and the NEC, the priority is to proceed with the scheduled assembly and elections under the association’s existing constitutional framework.

World.title: Liberia: 2,718 Civil Servants Set for December Retirement as Government Reports Pension Reforms
World.content:
MONROVIA – The Government of Liberia says it has made significant progress in addressing longstanding challenges in the country’s public service retirement system, with 2,718 civil servants expected to retire at the end of December 2026 under a nationwide exercise intended to improve pension administration and ensure timely payment of retirement benefits.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

Director General of the Civil Service Agency (CSA), Dr. Josiah F. Joekai Jr., disclosed that the employees were identified through a nationwide pre-retirement counseling and data collection exercise conducted in collaboration with the National Social Security and Welfare Corporation (NASSCORP).



According to Dr. Joekai, the exercise, which covered all 15 counties and 67 Government spending entities, was successfully concluded on October 17, 2026, marking what he described as an important step toward establishing a more organized, transparent and predictable retirement administration system.

The exercise captured a total of 2,835 employees, including 2,718 individuals scheduled to retire effective December 31, 2026, while the remaining 117 represent outstanding retirement cases involving public servants who left active Government service between 2020 and 2024 but have yet to commence receiving their pension benefits.

Speaking during an official press briefing in Monrovia in November, Dr. Joekai said the latest results demonstrate the Government’s determination to correct administrative weaknesses that for years left retiring public servants uncertain about their financial future. He said the retirement process had historically been characterized by inadequate personnel documentation, delays in processing retirement records, weak institutional coordination and prolonged waiting periods before eligible retirees could access their pension benefits.

According to him, some civil servants remained in active Government service beyond the statutory retirement age because their records had not been properly processed, while others completed their years of service only to encounter difficulties accessing benefits to which they were entitled.

Dr. Joekai said those challenges created unnecessary hardship for former public servants and their families, particularly individuals who depended on their monthly retirement income to meet basic household responsibilities. However, he maintained that the administration of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai Sr. had begun addressing the situation through improved coordination between the CSA and NASSCORP, with particular emphasis on identifying employees approaching retirement age before their departure from Government service.

He explained that the new approach involves identifying retirement-eligible employees, reviewing their employment records, providing pre-retirement counseling and facilitating the documentation required for pension enrollment ahead of their effective retirement dates.

The CSA Director General said the intention is to move away from a system in which employees begin pursuing retirement documentation only after leaving their positions to one in which the process is initiated and completed in advance.

Under the arrangement, employees scheduled to retire on December 31, 2026, are expected to begin receiving their monthly pension benefits in January 2027, provided they successfully complete NASSCORP’s verification and enrollment requirements.

In addition to their monthly pensions, eligible retirees are expected to receive a one-time Government Retirement Handshake Package, with the amount determined by their qualifying years of public service. Dr. Joekai said the package is intended to recognize the contributions of employees who have dedicated years of their productive lives to serving the country and provide additional financial support as they transition out of active employment.

He emphasized that the Government considers retirement security an important component of public sector employee welfare, arguing that individuals who have served the Republic should not be subjected to unnecessary administrative obstacles when accessing benefits earned through years of service.

The 2026 exercise also revealed significant differences in the number of employees approaching retirement across Government institutions, with the Ministry of Education accounting for more than half of the entire retirement batch.

According to the CSA’s figures, the Ministry of Education has 1,493 employees scheduled to retire, representing approximately 54.9 percent of the 2,718 individuals expected to leave active Government service at the end of December.

The Ministry of Health follows with 300 employees, representing 11 percent, while the Ministry of Local Government accounts for 297 employees, or approximately 10.9 percent. The remaining 628 employees, representing 23.1 percent, are distributed across other Government spending entities.

Combined, the Ministries of Education, Health and Local Government account for approximately 76.9 percent of the employees scheduled to retire during the period.

The figures have raised the importance of succession planning within these institutions, particularly because of their central responsibilities in delivering education, healthcare and local administrative services throughout the country.

The CSA said it intends to work with human resource directors and other relevant authorities to ensure that the departure of experienced employees does not unnecessarily disrupt institutional operations. The agency believes that early retirement identification should allow Government institutions sufficient time to prepare for personnel changes, transfer institutional knowledge and make appropriate arrangements for replacing employees whose departure could affect service delivery.

Of the 2,718 employees scheduled to retire in December, 2,125 are males, representing 78.2 percent, while 593 are females, accounting for 21.8 percent. Beyond preparing the current retirement batch, the Government says it is also prioritizing the resolution of pension cases inherited from previous years.

Dr. Joekai disclosed that the nationwide exercise identified 117 former public servants who retired between 2020 and 2024 but have not yet started receiving their monthly pension payments. The cases involve 92 males and 25 females spread across 13 Government spending entities.

The Ministry of Education accounts for the largest number of outstanding cases, with 42 individuals, followed by the Ministry of Local Government with 33 and the Ministry of Health with 19.

The remaining cases are distributed among other Government institutions. Dr. Joekai said the CSA has begun reviewing, compiling and transmitting the relevant documentation to NASSCORP for verification and further processing. He said the Government recognizes the difficulties confronting individuals who have already completed their years of service but remain unable to access their retirement benefits.

The CSA Director General assured that the outstanding cases would receive attention through continued collaboration between the two institutions, although the processing and commencement of payments remain subject to the required verification and enrollment procedures.

He pointed to the 2024 nationwide retirement exercise as evidence that coordinated administrative intervention could produce measurable results in addressing long-standing pension delays.

During that exercise, the CSA and NASSCORP identified 294 individuals who had retired between 2018 and 2023 without receiving their pension benefits.

Dr. Joekai said all 294 cases were subsequently processed through institutional collaboration, and the beneficiaries are now receiving their monthly pension payments.

He described the development as an important demonstration of the Government’s capacity to address inherited administrative problems when relevant institutions work together and maintain consistent follow-up.

The latest identification of 117 outstanding cases, however, suggests that challenges associated with retirement documentation and pension enrollment have not been completely eliminated. The CSA is therefore seeking to ensure that the newly identified cases are processed while preventing similar situations from affecting the 2026 retirement batch.

In a related development, the Government has extended the period for retirement registration and documentation to November 30, 2026, to accommodate eligible employees who were unable to participate in the nationwide field exercise. The extension is intended to provide an additional opportunity for civil servants approaching retirement to have their records captured and included in the processing arrangements.

Dr. Joekai urged eligible employees who have not yet completed the exercise to submit their required documents to the CSA before the November 30 deadline.

He also called on human resource directors and officers across Government institutions to assist eligible employees in completing the necessary procedures, warning against administrative lapses that could prevent qualified individuals from accessing their retirement benefits on time.

Employees captured under the extended registration period will form part of a second batch and are expected to commence receiving their monthly pension benefits in February 2027.

Their January 2027 pension entitlement is also expected to be paid retroactively, subject to successful verification and enrollment by NASSCORP. The extension is particularly important for employees whose retirement eligibility may not have been captured during the initial exercise or whose documentation remains incomplete.

The CSA said it wants to ensure that no eligible public servant is unnecessarily excluded from the retirement process because of documentation or administrative challenges that could have been resolved before the deadline.

Dr. Joekai maintained that the reforms are part of the Boakai administration’s broader commitment to improving conditions within the public service and strengthening institutional accountability.

He said retirement administration is not simply a personnel management responsibility but an important component of Government’s obligation to protect the welfare and lawful entitlements of individuals who have served the country.

According to him, the reforms are also expected to improve the Government’s ability to maintain accurate personnel records, manage workforce transitions and coordinate retirement-related responsibilities across spending entities.

World.title: Liberia: Vice President Koung Visits China as $25-$30 Million Hygiene Products Factory Targets 2027 Completion
World.content:
FOSHAN, China – Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung welcomed plans for a $25 million-$30 million hygiene products factory in Liberia during a visit to Chinese manufacturers KEDA Industrial Group and Sunda Group, where company officials said the project is targeting completion between May and June 2027.

By Jaheim T. Tumu- [email protected]

The facility, which will produce sanitary pads, baby diapers, wipes and other hygiene products, is being developed by Softcare at the Free Zones area on Bushrod Island near Monrovia.



Prince Wreh, Chairperson of the Liberia Special Economic Zones Authority (LSEZA), said an investment agreement with Softcare was signed in August 2026 after due diligence missions to Ghana and China. He said the designated land has been handed over to the company and initial implementation activities have begun.

Company representatives said the project is expected to include four production lines, with about 40% of output planned for the Liberian market and 60% for export, particularly to Sierra Leone and Guinea.

The project would establish Liberia as a production and distribution base for hygiene products serving West African markets, officials said.

Vice President Koung and his delegation toured KEDA’s exhibition facilities and manufacturing workshops before holding discussions with senior executives on the Softcare project and additional investment opportunities in Liberia.

Koung welcomed the investment and urged the company to meet its construction timetable, saying job creation remains a priority of President Joseph Boakai’s administration.

He also encouraged the investors to consider opportunities for future expansion, citing Liberia’s access to regional markets including Sierra Leone, Guinea and Côte d’Ivoire.

Responding to concerns raised by company executives over electricity and port services, Koung said the government is working to improve infrastructure needed to support manufacturing and attract investment.

The Liberia Special Economic Zones Authority said additional land could be considered for future expansion if the company meets its obligations under the existing agreement.

Wreh said the arrangement includes provisions aimed at creating employment opportunities for Liberians.

Dr. Peng Zhou, Vice President of KEDA Industrial Group, said the company is interested in exploring further cooperation with Liberia.

He said KEDA has expanded from machinery manufacturing into integrated industrial production solutions, with operations covering building materials machinery, building materials and new energy materials.

Y.C. Shen, chairman of Sunda Group, director of KEDA Industrial Group and chairman of Twyford International, said the partners’ experience across Africa has emphasized the importance of local employment, skills development and technology transfer.

Liberia’s ambassador to China, Dudley McKinley Thomas, described investment as an example of economic cooperation between Liberia and China. He said future partnerships should support domestic production, technical skills development and sustainable employment.

During the visit, the Liberian delegation received briefings on automated manufacturing systems, ceramics production equipment and integrated factory solutions that could contribute to Liberia’s industrial development.

VP Koung reaffirmed the government’s commitment to supporting investment that generates jobs and expands Liberia’s manufacturing sector.

World.title: Lufuma Warns Of Gold Militias As Military Ordered To Crush Illegal Mining
World.content:
Defence Minister Mr Ambrose Lufuma says the military has been ordered to crush illegal mining Zambia across the country. He warned that the trade, if left unchecked, could give rise to armed militias and push Zambia towards anarchy.

The order came from the top. Mr Lufuma said President Hakainde Hichilema had directed the Ministry of Defence to curb illegal mining Zambia in the national interest, and the military had been handed the task of restoring order wherever the trade had taken root.

“We’re not going to tolerate illegal mining Zambia and so the military has been given the responsibility to bring sanity in the country,” Mr Lufuma said.

The minister pointed to the experience of other gold-rich nations to explain the urgency. Countries with minerals such as gold had spiralled into confusion, he said, and the military had been tasked with containing the problem before Zambia reached the same point.

His sharpest warning was about what could grow out of the pits if nothing is done. Illegal mining, the minister said, was a danger to the nation and could give birth to armed militias loyal to whoever controls the gold.

“We don’t want to see a situation where militias and tribal chiefs are formed because of minerals which may later become a menace to society,” he said.

That danger is no longer theoretical. Last week, rival factions of suspected United Party for National Development (UPND) cadres fought running battles in Mpika District, Muchinga Province, over control of illegal gold mining. They left behind the shells of burnt-out vehicles and demolished makeshift shelters used by illegal miners.

The Mpika fighting has been linked to known figures with connections to the ruling party. Asked about the clashes, Mr Lufuma said the problem went beyond party cadres. He described illegal mining as a national problem drawing in young people from all walks of life.

The Kabompo East lawmaker put a number on the scale of the trade in North-Western Province. There were more than 80,000 illegal miners in Mufumbwe alone, he said, and most of them were not politically affiliated.

Political connections, the minister made clear, would offer no shelter once the operation moves in. There would be no sacred cows, and the army would carry out a thorough clean-up.

“Illegal mining leads to instability in the country and I personally will not tolerate that vice. That is why the military has been tasked to deal with this scourge,” Mr Lufuma said.

He also looked beyond Zambia’s borders for the money behind the pits. Foreign elements, the Defence Minister said, were operating in the background and sponsoring illegal mining in the country.

The crackdown will not be fought by one ministry alone. The Ministry of Defence has agreed with the Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development that all forms of illegal mining will be dealt with, a joint position that takes the military’s role beyond any single district or gold field.

Mufumbwe is familiar ground for the security forces. The military previously led a joint operation to clear illegal miners from the Kikonge gold fields in the district. The minister’s latest remarks extend that mandate to illegal mining wherever it is found.

For the miners in Mufumbwe and the factions that clashed in Mpika, the message from the Ministry of Defence is direct. The President has issued the order and the military has the task. In Mr Lufuma’s words, the soldiers are coming.

World.title: High Court Throws Out State Objection, Clears Way For Mundubile And Zulu Bail Hearing
World.content:
The Lusaka High Court has dismissed the State’s attempt to block the constitutional bail application of opposition leaders Mr Brian Mundubile, Mr Makebi Zulu and 16 others. It ruled that the matter is properly before the court and must now be heard on its merits.

The decision removes the procedural wall that has stood in front of the 18 detainees since they filed for bail. It opens the way for the hearing to begin on Wednesday.

A panel of three judges, Judge Derrick Mulenga, Judge Davies Chibwili and Judge Ireen Wishimanga, delivered the ruling. The panel threw out a preliminary objection in which the State challenged the manner in which the application had been filed.

Mr Mundubile was the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) presidential candidate in the August election and finished second. Mr Zulu was his running mate. Lusaka business executive Mr Harry Findlay is among their co-applicants.

The group has petitioned the High Court alleging gross violations of their constitutional rights and freedoms. Through the bail application, they are asking to be released while that petition is determined, either unconditionally or on such terms as the court considers appropriate.

The 18 face charges that include treason, sedition and terrorism-related offences, laid after their arrest in the aftermath of the polls. They are being held at Mukobeko Maximum Correctional Facility in Kabwe and have been brought from there to the court in Lusaka.

The failed objection came from the highest legal office in Government. Attorney General Mulilo Kabesha told the court that the bail application was improperly before it because it had been filed as part of a civil constitutional petition rather than through criminal proceedings.

Acting Chief State Advocate Chibesa Mulonda took the same line. He submitted that constitutional bail could not be sought under a constitutional petition and urged the court to dismiss the application for want of jurisdiction.

The defence resisted. Lawyers for Mr Mundubile and the other applicants, among them State Counsel Bonaventure Mutale, Chifumu Banda and Sakwiba Sikota, opposed the objection and maintained that the matter was competently before the court.

The judges sided with the applicants. They held that the court had jurisdiction to hear the bail application because it arose from a constitutional petition that was already properly before it.

The panel went further. It ruled that hearing the application within the petition would prevent unnecessary duplication of proceedings and promote the efficient administration of justice. The application therefore stays within the petition rather than being sent to the criminal courts, as the State had sought.

The ruling settles the jurisdiction question that has hung over the application since it was filed on 14 October. The process has moved slowly. At one sitting, the hearing failed to proceed after the State told the court it was not ready.

At another, the State and the defence agreed by consent to join Director of Public Prosecutions Gilbert Phiri to the proceedings, after Mr Kabesha insisted that the application was criminal in nature. Mr Zulu, himself a lawyer, has also told the court that he will represent himself in the bail proceedings.

With jurisdiction settled, the hearing now moves to the questions that matter most to the detainees. The State has already set out its opposition to bail on the merits. It contends that the applicants pose a flight risk and could interfere with prosecution witnesses because of their political influence.

The State also maintains that the time the applicants have spent in detention does not amount to the unreasonable or inordinate delay needed to justify constitutional bail. Those claims will now be tested before the same three judges who dismissed its objection.

Ahead of the hearing, Mr Mundubile and Mr Zulu appealed for openness, fairness and justice in the proceedings.

The panel will now hear both sides on whether the 18 should walk free while their petition is decided. The applicants want release, unconditional or on terms. The State wants them kept in custody. That contest opens on Wednesday.

World.title: Govt. calls for strengthened family systems
World.content:
Ministry of Community Development and Social Services Director of Child Development, Joshua Kamanya has called for strengthened family systems to ensure children grow up in safe and supportive environments.

Mr Kamanya says children’s voices should be strengthened from an early age to enable them to participate in decision-making processes.

Mr Kamanya was speaking when a combined team from UNICEF and various government Ministries paid a courtesy call on North-Western Province Deputy Permanent Secretary, Luckson Mulumbi in Solwezi today.

He said society today has many adults who are unable to effectively participate in decision-making due to weak family foundations.

“We need to sensitise our people so that children can have voices, and be part of the decision making at an earlier stage,” Mr Kamanya said.

He further said the team is in the province to launch the ‘Mwana Nimuntu Project,’ which seeks to advocate for children to be raised in safe and supportive environments.

“Our programme here in North-Western Province, particularly here in Solwezi and Mushindamo District, will run from the 9th to 13th November 2026 to launch the Mwana Nimuntu project and also the Equal Chances for Human Development,” Mr Kamanya said.

He said the programme is designed to create an environment where children can play, dream and realise their dreams so that they grow into responsible citizens.

And Mr Mulumbi expressed happiness with the introduction of the new project in the province, in addition to the already running Equal Chances for Human Development programme.

He said the Equal Chances programme, is already helping the province address various challenges in sectors such as health and education, among others.

“We are happy for this project and now that you have come to look at the issue of children, which is very important because when you look at the cultural dynamics of this province, it just makes sense that we invest in programmes that promote the welfare of our children,” Mr Mulumbi said.

World.title: ZDA calls on French companies to invest in Zambia
World.content:
Zambia Development Agency (ZDA) has called on French companies to invest in Zambia through partnerships and joint ventures to support the country’s economic growth ambitions under the Grow Zambia Agenda.

ZDA Director General, Albert Halwampa says partnerships with French companies would enable Zambia to expand local production, supply the domestic and regional markets, and increase exports to international markets, including France.

Speaking during the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the Zambia Development Agency (ZDA) and the Movement of the Enterprises of France (MEDEF) in Lusaka, Mr Halwampa noted that Zambia has a stable economic environment, improved investor confidence and access to regional markets.

“I am sure you all agree that our economy is very stable, looking at all the macroeconomic fundamentals,” Mr Halwampa added.

He cited the country’s strategic location, sharing borders with eight neighbouring countries, as well as its membership in regional trade blocs such as the Southern African Development Community (SADC) and Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA), as key advantages for investors

Mr Halwampa also encouraged French companies to explore opportunities in renewable energy, including solar, wind, hydropower and waste-to-energy, as well as manufacturing, mining and mineral value addition.

He assured investors that ZDA would facilitate their entry into the Zambian market, support the implementation of investment commitments and provide aftercare services to ensure their businesses thrive.

“We are very happy that today we are able to come to this moment, and we are committed as ZDA to ensure that we facilitate the investment of French companies in Zambia,” he further added.

Mr Halwampa further assured the delegation that Zambia remained a peaceful and secure investment destination where investors could enjoy returns and repatriate profits after meeting their tax obligations.

Meanwhile, President of the France East Africa Business Council of MEDEF International, Céline Gouveia, said the delegation of French companies had identified investment opportunities in Zambia following engagements with various government ministries and institutions.

Ms Gouveia highlighted that the delegation, comprising companies from different sectors, including mining, energy and transport, was interested in establishing long-term partnerships with Zambian businesses.

“Companies such as Alstom, Imerys and Africa Global Logistics (AGL) which are already established here in Zambia, are definitely here to support you,” she added.

Ms Gouveia thanked ZDA for facilitating meetings with relevant stakeholders, saying the signing of the MoU marked the beginning of stronger economic cooperation between Zambia and France.

She disclosed that the delegation was keen to move beyond diplomatic engagements and translate the growing relationship between the two countries into concrete business partnerships and investments.

World.title: Kalila pledges to work with stakeholders to address housing challenges
World.content:
The Transition of leadership in the Housing and Infrastructure sector has taken center stage as the outgoing Minister of Housing and Infrastructure Development formally hands over office to two Ministers now overseeing the separate portfolios of Housing and infrastructure and Urban Development.

The handover Ceremony marks an important moment ensuring continuity of government programmes, policy implementation and service delivery under the two ministries.

Speaking during the handover ceremony, the newly sworn in Minister of Housing Christopher, Kalila reaffirmed his commitment to building on the progress made while prioritising outgoing Minister’s programmes and reforms.

Dr Kalila said that he will be working collaboratively with all stakeholders to address the Housing needs of citizens.

Dr Kalila says he is looking forward to the Ministry’s staff support and cooperation as they strive to provide affordable, decent and sustainable housing for all in line with the Grow Zambia Agenda.

And the Minister of Infrastructure and Urban Development, Collins Nzovu, has pledged to strengthen monitoring of ongoing infrastructure projects to ensure timely completion and accountability in the use of public resources.

Eng Nzovu has identified inadequate funding, project delays, outstanding financial obligations and shortages of technical personnel as some of the major challenges affecting Infrastructure development.

He has commended progress made through Public- Private Partnership projects, saying government will continue strengthening the programme to support infrastructure development.

The Minister says Government will prioritise orderly urban development, upgrading informal settlements and improving access to basic services while promoting safe, resilient and sustainable public infrastructure.

Meanwhile, the outgoing Minister of Housing and Infrastructure Development, Charles Milupi, has called for collaboration among government ministries and stakeholders to accelerate infrastructure development and improve urban planning in the country.

He says the realignment of the Ministry presents an opportunity for a sharper focus on public infrastructure and Urban Development urging the incoming Ministers to build on the progress already made.

He has further emphasised the need for continuous maintenance of public infrastructure, stating that proper maintenance is more cost-effective than rehabilitation or complete replacement of Infrastructure.

The Minister has urged the new Minister of Housing to prioritize the completion of ongoing projects, finalise the Housing policy and strengthen estate management standards to improve housing delivery in the country.

He disclosed that construction of homes for the elderly people in Chinsali and Choma districts have reached 87 and 84 % completion respectfully.

World.title: Vubwi residents urged to reinforce buildings
World.content:
Vubwi Town Council Chairperson, Debby Zulu has urged the residents to reinforce their buildings and take precautionary measures ahead of the rainy season.

Mr Zulu says residents, schools, churches and government institutions need to institute measures to prevent damage to infrastructure caused by strong winds and heavy rains.

He said institutions and households should inspect their rooftops and ensure that buildings are structurally sound, warning that extreme weather conditions could damage infrastructure and disrupt household activities and government operations.

Mr Zulu was speaking after visiting a family whose house was damaged by strong winds in Chikoma Two Village in Vubwi Ward.

The incident occurred while a four-day-old baby and the mother were inside the house.

However, all family members escaped unharmed.

Mr Zulu advised residents to consider using quality building materials and constructing structures that can withstand harsh weather conditions associated with climate change.

He also encouraged residents and authorities to plant trees around their premises, saying the practice could help protect buildings and surrounding infrastructure from damage during the rainy season.

“What has happened here is quite unfortunate. As a family, you should remain strong and hopeful that you will overcome this challenge,” he said.

Mr Zulu also appealed to well-wishers to support the affected family to repair the damaged house, pledging to facilitate its renovation in his personal capacity.

Meanwhile, the affected homeowner, Elias Miti, said he needed at least K3,000 to renovate the house.

Mr Miti expressed concern that failure to raise the required funds in time could delay the repair works and affect his preparations for the farming season.

He said the family was fortunate to have escaped without injuries despite the frightening incident.

According to reports, Vubwi District is prone to storms and heavy rainfall, which have previously resulted in damage to residential houses, schools and church buildings, highlighting the need for communities and institutions to strengthen their infrastructure ahead of the rainy season.

World.title: Chifunabuli woman gang-raped
World.content:
A 31-year-old woman of Chifunabuli District has been allegedly gang-raped by three unknown men.

Luapula Province Police Commissioner, Lucky Munkhondya has confirmed the incident which occurred early this morning, November 10, 2026 around 04:00 hours at Lubwe market.

Ms Munkondya said the victim left home with her three months old baby to Lubwe market to drink alcohol around 18:00 hours yesterday, November 09, 2026.

He said after the victim got intoxicated, and fell asleep in one of the corridors at the market where unknown men took turns in raping her.

Ms Munkhondya explained that two women who were passing-by heard screams and saw the victim being raped after which they alerted a nearby security guard who managed to apprehend one of the three assailants while the other two accomplices escaped.

“The security guard together with others rescued the baby and later took the suspect to the police station,” Ms Munkondya said.

Police visited the crime scene where they found the victim still intoxicated and took her to Lubwe Mission Hospital where she is currently receiving medical examinations and treatment.

Ms Munkhondya identified the man who has been arrested as Oswald Chanda aged 31 of Mwelwa Kanina village in Chief Chitembo’s Chiefdom.

A manhunt has been launched to locate and arrest the two remaining suspects.
