World.title: FAZ Clarifies Under-15 national team winning allowances Issue
World.content:
The Football Association of Zambia (FAZ) has clarified issues surrounding the winning allowances for the Under-15 national team that emerged champions at the Tier-B World Cup in Baku, Azerbaijan.

In an exclusive interview with the media at Football House in Lusaka, FAZ media Manager, Godfrey Chikumbi, said no money came from International Federation of Association Football (FIFA) to pay the age-group team for winning the global competition.

Chikumbi said the action taken was within the provisions of the law.

He was reacting to accusations leveled against the local football governing body by members of the public, alleging that the winning allowances intended for the Under-15 players who won the recently concluded Tier-B World Cup tournament in Baku, Azerbaijan, had been misappropriated.

The Media manager explained that any player aged 17 and below is considered to be playing in a developmental competition and not a commercial one because of their age.

He said it is against international labour law to engage a person under the age of 17 in commercial activities.

“It is against this backdrop that our national team were not paid anything by FIFA despite their victory,” Chikumbi said.

He however advised parents and all stakeholders to nurture their children by ensuring they avoid illicit activities if they are to see them play in higher competitions in future.

Chikumbi said FAZ only spends little time with young players as most of the time they are in the communities with parents, hence the need to continue encouraging and counselling them.

Meanwhile, the Media Manager also indicated that the FAZ technical team has continued with its programme of talent identification across the country.

World.title: Developers’ body lobbies for statutory register to protect land buyers
World.content:
The Property Developers Association of Zimbabwe has called for a law compelling all land and property developers to register with a statutory body to restore public confidence in the property sector and protect land buyers from fraud.

Interim chairperson Arnold Khanda made the call on Wednesday in response to a recent government directive for local authorities to demolish all illegal structures in their areas of jurisdiction.

The move has left several families without shelter or a source of livelihood.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 11, 2026
World.content:
DR Congo Faces Growing Fears of a Cholera Resurgence

The Democratic Republic of Congo has reported more than 60,000 cholera cases since the beginning of the year, including 1,800 deaths. World Health Organisation (WHO) Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the situation represents the "worst cholera outbreak in decades." The eastern provinces of North and South Kivu have been hit particularly hard, with violence and insecurity hindering efforts to contain the outbreak. There are also growing concerns over the spread of the disease to the densely populated capital, Kinshasa, amid the rainy season. Health experts have cited poor access to clean water and sanitation, and called for greater prevention, better water systems and vaccination campaigns. Doctors Without Borders has increased its response by providing medical assistance, safe drinking water and sanitation support in affected communities, the agency said. However, insecurity, poor infrastructure and limited access to health care continue to hinder efforts to contain the outbreak.

UNICEF Warns Drones and Drought Are Deepening Sudan's Child Crisis



UNICEF has warned that escalating drone attacks on Sudan's power infrastructure, combined with severe drought, are creating a devastating humanitarian crisis for children. The agency said that up to 15 power stations were hit in October, disrupting water supplies, healthcare, irrigation and food production. Failed rains have severely damaged prospects for the 2026-27 harvest. An estimated 825,000 children under five are expected to suffer from severe acute malnutrition this year. UNICEF said that it has supported millions with healthcare, clean water, vaccinations and education but warns its response is only one-third funded. It said that two in three child casualties recorded this year have been caused by drone attacks, bringing the conflict into areas previously considered safe. The agency is calling for an end to attacks on civilian infrastructure, safe humanitarian access and urgent international funding to sustain essential services.

Violence in Northern Nigeria Forces Over 64,000 to Flee Across Borders

More than 64,000 people have fled violence in northern Nigeria to neighbouring Niger, while several hundred others have sought refuge in Benin since the beginning of the year, according to the UN refugee agency. The displacement is being driven by jihadist insurgencies, armed banditry and farmer-herder clashes, placing additional pressure on countries already facing insecurity and climate-related challenges. Many newly arrived refugees, including children, face food shortages, malnutrition, limited access to clean water and inadequate shelter. UNHCR said that only about five percent of this year's Nigerian arrivals have been registered because of funding constraints and is appealing for 11.4 million dollars to support humanitarian operations across Nigeria, Niger and Benin. Conditions are particularly difficult in Niger's Diffa region, where insecurity and drought have further weakened food production and livelihoods. The agency warns that without additional funding, thousands of vulnerable families could be left without essential humanitarian assistance and protection.

U.S. Issues Highest Travel Warning for 11 African Countries

The United States has issued its highest-level travel warning against 23 countries. It advised American citizens not to travel there under any circumstances because of security threats, unstable conditions, and limited consular assistance. The countries include several African nations: Burkina Faso, the Central African Republic, Chad, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Libya, Mali, Niger, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan and Uganda. The Level 4 advisory is the highest category in the US State Department's four-tier travel warning system and urges citizens to avoid all travel to the affected destinations. The department said that the warnings are based on local security conditions and the US government's ability to provide assistance to its citizens. Americans have been urged to consult the State Department's travel advisory website for country-specific updates before making international travel arrangements.

How Egypt's Laws Are Being Used to Silence Independent Media

Egyptian authorities are facing renewed criticism over their crackdown on independent journalism following the conviction of Mada Masr editor-in-chief Lina Attalah. A court ordered the closure of the independent news outlet, fined Attalah three million Egyptian pounds (about U.S.$54,000) and ordered the confiscation of its equipment for operating without a licence, despite repeated attempts by the publication to obtain registration. The Committee to Protect Journalists said that the case highlights how licensing requirements, criminal penalties and website blocking are being used to restrict press freedom. Attalah's legal team disputes claims that she waived her right to appeal, with the first appeal hearing scheduled for November 25. The case has also raised concerns about other independent outlets facing similar licensing difficulties and restrictions.

WHO Warns of Critical Gaps in Africa's Health Data Systems

The World Health Organisation has warned that critical weaknesses in Africa's health information systems are undermining efforts to identify health threats and improve healthcare delivery. A new report assessing 40 countries found that fewer than half notify authorities of at least 80% of deaths, while only 21 countries record causes for a similar proportion of registered deaths. The report also highlights limited capacity to analyse and verify health data, inadequate funding and shortages of trained professionals. However, progress is being made, with 43 of the WHO's 47 African member states having adopted digital platforms to collect and report routine health information. The findings were presented at the first African Health Data Forum in Nairobi, where officials are also discussing how digital technology and artificial intelligence can strengthen healthcare systems. WHO said that responsible use of AI will require appropriate legislation, safeguards and regulatory frameworks.

Close 

South African Olympic Champion Tatjana Smith Switches Allegiance to Netherlands

South Africa's most decorated Olympic athlete, Tatjana Smith, has announced she will switch her sporting allegiance to the Netherlands. She cited financial and practical challenges in sustaining her swimming career. The two-time Olympic gold medallist said she understood the decision could disappoint South African supporters but viewed it as an opportunity to explore her Dutch heritage and access better high-performance support. Smith, who holds dual citizenship, retired after the 2024 Paris Olympics but recently announced her comeback, targeting the 2028 Los Angeles Games. She will continue training in South Africa while representing the Netherlands. She won gold in the 200-metre breaststroke at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics and the 100-metre breaststroke in Paris in 2024. She also claimed two silver medals across the two Games, making her South Africa's most successful Olympic athlete.

Matlala Says He Didn't Know Impalas Were for Sibiya

World.title: Nigeria: Nigerian-Born Emehelu Makes History As New Jersey's Lieutenant Governor
World.content:
Nigerian-born American lawyer, Shirley U. Emehelu, has made history as the first immigrant to become Lieutenant Governor of New Jersey, U.S.

Emehelu, who emigrated from Nigeria as a child, was appointed by Gov. Mikie Sherrill on Monday, becoming the fifth Lieutenant Governor of the state.

The appointment also makes history, as New Jersey's two highest executive offices are occupied by women simultaneously for the first time.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The appointment represents a milestone for Nigerian-Americans, whose participation in U.S. public life now includes one of the highest executive positions in American state government.

Emehelu also assumed the position of Secretary of State, consolidating responsibilities in government administration, electoral oversight and public service.

She was sworn in at the New Jersey Statehouse in Trenton by Chief Justice Stuart Rabner, with her husband and children participating in the ceremony.

Announcing the appointment, Sherrill described Emehelu as an experienced public servant whose career demonstrated integrity, accountability and a commitment to protecting residents.

"Shirley embodies those values," the governor declared, referring to her administration's emphasis on accountability and public service.

Sherrill said Emehelu's record in prosecuting financial crimes, protecting consumers, defending civil rights and combating government waste informed her selection.

The governor explained that Emehelu had also demonstrated effective leadership while overseeing the administration of New Jersey's recent elections as Acting Secretary of State.

Accepting the appointment, Emehelu expressed appreciation for the confidence reposed in her and reaffirmed her commitment to serving the state's diverse population.

"I've spent my career upholding the law, protecting families, and rooting out fraud, abuse, and corruption," she said.

Emehelu also acknowledged the significance of her Nigerian heritage and the opportunities her appointment represented for immigrant and minority communities.

"As a Black woman and Nigerian American, I'm proud of what this appointment represents for our state, and especially for the communities that share my heritage," she said.

She expressed hope that the occasion would encourage younger generations to pursue public service and contribute meaningfully to their communities.

"I hope we can inspire the next generation to find their own ways to serve and make a little history of their own too," she said.

The lieutenant governor pledged to support Sherrill's administration in addressing living costs, expanding economic opportunities and ensuring more responsive government.

Reflecting on her years in public service, Emehelu identified the protection of ordinary citizens as the central motivation behind her professional career.

"The throughline across my federal and state service has been defending the people who are counting on government to do right by them," she said.

Emehelu previously served as New Jersey's Acting State Comptroller, overseeing efforts to combat fraud, financial mismanagement and waste involving public resources.

Between 2022 and 2024, she was the state's Executive Assistant Attorney General, the third-ranking official in the Attorney General's Office, overseeing major civil litigation and enforcement matters.

Close 

She also served for nine years as a federal prosecutor in the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of New Jersey, handling complex financial fraud cases.

During her federal service, she became Chief of Asset Recovery and Anti-Money Laundering, overseeing programmes involving forfeited assets, money laundering and restitution for victims.

A graduate of Yale University and Yale Law School, Emehelu also worked in private legal practice and served as a judicial clerk in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia.

Her appointment followed the September resignation of former lieutenant governor Dale Caldwell after allegations of misconduct and violations of state ethics rules, which he disputed.

Emehelu is married to Ikenna Emehelu and they have two children, Nnamdi and Amara. (NAN)

World.title: Liberia: Senate Opens Public Hearing On War Crimes, Anti-Corruption Courts
World.content:
The Liberian Senate has invited civil society organizations, victims' groups, human rights advocates, legal practitioners and other stakeholders to participate in a public hearing on proposed legislation seeking to establish a Special War Crimes Court for Liberia (SWCTL) and a Special Economic and Corruption Crimes Court under the proposed National Anti-Corruption Court Act.

The hearing, scheduled for November 25, 2026, at the Senate Chamber Annex in Monrovia, is intended to provide a platform for public consultation, allowing stakeholders to present recommendations and express their views on the proposed laws before they are forwarded to the full Senate for consideration.

The legislative initiative seeks to establish accountability mechanisms for addressing atrocities committed during Liberia's civil conflicts, alongside specialized judicial arrangements for prosecuting economic and corruption-related offenses.

The invitation was extended by the Senate Standing Committee on Judiciary, Human Rights, Claims and Petitions as part of efforts to gather public input and conduct further consultations on the harmonized bills.



The proposed hearing is expected to bring together representatives of civil society organizations, victims' associations, human rights defenders, legal professionals, government institutions and other national and international stakeholders whose contributions could help shape the proposed judicial frameworks.

Welcoming the Senate's decision, Adama K. Dempster, National Secretary General of the Civil Society Human Rights Advocacy Platform of Liberia and a longstanding advocate for the establishment of a War and Economic Crimes Court, described the invitation as an important development in Liberia's pursuit of justice, accountability and the rule of law.

In a statement issued on November 9, Dempster expressed appreciation to the Senate for opening the legislative process to broader public participation, noting that meaningful engagement with citizens and relevant institutions is necessary to ensure that the proposed courts reflect national expectations and accepted international standards.

"We want to thank the Senate for engaging a broad range of stakeholders and conducting due diligence in the legislative process on this matter. This public hearing represents an important milestone in Liberia's quest for justice and accountability," Dempster stated.

He emphasized that consultations involving victims, survivors, legal experts and other citizens would be essential to ensuring that the proposed judicial institutions are appropriately designed, independent and capable of fulfilling their intended mandates.

According to him, the legislative process must adequately address the rights and interests of victims while guaranteeing due process and fair trial protections for accused persons.

He further stressed that the proposed courts should be consistent with international standards, strengthen public confidence in the justice system and establish credible mechanisms for addressing Liberia's history of conflict-related atrocities and corruption.

Dempster said the proposed Special War Crimes Court represents a longstanding demand of Liberia's human rights community, transitional justice advocates and civil society organizations, particularly those calling for the implementation of recommendations contained in the report of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC).

The TRC, established following Liberia's civil conflicts, made recommendations intended to address the country's history of human rights violations, promote national reconciliation and establish accountability for serious crimes committed during the war years.

Dempster noted that the November 25 hearing would also provide an opportunity for national and international experts to contribute technical perspectives on the proposed court's mandate, jurisdiction, institutional independence, organizational structure and operational effectiveness.

He said such contributions would be important in ensuring that the final legislation provides a sound legal and institutional foundation for the proposed accountability mechanisms.

The civil society advocate also commended the Senate for acknowledging the initial submission of a draft War Crimes Court bill by civil society organizations and the Independent National Commission on Human Rights (INCHR) in 2025.

He described the recognition of that submission as an important part of the consultative process, emphasizing that civil society and human rights organizations have consistently advocated for the establishment of accountability institutions to address the consequences of Liberia's civil conflicts.

"We therefore want to appreciate the Liberian Senate for creating this space for public engagement through dialogue and recognizing civil society and the Independent National Commission on Human Rights initial submission of the war court crimes draft bill in 2025.

"Civil society and the human rights community remain committed to participating constructively in these processes and supporting efforts aimed at delivering justice for victims while promoting reconciliation, accountability, and lasting peace," he added.

Dempster further linked the Senate's current legislative initiative to the Joint Resolution adopted in April 2024 by both Houses of the 55th National Legislature, which supported the process toward establishing war and economic crimes courts in Liberia.

The resolution provided a legislative basis for advancing the national conversation and institutional process surrounding accountability for war-era atrocities and economic crimes.

Close 

Against this background, he urged victims' associations, youth and women's organizations, religious institutions, traditional leaders, development partners and members of the wider Liberian public to take advantage of the November 25 hearing to contribute to the national dialogue.

He stressed that the establishment of the proposed courts should not be viewed solely as an effort to address crimes committed during the country's past conflicts but also as part of broader efforts to strengthen democratic governance, combat impunity and promote respect for human rights.

"We believe the establishment of these accountability mechanisms is not only about addressing the crimes of the past; it is about strengthening democratic governance, combating impunity, promoting national healing, and ensuring that future generations inherit a society founded on justice and respect for human rights," Dempster stated.

He maintained that the public hearing represents a significant opportunity for Liberians to participate directly in shaping the country's accountability framework and contribute to the development of institutions capable of addressing serious violations and economic offenses.

The Senate's planned consultation comes amid longstanding national discussions over the implementation of the TRC recommendations and the establishment of specialized judicial institutions to address war-related atrocities and economic and corruption crimes.

World.title: South Africa: Ministers Pocket Pay Hikes As Millions Battle to Survive
World.content:
The increase adds about R97,725 a year to a minister's remuneration package and R46,304 to an ordinary MP's package.

The announcement came on the same day Stats SA reported that unemployment had risen to 33.7%, with 8.6 million people officially unemployed.

Ministers will get nearly R98,000 more a year after President Cyril Ramaphosa approved salary increases for politicians, a decision unions have condemned as millions struggle to make ends meet.

The South African Federation of Trade Unions (Saftu) wants the 3.5% increase reversed, arguing that political leaders should put struggling households first.

The Presidency announced the increases on Tuesday, 10 November. They are backdated to 1 April 2026.



The 3.5% adjustment covers ministers, deputy ministers, members of Parliament, premiers, members of provincial executive councils and provincial legislators.

Based on previously gazetted remuneration, the increase adds about R97,725 a year to a minister's package and R46,304 to an ordinary MP's.

These are increases in total remuneration packages, which include pension contributions, rather than additional take-home pay.

Saftu general secretary Zwelinzima Vavi said the decision could not be justified against the country's unemployment crisis.

"This decision is indefensible in a country where, in the second quarter of 2026, 8.5 million people were officially unemployed and another 4.6 million formed part of the potential labour force. That means 13.1 million people were unemployed or part of the potential labour force," Vavi said, according to The Citizen.

Those figures refer to April to June. Newer figures released by Statistics South Africa on Tuesday show that official unemployment rose to 33.7% in the third quarter, with 8.6 million people unemployed.

The number of unemployed people increased by 97,000, even though employment also grew by 101,000 to 16.8 million.

The potential labour force is counted separately from official unemployment. It includes discouraged jobseekers and others who meet some, but not all, of the criteria for being officially unemployed.

Ramaphosa also approved a separate 4% increase for judges, magistrates, traditional leaders and members of national and provincial houses of traditional and Khoi-San leaders.

The Presidency said the decision followed recommendations from the Independent Commission for the Remuneration of Public Office-Bearers.

The commission considered factors including inflation, the affordability of increases for the state, previous pay decisions and average annual wage increases.

The Presidency said Ramaphosa urged public office-bearers to uphold their responsibilities and honour the public's trust.

Close 

Saftu accepted the separate increase for judges but called on Ramaphosa and Parliament to reverse the 3.5% adjustment for politicians.

"At a time when millions are unemployed, and households are being pushed deeper into hardship, leadership must be measured by service to the people, not by higher pay for those already entrusted with governing them," Vavi said.

World.title: Uganda: Erratic Museveni Son Deactivates X Handle After Threats Against Uganda VP
World.content:
Nairobi — Uganda's Chief of Defence Forces Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba has deactivated his X account following a series of threats against Vice President Jessica Alupo, adding to a record of provocative online pronouncements by President Yoweri Museveni's son.

Muhoozi accused Alupo of supporting what he called the "treachery" of former deputy military chief Peter Elwelu, who was arrested on November over allegations of involvement in activities aimed at destabilising the country.

"There are already strong signals that Jessica was supporting the treachery of Elweru. If that is true she will account for it," he posted.

He subsequently threatened to remove her from government.



"As Deputy Commander-in-Chief, Jessica will be dismissed from our government soon. We have very many supporters in Teso. We don't have to rely on traitors."

In another post, Muhoozi suggested that Uganda would be governed on military terms if he became Vice President.

"As Vice President, the government will operate on military terms. There will be no more inefficiency," he wrote.

He later threatened to arrest Alupo if she was found to have supported Elwelu.

"We shall arrest Jessica, without hesitation if she is part of Elweru's treachery," he posted.

Muhoozi also invoked previous confrontations with opposition figures as evidence that his threats should be taken seriously.

"I told you I would arrest Besigye and I did. I told you I would defeat Kabobi and I did. I told you I would arrest Lukwago and I did. And many more. I think you should start believing me," he wrote.

The posts have drawn fresh attention to Muhoozi's use of social media to pronounce on political and security matters, including threats against senior government officials.

Museveni succession contest

The latest outburst comes as Muhoozi increasingly positions himself at the centre of Uganda's succession debate, with his Patriotic League of Uganda (PLU) movement mobilising support for a possible presidential bid in 2031.

Widely viewed as Museveni's presumed successor, Muhoozi faces competing political ambitions within the ruling National Resistance Movement (NRM), where supporters of both father and son have increasingly clashed over the country's political future.

PLU has insisted that it operates within the broader NRM framework rather than as a separate political party, even as it pursues a nationwide mobilisation drive for Muhoozi.

During a recent mobilisation meeting, a key PLU figure Jimmy Lwanga warned NRM supporters against attempts to frustrate the movement's activities or undermine Muhoozi's presidential ambitions.

"Everything PLU does has the president's endorsement, and we therefore call upon members of NRM to also join in support of Gen. MK," Lwanga said.

PLU has been distributing endorsement books through its structures across the country as it seeks to consolidate support ahead of the 2031 election.

Muhoozi, however, would have to leave military service before seeking elective political office.

Earlier controversies

Muhoozi's online conduct has previously triggered diplomatic criticism, including from Washington.

In January 2026, US Senator Jim Risch, Chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, rejected an apology issued by Muhoozi after a series of controversial posts directed at the United States.

Risch described the apology as hollow and insufficient, saying Muhoozi had crossed a "red line" despite deleting the posts.

The US Senator urged Washington to impose tougher sanctions on Uganda, arguing that an apology did not address wider concerns about the country's conduct and respect for democratic norms.

That same month, Muhoozi threatened to kill opposition leader Bobi Wine following Uganda's disputed presidential election.

"We have killed 22 NUP terrorists since last week. I'm praying the 23rd is Kabobi," he wrote, referring to the opposition leader by a derogatory nickname.

He also issued Wine a 48-hour ultimatum to surrender to police, threatening to treat him as an outlaw or rebel.

The remarks came as Wine remained in hiding following a security raid on his home and rejected the election results that handed Museveni another term.

Muhoozi has also intervened in government administration and military affairs.

In September, he directed ministers to obtain his permission before travelling abroad, threatening a fine of 30 million Ugandan shillings for those who left without his clearance.

The directive followed his questioning of a trip to Türkiye by Minister of State for Foreign Affairs Haruna Kasolo, who subsequently said he would seek Muhoozi's guidance and authority before undertaking future travel.

Close 

In November, Muhoozi announced that he intended to leave the position of Chief of Defence Forces within months and dedicate his life to Christ.

"My time as CDF is coming to an end. I have accomplished all the tasks my God gave me. In a few months I will handover this office to a qualified officer. I shall dedicate my life to Christ after that," he wrote, without specifying a handover date or naming a successor.

Days earlier, he had announced the demotion of his former deputy Elwelu from Lieutenant General to private.

Muhoozi's public pronouncements have also previously shifted. In March 2022, he announced his retirement from the army after 28 years of service, prompting speculation about his political ambitions.

"After 28 years of service in my glorious military, the greatest military in the world, I am happy to announce my retirement," he wrote.

He later walked back the announcement, indicating that he would instead retire eight years later.

Appointed Chief of Defence Forces in March 2024, Muhoozi has increasingly become a central figure in Uganda's political succession debate, with his public interventions drawing scrutiny both at home and abroad.

World.title: Malawi: South Africa Refuses to Let Bushiri Extradition Fight End
World.content:
The long-running legal battle over the fate of Prophet Shepherd Bushiri and his wife, Mary Bushiri, has entered a new phase after South Africa launched an appeal against a High Court ruling that blocked their extradition.

Pretoria has asked the High Court for leave to challenge the decision, arguing that the court misapplied both the law and the principles governing extradition proceedings.

The move underscores South Africa's determination to secure the couple's return to face fraud, theft and money laundering charges, allegations they have consistently denied.

Director of Criminal Litigation Dzikondianthu Malunda confirmed that South Africa had lodged an application setting out 14 grounds of appeal.



At the heart of Pretoria's argument is the contention that the High Court treated the matter as though it were a criminal trial, rather than an extradition proceeding whose purpose is to determine whether there is sufficient evidence for a case to be heard in another jurisdiction.

The appeal challenges several key findings made by the court.

South Africa argues that the judge applied the wrong standard of proof, improperly rejected documentary evidence and failed to assess whether the available material was sufficient to warrant a trial in South Africa.

It also disputes the conclusion that the Bushiris were denied a fair hearing, pointing to their participation in proceedings, including opportunities to cross-examine witnesses and present their own evidence.

Pretoria further contests the finding that extradition would be unjust or oppressive because of the passage of time.

According to the appeal, the court did not adequately establish whether delays had compromised the possibility of a fair hearing or whether the extradition request was politically motivated.

The case has become one of the region's most closely watched legal disputes since the Bushiris left South Africa and returned to Malawi in November 2020 while on bail.

South African authorities have since sought their extradition, while the couple have maintained that they would not receive a fair trial and have raised concerns about their personal safety if returned.

The latest appeal is therefore about more than the fate of one high-profile religious couple. It touches on wider questions of judicial cooperation, the interpretation of extradition law and the balance courts must strike between protecting individual rights and honouring international legal obligations.

The ruling now under challenge, delivered in October 2026, overturned an earlier magistrates' court decision that had cleared the way for the Bushiris' extradition.

Close 

With South Africa pressing ahead once again, the legal and diplomatic contest appears far from over.

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: Mounting Fears Over the Return of Cholera
World.content:
Three fresh cases of cholera have been reported on the outskirts of the capital Kinshasa. Amid the threat of a renewed outbreak, residents are concerned about how they can best protect themselves and their communities.

More than 60,000 cases of cholera have been recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) since the beginning of the year — including 1,800 deaths.

According to World Health Organisation (WHO) Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the situation accounts for the "worst cholera outbreak in decades" in the central African country.

The mortality rate to date in 2026 stands at around 3%, which the WHO says is quite high for cholera.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Eastern DRC at particular risk

Most of the infections so far have been detected in the eastern provinces of North and South Kivu.

Both regions have long been plagued by guerilla warfare waged by a multitude of armed groups, in particular rebels belonging to the Rwanda-backed M23 militia. Parts of the region are now under the control of the insurgents, which effectively are now tasked with addressing and coordinating public health measures.

These circumstances make a nationwide, government-coordinated response to the epidemic significantly more difficult, especially in North and South Kivu.

At the same time, the DRC is also facing the deadliest Ebola outbreak in its history, making public health one of the main priorities at the moment.

Millions worried across megapolis Kinshasa

Following the cases in North and South Kivu, further reports of cholera emerged along the Congo River basin. Most recently, three cases were reported in Kingabwa in the east of Kinshasa. Many worry that now, the ongoing rainy season could further facilitate the spread of the waterborne disease.

Fears of another cholera outbreak now feel palpable on the ground. One resident in the Kingasani district of the capital Kinshasa told DW that many people "are afraid."

"We wash our hands after every contact. Cholera is a disease that kills quickly," the man said, not wanting to share details about his name or identity.

Another resident meanwhile told DW that he was concerned because "there are no health authorities in Kinshasa" — although strictly speaking, this isn't true.

Kinshasa's health authority, Division Provinciale de la Sante (DPS), is either unknown to some residents or does not have a good reputation following previous public health crises.

During the last outbreak in February 2026, over 80% of infections were concentrated in the five Kinshasa health districts of Limete, Kingabwa, Kalamu II, Binza Ozone as well as Kingasani.

The WHO fears that the diarrheal disease could spread once again across the densely populated capital city, and that the DPS could become overwhelmed.

MSF: Protective measures needed across DRC

The Deputy Country Coordinator of Doctors Without Borders (MSF) in the DRC, Esther van der Woerdt, told DW that "the underlying problem often is the lack of access to safe drinking water and adequate sanitation," adding that "poor hand hygiene can also contribute to transmission."

"Cholera is primarily transmitted through the consumption of water or food that has been contaminated with the bacterium," van der Woerdt explained, stressing that MSF had significantly strengthened its response to the cholera outbreak, especially across North and South Kivu.

"Our response is providing medical care, providing access to safe drinking water to sanitation, as well as cholera prevention in the communities," she added.

However, in her view, this was not enough.

Instead, she argued, authorities across Congo need to move away from their predominantly reactive approach to outbreaks, and focus on investing more in prevention.

Cholera: A life-threatening illness if left untreated

Cholera leads to rapid dehydration and can, without sufficient medical care, be fatal — especially among vulnerable individuals and in overpopulated, poor communities.

Bernard Nsongolo, a senior doctor at a health centre in eastern Kinshasa, urges everyone living in such high-risk circumstances to "significantly step up hygiene measures."

"Drink safe water, especially treated water that is well protected," he told DW, stressing also that all food should be cooked thoroughly, and that raw vegetables and unpeeled fruit should be avoided.

Esther van der Woerdt also calls for urgent action, emphasizing the importance of treating water through chlorination, protecting water sources from contamination, and rehabilitating and maintaining water systems.

Close 

Furthermore, van der Woerdt remains a keen advocate of oral vaccination campaigns against cholera. Though efficiency rates might be limited, the vaccines can nevertheless provide another important layer of protection, particularly in high-risk communities, she said.

However, there's one challenge which seems to permeate much of the DRC: "Some areas ... simply have no access to health care at all," van der Woerdt said.

"In some areas, transporting supplies can cost approximately $15,000 (€13,500) per truck, and this can take several months due to difficult access routes and insecurity," she added.

With that in mind, van der Woerdt told DW that f or the time being, the official response to meet the scale of needs remains highly insufficient , particularly in underserved areas of the country. "Under these circumstances, communities in the DRC will continue to remain vulnerable to repeated cholera outbreaks."

DW correspondent Jean Noel Ba-Mweze (Kinshasa) contributed to this report.

World.title: LeBron James is gone, Bronny still can't play, and the Lakers need to finally cut him loose
World.content:
There are normally 60 players picked in the NBA Draft each year, and when the Los Angeles Lakers selected Bronny James out of USC in 2024, I thought "he's not a top-60 player...in the Pac-12."

We all know why the purple and gold took him late in the second round that June. It was to appease his father, LeBron James, who very well may have left L.A. if he couldn't play with his son.

The move was relatively low-risk for the Lakers, who picked Bronny 55th overall. It's rare that someone selected that late makes any meaningful contribution to his team. But now LeBron is in Philly, which begs the question: Why is Bronny still in the NBA?

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

LEBRON JAMES, BRONNY JAMES ARE ‘NOT A PACKAGE DEAL’ AFTER 76ERS MOVE, AGENT RICH PAUL SAYS

James is not like Shedeur Sanders — who's at least serviceable despite his name outshining his game. He'd likely be in his sport's top league regardless of who his father was. Bronny, on the other hand, would be lucky to play in Europe.

Let's take a look at the third-year Laker's stats.

In the 27 games Bronny played in his first NBA season, he averaged 2.3 points and 6.7 minutes (almost all garbage time) while shooting 31.3% from the field and 28.1% from deep. Keep in mind that these blatantly inefficient numbers came primarily against other NBA scrubs.

In the 42 games he played in his second season, Bronny averaged 2.9 points and 8.9 minutes while shooting 40.9% from the field and 38.6% from three. Yes, those numbers represented a modest improvement, but the sample size is so small and the competition so suspect that it's hard to judge whether he made strides toward becoming a legitimate NBA contributor.

Perhaps the better place to look is Bronny's production in the G League — the NBA's developmental league — where James got considerably more playing time per game.

In the 18 G League contests Bronny played in the 2024-25 season, he averaged 18.6 points, 4.5 rebounds, 4.8 assists and 31.4 minutes while shooting 41.5 percent from the field and 33.6 percent from deep. Not great. In the 20 G League games he played last season, he averaged 13.8 points, 3.4 rebounds, 3.9 assists and 29.5 minutes while shooting 50.2 percent from the field and 37.6 percent from deep. Scoring, boards and dimes were all down, although his shooting accuracy improved. But Bronny's Player Efficiency Rating of 12.9? It ranked 330th among qualified players in the freakin' G League.

LEBRON JAMES MAKES NBA FREE AGENCY DECISION, ANNOUNCES PLANS TO SIGN WITH 76ERS

This is basically the equivalent of the White Sox looking at Michael Jordan's .202 batting average in Double-A and saying, "Time to bring him up to The Show!" There is no world in which a G-Leaguer can be so underwhelming and keep getting NBA call-ups without a heaping helping of nepotism.

But now that LeBron is three time zones away from his firstborn, it's time for the Lakers to cut ties with Bronny for good. He's simply not an NBA-caliber player.

Yes, Bronny is making approximately $2.3 million this season on a guaranteed contract, meaning the Lakers would still owe him that money if they waived him. But cutting him would free up a roster spot for someone who might actually help the team win.

Oddly enough, the Lakers already waived another member of the 2024 draft class — 17th overall pick Dalton Knecht. And Knecht has actually produced in the NBA, averaging 7.1 points on 46.0 percent shooting while playing meaningful minutes over 132 games in L.A.

PHILADELPHIA ATHLETES, INCLUDING NEW TEAMMATES, REACT TO LEBRON JAMES JOINING 76ERS: 'WELCOME TO THE CITY'

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

He isn't a star, and he made more money than Bronny. But unlike LeBron's son, he actually contributed to the Lakers. So why was Knecht — who has since made the Knicks' roster — the one shown the door?

Maybe the Lakers see something in Bronny — who's averaging 0.8 points through five games this year — that the numbers don't reveal. Maybe they simply don't want to pay him to play somewhere else. Or maybe they're still worried about upsetting LeBron, even with the four-time MVP 3,000 miles away. Whatever the explanation, I haven't seen anything suggesting Bronny deserves an NBA roster spot. And though it's tempting to feel sorry for a man forever overshadowed by his generationally talented dad, that sympathy is starting to wane.

Despite accomplishing next to nothing beyond high school (he averaged 4.8 points per game at USC), Bronny has earned millions of dollars. And last weekend, he wasn't shy about flexing his financial muscle.

In response to a heckling Pistons fan at Little Caesars Arena, Bronny said, "How much money you make a year?"

Well, considering she was sitting near courtside, her answer could have been "a lot more than you if not for your old man."

World.title: Washington AG's office indicates it will defend girls' sports ballot measure after ACLU sues to block it
World.content:
Washington Attorney General Nick Brown’s office indicated it will fight to uphold a new voter-approved measure barring biological males from girls’ school sports, after the ACLU of Washington and other groups announced a lawsuit to block the measure.

"When a new law is passed by the people or the Legislature, our role is to ensure it is defended regardless of our personal views about the policy. We will review court filings as they come and discuss next steps," Brown’s office told OutKick.

However, the lawsuit to challenge the initiative involves Brown’s former law firm, a teachers union that supported his campaign and the former employer of his policy director. His office reiterated its position when OutKick asked follow-up questions about those connections and how the defense would be handled.

JACKSON THOMPSON: WASHINGTON STATE DEMOCRATIC PARTY CALLS GIRLS' SPORTS INITIATIVE UNCONSTITUTIONAL

"We’re discussing next steps and do not have more to add to the previous comment at this time. Again, when a new law is passed by the people or the Legislature, our role is to ensure it is defended regardless of our personal views about the policy," the office said.

The responses did not identify who would lead the defense or say whether the office had evaluated recusal or screening measures concerning those relationships.

Pacifica Law Group, where Brown previously served as a partner, is representing the Washington Education Association in the challenge, according to the Northwest Progressive Institute’s account of the filing.

Brown worked as a Pacifica partner from 2017 to 2021 before accepting President Joe Biden’s appointment as U.S. attorney for Western Washington, according to the firm. He returned in June 2023, and Pacifica identified him as a partner when it announced his election as attorney general in November 2024.

The Washington Education Association endorsed Brown’s 2024 campaign, according to Transparency USA.

The union’s political action committee was also among Brown’s campaign donors, according to The Spokesman-Review’s 2024 candidate profile, which cited Washington Public Disclosure Commission information. The profile did not specify the contribution amount.

Brown’s policy director, Enoka Herat, previously served as the ACLU of Washington’s policing and immigration policy program director.

Brown, a Democrat, also has a record of supporting transgender students’ participation in girls’ sports.

On Oct. 31, 2025, he led a coalition of attorneys general in filing an amicus brief supporting Minnesota’s policy in Female Athletes United v. Keith Ellison. The coalition urged the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to deny an emergency injunction that would have barred transgender students from most girls’ sports.

"I believe strongly in protecting the rights of all Washington kids—including transgender youth," Brown said in his office’s announcement of that amicus brief.

JACKSON THOMPSON: SEATTLE SCHOOL BOARD AUTHORIZES LEGAL CHALLENGE TO BALLOT MEASURE PROTECTING GIRLS' SPORTS

He argued that sports participation benefits children’s physical and emotional well-being and that excluding students based on gender identity perpetuates discrimination.

The lawsuit challenging Washington’s initiative was filed Monday in King County Superior Court. Plaintiffs include TransFamilies, the Washington Education Association and parents of transgender and nontransgender students who participate in girls’ sports.

The challengers argue the initiative violates state constitutional privacy protections and anti-discrimination law.

"Initiative 638 seeks to deny transgender girls equal opportunities simply because of who they are. It is discrimination, and it threatens all girls who play sports at school," the ACLU said in its announcement.

Let’s Go Washington, the organization behind the initiative, disputed the lawsuit’s claims Tuesday and argued existing sports physicals could satisfy the medical verification requirement.

Brown’s office also said it does not serve as legal counsel to the Washington Interscholastic Activities Association or local school districts.

"We don’t speculate on hypothetical events. Also, we only provide legal guidance to our state agency clients, which do not include WIAA or local school districts. We advise the state Office of the Superintendent of Public Instruction, and any such conversations would be attorney-client privileged," the office said.

World.title: ELI FEDERMAN: A boycott backfired when Philadelphia showed up for Jewish businesses
World.content:

The best response to antisemitism isn’t censorship. It’s philosemitism and exposing the truth.

I learned about the protests targeting Jewish-owned restaurants in Philadelphia on Nov. 8 when my friend Ari Engel posted on social media about going out to eat to support those establishments.

In Philadelphia, anti-Israel protesters organized a bicycle demonstration targeting six Jewish-owned restaurants and calling for a boycott. They wanted to discourage people from patronizing these businesses.

PHILLY DSA DECRIES BACKLASH OVER BOYCOTT TARGETING JEWISH EATERIES

Instead, the community turned their boycott upside down with a deluge of support and patronage for those Jewish-owned businesses.

The timing of the protest was chilling as it took place on the eve of the 88th anniversary of Kristallnacht, when Nazis attacked Jewish businesses, shattered storefronts and terrorized Jewish communities across Germany and Austria.

ANTI-ISRAEL SOCIALIST SILENT ON JEWISH BUSINESS BOYCOTT IN DISTRICT HE'S SET TO REPRESENT

Jewish organizations mobilized supporters in Philadelphia. The ADL encouraged people to eat at the targeted restaurants. JewBelong erected billboards urging residents to boycott the boycott. Hundreds of people showed up, packed restaurants and formed lines around city blocks. One restaurant worried it wouldn’t have enough food to serve everyone.

The protesters wanted to drive customers away. Instead, they drove customers in.

I’M AN ARAB MUSLIM — I STILL DON’T UNDERSTAND THE ANTISEMITIC BDS MOVEMENT

There’s a profound lesson here about the power of free expression. The protesters exercised their freedom to call for a boycott. The community exercised its freedom to reject it. Rather than demand censorship, ordinary citizens used their voices, their presence and their purchasing power to challenge prejudice.

That’s how a free society should work. We don’t need to silence hateful ideas to defeat them. We can expose them, challenge them and let them lose in the marketplace of public opinion. Censorship can turn extremists into martyrs. Public rejection can reveal just how little support their ideas command.

FORTY-FIVE PERCENT OF COLLEGE STUDENTS SAY VIOLENCE CAN BE JUSTIFIED TO STOP HATE SPEECH, POLL FINDS

And when non-Jewish neighbors stand alongside Jewish neighbors, antisemitism loses something essential: the illusion that it speaks for the majority.

Of course, criticizing Israel or advocating a political boycott isn’t inherently antisemitic. But targeting Jews because of their identity or holding them collectively responsible for Israel crosses a moral line. We can defend the right to peaceful protest while vigorously confronting prejudice.

WEAPONIZING THE CHARGE OF GENOCIDE FUELS AN INCREASINGLY DANGEROUS ANTISEMITISM

We need more than opposition to antisemitism. We need proactive philosemitism: people of every background celebrating Jewish culture, supporting Jewish neighbors and embracing Jewish life.

There’s a profound lesson here about the power of free expression. The protesters exercised their freedom to call for a boycott. The community exercised its freedom to reject it. Rather than demand censorship, ordinary citizens used their voices, their presence and their purchasing power to challenge prejudice.

And solidarity shouldn’t end when the protesters go home. Keep visiting those restaurants. Build friendships. Learn about one another. Turn a moment of outrage into lasting relationships.

The answer to people who want Jewish businesses to disappear isn’t to silence the protesters. It’s to fill those businesses with customers.

World.title: Common heart pill under scrutiny for older patients as study weighs risks of stopping
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Some older adults may be able to stop taking statins with little added risk over two years, but a new study raises concerns about longer-term safety.

That’s according to a randomized clinical trial that was presented on Nov. 7, 2026, at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions in Chicago, and published in The New England Journal of Medicine.

Statins are prescription medications that lower LDL, or "bad," cholesterol by reducing how much cholesterol the liver makes. They are known to help reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke, according to the National Heart, Lung and Blood Institute.

COMMON CHOLESTEROL DRUG LINKED TO LOWER DEMENTIA RISK WHEN STARTED EARLY

The study – conducted by researchers from the University of Bern in Switzerland, the University of California, San Francisco, and other institutions – included 1,880 adults aged 70 years and older, all of whom were taking statins to prevent a first heart attack or stroke.

All participants had at least two chronic medical conditions, but did not have established cardiovascular disease or previous cardiovascular events. Half of the participants stopped taking statins, and the other half continued.

After two years, the added risk from stopping statins was small enough to fall within the limits researchers had set for the study. However, that did not mean stopping carried no added risk.

5 HABITS THAT COULD HELP KEEP YOU OUT OF A NURSING HOME, FROM AN ORTHOPEDIC SURGEON

Over the full follow-up, which lasted about two years for the typical participant and up to four years for some, about 13% of those assigned to stop statins had a heart attack, an ischemic stroke or died from any cause, compared with 9% assigned to continue treatment.

The study’s safety monitoring board also recommended that participants who were assigned to stop statins discuss restarting treatment with their healthcare team, according to the American College of Cardiology.

For other outcomes, the researchers found no meaningful differences between the two groups in reported quality of life, muscle pain, falls, or loss of muscle mass and strength.

Dr. Christopher Kelly, a UNC Health cardiologist, emphasized that continuing statins did not worsen reported muscle pain or quality of life in the trial.

CLICK HERE TO 

Although guidelines support lowering high cholesterol earlier in life, the benefits of continuing statins in older age are less certain, said study author Dr. Rita F. Redberg, a cardiology professor at the University of California, San Francisco, in a press release.

"This small, increased risk of cardiovascular events means that one cannot make a general recommendation about stopping statins in this patient population."

Earlier studies found no difference in mortality after adults 70 and older stopped statins for primary prevention, she noted.

"One study suggested quality of life improvements after stopping statins," Redberg said, adding that her team explored whether stopping was safe for older adults taking the drugs to prevent a first cardiovascular event.

Study limitations

The study had several limitations. About 14% of participants did not stick with their assigned treatment plan. Some who were told to stop taking statins resumed them, while others assigned to continue treatment stopped taking the drugs, according to the researchers.

The findings also may not apply to all older adults, as the study was limited to people aged 70 and older who had multiple chronic health conditions but no history of heart disease or stroke.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Although some participants were followed for up to four years, the study primarily assessed outcomes over about two years. Longer follow-up is needed to determine how stopping statins affects patients over many years.

Weighing the risks

"This small, increased risk of cardiovascular events means that one cannot make a general recommendation about stopping statins in this patient population," Redberg said.

"There should be shared decision-making between the patient and the healthcare professional to know if it is appropriate for an individual to discontinue the medication. In general, however, discontinuation is safe for most people who are in this age group and without a previous CVD event."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Kelly, who was not involved in the study, noted that a healthy 70-year-old could live another 20 years, leaving questions about the effects of stopping treatment over that longer period.

The doctor also emphasized individualized decisions based on overall health and expected lifespan, noting that he "errs on the side of caution" with his own patients.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I typically recommend that they continue taking it unless they have specific concerns about that medication, such as side effects, or if they are taking a lot of medicines, and they're just really eager to stop taking one of them."

World.title: The election is over: It's time for young Jews to step up and lead
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A week has passed since election day. The votes have been counted. But no election can decide how proudly we live as Jews, how we support one another or what kind of leaders we become. Those decisions belong to us.

As the former student body president at the University of California, Santa Barbara, I know what it means to lead while your Jewish identity becomes a target.

My experience, featured in the documentary "October 8," taught me how urgently institutions need to confront antisemitism — and how much courage it can take to speak up when they fail. It also taught me that we cannot put our lives or our leadership on hold until someone else finds that courage.

JEWISH TEENS PREPARE TO COMBAT ANTISEMITISM ON CAMPUS WITH HISTORY, HUMOR AND COURAGE

Recently at the Jewish Student Union Presidents Conference in Stamford, Connecticut, I saw hundreds of Jewish high school students putting that principle into practice.

They had gathered as the country headed into Election Day. But their leadership did not depend on who would win.

They were already building Jewish communities in their schools. Already taking responsibility for something larger than themselves. Already choosing to show up.

I recognized myself in them. I am a Jewish Student Union alumna. Before I became a student body president, I needed opportunities to understand my Jewish identity, develop my voice and discover that I had something worth contributing.

BACK TO SCHOOL SHOULD NOT MEAN BACK TO FEAR FOR JEWISH STUDENTS

Returning to speak with these students reminded me why that early investment matters. Leadership grows through practice: inviting someone to a first meeting, organizing a program, asking a difficult question or standing beside a classmate who feels alone. Those actions can seem small. For the person on the receiving end, they can change everything.

Too often, we talk about young Jews only in terms of what is happening to them. The harassment they face. The friendships they lose. The pressure they feel to distance themselves from Israel or explain away a part of who they are.

Those experiences deserve attention. Antisemitism must be exposed and confronted. But young Jews also deserve to be seen for what they are creating.

CAMPUS ANTISEMITISM EXTENDS BEYOND STUDENT PROTESTS AND INTO CLASSROOMS, ADL WARNS

In Stamford, I saw students developing the skills and relationships that will shape their schools now and their college campuses later. They were learning to lead before a crisis demanded it of them.

That preparation matters. A strong Jewish identity gives us something to draw on when others challenge our belonging. A community gives us people to turn to. The experience of speaking up once can help us do it again. We should be giving more young Jews those opportunities. We should also make room for the joy that makes Jewish life worth building in the first place.

A student who encounters the Jewish community through music, sports or a celebration may discover a connection that a discussion about antisemitism could never provide. Those experiences give us friendships, memories and reasons to keep showing up for one another.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Last week’s Omer Adam concert at Barclays Center offered a powerful example: thousands of people gathering around Hebrew music, Jewish pride and a shared connection to Israel. Among those celebrating were wounded Israeli warriors. Their presence brought another dimension to that joy: the opportunity to stand alongside people who have sacrificed so much and welcome them into a shared celebration.

That is why I want to thank Warriors of Israel, which supports Israel’s wounded warriors. Its work reminds us that building Jewish community means taking responsibility for one another, including helping those living with the consequences of their service find support, connection and joy.

For young Jewish leaders, there is a lesson in that kind of commitment. We can build communities that celebrate who we are while making sure people who need us feel included and supported. That spirit belongs in our schools and on our campuses, too.

We need Jewish life that welcomes people in. We need students who know how to organize, build friendships across differences and explain what they believe. We need leaders who can confront hatred without allowing it to consume their entire sense of purpose.

None of this releases elected officials or university administrators from their responsibilities. They must enforce rules against threats and harassment. They must confront antisemitism within their own political circles. Jewish students have every right to demand accountability from the institutions that serve them.



And we can make those demands while taking responsibility for the communities we want to build. Run for student government. Start the club your school is missing. Invite the student who is hesitant to join. Learn enough about your history to speak about it with confidence — and enough about someone else’s experience to listen with care.

You do not need a title to begin. You need a willingness to act and the humility to keep learning. The students I met in Stamford will enter a world full of challenges. They will also enter it with ideas, conviction and the ability to make a difference.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

My message to them, and to young Jews across this country, is simple: Become the leaders you want to see in the world, regardless of who holds political office.
