World.title: What are childhood vaccination rates in your community and schools?
World.content:
This is part of The Vaccine Divide, an updated data investigation into America potentially losing its measles-free status as the deadly virus roars back and childhood vaccine defenses continue to crack and crumble.

As vaccination rates among children go down, the risk of getting sick from a vaccine-preventable illness such as measles goes up.

Use these maps to see the childhood vaccination rates for your community.

World.title: Behind the data: How NBC News tracked the decline in childhood vaccinations
World.content:
Editor’s note: This 2026 NBC News data investigation is an update of The Vaccine Divide, which was originally published in September 2025. The methodology for both projects is similar. The new data was collected from June to October 2026.

For “The Vaccine Divide,” NBC News gathered massive amounts of data from state governments and archives of public records. With the help of infectious disease researchers at Stanford University, NBC News filed scores of requests for documents, including materials obtained under the Freedom of Information Act, and wrestled different types of data into a standardized format to map and compare rates across thousands of counties.

Methodology

How NBC News collected the data

NBC News built a database of childhood vaccination and exemption information using data provided by state governments, primarily health agencies. The data combines public information available for some states and data provided directly to NBC News.

The data covers kindergartner vaccinations for each academic year.

After collection, the data was collated, and exemption rates were calculated in order to be analyzed. The analysis focuses on four facets of the data:

Medical exemptions: Exemptions granted when students have medical conditions that could make vaccination harmful. Nonmedical exemptions: Exemptions for students who opt out of required vaccinations because of personal beliefs or religious convictions. MMR (measles-mumps-rubella) vaccinations: For states where data is subdivided by number of doses, MMR vaccination is counted by the second dose. Some states track measles, mumps and rubella immunization separately; in those states, measles was used to represent MMR rates. Up-to-date vaccinations: Students are considered “up to date” with their vaccinations if they have received the full vaccination series required for enrollment in their schools.

How the data was processed

With a hodgepodge of formats, jurisdictions and collection practices across states, the task required extensive work to ensure that possible inconsistencies in the data were managed.

Certain states, such as Ohio and New York, required further calculations to aggregate the state-supplied data.

Other states required hand input of hundreds of rows of tabular data.

All data was checked for accuracy.

Analyzing the data

This analysis of childhood MMR vaccination rates focused on states that provided MMR figures for the 2025-26 school year. Accompanying the analysis were several variant analyses, which confirmed that the results were robust. The variant analyses all yielded similar results, mostly within 1 percentage point. We also examined the scale of MMR vaccination rate decline across counties, with almost 4 in 10 counties declining by over 5 percentage points since 2019 and about 1 in 8 declining by that amount since 2024. Fewer than 2% of counties declined by 0.1 percentage points or less since 2019.

Variations in the data

Many states collect and report their data differently. Some use health districts instead of counties. Some states provided over a decade of data; others provided only two years’ worth. Some states redacted certain data because of privacy concerns.

World.title: House votes to block motion to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth
World.content: The Republican-led House narrowly rejected a push to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over how he has carried out the war in Iran and other military hostilities in Yemen, Venezuela and the Caribbean. NBC News' Sahil Kapur and Courtney Kube discuss the tactic the GOP used to send the motion to the House Judiciary Committee and how Hegseth disputed the impeachment articles.Nov. 10, 2026

World.title: Bernie Sanders says he won’t support Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader
World.content:
WASHINGTON — Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., announced Tuesday he won’t support Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., to be majority leader for the next two years after Democrats’ big 2026 victories.

“I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. [There’s] nobody who works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view, the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be re-elected as the Democratic leader,” Sanders said at a news conference.

Sanders, who is in line to chair the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, becomes a high-profile opponent with inside power and grassroots clout when it comes to Schumer’s staying on as leader.

Schumer has spent a decade as caucus leader and is vying for another two years after having led his party to a net pickup of at least seven Senate seats in the midterm elections, with Mississippi and Alaska still counting votes as two more prospects. Senate Democrats won’t elect their new leadership until next month.

The progressive wing of the party has been calling for Schumer to step aside, while some new Democratic senators haven’t committed to support him. He’ll need a majority of the caucus to win another term as leader.

Standing next to Sanders at Tuesday’s news conference was Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who has similarly called for a change of leadership without backing an alternative candidate.

“I am not actively seeking this job. I am seeking change,” she said. “I’ve been very consistent for a very long time that we need a new generation of leadership. ... It’s important to demonstrate that we’ve heard what people want from this last election.”

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., whom grassroots progressive advocates are drafting to challenge Schumer, said Tuesday he’s still “actively listening” to colleagues about a potential run.

But he wouldn’t say whether he’ll jump in the race.

“We should not have a coronation,” Van Hollen told reporters in the Capitol. “We should not support anybody for leader without a very clear plan, and as you know, there are many people who think change is required.”

Until a challenger jumps in and gains traction, Schumer is the clear favorite to win and become majority leader. Despite grumbling in his own caucus, Senate Republican leader John Thune of South Dakota was re-elected by his colleagues Tuesday after detractors failed to recruit an opponent.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., faces some opposition in his bid for another term as leader. Tom Williams / CQ-Roll Call via Getty

“Our caucus is really united in focusing on bringing down costs, on ending the corruption, on ending the chaos, on ending the war,” Schumer told reporters Tuesday afternoon. “We have great unity in our caucus, and I’ll be proud to lead it as majority leader.”

Some Democrats credit his role in the election victories and believe he deserves the post.

“When the manager takes you to the World Series, you give them another contract,” Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., told reporters. “Chuck and I have had our differences, but at the end of the day, it’s time to unify.”

Asked whether he’s supporting Schumer for majority leader, former and returning Sen. Sherrod Brown of Ohio replied simply: “Yes.”

Sanders wouldn’t say when he was asked by NBC News whether he favors abolishing the filibuster for the upcoming two-year session, a cause that some on the left are pushing for. It would allow Democrats to pass most legislation without any Republican support, but the same power could be used against them the next time the GOP takes the majority.

“That’s a very important question, and I haven’t reached an answer on it. I think there are a lot of reasons to support it, and that is the majority — we believe the majority rule, not necessarily having 40 people be able to deny what the majority wants,” Sanders said. “I am worried about protecting minority rights, as well.”

Sanders pointed to the “reconciliation” process, which allows the majority party to pass some legislation on its own, as long as it’s related to spending and taxes; Republicans used the process to pass President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill.”

“What I do believe, absolutely,” Sanders continued, “is that we can, with a major budget reconciliation bill, do a whole lot.”

World.title: GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar wins re-election in Florida after clashing with Trump
World.content:
GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar has won re-election in her Miami-based congressional district, NBC News projects, after having clashed with President Donald Trump over his immigration agenda.

A recount that was completed Tuesday, one week after Election Day, showed that Salazar was narrowly ahead of her Democratic challenger, Eliott Rodriguez, by roughly 1,000 votes. In 2024, Salazar won re-election by nearly 20 percentage points.

Salazar drew national attention in September when she released an ad criticizing Trump’s aggressive deportation policy. She said that many Hispanics felt “betrayed” by the crackdown and that the administration’s tactics had “gone too far,” with many deportations targeting individuals without criminal records.

Trump carried Salazar’s district, which is heavily Hispanic, by 15 points in the 2024 presidential election. He responded to the ad by amplifying social media posts that labeled Salazar a “backstabber” and called for her to be replaced as the district’s GOP candidate.

Rodriguez, a former local news anchor, tried to capitalize on the rift. He said Salazar had become “so politically toxic that now even Daddy Trump appears to be distancing himself from his problem child.”

But Trump never officially rescinded his initial endorsement of Salazar.

Democrat Eliott Rodriguez. Marta Lavandier / AP

The close election spurred a legal battle after Rodriguez sued Miami-Dade’s election supervisor, Alina García, last week, alleging that she was biased in favor of Salazar and should recuse herself from the recount. Rodriguez claimed that García’s son-in-law was representing Salazar in the recount, which he said raised concerns about impartiality. Rodriguez also cited an interview in which García told The Miami Herald, “Maria Elvira is the winner, with or without a recount.”

A federal judge dismissed the lawsuit Monday, saying the allegations Rodriguez laid out were not adequate grounds to remove García from carrying out her duties, while adding that García’s remarks had been “perhaps unwise.”

With one of the largest concentrations of immigrants in the U.S., Miami has been on the front lines of Trump’s deportation campaign, with more than 130,000 pending removal cases — the most of any county in the country. Salazar’s district has been heavily affected, as it spans multiple working-class, largely Hispanic enclaves, though it also encompasses some of the wealthiest ZIP codes in the nation.

Notably, the district is also home to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who previously represented Florida as a U.S. senator.

In 2024, Trump became the first Republican presidential candidate to carry Miami-Dade County in 36 years. Florida’s 27th District is now set to be home to Trump’s presidential library.

Salazar was first elected to the seat in 2020, when she defeated former Health Secretary and former University of Miami President Donna Shalala in a major upset. The victory foreshadowed the Miami area’s rightward shift in the years that followed.

World.title: Pro-Palestinian protesters pelt objects at Joe Biden outside Irish university
World.content:
Three men have been arrested after protesters pelted objects at former President Joe Biden outside a university in Dublin, police in Ireland said Wednesday.

Videos showed protesters, some waving Palestinian flags, chanting “blood on your hands” and scuffling with police officers outside Trinity College Dublin on Tuesday, as he attended a ceremony honoring his son, Hunter, alongside former first lady Jill Biden. White liquid, believed to be milk, could also be seen flying through the air towards the group.

Hunter was being honored by its traditional Hist debating society, which dates back to 1770. Previous recipients of the Gold Medal for Outstanding Contribution to Public Discourse include Irish musician Bob Geldof, South African bishop Desmond Tutu, WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange and the late U.S. Senator Ted Kennedy.

Protesters gather as Joe Biden visits the College Historical Society in Dublin to receive the the Gold Medal for Outstanding Contribution to Public Discourse. Niall Carson / PA via Getty

During his acceptance speech in the university’s Exam Hall, Hunter discussed his addictions, family life and being in the public eye. “We are living in an age of bullies,” he said, adding that he had learned this from “my own scars.”

Shortly after the ceremony a “protest took place in Trinity’s Front Square,” Catherine O’Mahony, a spokesperson for the college said in a statement to NBC News on Wednesday.

She said “the protest escalated while the Bidens were leaving,” and Irish police, known as the Gardaí, arrived at the scene. “The Biden family left without incident. The protest dispersed soon after,” she added.

Police said in a statement Wednesday that three adult males were arrested “in relation to a public order incident” at Trinity College Dublin. One man in his 50s “has since been charged and is due to appear before Court. The two other males have been released without charge.” They did not say what the man had been charged with.

Representatives for Joe Biden did not immediately reply to a request for comment about the incident.

Joe Biden and Hunter Biden at the College Historical Society in Dublin on Tuesday. Niall Carson / PA via Getty

Ireland has long had a historical solidarity with the Palestinian cause, with pro-Palestinian flags, murals and graffiti a common sight around the country.

Many in the country compare the current situation in Gaza and the occupied West Bank with Ireland’s experience of British colonial rule and struggle for self-determination. Ireland was also the recent venue for American rapper Macklemore’s sold-out “Free Palestine Tour,” which opened in Dublin last month.

The Bidens, who have Irish heritage, also met with Ireland’s Taoiseach, or prime minister, Micheál Martin.

“We reflected on his strong Irish roots and previous visits, appreciating his lifelong support for Ireland,” Martin said in a post on X, of his meeting with Biden.

During a 2023 visit to the country while he was president, Biden told the Irish parliament in an emotional address that he was “home.”

Biden’s great-great-grandfather Owen Finnegan left the Irish county of Louth for the United States in 1849, and he also has relatives from another side of his family in County Mayo, on Ireland’s west coast.

Earlier this week, Biden, 83, signaled he was scaling back public tours to promote his upcoming memoir “Promise Me, America,” as he continues his treatment for cancer.

“Some days are better than others,” Biden wrote Sunday in a lengthy post on X. “It hasn’t stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down.”

Biden announced that he had been diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer months after he left office in January 2025 and has since undertaken courses of radiation therapy and hormone treatment.

He said his doctors were “encouraged by how I’ve responded to treatment” and thanked the public for their prayers and well-wishes.

World.title: U.S. charges 3 men with plotting multiple terror attacks, including on British air base
World.content:
Three men, including one already jailed in the U.S., were accused by U.S. authorities Tuesday of being Iran-supported operatives who plotted nearly 20 attacks on Jewish communities in Europe and the U.S., as well as a planned assault on a British air base used by the U.S. Air Force.

Charges against Mohammad Al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali Al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, were outlined in a superseding indictment unsealed in federal court in New York City.

Only Al-Saadi — an alleged pro-Iranian terrorist who is believed to have plotted attacks across Europe, Canada and the U.S., as first reported by NBC News — is in custody.

U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald in New York said in a news release that Al-Saadi, who was arrested in the spring, continued to coordinate with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted September terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, where U.S. bombers and troops had been stationed.

“As alleged, these defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” said McDonald, whose office is handling the case.

“The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real,” he added in the statement.

A USAF Rockwell B-1 Lancer bomber takes off on a sortie from RAF Fairford over the Cotswold village of Kempsford and the village church of St. Mary the Virgin, in Fairford, England, on March 21, 2026. Christopher Furlong / Getty

The new indictment offers fresh insight into an episode that has been shrouded in mystery for more than a month after five men were detained after midnight Sept. 27 on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward the base in western England.

The Justice Department indictment alleges that Al-Hassani paid associates to carry out surveillance of RAF Fairford in August and paid several people to move forward with the plot in September “by procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel.”

The group even made custom decals to give the vans the appearance that they were used by a fuel company and a swimming pool supply business, authorities say.

Al-Hassani is alleged to have then tasked the people to go to the base with the fuel when U.K. law enforcement took the men into custody.

Al-Saadi was helping direct the RAF Fairford plot while he was in a U.S. prison, according to the indictment. He made video and phone calls to his family members in Iraq, who are alleged to have passed coded messages to Al-Hassani and Mohajeri.

In a July call with his sister, Al-Saadi asked, “What are we doing about all our old work?” — a reference to terrorist activity — according to investigators.

His sister replied, “It isn’t cancelled,” investigators said.

The indictment alleges that the three men conspired to use a network of contacts in the United Kingdom to commit terrorist attacks on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata’ib Hizballah.

In June, Al-Saadi pleaded not guilty to charges that he plotted at least 18 attacks in Europe in retaliation for the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran.

The U.S. government has designated Kata’ib Hizballah and the Revolutionary Guards as foreign terrorist organizations.

World.title: Did GOP efforts to redistrict the House turn into a dummymander?
World.content:
Republicans undertook a historic effort to redraw several states' congressional districts mid-decade in an attempt to maintain control of the House. That effort was rebuffed on Tuesday night as the GOP was on track to lose many of the districts it tried to gerrymander last year.

There were several reasons that states undertook what had previously been a rare practice of mid-decade redistricting. Republican efforts started when President Trump ordered Texas lawmakers to redraw their map to net up to five seats for the GOP.

But despite the all-out effort, Democrats won control of the House on Tuesday, with CBS News estimating Democrats could end up with 251 to 268 House seats.

With the House decisively swinging toward Democrats and Democrats undertaking measures in a few states to counter the GOP's efforts, Republicans are faced with the possibility of having created a so-called "dummymander," a situation in which a party tries to gerrymander, but ends up benefiting the other party.

Here's a state-by-state breakdown of how the redistricting efforts panned out:

Texas

Texas Republicans went into Election Day controlling 24 seats, while Democrats controlled 13 seats and there was one seat in a GOP-leaning district that was vacant. In redrawing the map, Republicans sought to emphasize Mr. Trump's gains in South Texas to win five more seats.

Republicans won 24 seats and Democrats won 14 seats in the midterms, making Texas a dummymander.

Ohio

A commission comprising mainly Republicans hand-picked by GOP lawmakers redrew Ohio's map to net two more seats for their party. Republicans heavily targeted longtime Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur's district in the northern part of the state and Rep. Greg Landsman's Cincinnati-area district.

Heading into Tuesday night, Ohio Republicans controlled 10 seats and Democrats controlled five. Eight Democrats, including Kaptur and Landsman, won Tuesday night. Republicans only won seven districts, making Ohio a dummymander.

North Carolina

Although North Carolina has a Democratic governor, Republican lawmakers have a veto-proof majority in the statehouse and pushed through a new map that attempted to oust Democratic Rep. Don Davis.

North Carolina Republicans controlled 10 House seats going into Election Day, while Democrats controlled four, including Davis' district. As of a week after the election, nine Democrats had won — including Davis — while one Republican won reelection and CBS News estimated four districts with GOP incumbents were toss-ups, making the state a dummymander.

Louisiana

Louisiana lawmakers redrew their districts after the Supreme Court ruled in June that compliance with Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act could not justify the state's use of race in redrawing its House district lines.

Louisiana went into Election Day with four House seats controlled by Republicans and two controlled by Democrats. The new map aimed to eliminate one of the majority-Black districts that currently has Democratic representatives — the 6th District.

As of Monday, Republicans had won three districts, while Democrats had won one. CBS News estimates Louisiana's 5th and 6th Districts will go to runoffs. If Democrats ultimately win either of those districts, the redistricting effort will not have netted the GOP any extra seats.

Alabama

After the same Supreme Court decision, Alabama Republicans sought to eliminate the state's two majority-Black districts, both of which are represented by Democrats. Both incumbents won reelection on Tuesday, so Republicans did not net any more than the five they already controlled.

Tennessee

Tennessee lawmakers also redrew their map after that Supreme Court decision to target the lone Democratic district in Memphis.

Going into Election Day, Republicans had eight seats, and Democrats had one. As of Monday, Republicans had won eight seats, including the newly drawn 9th District that includes Memphis, and one seat is estimated as a toss-up. If Democrats win the remaining toss-up race, the state's House delegation will remain the same.

Florida

Led by Florida's Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, GOP lawmakers redrew their map to net up to four more seats for their party.

Heading into Election Day, Republicans controlled 20 seats and Democrats controlled eight. In the midterms, both parties won the same number of seats as before, with Democrats winning in all four districts that Republicans had targeted, meaning the redistricting effort did not net the GOP any seats.

Missouri

Missouri's GOP-led legislature last year redrew its map to make one of the state's two Democratic-held districts more friendly to Republicans. But the map's legality was challenged, and a state court ruled the map could not be used unless it was approved by voters. The Supreme Court three times blocked Missouri from using the new map, leaving the 2022 congressional districts in place for Tuesday's election.

Heading into Election Day, Republicans controlled six districts while Democrats held two. Democrats flipped another district, giving them three seats to the Republicans' five.

Indiana

Mr. Trump had also pushed lawmakers in Indiana to pass a map that would edge out the state's two Democratic lawmakers and make it a 9-0 Republican delegation. Despite pressure from Mr. Trump, the GOP-led state Senate rejected the new map.

Using the same boundaries as the last two cycles, Democrats held on to their two seats and flipped a third, making the state's representation 6-3.

South Carolina

South Carolina Republicans also sought to redraw their map after the Supreme Court decision in an effort to edge out powerful Democratic Rep. Jim Clyburn and make the state's representation 7-0 for Republicans. But the measure failed in the state Senate, and Clyburn won reelection on Tuesday. Democrats have picked up one other seat, and another race is considered a toss-up.

California

In response to Texas' redistricting efforts, California's Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom put forth a ballot measure to redraw the map to gain five seats for Democrats, which was decisively approved by voters.

Heading into Election Day, Democrats held 43 districts and Republicans held nine. A week after the election, Democrats won in 46 districts, while CBS News estimates another two are likely Democratic. Republicans have won three districts, and one is a toss-up.

Since Democrats picked up seats in California, it is a successful gerrymander for Democrats.

Utah

A judge in 2025 rejected Utah's congressional map that favored Republicans in all four districts, and then a district court rejected the redistricting map selected by the GOP-controlled legislature and instead selected a map that would create a Democratic-leaning congressional district in Salt Lake City.

Under the new map, Democrat Ben McAdams won the 1st District in Salt Lake City by 47 points.

Virginia

Virginia voters decisively approved a ballot measure in April to redraw the congressional map to favor Democrats in 10 districts and Republicans in one. But the map was thrown out by the Virginia Supreme Court, putting back in place the map drawn in 2021.

Heading into Tuesday, Democrats held six seats while Republicans held five. Using the same boundaries as the past two cycles, Democrats won eight seats and Republicans won three.

Maryland

Maryland's state constitution requires that congressional districts be compact and connected, and Democratic Gov. Wes Moore and other Democratic lawmakers championed a ballot initiative to remove those restraints on redistricting.

The ballot initiative, known as Question 3, passed by 20 points on Tuesday, so Democrats are likely to redraw their map now to edge out their sole GOP representative.

World.title: Why women get more migraines, and what to do about it
World.content:
Thirty-seven million Americans suffer from migraines, and women are three times more likely to get them than men.

Not only are migraines physically debilitating, they are very costly in terms of medical expenses and lost productivity. The World Health Organization even states that migraines are one of the top 10 most debilitating illnesses globally.

Despite being such a common illness, doctors and researchers don't know exactly what causes migraine.

Dr. Jessica Ailani is a board-certified neurologist with a specialty in headache disorders. As the director of MedStar Georgetown Headache Center in Washington, D.C., she studies migraines and treatment.

What are migraines?

Ailani wants to make abundantly clear that a "migraine is more than a headache." The condition can last from hours to days and have several phases.

The "prodrome" phase can start up to a day before the migraine, with over 36 potential symptoms like irritability, sensitivity to light and sound, nausea, neck pain, and even food cravings. Some individuals experience an "aura" — vision changes like flashing lights — during migraine attacks.

During a migraine, patients experience debilitating head pain, sensitivity to light and sound, nausea and insomnia, among other symptoms, sometimes for upwards of 72 hours.

The final phase is called "postdrome" and includes an inability to concentrate, fatigue and low mood. The symptoms can last up to two days.

All three phases make up the migraine and often lead to people missing school, work and events to cope with the pain.

What causes migraines?

While there is still some mystery around what causes migraines, Ailani believes they are "primarily a genetic disorder." However, there are several different genes related to migraines "in one way or another," and scientists have found it challenging to pinpoint which specifically cause them.

"Somewhere in the early '90s, there were a couple of big discoveries … where they started to realize that migraine is not an abnormality of blood vessels, but actually an abnormality of proteins that are released that can increase inflammation and cause this network error to occur," she explained.

People with a family history of migraines have genes that make "the brain more sensitive to having these cycles where there's more abnormal electric activity," Ailani said. "A release of proteins at the wrong time that are causing inflammation and network problems" is experienced as these intense headaches called migraines.

How hormones influence migraine attacks

Ailani said little was taught about hormones when she was in medical school. But she has come to realize "hormones are so incredibly important in everything."

This interaction between hormones and migraines may provide an explanation as to why women are three times more likely to suffer from migraines than men.

Before puberty, boys are actually more susceptible to migraines than girls. But, once the first menstrual cycle occurs, a female's "chance of developing migraines starts to increase tremendously."

A second peak of migraine attacks in a woman's life occurs in their 40s, when there seems to be "a lot of shifting hormones" and estrogen levels become unstable. This instability is also an indication of why when a woman is pregnant there "is almost a complete resolution of [migraine] attacks," according to Ailani, because estrogen levels tend to be steady and strong.

On the other end of the hormone spectrum, there are theories that testosterone might be a protective hormone against migraines.

Interestingly, at menopause, when women often experience other symptoms because of imbalanced hormones, "for many women migraine improves," Ailani said. If a woman starts getting migraines at menopause, she recommends consulting a doctor about the possibility of using menopausal hormone therapy.

Botox for migraines

There has been a lot of progress in finding better treatment for migraines and offering symptom relief to patients. Botox is a common and effective treatment that can help manage chronic migraines.

The injection is not the same as ones used for aesthetic procedures. The needle needs to go deeper and can be temporarily painful. Ailani says the treatment is so "effective that people keep coming back."

Ailani notes that Botox — a form of botulinum toxin — is the only FDA-approved toxin for treatment of chronic migraines, but there are others being studied that show promise as possible treatments for chronic and episodic migraines.

Innovations in migraine treatment

"One treatment doesn't work for every patient," Ailani said. Her team at MedStar has been on the forefront of developing new technologies and treatments to manage and even prevent migraine occurrence.

The goal, as Ailani puts it, is to "get a person to zero, to migraine freedom, to living their fullest life."

One of the biggest developments in the field is a CGRP inhibitor. This type of prescription medication blocks calcitonin gene-related peptide, a small protein in the nerves in your head and neck that scientists believe plays a role in migraine pain.

What's particularly "unique," according to Ailani, is that taking CGRP inhibitors will also help prevent future migraines, becoming more effective over time.

There are also non-pharmaceutical options that Ailani recommends to patients, like Remote Electrical Neuromodulation, or RENs. These devices are applied to a patient's upper arm and send electrical charges into the muscle to stimulate nerves that "turn off the brain's pain button."

Advances in the field give Ailani hope that someone with migraines "can definitely live a much better life under the right treatment."

"Put yourself first"

Ailani had a message specifically for women living with migraines: "We're very good at … not taking care of ourselves and taking care of everyone else and saying that whatever's wrong with us is just nothing."

Women sometimes remain silent about their health issues, thinking their pain is normal or part of being a woman.

"Put yourself first," Ailani said, calling it one of the "most important things to remember."

World.title: What stores are open and closed for Veterans Day 2026?
World.content:
Veterans Day, observed annually on November 11, honors Americans who have served in the U.S. military. Formerly known as "Armistice Day," the holiday was celebrated nationally for the first time in 1919 at the direction of former U.S. President Woodrow Wilson. Congress officially recognized it as a federal holiday in 1926.

This year, Veterans Day falls on a Wednesday. Read on to see which businesses are operating and some of the deals they are offering veterans and active military members to thank them for their service.

What stores are open on Veterans Day?

Most major grocery chains are open, including Aldi, Food Lion, Publix, Stop & Shop, Trader Joe's, Wegmans and Whole Foods.

Walgreens confirmed that it will welcome customers on Wednesday. CVS locations will be open, although some stores and pharmacies may have reduced hours, a spokesperson said.

Other retailers are also generally open on Veterans Day, although it's a good idea to check your local retailer's hours ahead of time.

Is Costco open?

The big-box store will be open for Veterans Day, according to its holiday schedule.

Is Target open?

Target stores will be open on Wednesday during regular business hours, a company spokesperson confirmed.

Is Walmart open?

Walmart stores will operate during their regular hours on Veterans Day, according to a company spokesperson.

Are banks open or closed today?

Major banks such as Bank of America, Chase and TD Bank are closed on Wednesday, as Veterans Day is a federal holiday observed by the Federal Reserve.

Americans can still visit ATMs and check online account activity. However, the holiday may affect the time it takes to process certain transactions, Bank of America says on its website.

Is the post office open or closed on Veterans Day?

All post office locations will be closed, and mail will not be delivered on Wednesday due to the federal holiday. Mailing and retail services will resume on Thursday, Nov. 12, according to the USPS.

Is the stock market open?

The U.S. stock market will be open, with Veterans Day not among the holidays observed by the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq. The next time markets will be closed is on Thanksgiving, which falls on Thursday, Nov. 26.

Veterans Day deals at retailers, grocery stores and restaurants

Here are a few discounts and freebies retailers are offering on Tuesday to veterans and active service members. Be prepared to show your military identification.

Applebee's: Complimentary full-size entree for active-duty military, veterans, reserves and National Guard members

Complimentary full-size entree for active-duty military, veterans, reserves and National Guard members Chili's: Free meal for veterans and active military members

World.title: Nima Momeni gets 16 years to life for murder of Cash App founder Bob Lee
World.content:
Nima Momeni, the man convicted in the 2023 killing of Cash App founder Bob Lee in San Francisco, was sentenced to 16 years to life in prison on Tuesday.

Momeni was convicted of second-degree murder in December 2024 for fatally stabbing Lee in the city's East Cut neighborhood under the Bay Bridge in April 2023, a killing that fueled a "doom loop" narrative about San Francisco street crime following the COVID pandemic.

Prosecutors said Momeni stabbed Lee following an argument about Momeni's sister and her relationship with Lee, along with their ongoing drug use.

(L-R) Nima Momeni, Bob Lee Pool/San Francisco Chronicle/MobileCoin

Momeni was found not guilty of premeditated first-degree murder. During the trial, his lawyers claimed he acted in self-defense, alleging that Lee had lunged at Momeni with a knife while under the influence of drugs and that Lee became aggressive after Momeni made a "bad joke" at the expense of Lee's family.

Aside from creating the Cash App digital wallet, Lee was a former chief technology officer for e-commerce company Square, Inc. and was chief product officer of the cryptocurrency MobileCoin at the time of his death.

His killing amplified a narrative of San Francisco spiraling into lawlessness, with high-profile figures such as Elon Musk driving the perception on social media. City officials aggressively pushed back against the sensationalist nature of the narrative, especially after it was quickly determined the stabbing was not a random street crime but rather stemmed from a personal dispute.

The sentencing was delayed extensively following a series of post-trial maneuvers from Momeni's defense team that included motions for a new trial and a new group of defense attorneys. The judge ultimately dismissed the challenges and requests for a retrial.

World.title: U.S. soldier accused of spying linked to Russia arrested in the U.K.
World.content:
A U.S. Army soldier has been arrested in the U.K. on suspicion that he engaged in espionage linked to Russia, British and U.S. authorities announced Tuesday.

The 41-year-old suspect was not identified, but a U.S. official told CBS News he is a senior officer based at Imjin Barracks, home to the headquarters of NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. He was arrested Tuesday near Gloucester, about 100 miles west of London.

The soldier is suspected of violations under Section 1 and Section 3 of the U.K.'s National Security Act of 2023 — obtaining or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service, respectively. The London Metropolitan Police said the suspected activity relates to Russia and that the force was carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire — the county where the base is located — related to the investigation.

The suspect was in custody in a London police station as of Tuesday, according to Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command.

"The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing," Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for the U.K.'s Counter Terrorism Policing force, said in a statement. "This activity demonstrates the strength of our UK and US law enforcement and national security partnerships, and I commend the work of all the teams involved. We will work together to take robust action against those we suspect of any criminal activity that could undermine our national security."

FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement that "this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners."

Speaking to reporters Wednesday in Moscow, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia had "nothing to do with" the detention of the U.S. soldier.

In an annual threat update last month, Sir Ken McCallum, the head of Britain's MI5 spy agency, accused Russia of "escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare," calling them "aggressor number one" when it comes to threats against the United Kingdom.

The arrest came as the U.S., Russia and Ukraine began a new round of trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi, the first such talks aimed at ending the war between Russia and Ukraine in about nine months. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the discussions "constructive and quite substantive," although it seems none of the participants expect any immediate breakthroughs, with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov rejecting European demands for an immediate ceasefire.

U.K. police said the arrest was not related to "any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations," meaning it appears to be unrelated to the recent suspected plot at RAF Fairford, which officials have said is linked to Iran. The U.S. military last month removed its bombers from that base after a security incident that led to the arrests of five British men and one U.K.-Iranian national in late September. There are U.S. troops stationed at RAF Fairford, a British Royal Air Force base.

On Tuesday, the U.S. Justice Department announced that three people it accuses of being Iran-backed operatives were charged with plotting a terrorist attack at RAF Fairford. One of the suspects is in custody in New York. However, the other two are not in custody at this time, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

World.title: 4 grizzly bears killed mom and daughter in Canada, DNA confirms
World.content:
Four grizzly bears captured in western Canada were responsible for killing a mother and her adult daughter this month in what investigators believe was a rare predatory attack, wildlife officials said Tuesday.

DNA tests conclusively linked a female grizzly and her three yearling cubs to the deaths of Jenny Balcarras, 48, and her 20-year-old daughter, Selah Reed, the British Columbia Conservation Officer Service said. All four bears were killed to protect the public.

"Our investigation also found that this attack likely involved predatory behavior, which I can tell you is very rare," Inspector Jeff Tyre told an online briefing.

"That is to say, we don't know how it started, but we know how it ended."

The women's remains were found about 150 meters (490 feet) apart near a trail outside Bella Coola, a remote community about 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) north of Vancouver.

Family members raised the alarm after Reed missed a routine Saturday night call with her sister. Searchers found her mother's remains first, then discovered Reed's remains in a bear cache, where bears store food.

This undated photo provided by Matthew Balcarras on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, shows Selah Reed, left, and her mother, Jenny Balcarras. AJ Reed via Matthew Balcarras via AP

Tyre said the bears were not involved in a separate grizzly attack last November on a group of about 20 elementary school students and teachers in the same area. Eleven people were injured, including two critically.

The latest killings have shaken the Nuxalk Nation community, which is still recovering from last year's attack. Local authorities imposed a voluntary curfew, and police escorted children to school.

"This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year's attack," said Tlhmtimut Samuel Schooner, the Nuxalk Nation's elected chief councilor.

He said community support services would remain available as long as needed.

Tyre said bears involved in fatal attacks cannot be rehabilitated or relocated because they pose an extreme risk to public safety.

"This was a heartbreaking event for the families, the Nuxalk Nation and the Bella Coola community. We hope the efforts of everyone who responded, along with these findings, bring some measure of closure," Tyre said.

Other bear attacks in British Columbia

There are between 10,000 and 13,000 grizzly bears estimated to live in British Columbia, according to the province's Ministry of Environment, Lands and Parks. The species is classified as vulnerable. Conflicts between grizzly bears and humans are considered "relatively rare," the ministry said, unless the animals are startled or protecting their cubs or food. Still, there have been a number of grizzly bear attacks in the province in recent years.

In October 2025, a grizzly bear injured two hikers in British Columbia's McGregor Mountain area, northeast of Prince George. One of the hikers was transported to the hospital in critical condition and died a few weeks later due to complications from the injuries. The grizzly bear was later found dead, according to the B.C. Conservation Officer Service.

A man suffered "significant injuries," including broken bones and lacerations, after being attacked by a grizzly bear while hunting in British Columbia's Elkford region in May 2024. He was able to shoot the bear to defend himself. The animal was later found dead. The man was flown to an area hospital for treatment.

A 21-year-old woman was seriously injured by a grizzly bear near Tumbler Ridge in British Columbia in July 2023. Authorities described the incident as a "defensive attack." The victim was transported via helicopter to an area hospital.

World.title: Judge denies motion to dismiss Trump's defamation case against BBC
World.content:
A U.S. federal judge denied a motion on Tuesday to dismiss President Trump's defamation case against the BBC, allowing the case to proceed.

In December 2025, Mr. Trump filed a $10 billion lawsuit against the British Broadcasting Corporation, the U.K.'s public broadcaster, over a documentary that featured edited parts of the speech he delivered on Jan. 6, 2021, as his supporters massed around the U.S. Capitol in what would become an assault on the heart of the government.

In the lawsuit, filed in the Southern District of Florida, attorneys for Mr. Trump accuse the BBC of publishing a "false, defamatory, deceptive, disparaging, inflammatory and malicious depiction" of him in an episode of the network's "Panorama" program, which aired a week before the 2024 election.

The case alleges the BBC "intentionally and maliciously sought to fully mislead its viewers" by "splicing together" two clips of the same speech Mr. Trump gave to supporters before the riots began. The president's legal team claims the two clips were 55 minutes apart and the edit omitted "his statement calling for peace."

President Trump speaks during a rally protesting the electoral college certification of Joe Biden as president, Jan. 6, 2021, in Washington. Evan Vucci/AP

On Tuesday, Judge Jeffrey Kuntz denied the BBC's motion to dismiss the defamation case, effectively allowing it to proceed.

"Whether President Trump can prove these claims and establish he sustained damages at summary judgment or trial is left for another day," Kuntz wrote in his decision.

Mr. Trump hailed the decision as "A Huge Victory against Fake News BBC, a terrible abuser of the truth," in a post on his Truth Social platform.

A spokesperson for the BBC, quoted by the network's news division, said: "We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court's authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage."

"We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process," the spokesperson added.

On Oct. 22, a federal judge in Miami said Mr. Trump must sit for a deposition with BBC lawyers by Dec. 11, warning that if he did not, he could face penalties, including possible dismissal of the lawsuit, unless the period for the president and the network to collect information in the case is extended.

Mr. Trump had been due to sit for a deposition in October, but his lawyers told the BBC in late September that he would no longer be available to answer questions, "due to other matters of national importance."

The president has said he will be available for the deposition in the second or third week of January, according to the BBC.

In November 2025, the BBC issued an apology to the president over the editing of his speech as featured in the documentary.

"BBC Chair Samir Shah has separately sent a personal letter to the White House making clear to President Trump that he and the Corporation are sorry for the edit of the President's speech on 6 January 2021, which featured in the programme," the BBC Press Office said in its statement at the time.

"While the BBC sincerely regrets the manner in which the video clip was edited, we strongly disagree there is a basis for a defamation claim," the press office added.

World.title: Trump's judicial confirmations to face resistance in Democratic-controlled Senate
World.content:
Washington — After seeing success in reshaping the federal judiciary in his first term and the initial two years of his second administration, President Trump and Republicans' campaign to shift the courts to the right could be coming to an end with Democrats poised to take control of the Senate next year.

During his first term in office, Mr. Trump successfully put more than 230 judges on the federal bench, including three justices on the Supreme Court, remaking the judicial branch for decades. So far during his second term, the Senate has confirmed 57 of the president's judicial picks. In total, Trump nominees make up about one-third of active federal judges.

But Democrats are now poised to control at least 54 Senate seats, and as many as 56 depending on the outcome of races in Mississippi and Alaska, making it unlikely that Mr. Trump will fill many more vacancies on the U.S. district and appeals courts.

"No one, or nearly no one, is going to get confirmed, so what he does in terms of nominating people, we'll see," Ed Whelan, a distinguished senior fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center and former law clerk to the late Justice Antonin Scalia, told CBS News.

There are currently 28 vacancies on the federal courts and another 15 seats that will open up in the coming weeks and months. So far, the president has formally sent to the Senate 16 nominees for those existing and future vacancies, though it's possible he submits more names for consideration before the current Congress finishes its work. Mr. Trump announced on Truth Social earlier Tuesday three more nominees to district courts in Texas and South Carolina.

The GOP-led Senate Judiciary Committee is moving quickly to advance those picks before control of the upper chamber changes hands. It voted to advance four of the president's district court candidates and held confirmation hearings for four other judicial nominees Tuesday.

The panel is expected to hold more confirmation hearings next week, a break from committee practice of holding those proceedings every other week, according to a source familiar with the panel's workings.

Republicans are violating "numerous longstanding standards in a desperate attempt to confirm more than 30 qualified loyalists to lifetime appointments before Democrats take the majority," Sen. Dick Durbin, the top Democrat on the Judiciary Committee, said Tuesday.

Durbin raised concerns about two of Mr. Trump's latest picks to serve as federal judges in Texas: James Sullivan, who lost his bid for reelection to the Texas Supreme Court last week, and T. Elliot Gaiser, the head of the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel whose only tie to Texas is a one-year clerkship for a judge on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit.

The Judiciary panel received information from Sullivan after he lost his campaign for Texas Supreme Court justice last week and from Gaiser on Nov. 8, before the president announced his intent to nominate each man, according to the source. Both are slated to appear before senators for confirmation hearings next week.

"There are many things we still can do, and I hope we'll use them. And one of them is not to expedite nominees who have not been carefully vetted," Durbin said. "I hope we don't accept that as a standard in this committee."

But Sen. Chuck Grassley, an Iowa Republican who chairs the Judiciary Committee, pushed back on Durbin's claim that he is departing from its typical practices. He argued that there are no committee rules about how quickly it can move to hold confirmation hearings or when those proceedings are held, and said chairs have discretion to set the panel's schedule.

"Historically, this committee has shortened timelines when circumstances warrant it," he said.

In anticipation of Democratic control of the upper chamber, Republicans are expected to make judicial nominees a focus of the lame-duck period.

"The priority is going to be getting the judges across the finish line," Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters Monday.

But seats on the federal bench that remain open come the end of the current Congress are likely to remain unfilled for at least the next two years.

"For the past two years, we've seen Trump seeking to stack our courts — district courts, circuit courts — with loyalists to him and not to the Constitution, and I think he's going to try to continue to do that," Rachel Rossi, president of the Alliance for Justice, a progressive judicial advocacy group, said. "In this moment, when Trump has clearly created this litmus test that there must be loyalty to him and not the Constitution, it's hard to see how Democrats can support nominees going forward."

It is not unprecedented in the Senate for the party in control to stymie the nominations of a president in the opposing party. During the final two years of former President Barack Obama's administration, when Republicans held the Senate majority, just 20 of his nominees to the district and appeals courts were confirmed. Obama's final judicial confirmation came six months before the end of his second term. Among the candidates that did not get a vote from the GOP-led Senate was Merrick Garland, who was nominated to replace Scalia on the Supreme Court following his death in February 2016.

"What we've seen is the federal courts being stacked with extremists and loyalists, and now Democrats have the power to stop the reshaping of our courts in a very dangerous direction," Rossi said. "I think there's increasing visibility on what judges mean and what these lifetime seats mean, and the hope is that Democrats use their power and stand against any further reshaping of our judiciary."

Of the 43 current and future vacancies, Mr. Trump has not yet announced candidates for more than half of those seats. Many of those are in states that will be represented by either two Democratic senators or one Republican and one Democratic senator next year.

Democrats could work with the White House to find consensus on candidates to serve on the district courts in their states, but it's unclear whether there is an appetite from either side to do so.

"Republicans on the Senate Judiciary Committee and the Trump administration have gutted the committee's oversight and confirmation authority," Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a Rhode Island Democrat who is expected to lead the panel next year, said in a statement. "There needs to be accountability for years of Republican bad behavior, and a hard reset on the nominations process next Congress."

Democrats' rout of Republicans in last week's midterm elections also makes it unlikely a Supreme Court justice appointed by a GOP president steps down in the final two years of Mr. Trump's term, given that a successor would likely not clear the Senate.

The president made a significant impact on the nation's highest court, appointing three of the nine justices. Among those was Justice Amy Coney Barrett, who filled Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg's seat following her death in September 2020, during Mr. Trump's first term.

Justices Clarence Thomas, 78, and Samuel Alito, 76, are the two oldest members of the high court, but Alito told The Wall Street Journal in August, "I'm here for another term." Alito also told CBS News chief legal correspondent Jan Crawford last month that while he considered retirement earlier this year, he feels he can still make a contribution to the Supreme Court.

With neither justice expected to step down during the lame-duck session, it could be several years before there is both a GOP president and Senate in place to confirm their potential successors on the Supreme Court, raising concerns among conservatives that a Democratic president and Senate could fill the seats of the influential conservative justices.

"Trump has managed to put in jeopardy his biggest achievement," Whelan said.

World.title: Iran-backed trio accused of plotting attacks on U.K. base hosting U.S. jets
World.content:
Iran-backed trio accused of plotting attacks on U.K. base hosting U.S. jets

toggle caption i Alastair Grant/AP

Federal prosecutors in New York have charged three men with terrorism offenses over what they describe as an Iran-backed campaign of nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks across Europe and the United States. The charges include a September plot against a British air base where American forces were stationed.

The indictment, unsealed on Tuesday, names Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi, 32, who holds Iranian and Iraqi citizenship, Mohsen Mohajeri, 48, an Iranian, and Mohammed Ali Al-Hassani, 35, an Iraqi.

Prosecutors allege the men acted on behalf of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the Iraqi militia Kata'ib Hezbollah to orchestrate, plan and conduct the attacks through a network of associates across Europe and the U.S., targeting Jewish communities and a British base hosting American troops. The indictment cites plots against synagogues in London and in New York. Both Iran's Revolutionary Guard and Kata'ib Hezbollah are designated by the United States as foreign terrorist organizations.

Sponsor Message

The court filings describe an operation that was directed, in part, by the suspects who were thousands of miles away. In April, prosecutors have alleged, the three men gathered in a room and watched an attack unfold live on a large screen via Apple's FaceTime video calling app. Al-Hassani allegedly coached the attacker through igniting and hurling a series of seemingly incendiary devices while Al-Saadi filmed.

The following day, Al-Hassani is accused of guiding another man on a video call as he lit an improvised explosive and threw it at a synagogue in London.

The men "helped orchestrate a campaign of terror" on behalf of the two designated terror groups, according to U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Jamie McDonald.

The RAF Fairford plot

The United Kingdom seems to have been a central target of the plot allegedly perpetrated by the three men: among the roughly 18 attacks claimed last spring by a group calling itself Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya, which prosecutors say was a front for Kata'ib Hezbollah, as many as seven took place in the U.K. It was the most intensely targeted country in Europe, though the indictment does not specify the location of other plots or attacks.

Sponsor Message

These included arson attacks, the use of explosives, and a near-fatal stabbing of two Jewish men in London - one of whom was a dual U.S.-British citizen.

Prosecutors say that in April the men sat in a room, and directed an attack remotely, in real time, over FaceTime, telling the attacker when to light and throw what seems to have been some kind of incendiary device.

The next day, one of the men, Mohammed Ali Al-Hassani, allegedly told another man attacking a London synagogue to quote "light it up like a Christmas tree."

According to the indictment, Al-Hassani was operating from Iran, but he began paying associates in Britain in August to film the perimeter of RAF Fairford, in Gloucestershire, several hours west of London.

They allegedly obtained vans and drums of fuel, looked into buying chemical accelerants, and gathered metal items that could potentially serve as shrapnel. The vans were fitted with sham branding for a fuel delivery firm as well as a pool supply company.

On September 26, three of these vans had set off toward the base that housed large numbers of U.S. military aircraft. At least two vehicles were stopped at a security roadblock, and British authorities seized all three early the next morning and arrested those inside.

The U.S. almost immediately redeployed several of its long range bombing aircraft from the base at the time of this incident.

The indictment said Al-Saadi had been detained abroad in May and brought to the United States, where prosecutors say he kept directing the network from his jail cell by relaying coded messages through phone calls with relatives in Iraq. He used aliases to refer to his alleged co-conspirators and referred to terrorist activity, including ongoing alleged plots, as "work," while those he spoke to used the phrase "international section" to mean overseas travel, according to the indictment. His sister and mother were among his interlocutors on some of those calls. Three days before the plot, in late September, he allegedly asked them to get money to Al-Hassani for the RAF Fairford operationBritish authorities had earlier charged two men with national security related offenses tied to the incident.

Sponsor Message

U.S. soldier held over Russia allegations

In a separate case, British counter-terrorism police said on Tuesday it arrested a 41-year-old member of the U.S. Army on suspicion of offenses under Sections 1 and 3 of Britain's National Security Act 2023. Officers have been searching two addresses in the same region of Gloucestershire, to the west of London. The man, who has not been named, has been held at a London police station. Police said the allegations concern Russia, and the investigation was "very much ongoing," according to Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK.

FBI Director Kash Patel called the arrest important in the context of an uptick in FBI counter-intelligence arrest, and said it "involves allegations of espionage"--- without giving further details.

The man who's been held was a senior soldier, according to Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command. His arrest was, he added, a "sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent."

The U.S. footprint in Britain

Though unrelated, both these cases have occurred in the U.K., a country which hosts a large American military presence. At the start of the war in Iran, Britain's Ministry of Defence confirmed to the U.K. Parliament in March that U.S. forces operate eleven RAF bases across the country, with approximately 12,300 American military and civilian defense personnel at various sites. Responding in January to a written question from a member of Parliament, the ministry said that there were around 11,000 uniformed U.S. personnel in the country, excluding families, civilians and contractors. The ministry has declined to give figures for individual bases, citing the security of personnel.

The U.S. Air Force's two main operating bases are RAF Lakenheath and RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk, in eastern England. Other sites include RAF Croughton, a communications station in Northamptonshire, and RAF Menwith Hill in North Yorkshire, used primarily by the National Security Agency, according to a House of Commons Library briefing . RAF Fairford serves as a forward operating base for the U.S. Air Force Global Strike Command.

Sponsor Message

In March, the British government allowed the U.S. to use British bases for limited strikes against missile sites in Iran, according to a parliamentary research service, which identifies Fairford as one of the bases potentially involved.

World.title: Oil giant ExxonMobil left Venezuela years ago. Now it's considering a return
World.content:
Oil giant ExxonMobil left Venezuela years ago. Now it's considering a return

toggle caption i Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images

ExxonMobil, the biggest U.S. oil company, is exploring a return to Venezuela after leaving almost two decades ago.

On Monday, the company announced it had signed a memorandum of understanding with the Venezuelan government and its state-owned oil company, Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A. The MOU, which is typically a non-binding agreement, involves ExxonMobil examining potential "upstream opportunities" – that refers to oil exploration and production.

ExxonMobil said in a statement, "We welcome the opportunity to evaluate potential upstream opportunities with the Venezuelan government and PDVSA."

A lot has happened in Venezuela's oil sector in the past ten months. In January, shortly after the Trump administration captured Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro, Trump gathered U.S. oil company executives in the White House and urged them to invest in the country. At that time, ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods said the country was "uninvestable."

Sponsor Message

But the country overhauled its petroleum law this year to make it more attractive for international oil companies. Those changes included allowing private oil companies more operational control in partnerships, as well as reforming taxes and royalties. The country has also welcomed the expansion of other U.S. oil companies, including Chevron and Continental Resources.

Still, ExxonMobil executives have maintained a cautious tone. On a call with analysts last month, Woods said that while there is "progress being made on those areas– working on fiscal regimes, working on legal regimes, working on investor protections, a number of things that are kind of in progress. But there's a way to go."

"This memorandum is a meaningful first step," ExxonMobil's statement reads, "But any future investment would require stable policies, clear regulations, strong investment protections and competitive returns."

ExxonMobil, which grew out of Standard Oil, operated in Venezuela for much of the 20th century. But over the years, the company's relationship with the Venezuelan government has been rocky. Beginning in 2004, then-President Hugo Chávez forcibly renegotiated contracts with international oil companies and ordered the nationalization of ExxonMobil assets. In 2007, ExxonMobil left the country.

Since then, ExxonMobil has been in international arbitration with the Venezuelan government. In September 2025, a U.S. court ordered Venezuela to pay ExxonMobil over $985 million for the past expropriations.

Sponsor Message

Energy analysts tell NPR that ExxonMobil may be looking at oil fields in Venezuela's Orinoco Belt, an area with sizable oil reserves and where the company has operated in the past.

The oil extraction process in this region generates a lot of greenhouse gas emissions, says Paasha Mahdavi, a political science professor at UC Santa Barbara who studies the oil industry.

Mahdavi says oil production in the Orinoco Belt has particularly high methane levels, a potent planet-heating gas. " This really matters from a global climate story," Mahdavi says.

ExxonMobil also has large oil investments in Venezuela's neighbor, Guyana, a key emerging player in the international oil industry. For years, Venezuela and Guyana have had a territorial dispute that has also been related to oil rights.

World.title: AI hoaxes are deceiving 911 dispatchers, and they're only getting harder to detect
World.content:
AI hoaxes are deceiving 911 dispatchers, and they're only getting harder to detect

toggle caption i Alex Edelman/AFP via Getty Images

In August, a caller made a bomb threat to Wheatland Union High School in Yuba County, Calif.

Police responded overnight and classes were canceled. There was no bomb and no one was hurt.

Authorities said it was part of a series of hoax calls — also called swatting — made to schools across the country over the summer.

Swatting calls can be made to 911 or police departments, with callers reporting a bomb threat, mass shooting or some other kind of life-threatening emergency with the intention of initiating a massive emergency response, according to the FBI.

911 dispatchers have long dealt with this problem. But the incident in Yuba County was different: The call was made by an AI-generated voice, a new and growing challenge for emergency responders.

Sponsor Message

"Those voices [of swatting callers] used to be pretty easy to recognize, but now they're natural sounding. They can insert pauses. They can use words like, 'uh', or 'maybe, um, let me think about it.' And it sounds very natural," says Mel Maier, the CEO and executive director of APCO International, the Association of Public Safety Communication Officials.

The goal of swatting calls is to harass or retaliate against the targets of the calls — like a public official. They usually trigger a big, chaotic response from police, redirecting public safety resources from real emergencies.

People also have been killed and injured in swatting attacks, Maier notes.

Swatting calls made by people using AI-generated voices or background sounds are making these hoax calls sound even more realistic, and harder to determine what's real and what isn't.

APCO and NENA: The 9-1-1 Association, which both represent 911 dispatchers, say incidents like the one in Yuba County reflect their growing worries over how AI could be used by bad actors.

APCO and the Public Safety Threat Alliance, an information-sharing and cybersecurity group, looked into the prevalence of swatting to 911 call centers. They published their findings in June based on 766 responses from public safety communications professionals. About 14% of dispatchers said they were targeted using AI tools. Maier says he thinks that number is going to keep going up with increasingly advanced tools

Sponsor Message

Signs of a swatting call

Companies like ElevenLabs, an artificial intelligence company creating synthetic voice software, offer AI tools that are incredibly cheap and readily available, according to Brandon May, an assistant professor of forensic psychology at the Florida Institute of Technology.

"I'm able to clone my voice on ElevenLabs for less than $20, and I can change the intonations. I can change how deep or high-pitch my voice is. I can change the pauses," he says.

And this makes it hard for anyone to detect these AI fakes.

"It is no longer simple to just look at an image or hear a video or hear a voice and go, 'That is AI.' People are duped by this all the time," he says.

Elaborate fraud callers using AI chatbots are even tricking people into handing over their life savings, May says.

And the increasing sophistication of these fake voices and sound effects makes it especially difficult for emergency dispatchers to deduce what is real or not during what May calls "high-stakes, high-consequence" calls. "It is going to be nearly impossible to detect," he says.

Despite the difficulty, APCO and NENA are developing ways to train their members to deal with these new threats.

April Heinze, NENA's vice president and chief of 911 operations, says there are some hallmarks of a swatting call.

For example, most swatters do not dial 911 directly.

"The reason being is 911 provides location. It provides a callback number. It provides the name of the person who owns the phone. It provides a lot of extra data, and it's really impossible to spoof your location on 911," she says.

Swatting calls are usually made to police departments or courthouses, Heinze explains. These callers are then ultimately transferred into the 911 centers. So trying to trace those calls is impossible, she says.

Sponsor Message

Training evolves to address new AI threat

Both Heinze and Maier decline to describe the specifics of training to identify potential AI swatting calls. The more information available, they say, the easier it will be to train AI to fool dispatchers going forward.

Maier does note one idea for training. APCO is working to create training criteria on caller interrogations where the dispatcher asks the caller specific questions at "such granular level that an AI cannot scoop that information from a public database, cannot capture it from a social media post, or simply make guesses," he says.

Despite the growing concerns about the use of AI, both Maier and Heinze emphasize that dispatchers will always assume calls reporting a life-threatening situation are real — and will continue sending emergency resources to any call for help.

"It's important to understand that no matter what, public safety is going to have a very strong response," Heinze says. "Even if there are indicators that it is a swatting incident. They are always reporting a life-or-death situation, and if it's a life-or-death situation, you cannot ever take chances on that."

World.title: Volunteer musicians play songs for veterans who are hospitalized
World.content:
Volunteer musicians play songs for veterans who are hospitalized

toggle caption i Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Dante Ciolfi unzips his guitar case in a courtyard of the Veterans Medical Center in Washington, D.C.

"I'm about to tune my guitar," he says.

He is getting ready to play some songs for patients in the hospice wing of the hospital. Ciolfi is a musician volunteer with Musicians On Call or MOC, a non-profit that brings live music to hospital patients nationwide, both bedside and virtually via zoom. The group's motto is "delivering the healing power of music." When Ciolfi isn't volunteering, he teaches computer science to graduate students.

He meets up with Ellen Morris, another volunteer with MOC. She trains musician volunteers on hospital protocols and guides them from room to room.

Sponsor Message

Once they reach the hospital's hospice unit, Morris takes the lead and knocks on a patient's room door. "Hi there, how are you doing today? My name is Ellen with Musicians on Call," she says, "I have my friend Dante here that would love to play a song for you today, would that be OK?"

The patient, 93-year old Army veteran Lawrence Ludden, agrees. He is sitting in his room reading the newspaper, but he's quick to extend his hand to visitors.

Ciolfi thanks Ludden for the sacrifices he's made then he adjusts his guitar and begins singing, "Desperado," by the Eagles.

Ludden's room is filled with sunlight. His daughter Eillen Ludden is here on her daily visit.

toggle caption i Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

He's the father of 4 and his shelf is full of family pictures — five grandchildren, two great-grandkids, a picture of him and his late wife on their wedding day and a couple of pictures of Ludden with England's Prince Harry who visited the VA this past August.

Once the song ends, and with a smile on his face, Ludden claps and thanks the volunteers. He also shares a memory with visitors.

"When I was a young boy I played piano, I used to like to sing quite a bit on the stage and I was in some light operas," Ludden says. "You never told me that," Morris replies.

Sponsor Message

Making the rounds while feeling gratitude for veterans

The volunteers move on to the next patient's room.

Ellen Morris says Ciolfi is an excellent volunteer. "The first time he played a song, and I watched him watch the reaction of the patient, it was overwhelming for me to see him be overwhelmed," Morris says. She knew right then that he was perfect for the group's mission.

Ciolfi says that playing music for veterans bedside is profound. He tries to hold emotional space with the patient, he says, even with those who can't speak.

"When I play, I try to mentally establish a conduit," says Ciolfi, "so the energy is kind of flowing back and forth. And to me that is so special … that energy is powerful."

toggle caption i Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

That's clear when he plays for Marine veteran John Fay, who is in bed and non-verbal. Fay taps his heart with his hand as he listens to the music.

"To me that signals that he felt the music," says Nicolette Rubin, a music therapist in charge of the music program at the VA Medical Center in Washington, D.C.

"I think he was grateful, he wanted to kind of keep the beat and feel it in his body, and his soul. I think he felt it in his heart," Rubin says, adding that music is not only uplifting to the spirit, but it's a restorative treatment that helps patients recover from and cope with emotional and physical trauma.

Ciolfi says he's witnessed a multitude of reactions to his music in patients. "A woman all of a sudden broke into tears," he says, "and at first I was wondering what's going on. But then a smile came on her face and it was like, no need for words."

U.S. Airforce veteran Sidney Nichols whispers yes, when volunteer Morris asks if he wants to listen to music. He served as a pararescue specialist for four years in Southeast Asia, including in Thailand, Vietnam and the Philippines.

Sponsor Message

Nichols is in bed, his eyes half-closed, but when Ciolfi starts singing "Crazy Love," by Van Morrison, he perks up and taps his hand on his leg as he silently begins mouthing the song's lyrics.

"You know that song, don't you? You were singing along," says Morris. Nichols responds, "I like it."

When asked how much Ciolfi knows about each patient's medical condition or their life, he's quick to respond. "I don't know anything about their circumstances," Ciolfi says. "Technically, I could probably read it on the chart that is outside their room. I intentionally don't because I want to stay focused on the music."

toggle caption i Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

Musicians On Call volunteers have performed for more than a million patients across the country since the organization was founded in 1999. Musician volunteers typically go into hospitals 3 to 4 times a month.

"I appreciate the opportunity to do it. You know, to me it's a gift," Ciolfi says.

His immigrant parents came from Italy, he says early on they drilled into him how lucky he is to be a U.S. citizen.

"Every single day I'm experiencing freedoms that other countries have no concept of," Ciolfi says.

And those freedoms, he says, are protected by our veterans.

"If I can do one tiny thing like play a song, my gosh, I'm there."

Editor's note: Since reporting this story U.S. Airforce veteran Sidney Nichols has died.

World.title: Both sides now? Critics slam DOJ moves to dismiss convictions of Trump allies
World.content:
Both sides now? Critics slam DOJ moves to dismiss convictions of Trump allies

toggle caption i Steven Hirsch/POOL/AFP via Getty Images

The Biden-era Justice Department portrayed the contempt of Congress case against Steve Bannon as open and shut.

Bannon declined to cooperate with the House committee that investigated the siege on the U.S. Capitol, flouting a subpoena and refusing to show up for an interview. A trial jury in Washington, D.C., deliberated for less than three hours before delivering a guilty verdict. A federal appeals court upheld that verdict.

Now, four years later, the DOJ is asking a court to drop the case and erase the conviction "in the interests of justice." Bannon's lawyers do not oppose the move.

Sponsor Message
