Legal experts said it follows a pattern where the Justice Department is helping to wipe the slate clean for allies of President Trump—with no one defending the cases, and without courts hearing arguments to the contrary. That violates the U.S. legal system's tradition of hearing views from opposing parties and comes as the Justice Department has also pursued investigations of Trump's perceived enemies.

"No adversity remains in this serious and high-profile criminal matter between, on the one hand, the U.S. Department of Justice overtly acting at the behest of the president of the United States, and on the other hand, Bannon, the defendant, who is a close political ally and adviser to the same president," said Bruce Searby, a defense attorney in Washington and a former federal prosecutor.

The Justice Department did not respond to a request for comment about its decision to walk away from the conviction and the lack of adversity, or truly opposing parties, in the case. Bannon's lawyers did not return messages seeking comment.

Vacating convictions, issuing pardons

Searby first noticed the issue in April, when the DOJ asked to vacate the convictions of about a dozen leaders and deputies of the far-right Oath Keepers and Proud Boys groups.

Those seditious conspiracy trials took months to unfold, as juries heard details about how some of those extremists gathered weapons, recruited followers and even breached the Capitol in the worst attack since the War of 1812.

Trump pardoned the vast majority of Jan. 6, 2021, defendants on his first day back in office, calling them "patriots."

Sponsor Message

In a recent interview with the CBS newsmagazine 60 Minutes, Trump took credit for those pardons. "I don't think any group's been treated more unfairly than them, and to this day, when they see me they cry," he said.

The administration took another route in seeking to drop the cases of more senior members of the Oath Keepers and Proud Boys—telling judges the move was in "the interests of justice." That was the same rationale it went on to use in the Bannon case.

Lawyers for Representative Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who served on the House Select Committee investigating the events of January 6, told a federal appeals court last spring this was not an ordinary set of cases—and that it should exercise its power to appoint a friend of the court, or amicus, to defend the convictions.

"The established path forward is for this Court to appoint an amicus to present opposing argument and defend the judgment being ambushed," wrote attorneys Justin Sher and Douglas Jensen.

Their court filing said judges have authority to take that step. And they pointed out two other controversial times that judges named outside lawyers to evaluate a bid to dismiss criminal charges: one in the case of former Trump national security adviser Michael Flynn; and another in the case of former New York City Mayor Eric Adams.

Ultimately, judges reluctantly dismissed the Jan. 6 charges without appointing a friend of the court.

"Today's epilogue diminishes the gravity of that day, denigrates the work of the prosecutors and law enforcement officers who secured these convictions, and excuses criminal acts that caused a centuries-long pillar of our democracy—the peaceful transfer of presidential power—to buckle," wrote U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta.

Leeway for prosecutors

Now, the issue has resurfaced in the courtroom of U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols, who presided over Steve Bannon's trial in 2022.

Sponsor Message

In a court filing last week, DOJ said it would exercise its prosecutorial discretion to dismiss Bannon's indictment. Courts have recognized wide leeway for prosecutors in making decisions about their resources.

Deputy Associate Attorney General Michael Weisbuch wrote it was not appropriate to pursue the contempt case against Bannon because Bannon said he believed he was protected by executive privilege.

Weisbuch said the judge lacked authority to reject the unopposed motion to dismiss. "But even assuming any review could be proper, the policy-laden grounds for dismissal asserted above are not susceptible to judicial second-guessing," he added.

Searby, the former prosecutor, said the judge should not accept the DOJ argument "at face value" and dismissing the case should not be a "foregone conclusion."

An outside lawyer, he said, could assess whether the Justice Department's actions amount to an abuse of prosecutorial discretion: if they are taken in bad faith, tainted with impropriety or contrary to public interest.

Critics and good government groups said the Trump administration has been exploiting the legal system, which is designed to hear views from two opposing parties. The president famously sued his own government over the leak of his tax returns, and then negotiated a settlement with the Justice Department that handed him and his sons immunity from tax audits.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, who previously served as a defense attorney for Trump, confronted serious questions about that deal and his sign-off during a confirmation battle in August. The Senate went on to approve his nomination by a single vote.

World.title: Your guide to hosting a flavorful, cozy and stress-free Thanksgiving
World.content:
Your guide to hosting a flavorful, cozy and stress-free Thanksgiving

toggle caption i filadendron/Getty Images

Every time I host Thanksgiving, it feels like a debate between what to repeat from last year and what to do differently this year.

Should I cook that turkey recipe again, or try a new one? Should I decorate the table with mini gourds again, or shake things up with a big sunflower centerpiece?

Let Life Kit help you decide. As you plan your Thanksgiving, friendsgiving or harvest-themed dinner party menu and decor, here are a few fresh ideas to add flavor, color and calm to the day. That includes two foolproof turkey recipes, advice on how to stay present while hosting, and directions on how to create a stunning floral arrangement with supermarket flowers.

Sponsor Message

Crowd-pleasing Thanksgiving recipes

Combine these recipes with sides and desserts — and you've got a whole feast. Don't forget to make Mama Stamberg's cranberry relish!

Easier roast turkey and gravy. Chef and writer Lan Lam shares the recipe she developed for America's Test Kitchen. It involves roasting the turkey on a pre-heated pizza stone to avoid the dreaded task of flipping the piping hot bird midway through the cooking process. It's the perfect recipe for first-timers. Get the recipe here .

Salt-and-pepper roast turkey breast. Don't feel like fussing over a whole bird? Try a bone-in turkey breast. It's "significantly easier to cook, it takes a fraction of the time and it still feeds a group comfortably," says New York Times food writer Eric Kim. Get the recipe here.

Stuffing with a cheesy pizza twist. Kim's fun spin on traditional stuffing is sure to be a crowd pleaser. Day-old bread gets tossed and baked with tomato paste, oregano and mozzarella cheese. Get the recipe here .

Pane criminale, or pull-apart garlic bread. This is one of chef and writer Samin Nosrat's favorite things to bring to a group meal. In this recipe, the bread is sliced vertically instead of horizontally, guaranteeing that each slice of bread has garlic butter. Once you set it at the center of the table, "everyone just starts pulling it apart," she says. Get the recipe here .

Sponsor Message

Vegan mushroom-coconut vegetable pot pie. Don't leave your meatless friends behind. This pot pie recipe from Tracye McQuirter's book, Ageless Vegan, uses coconut milk and mushrooms to add heft and flavor. Be sure to use a vegan pie crust for the recipe. Get the recipe here .

Roasted vegetables with Korean-inspired magic sauce. This is chef and writer Roy Choi's version of his mom's magic sauce. It uses Korean ingredients like gochugaru and gochujang, and tastes terrific spooned over roasted vegetables. Get the recipe here .

Make hosting fun, easy — and less stressful

toggle caption i vgajic/Getty Images

Host with "generous authority." When it comes to the event itself, a host should absolutely be able to enjoy themselves, but that doesn't mean stepping back entirely, says Priya Parker, author of The Art of Gathering.

The most meaningful gatherings tend to be run by what Parker calls "generous authority." She defines this as "imposing in a way that serves your guests."

It's about finding a balance between encouraging new connections and letting them happen naturally. "When you give guardrails, people then [are] allowed to actually be incredibly spontaneous because they feel safe." 3 ingredients for hosting with "generous authority."

Ask your guests "magical questions" to spark engaging conversations. It's "a question everyone in your group is interested in answering" and hearing the answers to, says Parker. For example: What's the weirdest thing you've ever found in your pocket? What topic could you give a 20-minute talk on with no preparation?

She likes asking them in group settings because they have the power to cut through small talk and reveal people's personalities. And people don't need to agree or have the same tastes or experiences to answer. Parker shares a few favorite magical questions here .

Pick three moments you want to be present for. You probably won't have the time and attention for everything on your to-do list, so shorten it down to the moments that matter to you most, says Niro Feliciano, a psychotherapist and author of All is Calmish: How to Feel Less Frantic and More Festive During the Holidays .

Sponsor Message

Maybe that's decorating the Thanksgiving table, serving homemade roasted turkey, and watching the football game. In those moments, show up as much as you can. How to focus on what matters during the holidays .

Decorating tips to make your house feel cozy and festive

toggle caption i Janina Steinmetz/Getty Images

Put holiday decor in the first spot people see when they enter your house. "Designers never leave that empty because the eye has to have somewhere to land, and it needs to land on something very pretty," says Elaine Griffin , interior designer and author of Design Rules: The Insider's Guide to Becoming Your Own Decorator .

So place a centerpiece in that spot, she says. It can create the same effect as filling a room up with holiday knickknacks. You can make a centerpiece by thrifting a glass vase and filling it with, say, pinecones or cranberries.

Decorate for all five senses. If you want your home to feel like a fall celebration, infuse the vibe more deeply throughout your home through sight, sound, scent, touch and taste .

That might mean throwing a velvety blanket over the couch; getting a candle with a loud, crackling wick; hanging up a cinnamon broom and displaying decorative gourds. More holiday decorating tips here .

Arrange supermarket flowers like a pro. Florist Alexander Campbell of AC Floral Studio explains how to make a professional-looking floral arrangement for your tablescape using store-bought flowers.

First, look for one to two types of greenery with different textures and three to four types of flowers in your color palette. Then, to build your bouquet, add each item in this order. See the infographic below for examples.



Start with greenery. Then add filler flowers. Next, add tall flowers to create a high point. Then add "star" flowers that really speak to you. Finish off your arrangement with dainty flowers.

Enlarge this image Photo Illustration by Becky Harlan/NPR Photo Illustration by Becky Harlan/NPR

See a step-by-step guide on how to make an arrangement here.

Sponsor Message

This story includes reporting and writing from Marielle Segarra, Andee Tagle, Beck Harlan, Margaret Cirino, Lennon Sherburne, Audrey Nguyen, Lauren Migaki, Meghan Keane, Maria Godoy, Clare Marie Schneider, Diba Mohtasham and Sam Yellowhorse Kesler. It was edited by Clare Marie Schneider. The visual editor is CJ Riculan.

World.title: U.S. officials look to Europe to learn how to make prison better
World.content:
U.S. officials look to Europe to learn how to make prison better

toggle caption i Lena Mucha

More than a dozen New Yorkers crowded into an empty prison cell in Berlin, Germany, this October. Inside, they found many contrasts to U.S. prisons: For one, prisoners held at this German facility, Tegel Prison, have keys to their own cells.

The reason, prison director Martin Riemer told the group, is so the men held here can lock their own door when they go to work or school, just like someone might at home. The guards still have keys, but Riemer said this gesture offers a semblance of privacy.

Riemer also noted that every prison cell in Germany must have natural light and ventilation. In the cell the tour group inspected, the large window still had bars on it, but it opened. A breeze was blowing in.

Sponsor Message

The purpose of this trip was to inspire key players in the criminal justice system — a judge, a prosecutor, a prison official, among others — to see new ways of improving New York City's troubled jail system, which officials are in the process of reimagining.

The trip, organized by the Vera Institute of Justice, a criminal justice reform nonprofit, is part of a larger trend: U.S. officials are increasingly looking abroad for how to design a better prison or jail system. In fact, at least 10 U.S. states now model some of their prison units or practices after prison systems in Western Europe and Scandinavia.

"It's what happens when they get there that makes a world of difference, really seeing it with their own eyes," says Nancy La Vigne, dean of the Rutgers School of Criminal Justice. "Touring the facilities, talking to the officers, talking to the incarcerated population, witnessing rehabilitation in real time is very inspiring."

toggle caption i Lena Mucha

On the tour of Tegel Prison, the group from New York kept finding tangible differences. Jails and prisons in the U.S. often have a distinct smell — the result of many bodies held in a poorly ventilated space. This German prison did not. Jails and prisons in the U.S. are often noisy. This prison was quiet.

Sponsor Message

Aisha Elliott, a tour member who spent more than 20 years incarcerated in New York state prisons, noticed the furniture.

"There's a lot of wood and movable objects, which I think makes it more bearable. Everything in New York is steel, metal, thin and painful," said Elliott, chief program officer at the Women's Prison Association, an advocacy group.

Tina Luongo kept peeking at the cell toilets. In American jails, she says the toilets remind her of a metal dog bowl. In Berlin, most were porcelain, like in a home.

"It's speaking to me because it's the smallest thing," said Luongo, who leads the Legal Aid Society's criminal defense practice, the largest public defense provider in the U.S. "I have to believe that makes a difference in how you show up in those places."

The German prison system

European prisons aren't perfect. In countries like Norway and Denmark, prisons still experience overcrowding, understaffing and lockdowns. Officials at several German prisons were quick to tell the New York group that correctional officers often still have to deal with things like violence between prisoners and issues with drug overdoses.

German prisoners say that what they are experiencing is still prison: They long for more human touch, for instance, and better food.

But the country is often regarded as an international model. After the Holocaust, Germany adopted a new constitution that centers on protecting human dignity, including in its prisons. In Germany, the loss of freedom is seen as the punishment, not the conditions inside.

In contrast, prison conditions in the U.S. are often plagued with inhumane conditions and violence. The Department of Justice has dozens of open investigations into jails and prisons across the country for constitutional violations.

By law, life inside a German prison has to resemble life outside prison as much as possible, a concept known as normalization.

toggle caption i Lena Mucha

Lauren-Brooke Eisen, senior director of the Justice Program at the Brennan Center for Justice, says normalization might look like allowing prisoners to cook their own food, or wear street clothes instead of a uniform. It could also be that a toilet inside a cell has a door or curtain on it for privacy.

Sponsor Message

German prison staff also go through years of training, and many have backgrounds in social work or law. In the U.S., correctional officers often only train for a few weeks or months. All of this, Eisen says, creates a culture of rehabilitation in German prisons.

"In many other countries, when you are incarcerated, you don't lose your humanity the same way that you do necessarily in the United States," Eisen says.

European models in the U.S.

Over the last decade, the Vera Institute's own initiative, called Restoring Promise, has launched prison units modeled after Europe in six states: Connecticut, Massachusetts, South Carolina, North Dakota, Colorado and Idaho.

Its initiative focuses on 18- to 25-year-olds, a group that is more likely to make impulsive decisions, including resorting to violence to solve a conflict.

Ryan Shanahan, chief research officer at the Vera Institute, says prioritizing safety is necessary when any change happens inside a prison.

"But what does that mean? Traditionally in U.S. prisons, safety is keys, locks, cameras, barbed wire fences," says Shanahan, who helped start Vera's initiative.

But, Shanahan says, skills like asking questions, listening and relationship building can make an environment safer, too. The goal of the Vera Institute's prison units is to build that culture. Older prisoners serving long sentences act as mentors for young people in the program. Staff members engage with families on the outside.

toggle caption i Lena Mucha

There are daily schedules that include discussion groups and activities aimed at "learning conflict resolution and being able to practice it, learning to care for each other and be vulnerable and practice that, so that you can care and be vulnerable when you go home," Shanahan says.

That matters. Almost everyone who goes to prison in the U.S. is eventually released.

A cost-benefit analysis

But these types of programs are still in only a small percentage of U.S. prisons. One barrier to launching more of them is the sheer size of the U.S. prison system.

Sponsor Message

Around 2 million people are behind bars in the U.S. at any given moment, the most in the world. The German system is about 3% of that size. People in German prisons also generally serve sentences that are far shorter than those in the U.S.

Shanahan says for many U.S. prison leaders, the desire for change is there, but "there has to be a level of risk tolerance. There has to be a commitment to try to do something different."

Other key barriers include cost and staffing, says La Vigne, the Rutgers professor. Many U.S. prisons are currently facing staffing shortages.

"Most of the programs that have been piloted have a pretty high ratio of correctional officers to incarcerated persons," she says. "But investing those resources is probably cost beneficial because you'll also be retaining your officers and your staff, because they'll be more likely to feel like this is a place where I want to be."

There is evidence to suggest that both staff and prisoners benefit from programs like the German model.

In a 2023 study of one of its units in South Carolina, Vera found prisoners there were far less likely to commit violence, and also less likely to end up in solitary confinement.

In Washington, a program modeled after Norwegian prisons in partnership with the University of California, San Francisco, also resulted in less violence among prisoners, and correctional staff began coming to work more consistently.

toggle caption i Meg Anderson/NPR

When Maine remodeled its prisons around the concept of human dignity, it found prisoners were less likely to commit new crimes once they were released.

In Pennsylvania, a reform unit called Little Scandinavia saw almost no violent incidents in 2024, even as violence rose in other facilities, according to preliminary data cited in a Brennan Center report.

On its tour of Tegel Prison in Berlin, the New York group passed through a greenhouse that smelled like fresh dirt and lemon basil.

Sponsor Message

Inside, Lenny Albrecht, who has been incarcerated there for four years, was repotting plants. He said his job as a landscaper requires a lot of trust: He can use scissors and knives in his work, and he can walk the grounds without being supervised by an officer.

Mostly, though, he said he likes that the work makes him feel comfortable and relaxed.

"Before, I was very aggressive," Albrecht said. "The work here makes you calm down and relax. And that's a thing I never had before."

toggle caption i Meg Anderson/NPR

Nearby, Elliott, the women's prison advocate, is taking in the freshness of the place. The yards in New York prisons, she said, are mostly concrete.

"This feels good because they're treating people like people," she said. "I feel like they are headed in the right direction, which is toward release, supporting people toward their release."

She said a person in prison might not feel good about where they are, but the goal should be to make them feel good about who they are, or who they can become.

World.title: Canadian family finds long-lost WW II baby in England after 81 years
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Rod Anderson grew up in England always wondering who his father was.

He was born at the end of the Second World War to a British mother.

At 81 years old, he received a call out of the blue this year with news he never expected — his dad was actually a Canadian soldier.

"I was knocked down by it all. It was just such a shock," Rodney told CBC News.

"Still, you could knock me down with a feather. Even today."

Anderson learned the truth about a family secret buried for generations. He was one of thousands of babies born in England and other countries where Canadian troops and allied forces were stationed during the Second World War.

WATCH | British man discovers his father was Canadian WW II soldier: He discovered his father was a Canadian soldier — 81 years later | Duration closed caption 6:11 After 81 years, Englishman Rod Anderson discovered a stunning truth: his father was a Canadian soldier during the Second World War stationed in Britain, but he had a family back home in New Brunswick. CBC's Ashley Burke speaks to Anderson and the Canadian relatives who searched for him for 20 years.



In the 1940s, mothers were blamed and shamed for these pregnancies out of wedlock. Children were given up for adoption. Families were torn apart. Some parents hid the truth until the day they died.

"My grandmother, my mother, none of them said a word," Anderson said.

Rod Anderson when he was a baby in his mother Yvonne Anderson's arms. He was born in 1945. (Submitted by Dawn Anderson)

But little did Anderson know, a family on the other side of the Atlantic Ocean spent almost two decades searching for him, hoping it wasn't too late.

Now after a remarkable turn of events, Anderson has connected with family in Canada he never knew existed.

An 18-year search

Canadian Bethany Allen spent almost two decades searching for Rodney Anderson.

She said it all started with a "persistent" family rumour about her grandfather Charles Blakney that never went away.

"After the war, there were rumors that my grandfather had a child with a woman in England," said Allen. "Some people heard it. Some people were well aware of it. While others have never heard a whisper of it."

Blakney was married and had a baby girl in New Brunswick when he stepped aboard the HMT Andes to travel across the Atlantic to serve in England in 1942.

Charles Blakney in uniform with his Canadian wife and baby (Bethany Allen's mother). (Submitted by Linda Rowe)

His military records describe him as a "very soft spoken" and reliable soldier. He served as a motor and driver mechanic with the New Brunswick Rangers until he returned home in 1945.

Rod Anderson was born in Farnham, England, that same year.

Allen requested her grandfather's divorce records from the archives in 2008. She says they contained the "mother lode of information." The documents confirmed the baby in England was indeed real.

"The moment that I saw it, I was so surprised because it was so obvious," said Allen. "It was so definitive … turned all the rumours into fact."

Bethany Allen in New Brunswick holding her grandfather's divorce records that confirmed he had a baby during the Second World War while stationed in the United Kingdom. (Pierre Fournier/CBC)

But the mystery was far from over. Allen had no idea who the baby was.

Before Allen's mother died, she asked her daughter to keep searching for her sibling overseas no matter what.

"My mother had always wanted to know that he had a good life and was happy," she said.

Suddenly this past spring, "everything changed very quickly" when she did a DNA test through the U.S.-based company Ancestry, Allen said.

The results pointed to Rod Anderson as her half-uncle.

"I was like, oh my god, there he is," said Allen. "Oh my god, his name is Rodney!"

'I thought this is a wind up'

That same day, she managed to track down Rod Anderson's daughter, Dawn Roberts, in England.

Roberts called her dad and asked if he was sitting down.

"She said I had a phone call from a lady in Canada who said that you're her long lost relative," Rod Anderson said.

"I thought this is a wind up. It has to be. But it wasn't. You can't believe what a shock it is to get that knowledge."

Anderson had once done his own DNA test. For 50 years he tried to find the man he always suspected was his father. But in a crushing blow years ago, the test results found they weren't related.

In the end, that DNA test was the key that connected him to his newfound family in Canada.

WATCH | Rod Anderson describes a stunning call from his daughter with the news: British man finds out at 81 his father was a Canadian soldier in WW II | Duration closed caption 0:36 Rod Anderson in Surrey, U.K., says he got a call out of the blue from his daughter in March with news he never expected. At 81 years old, he learned his father was a Canadian soldier stationed in England during the Second World War and that he has family in Canada he never knew existed.

Second World War historian Jeff Noakes at the Canadian War Museum says the parents of wartime babies whose fathers were Canadian or allied soldiers often kept the details about these children hidden.

'Unbelievable amount of stigma'

There was an "unbelievable amount of stigma," he said, back in the 1940s around having children outside of marriage.

"Eighty years ago, there would have been a tremendous amount of shame for many people attached to this," Noakes said.

"The blame also fell disproportionately on women who were involved rather than the men."

A photo of Charles Blakney taken during a family gathering. (Submitted by Bethany Allen)

Noakes said there was so much public attention around it, Canadian military commander Lt.-Gen. Guy Simonds held a news conference in 1945 to defend his troops. Dutch newspapers had written editorials about an alleged decline in Dutch morality because of the Canadian soldiers stationed in the Netherlands.

Now, decades after these parents have died and there's far less stigma, some Canadian relatives are searching for these war babies before it's too late.

Toine van der Weerden lives in the Netherlands and helps families do the detective work needed to track down the truth.

"They are always happy when they find out," said van der Weerden.

"Everybody wants to know where they come from. Where you got those gestures from, where you got your posture from."

'You've got the same ears'

Since Anderson's revelation about his father, he's connected with his 77-year-old half-sister Barb Lowe in St. Thomas, Ont. They now talk every week.

They said they felt instantly connected the first time they spoke. They both like to laugh, share the same sense of humour and joke about the mischief they got into growing up.

Lowe said he reminds her of their father, who died in 1987.

"You've got the same ears," Lowe told him on one of their calls that CBC News filmed.

'Everything you do is a challenge, especially when you've got one arm and one eye. You have to conquer those challenges no matter how,' said Anderson. (Luke Wolagiewicz/CBC)

Rodney joked she once called them big "elephant-like" ears.

Despite never knowing his biological father, Anderson was amazed to find out he takes after him.

Like father, like son

As a child, Anderson lost his eye and an arm in a rail accident.

In the 1960s, a government assessment found the only job he couldn't do because of his injuries was work as a mechanic.

In true Rod Anderson fashion, he proved them wrong and became one.

Rod Anderson's photos that show his work as a motor mechanic over the years. He eventually opened his own business. (Luke Wolagiewicz/CBC)

It turns out, that's the exact job his Canadian father did for a living and during the war.

"That did surprise me. Isn't it strange?" Anderson said.

These newfound siblings can't quite believe they found each other before it's too late.

"I means the world," Lowe said. "My sister had passed away, my half-sister had passed away. And I finally found Rod. He's everything."

"Don't give up. You never know what the DNA can do."

Barb Lowe lives in St. Thomas, Ont., and said it means 'the world' to her that she's connected with her half-sibling Rod Anderson in England. She's photographed on a video call with Rod. They speak every week. (Yan Theoret/CBC)

But for this family, the mystery may not be over yet.

The divorce records that helped the Canadians find Anderson said his father had another baby in Britain during the war.

"There's still more mysteries to be had," said Allen while laughing. "There's still a search going on, and now we have two sides of the Atlantic trying to solve that mystery."

For now, Anderson's booked his plane ticket to New Brunswick this summer.

He's bringing his granddaughter Samantha Eldridge with him to finally meet the extended family he almost never knew.

"It'll make a difference to my children and their children and their children's children. It will go on," Anderson said.

"Never give up looking."

World.title: Canadians fought a war in Afghanistan. Why do we struggle to talk about it?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It's not much of a stretch to say the federal government has trouble saying the word Afghanistan.

A couple of weeks ago, late on a Friday, Defence Minister David McGuinty and Veterans Affairs Minister Jill McKnight issued a statement to quietly defuse what some in the veterans community might view as a Remembrance Day bomb.

They announced that a Senate bill (S-246) currently before the House of Commons — designating service in both the first Gulf War and Afghanistan as wartime service — would be the subject of public consultation in the coming months.

While it is most definitely about Afghanistan, the word Afghanistan does not appear anywhere in the 335-word joint statement.

In the eyes of Canadian law, at the the moment, the service of 40,000 troops over 13 years, the deaths of 158 of them, the wounding of an estimated 2,000 soldiers is reduced to the banal catch-all designation of "special duty area."

The fact the federal government doesn't recognize the Afghan war as a war — and needs to ask the public what it thinks — is jaw-dropping for many people, especially veterans.

WATCH | Mission was 'a war by every metric': Afghan mission was 'a war by every metric,' says vet fighting for recognition | Duration closed caption 1:38 Retired colonel Mark Gasparotto says veterans of Canada's mission in Afghanistan 'paid the price in blood, sacrifice and psychological injury.' Gasparotto is among a class of veterans advocating for the passage of Bill S-246 which would develop a framework for the recognition of military service in places like Afghanistan and the Persian Gulf as wartime service.

"The Afghan mission was a war by every metric, and the current terminology of 'special duty area' rings hollow and judged against the life-and-death realities we faced on the ground," said retired colonel Mark Gasparotto, who led combat engineers during one of the bloodiest battles of the war, Operation Medusa. He spoke on Parliament Hill last week.

Those life-and-death realities are day-to-day realities for people like retired corporal Bruce Moncur. There's no debating semantics for him because the war is etched into his body.

He was nearly killed during Operation Medusa when an American warplane mistakenly strafed his position. The attack left him with a catastrophic brain injury.

"I'm sitting there eating, and my fire team partner comes to sit next to me, Fraser Gill, and I'm eating, and I just remember being tossed in the air like a rag doll," Moncur recalled in a recent interview with CBC News.

Retired corporal Bruce Moncur in Afghanistan. He was wounded by friendly fire in 2006. (Submitted by Bruce Moncur)

"I landed and I got thrown down the mountain … I'll never forget the sight of the coagulating sand with the blood mixing together. And I'm thinking, this is it. I'm probably going to die on this mountain in the middle of nowhere."

Retired sergeant Matt Snoddon served multiple tours as a psychological warfare officer, meeting local Afghans and trying to convince them to support the government.

For him remembrance isn't something reserved for one day in November.

Asked to relate the toughest day he faced during the war, Snoddon paused for a long time before relating how he and other soldiers and medics scrambled one night to save a group of Afghan children horribly maimed in an accidental explosion.

For the most part, the military itself and private organizations, such as the NATO Association of Canada, have been left to quietly mark significant anniversary events on their own this year, including the commemoration of Operation Medusa, the largest battle Canadians fought, in September.

Retired sergeant Matt Snoddon served multiple tours in Kandahar as a psychological warfare officer trying to convince local Afghans to support the local government. (Submitted by Matt Snoddon)

Increasingly, it seems Canada has left those who fought in the country's name to carry not only its wounds, but its memory.

"You know, we can't ignore the fact that there is a price to pay now and through the next generations," Snoddon said.

"I and many others like me have been stuck with the bill for that. And unfortunately my kids will have to pay a part of that bill and the people around me will have to pay part of the bill. I think that can't be forgotten."

One of the hallmarks of the war that sticks with veterans is the cruelty the Taliban inflicted on ordinary Afghans.

Former Canadian commander — retired major-general Denis Thompson — recalled how in 2008 insurgents used a 10-year-old boy as a suicide bomber.

"There was a lot of very cynical and vicious attacks," Thompson said, noting how the boy did not control his suicide vest and was remotely denotated by an old, nearby Taliban fighter as the child got close to a Canadian patrol.

"There are no limits, if you will, to one's imagination when they're coming up with ways to terrorize the population or to get at the security forces."

Canadian and U.S. troops in 2011 on the last joint patrol of Canada's Afghan war. (Murray Brewster/The Canadian Press)

It is fair to say, however, for many veterans Afghanistan risks becoming the war Canada has already forgotten as a collective institutional amnesia settles over most of Ottawa.

This year saw a remarkable convergence of anniversaries.

It has been 25 years since Canadian troops first set foot in Afghanistan following 9/11, 20 years since the beginning of major combat operations, 20 years since the first female soldier was killed in combat, 20 years since Operations Medusa, 15 years since combat ended and five years since the South Asian country fell back into Taliban hands.

And yet as those important milestones passed this year, there was mostly silence from Ottawa.

A forgotten war?

Unlike wars and major battles of the last century, there was no major national public commemoration to mark Afghanistan.

Canadians were uniformly outraged when U.S. President Donald Trump blithely dismissed allied contributions to Afghanistan, including Canadian sacrifices.

WATCH | Afghanistan 25 years later: Canada's forgotten war: Afghanistan 25 years later | Duration closed caption 10:00 158 Canadian soldiers died in the war in Afghanistan, a conflict fading from memory 25 years after it started. CBC's Murray Brewster speaks to Canadian veterans who can't forget their experiences, even though their country has moved on.

"We have never really asked anything of them," Trump said in an interview last January. "You know, they'll say they sent some troops to Afghanistan or this and that. They did. They stayed a little back."

Trump's remarks provoked a backlash across Canada. But beneath the anger lay an uncomfortable contradiction.

While Canadians were quick to defend the war's sacrifice online, they have been far less willing, it seems, to talk about the war itself.

Only a handful of federal statements have been issued — five in all. The federal government did mark the anniversary of the end of major combat and the beginning of construction of the long-delayed national memorial.

The prime minister's Veterans' Week statement, released on Nov. 5, specifically mentions the Gulf War and the four soldiers killed last month in Wainwright, Alta., but not Afghanistan.

Historian Sean Maloney, at the Royal Military College of Canada in Kingston, Ont., said we struggle as a nation to talk about war in general and find it particularly tough to sort out our feelings about Afghanistan.

Canadian and U.S. troops on one of the last joint patrols of Canada's Afghan war in 2011. (Murray Brewster/The Canadian Press)

"Why are we afraid to talk about it?" Maloney asked.

He spent a decade battling the Defence Department for permission to publish his history of the war.

"What are we embarrassed about? Who's embarrassed? Is it the bureaucracy? Is it elected officials? Is it both? Is it cultural mavens that this doesn't fit in with?"

Retired general Wayne Eyre, the former chief of the defence staff who led a team to train Afghan soldiers during the war, said Maloney's questions are not easy to answer.

"Part of it is because of how it ended up," Eyre said, in reference to the Taliban victory in 2021.

"Canada has gone through various waves of understanding and commemoration based on the national mood and who's to say that's not going to change in the future with respect to Afghanistan? My hope is that we learn from it, we continue to venerate those that we lost over there."

WATCH | 'This is war,' says former CDS: 'This is war,' says former CDS Eyre of his time commanding troops in Afghanistan | Duration closed caption 1:58 Retired general Wayne Eyre recounts one of his worst days during the Afghan war — the moment in 2007 when six Canadian troops and one Afghan interpreter were killed in a massive roadside bombing. Eyre led a team to train Afghan troops to fight the Taliban.

The last major public commemoration directly related to the war was the hastily organized national day of honour in 2014, a tribute by the former Conservative government after the last Canadian troops were withdrawn from the country.

Unlike some of our allies, Canada has never undertaken a comprehensive public accounting of the mission.

There have been internal assessments at both the defence and foreign ministries, but no national examination of the political decisions, military strategy, money spent — or why it ended the way it did.

Maloney said he believes the reluctance reflects something deeper and that the Afghan war challenges the comfortable story Canadians tell themselves about their country.

"We're peaceful people in the middle, we're trying to be reasonable, and we're a middle power, da-da-da. Well then you go back and look at the history of the country, it doesn't fit with that," Maloney said, pointing to Canada's participation in the world wars and Korea.

A Canadian soldier in Zangabad, Afghanistan, in 2011 preparing for the handover of a base to U.S. forces. (Murray Brewster/The Canadian Press)

Former diplomat Pam Isfeld said she has noticed the same thing and wonders how well equipped Canadians are to face a world that's increasingly more dangerous when they are reluctant to acknowledge their past.

"It's an important part of our history, and the idea that nobody really wants to talk about it, I don't understand," said Isfeld, who served as a civilian adviser to Canada's combat commander in 2006.

Awarding-winning photojournalist Louie Palu, who spent almost 15 months — over five years — embedded with the Canadian army in Kandahar, said there's often more interest in the United States and Europe about the exploits of Canadian troops than there is at home.

"It's still shocking to me how few people either talk about Afghanistan or Canada's experience in Afghanistan, or acknowledge that we were at war," he said.

A decade ago, Palu produced a documentary focusing on Canadian troops using his remarkable photos. It was a film that won multiple international awards and was screened all over the world and yet was rejected by every Canadian film festival which it tried to enter.

Canada accepted over 54,700 Afghan refugees who fled the 2021 Taliban takeover, many of them deeply invested in the Western political and social value promises of a better future.

Abdul Razaq Khan, a former translator for Canadian media outlets, said he was grateful for finding a safe haven and often thinks about what his home country could have become.

"Canadians were helping to build our country, and we had to step up for that," Khan said.

Asked if he was angry about the way life has turned out, he replied: "No one leaves their country happily."

World.title: Carney embarks on a worldwide summit tour to build bridges with Europe and Asia
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney will clock about 36,000 kilometres over the next 10 days as he takes part in a series of European and Asian summits, and doubles back across two oceans to avoid crossing Russian airspace.

A meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping is perhaps the most consequential item on his agenda. Shenzhen, China, is the last stop on his agenda for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders' meeting.

"We will discuss many things," Carney said in Montreal on Tuesday, listing the "security situation around the world" as well as the two countries' economic partnership — "something that is deepening but has clear guardrails."

Carney also said that Canada would finally replace its ambassador to China. The post has been unfilled for six months, but Carney said the person has been selected and they're in the process of agreeing with China on the appointment, which is a standard diplomatic process.

"It's a little longer than we would have liked" since the post was filled, he said. "We would hope to make the announcement in very short order."

A summit in Dublin

Carney's first destination is Dublin, Ireland, where the European Political Community is holding its ninth summit on Thursday. The EPC is a venue where EU members can meet with non-members such as the U.K., Turkey, Iceland, Norway and Switzerland.

Since 2022, Ukraine has often been the main topic at EPC events, and that is expected to be the case in Dublin too, with Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelenskyy in attendance.

Ireland has suffered a wave of bomb threats and cyberattacks in recent days that the government of Taoiseach Micheál Martin has said have a "Russian dimension." Several flights on national carrier Aer Lingus and Irish discount airline Ryanair were delayed or diverted as a result of threats. In Dublin, office buildings, including national broadcaster RTÉ, had to be evacuated.

Carney is joining the summit as the only non-European invitee. It will be his second EPC summit, after attending one in Yerevan, Armenia, in May. It follows hard on the heels of a Canada-EU summit in Montreal, and fits neatly into the Carney agenda of greater integration with Europe.

WATCH | Canada working toward EU associate membership, Carney says: Carney makes it clear: Canada is working toward EU associate membership | Duration closed caption 2:45 After days of semantic gymnastics, Prime Minister Mark Carney makes it clear that Canada is working toward associate membership in the European Union, with the goal of holding regular meetings in Canada and Europe in the months ahead.

As summits go, the EPC is considered fairly informal. There is no joint communiqué or statement to be negotiated, and a space called the leaders' lounge is set up to facilitate spontaneous bilateral discussions.

The security around the event is less likely to be relaxed, however.

Last year's summit in Copenhagen was preceded by incursions of large drones, forcing the closure of the city's airport.

Europe has experienced a significant escalation in drone overflights and cyberattacks since then.

Talk of building a European "drone wall" to resist such incursions is ongoing and likely to be a major topic in Dublin.

Free trade talks with 'Bongbong'

From Dublin, Carney will travel to Manila for the 49th summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).

The shortest way to reach the Philippines from Ireland is to fly east, but that route would take the PM's plane thousands of kilometres across Russia. So instead, Carney will cross back over the Atlantic, refuel in Anchorage, Alaska, and then cross the Pacific.

Canada is currently negotiating a free trade agreement with the ASEAN bloc, and also separately with host nation the Philippines.

The second of those two deals is much closer to fruition. Carney will meet with Filipino President Ferdinand (Bongbong) Marcos Jr. on Saturday.

Carney is seen with President of the Philippines Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at the ASEAN summit last year. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

"I think we can expect that there will be a bilateral trade agreement of some kind that will be announced," said Guy Saint-Jacques, former Canadian ambassador to China.

"It's a developing country and they are looking for investment, they are looking for technologies to help them to develop, to protect their environment. They are probably looking also to get more Canadian food products, and also to export more of their products. They want to develop other export markets than China."

Canada is keen to expand its agri-food exports to Asia, and to overcome trade obstacles that have emerged in recent years for Canadian pork, pulses and other products.

Currently, pork exports to the country are expected to drop, and Manila is set to impose a 60-day ban on pork imports starting a week after Carney's visit.

But defence is also on the agenda in the Philippines. Canada has appointed a defence attaché to the region, based in Manila, a sign of the importance it gives to its missions in the area, which include dark vessel detection and presence patrols in contested waters.

The Philippines has had many issues exercising sovereignty over some of its waters and islands.

"We know that there will be more military-to-military exchanges," Saint-Jacques said. "So the fact that the prime minister is visiting the country is a confirmation that we want to support and help the Philippines."

China is not a member of ASEAN, but it is a "dialogue partner" and Chinese Premier Li Qiang is expected to be in Manila.

PM to meet PSPP in Cambodia

Carney will then move on to Siem Reap, Cambodia, to attend the Summit of the Francophonie, where he's expected to meet with the new premier of Quebec, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon.

Carney is likely to use the summit for other bilateral meetings, with a focus on trade and investment. But Canada is also interested in hosting the Francophonie in 2028, and it's possible that will be announced in Cambodia.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon will also be in Cambodia for the Francophonie summit. (Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press)

From Cambodia, Carney will fly 1,500 kilometres to Shenzhen, where Xi will host the APEC summit.

Shenzhen, which grew from a network of rural villages less than 50 years ago to a vast economic hub of nearly 19 million people, is a symbol of China's rapid growth — now surpassing both Hong Kong and Singapore in GDP.

Carney is expected to meet privately with Xi at the summit.

Jeff Nankivell, president and CEO of the Asia Pacific Foundation of Canada, spent years as a diplomat in the Canadian Embassy in Beijing. He says the relationship is recovering from a difficult decade marked by allegations of foreign interference and the detention of Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor.

"We lost a lot of trust in the last decade. That's true on both sides," he said.

"There is clearly a desire on the part of both governments to advance the relationship. And on the Canadian side there's a note of caution, but the emphasis right now seems to be leaning forward to move further and faster in areas that are considered to be safe from a national security point of view."

The "clear guardrails" that Carney referred to on Tuesday remain necessary, he said, and Canada's allies expect it.

"We have to be careful really not to co-operate in areas that touch on national defence, on artificial intelligence, particularly anything to do with implanting artificial intelligence from China into core systems that are used by Canadians, and certain other aspects of high technology like areas of quantum research that could have a military application."

U.S. President Donald Trump will also meet with Xi in Shenzhen, the White House has confirmed.

There is no word yet on a three-way Xi-Trump-Putin meeting proposed by the Russians — a meeting that most Western allies would prefer not happen.

Trump will also be in Manila, and will likely cross paths with Carney both there and in China, but no meetings between the two are on the schedule.

World.title: This veteran thinks his brain cancer is linked to his deployment. He pushed for special benefits — and won
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Medals and framed family photos on display in retired major Bruce Mayo's Ottawa living room pay tribute to generations of military service.

"We are veterans of every conflict that Canada has participated in since 1900," said Mayo, 70, who joined the Canadian Forces as a teenager and later became a military lawyer.

His father was a pilot during the Second World War, his grandfather fought in France during the First World War and his wife, retired major Dr. Sandra West, served as a medical officer in Afghanistan.

While Mayo served overseas, too, his most recent battle has been with the federal department tasked with protecting those who serve, Veterans Affairs Canada.

For two years, he fought to secure "pain and suffering" benefits after being diagnosed with glioblastoma (GBM), a terminal brain cancer he believes is linked to his deployment to Southwest Asia almost 25 years ago.

"I couldn't stop fighting. I'm a trained lawyer and I had a case and I was like a dog with a bone."

Mayo was part of the military police force at Canada’s base in Germany in the 1980s. (Submitted by Bruce Mayo)

Mayo grew up in a small village in eastern Ontario, destined to follow in the family footsteps.

"When I was 18, my mother drove me to the recruiting centre and said, ‘Go in there. You'll be as free as a bird.' Those were her exact words, and it pretty much worked out."

On Sept. 11, 2001, Mayo was the deputy chief advocate at National Defence Headquarters in Ottawa.

"Everyone who saw those aircraft fly into those towers knew that the world had changed. We just didn't know quite how," he said.

In the wake of the 9/11 attacks, Canada started to deploy troops as part of its commitment to the U.S. "war on terror."

In the summer of 2002, Mayo became legal adviser at Camp Mirage, a logistics base in the United Arab Emirates that supported Canadian operations in Afghanistan. He served at Camp Mirage for seven months.

Canadian Forces lawyers Mayo, left, and Randy Callan, right, in Afghanistan in 2002. (Submitted by Bruce Mayo)

Some 20 years later, in July 2023, Mayo was rushed to hospital after a seizure and soon diagnosed with brain cancer. Surgeons removed the tumour, but it's a terminal diagnosis with an average life expectancy of 18 months.

From the outset, Mayo and his wife asked doctors if his cancer could be connected to his deployment.

No one knew, so Mayo started digging. He joined a Facebook group for people living with GBM and what he discovered stopped him in his tracks.

"Someone mentioned that the U.S. Veterans Administration had discovered a 26 per cent greater incident rate of GBM among veterans who had served in Southwest Asia. So that area includes Afghanistan, and it also includes Dubai," said Mayo.

WATCH | Why Bruce Mayo fought for years to receive benefits : This veteran with cancer spent years fighting for special benefits | Duration 1:23 It took three attempts for Bruce Mayo, a retired military officer diagnosed with a rare brain cancer, to receive special benefits from Veterans Affairs Canada.

That American research came out in early 2022, about six months before former U.S. President Joe Biden signed the Promise to Address Comprehensive Toxics or PACT Act. One feature of that law is providing expanded veteran benefits by presuming a glioblastoma diagnosis is related to military deployment in Southwest Asia.

American studies cite a number of potential risk factors for various cancers, including burn pits, depleted uranium, fine particulate matter and aircraft fumes.

Biden's son, Beau Biden, served in Iraq and died of glioblastoma in 2015.

"If you could prove two things, that you had service in Southwest Asia and that you had a GBM diagnosis, they automatically awarded under their scheme 100 per cent disability. Well, I was gobsmacked when I saw that," said Mayo.

In 2024, citing the U.S. law and research, Mayo applied to Veterans Affairs Canada for special benefits. The monthly amount payable ranges between $500 to $1,500 depending on the scale of a veteran's impairment.

U.S. Vice President Joe Biden, right, talks with his son, U.S. army Capt. Beau Biden, at Camp Victory on the outskirts of Baghdad, Iraq, in the summer of 2009. (The Associated Press)

The response was swift.

"It just simply turned me down," said Mayo.

But he wasn't ready to give up. Through social media connections, Mayo found two other Canadian Forces members he'd served with at Camp Mirage during the same time period had recently died of glioblastoma.

Next, Mayo filed an appeal to the Veterans Review and Appeal Board, asking it to reconsider his request for special benefits.

He was turned down again. Meanwhile, stories via social media kept coming.

"I learned of this pattern that emerges over and over again. So someone would serve in Afghanistan, in Southwest Asia, come back, and within a year they were dead of GBM, and they left widows and orphans behind," said Mayo.

Medical oncologist Dr. Garth Nicholas has treated Mayo at The Ottawa Hospital Cancer Centre since 2023. (Robyn Bresnahan/CBC)

Two years into his diagnosis, Mayo took his ever-expanding research to his oncologist, Dr. Garth Nicholas, at The Ottawa Hospital Cancer Centre.

"He has lived longer than most people with glioblastoma," said Nicholas, remarking on Mayo's impressive cognitive function that's allowed him to keep investigating.

Nicholas analysed Mayo's research.

"It's not well understood exactly what their exposures were in that place that led to that, but certainly there seem to be excess cancers in that population compared to the general population," he said.

Support for an appeal

In a letter, Nicholas supported Mayo's next appeal.

Almost three years after his diagnosis, on May 5, 2026, the veterans appeal board sent him a 12-page decision, granting him the benefits he was requesting and placing him into the Veterans Independence Program . It helps subsidize grounds maintenance, housekeeping and personal care for sick and injured veterans.

"Most GBM patients aren't going to get that much assistance because they're not going to live long enough," he said.

Sandra West, left, and Mayo at their Ottawa home. (Robyn Bresnahan/CBC)

Luckily, Mayo has outlived his medical prognosis. Plus he had the legal skills to help him succeed.

"But you shouldn't have to be a blue ribbon candidate to do it," said Mayo.

His wife, a veteran herself, is frustrated by what became such an onerous process.

"It angers me when I see someone who is truly deserving of our support being made to jump through all these hoops, being delayed, being disbelieved," said West.

No precedent set

The decision in Mayo's case doesn't officially set precedent because the Veterans Review and Appeal Board is a quasi-judicial tribunal. Unlike a court, it is not bound by its own decisions.

Mayo still hopes his case will help others.

"If you have a very similar case they would be hard-placed to turn it down based on the evidence that's in my case," he said.

But what he'd really like to see is a formal change to government policy.

Veterans Affairs Minister Jill McKnight, centre, meets with members of the Royal Canadian Legion Saskatchewan command. (Kirk Fraser/CBC)

In a statement, Veterans Affairs Minister Jill McKnight said the department continually reviews research on the links between military service and veterans' health outcomes, but she made no mention of any intended policy change, such as the development of a presumptive injury list similar to that of the U.S.

According to Conservative MP Michael Barrett, who is his party's Veterans Affairs shadow minister, this is on the opposition's radar.

"We've previously called on Veterans Affairs Canada to develop that presumptive injury list," Barrett told CBC in a recent interview.

For Mayo, winning his appeal is bittersweet. The benefits will only sooth what is coming since there is no cure for glioblastoma.

"The mantra is it always comes back and it's unpredictable," said Mayo.

It's difficult to talk about, but West says when her husband is gone, his memory will be recognized as a service-related death, now that Veterans Affairs acknowledges his illness stems from his deployment.

While Mayo is grateful for the recognition, that's not why he continued to appeal.

"I just viewed it just as an inequity that needed to be addressed," he said. "I don't bear any malice towards the military."

World.title: Are we alone? Institute searching for alien signals is using a new way to answer that age-old question
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It’s lonely being the only voice in the cosmos.

In case you didn’t know, the search for life — specifically intelligent life — has been ongoing for decades. But so far, it’s just us.

Astronomers look for life in two ways: searching for biosignatures, evidence of past or current biological processes (think Mars rovers); and technosignatures, evidence of technology created by an intelligent civilization. Looking for the latter primarily involves radio astronomy, not optical, because any activity would be happening too far away for us it see it. Basically, astronomers are listening for something.

One of the organizations at the forefront of that has been the SETI Institute . Since its founding in 1984, it has scanned the sky for radio signals that might be crossing the great cosmos just to say “hello” to us humble earthlings. It’s pointed at star systems with known exoplanets, but so far, no signals from ET have been detected.

But now, scientists at the organization, based out of Mountain View, Calif., have come up with a novel method to look for these signals, incorporating game theory. Not only does this method look at where we should be searching for these signals, but also when.

Game theory is a branch of mathematics that studies interactive decision-making, where there is an interdependence between the two “players” or “agents.” Each player considers the other player’s strategy while not knowing what the other is doing. The winner depends on the collective strategy.

WATCH | Game theory explained:

In the case of the SETI Institute, it is using the “Schelling point” of game theory. The example most cited by American economist Thomas Schelling is this: Imagine you’re meeting someone in New York City, but you haven’t communicated a time or place. Both of you might choose to go to Grand Central Terminal at noon, as it’s a common meeting place and a reasonable time.

Now apply that to listening for an alien civilization, and consider the anti-solar point, an imaginary spot on the celestial sphere that is opposite the sun (180 degrees away). Think of a straight line from the sun that passes through Earth out into space.

What if there was an alien civilization that could see Earth cross in front of the sun, which is called a transit? What if they knew there was a planet around our particular star and they sent a signal toward us?

We have the where — Earth — and the when — during a transit.

Basically, we're meeting at Grand Central at noon.

Voices in the void

This anti-solar method had been suggested years ago, but there wasn’t enough funding to attempt it until now.

“I thought about these ideas that have been percolating for a long time in the literature,” said Sophia Sheikh, technosignature research scientist at the SETI Institute, and lead author of the paper. “And so now the anti-solar point idea is sort of finally getting its time in the sun.”

In their new paper released Nov. 3, SETI Institute astronomers reported that they detected 1.9 million radio signals using this method. However, after filtering them all out, they did not detect any that matched extraterrestrial technology — the signals were all us. It turns out that we earthlings, with our satellites and radio transmissions, are pretty loud.

The study ruled out that small part of the sky — but that doesn’t mean that there’s nothing out there. Space is pretty big.

So they plan on continuing this method to search for at least four years, said Sophia Sheikh, technosignature research scientist at the SETI Institute, and lead author of the paper.

The Sun and our solar system in relation to the Milky Way galaxy. The white circle indicates the area where the majority of exoplanets have been found with current telescopes. (NASA/JPL-Caltech/T. Pyle)

They're looking for something called a narrowband signal, said Sheikh, who described it as a "'we are here' ... like an air horn, almost, in the radio frequencies."

“Maybe there is information contained in it, or maybe the signal that we find is what we'd call a carrier wave. So the air horn, that says, 'Hey, there's something interesting here.'"

But don’t think of astronomers sitting with headphones on, like Ellie Arroway in 1997's Contact. Instead, computer programs sift through the data.

The SETI Institute is using the Allen Telescope Array , a collection of 42 fully steerable 6.1m-diameter telescopes at the Hat Creek Radio Observatory in California — which has been used to look for alien signals since the 1980s — to do the search.

Pictured here is the Allen Telescope Array, the first radio telescope built specifically for searching for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI). Located at the Hat Creek Radio Observatory in northern California, it features 42 antennas. (Simon Steel)

Science fiction?

Searching for extraterrestrial signals may seem like something out of science fiction. But with our Milky Way galaxy holding 100 billion stars or more, there’s a belief that there ought to be someone out there, especially considering that we now know that most stars contain at least one exoplanet .

Then there’s the Drake equation, devised by American astrophysicist Frank Drake in 1961. His aim was to estimate the number of potentially communicative civilizations in the Milky Way.

The answer is dependent on many unknown variables, but it's not zero.

Adam Frank, professor of astrophysics at the University of Rochester in New York, is also searching for technosignatures. He was awarded NASA’s first grant to study non-radio technosignatures. Instead, he looks at the chemical signatures or other indicators of an intelligent civilization.

He's talked about how the search for extraterrestrial intelligence wasn't taken seriously in the past.

“The giggle factor, which existed through almost my entire career, is gone," said Frank, referring to the fact that the possibility wasn't taken seriously decades ago. "And it never made sense."

That's particularly true after the first discovery of exoplanets in 1992, and the first discovery of an exoplanet around an sun-like star in 1995.

In the event of a detection...

Let’s say there was a detection. What then?

Believe it or not, there are protocols in place set out by the International Academy of Astronautics . Aside from the obvious — confirming and authenticating the finding — there’s a pretty big one: Do not answer. (If you've read or watched 3 Body Problem by Lui Cixin, you'll understand why that's probably a good protocol.)

Turns out that’s not exactly a major issue. Signals will be crossing distances of light-years. So, imagine we receive a signal from a star system that is 100 light-years away, and we on Earth agreed to send a response. It would take 100 years for our signal to get to the alien civilization, and then another 100 to receive their response. That’s 300 years just to say, “Hey.”

"Communication is not Job 1," Frank said.

Frank’s research involves searching for evidence of technosignatures by studying an exoplanet’s chemistry.

“For example, we can look in the atmospheres of alien planets and we could look for something like chlorofluorocarbons ... a chemical that only industry produces,” he said. "You'll never get it from just nature, from a biosphere.”

So it will be more about taking comfort knowing that we’re not alone.

This image shows the printout of a strong signal received at the Big Ear Radio Observatory in 1977. Astronomer Jerry Ehman circled the unusual signal and wrote, 'Wow!' in the margin. (Big Ear Radio Observatory and North American Astrophysical Observatory)

While we haven’t detected a definitive radio signature that might indicate an alien civilization, there was the famous “ Wow! Signal .” This powerful radio signal was detected in 1977 by the Big Ear telescope in Ohio. It lasted for 72 seconds but was never detected again. Since then, there has been some speculation that it was the result of passing comets .

So when could we detect an alien signal?

"The thing I like to say," said Sheikh, "is I hope that by the end of my career, we have a sense of whether there are any radio signals in the galaxy being produced by other technology-having civilizations."

World.title: U.S. comedian Josh Johnson surprised by CBC journalist in viral video
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A CBC News copy editor turned into one half of an unexpected comedy duo in a video posted to social media Tuesday.

American Josh Johnson, a standup comedian and occasional host of The Daily Show, was cracking jokes about CBC's coverage of a bodega cat getting evicted due to health concerns, during his show at the Vogue Theatre in Vancouver last month.

"I want so badly to meet the editor," Johnson quipped.

A voice from the audience shouted out: "He's here!"

A befuddled Johnson replied: "The cat's here?"

Nope.

"The editor's here!" shouted the crowd.

Enter Jon Azpiri.

Wearing a dark grey hoodie, coincidentally mirroring Johnson's signature light grey hoodie, Azpiri walked onstage for a 10-minute back-and-forth filled with jokes about cats, disappearing islands and journalism.

Johnson started to ask Azpiri about the bodega cat situation before Azpiri interrupted.

"We do a lot of stories about cats. So I need to know the specific cat."

WATCH | The cat in question:

Azpiri, a copy editor and reporter, answered Johnson's various questions about how a newsroom chooses what to cover.

"We're a public broadcaster," Azpiri said. "So we have a thing called Journalistic Standards and Practices."

"There's really no need to brag," Johnson replied.

As of 2 p.m. PT, Johnson's video has more than 2.4 million v iews on Instagram, and it's been seen more than 860,000 times on TikTok.

Johnson ended the exchange, and the two shook hands.

As Azpiri left, he reminded Johnson the province was set to have an election the next day.

"That's a real editor right there, too," Johnson said. "Even as he's leaving, [he's like] 'We do have an election tomorrow.'"

WATCH | Exchange with CBC journalist goes viral: U.S. comedian Josh Johnson’s CBC surprise goes viral | Hanomansing Live | Duration closed caption 14:19

Johnson told CBC's Hanomansing Live that he had a whole routine prepared about the cat story, about how the coverage was so local and quaint, and he decided instead to ask Azpiri about it since he was involved.

"The whole thing just felt like serendipity," he said, describing asking the copy editor about various CBC stories as a gift.

"When you're very open to the possibility of, like, spontaneous moments being gifts, it happens more often," he said. "And we get more of the things that we look for."

When asked what stands out to him about Canada, as an American comedian, Johnson says that there's a general understanding that people are more neighbourly to each other.

'My eyes kind of bugged out'

Azpiri said he didn't expect Johnson's video to be posted — let alone go viral. He didn't even know the show had been recorded.

He told CBC's BC Today he had just come off his copy editing shift before heading to the show.

As he was walking to the theatre with his wife, he told her he hoped they weren't sitting too close to the stage.

"Sometimes comedians do that thing where they talk to people in the audience," Azpiri said. "And I said 'I don't want to be one of those people.' "

Their tickets were for the lower deck, his wife said.

The show started, and when Johnson said he wanted to talk to a CBC editor, Azpiri reacted.

"My eyes kind of bugged out," Azpiri said.

"My wife couldn't help herself and shouted, 'Oh, he's here.' "

LISTEN | Azpiri on his viral Josh Johnson interaction: As It Happens 6:00 When Josh Johnson invited this CBC editor on stage, he just 'rolled with it'

Azpiri said everything happened so quickly, there was no time for stage fright.

"As I walked toward the stage, I did kind of realize, 'What have I gotten myself into?' "

He estimated 1,000 or so people were in the theatre, but he didn't realize there were cameras rolling.

"That seemed crazy to me … I thought that was a very pleasant thing I could tell my kids about. And then this happened this morning."

While he's been a hit in the comment section on social media, Azpiri has no plans to try one-upping Johnson on the comedy circuit.

"[I'm] very much second-billing to Josh."

World.title: Stellantis auto plant sale draws optimism, hurt in Brampton, Ont., after 2,000 jobs lost
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

For three years, Shelly Lewis has been trying to increase foot traffic at her restaurant after it dwindled following the 2023 closure of the Stellantis auto plant in Brampton, Ont.

Shelly's Kitchen on Chrysler Drive is among the many food shops that relied on business from thousands of Stellantis workers, but Lewis said she's had to lay off a staff member and admits she has struggled to pay bills some months.

"The Stellantis plant made business for me because I had staff at all hours come in and I had lots of specials," she said. "I'm so sad that they shut down operations."

Now, however, she's hopeful that news the automaker is expected to have a new owner will result in more customers at her eatery and rejuvenate the area.

On Monday, it was announced that Canadian armoured ⁠vehicle maker Roshel Inc. will buy the auto plant, acquiring the idled facility and equipment from Stellantis for an undisclosed amount.

That appears to be positive news, as more than 2,000 workers were laid off when operations were halted in in 2023 to retool the plant for Jeep production, a plan that was paused in early 2025.

Baltej Bajwa, among the over 2,000 workers laid off from Brampton's Stellantis facility, says it's great that Roshel is offering jobs to workers in the city, but fears there will be lots of uncertainty for colleagues. (CBC)

But Baltej Bajwa, one of the laid-off workers who has been left in limbo since the plant's closure, remains uncertain of his future and said he was shocked to hear about the sale.

"Any hope that we had of potentially coming back when we heard the news kind of just got shattered," Bajwa said.

Roshel Inc. CEO Roman Shimonov did say the company plans to employ thousands of people and will give first priority to the workers who lost their job in Brampton.

However, Bajwa said, Roshel's production capacity will be far fewer than the 400 to 800 vehicles that the 2,200 Stellantis workers produced daily.

"So yes, it's amazing that Roshel is giving us those job opportunities, but it still does kind of leave the other half of the plant in a state of disarray where we don't know where we're going to go."

'They can't cut and run,' mayor says

Roshel's purchase of the plant has garnered harsh words from union leaders and politicians.

Prime Minister Mark Carney called it a "betrayal" to all Canadians.

Lana Payne, national president of Unifor, said Monday that the sale is an "unacceptable outcome" for the union and its members, calling it the "worst-case scenario."

Brampton Mayor Patrick Brown echoed those sentiments. He said Stellantis has received "bailouts" from various levels of government over the years, including most recently in 2022, "on the basis of production in Canada."

"Brampton residents are rightfully angry. I think Canadians should be angry," he told CBC News on Tuesday. "This is a company that has depended on Canadian taxpayer generosity for decades. They can't cut and run without consequences.

"Stellantis has abandoned Canadian workers — they got bullied by the Trump administration. If we allow Stellantis to leave easily and ignore their legal obligations, this will not be the last auto plant that falls in Canada. Really, this is ground zero of protecting auto jobs."

In a statement, Stellantis said it would voluntarily repay the subsidies.

Purchase will drive up economic activity: Board of Trade

Brown said he thinks Roshel is a great local company that has ambitions to create thousands of jobs, but doesn't believe it should have purchased Stellantis.

However, Jaipaul Massey-Singh, CEO of the Brampton Board of Trade, believes this will be a boon to the city and the local economy.

He said the impact of Stellantis's closure goes beyond just workers, affecting their families and the local businesses they were supporting. He has heard from many shops that have laid off staff, lost orders and reduced their hours to stay afloat.

"Knowing that it's going to result in activity in that plant once more, creating employment for those who are going to be there but also additional employment and economic activity for the community in general, is absolutely welcome news," Massey-Singh said about the sale.

"For every employee that's affected, it's up to, five to six additional employees or workers in that community that are impacted. So in a place like Brampton, we're talking minimum [12,000] to 15,000 individuals who were impacted by Stellantis's decision to walk away."

The Chrysler Brampton Assembly plant is seen Nov. 10 in this image taken by drone. Local leaders have condemned Stellantis's decision to sell the plant, leaving over 2,000 workers without jobs. However, local businesses hope the sale will bring more foot traffic to the area. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

Massey-Singh hopes all laid-off Stellantis employees get their jobs back, and believes reopening the plant under new ownership will drive more investment and business in the form of new workers, retraining and additional resources.

Lewis remains optimistic that Roshel joining the community will help boost business for her restaurant and other local establishments.

"I'm happy that something else will be there again because they'll have people working there again and this plaza has lots of different businesses, so I know it's going to be better for everybody."

World.title: Joining lawsuit, Kennedy family members say Trump's arch would be 'denigration' of JFK, RFK plots at Arlington
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Nine family members of the Kennedy political dynasty asked a judge on Tuesday to block U.S. President Donald Trump's plan to build a towering memorial arch, saying the 250-foot (76-metre) structure would cast a shadow over their relatives' gravesites at Arlington National Cemetery.

The shadow would "fundamentally alter the experience of visiting the gravesites," the relatives argued. They filed a motion to intervene in two existing lawsuits seeking to block construction of the arch.

U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan last week prohibited the Trump administration from breaking ground on the structure for 14 days.

The nine Kennedy family members who filed suit are children and grandchildren of Robert F. Kennedy and Edward M. Kennedy, brothers of the slain U.S. president John F. Kennedy, both of whom served in the U.S. Senate. They are buried close to the eternal flame that marks JFK's gravesite, a trio of memorials that are a major draw for the millions of people who visit the Arlington cemetery each year.

Sen. Tammy Duckworth, of Illinois, speaks at a demonstration against U.S. President Donald Trump's proposed arch on Oct. 1 in Washington. (Kylie Cooper/Reuters)

Building the arch would be a "permanent denigration" of the gravesites, lawyers for the relatives wrote.
