World.title: A Quiet Island Escape in Costa Rica’s Gulf of Nicoya
World.content:
A three-hour journey and a short boat ride from my home in Costa Rica took me somewhere that felt much farther away. Isla Jesusita sits in the Gulf of Nicoya near Paquera, surrounded by forested hills, calm water and small islands crowded with birds. I went there for two nights at Isla Chiquita Glamping Hotel, expecting a comfortable little escape.

What I found was one of those places where the surroundings quickly became more important than the accommodation.My arrival was gray, misty and cooler than I expected. I had pictured bright tropical sunshine, but the hills were wrapped in clouds and the Gulf had an almost rainforest feel. I immediately wished I had packed a light jacket.

A few hours later, the rain stopped and the sky produced one of the most beautiful sunsets I have seen in Costa Rica. By the next morning, the water was calm and the sun was shining. I liked the changeability of it. Nothing felt staged. The island seemed to shift with the weather.

The setting reminded me of Tsowa Safari Island, a tented camp where I stayed on the Zambezi River near Victoria Falls. Obviously, the Gulf of Nicoya is very different from the Zambezi, but the feeling was remarkably similar. In both places, I felt as though I was staying inside the landscape rather than looking at it from a conventional hotel.

My air-conditioned canvas tent was comfortable without separating me from what was happening outside. I could hear the sounds of the island, walk down to the water within minutes and spend much of the day outdoors. The property is small enough that it never felt crowded during my stay, which became one of the things I appreciated most.

The beach itself is not the kind of broad white-sand beach people often picture when they think about Costa Rica. It is smaller and quieter, and I found myself paying attention to things I might normally have walked past. At low tide, for example, the wet sand was covered with elaborate flower- and fern-like patterns created by tiny crabs feeding beneath the surface. At first, I wasn’t quite sure what I was looking at. Once I realized what was making them, I kept stopping to examine the patterns.

There is also a forest trail through the island. I had intended to explore it, but after the rain, I took one look at the mud, exposed roots and steeper sections and reconsidered. I had brought water shoes rather than proper walking shoes, so the beach won. It was a good reminder that glamping does not necessarily mean every part of the experience is manicured.

One of my favorite parts of the stay was actually how little I felt I needed to do. I slept incredibly well. One morning, I woke around five to the sound of howler monkeys somewhere in the distance and stayed in bed listening to them for a while. Eventually, I wandered down for breakfast and spent much of the morning simply enjoying the water and the quiet.

That pace worked particularly well for me as a solo traveler. There was enough privacy that I could disappear with a book or walk by myself, but I never felt isolated. The excursions provided natural opportunities to meet other people without requiring me to organize my trip around a group.

I met a couple from Austin on a sunset cruise through the Gulf. As we traveled among the small islands and rocky shoreline, we watched frigatebirds circling overhead, large groups of birds filling the trees and bright red crabs clinging to the rocks. Then the sky began to change. Orange, pink and lavender spread across the water while the islands became dark silhouettes. Every few minutes, the colors shifted again. I have lived in Costa Rica long enough to know that the country does spectacular sunsets very well, but this one was exceptional.

Later that evening, we went back onto the water for a bioluminescence excursion. We were given nets to move through the water, triggering flashes of light from the tiny organisms below the surface. The glowing water was fascinating, but what surprised me just as much was the sky. Away from the brighter lights, the stars were spectacular. For a few minutes, there was light above me and light below me.

That was probably my favorite moment of the trip. The Gulf of Nicoya does not always get the attention given to Costa Rica’s more famous beach destinations. That may be part of its appeal. From the water, the landscape feels less like a beach resort corridor and more like a collection of islands, forest, fishing communities and stretches of undeveloped coastline.

It also felt refreshingly uncrowded. There were no lines, no packed beaches and none of the sense that everyone was competing for the same photograph. The experience was quieter and more intimate than that. For travelers interested in making a similar trip, Isla Chiquita is located on Isla Jesusita near Paquera. Guests arriving from the Guanacaste side travel by road to a mainland meeting point at Punta Cuchillos, where a small hotel boat provides the final transfer to the island. The boat ride is short, but it creates a definite psychological break between the mainland and the stay.

My two-night air-conditioned tent stay, including breakfast, cost $460. My share of the sunset cruise and bioluminescence excursion brought my accommodation-and-activity total to a little over $556 before additional meals, drinks and incidentals. Those were the prices during my November 2026 visit and should be checked directly before planning a trip.

I would also pack differently next time. Comfortable walking shoes would make the forest trail much more practical, particularly during the rainy season, and I would bring a light sweater or jacket. Costa Rica may be tropical, but an evening on the water after rain can feel surprisingly cool.

I would return, but not because Isla Jesusita offers a checklist of things to do. In fact, almost the opposite was true. What I enjoyed was waking to monkeys, watching the tide expose tiny signs of life on the beach, seeing islands filled with birds and sitting on the water as the sky changed color. It gave me the scenery and solitude I wanted, but enough interaction with other travelers that being there alone never felt lonely.

Sometimes a short trip does not need to be packed with activities to feel like an adventure. Sometimes it is enough to go somewhere quiet and pay attention.

About the Author

Jennifer Pietrzak-Wahl is a retired technology executive and solo traveler living in Costa Rica. She writes about independent travel, immersive experiences and the practical realities of exploring the world later in life. Her travels have taken her from safari camps in Africa to the Scottish Highlands and islands throughout the Caribbean, with a particular interest in experiences that combine culture, nature and a strong sense of place.

World.title: Costa Rica Has Seized 74 Tons of Drugs This Year, a Total the US Calls Historic
World.content:
Costa Rican police have seized more than 74 metric tons of drugs so far in 2026, according to the government, a total the United States Embassy described as historic and higher than in previous years. The figure was released Monday after President Laura Fernández held a security meeting at the US Embassy in Pavas, in western San José, with Ambassador Melinda Hildebrand, embassy political and counternarcotics officials, and representatives of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA).

The session resumed the meetings of what the Presidency calls its “Fuerza Élite,” a group of senior security officials that the president convenes weekly to review the country’s security situation. According to the Presidency, the discussion covered drug seizures, coordinated operations against drug trafficking and strategies to dismantle transnational criminal groups.

Photos released by the Presidency showed Foreign Minister Ana Elena Pinto, Public Security Minister Gerald Campos, Justice and Peace Minister Gabriel Aguilar and Communication Minister Arnold Zamora at the meeting. The government did not announce any new operations, agreements or funding.

The US Embassy credited Costa Rican police and security forces for the seizures and said Washington would keep supporting the country, adding that neither side could afford to let its guard down. The government linked the results to Costa Rica’s participation in the Coalition Against Cartels of the Americas and the Shield of the Americas, two regional security frameworks it joined this year.

Costa Rica backed a regional security declaration in March and a multilateral declaration in September that included migration restrictions and mechanisms to freeze criminal assets, according to the government.

The meeting followed the interception of a fast boat in the South Pacific on Sunday night. The Ministry of Public Security said officers from its Special Operations Group and the Coast Guard, supported by a US aircraft, stopped the vessel about 41 nautical miles (76 kilometers or 47 miles) southwest of Sierpe de Osa.

Two Colombian men, aged 55 and 52, and a 38-year-old Ecuadorian man were detained, according to the ministry. The unflagged boat, about 9.75 meters (32 feet) long with two outboard motors and satellite communications equipment, was taken to Golfito. The Drug Control Police will determine the type and quantity of the suspected cargo, and the ministry has not said what legal measures it will seek against the suspects.

Days earlier, authorities seized marijuana off Punta Burica, near the Panama border, and detained two Ecuadorian nationals. The growing volume has also strained the country’s ability to dispose of what it seizes. In late September, the two governments announced that a US military plane would carry 45 tons of seized drugs to the United States for destruction because the country lacked the capacity to incinerate them.

Security cooperation with Washington has deepened under the Fernández administration. The president has said that US ground operations would benefit national security. Hildebrand, who arrived in Costa Rica as ambassador in January, hosted Monday’s session. Officials have presented the record seizures as evidence that joint operations are working. The larger figure also reflects how much cocaine continues to move along Costa Rica’s Pacific coast toward North American and European markets, a flow authorities have tied to much of the country’s violence in recent years.

World.title: Costa Rica Can’t Build Its Way Out of Traffic, Public Works Minister Says
World.content:
Costa Rica has spent decades underinvesting in its road network, and the gap has pushed Costa Rica’s traffic problems well beyond long commutes, Public Works and Transport Minister Efraím Zeledón said this week. Zeledón acknowledged that Costa Rica has not put enough money into roads to keep pace with the growth in vehicles, leaving a deficit that has built up over several decades. He argued, however, that wider highways alone will not solve the problem.

No country has managed to end its congestion by adding lanes, the minister said, because more road capacity draws more drivers. Transport planners call this induced demand, and Zeledón cited it as the reason the Ministry of Public Works and Transport (MOPT) is betting on trains, buses and digital mobility platforms rather than road expansion alone.

He also pointed to a newer pressure on the network. The exchange rate has pushed vehicle prices down sharply, Zeledón said, making it easy for more people to buy a car or motorcycle and adding traffic to roads that were already over capacity. The cost of congestion is showing up in the workplace. A recent study by the Federation of Chambers of Commerce of the Central American Isthmus (FECAMCO), based on consultations in five cities across the region, found that 60% of workers said a company’s location influences whether they accept or keep a job. About one in four, or 24%, had considered changing jobs because of commuting problems.

Employers described similar strain. Half of the business owners consulted said mobility conditions or their company’s location had made it harder to attract or retain staff, and eight in ten identified added costs tied to those problems. Seven in ten participants overall reported a moderate or high impact on their family, personal or rest time. In the Greater Metropolitan Area, where daily commutes link San José, Heredia, Alajuela and Cartago, those hours on the road come directly out of time for work, study and family.

The government’s main bet is the electric passenger train known as Tibi, which Zeledón has described as the backbone of a future public transport network and which authorities aim to have 80% complete by 2030. The project still faces hurdles, including more than 400 buildings that sit in its right of way.

MOPT is also exploring a cable car that would connect southern San José areas such as Desamparados and Aserrí with the future train. Zeledón has said the ministry is seeking financing for the prefeasibility and pre-investment studies needed to determine whether the project is viable. The minister framed the task ahead as recovering years of lost investment while building a public transport system reliable enough that commuters choose it over their own vehicles.

World.title: ATP Finals 2026 Set for Turin Without Sinner as Four Newcomers Join Field
World.content:
The 2026 ATP Finals will begin Sunday, November 15, with a different look from recent years. World No. 1 Alexander Zverev leads an eight-player field that includes Carlos Alcaraz, two Americans and four first-time qualifiers, while defending champion Jannik Sinner will miss the season-ending tournament because of a knee injury.

The tournament runs through November 22 at the Inalpi Arena in Turin, bringing together the season’s leading players for one of the most prestigious titles outside the Grand Slams. With the field now confirmed, attention turns to Thursday’s group draw and the opening matches this weekend.

Sinner’s absence is the biggest change. The Italian, who won the ATP Finals in 2024 and 2025, has not competed since capturing his fifth Grand Slam title at Wimbledon in July. Speaking at a press conference in Milan on Tuesday, November 10, Sinner said he hopes to return for the 2027 Australian Open but will not rush his recovery. He is following medical advice and wants to protect his long-term career rather than risk returning too soon. His withdrawal means Turin will crown a different champion this year and removes one of the tournament’s leading attractions, particularly for Italian fans.

Zverev enters as the highest-ranked player and one of the most experienced competitors in the field. The German has won the ATP Finals twice, in 2018 and 2021, and will be making his ninth appearance at the year-end championships. Alcaraz arrives with renewed confidence after defeating Ben Shelton in Sunday’s Paris Masters final. The Spaniard, who reached the ATP Finals championship match in 2025, is still chasing his first title at the event.

Daniil Medvedev, the 2020 champion, is the other former winner competing this year. For American tennis, the tournament offers another opportunity to end a long wait for a champion. Shelton and Frances Tiafoe will both compete in Turin, marking the second consecutive season that two Americans have qualified.

Shelton returns for his second appearance, while the 28-year-old Tiafoe makes his debut. No American has won the singles championship since Pete Sampras in 1999. The remaining newcomers bring several compelling stories. Italy’s Flavio Cobolli will make his first ATP Finals appearance in front of a home crowd after a breakthrough season that included reaching the French Open final.

France’s Arthur Fils becomes the first Frenchman to qualify for the tournament since Gael Monfils in 2016. Fils won titles in Barcelona and Cincinnati during a season that established him among the leading young players on the ATP Tour. Perhaps the most unexpected qualifier is Spain’s Rafael Jodar, who was still playing college tennis at the University of Virginia a year ago.

Jodar, 20, began the season outside the established elite but climbed high enough in the ATP Race to secure the final position in Turin. He follows Alcaraz in progressing from the Next Gen ATP Finals to the season-ending championship the following year. The ATP Finals use a format different from regular tournaments. The eight singles players are divided into two groups of four, with each competitor playing three round-robin matches. The top two players from each group advance to the semifinals.

The format allows a player to lose a match during the group stage and still compete for the championship. There is also considerable prize money at stake. The tournament carries a total purse of $15.75 million, with an undefeated singles champion eligible to earn $5.171 million. The group draw is scheduled for Thursday, November 12, and will determine the opening matchups. Round-robin play begins Sunday, November 15, followed by the semifinals on November 21 and the championship match on November 22.

With Sinner sidelined, Zverev seeking a third title, Alcaraz chasing his first and half the field making its debut, this year’s ATP Finals offer a different mix of established champions and emerging contenders.

World.title: Marino Ballena Closes Piñuela Entrance for Six Months, Whale Tail Still Open
World.content:
If you’re heading to Marino Ballena National Park in the coming months, one of its four entrances is off limits. The Piñuela sector on Costa Rica’s southern Pacific coast closed Monday and is expected to stay shut for six months. The rest of the park is open and you can still enter through the Uvita, Colonia and Ballena sectors, and Uvita remains the closest entrance to the park’s famous whale-tail sandbar.

At Piñuela, the closure is total and you can’t walk in, and boats can’t drop off or pick up passengers there. The bathrooms and showers at that entrance are closed too. The reason is damaged infrastructure. The National System of Conservation Areas (SINAC) said the sector’s facilities have deteriorated enough to put visitors and park staff at risk.

If your tour includes a boat landing or a stop at Piñuela, check with your operator before you go. Your trip may need to move to another sector. The timing is important to note since the closure runs through Costa Rica’s busiest travel months, which typically start in December. It also overlaps with the season when humpback whales from the Northern Hemisphere pass through these waters, roughly December through April.

Marino Ballena sits near Uvita in the canton of Osa, Puntarenas. It protects about 15 kilometers (9.3 miles) of coastline between the mouth of the Morete River and Punta Piñuela, the park’s southern end. Its whale-tail sandbar, visible at low tide, is one of Costa Rica’s best-known coastal landmarks.

Guided tours, hotels and restaurants in Uvita and nearby communities depend heavily on park visitors, and the park is home to the annual Whale and Dolphin Festival. The Osa Conservation Area, which manages the park for SINAC, asked visitors to respect the restrictions and follow instructions from park rangers.

Officials have not said which facilities will be repaired or released a detailed work schedule. If the six-month timeline holds, Piñuela would reopen around May 2027, though that date still needs official confirmation.

World.title: Central America – Where Soccer Is Stuck in Time
World.content:
Bryan Oliva, 12, runs across a field of yellowing, overgrown grass in a densely populated neighborhood of San Salvador. He dreams of becoming a professional soccer player, but talent alone is not enough to make that happen in a Central America where the sport is moving backward.

Eleven-year-old Darixon Rivas of Honduras shares that dream. Every afternoon, he trains on a muddy field, but first he must work on his family’s ranch in La Abisinia, a remote village in the northern department of Colón. “You make a lot of money as a soccer player, but I don’t feel like it’s possible for me,” Bryan admits in Zacamil, a neighborhood of apartment buildings in the Salvadoran capital.

Hoping to help his family financially, he believes it is “really difficult” for young people from poor communities like his to get noticed by scouts, since the few opportunities available tend to reach more privileged areas. Poverty touches almost everything in Central America, where roughly half the population lives in those conditions. But soccer’s problems go further: with few exceptions, investment in infrastructure and player development is scarce.

“We have a long way to go,” Salvadoran Soccer Federation President Yamil Bukele recently acknowledged. He is promoting a plan to strengthen the youth divisions.

Moving Backward

The consequences are plain to see: only Panama and Guatemala qualified for the Concacaf Nations League quarterfinals, which begin Thursday. In fact, Panama was the only Central American team at the recent World Cup in North America, where Caribbean nations Curaçao and Haiti also represented Concacaf.

El Salvador last appeared at a World Cup 44 years ago, during the rise of striker Jorge “Mágico” González, considered Central America’s best player of the 20th century. More than 40 coaches have led the team since then. The job is currently held by Colombia’s Hernán Darío Gómez, who has coached at the World Cup.

Honduras, led by Spain’s José Francisco Molina, has also spent years living on memories. Its last World Cup appearance was in Brazil in 2014. That tournament was also where time stood still for Costa Rica, which has never again fielded a team like the one that stunned the soccer world by reaching the quarterfinals. Guatemala, Nicaragua and Belize have never played at a World Cup.

“There has been a regression,” Argentine coach Diego Vázquez, who led Honduras from 2022 to 2023, tells AFP. “Youth leagues need to be organized, and governments need to invest too,” he adds. Former Panama international Víctor René Mendieta says El Salvador, Honduras and Costa Rica “neglected” the development of new talent.

Costa Ricans and Hondurans in particular “think the coaches are to blame, when the reality is that their talent pool (…) has been drying up, and they can’t compete with the emerging forces in the Caribbean,” Salvadoran journalist Bruno Porzio said.

No One Taking Responsibility

With nearly 50 million inhabitants, Central America has around 4,400 professional soccer players, most of them spread across 68 teams, according to FIFA figures from 2024. Yet domestic competitions, lacking stars or prominent coaches, are of a modest standard, and only a handful of players earn more than $5,000 a month.

Most teams lack youth affiliates and training centers. Many clubs also play in small stadiums with artificial turf. “In El Salvador, major business owners stopped taking an interest in soccer,” and club officials have no interest in “leaving a legacy,” Porzio says. In Honduras, meanwhile, executives “want to stay for life,” Honduran coach Reynaldo Tilguath tells AFP.

Central America also lacks players in major leagues who could raise the standard of its national teams, unlike Haiti, Suriname and Curaçao, whose squads are filled with players developed in Europe. Panama is “doing a better job” of developing players, while “the rest of us are falling behind,” Tilguath says.

Meanwhile, high in the mountains of La Abisinia, Darixon and his friends share their field with horses and cows, trying to score in goals made from rusty metal posts. One wears a Lionel Messi jersey, while another sports clothing covered in images of Cristiano Ronaldo.

“Honduran soccer is broken (…). Look at the state of this little field. Our fathers used to come and play here too,” Darixon says.

World.title: DEA Traced Costa Rica’s First Female Extradition Case to a 2-Ton Jungle Lab
World.content:
A U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration investigation that reached a jungle cocaine lab in Colombia and a fishing boat anchored off Peru lies behind the case of Shirley Yesenia Gómez Parra, the first Costa Rican woman approved for extradition to the United States on drug charges.

Gómez Parra, 39, and her partner, Viveros Viveros, 50, a Colombian-born naturalized Costa Rican, are among six people named in a single indictment returned by a federal grand jury in Arizona on Oct. 1, 2025, according to the federal court docket in United States v. Arredondo et al. The indictment carries one count and a forfeiture allegation.

Investigators allege the pair acted as local leaders of a network that moved cocaine from Colombia through Panama, Costa Rica and Mexico to the U.S. market. Neither has been convicted, and the allegations have not been tested at trial. According to case records reported in Costa Rica, a confidential DEA informant met in Bogotá on July 31, 2024, with Edgar Santiago Barbosa Andrade, who investigators say acted as an emissary for Colombian supplier Jorge Sánchez Gamboa. The meeting was recorded.

On Oct. 3, 2024, the informant met Francisco Mantilla Angulo, known as “Frank,” and a second man known as “Primo” in Cali, investigators allege. The informant was then taken about an hour and a half to a jungle complex that could hold up to 2 metric tons (about 4,400 pounds) of cocaine and was watched by roughly six lookouts.

During that visit, according to the allegations, the suppliers set a price of 5.8 million Colombian pesos per kilogram, or about $1,350. On Oct. 18, 2024, an emissary handed over 7 kilograms (15.4 pounds) of cocaine for $10,000 in cash at a shopping center in Cali. DEA laboratory tests later confirmed it was high-purity cocaine hydrochloride.

In December 2024, investigators allege, the group’s leaders offered a fishing vessel anchored in Peru to move drugs across the Pacific. The DEA also recorded Gómez Parra on video negotiating a 100-kilogram (220-pound) cocaine shipment to Arizona, investigators allege. U.S. authorities further link the network to biweekly flights from Colombia, a set of safe houses and the seizure of 273 kilograms (602 pounds) of cocaine from two vehicles in August 2024.

Colombian investigators, working with the it’s navy and a military anti-kidnapping unit, located Sánchez Gamboa, Barbosa Andrade and Mantilla Angulo in Bogotá, Cali and Buenaventura and served them with the U.S. request, Colombia’s Attorney General’s Office said in March.

In Panama, authorities detained Oscar Enrique Virula Arredondo, a Guatemalan national who prosecutors allege offered safe houses and transport routes in Costa Rica. He is listed as the first defendant in the Arizona case. Gómez Parra was detained in Ciudad Neily and Viveros Viveros in La Sabana, both on March 13, 2026. She is held at the Vilma Curling Rivera women’s prison, and he is in the maximum-security module at La Reforma.

The San José Criminal Court approved the extradition of both on Sept. 14. Their defense appealed within three days, arguing that the alleged acts date to July 2024, before the constitutional reform that allowed Costa Rica to extradite its own citizens took effect. The defense also argued that DEA agents made covert purchases without a formal cooperation agreement endorsed by Costa Rica’s Foreign Ministry.

The trial judge rejected the retroactivity argument, finding that drug trafficking is a continuing offense and that the alleged conduct ran until Oct. 1, 2025. The judge also ruled that the validity of the DEA’s evidence is a matter for the courts in Arizona, not for an extradition hearing.

The appeal is pending, and neither defendant can be handed over until it is resolved. The case adds to a widening set of U.S. drug investigations that run through Costa Rica. If the appeal fails, Gómez Parra and Viveros Viveros would follow former Public Security Minister Celso Gamboa, who was extradited to Texas in March, among the Costa Ricans sent to face trial in U.S. courts since the reform.

World.title: Strong Winds Up to 75 km/h and Rain Forecast for Costa Rica
World.content:
Hold on to your hat if you’re in northern Guanacaste today. Trade winds pick up across Costa Rica on Tuesday, Nov. 10, and gusts could reach 75 kilometers per hour (47 mph) in the country’s northwest corner, according to the National Meteorological Institute (IMN). In the Central Valley, the North Pacific and the mountain ranges, expect gusts of 30 to 50 km/h (19 to 31 mph). That’s strong enough to bring down weak branches, rattle loose roofing and signs, and push motorcycles and high-sided vehicles around on open stretches of road.

The wind isn’t the only thing to watch. On the Central and South Pacific coasts the day starts mostly clear, but sea breezes will build clouds through the morning. By afternoon you can expect isolated showers and downpours, some with thunderstorms. In the Central Valley, skies will be partly cloudy with moderate morning winds and only light, scattered rain in the afternoon. San José should range from 19°C (66°F) to 28.5°C (83°F).

Guanacaste will be the windiest and hottest part of the country. Skies stay mostly clear, with the strongest gusts over high ground in the morning and moderate winds into the afternoon. Liberia is forecast to hit 35°C (95°F). Along the Central Pacific, clouds thicken through the morning, and showers and possible storms form over the mountains in the afternoon. Quepos tops out near 31.5°C (89°F), and coastal showers are possible after dark.

The South Pacific follows the same pattern. Isolated downpours with possible thunderstorms develop in the afternoon, followed by showers along the coast at night. Golfito expects a high of about 30°C (86°F). On the Caribbean side, moisture coming off the sea brings partly cloudy skies and scattered rain in the morning. In the afternoon the rain stays close to the mountains, and Limón and Guápiles both top out around 29°C (84°F).

The Northern Zone gets a similar mix, with scattered morning rain and possible afternoon showers in the mountains. Ciudad Quesada ranges from 17°C (63°F) to 28°C (82°F). If you’re driving in northern Guanacaste, keep both hands on the wheel and give trucks and motorcycles extra room. Gusts hit hardest on open roads and ridgelines, where nothing breaks the wind. Bring in or tie down anything loose on balconies, patios and rooftops.

If you’re headed to a Pacific beach, plan to be off the sand and out of the water by early afternoon, when storms are most likely to form. Lightning is the main danger, and it can strike before the rain arrives. Looking ahead, IMN expects the trade winds to stay strong through Wednesday, ease for a short time midweek, and pick up again Saturday and Sunday. That weekend push comes from a weak cold front system to the north that speeds up the winds over the Caribbean. Rain should decrease nationwide over the week.

This is the usual pattern of the shift from the rainy season to the dry season. Sunny days, occasional showers and bursts of strong wind take turns until the dry months settle in. IMN has also forecast warmer-than-normal temperatures from November through January.

World.title: Anthony Carballo Jr. rejects sentencing indication of life imprisonment, will stand murder trial in January 2027
World.content:
Anthony Carballo Jr. rejects sentencing indication of life imprisonment, will stand murder trial in January 2027

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Anthony Carballo Jr. has rejected a sentencing indication that could have seen him serve life imprisonment with the possibility of parole after 20 years, opting instead to proceed to trial alongside his co-accused, Christopher Pitts Jr., for the 2023 murder of Sylvian Nigel Swift.

The two men appeared before High Court Justice Nigel Pilgrim on Tuesday, November 10, where their murder trial was scheduled to begin on January 27, 2027, and is expected to last approximately one week.

Carballo’s attorney, Nazira Myles-Espat, informed the court that an agreement could not be reached, stating, “We were unable to reach an agreement and so we will proceed to trial.”

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, Carballo had sought a sentencing indication while exploring the possibility of entering a guilty plea. On October 8, Justice Pilgrim reportedly indicated a sentence of life imprisonment with the possibility of parole after serving a minimum of 20 years.

However, Carballo has now decided against accepting the indication and will proceed to trial.

Meanwhile, Pitts Jr., who maintains his innocence, is represented by attorney Andrew Bennett, who informed the court of his intention to call alibi witnesses during the trial. Myles-Espat also indicated that she intends to file amended case management documents to challenge certain issues in the proceedings.

The charges stem from the April 27, 2023, murder of 20-year-old Swift, who was fatally shot near his home in Belize City. Reports indicate that Swift was standing a short distance from his residence when two men riding a motorcycle opened fire, fatally injuring him.

World.title: Alleged ‘Grabby Cabbie’ Herbert Taylor, previously charged with sexually assaulting passenger, charged again for kissing another passenger without consent
World.content:
Alleged ‘Grabby Cabbie’ Herbert Taylor, previously charged with sexually assaulting passenger, charged again for kissing another passenger without consent

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 52-year-old Belize City taxi operator, Herbert Garreth Taylor, is facing a new sexual assault charge after an 18-year-old woman accused him of touching and kissing her without her consent.

Taylor, a resident of the Saint Martin de Porres area, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday, November 9, where he pleaded not guilty to the charge.

The allegation stems from an incident on November 5, 2026, during which Taylor allegedly touched the young woman inappropriately before kissing her without her consent.

The prosecution raised concerns about a previous sexual assault charge against Taylor but did not object to bail after it was established that the earlier charge had been dismissed.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, Taylor was arraigned in October 2025 after another woman accused him of inappropriately touching her leg during a taxi drop-off on September 9, 2025. He denied that allegation in court, stating, “I never touched her on her leg.” He was granted bail of $6,000 at the time, and the charge was subsequently dismissed.

In the latest case, Taylor was granted bail of $3,000 with one surety or two sureties, subject to conditions prohibiting him from contacting the complainant, her family or prosecution witnesses. He must also remain at least 100 yards away from the complainant.

Taylor, who has reportedly posted bail, is scheduled to return to court on December 30, 2026.

The latest allegation against him has not been proven in court.

World.title: ‘Easy Glen’ committed to stand trial for 2025 Shaniele Faber murder, claims family paid attorney who failed to represent him
World.content:
‘Easy Glen’ committed to stand trial for 2025 Shaniele Faber murder, claims family paid attorney who failed to represent him

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Well-known UDP activist Goldburn Adolphus, better known as “Easy Glen,” has been committed to stand trial at the High Court for the October 2025 murder of 42-year-old school warden and mother of four, Shaniele Faber, whose mutilated body was discovered stuffed inside a blue garbage drum in Belize City.

Adolphus, 56, appeared unrepresented before the Chief Magistrate on Tuesday, November 10, where his preliminary inquiry was finally conducted following several adjournments. At the conclusion of the proceedings, the court committed his case to the January 2027 session of the High Court.

However, Adolphus expressed shock and disappointment over the absence of his attorney, claiming his aunt had paid $1,200 for legal representation during the preliminary inquiry.

His former attorney, Norman Rodriguez, submitted a letter informing the court that he no longer represented Adolphus. When approached for comment, Rodriguez disputed the amount reportedly paid, saying he had received only $800 and that Adolphus subsequently indicated his aunt would handle the matter.

Adolphus said he intends to report the matter to the Bar Association and seek new representation, possibly from prominent criminal attorney Richard “Dickie” Bradley.

During the preliminary inquiry, the prosecution submitted 16 witness statements, 12 documentary exhibits and seven additional exhibits, including forensic evidence, surveillance footage and materials recovered during the murder investigation.

Adolphus also provided the court with the names of four witnesses, two men and two women, whom he intends to call during his High Court trial.

Faber’s partially decomposed body was discovered on October 4, 2025, after a bottle collector searching a garbage drum at the corner of Amandala Drive and Cemetery Road made the horrifying discovery.

According to previous reporting by Breaking Belize News, investigators recovered a bloodstained machete, trolley and suspected blood evidence from a nearby apartment. Police also obtained surveillance footage allegedly linking Adolphus to the disposal of the drum.

Adolphus was initially arraigned on October 7, 2025, and has remained on remand at the Belize Central Prison since then.

He is presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

World.title: KHMH denies admitting negligence in newborn’s death, acknowledges delay in responding to mother’s complaints
World.content:
KHMH denies admitting negligence in newborn’s death, acknowledges delay in responding to mother’s complaints

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital Authority (KHMHA) has denied admitting negligence or wrongdoing in connection with the death of a newborn, following allegations raised during a recent social media live broadcast.

In a statement issued Tuesday, November 10, the hospital confirmed that its representatives had previously met with the woman involved to hear her concerns and discuss the possibility of a resolution. The woman subsequently submitted written correspondence outlining her complaints and requests.

However, KHMHA emphasized that no admission of negligence, wrongdoing, or liability was made during those discussions, stressing that efforts to address complaints should not be interpreted as an acknowledgment of fault.

The hospital also acknowledged that it failed to provide a timely formal response to the woman’s correspondence and expressed regret over the communication delay.

KHMHA confirmed that the matter has since been referred to its legal counsel for review and guidance.

While extending condolences to the grieving family, the Authority said it would not publicly discuss individual medical circumstances because of patient confidentiality.

The hospital urged the public to refrain from drawing conclusions before the facts have been properly reviewed, reaffirming its commitment to accountability, due process and quality patient care.

The specific circumstances surrounding the newborn’s death and the allegations made during the live broadcast were not detailed in the hospital’s statement.

World.title: Belize participates in Commonwealth Women’s Forum in Antigua and Barbuda
World.content:
Belize participates in Commonwealth Women’s Forum in Antigua and Barbuda

By Zoila Palma: Belize participated in the Commonwealth Women’s Forum held in Antigua and Barbuda from November 2 to 4, 2026, alongside the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM).

The delegation included Special Envoy Rossana Briceño, Chief Executive Officer Adele Catzim-Sanchez, and Starla Bradley of the Ministry of Human Development, Family Support and Gender Affairs.

The forum brought together representatives to discuss key issues affecting women across the Commonwealth, including women in leadership, economic empowerment, gender and climate change, ending gender-based violence, and strengthening accountability for gender equality commitments.

The Special Envoy delivered a high-level reflection during a session titled “The Health Sector Response to Gender-Based Violence in the Commonwealth,” highlighting the important role healthcare systems play in identifying and supporting survivors.

During her remarks, Briceño stressed that gender-based violence is not simply a private matter but a violation of women’s rights, a public health concern, and an obstacle to equality and development.

She highlighted Belize’s newly enacted Domestic and Intimate Partner Violence Act and called for survivor-centred healthcare, improved mental health and psychosocial support, greater investment in trained healthcare professionals, and stronger coordination among health, social and justice services.

The Special Envoy also highlighted the need to move beyond condemning violence and establish systems that protect women, support survivors and hold perpetrators accountable.

The forum was funded by the Caribbean Development Fund, which will invest in establishing Belize’s first One-Stop Resource Centre for victims of gender-based violence, alongside intervention programmes for batterers.

World.title: Belize Department of Civil Aviation launches study to expand Air Traffic Capacity and improve Route Efficiency
World.content:
Belize Department of Civil Aviation launches study to expand Air Traffic Capacity and improve Route Efficiency

Six-month project with Tetra Tech and The Aviation Group will produce a roadmap for safe, sustainable aviation growth across Belize’s airports and airspace

The Belize Department of Civil Aviation (BDCA) today announces the kick-off of a technical assistance project to develop a Concept of Operations (CONOPS) for the country’s inter-airport system capacity and route efficiency. The work is being carried out by Tetra Tech, an international aviation and engineering consulting firm,

and is expected to take approximately six months.

The study will examine how aircraft move through Belize’s airports and airspace today. It will then recommend practical ways to handle more flights safely and with fewer delays. The goal is to get the most out of existing runways, routes and air traffic systems before the country commits to major new infrastructure spending.

The project covers the Philip S. W. Goldson International Airport and domestic airports with scheduled service, including San Pedro, Caye Caulker, Placencia, Dangriga, Corozal and the Belize City Sir Barry Bowen Municipal Airstrip. Particular attention will go to the busy PGIA–San Pedro corridor. International links to the United States, Canada, Mexico and Central America are also in scope.

“This CONOPS is a first of its kind for Belize. It is intended not just to bring order to airspace management for a thriving aviation sector, but also to prepare us for a possible doubling of air traffic by 2045 as projected by the International Air Transport Association (IATA),” said Nigel Carter, Director of Civil Aviation.

The work will proceed in four phases:

Kick-off and data gathering (Month 1). A three-day on-site visit to Belize, including a kick-off meeting at BDCA offices in Ladyville, interviews with stakeholders, and visits to air traffic control facilities and selected airports. Capacity assessment (Months 2–3). Analysis of current and future traffic demand, delays, peak-hour operations, air navigation technology and procedures, compared against International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) standards. Tetra Tech will use 3D visualization tools to map air traffic movements. Draft Concept of Operations (Months 4–5). A plan focused on efficient route use, demand management, coordination among stakeholders and safety, prioritizing improvements that need little capital investment. Final report (Month 6). A final CONOPS with recommendations, alternatives and a prioritized implementation roadmap, presented in person to the BDCA and stakeholders.

The BDCA will work closely with the Central American Corporation for Air Navigation Services (COCESNA), airlines, airport operators and other stakeholders throughout the project.

The study will not affect flight schedules or airport operations. Travelers and the public should notice no disruption while the work is under way.

About the Belize Department of Civil Aviation

The Belize Department of Civil Aviation regulates and oversees civil aviation in Belize, working to keep the national airspace system safe and efficient.

World.title: Belize Coast Guard officers return with international academic achievements
World.content:
Belize Coast Guard officers return with international academic achievements

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Coast Guard is recognizing two of its officers, Lieutenant Melissa Jones and Lieutenant Junior Grade Rasheed Broaster, for successfully completing their academic studies abroad. Their achievements mark important milestones in their professional development and reflect the institution’s continued efforts to build a highly educated and professional officer corps.

Lieutenant Jones earned a Master’s Degree in Maritime Affairs from the World Maritime University. The advanced qualification is expected to strengthen her maritime knowledge and expertise, contributing to the continued development and operational capabilities of the Belize Coast Guard.

Meanwhile, Lieutenant Junior Grade Broaster completed four years of academic and military education at the Taiwan Naval Academy, earning a Bachelor’s Degree in Foreign Language. His accomplishment reflects the discipline and commitment required to complete a demanding programme at an international naval institution.

The Belize Coast Guard commended both officers for their dedication, academic excellence and for representing Belize abroad.

World.title: International News: CARICOM Sec-Gen participates in high-level climate finance discussions at COP31
World.content:
International News: CARICOM Sec-Gen participates in high-level climate finance discussions at COP31

By Zoila Palma: CARICOM Secretary-General Dr. Carla Barnett is participating in a series of high-level engagements at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), currently underway in Türkiye.

Held under the theme “Dialogue | Consensus | Action,” the conference brings together world leaders and climate stakeholders to discuss climate action, resilience and financing. Dr. Barnett has been taking part in forums focused on climate resilience, financing and regional cooperation.

Today, Dr. Barnett addressed a high-level ministerial dialogue hosted by the Caribbean Catastrophe Risk Insurance Facility (CCRIF) at the CARICOM Pavilion at the Antalya Expo Centre. The discussion focused on the topic, “The Resilience Financing Imperative: Who Pays When Climate Disasters Strike?” Following the engagement, CCRIF Chief Executive Officer Isaac Anthony presented Dr. Barnett with a copy of the organization’s Strategic Plan.

The CARICOM Secretary-General also delivered remarks at a side event hosted by the Caribbean Development Bank (CDB), focusing on “Financing Caribbean Climate, Energy and Transport Transformation: From Ambition to Implementation.” The event brought together regional development and climate finance leaders, including CDB President Daniel Best, Caribbean Centre for Renewable Energy and Energy Efficiency Executive Director Dr. Mohammad Nagdee, and CARICOM Development Fund Chief Executive Officer Rodinald Soomer.

Dr. Barnett’s participation highlights CARICOM’s continued engagement in international discussions on climate financing and the need for stronger regional cooperation to address climate challenges.

World.title: Stabbed, robbed student loses case against UWI
World.content:
The main entrance to The University of the West Indies, Mona campus. (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

A student who sued The University of the West Indies (The UWI) for negligence after being robbed and stabbed while studying on the Mona campus 11 years ago, lost his case after a Supreme Court judge found that he failed to provide sufficient evidence that the institution had breached its duty of care or been lax in its security obligations.

According to the evidence in the case, the student was studying at a gazebo between the Confucius Institute and the Carimac Annex Lab on June 29, 2015, when two men came up to him and stole his laptop. They stabbed him twice in his chest and once in his abdomen, about 100 metres from a manned security booth at the campus’s post office entrance which, the student said, was within his line of sight. He said that before he was cut, he was not aware that the attackers were armed.

According to the account of another student, who was a witness in the matter, the two men had first appeared on bikes and called out to them “asking for free Wi-Fi”. She said her colleague responded and the two men rode away but returned on foot some moments later and sat in front of them. She said one of the men then demanded the male student’s laptop. She said when he reached for the laptop to secure it, the man pulled a knife and cut him on his arm while the other man attacked her.

According to her, their attackers then ran. They gave chase. She said while running she saw a friend and “called out to him”. She said they both helped her injured colleague to a vehicle and took him to hospital.

According to the injured male student, he chased the men because the weapon fell and he thought he was out of danger. He further said he did not call out to the security guard stationed at the post office gate, so that individual was unaware of what had transpired.

In his suit, the male student sought to recover damages on the basis that the university did not provide adequate security for its students.

Supreme Court judge Justice Tara Carr, who heard the matter in open court on three dates between June and early November this year, said the issues for determination were whether the university owed a duty of care to the student, either by virtue of statute or at common law in negligence and, if so, whether it breached that duty resulting in injury, loss, or damage to him and whether he was entitled to damages.

The student, in his defence, also relied on a letter from the campus registrar which stated, “As a result of this incident we have revisited and changed the protocols surrounding visitors to the campus who travel on motor bikes. We believe that this will go a far way in preventing incidents of this nature in the future.”

According to Justice Carr, this “tacit admission” was the lynchpin of the case for the student whose attorney argued that “this is sufficient for the court to find that the university did not do all that it could have to prevent the unfortunate incident which occurred”.

However, the university, in its defence, stated that it took reasonable care to ensure the safety of the student by implementing adequate and appropriate security measures.

An expert report and answers to questions posed from criminologist Dr Jason McKay formed a part of the evidence on behalf of the university. In his expert report, McKay stated that the university’s property is approximately 650 acres, with 67 security guards deployed at night on the campus which, he said, was, by any standard, a generous allocation of security personnel. McKay said he found that the property was secure and had security personnel posted at the entrances while noting that a property of this nature and size cannot facilitate a close protection security detail. He opined that the security arrangements at the university on the date of the incident were adequate and could be functional if all persons adhered to the directives as stated in the handbook.

Meanwhile, retired Assistant Commissioner of Police (ACP) Marlon Nesbeth, who is campus security manager, in his evidence, outlined that the university maintains a structured security system tailored to ensure the safety of all staff, students, and visitors to the campus. He said at the time of the incident the security team was comprised of 20 cops at the Mona Police Post and 200 security guards strategically stationed around the campus.

Furthermore, he said the university has designated areas for students outside of the operational hours of the campus, which are equipped with surveillance cameras and are well-lit. He also noted that the faculties have a security presence until 10:00 pm and the main library has 24-hour security.

Said Justice Carr: “There is no allegation that the physical conditions of the university caused the incident; neither can it be said that the university failed in its duty, whether by things done or undone, to provide a safe environment for all students to include [the student who was robbed and stabbed].”

“It is fair to say, based on the evidence, that the university provided spaces that were secure and safe for students to study throughout the day and night. The deployment of security guards and the erection of security posts over a 24-hour period is also accepted. The evidence [of the student] confirmed that there was a patrol that passed shortly before the incident. There is no evidence that contradicts these factual findings. Nor is there any evidence to suggest that the arrangements made by the university are insufficient or inadequate,” she noted further.

In disposing of the matter, Justice Carr said: “There is evidence to suggest… that the university employed several strategies to combat the rising level of crime on the Mona campus.”

Pointing out that it was the duty of the student’s attorneys to “put forward evidence to contradict this, or at the very least, to suggest that there were alternative options or arrangements that would have increased the security measures on the campus”, she said the claimant “did not provide the court with any evidence to support his case that the university did not do all that was reasonable in the circumstances to secure the campus and to provide a safe environment for all students”.

Said Justice Carr, in ruling in favour of the university, “The combination of the security measures outlined by Mr Nesbeth, the student handbook, and the warnings given are reasonable methods to prevent criminal activity at the university. [This student’s] injuries are a direct result of criminal conduct which, in our society, unfortunately is far too commonplace. I cannot say, however, that, based on the evidence as presented, the university was negligent or that they breached their statutory duty under the Act. In the round, therefore, I find that the claim has not been proved to the requisite standard and judgment is entered for the defendant.”

World.title: Swaby hits back
World.content:
SWABY... I have observed that Minister of Works Robert Nesta Morgan has developed what appears to be a rather special interest in the affairs of the KSAMC, and in me personally.

KINGSTON Mayor Andrew Swaby has challenged Works Minister Robert Morgan to acknowledge the funding challenges facing municipal corporations across Jamaica, arguing that the deteriorating state of the country’s roads cannot be blamed on local authorities without recognising the inadequate resources available to them.

Swaby, speaking at Tuesday’s sitting of the Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation monthly meeting, continued his public joust with Morgan, accusing him of singling out the Opposition-led corporation for criticism while appearing to overlook similar difficulties facing municipalities controlled by the governing Jamaica Labour Party (JLP).

“I have observed that Minister of Works Robert Nesta Morgan has developed what appears to be a rather special interest in the affairs of the KSAMC, and in me personally. Judging from how frequently he speaks about the KSAMC, one would assume that he was given the responsibility for local government. I trust that Minister [of Local Government Desmond] McKenzie has been advised of this apparent expansion of his colleague’s responsibility,” Swaby commented, drawing murmurs of agreement and chuckles from councillors within the chamber.

“What I find particularly interesting, however, is that I have heard little from Minister Morgan about the challenges facing municipal corporations led by his own party,” he continued.

Swaby’s scrutiny comes as a direct response to Morgan’s September media comments, in which the works minister claimed the KSAMC was not doing enough to effect change on municipal roads.

At the time, Morgan admitted that several major thoroughfares in the Corporate Area were in need of repair but argued that many, including South Avenue, Lindsay Crescent and Beechwood Avenue, are municipal corporation roads and are to be fixed by the KSAMC.

“For example, most of the roads that the Government has fixed in Kingston and St Andrew are not NWA (National Works Agency) roads, they are KSAMC (Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation) roads, and before this new mayor [Andrew Swaby] came in, the Parochial Revenue Fund was about $700 million a year; it is now over $1 billion, and we have not seen a commensurate increase in the allocation for repairing roads,” Morgan told the Jamaica Observer.

But on Tuesday, Swaby argued that the challenges facing the KSAMC were not unique, pointing out that discussions with JLP mayors and councillors had revealed widespread concerns about insufficient funding for road maintenance and other necessary services.

“They too are struggling with inadequate resources to maintain roads and provide essential services to their municipalities. Some may not enjoy the same freedom to speak publicly about these difficulties, but their silence should not be mistaken for the absence of concern. So I would encourage Minister Morgan to turn some of his attention to those municipalities. He may discover that the concerns I have raised are shared by many of my colleagues on his side,” urged Swaby.

The mayor further questioned how Morgan could expect the KSAMC to adequately address its decrepit road network when the Government’s $40-billion Shared Prosperity through Accelerated Improvement to our Road Network (SPARK) programme was insufficient to rehabilitate all roads requiring attention nationally.

“Nobody expects the SPARK programme to fix every road in Jamaica. So if $40 billion cannot address all our road rehabilitation needs, how does Minister Morgan expect the KSAMC to do so with the meagre resources at his disposal?” he asked.

The mayor explained that during the 2025-2026 financial year, the corporation received an average $85 million monthly from the parochial revenue fund (PRF) which must finance not only road maintenance but also drain cleaning, and de-bushing across its 40 divisions.

According to Swaby, rehabilitating a single kilometre of parochial road, approximately 6.5 metres wide, costs about $40 million.

With more than 100 kilometres of roads requiring attention across Kingston and St Andrew, Swaby said a project of that magnitude would require at the very least a supportive budget of $4 billion.

“If that programme were to be undertaken in over 12 months, it would require an expenditure of an average of $333 million every month. Compare that with $85 million we received monthly from the Parochial Revenue Fund in the last financial year, which must also cover drain cleaning, de-bushing and other things. The difference is substantial. It illustrates the inadequacy of the present financial arena,” remarked Swaby.

He maintained that no amount of administrative efficiency could overcome the existing funding shortfall, stressing that the core issue remains an inadequate budget.

“We can establish a new authority, reorganise existing agencies, and change administrative arrangements under which roads are managed. But unless we confront the underlying financial problem, we risk transferring responsibility for deteriorating roads from one institution to another without providing the resources necessary to improve them. That would hardly constitute meaningful reform,” charged Swaby.

The inaugural staging of the Jamaican Rising Day Parade in New York was a resounding success, attracting an estimated 70,000 people last August.

Buoyed by the positive response, organisers have their sights set on an even bigger and better celebration for Jamaica’s 65th independence anniversary in 2027.
