World.title: Trough to bring showers, thunderstorms across Jamaica
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — Showers and thunderstorms are expected across sections of Jamaica over the next few days as a trough continues to influence weather conditions across the island, the Meteorological Service of Jamaica says.

The Met Service said windy conditions are also expected, mainly across southern parishes, from Wednesday through Thursday morning as a low-level jet moves closer to the island.

The forecast for Wednesday is isolated morning showers across eastern parishes, with partly cloudy conditions elsewhere. In the afternoon, mostly cloudy conditions with showers and thunderstorms are expected across western parishes, while windy conditions are forecast for southern parishes and hilly areas elsewhere.

On Thursday, isolated morning showers are expected across sections of eastern parishes, with afternoon showers and thunderstorms across central and western parishes.

Friday is expected to bring cloudy conditions with showers across most western, south-central and eastern parishes in the morning, followed by scattered afternoon showers and thunderstorms across most parishes.

Meanwhile, the trough is expected to persist into the weekend, with a cold front projected to move into the western Caribbean by Saturday.

World.title: Privy Council overturns anti-gay laws in Trinidad
World.content:
Jason Jones (Photo via IG)

LONDON, United Kingdom (CMC) — The London-based Privy Council Tuesday ruled “unanimously” in favour of Jason Jones, who had challenged the laws criminalising consensual same-sex relations between adults in Trinidad and Tobago.

In a statement issued before the Privy Council hearing, Jones had said he was confident the country’s highest appellate court would uphold his claim, saying, “The Privy Council will never uphold a 500-year-old homophobic piece of British law that goes against the rights of the individual! Not in 2026! I’m going to win.”

Jones, 62, who was born in Trinidad and Tobago and now lives in Britain, welcomed the ruling but noted that it did not address wider issues of “human rights and equality for LGBTQ+ people which have been denied using British colonial era laws across the Commonwealth and beyond”.

Former Trinidad and Tobago attorney general, Anand Ramlogan SC, who represented Jones, said the judgement was a “landmark victory for gay rights, equal dignity and respect for private and family life in Trinidad and Tobago”.

Jones, a gay man, had sought a declaration that sections 13 and 16 of the Sexual Offences Act 1986 Act infringe his fundamental rights under the Trinidad and Tobago Constitution.

Section 13 of the Act prohibits “buggery” while Section 16 prohibits “sex acts” other than sexual intercourse. Section 16 also makes an exception to this prohibition for sex acts carried out in private between a male and a female who are both over the age of 16 and consent to the act.

Jones sought a declaration that sections 13 and 16 of the Act are unconstitutional, arguing that these sections infringe a number of his fundamental rights and freedoms, especially his right to respect for his private and family life.

The High Court held that sections 13 and 16 of the Act were unconstitutional, finding that Jones’s fundamental rights under section 4(c) of the Constitution were violated by sections 13 and 16 of the 1986 Act; those provisions were not immunised by section 6 of the Constitution from a challenge based on those rights; and nor were those provisions immunised from such a challenge by section 13 of the Constitution, because Jones had shown that they were not reasonably justifiable.

But by a majority, the Court of Appeal allowed the Attorney General’s appeal to a material degree in relation to his argument based on section 6(2) of the Constitution, to the extent that sections 13 and 16 of the 1986 Act reflected the law in existence when the Constitution came into force.

However, the Court of Appeal unanimously held that, in so far as those provisions went beyond existing law when the Constitution came into force, they were not reasonably justifiable within the meaning of the proviso and were to that extent incompatible with Jones’s fundamental rights and therefore, to that extent, had to be disapplied.

Jones appealed to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in relation to the Court of Appeal’s ruling based on section 6 of the Constitution.

The Attorney General does not appeal against the disapplication of sections 13 and 16 of the 1986 Act as ordered by the Court of Appeal but cross-appeals to contend that the Court of Appeal’s order to confirm the validity of those provisions to a material degree should also be upheld by reference to section 13 of the Constitution, maintaining that Jones has failed to show that the provisions are, to that extent, not reasonably justifiable, according to the test in the proviso.

But the Privy Council unanimously allowed Jones’s appeal and dismissed the Attorney General’s cross-appeal. It holds that sections 13 and 16 of the 1986 Act are not protected as existing law by section 6 of the Constitution, nor are they protected to any extent by virtue of section 13 of the Constitution, because Jones has shown that they are not reasonably justifiable. according to the test in the proviso.

Lord Sales and Lord Burrows gave the judgment, with which the other members of the Judicial Committee agreed.

In outlining the reasons for its ruling, the Privy Council said that under section 6(1) of the Constitution, laws which existed immediately before the Constitution came into force in 1976 are protected from a fundamental rights challenge.

The same protection from a challenge based on fundamental constitutional rights applies to subsequent legislation which repeals and re-enacts existing law with modifications: section 6(2) of the Constitution, the Law Lords said.

They said it is common ground that sections 13 and 16 of the 1986 Act do not fall within the meaning of existing law in section 6(1) of the Constitution and with respect to section 6(2), the Court of Appeal erred in their finding that sections 13 and 16 of the 1986 Act were protected as laws which merely repealed and re-enacted existing law with modifications.

The Privy Council said rather, those provisions constituted new law and were therefore not immunised from a challenge based on the fundamental rights in section 4 of the Constitution.

“The Judicial Committee holds that constitutional provisions which immunise old laws from challenges based on fundamental constitutional rights should be interpreted narrowly so as not to protect large areas of old law from constitutional scrutiny even after Parliament has comprehensively reviewed and sought to modernise them.”

The Privy Council said that the 1986 Act as a whole reflected Parliament’s assessment in 1986 of the whole of the law of sexual offences in light of the circumstances at that time and was a new and comprehensive regime for Trinidad and Tobago.

The Law Lords said the correct categorisation of the 1986 Act is that it is new law enacted after the Constitution came into force and so is not made exempt by section 6(2) of the Constitution from a challenge based on the fundamental constitutional rights in section 4 of the Constitution.

Section 13 of the Constitution permits Parliament to pass legislation which is inconsistent with fundamental rights if certain legislative conditions are met. The 1986 Act was passed into law using the correct procedural conditions as specified in section 13. However, by virtue of the proviso, such legislation will not be protected from a challenge based on the fundamental constitutional rights in section 4 where it is shown not to be reasonably justifiable in a society that has a proper respect for the rights and freedoms of the individual.

The Privy Council said that the Attorney General’s contention, that the question whether sections 13 and 16 of the 1986 Act were not reasonably justifiable, according to the test in the proviso, should be assessed according to the circumstances which existed when the legislation was enacted in 1986, could not be accepted.

“The relevant time for that assessment is when the rights of the individual bringing the challenge are in issue and the question of justifiability is before the court. In the assessment whether sections 13 and 16 of the 1986 Act meet the reasonably justifiable standard in the proviso, the rights and interests of Mr Jones which are at stake involve a particularly important facet of his existence and identity since the ability to form an intimate and loving relationship with another person lies at the core of the right to private and family life.”

The Law Lords said that the Constitution affirms the dignity of the human person and the importance of respect for family life.

“The criminalisation of private, consensual same-sex relations interferes with a fundamental aspect of Mr Jones’s life and identity.”

They said that for sections 13 and 16 of the 1986 to be immunised by section 13 of the Constitution from a challenge based on the fundamental constitutional rights in section 4, in light of the test in the proviso, the Attorney General would need to demonstrate that the interference with Jones’s rights was in furtherance of a legitimate aim.

“To that end, the Attorney General argued that sections 13 and 16 of the 1986 Act reflected earlier laws which were traditional and of long standing. However, in order to justify a law on that basis, evidence would be required to explain the strength of the tradition and its consistency with prevailing societal values.

“No such evidence was put forward by the Attorney General. In any event, the interference with the most intimate aspects of Mr Jones’s private life is too severe for the relevant provisions to be considered as striking a fair balance and to be reasonably justifiable according to the test in the proviso,” the Law Lords noted.

The Privy Council therefore agreed with the High Court and the Court of Appeal that sections 13 and 16 of the 1986 Act are not reasonably justifiable in a society which has a proper respect for the rights and freedoms of the individual.

“The Judicial Committee will receive further written submissions from the parties before making its final order as to any modifications to sections 13 and 16 of the 1986 Act to ensure their compatibility with Mr Jones’s fundamental constitutional rights in section 4 of the Constitution.”

World.title: Guilty after jury fury
World.content:
A photo of Andre Ruddock captured while he lay on the ground at Pathways International Kingdom Restoration Ministries in St James on the night of October 17, 2021, after he cut the throat of fellow church member Taneka Gardner.

POLICE personnel were forced to rush in and restore order in the jury room at the Supreme Court on Monday after tensions boiled over following a split in their verdict during deliberations in the Andre Ruddock murder trial.

Eventually, after two hours of deliberations, the jury ultimately found Ruddock guilty of murder in the gruesome killing of 39-year-old Taneka Gardner, whose throat was cut at Pathways International Kingdom Restoration Ministries in St James on October 17, 2021, in what was said to be a human sacrifice ritual.

Earlier, after trial judge Justice Leighton Pusey completed his summation, the jurors were sent off to deliberate at 12:46 pm.

At 1:25 pm police who were guarding the jury room indicated to the court registrar that the panel was ready to deliver the verdict. They were readmitted into the courtroom at 1:37 pm

— 51 minutes after retiring

— at which time the registrar asked the lead juror if they had arrived at a unanimous verdict. The lead juror indicated that they had not, pointing out that five among them believed Ruddock was guilty while two jurors weren’t satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that he had killed Gardner.

Justice Pusey informed the jurors that they would have to spend at least two hours in deliberations before they could return to the courtroom and deliver the verdict. They were subsequently sent back to the jury room by the judge.

At 1:49 pm the registrar again indicated that the jurors were ready to deliver their verdict, leaving everyone inside the courtroom to believe that they had arrived at a unanimous verdict. However, when they entered the jury box and the lead juror was asked if a unanimous verdict had been reached, she again said ‘No’, prompting the judge to explain to them that if the verdict was not unanimous, they would have to spend two hours or more deliberating. Pusey again sent them back to the jury room.

At approximately 2:09 pm, about five members of the Jamaica Constabulary Force were spotted rushing into the jury room where a heated argument was unfolding.

One juror was heard blurting out: “You want to be the boss of everything!” The police managed to cool the tension, then exited to give the jurors space to arrive at a final decision.

However, additional police personnel were called in to join the two who were already standing guard outside the door of the jury room.

At 2:52 pm, the jurors returned to the jury box where the lead juror indicated that there was a slight change in the decision, pointing out that six among them were convinced that Ruddock was guilty of killing Gardner and only one was not so convinced.

Judge Pusey then thanked the jurors for their service before dismissing them. The judge ordered that a social enquiry be done on Ruddock, with a report to be produced in the next six weeks.

Ruddock is to return for sentencing on January 22, 2027.

Lead prosecutor Latoya Bernard told the media that she would not be making any extensive comments on the matter following the verdict. All she offered was that, “The jury has spoken.”

Bernard was supported by prosecutor Carolyn Wright, while Venice Brown supported lead defence attorney Anthony Williams.

After the verdict, Williams breathed a sigh of relief saying, “Boy, the case is finally over.”

“The prosecution’s case essentially is that Mr Ruddock was the one who slashed the throat of Miss Taneka Gardner with a knife on instructions of Mr Kevin Smith. They also alleged that Mr Ruddock gave a caution statement as well as a question and answer document. We contend that, in the first place, it was Mr Kevin Smith who was the person who actually slit or cut Taneka Gardener’s throat.

“We denied it vehemently and that was the defence. We also say that the alleged caution statement and question and answer were, in fact, done under duress. He was forced and intimidated by a policeman in question who held him on the compound of the church. We made very, very heavy waters in this case. It was a very tough case. The jury retired once, it was a 5-2 verdict. They retired twice and in the end they came back with a 6-1 verdict of guilty,” the attorney pointed out.

Williams said the defence was proud of its performance and had given Ruddock the best possible representation in a very challenging case.

“We felt very optimistic of a not guilty verdict, and I say that because of the intensive cross-examination we did of the main witness in particular, as well as the other prosecution witnesses. They were discredited, undermined, and we think we made very good progress. At the end of the day, the jurors are the judges of the fact, and they have concluded that our expectation was not theirs,” Williams said.

Ruddock cut Gardner’s throat on the compound of Pathways International Kingdom Restoration Ministries allegedly on instructions from his now deceased pastor, Kevin Smith. It was disclosed during the trial, through a witness, that Gardner’s name appeared on a piece of paper alongside other names. The witness said that Gardner was called onto the compound of the church and instructed by the pastor to write 999 beside her name.

The pastor then told her that she would have to die because her blood was unclean. He then proceeded to ask her if she believed that he could bring her back to life if her throat was to be cut. Gardner reportedly told the pastor “Yes” in response to his question. Smith then instructed a male member of the church to cut her throat. When that member hesitated, Ruddock took a knife from him and carried out the pastor’s order.

Pastor Smith died on October 25, 2021 in a motor vehicle crash on the Linstead bypass in St Catherine while being transported to Kingston by police to face charges.

Authorities reported that he died along with Constable Orlando Irons, who was among the lawmen transporting the cult pastor.

In May 2024 a coroner’s inquest found that the crash did not occur because of excess speed and as such the policemen, who were placed before the inquest, were credible witnesses.

The inquest found that Smith assaulted the cops who were transporting him, and the judge ruled that his actions were unlawful, dangerous, and caused the death of Constable Irons.

World.title: Merl Grove dispute boils over
World.content:
Merl Grove High teachers with placards on Constant Spring Road on Monday morning. (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

THE smouldering dispute at the all-girls Merl Grove High School in St Andrew boiled over into the public space on Monday, with scores of teachers taking to the streets to stage a silent protest.

Teachers at the school, who refused to speak to the media during their protest, left little doubt that they were opposed to the actions of Principal Dr Marjorie Fullerton who returned to the post in March following a Supreme Court ruling.

Fullerton was first appointed to the post in 2016 but was ousted by the school’s board — based on a recommendation of its Personnel Committee — in 2022 after she was suspended in September 2021.

The veteran educator took her dismissal to the courts which ordered her reinstatement on the basis that the board did not follow procedures of the Education Regulations.

The ruling marked a setback for the school board, the Ministry of Education and the Associated Gospel Assemblies Church, which owns the institution. All had upheld her dismissal following a dispute with staff over her leadership style.

Three months after returning as principal, Fullerton told the Jamaica Observer that the job remains challenging, given that she is still working with the same board that recommended her dismissal four years ago.

“It is not easy at all, because I thought that coming back after six years — and six successful years, and I’m saying successful because the school has moved in terms of ranking and academic performance. And coming back, I thought I was going to see a new board, but I’m facing the same school board, and there were teachers here before who are still here,” said Fullerton.

“It is very difficult if I’m not getting the support that I need. It’s not easy, but I have been through many fights, because I’m a breast cancer survivor, and during the time I was fighting for my job I was also fighting for my life. I believe that, even though it’s not the same thing, it’s still a fight,” she said then.

With the dispute simmering a meeting was organised last month with administrators at the institution and the education ministry’s Regional Educational Services, which mobilised an estimated 100 Merl Grove stakeholders and interested parties to the dispute.

According to Observer sources, the meeting was being spearheaded by the ministry not as a formal hearing, but to allow internal stakeholders to express their concerns and work towards achieving a more harmonious and conducive environment.

The ministry later indicated that it would be reviewing the outcome of the discussions for a follow-up meeting to be decided.

Some stakeholders said they were hopeful that the meeting would achieve a resolution but suggested that some of the issues were controversial and would require patience and a willingness to end the dispute.

When the Observer visited the institution on Monday, teachers were observed bearing placards calling for the resignation of Fullerton, but remained tight-lipped about what prompted the morning’s protest.

Efforts to speak with Fullerton were unsuccessful.

World.title: Resilience takes centre stage
World.content:
Protoje delivers a masterful set at the Treasure Beach Food, Rum and Reggae Festival at Breds Sports Park last weekend. (Photo: Brian Pitter)

If Friday night’s Dubwise session at Jack Sprat was the spark that ignited the 2026 Treasure Beach Food, Rum & Reggae Festival, then Saturday’s main stage concert at Breds Sports Park was a full-on fire.

Riding high on a wave of resilience, the Treasure Beach community pulled off a seamless post-Hurricane Melissa event, proving that a parish twice ravaged by back-to-back natural disasters simply refuses to lose its spark.

Through powerhouse performances from Lila Iké and Protoje the event transcended expectations. Song after song the concert became more than just another item on the annual entertainment calendar; it was a profound celebration of resilience, musical lineage, and cultural preservation.

Sporting her signature Afro, Lila Iké stepped into the spotlight, and the atmosphere inside the venue shifted instantly. Known for her remarkable ability to cater to a diverse cross section of fans, Lila Iké delivered a beautifully balanced set list that bridged the gap between sweet, vulnerable love songs and hard-hitting social commentary.

Opening her set with a soulful rendition of her powerful hit single Scatter, the artiste immediately captivated the crowd and established the tone for the rest of her performance. Building on that momentum with each successive track, the reggae songstress stamped her class on the evening. Songs such as Thy Will Be Done, Forget Me, Solitude, and Second Chance were well received by patrons, but it was her spirited performance of Where I’m Coming From that proved the highlight of her set.

As she introduced the track, she was met with screams of approval from the crowd. The single took on an added layer of purpose, resonating deeply with the St Elizabeth audience.

“Weh di people dem deh weh glad weh dem a come from dung a St Bess tonight? No disaster cyaan mash dis dung,” she said, sending the crowd into a frenzy.

“Yeah, St Bess, a we say resilience,” she continued before launching into the track.

Its lyrics, which speak to struggle, identity, resilience, and divine timing, struck a chord with the audience. The response was unmistakable, as Lila Iké’s set was punctuated by massive forwards and gun-fingers in the air from patrons who had connected deeply with her message.

By the time she brought her performance to a close the singer had further cemented her place among the leading voices of the modern reggae movement.

But the night’s musical treats didn’t end there. St Elizabeth was in for more, this time from one of its own, as Protoje took to the stage. As the headlining general of the In.Digg.Nation Collective, Protoje’s arrival was greeted by a thunderous roar that echoed across the sports park. With his signature effortless command, he delivered a structurally brilliant set, drawing heavily from his catalogue of “message music” and urgent social commentary, while seamlessly weaving in the relaxed, party-centric sounds that keep a festival crowd moving.

Protoje commanded the stage with precision, launching into conscious anthems such as Blood Money and Kingston Be Wise. The tracks, which highlight the socio-political issues affecting Jamaica, made quite an impact on the crowd. Chanting lyrics of resistance word for word, patrons transformed Breds Sports Park into a unified space of collective consciousness.

Recognising the assignment of a weekend festival fuelled by premium Jamaican rum, Protoje masterfully shifted gears into his lighter, feel-good catalogue. The weight of the socio-political commentary gave way to pure relaxation when the band struck up the infectious party anthem Big 45. The smooth, celebratory rhythms of Switch It Up and Who Knows continued to transform the atmosphere into one massive skanking party, allowing patrons to lose themselves in the sweet sounds of reggae.

But the true climax of Saturday night came when the catalogues of both main acts collided. The synergy between Protoje and Lila Iké was undeniable as the pair shared the stage. Bringing an entirely different level of artistic chemistry, the duo performed their collaboration All Over The World. Energy levels peaked as the two artistes traded verses with a seamless, almost familial rapport that spoke to their mutual artistic respect and the strength of their musical connection.

What’s more, patrons were treated to a little ‘brawta’ when Jesse Royal made a surprise appearance. The Small Axe artiste delivered a short but spicy set, joining Protoje for a performance of Sudden Flight, a collaboration the two entertainers recorded alongside Sevana more than a decade ago.

As the curtains closed on a successful staging of the St Elizabeth music festival, it became clear that the event was never just about entertainment. It was a declaration that the culture of the south coast cannot be washed away.

According to Gregory Wright, festival director, through the power of reggae’s finest contemporary voices, Treasure Beach didn’t just celebrate its recovery; it danced its way into a new chapter.

“Returning the festival to its home in St Elizabeth this year was especially meaningful for us, particularly after the parish was impacted by Hurricane Melissa last year. We are incredibly grateful for the opportunity to return and for the tremendous support and turnout we received, which exceeded our expectations,” he said. “The atmosphere throughout the festival was truly special, with the DJs delivering strong sets and the artistes putting on great performances, engaging with the audience and creating an experience that felt both celebratory and meaningful.

“We were also grateful for the artistes’ support beyond the stage, including our headliners, Lila Iké and Protoje, who took the time to interact with patrons and experience different aspects of the festival weekend,” he continued. “We are excited about what this means for the parish and look forward to building on this momentum in the years ahead.”

World.title: US to seek Putin’s ‘blessing’ for Europe to join Ukraine talks
World.content:
After two days of talks in Abu Dhabi, Russia and Ukraine have agreed a major prisoner swap, with final numbers to be confirmed, U.S. officials say.

ABU DHABI — U.S. officials will head to Moscow in person on Thursday to ask Russia’s Vladimir Putin to give his “blessing” to allowing European representatives to join future peace talks for Ukraine.

Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law who has been mediating talks in Abu Dhabi, told reporters he and White House envoy Steve Witkoff will head to Moscow to meet the Russian leader. They aim to agree a date for the next round of negotiations and to secure Putin’s approval for Europe to get a seat at the table.

“We need to have the Europeans at the table,” Kushner said, answering a question from POLITICO. “We have relayed to President Putin directly several times and to his team that the only way to get this done is to have them by our side and I think they are receptive to it.

World.title: Burnham: Good COP or bad COP?
World.content:
As the prime minister heads to COP, the UN’s annual climate change conference, does the government have a coherent message?

With the cost of the green transition starting to bite, the government faces tough questions on its policy decisions and delays around oil, gas, and electric cars. Are Labour’s climate ambitions slipping because of hard economic choices?

Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy examine the political divisions and why COP could matter far more for Labour than it at first appears.

Elsewhere, Nigel Farage has reportedly appointed Amar Johal as Reform UK’s new policy chief – but was he already pulling the strings?

Plus cabinet secretary Antonia Romeo has described a brutal lesson in Whitehall hierarchy, following a run-in over chairs.

World.title: How to bypass unruly MEPs
World.content:
The European Parliament has figured out how to pass controversial legislation … just bypass the full vote of all 720 MEPs.

Today on the show, Zoya Sheftalovich and Ian Wishart discuss how cross-party leaders are worried that the plenary’s shifting alliances — particularly with the rise of the far right — could blow up legislation that expert lawmakers have already negotiated at the committee stage. The bypass method could come in handy for the EU’s next long-term budget.

Next, NATO allies are considering the biggest overhaul of their military planning in at least two decades — by prioritizing Russia and deprioritizing conflicts further away. We go inside the ongoing talks.

Finally, the EU today unveils its new Digital Fairness Act, which aims to help consumers online. But NGO Finance Watch says the proposal falls short when it comes to protecting people from fin-fluencers.

Have you ever fallen for an online get-rich-quick scheme? Let us know! Message us on WhatsApp here or at +32 491 05 06 29.

Articles mentioned in this episode:

World.title: How Health Systems Can Spot Risk Before a Crisis
World.content:
Cancer claims 10 million lives each year, the global shortage of health workers runs into the millions, and in some parts of the world, a single mosquito bite can be fatal.

These challenges may seem very different. Yet they share a common element in how many health systems operate: risk is often recognised only after it has become illness, outbreak or crisis. By then, a disease may have advanced, transmission of disease may be under way, or an already stretched workforce may be managing consequences that earlier action could have reduced.

The opportunity is to move that point of intervention earlier. This is what anticipatory health means in practice: using signals that already exist, at the bedside, in communities, and in routine health data, to help people and health systems act sooner. It is not prediction for its own sake. The value lies in connecting early and everyday signals to a timely, practical response.

World.title: Spanish election: How bad is the housing crisis?
World.content:
“We must look upwards at those in the penthouses and those who run vulture funds and put an end to their speculative practices and abuses,” he added, calling for voters to unite to protect “small property owners and tenants.”

It is no wonder Sánchez has attempted to seize on the topic of housing in a bid to be reelected. The high price of homes is at the forefront of voters’ minds: the most recent data shows house prices are double what they were at the same time in 2015; the average Spaniard doesn’t leave their parental home until after their 30th birthday; and in some historic centers tourist accommodation accounts for 45% of the rental market.

His big challenge, however, is that he could end up blamed for the problem exploding during his more than eight years in office. Between 2015 and 2025, average home prices in Spain rose by 80%, while salaries increased by only 30%. A pledge to use “all state resources” to provide 184,000 public and affordable rental homes has been difficult to realize.

And yet, on many metrics, Spain’s housing struggles are not even the worst in Europe. Rising rents and home prices across the bloc are fueling discontent and setting the stage for affordability to become a key issue in a string of elections set for the coming year.

Here’s everything you need to know:

Between 2015 and 2025, house prices in Spain rose 80%, according to Eurostat’s house price index. The first half of 2026 made this figure even starker: by the second quarter of this year, prices were around double what they were at the same time in 2015.

World.title: Turkey-Greece maritime spat threatens to intrude on EU summit
World.content:
“Greece has explicitly stated ... that in the event of any escalation, it will request sanctions and support from the European Union,” Greece’s Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis said last week in an interview with local TV.

Despite being NATO allies, Greece and Turkey have quarreled over maritime boundaries and overlapping claims to their continental shelves. Athens fears Ankara could invoke the Libya deal to challenge offshore exploration south of Crete and the EU-funded undersea electricity cable linking Greece and Cyprus, turning both projects into flashpoints.

Turkey signed the agreement in 2019 with Libya’s U.N.-backed government in Tripoli, and it was unanimously ratified by rival authorities in eastern Libya on Oct. 20.

The EU immediately responded.

"This agreement infringes upon the sovereign rights of third states, it does not comply with the Law of the Sea, and is null and void," said a joint statement on Oct. 20 from the heads of the European Commission and Council.

Egypt also rejected the border pact, as did Bahrain, Cyprus (which has its own separate disputes with Turkey over Ankara's occupation of the northern part of the island since the 1970s), Israel and the United Arab Emirates.

World.title: Farage cries foul after Reform slips to a tie with the Tories
World.content:
It’s a major test of Reform’s claim to be the best-placed right-wing vessel to stop another Labour victory.

So what’s Farage’s answer? He is increasingly trying to remind voters how the Conservatives operated in government — and claiming the polls themselves are bogus.

POLITICO spoke to half a dozen figures on Reform’s frontline to try and understand their gripes with the polling. All were granted anonymity, like others in this piece, because of the generally held convention in Westminster that parties don’t discuss polling.

Farage goes after the number-crunchers

“The jiggery-pokery that is going on with polling is utterly astonishing,” Farage told journalists after a speech last week. “What you’ve seen from the polling industry is nonsense, and I mean that.”

The Reform UK leader claimed that the “raw data” shows his party is really eight points clear of the Tories — and berated a “desperate push from the establishment” to get back to the “Tweedledum and Tweedledee” state of two-party politics.

Two senior Reform Party insiders challenged the methodology used by Britain’s pollsters. They argued that Reform’s polling is suppressed because of the way undecided voters are partially stacked with the party they voted for at the last election. Both insiders argued this would harm the party because it was a much more nascent outfit back in 2024.

World.title: Zelenskyy tells Europe to hurry up and pick a rep for peace talks with Russia
World.content:
With Europe set to take on a more important role in talks with Russia and the United States, Zelenskyy’s comments join a growing chorus of demands for the EU and others to unite behind one top negotiator or a small team at the highest level.

Speaking to reporters during his trip to Denmark on Tuesday, the Ukrainian leader said he wanted a “dialogue” with the EU and other European powers over who will represent them. He said it would be “better” this way, rather than just presenting their answer to Ukraine, which is “not good, really.”

“I hope that not later than the end of November — better in Germany on 19th [at a Coalition of the Willing meeting] — fix it. We will see.”

Europe has been struggling to work out a plan for how to engage in top-level dialogue with Moscow and Washington over ending the war in Ukraine. Despite providing most of the foreign financing for Ukraine’s war effort, EU countries have been split over who should represent them, or whether they should be talking to Russian leader Vladimir Putin at all.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni last week blasted the European Union’s engagement with the peace talks as “all over the place.”

Leaders are due to grapple with these questions at a summit in Dublin later this week.

As talks with Ukraine, Russia and the U.S. resumed in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, American officials made clear they wanted Europe fully at the table next time the negotiations take place. That is partly because the U.S. wants to bring a review of wider European security arrangements for Europe into the negotiations over peace in Ukraine — a longstanding Russian demand.

World.title: Abu Dhabi peace talks end with prisoner exchange agreement as US envoys prepare to meet Putin
World.content:
Ukraine and Russia have agreed in principle to a major prisoner exchange following two days of US-mediated peace talks in Abu Dhabi, although negotiations ended without a breakthrough on the central issues dividing the two sides, Euronews reports from the UAE.

 

US envoy Jared Kushner announced the agreement on Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, saying the final number of prisoners to be exchanged would be determined on Thursday.

"One of the positives is we agreed that we're going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which we're going to finalise the numbers tomorrow," Kushner said.

Ukraine's chief negotiator Rustem Umerov and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Medinsky also confirmed the planned exchange, although neither side provided further details on its timing or scale.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that negotiators had been discussing an exchange of 1,000 prisoners from each side, potentially rising to 1,500 each.

The agreement marks the most concrete — and so far the only — outcome of the first direct negotiations between Kyiv and Moscow in nine months, following an earlier round in Geneva in February this year that failed to produce a breakthrough.

During negotiations in Istanbul in May 2025, the two countries also agreed to exchange 1,000 prisoners each despite failing to reach a ceasefire agreement.

US envoys head to Moscow

Kushner said he and Steve Witkoff would travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin, before heading to Dublin for talks with Zelenskyy.

Russia continues to insist that Ukraine withdraw from territory in the eastern Donbas region still under Kyiv's control, while Zelenskyy has maintained that territorial decisions must be addressed at the leaders' level.

Moscow has also rejected calls for an immediate ceasefire, insisting on broader security arrangements before agreeing to halt hostilities.

European representatives were present in Abu Dhabi for separate consultations with Ukrainian and US officials but did not participate directly in the trilateral negotiations.

Russia's chief negotiator Vladimir Medinsky said his delegation had not held talks with European representatives and questioned their presence.

"No, we did not communicate with them. We don't really understand in what capacity they are here," Medinsky told reporters.

He also said Moscow received no concrete peace initiatives or proposals from European countries, questioning what there was to discuss with them.

"We don't really understand what there is to discuss with them," he told reporters.

Umerov said Kyiv's delegation would hold further discussions with European partners on Wednesday.

Washington indicated that European countries should eventually join the negotiations, particularly as discussions expand to the continent's future security arrangements.

World.title: Princess Diana’s iconic ‘Revenge Dress’ goes on display ahead of auction
World.content:
It's a little black dress that became one of the most talked-about outfits in royal history. Princess Diana’s iconic ‘Revenge Dress’ is on display at Sotheby’s in Geneva ahead of its first auction in nearly 30 years.

 

The black silk dress, designed by Christina Stambolian, was worn by Diana on 29 June 1994 – the same evening Prince Charles publicly admitted to being unfaithful during their marriage.

Diana later sold the dress at a charity auction in 1997, and it has remained in private hands ever since. Now, it is expected to fetch up to $300,000 (€270,000) when it goes under the hammer in New York on 9 December.

World.title: Santorini seeks year-round tourism by promoting gastronomy, wine and culture
World.content:
Santorini is considered the most popular Greek island worldwide. Its distinctive volcanic caldera, whitewashed houses and sunsets in Oia consistently place it among the top choices for international travellers. However, over the past two years local hoteliers have been complaining that their hotels are not filling up with tourists.

 

"After the Covid pandemic we had intense tourist activity on our island, but because of some unrelated events, one was the seismic activity on the neighbouring islands and later on the war in the Gulf, we experienced a drop in tourism," hotel owner Thomas Giannis tells Euronews. "For me personally it was around 30 to 40%."

The biggest decline was recorded in arrivals of tourists from the United States and, of course, from Israel. The former in particular, who tend to spend a lot of money in the destinations they visit and are therefore especially sought after by people working in tourism, book their holiday packages up until early spring, in other words during the periods that coincided with the seismic activity events of 2025 and the start of the war with Iran this year.

Greece may have been far from the centre of operations, but this is not immediately obvious to the average American planning a holiday.

Despite the downturn, the situation improved after the summer, according to Thira Mayor Nikos Zorzos. "Tourism in Santorini started this year with a sense of numbness, but the situation then stabilised. September and October are strong tourist months and attract visitors who have a special interest in the island," the mayor tells Euronews.

Gastronomy and culture

What do we mean by "special interests"? Thomas Giannis explains: "Santorini is not just a summer destination to watch a sunset. It is also a gastronomic and cultural destination. And it can now offer tourism all year round."

With this in mind, it was recently announced that a new digital campaign of 32 short videos will be launched, aiming to broaden the island’s international tourism image by showcasing experiences that are often overshadowed by its famous sunsets and luxury accommodation. These include its distinctive wine tradition, closely linked to the volcanic soil and climate of the island, its gastronomy, and visits of cultural and religious interest.

In fact, this is now what most visitors are looking for, both from the US and from the United Kingdom, Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Austria, the Netherlands, Poland, Belgium and Romania, the European countries from which most visitors come. They are joined by tourists from Australia and Asian countries such as China, South Korea and Japan, from which group trips are often organised.

In Santorini, July in particular had a strong Italian "flavour". Traffic to and from Italy reached 93,315 passengers, placing the country first among foreign markets. It was followed by the UK with 59,362 passengers and France with 35,158, while Germany recorded 17,746 passengers. Traffic with Spain was also significant at 14,443 passengers, followed by Austria with 11,211 and Romania with 10,594.

Furthermore, Thomas Giannis argues that Santorini is no longer the very expensive destination people imagine if they have never visited. "Santorini is for every budget. It can cater for everything. It has rooms from very cheap to extremely expensive," he says, disagreeing with the widespread perception that it is an off-limits destination for those on lower incomes, and stressing that especially outside the peak season there are many excellent deals.

As he also revealed, there has been a drop in tourist arrivals over the past two years, even if this is due to unrelated factors. However, this comparatively lower occupancy than in previous periods is also attributed to another factor, the constant construction of new hotel units.

"The increase in the number of beds creates an issue with accommodation occupancy," the mayor comments, adding that he has used Euronews to call on the government to take measures to stop unregulated building on the island.

Cruise tourism: 'A blessing and a curse'

On visitor numbers, Nikos Zorzos adds: "The figures are roughly the same. Santorini receives 3.5 million visitors a year including those who arrive by cruise ship."

However, locals have raised a counter-argument with the Ministry of Tourism. Because of the airport and direct flights to it from European destinations, a significant number of those recorded as landing and taking off for Santorini in fact do not stay on the island but on neighbouring ones, simply using it as a gateway into and out of the country, which in turn distorts the real figures.

Even so, there is no doubt that Santorini has plenty of tourists every year and, for cruise ships in particular, a stop there is considered a must. However, for islands like Santorini, cruise tourism is seen by many as both a blessing and a curse.

On the one hand it pushes up visitor numbers, but on the other it does not bring money to the local population and is the main reason behind the severe overcrowding that is often seen in the narrow alleyways and at times becomes unbearable.

What has the municipal authority done about this? "Look, we regulated cruise tourism," Nikos Zorzos tells Euronews. "About 10 years ago, with a study we carried out with the University of the Aegean, we set the maximum number of visitors who can visit Santorini every day. As a result there are no longer crowds in different parts of the island and movement is easier. So cruise tourism is no longer the problem it was in the past."

Cruise ship in Santorini Copyright 2007 AP. All rights reserved.

Now, up to 8,000 tourists a day can disembark from cruise ships. Even so, it is estimated that around half of all tourists in Santorini each year come from the cruise sector. Local residents complain that this type of visitor does not spend money on the island, since they do not stay overnight and, for the most part, do not even visit local shops. In recent years a further trend has emerged, with some not even going ashore and instead enjoying the famous caldera sunset from the ship.

"Of course, those who stay in hotels or other accommodation spend more money than visitors on short cruise stopovers," admits the mayor of Thira.

According to a ministerial decision, however, a new increased "cruise levy" has been in place since last year, essentially a per capita tax on each disembarkation. It amounts to 20 euros per person in the summer period (1 June to 30 September), drops to 12 euros in April, May and October, and is reduced to 4 euros in the winter period (1 November to 31 March). However, only one third of this money reaches the municipal coffers, as the remainder is shared between the Ministries of Tourism and Shipping.

World.title: EU lawmakers push to reduce Europe's dependence on foreign cloud providers
World.content:
A joint draft report on the European Commission's proposed Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) was presented at the European Parliament on Wednesday, calling for common EU rules on cloud and AI infrastructure, greater support for European technology companies and reduced dependence on foreign providers.

 

The proposal aims to strengthen Europe's digital infrastructure and international competitiveness amid concerns that reliance on foreign technology providers could undermine the bloc's control over critical services.

"This is not only a matter of economic competitiveness, it is also a matter of our capacity to make our own decisions," Spanish conservative MEP Diego Solier said during a press conference on Wednesday.

"Technological sovereignty does not consist in closing Europe to the rest of the world, it consists of ensuring that Europe has the capacity to act, compete and choose."

The proposal comes as the EU is making significant efforts to reduce its reliance on other countries for critical services, infrastructure, materials and security, with a slew of proposals currently in the works.

European leaders have been worried since Donald Trump returned to office, making the US an unreliable partner and exposing how reliant the bloc is American goods and services, especially big tech.

In June this year, Trump ordered Anthropic to block access to its widely used Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 AI models from outside the US, citing security concerns.

Access was restored later that month but conversations over so-called "kill switches" that the US government and tech companies held over critical European civilian and military infrastructure only intensified.

Boosting Europe's digital independence

The draft report calls for greater investment in European cloud and AI infrastructure, including measures to help European technology companies grow.

It also seeks to establish common EU standards for cloud services and strengthen protections for critical sectors, including healthcare, energy and transport.

"Our critical systems run on someone else's technology, and someone else can switch it off. Today a court, tomorrow a ministry, a hospital, a grid operator?," Dutch green MEP Reinier Van Lanschot warned.

The lawmakers also want public authorities to buy more cloud services from European providers to help them compete with foreign companies.

"Europe has brilliant businesses and they are not asking for subsidies, they are asking for customers. That's at the heart of our proposal," Van Lanschot said.

The report also calls for faster approval procedures for new data centres, while ensuring that projects respect environmental requirements and benefit local communities.

Under the Commission's proposal, the EU aims to triple its data centre capacity over the next five to seven years.

The proposed legislation comes amid concerns over Europe's dependence on non-EU technology companies.

According to the Commission, three non-European hyperscale cloud providers control more than 70% of the European cloud market, raising concerns about data sovereignty, security and operational autonomy.

What happens next?

The draft report is expected to be published on Thursday and discussed by European parliamentary committees on 1 December.

A committee vote is provisionally scheduled for mid-March 2027, followed by a plenary vote in April next year.

World.title: Protesters outside Israel’s Knesset oppose Arab lawmakers, call for new elections
World.content:
Demonstrators gathered outside Israel’s parliament, the Knesset, in Jerusalem, calling for new elections and voicing opposition to the presence and political role of Arab lawmakers.

The slogans and accusations displayed during the protest reflected the demonstrators’ own views and were not established facts about the lawmakers concerned.

World.title: The 500 best bars in the world have been revealed – and 13 of the top 25 are in Europe
World.content:
We all have different opinions on what makes a good bar. For me, my priorities are a chatty mixologist (I love sitting at the bar and watching all the action), moody lighting (I’m very staunchly anti-big light), and a mix of unique and classic concoctions on the menu.

 

You, however, might disagree, as might your friends or your family.

Luckily for us, Top 500 Bars has pulled together the thoughts of thousands upon thousands of people across the internet to create a definitive list of the best watering holes.

Using opinions from journalists, experts and influencers, plus reviews across social media and search engines, the team created a ranking based on “the wisdom of crowds”.

After all that number crunching, the number one spot went to Bar Leone in Hong Kong.

Co-founded by Lorenzo Antinori, who also owns Montana – which ranked third – the cocktail spot focuses on the classics, with Italian pop culture-themed interiors. Bar Leone has previously claimed the 50 Best top spot twice, including in 2026.

Where are the best bars in Europe?

The best bar in Europe accolade went to HIMKOK, a distillery bar in Oslo, which placed second overall.

Making use of their own aquavit, gin and vodka, the drinks on the menu have been “inspired by Norway’s nature, ingredients, culture and traditions”.

Next up is Line in Greece, which ranked fifth overall, having been named the best bar in Europe by 50 Best back in July.

Located in Athens, Line is known for its fruit wines, which are made and bottled on-site using ingredients from local producers.

Another European spot to make the top 10 is Panda & Sons in Edinburgh, placed seventh.

Hidden behind the façade of a barbershop, the speakeasy-style bar is best known for its use of freezing techniques.

Rounding out the top 10 are Moebius in Milan (ninth) and Paradiso in Barcelona (10th).

Mixologists at the former have more than 300 spirits at their disposal, which they use to create unusual beverages like the pesto martini, while the latter is a speakeasy (this time hidden behind a fridge door in a pastrami bar) with a themed menu that changes yearly.

World.title: 'No longer science fiction': Flying cars could launch in China in months, says Xpeng
World.content:
People could start travelling in so-called flying cars in China as soon as summer 2027, the manufacturer of a two-seater autopilot vehicle told Euronews Next.

 

The low-altitude flying device by XPeng Aridge is close to large-scale commercialisation, with limited deliveries to partners in China expected within months and a wider roll-out to follow, and has been approved by China’s civil aviation authorities for limited use.

"It’s no longer science fiction or just a single demo aircraft," vice president and chief financial officer of Chinese company XPeng Michael Du said at the Web Summit technology event in Lisbon. "It’s really a commercial model."

The two-seat electric vehicle costs $300,000 (€270,000) and has a cockpit the size of a small car.

The company has received more than 7,000 pre-orders worldwide, "most of them in China, but also some from the Middle East," Du said.

The device was shown off at Web Summit Lisbon 2026. XPeng

Buyers include individuals interested in personal flying and air tourism, as well as operators in emergency rescue and public services. "It showcases how wide a range of applications our products are capable of," he said.

The aircraft has completed its technical test flights across a range of conditions. "We tried it at sea level, high altitude, cold areas, hot areas, extreme wind or even rainy areas, a lot of extreme cases, so it’s safe," Du said.

The company has spent a decade building the technology from its own mass-production factory in Guangzhou.

The aircraft has completed its technical test flights, including at sea level and high altitude and in cold, hot, windy and rainy conditions.

It has also received a type inspection authorisation from the Civil Aviation Administration of China, whose test pilots completed all the test items. The company is now going through final type certification.

The future of mobility

Electric aircraft will reshape transport the way electrification reshaped cars, according to Du.

"Electrification has transformed and advanced the development of the car industry. Similar patterns will happen in the aircraft industry," he said, citing better power distribution, more redundancies and quieter operation.

Asked how the aircraft could change mobility in the long term, the executive used a Chinese saying about roads.

"In China, there’s a saying: if you want to develop the economy, you’d better build the roads," the executive said. "When you have better roads, it’s more accessible to everyone else."

That logic held while most travel happened on the ground, he said, but air mobility offers "a different format to improve transportation efficiency".

It "will completely change how people travel over time, from an efficiency perspective, from an economics perspective," he said.

The two-seat electric vehicle costs $300,000 (€270,000) and has a cockpit the size of a small car. XPeng

The main advantage, the executive said, is that aircraft skip the need for continuous infrastructure. "You don’t actually need to build infrastructure inch by inch from the starting point to the end," he said. "That’s the case for cars. That’s the case for high-speed rail."

The device could also benefit island nations and sparsely populated regions, Du said, "those areas will become so valuable" once air mobility arrives, as it will create economic value.

When will it come to Europe?

After China, the company plans to work with overseas regulators and partners, with the Middle East and Southeast Asia as the clearest early markets.

But Europe is "definitely a very attractive market", Du said, adding that the company hopes Web Summit will introduce European consumers, regulators and partners to the product.

However, Du said there were hurdles to overcome before entering Europe, including launching an affordable product at launch, and having the right infrastructure and places to fly to.

Geopolitics

Asked about US-China tensions, Du said the company would welcome more open markets and would be happy to enter the United States if regulations allow.

He noted that China, the US and Europe together account for only about half of the global aircraft market, so a temporary lack of access to one still leaves plenty of room to grow.

Du compared the situation to Chinese electric cars, which have now become widely accepted in Europe.

"Starting small, starting from outside the city, starting with some cargo, some passenger carrying, gradually into larger ones, entering into cities," Du said. "I think that could be one way the industry develops more positively."

World.title: ‘Monstrous injustice’: King Charles condemns slavery as UK agrees to talks
World.content:
In this episode of Spotlight on Africa, we talked to scholars from the continent and the Caribbean about slavery reparations – a key topic discussed at this year’s Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda.

Advertising

The Commonwealth is a 56-nation group of mostly former British colonies, 21 of them in Africa. King Charles III remains head of state in 15 of them, including the UK.

Its biennial Heads of Government Meeting took place from 1 to 4 November 2026 in Antigua and Barbuda.

In a final communiqué issued on Wednesday, the group said the time had come for “meaningful, truthful and respectful conversation towards forging a common future based on equity”.

Timetable of talks

While no timetable for talks was announced, the group welcomed the United Kingdom’s willingness to engage “in a structured, time-bound, inclusive and good-faith dialogue with affected parties addressing the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and its historical harms”.

In his opening speech, King Charles III, who is politically neutral, called the slave trade “a monstrous injustice” that filled him with “profound personal sorrow”, but stopped short of a formal apology.

UN backs resolution calling slave trade ‘gravest crime against humanity’

For his part, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was open to saying sorry but ruled out paying the financial reparations demanded by some Caribbean countries.

Britain’s Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband also said it was “not feasible” for the country to pay reparations for slavery, but that “there are things we can work on co-operatively”.

According to reports, Britain could issue a formal apology next year, during its G20 presidency.

Britain played a pivotal role in the slave trade, which saw between 10 and 15 million enslaved Africans taken to the Americas over four centuries.

The country abolished the slave trade in 1807 and slavery throughout the British Empire in 1833. It paid financial compensation, but to plantation owners rather than to the enslaved people themselves.

UN resolution

In March this year, the United Nations adopted a resolution recognising the transatlantic slave trade and the enslavement of Africans as the “gravest crime against humanity”, in a motion spearheaded by Ghana.

Ghana backs Jamaica’s petition to push UK for slavery reparations

For many countries, the time has come for formal apologies and concrete plans for slavery reparations.

To find out how these issues are being tackled on the African continent and in the Caribbean, RFI spoke to a panel of four guests:

Edem Adotey: professor at the Institute of African Studies in Accra, Ghana,

Joel Kibazo: Commonwealth spokesperson,

Matiangai Sirleaf: professor at the University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law in the United States,

Verene A. Shepherd: Jamaican historian and one of three vice-chairs of the Caricom Reparations Commission.

This episode was mixed by Nicolas Doreau.

World.title: Turkey courts Egypt to tip the scales in eastern Mediterranean power game
World.content:
This week’s joint naval exercises between Turkey and Egypt in the eastern Mediterranean are the latest move in a burgeoning partnership, as Ankara intensifies its efforts to draw Cairo closer and loosen its bonds with Turkish rivals Greece, Cyprus and Israel.

Advertising

The "Sea of Friendship 2026" naval drills, held from 4-9 November off the coast of Alexandria, follow five years of rapprochement after nearly a decade of mistrust sparked by the 2013 ouster of Mohamed Morsi, a close ally of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, by Egypt's President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi.

It is the second year in a row that Turkey and Egypt have held the joint drills, after a 13-year break.

“I think it's already a sign that the two countries are getting closer,” said Africa expert Elem Tepecikoglu of Ankara’s Social Sciences University. In her view, the naval exercises are part of an evolving partnership.

“This normalisation process started five years ago in the diplomatic realm,” she explained. “And then we see cooperation in the security domain as well. So this is why I say I'm optimistic that Egypt might come closer to the Turkish side.”

The strengthening alliance between Turkey and Egypt is stirring unease in Israel, at a time when Israeli-Turkish relations are already frayed by the war in Gaza and Ankara’s support for Hamas.

“Obviously, Israel does not see this as necessarily positive, because of the heightened tensions between Israel and Turkey,” warned Turkey analyst Gallia Lindenstrauss of the Institute for National Security Studies at Tel Aviv University.

She noted that Israel is growing ever more wary of Turkey’s expanding reach in the eastern Mediterranean. “There is concern that Turkey and Egypt can cooperate in ways that will squeeze Israel’s room to manoeuver, politically but also militarily.”

Lindenstrauss said she does not see this as a likely scenario, affirming that the 1979 peace agreement between Israel and Egypt is “still very much in place, despite many geopolitical turnovers”.

“But there was always a fear that the other countries surrounding it would unite and act against Israel,” the analyst added.

Lindenstrauss believes Egypt’s strong ties with Turkey’s rivals, Greece and Cyprus, allay fears of Israeli encirclement. “It is very important that this relationship keeps going ahead because it is a source of stability in the eastern Mediterranean,” she said.

Houthi war risks dragging Israel and Turkey into Horn of Africa standoff

Turkish leverage

Egypt, Greece, Cyprus and Israel are bound by a tightly knit strategic energy alliance centred on the Eastern Mediterranean Gas Forum, a regional organisation formed in 2020 that has its headquarters in Cairo.

Just last month, they stood united in condemning the Libyan parliament's ratification of a maritime deal with Turkey that encroached on Greek and Egyptian waters.

Still, Jalel Harchaoui, a regional expert at the Royal United Services Institute for Defence and Security Studies, a London-based think tank, observes that Turkey and Egypt are forging ever-closer collaboration on issues ranging from Libya to the Sudanese civil war to the Horn of Africa. Harchaoui suggests this growing cooperation is steadily boosting Ankara’s leverage over Cairo.

“I think observers should ask, can Egypt afford to do without Turkey? And the answer is probably no, and Turkey probably is aware of it,” he said.

Even so, Harchaoui doubts Cairo is ready to pivot fully toward Ankara. “If [Egypt] switches 180 degrees, it would be a disaster for the other side. I'm talking about Greece and Cyprus and Israel. So you could also ask yourself, can Egypt afford to anger its traditional friends?”

Libya-Turkey maritime deal stokes tensions in eastern Mediterranean

Egypt's balancing act

Ankara is stepping up its diplomatic courtship of Cairo, hoping to lure Egypt away from its longstanding partners.

But Turkish ambitions stumbled when Egypt declined to join the Mecca Defence Alliance with Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in August. Analyst Lindenstrauss sees this as a clear sign of the boundaries in Turkish-Egyptian ties.

“Egypt has already moved closer to Turkey than was imaginable a few years ago,” she said. “However, at the end of the day, there are limits to how much it can accept greater Turkish influence. I think Turkey pretty much reached where Egypt is willing to agree to, and it will not give Turkey concessions in the eastern Mediterranean that will endanger its relationship with Greece and Cyprus, or its peace agreement with Israel.”

Lindenstrauss believes that despite diplomatic tensions with Israel over the war in Gaza, it still remains in Egypt’s interests to maintain ties with all sides. “Because of Egypt's importance in the region, I think it can definitely go ahead with this balancing act. It gives it all the gains and the risk is relatively low compared to having Egypt choose sides,” she added.

Ankara stands ready to ramp up its campaign to win over Cairo as the battle for influence in the eastern Mediterranean intensifies. In the unfolding rivalry between between Turkey on one hand and Greece, Cyprus and Israel on the other, Egypt is emerging as the pivotal player.
