World.title: Zagreb Airport Attraction Wins Yet Another Prestigious Award
World.content:
November the 11th, 2026 – Zagreb Airport has an attraction that has won yet another prestigious award. The Museum Zone took home silver and has done very well in attracting passengers.

The Museum Zone at Franjo Tuđman Airport, a commendable project realised in cooperation between the Croatian History Museum and Zagreb International Airport, has won the silver the! Award in the multi-stakeholder and multi-sectoral cooperation category at the KoMference of the Croatian Public Relations Association. Poslovni reports that this is otherwise the second professional recognition for that particular project, which in the spring of this year took home the Grand PRix.

The Croatian History Museum, located in Zagreb’s Upper Town (Gornji grad) palaces, was severely damaged in the March 2020 earthquake, because of which it could no longer use its space for exhibiting its museum holdings. On the initiative of the Val Group, cooperation between the Croatian History Museum and Zagreb International Airport began. It was then that the Museum Zone was formally established, within which the exhibition “Stars of Croatian History – The Sky Is Their Limit. Get to Know Them!” was officially opened.

The exhibition presents 24 important figures from throughout Croatian history who, with their work spanning four areas – science, culture, politics and society, and sport – contributed to the development of Croatia and left a mark on the European and global level. “We’re pleased that a project that connected a heritage institution with Zagreb International Airport has been awarded and that this has been recognised as a very good model of communication,” said Minister of Culture and Media Nina Obuljen Koržinek at the KoMference.

Director of the Croatian History Museum Matea Brstilo Rešetar emphasised that when they entered that project they wanted to prove that heritage can meet the public even outside museum walls. According to her words, the Museum Zone has become the second most visited exhibition space in all of Croatia. President of the Management Board of Zagreb International Airport Huseyin Bahadir Bedir said that passengers have been given the opportunity to get to know Croatian history and cultural heritage in an interesting and accessible way, turning the time spent at the airport into an educational experience.

World.title: Crafted in the Capital: Meet the Last Masters of Zagreb’s Old Trades
World.content:
November the 11th, 2026 – The last masters of Zagreb’s old trades keep the door to simpler times open, all while exposing the soul of the Croatian capital in an increasingly fast-paced world.

If you happen to take a stroll down Zagreb’s old main artery, Ilica, or into one of the (many) historic courtyards of Lower Town (Donji grad), you’ll notice a distinct shift in the bustling city’s rhythm. Beyond the hum of modern life, endless coffee shops and modern boutiques, lies a quieter Zagreb. I’d say the real Zagreb. Situated behind modest, easily overlooked and century-old wooden storefronts, a dedicated group of local master artisans is keeping the Croatian capital’s medieval guild traditions alive and well. In the face of modernity, which is frankly becoming more and more concerning in many ways, these artisans do far more than just preserve tradition.

For many centuries, Zagreb’s economy and civic identity were built and constantly maintained by its obrtnici the master craftsmen. Today, in an era of mass production, fast fashion and people insisting on robots doing absolutely everything for them, these last surviving workshops are grounding for very many people. They’re living, working museums of intangible cultural heritage, offering visitors a rare chance to witness authentic, slow-crafted artistry firsthand. If this is up your street, let’s take a peel inside the workshops of Zagreb’s fascinating master umbrella makers, hatters, and cobblers, as all of them shape the capital’s true artisanal soul.

the crimson canopy of the Šestine umbrella

TZGZ/Ernest Mazarekic

No visit to Zagreb is complete without seeing the iconic Šestine umbrella (Šestinski kišobran, if you want to go local). Towering in vibrant crimson over the stalls of the busy Dolac Market, this striking parasol with its multicoloured horizontal stripes and natural chestnut handle is the city’s most recognisable visual symbol. What many travellers fail to realise is that every single authentic Šestine umbrella is still handcrafted in one single location – the Cerovečki Umbrella Workshop. You’ll find it on Ilica. Founded back in 1912 and now led by the fourth generation of the Cerovečki family, this is the last remaining umbrella-making workshop out of the eight that once operated across the capital. Recognising its profound historical value, the Croatian Ministry of Culture inscribed the traditional craft of making the Šestine umbrella on the List of Intangible Cultural Heritage of the Republic of Croatia. Stepping inside the shop, you’ll immediately be struck by the aroma of steamed chestnut wood and fine cotton. It’s an instant sensory reminder that a true souvenir isn’t always a magnet or a keyring that will fall to bits quickly, it can still be something built to weather decades of rain.

zagreb’s hatters – crowning the capital

Sandra Simunovic/PIXSELL

The word “hatter” is often associated with the term “mad hatter” and little else anymore, and while we can’t 100% guarantee you won’t run into a mad hatter in Zagreb, we can guarantee you’ll be impressed by what they do. If you turn the clock back to the early 20th century, however, a refined gentleman or lady living in Zagreb would never dream of stepping out onto Ban Jelačić Square without donning a proper hat. Today, that bygone Central European elegance survives in the workshops of the city’s historic milliners and hatters (known as klobučari).

Tucked into the historic Octagon passage (Oktogon) and along Ilica, old institutions like Kobali Hat Shop and Salon Šešira Cahun continue to block, steam, and stitch headwear using century-old wooden molds. Whether crafting traditional wool felt fedoras, bespoke bridal fascinators, or the classic caps worn by very many regional folk ensembles, Zagreb’s hatters bridge the gap of time, linking historical preservation and contemporary high fashion. Visitors are welcomed directly into spaces lined floor-to-ceiling with what seems like endless hatboxes, where a master artisan will measure your head and fit a piece tailored specifically to your silhouette. You don’t get that in Primark.

the bespoke cobblers who aid life spent walking the city’s cobbles

Goran Stanzl/PIXSELL

Before industrial footwear flooded the market, Zagreb’s shoemakers (postolari) and bootmakers (čizmari) were among the most respected tradespeople in the entire city. While many have since transitioned into repair shops, a handful of master cobblers still practice the careful, painstaking art of bespoke shoemaking from scratch.

Along Ilica, workshops like Postolar Bočak continue to maintain the rigorous standards of traditional Central European leatherwork. Creating a single pair of handmade shoes requires dozens of individual steps, from carving custom wooden lasts (kalupi) to hand-stitching supple calfskin uppers and natural leather soles. For those seeking sustainable, buy-it-for-life luxury, commissioning a pair of shoes or leather goods in Zagreb connects you directly to generations of ergonomic mastery. These people know that wandering the cobbled streets of the much older parts of the city, such as Upper Town, can take quite the toll on the ankle without the right footwear. So, if you plan to get your steps in while wandering all over Zagreb, this might be the best place to start!

preserving zagreb’s soul in a world full of confusion

TZGZ/Julien Duval

We currently live in a world dominated by rapidly evolving tech, uncertainty and a lot of worries we wouldn’t have had a clue about even a decade ago. Most of us feel that insecurity and desire something to ground us to the good old days. That’s exactly why these workshops matter so deeply to modern Zagreb. They take us back to simpler times, all while anchoring the city’s identity. Through dedicated cultural preservation initiatives championed by the Zagreb Tourist Board and the Croatian Chamber of Trades and Crafts, these fantastic traditional businesses are actively protected as vital cultural assets. Many carry the prestigious “Tradicijski obrt” (Traditional craft) designation. This is a mark of authenticity guaranteeing that the techniques used inside have been passed down through many generations.

For visitors looking to trade mass-produced trinkets (and especially umbrellas and shoes that fall to bits after a few weeks) for genuine stories and something made to go the distance, exploring Zagreb’s old trades is an unforgettable way to spend an afternoon. In an uncertain world moving faster than we can keep up with every single day, Zagreb’s last master craftsmen remind us that the finest things in life, much like the many hidden gems dotted around the Croatian capital itself, are best appreciated slowly.

World.title: How to Claim Croatian Citizenship If Your Ancestral Records Were Destroyed in the War
World.content:
November the 10th, 2026 – Claiming Croatian citizenship is no easy feat without professional assistance, but it becomes even more of a quagmire when your ancestral records were destroyed during the war. Luckily, there’s help available to guide you through what’s often a difficult, lengthy process.

America is a melting pot and there’s a lot of Croatian “ingredients” within it. There are countless Americans who have Croatian descendants scattered across North America, and many have a desire to not only reconnect with their family histories, but cement that connection with a Croatian passport of their own. For all of them, the journey toward claiming a Croatian and as such EU passport begins with a simple request, and that’s obtaining an ancestor’s birth certificate (rodni list) from that usually long gone relative’s home village somewhere in Croatia. For many such would-be applicants, that’s where the journey typically ends.

the dead end… or is it?

There’s a reason why what sounds like such a simple procedure comes unstuck so often – the war. For families whose roots trace back to areas of the country which were particularly heavily impacted by the Homeland War, including Slavonia, Banovina, Kordun, or the Dalmatian hinterland, the first step is also the last.

When DIY applicants reach out to local municipal registry offices or consular officials, they’re frequently met with the response that the old local archives were burned, shelled, or simply became completely lost during the war, and the primary civil records simply no longer exist. For most diaspora applicants, this feels like the end of the road. They assume that without an original birth certificate of a relative who actually came from Croatia, proving their lineage under the Croatian Citizenship Act is impossible. Fortunately, a destroyed municipal archive doesn’t erase your legal right to Croatian citizenship, even if those who destroyed it during the 1990s had hoped that would be the case. It just means your application requires administrative (and often legal) reconstruction rather than standard document retrieval.

a missing birth certificate doesn’t have to mean the end of the croatian citizenship road…

Under current Croatian administrative law, the Interior Ministry requires an unbroken chain of evidence proving your ancestor’s identity, birthplace, and connection to Croatia. When primary civil registries end up being destroyed, the law does allow applicants to rebuild that proof using secondary historical records. However, you can’t simply submit a family story or a letter stating the records were burned or lost during the war. To satisfy Croatia’s somewhat strict legal thresholds, you need obtain an official certificate confirming the destruction of the primary registry, and then pair it with alternative, state-recognised proof of your ancestor’s birth and residency.

duplicate histories, and why croatia’s love of recording everything more than once leans in your favour…

Back during the 19th and early 20th centuries, vital events in Croatia (and there were very many) were rarely recorded in just one single book. This era was a very turbulent time for what is now Croatia, with regimes and empires coming and going fairly often. That means that even if a local town hall was destroyed in the 1990s, parallel records often survived in completely different institutions across the country. It’s finding them that can be tricky. Reconstructing a lost Croatian lineage often involves hunting down secondary evidence across four main repositories.

First, you usually need to begin with the Diocesan church archives. Catholic parishes usually held meticulous baptismal, marriage, and death registers. Parishes were, at least historically speaking, required to send duplicate copies of these books to regional bishoprics or archdiocesan archives in bigger cities like Zagreb, Split, or even (again, historically speaking) Đakovo. This largely kept them safe from localised village destruction.

Then comes the regional state archives. These often contain much older civil records. Usually older than 100, these records were frequently transferred out of local municipal offices and into regional state vaults long before the final fall of Yugoslavia in the 1990s.

Another particularly important area to explore are the property registries. These are historical court records detailing land ownership, agricultural plots, and inheritance deeds. Logically, they tend to list exact family lineages, birth years, and familial relationships.

Then comes the historical Census and conscription lists. Austro-Hungarian or early 20th-century regional tax rolls, school registries, and military draft lists can serve as vital corroborating evidence to establish an ancestor’s presence in a specific village. The interesting thing here is that you shouldn’t necessarily be put off if you don’t find your ancestor listed as even being Croatian. Given the period we’re talking about here, they very likely wouldn’t be.

why taking the diy approach often falls flat

While secondary reconstruction is completely legal, executing it from thousands of miles away is nearly impossible for a DIY applicant. Local municipal clerks in Croatia are rarely equipped (or obligated) to act as historical detectives on behalf of overseas applicants. Frankly, they’ll likely ignore a single rogue applicant from somewhere in America until you go away. If a record is missing from their immediate database, their job ends at telling you it isn’t there. Hunting down duplicate baptismal books in a diocesan vault or pulling 19th-century inheritance deeds from a regional court requires physical presence, archival knowledge, and proper knowledge of administrative Croatian – and that’s not something you can muster up overnight (trust me on that).

how croatian by descent‘s services can be your guide

All is not lost. There are services which aid would-be Croatian citizenship applicants in exactly this, and Croatian By Descent is one of them. Their guidance and knowledge of the process, particularly for US applicants, can turn what seems like an administrative dead end into a genuine, flowing path towards that Croatian and EU passport. Instead of accepting a “records not found” notice at face value, their team, comprised of diaspora Croats themselves, utilises local archival experts who not only understand how to trace where surviving duplicates are housed, but have the skills to grasp what that undertaking looks like. They navigate the regional state archives, coordinate with authorities, and help you to compile the combination of documents required by the Interior Ministry. They also work with lawyer partners who are on hand to help push through anything that ends up being trickier than expected.

By pairing this investigative archival work with document formatting, they give you the best chance possible of your application meeting the requirements, even if your ancestral village’s town hall didn’t survive the war.

World.title: Landlords in Top Croatian Tourist Spots Could Pay More Tax – Breakdown by City
World.content:
November the 10th, 2026 – Landlords located in the top Croatian tourist spots could find themselves paying much more out in tax next year – here’s a breakdown of what that looks like on a city by city basis.

As of 2027, private landlords who rent out their properties to tourists could face new rules for calculating their lump-sum tax. Lukrecija Zderic reports for Index that with the proposed amendments to the law, the minimum annual tax amounts per bed would increase, and how much landlords will pay will also depend on the decisions of cities and municipalities, should parliament adopt these amendments. The increase won’t hit all landlords equally. Here’s a full breakdown of exactly which Croatian tourist spots could see the future lump sum change and how much more apartment owners could pay annually depending on the number of beds they have.

four beds could mean 200 euros higher annual tax

According to the current proposal of legal amendments, the minimum annual lump-sum tax in the first category of tourist development would rise from 100 to 150 euros per bed, and in the second from 70 to 100 euros. Cities and municipalities that have so far prescribed lower amounts would have to align them with the new minima. That would mean at least 50 euros more annually per bed in the first, or 30 euros in the second category, but not an automatic tax increase for all landlords. In those categories, there are a total of 105 cities and municipalities, including the best-known tourist destinations. Below we bring an overview of the existing amounts and possible changes from 2027.

The largest increase in the first category would be felt by landlords who currently pay 100 euros per bed. If local authorities align that amount with the new minimum of 150 euros, the owner of an apartment with four beds would see the annual tax rise by 200 euros.

Ston, Kaštela, Senj, Vir and Trogir…

In the second category, the largest change would affect Ston, Kaštela, Senj, Vir and Trogir. There landlords with four beds, with the application of the new minimum, would pay 120 euros more annually. Changes will not be equal in all parts of individual cities. Where the lump sum differs according to zones, the increase would apply only to zones in which the current amount is lower than the new minimum. For example, in Split the lump sum could increase in zones where it is now lower than 150 euros per bed, while in others it would remain unchanged. On the other hand, in Zagreb, Makarska and Rijeka, the existing lump sum is already higher than the proposed minimum, so it would not have to rise solely because of the legal amendments. The final amounts will nevertheless depend on the decisions of cities and municipalities, which can prescribe even higher lump sums than the legal minimum.

a higher lump sum even if the cities themselves fail to make a decision

The draft law also provides for an increase in the amounts that are applied if city or municipal councils do not make a decision on the amount of their lump-sum tax. In the first category of tourist development, that amount would increase from the previous 200 to 225 euros per bed or accommodation unit, while in the second category it would rise from 135 to 150 euros. For example, a landlord with six beds in the first category, to whom that legal amount would apply, would instead of the previous 1,200 euros pay 1,350 euros annually, or 150 euros more. These are legal amounts provided for in the proposal, and not the final tax obligations of all landlords.

Since 2025, the lump-sum tax for private landlords has been determined according to the tourist development of the city or municipality in which the accommodation is located. Four groups were introduced, and for each a special range of amounts per bed was prescribed, within which cities and municipalities themselves determine the amount of tax. Before that, all units of local self-government had the same legal range, from 150 to 1,500 kuna, (or from approximately 19.91 to 199.08 euros per bed). Local authorities even then independently determined the final amount, but regardless of the tourist development of their specific area.

as expected, the smallest landlords will actually be hit hardest…

Vedran Tomić, representative of the association Save Small Family Landlords, considers that with the proposed amendments the state is forcing cities and municipalities to increase the lump-sum tax. He emphasises that in the association they are not against lump-sum taxation, but warns that the increase in the legal minimum would hit precisely the landlords who offer the cheapest accommodation the most.

“More than 90 percent of beds are in the first and second category. Thereby, the lower limit of the lump-sum tax is practically shifted for all landlords. We consider the shifting of the lower limit absurd because units of local self-government already had the possibility to increase the amounts, and they did not. Now the minimum is increased by 50 percent, that is to 150 euros. I’ll give a concrete example. I’m from Crikvenica and I know the situation there very well. The lump-sum tax per bed there first amounted to 45 euros, then it was increased to 100, and then to 150 euros. Such an increase is contrary to the interests of the residents of Crikvenica and all political options in the city.

Regardless of whether it is the government or the opposition, no one considers that the tax on rental, which is one of the main economic activities of Crikvenica, should be additionally increased. One should look at that more broadly. Units of local self-government should find it important that people understand that in smaller places on the Adriatic that tax is not such a significant source of revenue for the local budget. The goal should be to encourage people to work and earn, and then spend that money precisely in their community. These are people who live in those communities and spend their money there. We consider that the state should not force cities and municipalities to increase tax on their own population,” Tomić believes.

will this result in the loss of the local guest?

When asked about how the proposed increase in the lump-sum tax will be reflected in the business of landlords and whether the additional cost will spill over into accommodation prices, he believes Croatian guests will be among the first affected.

“First of all, the tax increase will at least partially spill over into accommodation prices, which will additionally encourage inflation. It is a pro-inflationary, and not an anti-inflationary measure because every additional tax cost someone has to pay. The second important problem is the social effect of such an increase. It will hit landlords with lower incomes harder, as well as guests who use the most favourable private accommodation. It’s precisely in these most favourably priced apartments where Croatian guests like to spend their summer holidays. Due to the possible increase in prices the affordability of summer holidays will also be endangered because part of Croats could remain without the possibility of being able to afford the accommodation they have been used to so far and will choose other locations,” Tomić stated.

He also added that he fears that the increase in the lump-sum tax could encourage part of the landlords to move into the grey zone, that is unregistered rental of accommodation. “If the tax rises so much that landlords with the lowest incomes can no longer bear it, part of them could move into the grey zone, because of which the state, that is cities and municipalities, would ultimately collect nothing. In doing so all those costs are added up. For some the additional amount may not represent a great burden, but for many it will. Everything depends on the incomes they achieve. Ultimately, I consider that the system of lump-sum taxation according to the number of beds itself is quite unfair.”

Whether the announced increases will indeed be reflected in accommodation prices and supply will be known after the adoption of the law and the decisions of cities and municipalities, while a clearer picture of their real consequences will be given only by the next summer tourist season.

World.title: Should Pula Airport Follow Zadar’s Model?
World.content:
November the 10th, 2026 – Pula Airport is notoriously empty during the winter season, and some are saying over-reliance on just Ryanair might be more of an issue than we realise – should it therefore follow Zadar’s model?

Much has been said recently about the business model employed by Pula Airport, and the debate even reached the Croatian Parliament recently. Boris Bilas reports for Glas Istre/Voice of Istria reports that SDP MP Sanja Radolović proposed an initiative to establish a route between Pula and nearby Venice. Given the previous management’s neglect of the airport, Pula Airport is still far from reaching the passenger numbers it recorded just under a decade ago. It’s therefore hardly surprising that Istrian politicians, as well as the general public in Istria, are becoming quite concerned.

The new airport director, Marko Ražem, has quickly demonstrated that he is the complete opposite of his predecessor, and it seems that Pula Airport finally has a chance to recover under his leadership. At the same time, many people in Pula are calling for the Zadar model to be adopted, wondering why Pula cannot have an airport just as successful as Zadar’s, especially given that Istria is a much stronger tourist region than the Zadar area.

However, Marko Ražem himself has already stated publicly that he doesn’t consider Zadar’s airport management model particularly appealing and would rather develop Pula Airport in a completely different direction. Indeed, the two airports have completely different business strategies, and a comparison of passenger traffic at Zadar and Pula airports reveals a fundamental divide in their approaches to route development. Zadar’s rapid rise, which saw passenger numbers exceed 1.6 million in 2025 and 2026, has been built on the back of one dominant partner, the ultra-popular Irish low-cost giant Ryanair.

Pula, on the other hand, records stable but more modest passenger traffic of around 554,000, approximately 200,000 fewer than its record year of 2019. However, its strength lies in spreading risk and maintaining a network of traditional and diverse airlines.

the two different strategies employed by zadar and pula

Zadar Airport has become one of Ryanair’s key hubs in this part of the Adriatic coastline. According to estimates, Ryanair accounts for between 75 and 80 percent of Zadar Airport’s total annual passenger traffic. The Irish airline group connects Zadar with more than 70 destinations, bringing record passenger numbers to the airport during the summer season, but also leaving it completely exposed to the business decisions of a single board of directors in Dublin.

Pula Airport, on the other hand, has historically maintained a more balanced portfolio. Although Ryanair first entered the Croatian market through Pula in 2006, Pula does not allow its future to be determined exclusively by the low-cost model. Germany and the United Kingdom account for more than half of all arrivals, while, alongside Ryanair, a significantly larger proportion of passengers travelling to Istria are brought in by other airlines and numerous charter operators.

In the aviation industry, having 80 percent of your traffic dependent on a single airline is considered an extremely high-risk gamble. Ryanair operates according to a highly aggressive business model: it has no particular loyalty to destinations. Its bases are established wherever subsidies from local tourism boards are highest and airport fees are lowest. When an airport refuses to reduce its charges or a government raises taxes, Ryanair does not hesitate to withdraw aircraft and shut down routes overnight. Zadar is currently undergoing a massive infrastructure expansion of its passenger terminal. Investments in increased capacity are justified by the current overcrowding. However, if Ryanair were to decide to drastically cut its operations or relocate its base, as it recently announced reductions and withdrawals from cities such as Berlin, Bremen and Thessaloniki due to disagreements over airport charges, Zadar Airport could be left with an enormous empty terminal, high fixed costs for maintaining unused facilities and a dramatic drop in revenue.

a broader airline range

This is precisely what the new director of Pula Airport, Marko Ražem, wants to avoid. He has announced that the airport will attempt to further expand its range of airlines in the future, even if this might mean slightly fewer passengers in the short term compared with Zadar.

In the long run, however, this would mean a much more stable and secure business model that does not depend on the whims of a single person in Dublin. All things considered, Zadar is currently enjoying the fruits of its tourism boom and making headlines with record-breaking passenger numbers. However, its Ryanair “monoculture” is unsustainable in the long run without a strong Plan B. Pula, despite having fewer passengers, can sleep much more peacefully because losing any individual airline would not automatically mean the end of the airport’s operations. The lesson for Croatian tourism and aviation authorities is clear: low-cost airline partners are an excellent engine for growth, but turning an airport into the private runway of a single airline creates a vulnerability that could bring an entire region’s air connectivity to a standstill in an instant.

ryanair’s cautionary tale…

The risks of depending on a single airline are not merely theoretical. Several smaller European airports have experienced complete collapse after becoming dependent on Ryanair and subsequently attempting to make the airline pay market-rate prices. It’s no secret that Ryanair offers the best prices for the vast majority of its routes, and that making sure it is present at your airport has become paramount across Europe, but it shouldn’t imply total reliance. There are a few cautionary tales to keep in mind…

Frankfurt-Hahn Airport (Germany): Once a textbook example of Ryanair’s success outside Frankfurt. When the Irish airline began transferring flights to Frankfurt’s main airport and cutting routes at Hahn, the airport sank into debts amounting to millions of euros and eventually declared bankruptcy.

Altenburg-Nobitz Airport (Germany): A regional airport that invested millions in modernisation to meet Ryanair’s requirements. Following disagreements over marketing funding, Ryanair completely abandoned the airport in 2011. The airport was left without commercial flights, and the project ended in business failure.

Ciudad Real Airport (Spain): Although it also suffered from other structural problems, this so-called “ghost airport” attracted Ryanair with millions in subsidies. When the subsidies dried up and Ryanair left, the airport closed and ended up in insolvency proceedings. The recent wave of base closures and capacity cuts across Germany and Belgium clearly demonstrates that O’Leary’s management is not afraid to make radical cuts.

World.title: Pula Wins the Title of the Best 15-Minute City in the Region
World.content:
November the 10th, 06 – Pula has won the title of the best 15-minute city in the region, with around 60% of the people in this city getting from A to B within a quarter of an hour.

As many as 60% of Pula residents get from A to B within a quarter of an hour. In contrast, in Zagreb, more than 80% of citizens travel for much longer. There’s a coastal Croatian city in which one reaches their job, school, family obligations and more, all in the time it often takes a resident of Zagreb to leave a car park. Poslovni reports that this remains the case even as a city that receives hundreds of thousands of visitors from all over the world in summer. In spite of that, it has preserved what most European cities have long since lost – order and peace on the roads. That city didn’t win only in Croatia, as this Friendly City Index research spans 62 cities across 11 countries.

pula takes first place

The biggest city in Istria was victorious among 62 cities. This is because as many as 60 percent of surveyed Pula residents manage to reach most of their everyday destinations within 15 minutes. The research , which was carried out by Syno International in 62 cities across Croatia, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, Ukraine, Bulgaria and Azerbaijan, show that Pula residents live the everyday life that many desire: one in which less time goes on travel, and more remains for and free time.

“Pula was packed with events this summer, and thousands of visitors from all over the world week after week filled the Pula Arena at concerts of the biggest music stars. Despite the hustle and bustle, tourists and the expected crowds of the peak summer season, the average Bolt ride lasted 11 minutes, and almost 80 percent of all rides finished in less than 15 minutes. Our mobility and user movement data thereby additionally confirm what Pula residents highlighted in the Friendly City Index research: Pula is indeed a 15-minute city,” said Sanja Babić. Such a city rhythm is not a coincidence. Short distances and roundabouts, which in Pula at many key intersections have replaced traffic lights and enable more fluid traffic without long waiting, make Pula an example of how urban mobility can be simple and efficient.

zagreb remains the croatian record holder… at the very bottom of the list

Zagreb failed the 15-minute city test, and rather catastrophically so. The majority of surveyed Zagreb residents consider that the capital is still far from the vision of a city within a quarter of an hour’s reach, so it found itself at the bottom of the ranking, in 50th place, with a result of 18 percent. A surprise also came in the form of Zadar, which last year led the regional ranking with approximately 54 percent of respondents, and this year fell to ninth place, with 46 percent. This year’s analysis was also expanded to Pula and Dubrovnik, whereby the number of covered Croatian cities was increased from five to seven. In addition to first-placed Pula, Split occupies fourth and Osijek fifth place, both with a result of 50 percent. They were followed by Zadar, Rijeka in 16th place with 38 percent, Dubrovnik in 38th place with 23 percent, and Zagreb as the last among Croatian cities.

pula beats bucharest

The Friendly City Index research, in which residents of 62 cities in 11 countries assessed whether they reach their everyday destinations within 15 minutes, showed that at the opposite end of the ranking from the winner Pula is Romanian Bucharest, which took last place in the research. In Bucharest only six percent of residents reach destinations within a quarter of an hour, which means that that share in Pula is as much as ten times higher than in the Romanian capital. Among the capital cities Bratislava fared the best, but even it with a result of 26 percent occupies only 30th place in the overall ranking.

what is the Friendly City Index?

The Friendly City Index is an international research that compares the quality of life in cities of Central and Eastern Europe as the residents themselves see it: how much time they need to work, educational, health and sports facilities or the shop, how close green areas are to them, what the cycling and traffic infrastructure is like. The research was conducted on Bolt’s initiative by the company Syno International, and this year’s edition covers 62 cities in 11 countries: Croatia, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, Ukraine, Bulgaria and Azerbaijan. The ranking of 15-minute cities is based on the share of respondents who reach most everyday destinations within a quarter of an hour.

People who still want to live in cities move into them primarily because of practicality, but the accelerated growth and development of cities can make everyday life much more challenging. That’s why the concept of the 15-minute city is a good check of what the real situation is. It shows where cities succeed, and where there is room for improvement. The recipe for success is almost universal – fewer crowds, better public transport and more available alternatives to the private car. If people daily spend more time travelling, that indicates the negative consequences of urban planning that ultimately reflect on the quality of life, from the household budget to health.

World.title: Iraqi president participates in COP31 in Turkey
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi President Nizar Amidi arrived on Tuesday in the Turkish city of Antalya to participate in the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31).

Amidi is expected to deliver Iraq’s speech at the conference and meet with senior officials to discuss approaches to enhance international cooperation in environmental protection, according to a statement released by the Iraqi Presidency.

At the same time, the president of Iraq will discuss climate-related issues, specifically the effects that climate change will have on Iraq and the region.

On the sidelines of his participation in COP31, Amidi met on Wednesday with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.

Held between November 9 and November 20, 2026, COP31 brings together heads of state, government officials, and international leaders, though notable leaders from several G7 and European nations are absent.

The summit centers on climate change financing and adaptation for vulnerable nations, loss and damage funding, and clean energy transitions rather than just new targets.

World.title: Cathay Pacific orders 11 Airbus aircraft for $5.1 bn
World.content:
Hong Kong – Cathay Pacific has ordered 11 more Airbus jets in a deal worth $5.1 billion, the Hong Kong airline said Wednesday.

The 11 A330-900 jets “will support the growth of Cathay Pacific’s regional network and provide it with more passenger and cargo capacity”, the company said in a press release.

Its filing to the Hong Kong stock exchange put the deal at $5.1 billion, with the carrier saying the European plane maker had granted it “significant price concessions”.

Cathay also announced it was ordering three more Airbus A321neo narrowbody aircraft for its budget subsidiary HK Express, which would help build on its “growth potential with its focus on destinations in the Chinese mainland and other short-haul routes”.

Describing the 14 jets as “state-of-the-art, fuel-efficient”, CEO Ronald Lam said they would upgrade Cathay’s total fleet and “enhance connectivity at our home hub Hong Kong”.

The 11 A330-900 aircraft are expected to be delivered between 2031 and 2035.

The carrier said in the filing they will “progressively replace” its existing fleet of mid-size widebody aircraft, and primarily serve regional destinations in Asia.

The jets could also serve longer-haul destinations at a later stage, it added.

Cathay said this year it aims to add 150 aircraft in the next 10 years if market conditions are favourable, replacing the current jets and bringing the fleet to around 300 aircraft.

It reported a 71-percent surge in net profit in the first half of 2026, as more travellers chose to transit through Hong Kong due to the Middle East situation in the second quarter.

World.title: UK arrests US soldier suspected of spying for Russia
World.content:
London – A member of the US army suspected of spying for Russia was arrested in Britain on Tuesday, London police said, following an investigation with support from the American military and law enforcement.

The case is the latest espionage allegation involving suspected Russian agents in Britain, a close ally of Ukraine which Moscow invaded in 2022.

Police said in a statement the 41-year-old American soldier was detained near Gloucester on suspicion he had violated national security laws and was in custody at a London police station.

“This significant arrest and investigation is a result of close collaboration between UK and US authorities,” said Vicki Evans, London Metropolitan Police’s Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing.

“The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing,” she added.

US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) director Kash Patel thanked UK police and intelligence agencies.

“This important arrest involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies,” he said, according to the London police statement.

The Pentagon referred AFP to the US army, which did not provide an immediate response to request for further details on the case.

Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command in the police statement described the alleged actions of the “senior solider, entrusted with sensitive information” as a “sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent”.

Relations between Russia and Britain were frosty long before the Ukraine war began — marred by several spy and assassination scandals, including the 2006 poisoning of ex-Russian spy Alexander Litvinenko in London and the 2018 attempted poisoning of double agent Sergei Skripal in Salisbury.

In September, a British man appeared in court in London over allegations he was preparing to sabotage a drone factory and drone manufacturing sites on behalf of Russian military intelligence.

The investigation that led to the US soldier’s arrest was “not linked to any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations,” police said.

World.title: Chinese woman accused of spying on Nvidia boss entered Taiwan on Hong Kong passport
World.content:
Taipei – The woman accused of spying for China during an affair with Nvidia chief Jensen Huang used a Hong Kong passport to enter Taiwan, the island’s immigration agency said Wednesday, as authorities investigate the incident.

Jensen Huang has admitted to having an affair, reportedly with Alice Huang, a Chinese former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who US officials believe was working for Chinese intelligence. Beijing has rejected the spying allegations.

Nvidia’s board announced Sunday that it had opened a probe into Jensen Huang, the company’s chief executive and co-founder, who is no relation to Alice Huang.

“Our government’s relevant agencies are fully informed of the relevant records and information,” National Immigration Agency Director-General Lin Horng-en told reporters, confirming that Alice Huang used a Hong Kong passport to enter Taiwan.

“We were aware of all her relevant entry and exit records.”

It is generally easier for Hong Kong passport holders to enter Taiwan than those with mainland Chinese passports, who must also apply for special permission to travel there.

The additional restrictions are partly due to the complex relations between China and Taiwan, which Beijing claims and has vowed to bring under its control.

Taiwan’s Interior Minister Liu Shyh-fang said Alice Huang “did indeed enter the country, but she is currently overseas”.

“If we had known she was a spy, we certainly would not have let her enter Taiwan,” Liu told lawmakers in parliament.

“We will review our procedures, specifically our pre-screening, interim spot checks and interviews, and post-visit measures,” she said.

“As far as we understand, this Ms Huang has had her permit revoked, meaning it is impossible for her to enter Taiwan again.”

On Tuesday, Liu said Taiwan’s “national security units are actively investigating the matter”.

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was seen at a dinner in May 2025 hosted by Jensen Huang at a Chinese restaurant in Taipei during Computex, the island’s top tech expo.

Journalists stood outside the restaurant filming through glass windows and doors as Jensen Huang and a woman identified as Alice Huang, who was wearing a pink dress, mingled with other attendees.

At one point, Jensen Huang can be seen putting his arm around Alice Huang as she kisses him on the right cheek, press livestreams show.

World.title: Celtics beat Sixers 123-101 as Tatum outshines Brown
World.content:
New York – The Boston Celtics beat Philadelphia 123-101 to replace the 76ers at the top of the NBA Eastern Conference as Jayson Tatum outshone his former teammate Jaylen Brown in a much-hyped showdown Tuesday.

Brown’s first regular season clash against the Celtics team he called home for a decade played out against reports of a beef with his 2024 NBA title-winning partner Tatum.

The two men have exchanged cryptic public barbs, apparently disagreeing over Tatum’s knowledge of — or role in — Brown’s shock trade this summer to the Sixers.

Tatum greeted Brown moments before tip-off but was seemingly blanked, and the game began in feisty fashion, with a fired-up Brown making two steals but conceding two fouls in the opening minutes.

But Brown was ultimately restricted to just 13 points on a frustrating night, against Tatum’s 21, as Boston weathered a Philadelphia third-quarter comeback and rode to victory.

“No game is bigger than the other, definitely in the regular season, you know — it’s one game,” said Tatum.

“The hoopla is over, and now we get all ready for tomorrow.”

The Celtics took an early lead, even as the Philadelphia crowd booed Tatum’s every move, jeering loudly as he wildly misplaced a pass under pressure from VJ Edgecombe.

But as the game settled into its rhythm it was veteran Paul George — who went the other direction, from Philadelphia to Boston, as part of the Brown package — who dominated.

George racked up 36 points across the night, on superb shooting form including six three-pointers from 11 attempts.

In the third quarter, Tatum soared above LeBron James for a driving dunk.

But Philadelphia rallied, levelling the score at 76-76 and again at 79-79 with a monster Maxey three-pointer.

Boston regrouped and raced out of sight down the final stretch, with George paying credit to Tatum for soaking up the opposition’s focus, leaving him free to score.

“Obviously JT demands so much attention. Playing off him has allowed me to get a lot of easy opportunities,” he said.

“At this point in my career, there’s only one thing that I want to do, and that’s win. And so, for him, especially for JT, (my role is) to alleviate any pressure, any friction.

“I’m here to help you. I’m in a way here to serve you, make you become the best player that you can become.”

The battle of the top two teams in the East saw Boston move to 9-2 with a fourth straight win, with Philadelphia now 9-3.

Also in the NBA on Tuesday, the defending champion New York Knicks thrashed the struggling Milwaukee Bucks 117-85.

Jalen Brunson scored 23 and Karl-Anthony Towns continued his fine form with 21 points plus 16 rebounds.

The Bucks slump to 1-10, having lost their former star man Giannis Antetokounmpo this summer.

The Celtics had initially attempted to trade Brown for Antetokounmpo, kick-starting the saga, before Antetokounmpo ultimately moved to the Miami Heat and Brown ended up at Philadelphia.

World.title: Asian stocks fluctuate as US rate worries temper tech bounce
World.content:
Hong Kong – Asian stocks diverged Wednesday as renewed optimism over the AI trade was offset by forecast-topping US inflation data and the prospect of a bumper interest rate hike next month.

After last week’s rout fuelled by fears that Democrats would ramp up regulation of artificial intelligence, beaten down tech stocks have bounced this week on bargain-buying and a feeling their fears may have been overdone.

Sentiment was also given a boost by earnings from data centre operator CoreWeave, which said sales would come in at $13-$13.3 billion this year, beating estimates.

The news soothed worries about the company’s health after suffering heavy selling last month amid speculation that it could struggle to finance its vast debt pile as borrowing costs continued to rise.

That sparked a period of panic over the tech sector as firms rely heavily on debt to fund their eye-watering AI investments.

Also lifting confidence was Anthropic’s filing showing it planned to raise up to $64 billion in its upcoming initial public offering, valuing it at as much as $1.4 trillion.

The maker of AI agent Claude had been expected to raise up to $100 billion in its IPO, which would have made it the largest IPO on record.

The stock market debut is being seen as a gauge of how long the AI spending boom can last.

Its filing also revealed that revenue soared to $17 billion in the third quarter, up from just $1.4 billion a year earlier.

And in another sign of the sector’s health, Bloomberg reported that ChatGPT-maker OpenAI had earned $10 billion in quarterly revenue for the first time in July-September, thanks to demand for its software.

The figure marked an increase of nearly 50 percent from the previous three months and a near threefold jump year on year.

However, chip giant Nvidia was still in focus following the bombshell revelation of an affair between CEO Jensen Huang and a woman reportedly suspected of being a Chinese spy.

The firm is now the subject of an FBI investigation.

– ‘No shortage of catalysts’ –

All three main indexes on Wall Street ended in the red Tuesday, snapping a two-day rally, and Asia stuttered.

Tokyo, Seoul and Taipei — where most of Asia leading AI-linked firms are listed — continued to rise, with Singapore and Jakarta also up.

But there were losses in Hong Kong, Shanghai, Sydney, Wellington and Manila.

Traders are also now fretting over the possibility of a bigger-than expected rate hike by the Federal Reserve when it next meets in December.

US consumer prices rose 0.4 percent on-month in October, a slowdown from the previous month’s 0.6 percent but more than the 0.3 percent forecast.

While the reading reflected a significant moderation in energy price increases, food prices shot higher with medical care, household furnishings and several other categories.

Chicago Fed boss Austan Goolsbee told PBS Newshour the reading was “another distressing report, borderline disturbing”.

The report came hours after Fed Governor Christopher Waller called for a swift response to inflation, suggesting he could even support a 50-basis-point hike in December.

A second Fed official, Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, also signalled strong support for swift action to address inflation.

“Market participants continue to navigate the political implications of the Democratic sweep, and the economics of AI infrastructure,” said Pepperstone’s Chris Weston.

He said investors were “forced to reassess assumptions around future revenues, cash flows and funding conditions”.

“Add a hotter-than-expected US (consumer price) print, a heightened focus on Anthropic’s IPO, and a major buyers strike on Nvidia, and there’s no shortage of catalysts driving market price action,” he added.

Oil prices edged up after sinking again Tuesday on hopes for a US-Iran agreement to end their war and reopen the crucial Strait of Hormuz.

International benchmark Brent was hovering around $92 a barrel, after dropping below $90 for the first time since August.

Both contracts are down around 20 percent since the start of the month.

In company news, Japanese tech investment giant SoftBank tumbled as much as eight percent in Tokyo after reporting a more than $7 billion loss in the fiscal second quarter.

World.title: EU to make addictive app features easier to switch off
World.content:
Brussels – The European Union will on Wednesday unveil new rules to crack down on influencer marketing, ban online features that trick Europeans and force platforms to give users the right to turn off “addictive” features.

The EU already has a raft of laws covering data protection, artificial intelligence and online content but Brussels and campaigners argue there are gaps that leave consumers exposed to harmful digital practices.

The bloc’s executive will unveil a much-needed update of consumer rules dubbed the “Digital Fairness Act” (DFA) that will give it the power to slap fines on companies of up to six percent of their annual turnover in large-scale cases.

The financial harms to European consumers are vast: official data showed “problematic” digital practices led to losses for individuals reaching 10.3 billion euros ($11.5 billion) a year.

Based on draft documents seen by AFP, the proposal will include:

— a ban on “dark patterns”, the practice of tricking users into making unwanted purchases or opting in to certain settings without their knowledge

— stricter rules on how brands promote content through influencers, demanding clear labels such as “” on posts

— a ban on offering minors “pay-to-win” or “pay-to-progress” features, and a requirement for in-game virtual currencies to show their real-world value

— platforms must remind consumers when a free trial period ends with details about the end date and how much it will cost to continue

— access to human customer service operators when users demand it.

EU consumer protection chief Michael McGrath has previously said the new rules aim to “step up our fight against unfair commercial practices”, pointing to data that shows 97 percent of popular platforms use dark patterns.

The European Consumer Organisation’s Agustin Reyna said the proposal is a “much-needed tool to give consumers back control of how much time and money they spend online”.

– ‘Safety net’ –

Questions have been raised over the EU’s expanding digital rulebook after Brussels unveiled plans to ban children under 13 from social media, and force companies to make platforms safe for use by minors — in addition to sweeping rules already in place under the Digital Services Act.

But Spanish EU lawmaker Laura Ballarin Cereza said the proposal aimed to make a “safer online space for everyone, children and adults alike”, adding it will “fill the gaps” as “consumer law is meant to act as a safety net”.

The EU also wants users to know the full price of an order before checkout, banning a practice known as “drip pricing” where fees are hidden until the end.

The European Commission, the bloc’s digital watchdog, has faced pressure from EU lawmakers and consumer advocates who accuse it of failing to enforce its online content and competition rules.

“Strong rules only matter if they are properly enforced,” said the Euroconsumers group, which represents users’ rights across several EU countries.

NGO Finance Watch said the proposal on dark patterns goes “in the right direction, but they lack ambition to sufficiently protect consumers in financial services”.

The group also warned there were “significant holes” in the draft plans. “Firms could still pay influencers to promote risky investments,” it said.

Finance Watch in September raised concerns about financial influencers and the risks to consumers posed by “misleading” information.

World.title: Many AI companies will adopt advertising: ad chief Criteo
World.content:
Lisbon – Many AI platforms will end up eventually adopting advertising, the head of the online advertising agency Criteo told AFP Tuesday, as investors are focused on whether the technology will ever be profitable.

“I believe that a lot of AI platforms will find their way to advertising models over time,” said the group’s chief executive Michael Komasinski on the sidelines of the Web Summit in Lisbon.

“Advertising is the most scalable business model in the world. It has paid for most of the large platforms that we all use and enjoy today, whether it’s Google, Meta, Snapchat.

“The ad formats will continue to become more interesting, more innovative, and certainly more native to that conversational experience,” he added.

Pressure to boost revenue to cover its colossal spending pushed OpenAI to begin testing advertising in ChatGPT in February in the United States for free and low-cost tier subscriptions.

It has subsequently begun to progressively roll out ads worldwide, in cooperation with Criteo.

OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, which is set to imminently go public with a stock listing, has said it doesn’t plan to integrate advertising in its AI tools due to data protection concerns as well as to protect the interests of its users.

Microsoft has used ads in its public version of Copilot AI since 2023.

Perplexity has experimented with ads in the United States since 2024.

Google is considering integrating ads in Gemini.

Developing AI models and rolling them out requires massive investments.

The rally in AI-related stocks that has buoyed markets this year was testament to investor confidence, but both equity and bond investors have recently grown more wary as inflation and high interest rates are making the endeavour even more expensive.

Criteo works with OpenAI in 89 countries to develop advertising campaigns on AI chatbots.

Komasinski said some 3,600 brands have trialled AI advertising campaigns and they have noted a modest increase in their spending on ChatGPT.

He remains sceptical about AI agents being able to autonomously make purchases.

“It’s actually really easy to order unimportant things, and things that are very important you would tend to not delegate to a bot,” he said.

World.title: Late-arriving grooms put on notice as Kashmir's wedding chefs set 10 pm deadline for wazwan
World.content:
Representative image

Kashmir's traditional wedding chefs, popularly known as 'waza', have decided to stop serving the elaborate multi-course wazwan after 10 pm, citing long working hours and poor treatment at wedding functions.The decision was taken unanimously at a meeting held at a marriage hall in the Rajouri Kadal area of Srinagar. The chefs said they had been forced to work under difficult conditions for years, particularly because wedding feasts often get delayed by the late arrival of the groom and his relatives.Ghulam Nabi Waza, president of the Kashmir Waza Association, said the community had remained silent about its working conditions for too long."It takes several hours to prepare the dishes, and usually we work late into the night. Then we are expected to start serving lunch from around 1 pm till 6 pm, which is followed by dinner, which starts well into the night," Waza told news agency PTI.He explained that the situation becomes even more difficult when chefs are hired to prepare food at the bride's house. They often have to wait until the groom and his wedding party arrive, sometimes well past midnight, before they can begin serving the feast."There have been incidents where the maulvi left without solemnising the nikah because the groom did not turn up till 1 am. We are also humans. So we now set the 10 pm deadline," Waza said.Waza also criticised the growing trend of guests arriving late for wedding celebrations and urged people to change what he described as a bad habit."There are so many people attached with the wazwan, and they too have the right to dignified working hours," he added.Other chefs at the meeting also raised concerns about how they are treated by wedding hosts. One of them said they are often not given proper arrangements to rest despite working for long hours."For example, we are not provided a proper place to sleep. We work long hours and need some time to rest before we prepare ourselves for the next day's gruelling routine. The hosts should take care of that aspect," the chef said.

World.title: 2003 scandal resurfaces ahead of Uttarakhand polls: What is Harak Singh Rawat-Jenny case
World.content:
NEW DELHI: A two-decade-old controversy involving senior Congress leader and former Uttarakhand minister

has resurfaced ahead of the state's assembly elections next year. A woman identified as

has renewed her allegations of rape against Rawat and demanded a fresh DNA test to establish the paternity of her 23-year-old son.

The allegations, which first triggered a political storm in 2003, had forced Rawat to resign as a minister before a Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) probe gave him a clean chit in 2004.

Assam chief minister Himanta Biswa Sarma expressed support for Jenny, who is originally from Assam. After meeting her, Sarma described the alleged treatment she faced as âextremely wrong and reprehensibleâ and said he stood by her in her fight for justice.



Rawat, who currently heads the Congress's election management committee in Uttarakhand, has rejected the renewed allegations, maintained that he was cleared by the CBI and accused the BJP of reviving the controversy for political reasons ahead of the polls.

What are the allegations

Jenny has claimed that she arrived in Dehradun from Assam in October 2002, when she was 16. She alleged that a party worker took her to Rawat's residence in Yamuna Colony, where she stayed for around one-and-a-half to two months.





In an interview with ANI, she accused Rawat of sexually assaulting her and claimed that she subsequently became pregnant. She alleged that she was placed in a Nari Niketan (women's shelter) under the pretext of providing hostel accommodation, where she was kept among people with mental health conditions.

At a press conference, Jenny questioned the original investigation, claiming that she was not properly heard by the CBI and was made to sign documents without understanding their contents.

She said she had limited knowledge of Hindi at the time and struggled to understand the proceedings.

She also questioned the earlier DNA test, asking how it was conducted without collecting blood samples from her or her son.

âMy son is 23 years old today and has grown up without a father. I do not want anything for myself; I only seek justice for my son. I demand that the CBI re-investigate this case and that a new DNA test be carried out,â she said.

Jenny has submitted a written complaint to Uttarakhand DGP Deepam Seth, who forwarded it to the Dehradun SSP for further action. The inquiry has been assigned to Doiwala circle officer Vandana Verma.

How did the controversy first emerge

The case first surfaced in 2003, when Jenny gave birth to a child at a government hospital in Dehradun in June. She alleged that Rawat, then revenue minister in the Congress government led by chief minister Narayan Dutt Tiwari, was the child's father.

The allegations triggered a major political storm, forcing Rawat to resign. He also gave up his assembly membership and demanded a CBI investigation, saying he would stay away from public events until his name was cleared.

A subsequent CBI investigation and DNA test reportedly found that the child's DNA did not match Rawat's. He was given a clean chit in 2004.

World.title: Being underweight with high BP can be a problem too: Study
World.content:
Being underweight with high BP can be a problem too: Study

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

While obesity with hypertension is the most widely recognised high-risk category, a recent study has shown that being underweight with elevated blood pressure or hypertension may also be a high-risk sub-group in Asian populations.The study done in Japan and published in Hypertension Research, an open-source journal in the Nature group of journals, showed the combination of being underweight and having elevated blood pressure or hypertension was associated with increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events like heart attacks and strokes, particularly among women and among adults aged 40 and above. This is significant for India, where one in five men and women in the 15-49 age group is underweight (body mass index below 18.5)."Conventional prevention strategies for obesity with hypertension appropriately emphasise weight control and cardiometabolic risk reduction; however, the same approach may not be sufficient for underweight individuals with elevated BP or hypertension," stated the study, suggesting the need for additional assessment for unintentional weight loss, malnutrition, low muscle mass, frailty, and underlying chronic disease for those who are underweight with hypertension.Potential management strategies may, therefore, include nutritional assessment and support, resistance exercise or muscle-strengthening interventions where appropriate, and individualised BP control that considers frailty, and symptoms like dizziness or fainting when rising from sitting or lying down.The association between being underweight and cardiovascular events and mortality has been observed in previous studies but significance of high blood pressure was not as well studied or understood. This is of particular significance in Asia where being underweight is relatively common and the distribution of BMI is different from Western populations. In India, the latest National Family Health Survey of 2023-24 showed about 20% of men and women above 15 years had elevated blood pressure or were taking medicine to control it.Understanding cardiovascular risk across the full range of BMI, rather than focusing exclusively on obesity, is expected to enhance understanding of risk stratification in hypertension. The study used the nationwise claims and health-check database of Japan for the period Jan 2005 to Oct 2023 and analysed 62.6 lakh adults without prior cardiovascular disease, chronic renal failure, dialysis, or antihypertensive medication use.

World.title: 2008 CRPF camp attack convict shot dead by unknown gunman in UP
World.content:
NEW DELHI: An unknown gunman shot dead

, an accused linked to the 2008 CRPF camp attack, on Tuesday. Sharif was killed in Rampur, UP with bystanders alleging he was shot 16 times. The police have initiated a manhunt for the shooter/s.

Seven CRPF personnel and a rickshaw puller were killed in a pre-dawn terror attack, plotted by

, on the CRPF Group Centre in Rampur on the night of December 31, 2007-Jan 1, 2008. In May 2025, unknown gunmen had killed Abu Saifullah Khalid, a key Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) operative and the mastermind behind the 2006 RSS headquarters attack and multiple terror strikes, including one on a CRPF camp in Uttar Pradesh.

Sharif, who belonged to Badanpuri-Khajuria village in Rampur, went by aliases of Suhail, Sajid, Anwar and Ali, according to police records.



He was lodged in Bareilly central jail and released last Nov.

Arrested in the case in the aftermath of the attack, a UP court had in 2019 convicted Sharif and five others including two Pakistani nationals in the case. Four including Sharif were subsequently sentenced to death after they were found directly involved in the attack.

In Oct 2025, the Allahabad High Court, however, overturned the death sentences but upheld their conviction under the Arms Act for possessing prohibited weapons, sentencing them to ten yearsâ rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs 1 lakh each. The HC had noted procedural lapses by the police like failure to conduct a Test Identification Parade (TIP) and also found lapses in the handling of physical evidence, observing that firearms, cartridges, and grenades allegedly recovered from the scene were not securely preserved or properly traced through the chain of custody.

Key witnesses who should have verified storage and transfer of evidence were not examined.

World.title: Sonia Gandhi memoir: From Parliament attack to anti-terror bill passage, ex-Cong chief recalls conversations with Vajpayee
World.content:
NEW DELHI: In her memoir, "Belonging: A Journey of Love," released in India on Tuesday, senior Congress leader Sonia Gandhi has recalled several conversations with former Prime Minister and late BJP leader

.

Most of the anecdotes recounted by Sonia Gandhi date back to 1999-2004, when Vajpayee was Prime Minister and she was the leader of the opposition in the Lok Sabha.

Parliament attack

In her memoir, Sonia Gandhi recalled being "terrified" and calling PM Vajpayee to enquire about his safety after explosions and gunshots rang out during the terrorist attack on Parliament on December 13, 2001.

According to the Congress Parliamentary Party chairperson, he assured her that he was safe at home and later told many of his colleagues âappreciatively that I had been the first to call him.â



How Sonia Gandhi's views about Vajpayee changed

The former Congress president, who was leading the grand old party at the time, also recalled being "afraid" to âstand up and confrontâ leaders of the ruling BJP-led coalition, who had long viewed her as âthe foreign-born daughter-in-law of the Nehru-Gandhi familyâ â a reference to her country of birth, Italy.

Nearly four months after her December 2001 conversation with Vajpayee, Sonia Gandhiâs perception of the-then Prime Minister changed when the two leaders came face to face over the Prevention of Terrorism Ordinance (POTO).





In March 2002, the Vajpayee government convened a special joint sitting of Parliament to pass POTO into law after the legislation was defeated in the Rajya Sabha.

Sonia Gandhi drew a contrast between the BJPâs opposition to the legislation when the Congress was in office and the saffron party's stance when it was in government.

âIt was a measure the BJP's heavyweights had vigorously opposed as anti-democratic in 1985 when it had been brought into existence by our government to counter the Punjab insurgency,â she writes.

The Congress, in opposition at the time, argued that the ordinance âhad proved ineffective in dealing with terrorism, while giving the police wide-ranging powers that could be misused against our citizens."

She recounted that the joint sitting was held in the Central Hall of the old Parliament building, which was replaced by the new Parliament complex inaugurated in May 2023. She described the hall as âa much larger and more intimidating spaceâ, with "imposing" portraits of leaders of the freedom struggle adorning its walls.

âPrime Minister Vajpayee had chosen not to speak on this vitally important issue. Towards the end of the session, when the Speaker called out my name, I walked to the podium, full of trepidation. I had just finished reading out my speech, when the Speaker surprised everyone by calling out the name of the Prime Minister.â

Vajpayee then appeared in the Central Hall, âhis expression sullenâ, and began speaking. According to Sonia Gandhi, his speech focused not on the legislation but on questioning her âinexperience and lack of skill in oratoryâ.

âHe had taken offence at my asking whether he would âuphold the prestige of his high officeâ or be âsubmissive and weak in his leadershipâ. So that was his purpose in returning to the House! How dare I question his leadership abilities, who was I to place him in the dock?

âHe launched into a full-blown attack on my inexperience and my lack of skill in oratory, berating me so that our MPs rose to their feet in protest. The other side did the same, and soon all were not only vociferously shouting one another down but almost coming to blows.

I cannot deny I felt wounded,â Gandhi writes in the book.

The joint sitting ended with the passage of the bill, which was later repealed by the Congress-led UPA government in 2004.

When Sonia Gandhi felt her criticism of Vajpayee had gone 'too far'

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

A few months later, when Sonia Gandhi saw that Vajpayee had âaged visibly and was looking far from wellâ, she felt she had âgone a bit too farâ in her criticism of him.

â...he was a veteran leader, and though we belonged to opposing ideologies, he was the prime minister, and I should have been more moderate in criticising him,â she writes.

The 526-page memoir, published by HarperCollins India, traces Sonia Gandhiâs life, from her childhood in post-war Italy and marriage into the Nehru-Gandhi family to the assassination of her husband, Rajiv Gandhi, and her eventual entry into politics.

(With PTI inputs)

World.title: 'Silent on hate crimes against Indians': MEA tears into US agency over religious freedom report
World.content:
NEW DELHI: India on Tuesday strongly criticised the United States Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF) over its remarks on the alleged targeting of religious places, including Gurudwaras, churches and mosques, in the country.

Responding to a question from ANI, ministry of external affairs (MEA) spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal described the USCIRF as a âbiased and ill-informed organisationâ with a âblatantly political agendaâ.

He also accused the US-based body and its commissioners of remaining silent on attacks on religious places in the United States, as well as hate crimes and racial abuse targeting the Indian community there.

âIt is particularly telling, and you must note that the USCIRF and its commissioners have consistently kept silent on attacks on religious places in the United States, as well as on hate crimes and racial abuse that are targeted at the Indian community in the United States,â Jaiswal said.

Also read:

âPrejudiced entities like the USCIRF can hardly be taken seriously,â he added.

World.title: Top news of the day: Three injured after terrorists open fire on CRPF personnel in Kulgam; Cabinet approves development of North and South Block complex as museum; and more
World.content:
J&K attack: Three injured after terrorists open fire on CRPF personnel in Kulgam

Three CRPF personnel were injured as motorcycle-borne terrorists opened fire in south Kashmir’s Kulgam on Wednesday (November 11, 2026). Initial reports suggested that terrorists opened fire at a checkpoint around 2.15 p.m.

Cabinet nod to development of Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum with project cost of ₹3,230 crore

The Union Cabinet, in a meeting chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday (November 11, 2026), approved the development of the Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum through adaptive reuse of the North and South Block complex in Delhi, at an estimated total project cost of ₹3,230 crore.

Firecrackers still Delhi’s top pollutant after Deepavali, IITM finds

Firecrackers emerged as the biggest contributor to Delhi’s air pollution on both Monday (November 9, 2026) and Tuesday (November 10), accounting for 71.1% and 29.8% of the pollution load, respectively, according to source-apportionment estimates by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM).

Yogi Adityanath dismisses Deepavali pollution concerns, says it will subside

Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath on Wednesday (November 11, 2026) defended the bursting of firecrackers during Deepavali, saying people should be allowed to celebrate the festival without restrictions. He dismissed concerns over the pollution caused by firecrackers, arguing that it could be addressed, while accusing critics of overlooking pollution caused by corruption.

Several coaches of Sairang-Kolkata Express train derail at Digaru in Assam

Several coaches of Kolkata-Sairang Express train derailed at Digaru railway station in Assam early Wednesday (November 11, 2026) after the loco pilot failed to control the train’s speed while giving precedence to another train. All passengers are safe and no injuries were reported, Northeast Frontier Railway said.

Tamil Nadu may approach Supreme Court seeking greater powers for Cauvery Water Management Authority

Frustrated that the Cauvery Water Management Authority (CWMA) does not have the power to enforce its orders, Tamil Nadu is contemplating approaching the Supreme Court with a prayer that the Authority be given teeth. It wants the Authority to be modelled along the lines of the Bhakra Beas Management Board (BBMB), a case of which has been mentioned in the Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal’s report (Volume V).

Keralam to launch Family Sustainability Mapping to identify children in high-risk environments

The Keralam government will take steps to implement ‘Family Sustainability Mapping’ across the State to identify, at an early stage, children living in high-risk environments, Minister for Women and Child Development Bindhu Krishna has said.

Illegal oocyte collection racket: 27 ART centres inspected across Telangana, notices issued to seven hospitals

The Telangana Health Department has intensified its investigation into the alleged illegal oocyte (egg) collection racket, with inspections conducted at 27 of the 44 identified Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART) facilities across the State. Officials have detected 13 regulatory violations in seven hospitals and issued show-cause notices to their managements.

Vijayasai Reddy launches Parivartana Rajaneethi Party, vows to end ‘two-family’ politics in Andhra

Former YSR Congress Party (YSRCP) Rajya Sabha member V. Vijayasai Reddy on Wednesday (November 11, 2026) launched the Parivartana Rajaneethi Party (PRP) in Vijayawada, declaring that its principal objective would be to end the dominance of two political families in Andhra Pradesh and create opportunities for a new generation of leaders.

Two days past Deepavali, NPCI yet to announce a date for UPI MDR rollout

Two days since Deepavali, the National Payments Council of India is yet to notify a new date for the implementation of the Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on UPI transactions and The Hindu has learnt that “there is no announcement on this at the moment”. When it had put the proposed additional charge on hold nearly a month ago, the NPCI had said the new date would be announced “immediately” after Deepavali. The new rate was originally supposed to have been implemented on October 15.

Hardik Pandya traded to Punjab Kings in exchange of Arshdeep Singh ahead of IPL 2027

Hardik Pandya’s second stint with Mumbai Indians (MI) has come to an end, with the five-time champion franchise agreeing to trade its captain to Punjab Kings (PBKS) in exchange for India left-arm pacer Arshdeep Singh ahead of the 2027 Indian Premier League (IPL).

Khawaja withdraws from book interviews amid Sandpapergate row; ACA urges end to online abuse

Under-fire Usman Khawaja has withdrawn from interviews promoting his autobiography after facing criticism, while the Australian Cricketers’ Association (ACA) has urged an end to the furore that has been reignited following his claims that the entire team was involved in the 2018 ball-tampering scandal.

World.title: Opposition slams KCHR chairperson appointment amid allegations of search panel bypass and resignations
World.content:
A political controversy has erupted over the appointment of Vinodkumar Kallolikkal as chairperson of the Kerala Council for Historical Research (KCHR) with some members of the government-appointed search committee alleging that the prescribed selection process was bypassed.

Two members of the panel have formally objected to the appointment, stating that Dr. Kallolikkal’s name was neither proposed nor discussed at any of its meetings. Besides, three prominent historians have resigned from the KCHR executive council.
