Samushia supported his motion by citing the Organic Law on the Constitutional Court and the court’s rules of procedure. He sought to convince the judges that the law provides for a separate stage of examining evidence, which must take place before the question-and-answer session.

Under Article 20, paragraph 6 of the Constitutional Court’s rules of procedure, “after examining the evidence, the presiding judge gives the parties the right to question each other”.

“Put simply, they are trying to suppress political parties. That is exactly what is happening here from a legal point of view,” Samushia told the full bench of judges.

He urged the court not to skip this crucial stage, invoking the principles of a fair trial and the binding requirements of the law.

Other opposition parties backed Samushia’s motion, saying they had also planned to make a similar request.

From the outset, Constitutional Court Judge Revaz Nadaraya did his utmost to portray the motion as unfounded.

“So you want to start by examining the documents attached to the case file? Open all of them?” the judge asked.

“Yes,” Samushia replied.

“Criminal procedure law works differently here,” Judge Nadaraya insisted, showing no intention of backing down.

He was referring to the inquisitorial principle, arguing that, unlike in ordinary courts, the parties in the Constitutional Court do not have the exclusive right or responsibility to obtain or request evidence. The court itself plays the leading role in this process.

“The adversarial principle has not been abolished along with the inquisitorial principle,” Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Coalition for Change, interjected from his seat. “We must not skip this stage.”

“Are you suggesting that we open and watch every link? View programmes lasting half an hour or more?” Judge Nadaraya asked again. [*Georgian Dream’s application relies primarily on the findings of the parliamentary investigative commission, but it also includes numerous links. You can see how many by following this link – JAMnews.]

“The claimant should specify the exact minute and second in each programme. That way, we can save the court’s time,” Samushia insisted, sticking firmly to his position.

“What do I have to do with the events of 7 November? I was a first-year student” – Berdia Sichinava

Berdia Sichinava, a representative of the party founded by former prime minister Giorgi Gakharia, who previously served in Georgian Dream, also joined the discussion.

He pointed to what he described as the absurdity of holding him accountable and scrutinising him over cases in which he himself, as a prosecutor, had brought charges against the previous government.

“Take the case of Nora Kvitsiani, for example, which the investigative commission’s report mentions. Are the accusations directed at me, Berdia Sichinava? I was the prosecutor who issued a ruling in 2016 recognising that Nora Kvitsiani’s rights had been violated. I took part in the proceedings that ultimately led to her acquittal.”

He also referred to the case of Sulkhan Molashvili:

“I would like to know whether the case of Sulkhan Molashvili concerns me too. I was the prosecutor who recognised his family as victims and returned their country house to them.”

One of the main arguments in Georgian Dream’s application is that the United National Movement introduced systematic torture and inhuman treatment in penitentiary institutions while in power, and that the party should therefore face a ban. The application cites several high-profile cases from the previous administration, including those of Nora Kvitsiani and Sulkhan Molashvili. However, Georgian Dream does not specify which evidence relates to each individual. Instead, it claims that all the evidence applies equally to everyone named in the case. Sulkhan Molashvili was the former head of the Chamber of Control. Authorities arrested him in 2004, and he later said that he had suffered torture and inhuman treatment. Nora Kvitsiani was arrested after a special operation in the Kodori Gorge in 2006. Her arrest and prosecution formed part of wider concerns about repressive measures against opponents of the government then in power.

“What do I have to do with the events of 7 November? I was a first-year student,” Berdia Sichinava asked. [The application accuses the United National Movement of violently dispersing a protest on 7 November – JAMnews.]

“So what are we supposed to do now – read out the court rulings as well?” Revaz Nadaraya asked, seizing on a new argument and pointing out that the parliamentary commission’s report referred to specific court decisions.

“The court cannot base its decision on this report [by the parliamentary commission]. It could, however, rely on the facts presented in it – although those facts would still require further examination,” Gvaramia said. He reminded the judges that the report came from a temporary parliamentary investigative commission and represented a document containing political assessments.

“How dare you speak to me like that? I will file a motion to recuse you” – Gvaramia confronts judge

The discussion dragged on and repeatedly descended into heated arguments.

“Suppose I want to examine the records of my own questioning. How am I supposed to know whether you will rely on that testimony when reaching your final decision? How can I find that out without examining it together with you?” Gvaramia asked.

He also reminded the judge of previous motions that the court had rejected, pointing out that they concerned legal issues. [Since the start of the proceedings, the defence has submitted around 14 motions. The court has granted only one, and even then only in part – JAMnews.]

Judge Nadaraya grew angry and repeatedly interrupted Gvaramia.

“If we are going to argue, we will get nowhere. You have your procedural rights, and I have mine. I know them perfectly well. Please let me finish,” Gvaramia said.

“You seem to think you have the right to do whatever you please. That is simply not the case,” the judge replied.

“What tone are you using with me?! What makes you think you have the right to speak to me like that?! I will file a motion to recuse you. Please do not interrupt me!” Gvaramia exclaimed, no longer concealing his anger.

“Stick to the substance of the motion. There is no need to bring up what we have or have not granted in the past,” Nadaraya said sharply.

“It is not for you to decide what I can talk about!” Gvaramia retorted.

“It is precisely my job to decide that. Either you comply with the court’s instructions or…” The presiding judge left the sentence unfinished.

“I am explaining the grounds for my motion. Let me speak! You cannot conduct the proceedings in such a one-sided manner!” Nika Gvaramia insisted.

“Maya, would you like my seat?” Judge Nadaraya asks Maya Kopaleishvili

Constitutional Court Judge Revaz Nadaraya lost his temper again when Maya Kopaleishvili, an ally of Nika Gvaramia, tried to join the discussion. Kopaleishvili is a former Constitutional Court judge who frequently highlights cases in which judges have breached procedural rules.

Speaking from her seat, Kopaleishvili tried to explain why examining the evidence was important.

“Ms Kopaleishvili, perhaps I should give you my seat? Why are you speaking? Did you ask for permission to speak? Do you have some special privileges?” Judge Nadaraya asked sternly.

“I don’t have any, but apparently you do,” Kopaleishvili replied.

The judge did not allow Maya Kopaleishvili to put forward her arguments. Throughout the hearing, the presiding judge was particularly harsh towards her and repeatedly threatened to have her removed from the courtroom. He accused her of trying to discredit the court.

“There seems to have been a misunderstanding” – Eva Gotsiridze

“It seems there has been a misunderstanding,” Judge Eva Gotsiridze said, trying to make herself heard above the noise and defuse the tension. She explained that the examination of evidence actually formed part of the question-and-answer stage.

“For example, during cross-examination, you can ask: ‘What evidence supports the allegation that you are guilty?’” she suggested to the opposing side.

Gotsiridze repeated the argument that the Constitutional Court chairman had made several times. She noted that the court could not, for instance, check each of the 1,005 links listed in the footnotes to the application. She cited this figure as an example, although the actual number of links in the footnotes is indeed very large.

She also recalled another argument raised by a fellow judge: some of the evidence consisted of court rulings, and “you are hardly going to ask us to review those as well”.

“Then why does the examination of evidence stage exist at all? Why do other cases include it?” Nika Gvaramia asked Gotsiridze.

In response, Eva Gotsiridze said that lawmakers could not have anticipated exactly how proceedings before the Constitutional Court would unfold in practice when they drafted the legislation. She again stressed that the examination of evidence was “woven into the question-and-answer stage, particularly when the parties question each other”.

Maya Kopaleishvili also wanted to respond to this clarification. However, the presiding judge once again refused to let her speak.

“You are not allowing me to comment on this motion. That is wrong,” Kopaleishvili told Judge Nadaraya.

“Yes, yes, that’s right! Absolutely right! Enough has been said already,” the judge replied.

“Do you know what this tells us? It tells us that the court… is afraid,” Kopaleishvili retorted.

“Ms Kopaleishvili, this is the second time you have said that someone is afraid. I will have you removed from the courtroom! Out!” the judge snapped.

“Mr Chairman, are you trying to intimidate me now? Do I look like someone who can be intimidated?” Kopaleishvili replied, refusing to back down.

“No, no – I have absolutely no such intention,” the judge replied. But he still did not give her the floor.

No separate stage for examining evidence: the court’s ruling on the motion

After the heated exchanges, the panel of judges withdrew to deliberate. The half-hour they had requested stretched into an hour.

“Granted in part,” the judges announced when they returned to the courtroom. They explained that they would consider any evidence whose relevance to the case became disputed. However, they would not hold a separate stage devoted exclusively to examining evidence.

“The panel reached a unanimous decision,” Judge Nadaraya stressed.

“A legal absurdity”: the court rejects the opposition’s second motion

Before Nadaraya, who appeared pleased with the decision, could resume the hearing, Nika Gvaramia asked to speak and submit a second motion.

He proposed that, if the court upheld the application, it should delay enforcement of its ruling by at least one month. All the opposition parties joined the motion.

Gvaramia explained that this period would allow the parties to apply to the European Court of Human Rights for interim measures.

“Mr Gvaramia, you spoke for so long and presented so many arguments that you could write a separate article about them. These issues require examination and analysis. In my view, we cannot decide this today. It would be irresponsible. Let us leave these motions without consideration: rejecting them or granting them would be equally irresponsible,” Constitutional Court Judge Eva Gotsiridze replied.

“What kind of research would that require? If I had proposed something that called for setting up an entire scientific institute to resolve a single question, then, well, I am not quite that ambitious,” Gvaramia retorted.

Representatives of the ruling party opposed the motion. Archil Gorduladze argued that granting it would amount to prejudging the court’s final verdict.

“If the court grants this motion, it will effectively announce in advance that it intends to set a specific deadline – ‘X’ or ‘Y’ – for enforcing its decision. Nothing like this exists in legal practice,” Gorduladze said.

“If anything truly has no precedent in legal practice, it is banning five different political parties in a single court case,” Gvaramia replied.

The court rejected this motion too. Despite Eva Gotsiridze’s comment, the full bench reached its decision immediately, without even withdrawing to deliberate.

“Granting this motion has no constitutional or legal basis. It would be a legal absurdity,” Revaz Nadaraya said, stressing that “the full bench is unanimous in its position”.

He explained that the court could decide whether to delay enforcement in its final ruling, so there was no need for a preliminary decision.

Where does the state end and the ruling party begin? The question-and-answer session

After the court had dealt with the motions, the question-and-answer session began. Judge Vasil Roinishvili asked the first questions.

He asked Archil Gorduladze to clarify where the boundary between the state and the ruling party lay, and to explain how far a political party should be held responsible for government decisions and actions.

Gorduladze said that the state and the party were not the same thing. However, he argued that a party bears responsibility for the laws and political course that its representatives help shape. He cited the foreign agents law as an example, noting that Georgian Dream had still secured a mandate from voters in the election despite passing it.

Roinishvili raised an argument put forward by the opposition: responsibility for criminal acts should rest with the individual officials involved, not with the political party itself. Gorduladze replied that human rights violations under the United National Movement government had not been isolated incidents. He said an entire system had encouraged criminal behaviour and protected those responsible.

Judge Eva Gotsiridze then took over the questioning. She asked Gorduladze to clarify whether a party should be held responsible for failing to distance itself from its leaders’ actions or for failing to respond appropriately to their behaviour.

She also noted that most of the people mentioned in the case had faced criminal charges only after the change of government. The opposition regarded this as a leading question.

Gotsiridze also asked about the meaning of the term “constitutional order”. She wanted to know whether Euro-Atlantic integration, enshrined in Article 78 of the Constitution, could be considered an integral part of the constitutional order, and whether violating this provision could provide grounds for banning a political party.

Giorgi Kakhiani, another representative of Georgian Dream, replied that the court should interpret Article 78 alongside other constitutional provisions. Tornike Cheishvili, meanwhile, described it as a transitional provision designed to achieve a temporary goal.

The judge then asked: if the government violates Article 78, does that amount to a breach of the constitutional order? And could it justify banning a political party? The question prompted laughter in the courtroom.

Gotsiridze raised several more issues, including the circumstances in which a party could be required to distance itself from the actions of its own leaders. She postponed hearing the answers until the following day.

“The decision has already been made – they are just trying to dress it up nicely”: reactions after the hearing

After the hearing, Georgian Dream accused the opposition of turning the proceedings into a performance.

“They are trying to turn a legal process into something resembling a televised debate or show. They know perfectly well that their unconstitutional actions have absolutely no legal basis. They are trying to achieve their goals through demagoguery alone,” Archil Gorduladze said.

The opposition, meanwhile, focused on the question of examining evidence.

“The way the court is handling the evidence raises serious questions. I do not know how it intends to resolve this situation. Essentially, it has simply skipped an entire stage of the proceedings. This is completely unacceptable and does not comply with the law,” Nika Gvaramia said after the hearing.

He added that the decision to ban the parties had effectively already been made: “Now they are just trying to make the whole thing look respectable – rather like trying to make a corpse look presentable.”

“The Constitutional Court operates under the inquisitorial principle: it must examine all the evidence, including material that the parties themselves have not submitted but which is necessary for a well-founded decision. However, the court must examine this evidence during the proceedings, with the parties present, rather than behind closed doors in the judges’ deliberation room,” former judge Maya Kopaleishvili wrote on social media after the court refused to let her speak during the hearing.

During the hearing itself, she had warned the judge that if he refused to let her speak in court, she would present her arguments publicly on Facebook.

In her view, the court should have prepared better for a case involving a ban on political parties. “The court could have included a special section in its rules of procedure, for example, setting out how it should examine evidence.”

Berdia Sichinava said the proceedings had only made the court’s alleged bias more apparent. He added that the judges’ haste to reach a decision had also become unmistakable.

“Of course, there can be no other conclusion. This is a fundamental issue. A case of such importance to the country cannot proceed without examining the evidence. I am certain that the question-and-answer session will make it even clearer that this is all nothing but a bluff.”

The court will resume hearings on the application on 11 November. Further sessions are also scheduled for 12 and 13 November.

The Constitutional Court in Batumi began hearing the case to ban political parties on 21 October. The stage at which the parties presented their explanations and arguments has already concluded.

Last week, the court took a 10-day break to mark its 30th anniversary. The judges celebrated the occasion alongside senior representatives of the Georgian Dream party.

Georgia party ban trial: Day 9

World.title: ‘This restraining measure cost man his life’: Armenia debates opposition figure’s death in prison
World.content:
Death of opposition politician in Armenian prison

Arsen Gevorgyan, an opposition politician, died this morning at a prison in Armenia. Gevorgyan had stood as a candidate for head of the Stepanavan community in local elections, representing the opposition Strong Armenia party. However, authorities arrested him on suspicion of vote-buying just days before the election.

The prison authorities have not disclosed the cause of his death. Media outlets reported that Gevorgyan had apparently suffered a heart attack. His relatives said he had never “complained of any health problems”.

The opposition Strong Armenia party blamed the authorities for Arsen Gevorgyan’s death. It said his arrest on “groundless charges” formed part of a “smear campaign”.

“Those who ordered the unjustified discrediting and arrests of hundreds of people bear responsibility for the death of yet another opposition figure in prison,” representatives of Strong Armenia said.

Human rights defenders are calling for a thorough investigation into the circumstances of Arsen Gevorgyan’s death.

The issue has also sparked widespread discussion on social media. Some users argue that the authorities imposed an excessively harsh pre-trial measure on the opposition politician, which may have contributed to his death. They therefore hold the Armenian authorities responsible.

Stepanavan was the only community where Strong Armenia, led by pro-Russian businessman Samvel Karapetyan, fielded a candidate in the local elections. Authorities detained Arsen Gevorgyan, who was running for head of the community, on 21 October – four days before the election. A court ordered his pre-trial detention for two months that same day. According to the Anti-Corruption Committee, Gevorgyan had bribed several dozen voters, urging them to vote for Strong Armenia. He denied the charges. His party colleagues, meanwhile, described the case as political persecution.

What the authorities have said

The Penitentiary Service said that Arsen Gevorgyan, born in 1980, who was being held at the Nubarashen penitentiary, suffered a sudden deterioration in his health early in the morning. The medical officer on duty administered first aid.

“An ambulance was called at around 07:55. At approximately 08:30, medical staff pronounced Arsen Gevorgyan dead,” the statement said.

The authorities also said that Gevorgyan had not complained about his health during his time in the facility.

Journalists asked Justice Minister Srbui Galyan today who would be held accountable if an investigation found that Gevorgyan had not received adequate medical care. Galyan did not answer the question. However, she confirmed that Gevorgyan had not complained about his health while in the penitentiary.

“Unfortunately, incidents like this happen both around the world and in penitentiary institutions,” the minister said, offering her condolences to Gevorgyan’s family.

According to Galyan, 20 inmates died in penitentiary institutions in 2025 and four in 2026.

The Investigative Committee has opened a criminal investigation into Arsen Gevorgyan’s death. A forensic medical examination will follow.

Human rights defender’s view

Daniel Ioannisyan, a human rights defender and coordinator of the NGO Union of Informed Citizens, says the authorities must conduct a “thorough and transparent investigation” into the circumstances of Arsen Gevorgyan’s death.

In particular, he wants answers to the following questions:

“Did Gevorgyan have any chronic illnesses that he had reported to the prison administration?

When did Gevorgyan’s health begin to deteriorate? When did he (or his cellmates) alert prison staff? How did the staff respond, and exactly what steps did they take, minute by minute?

When did medical personnel learn about the problem, and what measures did they take, minute by minute?”

“The public should receive answers to these questions as soon as possible,” Ioannisyan wrote on his Facebook page.

Reactions on social media

Most comments on social media express outrage over the opposition politician’s death and the court’s decision to remand him in custody.

Here are some examples:

“Another political murder.”

“Look, the leader of Strong Armenia is to blame. He provided the money for distributing bribes during the election campaign. What does Nikol [Pashinyan] have to do with it?”

“Far more dangerous criminals are walking free, while they jailed a man for offering a bribe. They could have simply placed him under house arrest.”

“Pre-trial detention was clearly a disproportionate measure. And this measure cost a man his life. Where could he have fled from your so-called justice? And who can actually escape your justice – assuming it even exists?”

“The state is responsible for the life of anyone in its custody. And the head of state is Nikol Pashinyan. Nikol, this happened under your system. You must answer for it: what condition was the man in, did he receive medical care, and why did a man whose guilt a court had not established die in prison?”

“This is another stark reminder of the tragic consequences that political persecution can bring. We demand a full, independent and impartial investigation into all the circumstances surrounding his death.”

World.title: Which sectors of Georgia’s economy are most dependent on Russia?
World.content:
What does Georgia depend on Russia for?

Since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, remittances and other financial inflows from Russia to Georgia have risen sharply. Although these flows have declined somewhat in subsequent years, Georgia remains heavily dependent on Russia in several sectors.

The Russian market remains particularly important for Georgian wine and other traditional export goods. Russia has also increased its share of Georgia’s natural gas supplies.

A study by BM.ge examines Russia’s influence on Georgia’s economy over the past five years. It covers data on foreign trade, foreign direct investment, remittances, tourism and the energy sector from 2021 to 2026.

This article provides a brief overview of the study’s main findings.

Revenue from Russia has fallen, but dependence remains

One of the key indicators in the study is the ratio of revenue from exports to Russia, tourism from Russia and remittances from Russia to Georgia’s nominal gross domestic product (GDP).

According to BM.ge’s calculations, in 2022 these three sources accounted for 14.4% of Georgia’s GDP. By 2025, the figure had fallen to 5% – below the 6.2% recorded in 2021.

The main reason for the decline was a sharp drop in remittances from Russia. In 2022, people and businesses transferred $2.07bn from Russia to Georgia. By 2025, the figure had fallen to $468m.

Moreover, between January and September 2026, remittances from Russia fell by a further 11.5% compared with the same period a year earlier, reaching $304.8m.

However, these figures do not necessarily mean that Georgia’s overall economic dependence on Russia has declined by the same margin. The indicator does not account for imports from Russia, dependence on energy supplies or other economic ties.

Trade: imports are rising, while traditional exports remain concentrated in the Russian market

Between 2021 and 2025, trade between Georgia and Russia increased.

In 2025, Georgia’s exports to Russia totalled $749.3m, while imports from Russia reached $1.94bn. Total trade turnover stood at $2.69bn. Imports were approximately 2.6 times higher than exports.

Over the same period, Russia’s share of Georgia’s total exports fell from 14.4% to 10.3%. However, the picture looks different when it comes to exports of locally produced goods: Russia’s share of these exports rose from 17.7% in 2021 to 20.8% in 2025.

This means Russia remains an important market for goods produced in Georgia. Dependence is particularly high for traditional export products.

In 2025, Russia accounted for around 64% of Georgia’s wine exports and 56% of its exports of spirits. In the first nine months of 2026, Georgia exported $119.8m worth of wine and $92.9m worth of spirits to Russia.

According to the study, such a high concentration in the Russian market leaves Georgian producers vulnerable to changes in demand and potential trade restrictions.

Energy: Russia’s share of gas supplies has increased

One of the sectors most visibly dependent on Russia is energy, particularly natural gas supplies.

Citing data from GNERC (the Georgian National Energy and Water Supply Regulatory Commission), BM.ge reports that Georgia imported 397 million cubic metres of natural gas from Russia in 2021. By 2025, the figure had risen to 886 million cubic metres. Over five years, gas imports from Russia increased 2.2-fold.

As a result, Russia’s share of Georgia’s gas supplies rose from 15.3% to 27.9%. Nevertheless, Azerbaijan remained by far the largest supplier in 2025, accounting for 71.7% of Georgia’s natural gas imports.

Russia is also an important supplier of oil and petroleum products to Georgia. A key factor in this area is the oil refinery in Kulevi, which began operations in October 2025. Initially, the facility processed Russian crude oil.

The European Union added the refinery to its sanctions list in July 2026, but postponed the restrictions until 25 January 2027. According to the company that owns the facility, the refinery stopped processing Russian oil on 23 August 2026 and switched to non-Russian crude.

As for electricity, Russia supplied 62.4% of Georgia’s electricity imports in 2025.

However, these figures need to be considered in context: a significant share of the electricity imported from Russia goes towards supplying occupied Abkhazia.

According to BM.ge, around 74.5% of the electricity Georgia imported from Russia in 2025 went to Abkhazia.

Tourism: visitor numbers and revenue tell different stories

Russia remains one of the main sources of tourists for Georgia.

In 2025, Russian citizens made 1.58 million visits to Georgia, an 11.1% increase on the previous year. Between January and September 2026, they made 1.31 million visits, 4.9% more than in the same period a year earlier.

However, Russia’s share of Georgia’s tourism revenue has declined.

In 2022, Russia accounted for 25.3% of revenue from international travel. By 2025, this figure had fallen to 14.8%.

Georgia earned a total of $4.69bn from international tourism in 2025, with Russian visitors contributing $694m.

The study also notes that trends in arrivals from other countries affect the overall number of tourist visits.

Therefore, an increase in visits by Russian citizens does not necessarily mean that Russia’s share of Georgia’s tourism revenue is also growing.

Investment: Russia’s share of foreign capital remains relatively small

Russia accounts for a relatively small share of Georgia’s total foreign direct investment (FDI), compared with other economic indicators.

In 2021, Russian FDI in Georgia totalled $87.7m. By 2023, it had risen to $131.2m, before reaching $109.5m in 2025.

At the same time, Russia’s share of Georgia’s total FDI fell from 6.8% in 2021 to 5.8% in 2025.

In the first half of 2026, most Russian investment went into the property and construction sectors.

According to data that BM.ge obtained from Georgia’s National Statistics Office, 71.8% of Russian investment – amounting to $26.7m – went into real estate.

What does the study show? The key findings

The analysis concludes that falling revenue from Russia does not provide a complete picture of Georgia’s economic dependence on its northern neighbour.

On the one hand, Russia’s share of remittances and tourism revenue has declined, as has its share of Georgia’s total exports.

On the other hand, Russia’s share of Georgia’s natural gas supplies has increased, while it remains the main export market for Georgian wine and other traditional products.

The study’s author also stresses the importance of reducing economic vulnerability.

According to BM.ge’s analysis, this requires diversifying export markets, finding alternative energy suppliers and steadily reducing Georgia’s economic dependence on Russia.

The study also serves as a reminder that economic relations with Russia are not merely a commercial matter. Previous embargoes on Georgian goods have shown that Moscow can restrict access to its market for political reasons.

What does Georgia depend on Russia for? The Georgian-Russian border and the road towards Lars. Photo: Davit Pipia / JAMnews, 2022.

What does Georgia depend on Russia for?

World.title: Ukraine-Russia talks resume in Abu Dhabi after nine-month pause, with US mediation
World.content:
Russia-Ukraine talks resume

Trilateral talks between the United States, Ukraine and Russia aimed at ending the war in Ukraine resumed in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, on 10 November. The meetings will continue on 11 November.

The main issues on the agenda include security guarantees for the post-war period, a ceasefire and the future of Ukraine’s eastern territories.

This is the first meeting in this trilateral format since February 2026. The United States is mediating the talks.

Who is taking part in the talks?

Ukraine’s delegation is led by Rustem Umerov, head of the Foreign Intelligence Service. Russia’s delegation is led by Vladimir Medinsky, an aide to President Vladimir Putin. US President Donald Trump is represented by his special envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.

At the initial stage, the Ukrainian delegation held meetings with representatives from the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission. The talks then continued in a trilateral format involving Ukraine, the US and Russia.

According to Rustem Umerov, Ukraine’s main priorities include ending the fighting, securing reliable post-war security guarantees, rebuilding the country’s economy and resolving humanitarian issues.

At the start of the meeting, US representative Jared Kushner said recent contacts had helped narrow the differences between the sides. “He [Trump] asked us to make an extra effort to find a solution that, hopefully, will end the war and put both sides in a much stronger position, giving them the opportunity to realise the full potential of their countries,” Kushner said.

Meanwhile, Russian delegation head Vladimir Medinsky expressed hope that the talks would bring progress towards peace, in the interests of the people of both countries.

Donetsk and post-war security guarantees

One of the most difficult issues in the negotiations concerns control over territories in eastern Ukraine, particularly in Donetsk region.

Russia demands that Ukraine surrender the parts of Donetsk region it still controls. Kyiv, however, refuses to give up land that Ukrainian forces have spent years defending.

At a briefing on 9 November, an unnamed US official said both sides had shown some flexibility on territorial issues during closed-door discussions.

However, the official stressed that they could not reach an agreement on this issue until they had established what the post-war security arrangements would look like.

“They will not be able to resolve the issue of Donetsk or the territorial question until they understand what the post-war security architecture will look like. It is important to understand that neither issue can be finally agreed without the other,” the US official said.

According to the official, security guarantees for Ukraine could include a mechanism similar to Articles 4 and 5 of the NATO treaty, providing for consultations and defensive assistance in the event of a security threat.

A senior Ukrainian official told Reuters that Kyiv was not discussing territorial concessions. The official said the issue could only be addressed by the countries’ leaders and only in the context of providing Ukraine with appropriate security guarantees.

Europe seeks a role in the talks

Ahead of the trilateral meeting in Abu Dhabi, representatives of Ukraine, the US, the EU, NATO, the UK, France, Germany and Italy also gathered in the city.

On 9 November, following a conversation with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said:

“The European Union will be represented, together with our partners.”

She also backed efforts to restore freedom of navigation in the Black Sea and called for an end to attacks on food and energy infrastructure.

European leaders insist that Europe itself must have a say in decisions concerning the security of the continent.

In their view, lasting peace in Ukraine will be impossible without reliable security guarantees.

Russia, however, said that the ongoing talks in Abu Dhabi should involve only Russia, Ukraine and the United States, with European representatives excluded from the meetings.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the Americans had their own channels of communication with the Europeans, as did the Ukrainians.

Why have the talks resumed now?

The previous trilateral meetings between the US, Russia and Ukraine on the war took place in January and February 2026. The latest round was held in Geneva on 17–18 February, but the sides failed to reach an agreement.

One reason for the pause was the war between the US, Israel and Iran, which shifted Washington’s attention away from Ukraine to other developments.

On Thursday, 5 November, Donald Trump met Kirill Dmitriev, a representative of the Russian president, at the White House.

Following the meeting, Trump said a “big deal” to end the war in Ukraine could be reached. He suggested the agreement would go beyond Ukraine and involve other European countries.

“This will be a big deal, and it won’t be limited to Ukraine alone. You could say that all of Europe will be involved,” Trump said.

Ukraine remains sceptical that Trump’s proposed deal could deliver a just peace. Kyiv insists that the war must not end at the expense of Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

The talks in Abu Dhabi will continue on 11 November. It remains unclear whether the sides will reach a concrete agreement. Their main disagreements still concern territorial issues and the format of security guarantees for Ukraine.

Russia-Ukraine talks resume

World.title: Why did Abkhazia’s president travel to Russia to be baptised? Several theories are circulating, all political
World.content:
President of Abkhazia Badra Gunba and his wife and two sons have been baptised. The ceremony took place at the Sretensky Monastery in Moscow, prompting mixed reactions on social media.

Some saw it as a sign of the Kremlin tightening its control over Abkhazia. Others linked it to the church schism within the republic, while a third group pointed to the lack of fully fledged Orthodox institutions in Abkhazia.

The ceremony was initially due to take place at another Moscow monastery, the Donskoy Monastery. However, the organisers moved it to the Sretensky Monastery because the Donskoy site lacked suitable baptismal facilities.

Metropolitan Feognost, who also heads the Russian Orthodox Church’s (ROC) Synodal Department for Monasteries and Monasticism, baptised the Gunba family. He began his career as a priest in Abkhazia many years ago and later provided extensive support to Abkhaz students at the Moscow Theological Seminary.

Badra Gunba was baptised under the name Bogdan. Sergei Kiriyenko, first deputy head of the Russian presidential administration and the Kremlin’s official overseeing Abkhazia, attended the ceremony. Gunba’s decision to be baptised as an adult reflects the relatively “democratic” approach to religion in Abkhazia. Some Abkhaz people are Orthodox Christians, others are Muslims, while some remain followers of the traditional Abkhaz belief in the god Anцэа. Even Orthodox parents often choose not to baptise their children as infants, allowing them to grow up and decide for themselves which faith to follow.

Abkhaz society generally welcomed the president’s baptism, but most people felt he should have undergone the ceremony in one of Abkhazia’s own churches rather than in Moscow.

Some social media users saw this as one of the consequences of a long-running conflict between the two unrecognised churches: the Abkhazian Orthodox Church, led by Father Vissarion, and the Holy Metropolis of Abkhazia, headed by Archimandrite Dorotheos.

In effect, Abkhazia currently has no officially recognised church. The republic’s religious institutions lack international recognition, just as Abkhazia itself does. The Russian Orthodox Church (ROC) does not even recognise the Abkhazian Church as autocephalous.

Archimandrite Dorotheos believes this is precisely why Badra Gunba travelled to Moscow to be baptised.

“This sends a signal to the entire Orthodox world: until the issue of the Abkhazian Church is resolved and a fully fledged institution of the Orthodox Church of Abkhazia is restored, even the republic’s top officials cannot receive the Sacrament of Baptism from an Abkhaz bishop, however much they might wish to. This is simply because the entire Orthodox community’s unwillingness to address the issue for 33 years has left our country, our people and its leadership without episcopal pastoral care,” Dorotheos said.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: ‘An example of shadow justice’: another letter from jailed former Georgian prime minister Garibashvili
World.content:
New letter from Georgia’s former prime minister in prison

Former Georgian prime minister Irakli Garibashvili, who is currently in prison, has described the decision to hold his trial behind closed doors as an example of “shadow justice” driven by fear.

In another letter sent from prison – probably his tenth – the politician, who served two terms as prime minister, again speaks of political persecution, selective justice and discrimination against him.

“‘This is a violation. Cases involving other individuals, whether in the same context or over similar charges, have generally been heard in open court. My trial, however, is taking place behind closed doors. This shows that the procedure is being used not to uphold the rule of law, but as an instrument of selective justice. It is a clear example of “shadow justice” and an attempt to prevent public scrutiny,’ Garibashvili writes.

The former prime minister says he intended to use the court hearings to speak about the pressure he had faced and the political persecution he had experienced.

“‘The authorities have made this decision out of fear, seeking to keep the proceedings shrouded in “darkness”. I want to make this clear: I have nothing to hide. That is why I insist that the trial be open and brought into the “light”.’

In another statement, Garibashvili recalls telling the judge at the previous hearing that he had faced psychological pressure and blackmail. He describes it as ‘psychological terror, torture, moral suffering and interference in political activity’.

The former prime minister claims that the defence was not allowed to submit to the court a letter containing threats and blackmail that he had received. His lawyers were also denied access to some of the case materials.

Garibashvili writes that the prosecutor’s office failed to launch an investigation, despite receiving information from him about possible signs of a crime. He says the opposite happened: authorities brought new charges against him in line with the ultimatum mentioned in his letter.

Garibashvili also alleges violations of Articles 3, 6 and 18 of the European Convention on Human Rights. These articles concern, respectively, the prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment, the right to a fair trial, and the limits on the use of restrictions on rights. The former prime minister claims that, taken together, these rights have been violated in his case.

Why is the trial being held behind closed doors?

On 2 November, the Tbilisi City Court began hearing the bribery case against Irakli Garibashvili on its merits. It was the first hearing that the former prime minister attended in person.

At the start of the hearing, he stressed the importance of an open and transparent trial and opposed holding the proceedings behind closed doors.

The prosecution asked the court to hold the hearing in private. It argued that the case involved classified procurement by the Ministry of Defence, required the questioning of other senior officials and contained personal data.

The defence objected, pointing out that courts had previously heard similar cases in public. Judge Tamar Mchedlishvili ultimately ruled that the hearing should take place behind closed doors.

Garibashvili’s letters from prison

Irakli Garibashvili, once a favourite of Georgian Dream’s honorary chairman and oligarch Bidzina Ivanishvili, was arrested in the courtroom on 12 January 2026.

For several months after his arrest, the former prime minister and his family remained silent and made no comments to the media.

On 17 August, the former prime minister sent his first letter from prison. It marked his first major public statement, in which he accused Bidzina Ivanishvili and the government of blackmail. “They left me no other choice; I have no option but to fight,” Garibashvili wrote.

According to the letter, he had been offered a deal: if he pleaded guilty to a new corruption charge, authorities would release him on condition that he never return to politics.

More letters followed.

In his subsequent letters, the former prime minister gradually shifted from a defensive stance to making political statements. He accused several senior officials, including Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, of orchestrating a political vendetta against him.

He also referred to more serious offences, including cases in which people had been driven to suicide. In addition, he said he had no intention of returning to politics.

In one of his most recent letters, he even reflected on his time in office.

Criminal cases against the former prime minister

Irakli Garibashvili currently faces charges in two criminal cases.

In the first, prosecutors charged him with laundering a particularly large amount of illicit income. On 12 January 2026, he pleaded guilty and reached a plea bargain with the prosecutor’s office. The court sentenced him to five years in prison and fined him one million lari.

In the second case, prosecutors accuse the former prime minister of accepting a particularly large bribe. According to the prosecution, Garibashvili received 750,000 lari in connection with classified procurement by the Ministry of Defence.

The case is linked to the criminal proceedings against former Defence Minister Juansher Burchuladze. Garibashvili denies the charges and describes them as politically motivated.

Harsh prison conditions

Irakli Garibashvili and his family have repeatedly spoken about the harsh conditions of his imprisonment. On 7 November, his brother-in-law, Lekso Tamazashvili, said that the former prime minister had seen his children only twice in the past 11 months.

He called on the Special Penitentiary Service to show compassion and allow the children to see their father.

Meanwhile, Garibashvili’s lawyer, Lili Gelashvili, said that authorities had cancelled a planned meeting between her client and his children. She linked the decision to the publication of letters Garibashvili had written in prison.

The Special Penitentiary Service rejected the lawyer’s claims. According to the agency, Garibashvili had already used all the visits allowed under the law, including two extended visits and standard short-term meetings.

The service explained that authorities treat any additional visits as a form of reward, and the head of the correctional facility has discretion over whether to grant them.

The agency also said that no additional visit had ever been scheduled, so there could have been no cancellation. The issue of restrictions on visits with his children first became public in late August. The circumstances were similar then: authorities cancelled a planned meeting between Garibashvili and his family, although the Penitentiary Service denied the report at the time.

New letter from Georgia’s former prime minister in prison

World.title: ‘Democrats do not see TRIPP as project exclusive to Trump administration’: opinion from Yerevan
World.content:
US midterm elections and implementation of TRIPP

The US midterm elections, in which the Democratic Party won control of both chambers of Congress, have also become a major topic of discussion in Armenia.

Government officials and experts are discussing the Democrats’ victory in the context of developments in the South Caucasus. In particular, they are focusing on the implementation of the Armenian-American TRIPP project (the “Trump Route”).

TRIPP (Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity) is a road that will connect Azerbaijan with its Nakhchivan exclave through Armenian territory. The project also aims to reopen regional transport links. As a result, Armenia will gain access to third countries via Azerbaijani territory. For several years, Yerevan and Baku failed to reach an agreement on the issue. Azerbaijan demanded a road that it called the “Zangezur Corridor”. Armenia’s authorities said they were ready to reopen all transport routes. However, Yerevan rejected the term “corridor”, which implies that the country would lose control – and therefore sovereign rights – over this territory. The two sides reached an agreement in Washington on 8 August. Under the deal, the road will remain under Armenian sovereignty, while the US will join the process as a business partner. The initiative took the name “Trump Route” after the mediator.

Armenian Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan stressed that national interests must come first in such matters. Individual political figures and teams may adjust the course of policy, he said.

“I am confident that what we are now doing with the US benefits the United States itself. I do not think the Democrats will have no interest in getting TRIPP built as soon as possible,” he emphasised.

Political analyst Tigran Grigoryan explained that US presidents often lose ground in midterm elections. According to him, their approval ratings usually decline during the first year or two in office, as public dissatisfaction with their policies grows.

Grigoryan described the Republicans’ midterm results as “a historic-scale fiasco”. Nevertheless, he does not expect any significant changes to the implementation of TRIPP.

“There is bipartisan consensus in the US on TRIPP. Democrats do not see TRIPP as a project exclusive to the Trump administration. They recognise its importance for the South Caucasus and for maintaining peace,” the political analyst said.

At the same time, he noted that Yerevan should do more work with its American partners, both at official and expert level. He said Armenia needed to make one message clear to them: “Under no circumstances must the implementation of the Trump Route be put at risk.”

“There will be no problems” – Armenia’s Security Council secretary

Speaking at the Third World Armenian Summit, Security Council Secretary Armen Grigoryan recalled that the Trump administration had developed the TRIPP project.

“However, I am confident that TRIPP is not simply Trump’s personal business project. It is also a business project for the state.”

Grigoryan said Armenia and the US had agreed on TRIPP at state level. He believes the project will encounter no problems during implementation.

Journalists asked the Security Council secretary whether he was concerned that, after the elections, Trump might turn his attention to domestic issues and lose interest in the South Caucasus.

“TRIPP is not an initiative that depends on any one administration or a single factor. It is an important agreement that aims, among other things, to eliminate a casus belli – a pretext for starting a war,” Armen Grigoryan replied.

“The US will also have opportunities” – US chargé d’affaires in Armenia

At the same summit, David Allen, the US chargé d’affaires in Armenia, also discussed the TRIPP project.

Allen noted that TRIPP aligns with the Armenian government’s Crossroads of Peace initiative, which aims to turn the country into a regional trade and transit hub.

“For the US, it creates commercial opportunities for American companies and advances our strategic interest in seeing the South Caucasus become a stable, prosperous and interconnected region.”

The diplomat said the US believes that trade links between neighbouring countries reduce the likelihood of war.

“When roads and railways cross borders, they carry not only goods but also trust.”

Comment

Political analyst Tigran Grigoryan says:

“Many people link the midterm election results to the US decision to go to war with Iran. That move had a significant impact on oil and fuel prices and, consequently, on consumers. However, in a broader sense, the events of the past two years led to this historic outcome.

What should we expect in the context of Armenia? I believe oversight of the Trump administration’s policies will become much stricter.

The US system of government is essentially designed so that no branch of power can impose its policies on another.

In theory, even if a Democrat-controlled Congress tries to restrict the president’s decisions, he retains the power of veto and the authority to issue executive orders. During his second term, for example, Obama often governed through executive orders, bypassing Congress on many issues. However, on many other issues, the administration cannot make progress without congressional involvement.

The Democrats’ main advantage is their oversight role. They will now control key committees in the House of Representatives. This means that Democrats will scrutinise all matters relating to TRIPP, including its funding.

They will also pay much closer attention to possible corruption. Reuters recently published an interesting report examining the business interests of Konstantin Sokolov, head of the TRIPP+ Foundation, in Armenia and the potential for conflicts of interest.

This could, for example, become an important area of scrutiny for the Democratic majority.

The TRIPP+ Foundation operates as a separate investment fund. Its main purpose is to finance the Trump Route project. The 52-year-old financier and investor Konstantin Sokolov also heads Dynamic Frontier Holdings. The company recently acquired the Teghut copper and molybdenum mine in Armenia. Since 2024, Sokolov has also owned a 20% stake in Viva Armenia, a mobile network operator. Some experts also suspect him of having links to Russia. Sokolov was born in Russia and moved to the US at the age of 21. He is known for investments in telecommunications, energy and financial services.

The Trump administration’s characteristic approach to foreign policy, often based on nepotism and favouritism, has attracted the Democrats’ attention. This includes the involvement of Jared Kushner, Steve Witkoff and other figures close to Trump in various matters. We should therefore expect Democrats to take a much closer interest in this issue.

Of course, we want TRIPP to be seen as more than just a project of the Trump administration. We need to strengthen that understanding. And we should take active steps to achieve this.”

Background

The Trump Route offers Armenia an opportunity to reopen regional transport links in practice. For Azerbaijan, it provides the shortest route connecting the country with Nakhchivan.

The 43-kilometre section running through Armenian territory will include a railway. A motorway, energy infrastructure and digital communications networks will also run along the same route.

All infrastructure located on Armenian territory will remain under Armenia’s sovereignty and jurisdiction.

The ratified framework agreement provides for the creation of the TRIPP Development Company, which will oversee the project’s development and implementation.

Initially, the US will own 74% of the company’s shares and Armenia 26%. After 49 years, if the parties extend their cooperation for a further 50 years, Armenia’s stake will rise to 49%.

On 7 November 2026, Armenia, the US and Azerbaijan issued a joint statement outlining steps to advance the TRIPP project as quickly as possible:

“The parties agreed to launch the first two trilateral technical planning groups, focusing on areas such as transportation and electricity transmission. Establishing these technical groups marks an important step towards resolving complex technical issues and moving on to the next stages of implementation, including ensuring connections with other regional infrastructure.”

According to the statement, the format brings together politicians and technical experts from the three countries to work jointly and help ensure stability, economic viability and commercial prosperity in the region.

The statement came from US Assistant Secretary of State for European and Eurasian Affairs Brendan Hanrahan, Armenian Deputy Foreign Minister for Foreign Affairs and International Trade Vahan Kostanyan, and Azerbaijani Deputy Foreign Minister Elnur Mammadov. However, they provided no further details.

US midterm elections and implementation of TRIPP

World.title: Have people in Georgia become more cautious about what they say on social media? Street survey in Tbilisi (video)
World.content:
Street survey on social media in Georgia

We asked people walking the streets of Tbilisi whether they or those close to them had recently become more cautious than before about expressing their opinions on social media.

Background

On 1 June 2024, a unit tasked with combating “hate speech” was established in Georgia. It monitors people’s statements in the public sphere. According to the Georgian Dream party, the unit aims to reduce hate speech and online campaigns involving insults.

Since the unit began its work, authorities have launched numerous administrative proceedings based on social media posts, affecting hundreds of people. Most received fines ranging from 1,500 to 6,000 lari, and some were fined more than once.

The law also provides for administrative detention, although courts generally try to avoid imposing it.

To date, authorities have used this measure only a handful of times – twice against the same person, journalist Vakho Sanaia. He is currently in detention. A court first sentenced him to 14 days in detention and later handed him a 30-day sentence.

Lawyers have described the initiative as an attempt to restrict freedom of expression and legalise censorship. Meanwhile, social media users have nicknamed the unit the “scrolling and screenshot department”, reflecting the nature of its work.

What did people in the survey say?

Respondents were almost evenly divided over whether these restrictions had affected them. Half said the fear was tangible, whether or not people felt ready to admit it openly.

The other half insisted that this repressive measure had made no difference to them or their social circles.

Here are some notable responses:

* “Lately, I’ve been weighing my words carefully. It’s not exactly conformism, but at some point – I see it among my acquaintances, and I notice it in myself too – a thought creeps in: ‘Maybe I’ll wait a little; perhaps all this will somehow blow over.’ There is fear involved! Perhaps people have simply become frightened. Do you see what I mean? And yet there is a certain line: once you cross it, there’s no going back.” This was the view of writer Aleko Shugladze, whom we met on the streets of Tbilisi while conducting the survey.

* “Personally, I don’t restrict myself at all. I don’t even try to edit the opinions I want to post in any way. Because if we start worrying today that saying something could get us into trouble, tomorrow even the thought of expressing an opinion could become punishable.”

* “In a way, it does affect people. Knowing that restrictions, fines and the risk of arrest exist has an impact. I’ve always been afraid. Of course, you also start having doubts – you wonder what might happen next and what the consequences could be.”

We also met people who knew nothing about the new unit. As often happens, many avoided the camera and declined to take part in the survey.

Others told us they had never really used social media much.

Street survey on social media in Georgia

World.title: Kyrgyzstan honey exports rise 76.3% in January-October 2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 11. Kyrgyzstan's honey exports increased by 76.3% year-on-year in January–October 2026, according to the press service of the Ministry of Water Resources, Agriculture and Processing Industry.

Kyrgyzstan exported 572.41 tons of natural honey during the first ten months of 2026, compared with 324.74 tons in the same period of 2025.

Meanwhile, dairy product exports totaled 33,466.58 tons in January–October 2026, down 3.2% year-on-year. The decline amounted to 1,115.46 tons compared with the same period of the previous year.

The figures indicate contrasting trends in the country's agricultural exports, with honey shipments expanding rapidly while dairy product supplies to foreign markets experienced a slight contraction.

Kyrgyzstan's dairy industry remains a fundamental pillar of its agricultural sector. The country produces over 1.7 million tons of raw milk annually, though only a relatively small fraction is processed into finished, value-added dairy goods. Exports of domestically produced dairy items are primarily directed to Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) partner countries, particularly Kazakhstan and Russia. Major export items include butter, cheese, ice cream, milk powder, and traditional fermented dairy beverages.

Concurrently, beekeeping represents a rapidly growing segment with high export potential. Kyrgyz honey is currently exported across Central Asia, the Middle East, and East Asia, including key markets such as Uzbekistan, China, the United Arab Emirates, South Korea, and Japan. Furthermore, authorization by the European Commission allows domestic producers to export Kyrgyz honey to the European Union market.

World.title: Azerbaijan participates in 30th World Investment Conference in Geneva (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 11. Azerbaijan's First Deputy Minister of Economy Elnur Aliyev attended the 30th World Investment Conference (WIC 2026) in Geneva, Switzerland, on November 10–11, the Ministry of Economy reported.

During the visit, Aliyev also met with the Deputy Director General of Vietnam's Foreign Investment Agency.

The conference was organized by the World Association of Investment Promotion Agencies (WAIPA).

As part of the conference, a Ministerial Roundtable was held on the theme "The Next Decade of Global Investment." At the event, the First Deputy Minister of Economy provided an overview of the favorable business environment established in Azerbaijan, the key priorities of the country's investment policy, and the measures being taken toward economic diversification. Attention was drawn to Azerbaijan's advantageous geographical location, its transport and logistics capabilities, and the opportunities created for investors. The importance of expanding international cooperation in the field of investment promotion, including the role of international organizations such as WAIPA, was emphasized.

WIC 2026 brought together government representatives, international organizations, and members of the business community from various countries. Discussions at the conference focused on global investment trends, attracting investment amidst shifting geopolitical and economic conditions, and strengthening international investment cooperation.

On the sidelines of the conference, Aliyev met with Deputy Director General of the Foreign Investment Agency of Vietnam Bui Thu Thuy.

During the meeting, the parties exchanged views on prospects for expanding trade and investment cooperation between Azerbaijan and Vietnam. Key topics included increasing mutual trade, exploring cooperation opportunities in sectors such as energy, transport and logistics, and tourism, as well as fostering ties between the business communities of the two countries.

World.title: Solidcore plans three new power plants with 96 MW capacity in Kazakhstan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 11. Solidcore Resources plc plans to build two solar power plants and one gas piston power plant in Kazakhstan with a combined capacity of 96 megawatts (MW), according to the company's announcement.

The projects are intended to strengthen the company's self-generation capacity and ensure a more reliable electricity supply for its production facilities while reducing its carbon footprint.

The planned facilities include the 23 MW Syrymbet solar power plant, which will partially cover the electricity needs of the Syrymbetproject, and the 25 MW Ertis solar power plant, which will supply part of the electricity consumed by Ertis POX, the company's hydrometallurgical plant.

The third project involves a 48 MW gas piston power plant in the area of the Osakarovka settlement in the Karaganda region. The facility is planned to be connected to Kazakhstan's national electricity grid and gas transmission system.

The new projects follow the company's ongoing efforts to expand in-house power generation. A 23 MW solar power plant was commissioned at the Varvara hub at the end of 2025. A 40 MW gas piston power plant is under construction and is scheduled to be commissioned by the end of 2026. Another solar power plant, with a capacity of 17 MW, is being developed in Kyzyl.

Once all six projects have been implemented, Solidcore's total installed capacity of self-generation facilities will reach 176 MW.

The company said that expanding in-house electricity generation forms part of its climate strategy, which currently aims to reduce direct and indirect greenhouse gas emissions from existing assets by 45% by 2030 and ensure that renewable sources account for 30% of its electricity consumption.

Solidcore plans to integrate its growth projects into these climate targets and develop a pipeline of decarbonization initiatives for them as part of its long-term growth strategy and its commitment to achieving carbon neutrality in the future.

According to the company, Solidcore and Kazakhstan's Ministry of Energy have signed a memorandum of understanding to coordinate cooperation in preparing and implementing these projects.

Under the memorandum, the ministry will, within its remit, coordinate interaction with relevant government bodies, consider the company's proposals and facilitate its engagement with KEGOC JSC and NC QazaqGaz JSC on technical solutions and obtaining technical specifications for grid and gas system connections.

The memorandum is framework in nature and does not provide for project financing, gas supply, electricity or capacity procurement, tariff setting, or state support measures.

"Reliable energy supply is the foundation for the sustainable development of our production projects in Kazakhstan. The development of in-house generation, including solar and flexible power, aligns with Solidcore's strategy to enhance operational efficiency and increase production while consistently reducing the carbon footprint of our facilities. We are grateful to our partners - the Ministry of Energy of the Republic of Kazakhstan, KEGOC JSC, NC QazaqGaz JSC, and all involved government authorities and quasi-government entities - for their open dialogue, and we look forward to a constructive partnership in preparing and executing these projects," said Kanat Dosmukametov, CEO of Solidcore Eurasia and COO of Solidcore Resources.

The company noted that the specific sites, connection arrangements, technical parameters and implementation schedules would be determined following pre-project and design work, the issuance of technical specifications and the receipt of the necessary approvals.

Solidcore Resources is a gold producer registered in the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC) and listed on the Astana International Exchange (AIX). The company operates two producing gold mines in Kazakhstan and is developing two growth projects: Ertis POX, a gold concentrate processing hub, and Syrymbet, one of the world's largest undeveloped tin deposits. Solidcore is also pursuing greenfield exploration projects in Oman and Japan.

World.title: Iran's gas network stable after fire extinguishment at South Pars field – deputy minister
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 11. Gas supplies across Iran remain stable following the extinguishing of a fire on a platform at Phase 14 of the South Pars gas field, which Iran shares with Qatar, where it is known as the North Field, Deputy Oil Minister and National Iranian Gas Company Managing Director Saeid Tavakkoli said.

The Iranian Ministry of Petroleum reported his remarks.

"Through the unified coordination of the Iranian Ministry of Petroleum, the stability of the country's gas supply has been maintained, and there are no issues for consumers," he said.

The deputy minister noted that the stability of the national gas supply was preserved following the successful extinguishing of the fire on one of the platforms belonging to the National Iranian Oil Company and the implementation of appropriate follow-up measures. During the transition from the summer to the winter operational mode, it is common for gas demand to occasionally exceed forecasts.

"As of this morning, gas consumption in the residential and commercial sectors across Iran reached 450 million cubic meters, with 95 million cubic meters consumed in Tehran Province alone," he said.

Tavakkoli added that citizens in Iran are encouraged to maintain indoor temperatures at 20 degrees Celsius to help manage gas consumption. It’s possible to maintain stability in gas supply by keeping the temperature at this level.

To recall, a fire broke out last night on one of the platforms of Phase 14 of the South Pars gas field. The fire, which lasted for several hours, was subsequently extinguished.

The South Pars gas field, known as the North Dome in Qatar, is shared by Iran and Qatar. Its reserves are estimated at 51 trillion cubic meters of natural gas, of which 36 trillion cubic meters are considered recoverable. Iran's share is estimated at 14 trillion cubic meters of gas and 18 billion barrels of gas condensate.

The Iranian side of the field comprises 24 development phases. Iran began production there in 2002 and is currently reported to produce around 720 million cubic meters of gas per day across these phases. Total investment by Iran in the field is estimated at $90 billion.

Approximately 33% of the gas recoverable from the field is reported to belong to Iran. The Iranian side has been developed by Iranian companies, while the Qatari side has largely been developed with the involvement of foreign companies.

World.title: Sincere dialogue between President Ilham Aliyev and Recep Tayyip Erdoğan at COP31 (PHOTO)
World.content:
Photo: Press service of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 11. As previously reported, on November 11, President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev arrived at the Expo Center in Antalya to attend the Leaders' Summit of the 31st session of the Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31).

President of the Republic of Türkiye Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and UN Secretary-General António Guterres welcomed President Ilham Aliyev, as well as other heads of state and government, and leaders of delegations participating in the Summit.

President Ilham Aliyev and President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan shared a warm and friendly exchange during the joint photo session of the Summit participants.

World.title: COP31: Uzbekistan to receive €103.7M for climate resilience program
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 11. Uzbekistan is set to receive €103.7 million under a regional climate resilience program aimed at restoring degraded landscapes, improving agricultural sustainability and helping rural communities adapt to climate change.

According to the presidential press service, the funding is part of the seven-year Climate-Resilient Landscapes in Central Asia (CLiCA) program, which has a total budget of €264.4 million and was developed jointly by Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan with support from international partners.

The program was launched during the World Leaders' Summit on Climate Action in Antalya, Türkiye, held as part of the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31). Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev attended the summit's opening ceremony.

The funds allocated to Uzbekistan will support forest and pasture restoration, the introduction of climate-resilient agricultural practices, more efficient use of natural resources and expanded adaptation opportunities for rural communities.

The summit, held under the theme "Towards a Sustainable, Stable and Just Future," brought together heads of state and government, international organizations and financial institutions to advance global climate action.

COP31 is taking place in Antalya from November 9 to 20, bringing together government representatives, international organizations, businesses, scientific institutions and civil society to discuss implementation of the Paris Agreement, greenhouse gas emissions reductions, climate adaptation, climate finance and the transition to a green economy.

Climate resilience is a particular priority for Uzbekistan and Central Asia, where water scarcity, land degradation, glacier retreat and drought are increasingly affecting ecosystems and livelihoods.

Uzbekistan has pledged to reduce greenhouse gas emissions per unit of gross domestic product by 50% by 2035 compared with 2010 levels. The country joined the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change in 1993 and became a party to the Paris Agreement in 2018.

World.title: Regional flights cost 173pc more per km than city routes, inquiry finds
World.content:
Regional Australians are paying excessive fares to travel within their own state, with a new Productivity Commission report exposing the extraordinary cost of domestic travel.

One family of four paid $3,200 for a one-hour flight from Kalgoorlie to Perth — the cost of a single return airfare to Europe.

The interim report, released today, found short regional flights were, on average, 173 per cent more expensive per kilometre than major city routes.

"Many regional communities are frustrated by the high cost of flights," Commissioner Catherine de Fontenay said.

Regional communities are being hit with flights on average 173pc more expensive per kilometre than city routes. (ABC News: Mary Lloyd)

"Previous government inquiries have looked at the issue, but until now we haven't had the data or the evidence to understand what really sets the prices."

The report, commissioned by Federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers, comes as airlines continue to scrap regional routes across the country, due to high fuel costs and lack of demand.

Huge costs tearing families apart

The Determinants of Regional Airfares report received more than 100 submissions, with some revealing the devastating consequences of expensive airfares for families and remote communities.

The Northern Territory's Yalu Aboriginal Corporation warned high airfares were leaving children disconnected from their families.

"Expensive airfares mean that children in care are deprived of the opportunity to thrive and indeed will continue to suffer the effects of being disconnected from family, well into their adult years," the submission said.

Outback flights cost more than overseas trip Customers say outback airfares are not "fair dinkum" amid a delayed review and calls for airlines to be more transparent.

Regional Development Australia Mid North Coast in NSW said a last-minute airfare could be beyond the reach of some families.

Its submission highlighted problems related to custody disputes, and warned the cost of flights could prevent parents from attending court hearings, mediation and supervised visits with their children.

Missed appointments could potentially lead to "adverse legal actions including removal of children from family care".

The report also included evidence from a remote resident unable to afford flights to take their daughter for a critical medical appointment, stating the Patient Assistance Transport Scheme (PATS) did not cover the costs.

"There are things my daughter is supposed to attend but because PATS don't cover it and it cannot be done up here, I just haven't taken her," the submission stated.

One Western Australian resident said even with a state government scheme limiting the cost of regional airfares, a return flight to Perth could still cost about $600.

Limited competition and high operating costs

The report found more than 90 per cent of regional and remote passengers flew with the Qantas Group or Virgin Australia in 2025, while 72 per cent of routes were served by just one carrier.

Regional flights also cost more to operate, with airlines spending about 91 cents of every dollar earned on operating costs, including fuel, maintenance and airport fees, according to the report.

Regional flights cost more to run. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor )

"Half of regional and remote routes operate 10 or fewer flights per week and more than a third of their seats are empty," Commissioner Martin Stokie said.

"Operators are often choosing between charging higher fares or running them at a loss."

But profitability varied significantly between routes, the report said.

AI influences Qantas layoffs Qantas lay-offs are just the beginning of big changes for a tourism industry still trying to find its feet.

Mining routes were more profitable for airlines, while some short remote routes carrying fewer passengers had profit margins below 5 per cent.

Regional airline Rex went into administration in 2024, after expanding into capital city routes.

The airline was losing around $1 million a week and blamed high operating costs and difficulties competing with Qantas and Virgin when it collapsed.

Last month, Qantas and Virgin executives defended regional service cuts at a Senate inquiry into Australia's aviation sector.

Qantas Domestic CEO Markus Svensson told the committee regional flights were more expensive to operate because of fuel costs, aircraft requirements and airport fees.

"On a typical $197 fare, around $93 is made up by government, airport and security fees and charges and that's before the airline pays for aircraft, crew or fuel or maintenance," he said.

Calls for more support

In its recommendations, the commission said governments needed to do more to help patients with the up-front costs of medical travel and subsidise essential routes where airlines cannot provide a commercial service.

"Government assistance should focus on keeping communities connected, rather than supporting particular airlines," Commissioner Catherine de Fontenay said.

The commission is seeking further submissions and registrations for public hearings and will deliver its final report in April 2027.
