World.title: Singapore Airlines flight makes emergency landing in regional Queensland
World.content:
A Singapore Airlines flight has been forced to make an emergency landing at Rockhampton Airport on Wednesday after smoke was seen in the cabin.

The Singapore-bound plane had just departed Brisbane when the incident occurred.

It touched down safely just after 4pm. No injuries were reported.

Paramedics and fire crews were called to the scene.

Passengers reported seeing smoke fill the cabin and plane screens go black.

A group of school children going on an excursion were among the passengers. (ABC News: Vanessa Jarrett)

A Singapore Airlines spokesperson said the company was investigating the cause of the smoke.

"We are providing our customers with all necessary assistance, including on ground refreshments, arranging for a relief flight and rebooking onward travel where necessary," the spokesperson said in a statement.

"The safety of our customers and staff is our top priority."

Passengers who were on board the flight were contained to an internal lounge in the airport.

World.title: Young adult dies from meningococcal disease
World.content:
A young adult infected with invasive meningococcal disease has died.

SA Health confirmed the person's death on Wednesday, after the state's health minister and chief public health officer confirmed the case on Saturday, October 31.

SA Health said data confidentiality meant no details regarding the deceased person could be provided.

Chief Public Health Officer Nicola Spurrier had previously said close contacts of the infected person had been provided preventative antibiotics.

No further meningococcal cases have been reported to SA Health, with the deceased person the 22nd case in South Australia this year.

Failure to receive treatment for the disease once symptoms are detected can increase the risk of disability and mortality.

Susceptible groups include adolescents and very young children, though a 36-year-old South Australian man died from the disease in 2023.

Professor Spurrier and the state's health minister, Blair Boyer, have encouraged parents to vaccinate children younger than 12 months, or who are students in Year 10, as these groups are eligible for the state's free vaccination program.

World.title: VCAA investigating after website hacked during exam period
World.content:
The Victorian Curriculum and Assessment Authority (VCAA) is investigating after its website was hacked during the exam period.

Earlier this evening the VCAA home page was displaying an error message that has since been replaced with a message saying "We'll be right back".

"Our site is currently undergoing maintenance," the website states.

"We apologise for any inconvenience and appreciate your patience."

A VCAA spokesperson confirmed the page was hacked earlier today.

"The VCAA is conducting a forensic investigation to determine the extent of the attack," they said in a statement.

"There is no indication that exam papers from today or previous weeks have been accessed."

Exams for students in Victoria are scheduled through to November 18.

A hacker has claimed responsibility for the breach. (ABC News: Casey Briggs)

Hacker claims to have distributed exam papers

The compromised version of the VCAA website included an expletive-riddled message critical of the digital security standards of the VCAA and others, including providers of printing and legal services.

"The success of this campaign could not have been possible without all their help together," the hacker, who signed off as DaggerElite, wrote.

"I'm here to say a big THANK YOU to a much cooler group of people --- those who purchased an Official VCA 2026 Exam from me ahead of the Exam day this year.

"Thanks to the support of these awesome hundreds of students statewide, we will hopefully be able to prepare the exam pages to be sent out even earlier than we have been able to this year, so we can study the paper you will sit in 2027 well in advance!!"

The hacker claim they downloaded a copy of the 2026 exam papers from the printing provider's internal file servers and distributed copies using email details obtained from the legal service provider.

"And before anyone seeing this decides to go ask people on Reddit to share the papers for the next few exams, I would like to remind you that those holding a paper are very well aware that each sent copy is individualised with an identifiable signature embedded in it, and it's in their best interests to keep their papers to themselves," the text on the website said.

"This is DaggerElite, and it has been an absolute pleasure working with all of you this year."

In 2024 an exam blunder led to some questions being leaked in online practice material.

In April this year, the Victorian government announced more than $222 million to rebuild the VCAA with the aim of "safeguarding exams for the long-term".

World.title: Advocate who supported Peter Greste named ACT's Australian of the Year
World.content:
A human rights lawyer and advocate has been named the ACT's Australian of the Year for 2027, recognised for his work supporting vulnerable Australians, from First Nations people to prisoners with wrongful convictions.

Martin Hodgson, 46, represented hundreds of clients pro bono through the Foreign Prisoner Support Service and the Disappeared Project, which spotlights First Nations cold cases, and which he co-founded.

Mr Hodgson paid tribute to his mum, who he said "has made me who I am".

"When I was very little, we lived in a tent, and then we upgraded to a tractor shed in the bush, and shortwave radio introduced me to the world," he said.

"And I heard about Nelson Mandela and the troubles in Ireland and, at six, they were the things I wanted to solve."

"Mum was the one who encouraged us to be whatever we wanted to be, but just to be good people, and to help others, which she did her whole career."

Martin Hodgson with journalist Peter Greste's parents, Lois and Juris. (Supplied)

Mr Hodgson said when he was a university student he helped an imprisoned Australian "in trouble overseas" get home — and since then "the phone never stopped".

He has supported the Bali Nine and Australian foreign correspondent Peter Greste, who was imprisoned for 400 days in an Egyptian prison.

"I've had a real pleasure of working with Australians in trouble overseas, a lot of First Nations communities, and young Aboriginal mums who are doing it tough through no fault of their own and really being let down, and just being in their corner," Mr Hodgson said.

Using DNA in Indigenous cold cases Modern forensic techniques aim to solve Australian First Nations cold cases.

He also helped free First Nations man Kevin Henry, who was wrongfully imprisoned for more than 25 years.

Inventor wins Senior Australian of the Year

Food scientist Andrzej Kilian was awarded the ACT's Senior Australian of the Year for his dedication to tackling global food security.

Dr Kilian developed an efficient tool to analyse the DNA of organisms, helping farmers, scientists and ecologists improve crop yields.

Dr Andrzej Kilian was named the 2027 ACT Senior Australian of the Year.

He commercialised the invention in 2001 through the Diversity Arrays Technology social enterprise, located in Canberra.

Accepting the award, Dr Kilian, who immigrated from Poland three decades ago, said he drew upon his love for cooking nutritious food for his wife when starting the company.

"This is extending that to the global community, so the catchphrase is, 'Can we feed 10 billion people, project for 2050, without destroying biodiversity?'" he said.

Young Australian of the Year goes to man fighting loneliness

In 2021, Zakary Pino began a routine of walking around Lake Burley Griffin each Sunday, as a way to combat his own loneliness and anxiety during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Zakary Pino tapped into a widely felt loss of connection during the pandemic era. (Supplied)

He did not realise at the time that he was starting a movement that grew into the charity WITH-ME, bringing connection to thousands.

"The premise of it was to get people to walk and talk and also, for me, it was … to kind of learn off older people," Mr Pino said.

" Because I do believe that there's a lot to learn if you're older, speaking to younger people, and younger people speaking to older people. "

The 30-year-old also works to breaks down taboos around mental health by speaking with school students across the ACT.

Mr Pino was named Young Australian of the Year for ACT.

Founder of mothers' social enterprise is ACT's Local Hero

Micaela Centenera's impact extends overseas through the provision of supplies to impoverished communities. (Supplied)

Micaela Centenera has taken out the Local Hero award for her work advocating for community and connection among mothers.

Ms Centenera was recognised for her mission to create a "free community" for women through her co-founded social enterprise, The Little Capsule Co, which included an online marketplace for new and pre-loved children's wear.

Upon accepting the award, Ms Centenera recounted how her own experience inspired the organisation, which acted as "drop-in centre for women during those tough early days, where you just want to cry and you don't want to put your shoes on".

"I moved to the ACT almost seven years ago now, and I lost my mum tribe, and it kind of felt very isolating when you've got a small one. You need community — it's so important to have people around you," she said.

She also posts monthly medical, clothing, bedding and toiletry supplies to families facing extreme poverty.

The four recipients will attend the national Australian of the Year awards in Canberra next year.

World.title: Report shines light on what drives people to post hateful content
World.content:
Researchers have shed light on the characteristics of people who post hateful comments online, in a study published by the Australian Institute of Criminology.

The institute, a federal government crime research organisation, used the Australian eSafety commissioner's definition of online hate, framing it as "hateful posts or comments about a person or group based on discrimination or bias related to their identity or beliefs".

It surveyed almost 10,000 people between October and November 2024, and found 1.7 per cent of respondents had subjected others to online hate.

This group was also more likely to have hold misogynistic attitudes, engage in antisocial behaviour, consume fringe radical content, and have been a victim of online hate, compared to those who had not posted hateful online content.

"This cohort was also more likely to have experienced negative life events compared with those who had not subjected others to online hate," the report read.

"[They] were more likely to spend less time connecting with people offline and to be concerned about their internet use.

"These experiences align with previous research that has found online hate to be associated with close ties to online communities and low offline social capital."

Misogyny named as red flag for violent extremism A study finds violent attitudes towards women are not just a social issue but a matter of national security.

Perpetrators of online hate believe in 'superior groups'

The report also found the people more likely to indulge in online hate held strong beliefs about how "superior groups" should act in society.

They were more likely to agree with these two statements:

Superior groups should dominate inferior groups.

We should not push for group equality.

"After controlling for gender and age, these respondents were more likely to believe that some groups should hold greater dominance over others," the report read.

Researchers also measured the extent to which respondents: believed women to be manipulative and exploitative; were distrustful of women; and devalued women.

They found perpetrators of online hate were more likely to hold misogynistic attitudes, and almost twice as likely to agree with the following:

Women seek to gain power by getting control over men.

Women use their sexuality to manipulate men.

Women exploit men for their own agendas.

If things don't go their way, women will play the victim.

The study also found across all respondents there were no major demographic differences between perpetrators or victims of online abuse from place of residence, country of birth, or language spoken.

Antisocial behaviour and extreme content

The research found perpetrators of online hate were likely to have had contact with the criminal justice system both as an adult and as a juvenile.

"Those who had subjected others to online hate were more likely to have used violence against another person. They were also more likely to have threatened another person," the report read.

Manosphere warning Recent studies link exposure to extreme anti-women content to increasing misogyny among boys.

Perpetrators of online hate were more likely to have been diagnosed with a mental health condition, and engaged in antisocial behaviour, than respondents who did not.

The report also found many have been victims of hate speech, online harassment and abuse.

It found they were more likely to be engaging in antisocial behaviour online and creating fake social media accounts.

About half of those who subjected others to online hate did at least one of the following, compared to just two per cent of those who had not:

Bullied, harassed, stalked or abused someone online.

Gained unauthorised access to someone else's social media, email, streaming or shopping account (i.e. hacking).

Sent someone emails or text messages with the intention of tricking them into sending money or personal information (i.e. phishing).

The report also examined the relationship between viewing radical fringe content and engaging in online abuse.

It defined "fringe and radical" as online content that was political, ideological or religious in nature but viewed by wider society as unorthodox, radical or fringe.

When compared to the cohort who did not post online hate, it found those who did were almost two times more likely to have viewed fringe and radical content online.

World.title: Rescuers wrangling red tape as foxes pick off young swans south of Perth
World.content:
Wildlife rescuers are mounting a community-led effort to save more than 50 vulnerable or abandoned black swan cygnets at a drying lake south of Mandurah.

WARNING: This story contains images of dead birds some readers may find distressing.

Rescue groups spent most of today negotiating the terms of their operation with WA's Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions (DBCA), which manages McLarty Lake, about 90 kilometres south of Perth.

WA Seabird Rescue's Rachel Olsen vented her frustration with red tape as foxes picked off abandoned cygnets.

"We were only just made aware of the situation, but it is really quite urgent," she said.

"As of this morning, I went out really early; the water level is down, and there's only about 60 cygnets left."

Black swans are vulnerable to predation at Lake McLarty. (Supplied: WA Seabird Rescue)

Rescue efforts set to go ahead

While the department says wildlife rescuers can access the reserve, it was wary that a large-scale rescue operation could pose public safety risks.

"DBCA has also been in discussions with WA Seabird Rescue regarding the organisation of a larger event involving around 100 people, which may pose additional public safety risks that will need to be managed," a spokesperson said.

"DBCA continues to work with WA Seabird Rescue to facilitate volunteer wildlife rehabilitators accessing the reserve to monitor and rescue cygnets."

A dead cygnet was found at Lake McLarty, south of Mandurah. (Supplied: WA Seabird Rescue)

Ms Olsen said the situation had evolved quickly and rescue was set to take place this afternoon.

"Some of them have been abandoned, but we basically need to scoop them all up," she said.

"We know that in a few days all of these cygnets will be dead; the parents have no choice but to abandon them."

Lake dries up early

Ms Olsen said the lake was drying up earlier than usual, forcing adult swans to abandon their young because of the risk of predation.

Water levels are low at Lake McLarty. (Supplied: WA Seabird Rescue )

"Parents don't want to abandon their babies, but as they face increasing pressure and are running out of food, all the swans are getting concentrated into one area, and then the foxes come in," she said.

World.title: Victorian Liberals dump Williamstown candidate over offensive comments
World.content:
The Victorian Liberal Party has dumped Williamstown candidate Paul Lindemann over offensive comments it says he made about Indigenous Australians.

In a statement, the party says it has withdrawn its support and endorsement of Mr Lindemann over views he expressed, which had recently come to light.

"These comments are offensive, unacceptable and inconsistent with the values and standards expected of Liberal candidates," the statement says.

" All candidates are expected to treat Australians with dignity and respect. Mr Lindemann's comments fell short of that standard. "

The party was not previously aware of Mr Lindemann's comments, the statement says.

Yesterday One Nation dumped former Preston candidate Franco Guardiani over comments he made about Hitler.

The seat of Williamstown has been held by Minister for Jobs Melissa Horne since 2018, and has been won by Labor at almost every election since 1889 on very safe margins.

The former dockyard town is now one of the wealthier seats in the state.

Earlier today, Sport Minister Steve Dimopoulos said Opposition Leader Jess Wilson should dump Mr Lindemann over allegations he insulted and mocked a young basketball player while coaching the Bay City Lakers.

In a statement, Mr Lindemann apologised for his actions and acknowledged he should have "handled the situation differently".

The ABC has attempted to contact Mr Lindemann for comment.

Victorians are set to head to the polls on November 28.

The Victorian Curriculum and Assessment Authority has confirmed its website was hacked on Wednesday evening, but says there is no evidence that the hacker accessed this year’s exam papers as they have claimed. At about 6pm, a message laced with profanities appeared on VCAA’s homepage, authored by someone using the alias “DaggerElite”, claiming to have hacked the site and sold VCE exams to “hundreds of students statewide”. VCAA has confirmed its homepage was hacked on Wednesday night. Joe Armao The hacker claimed they had breached the security of not only VCAA, but the authority’s external printing providers, from which they had downloaded the VCE exams. They did not name the provider in the message. The hacker then claimed to have sent the exams to the students via an email address belonging to a law firm, whose system they said they also hacked.



“The success of their campaign could not have been possible without all their help together,” they wrote with mock gratitude. The message posted on VCAA website on Wednesday evening. VCAA website The hacker also claimed the “hundreds of students statewide” who participated in the scheme this year would allow them to start selling papers for 2027 “well in advance”. In a statement, VCAA confirmed its site had been the “subject of vandalism”, but an initial investigation had shown no evidence that sensitive data or exam papers had been accessed. “There is no indication that exam papers from today or previous weeks have been accessed,” it said in a statement. It also confirmed VCE exams would continue as normal and the incident had been reported to Victoria Police.



The website remained largely blank several hours after the hack, with a message telling visitors it was “undergoing maintenance”. On Wednesday evening, GoAhead lawyers said they suspected its email address had been spoofed by a third party. Email spoofing is the creation of an email with a forged sender address. Principal lawyer Sukhwinder Singh said his firm had not authorised any emails distributing VCE papers. “Our checks so far have found no record of the reported emails in our systems, and we cannot confirm that they were sent from a Go Ahead Lawyers account,” Singh said in a statement.



Singh said he had reported the suspected spoofing to VCAA and will assist with its inquiries. Related Article Exclusive

VCE Cover sheets and additional exams uncovered in VCE bungle Several VCE students and parents contacted The Age after discovering the hacker’s message. One of them, David Charlesworth, has a daughter in her final year who was alerted to the message by her friends. Charlesworth said even if the hacker was lying about selling exams, the hack itself was reason enough to worry and said it made it hard for him to have confidence in the system. “They’ve been through this before,” he said of VCAA. “They can do a better job.”



“Students are very upset about this,” said another parent on social media. “Some still have exams to go.” The hack comes two years after the government ordered a review into the 2024 exam period after VCAA unintentionally published 56 test papers that gave thousands of students an advantage over others. VCAA’s then-chief executive Kylie White resigned after the bungle, before the board was sacked in 2025. There were also errors in papers in the 2022 and 2023 exam periods. Education Minister Gabrielle Williams was contacted for comment.



The Coalition’s education spokesperson Brad Roswell said he had sought a briefing from the department and VCAA. The 2026 VCE exam period still has a week to run, concluding with language exams on November 18. Results are set to be released on December 10. Be the first to know when major news happens.

Tony Everett’s query regarding the third jewel-themed room (after Sapphire and Emerald) at the Australia Hotel (C8) is an entanglement. Clytie Williams of Randwick remembers her dad, key figure Bill Cullip, running front-of-house operations in the late1930s. “I recall having lunch there as a very little girl of about five in the Diamond Room, the third jewel-themed room your reader was looking for. I remember feeling very grown-up being in such a splendid chandelier-encased, white table-clothed and silver-laden-table room and certainly learned my early table manners there!” A deep dive on the establishment could not uncover a Diamond Room, but a major third room is listed by a number of sources as the Amethyst Room. Clytie?

Further complicating things is Steven Maher of Forster: “In response to the query about the third jewel-themed room at the Australia Hotel, I celebrated my 18th birthday in 1966 in the Jade Room at that establishment. The resident singer was Michael Klentos. I requested he sing More from the 1962 movie Mondo Cane, and he did. Memories are made of this. Gone are the days.” In this case, the Jade Room did exist, but did so after a renovation. Room for any more?

“Recently on radio, I heard an independent MLA suggest that ‘Sydney needs more articulate buses’,” notes Colin Taylor Evans of Lane Cove. “Well said!”

As far as ginger nut biscuits (C8) go, “the results are in,” according to Gregory Nell of Tamworth: “There are 11 more ginger nuts in a Queensland variety packet than there are in a NSW variety packet of the same net weight. That would possibly make purchasing the Queensland better value, unless one ends up dunking two Queensland variety biscuits into one’s cup of tea (because they’re thinner) for every one NSW variety biscuit. So endeth the investigation.”

Lance Dover of Pretty Beach writes: “Whilst my late mother was serving at the confectionery counter of David Jones (C8), Barrack and George Street store, laughter rang out from the workroom where they made up bags of DJ’s trademark ‘Mary Pumpkin’ sweets. The reason? One of the ladies’ dentures had fallen into the bin of hundreds and thousands. I forget if she told us whether the bin was discarded or not!”

World.title: Premier, police minister subpoenaed for court appearance five days before poll
World.content:
PoliticsNSWNSW State Parliament Premier, police minister subpoenaed for court appearance five days before poll Jessica McSweeney November 11, 2026 — 8:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. NSW Premier Chris Minns and senior ministers may be forced to testify in court just days before the March state election as part of the criminal case against demonstrators at the now-infamous Town Hall protest. The defence case says it has subpoenaed Minns, Police Minister Yasmin Catley and Tourism Minister Steve Kamper to answer questions about their role in decision-making in the lead-up to and on February 9, which resulted in confrontations between protesters and police. Police face protesters at Sydney Town Hall demonstrating against Israeli President Isaac Herzog in February. Kate Geraghty More than a dozen protesters are facing charges connected to the demonstration against visiting Israeli President Isaac Herzog, including assaulting police. The rally is also the subject of a Law Enforcement Conduct Commission investigation into police conduct. A subpoena is a legal order from the court, but one that can be challenged with a valid objection in a motion to the court. That can include relevancy, or if the terms of the subpoena are oppressive, and a judge can decide to set the subpoena aside on those grounds.



A government spokesperson said it would be inappropriate to comment given the matter was before the courts. Lawyer Nick Hanna, who is representing the protesters, said: “At the hearing we will argue that the police operation was unlawful and that the unlawful nature of it stemmed right from the top of the government.” Hanna said the date given on the subpoena, March 8, is the first day of hearings in the legal argument as to the lawfulness of police conduct at the protest. Hanna argued there were “cogent and compelling reasons” requiring Minns and the senior ministers to attend court. The election is set for March 13. The defence will highlight comments Minns gave about the police watchdog inquiry into police actions on the night of the protest, Hanna said. Minns said in February: “We can’t blame the police for doing what we asked them to do, and that is to keep the people of NSW safe, protect mourners who were down at the ICC on that evening.”



Related Article Protests Commissioner’s SCG briefing, police miscommunications in spotlight at Town Hall protest inquiry Police officers were operating with powers under multiple pieces of state legislation on the night of the protest, including a Public Assembly Restriction Declaration (PARD), which was part of now-struck-out legislation passed after the Bondi terror attack. The PARD prohibited protest marches within parts of Sydney designated by the police commissioner, but was later ruled invalid by the NSW Court of Appeal for burdening the implied right to freedom of political communication. The PARD was invoked by officers on the night and cited in fact sheets used in court cases against protesters, according to court documents seen by this masthead. Police were also given powers under the Major Events Act, a law which is still valid and one rally organisers failed to overturn in a court challenge in the hours before the protest. World.title: Former department head given contempt warning, as probe calls for new building code
World.content:
NationalQueenslandBuilding Bad Former department head given contempt warning, as probe calls for new building code Matt Dennien November 11, 2026 — 7:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Queensland’s CFMEU inquiry boss has warned lawyers for a former top bureaucrat that he was at risk of being found in contempt over his professed inability to recall details of discussions at the heart of two key concessions granted to the union. It comes as the $95 million Stuart Wood-led probe issued an interim report late on Wednesday making formal recommendations for the Crisafulli government to introduce a new state building code and establish a new regulator to monitor and enforce compliance. The inquiry this week returned to a case study into regulatory capture of the workplace safety regulator by the union, focusing particularly on the pressure exerted by the CFMEU during the short-lived tenure of one of Michael De’Ath’s deputies. Former Education Department director-general Michael De’Ath giving evidence at the commission of inquiry. Commission of inquiry Former Education Department director-general De’Ath, who in that role between 2021 and 2024 also oversaw the state’s industrial relations and racing offices, returned to the stand on Wednesday for a second full day.



His evidence included early efforts by the mega-department’s deputy director-general in charge of the Office of Industrial Relations, Kym Bancroft, to remove a CFMEU-favoured figure with responsibility for managing safety inspectors, which raised the ire of the union. De’Ath, the most senior former public servant called to date, said on Tuesday he could not recall calls and texts with since-ousted CFMEU state secretary Michael Ravbar in early August 2022, after it was put to him by counsel assisting that Ravbar had expressed disdain over the decision. Commissioner Stuart Wood pictured during hearings last month. Pool - NewsWire/John Gass After this and other efforts by Bancroft to address cultural issues within the office, union figures began calling her directly with site complaints and concerns, leading to a proposal for a general 1300 number to be established to field and triage complaints.



The inquiry heard on Wednesday that the union refused to engage in early consultation on this system, which was also backed and signed off by De’Ath in mid-March 2023, and that it was simultaneously pushing for Bancroft to be removed from an executive director selection panel. Related Article Updated

Queensland government Former workplace safety boss wanted to sack ‘friend of the CFMEU’, but couldn’t Around this time, Ravbar threatened to take his concerns to then-industrial relations minister Grace Grace, and attended a meeting with De’Ath and Bancroft that the director-general cut short due to Ravbar’s aggressive and inappropriate behaviour. The inquiry was then shown an invitation for a meeting sent by Grace’s office to Ravbar and other building sector union figures the same day of his threat, set for early April. Around the end of that meeting, on April 3, call records showed De’Ath was phoned by Grace’s office, and had a meeting of his own set with Grace for the following day. De’Ath said he could not recall what the pair discussed.



The inquiry was then shown an email by Bancroft from the morning of April 5, indicating the triage system was still being pursued. By that afternoon, following a call between De’Ath and Bancroft, it was to be paused with further consultation and an independent facilitator. Related Article Queensland government Crisafulli brushes off calls for special CFMEU probe prosecutor Counsel assisting, Dimitri Ternovski, put Bancroft’s version of events – that De’Ath told her Grace had considered the triage system and it would not be going ahead until the new executive director of compliance and field services was appointed – and asked if it was the truth. De’Ath said it was not, but could not remember the detail of the call, while conceding the shift from the 1300 hotline to an interim arrangement was “another accommodation” of the union’s demands, but that he believed he and Grace would have “problem-solved” to make that shift. At this point, Commissioner Wood reminded De’Ath’s lawyer, Emma Hoiberg, of a High Court opinion that the “feigned inability to remember”, if used by a witness to deliberately evade questions, can amount to an allegation of contempt.



Asked by Hoiberg if such a finding might be made against De’Ath, Wood said: “It seems to me that we’re getting very close to that position.” Hoiberg said the questions related to phone calls and conversations from, in some cases, four years ago in the context of De’Ath’s “wide portfolio across a range of matters” and that “it’s not unexpected for Mr De’Ath to not have specific recall”. After a break to allow Hoiberg to speak with De’Ath, Wood said he was effectively giving the warning required in some jurisdictions before a formal charge could be pursued either by an inquiry or the Supreme Court, but this did not mean it would be pursued. De’Ath said he understood the frustrations of the inquiry, but that he was “sincere and genuine in saying that I just don’t remember all of those conversations” and was “not trying to be in any way evasive”. He said he was not aware of any formal record of a decision to pause the pursuit of the triage system, nor that the department was required to keep one under the Public Records Act, but he rejected the suggestion this was an effort to obscure an intervention from Grace.



De’Ath earlier told the inquiry there was no influence from Grace’s office around either the pausing of the triage system or the eventual dismissal of Bancroft later that month relating to conflict of interest concerns De’Ath took to the Crime and Corruption Commission. After the conclusion of evidence, the attorney-general tabled an interim report from Wood on a question it had posed to stakeholders about the reintroduction of a state building code and a “suitably resourced” regulator to oversee it. Both were formally recommended by Wood. Despite suggesting during a hearing last month that it might not be prudent to wait until the inquiry’s final reporting date in December 2027 to start making broader recommendations to deal with evidence heard of wrongdoing, no such measures featured in Wednesday’s report. The inquiry continues on Thursday, with further evidence from De’Ath. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Absolutely false’: Another former coach denies knowledge of sandpaper plot
World.content:
Exclusive SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘Absolutely false’: Another former coach denies knowledge of sandpaper plot Andrew Wu and Christy Doran Updated November 11, 2026 — 7:39pm ,first published 1:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A member of Darren Lehmann’s coaching staff from the 2018 South Africa tour has denied having any knowledge of the sandpaper plot, slamming Usman Khawaja’s assertion it was known by all members of the touring party as “absolutely false”. As David Warner hit back at Lehmann for downplaying his knowledge of the scandal, Australia’s former batting coach Graeme Hick said he was not aware of the use of sandpaper until footage emerged of Cameron Bancroft on the big screen. Australia’s former batting coach Graeme Hick with Steve Smith during the 2019 Ashes series. PA The revelation came on a day when Khawaja pulled out of television and radio interviews to promote his memoir Sabr after his grilling from multiple Walkley winner Sarah Ferguson on the ABC’s 7.30 program, during which he failed to answer key questions about Sandpapergate. Test captain Pat Cummins is expected to speak publicly for the first time since Khawaja’s explosive claims on Friday, though Cricket Australia said that was yet to be confirmed.



Australia’s stand-in ODI captain Mitch Marsh is due to speak at his pre-game press conference on Thursday ahead of the first game against England, where he is likely to be quizzed on his knowledge of the events from eight years ago. Australia’s former batting coach Graeme Hick in 2018. Getty Images A close friend of Cummins and a former state teammate of Bancroft, Marsh has told national teammates he is nervous about how he will address the matter, according to a source with knowledge of the matter. The all-rounder was in the attack at the time South African broadcaster SuperSport aired footage of Bancroft hiding a piece of sandpaper down his trousers. Cameron Bancroft slid a yellow strip of sandpaper into his pants in Cape Town. Getty Images



Hick, Australia’s batting coach from 2016-2020, denied any involvement or knowledge of the plan to use sandpaper in Cape Town and, as claimed by Khawaja, in Port Elizabeth. Lehmann also denied knowledge of the plan and questioned Khawaja’s claim that all members of the team knew. Khawaja has said the entire squad was complicit in the use of sandpaper and should share the blame instead of allowing his close friend Warner, Bancroft and former captain Steve Smith, who all copped lengthy bans from Cricket Australia, to carry the burden. Loading Khawaja also claimed a member of the coaching staff had encouraged Bancroft to use sandpaper during an interval of the Cape Town Test. “I have seen the various statements around the coaches and I’m very disappointed with the broad nature of them,” Hick told this masthead.



“Khawaja puts it simply: ‘It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us.’ To me what Khawaja is implying here is absolutely false. “In regard to any discussions around the ball tampering in Port Elizabeth or Cape Town that took place, I will say in true honesty that I did not hear or know anything!! “My first knowledge of all this was, like many, when it appeared on the big screen in Cape Town as I was sat on the outside balcony at the time.” “I have seen the various statements around the coaches and I’m very disappointed with the broad nature of them. “Khawaja puts it simply: ‘It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us.’ To me what Khawaja is implying here is absolutely false.” Graeme Hick Victoria captain Peter Handscomb, who was on a walkie-talkie to Lehmann in Cape Town after vision emerged of Bancroft on the big screen in Cape Town, said he did not want to speak about the affair.



“I appreciate you have to ask these questions,” Handscomb said after making an unbeaten 131 against Western Australia at the MCG. “I’ve had a nice day today, it’s not really something that I want to comment on right now. I’ll sort of just let the powers of be do their thing.” Warner took to social media on Wednesday morning and agreed with former International Cricket Council match referee Chris Broad – the father of England great Stuart – that Lehmann should not have been Australia’s coach if he had no idea that sandpaper was being used in Newlands. Loading “Darren Lehmann surely knew all about it,” said Broad on Talk Radio, after Lehmann denied that “everyone” knew that sandpaper was being used during the infamous third Test between Australia and South Africa in Cape Town in 2018 on ABC radio. “And if he didn’t, he shouldn’t have been the coach at the time.



“I think he’s got away lightly … OK, he left his job a few months later, but he didn’t get any sanctions.” View post on X Broad, who played 25 Tests for England, also said Lehmann had double standards during his term as Australia’s coach, saying he was “very angry” at his response to his son’s decision not to walk during a controversial Ashes Test in 2013. “And there he was in 2013, taking the moral high ground against my son, where he played the Australian game of nicking the ball and waiting for the umpire to give him out, and he got given not out on that occasion, and then [Lehmann] came out in the media saying ‘we’re going to make him cry when he comes to Australia next,’” Broad continued. Former Australia coach Darren Lehmann (right) with batsman Dave Warner. Getty Images



“And here he is, the coach of the Australian cricket team that brought sandpaper out onto the field of play and denied any knowledge of this happening. “I’m very angry at Darren Lehmann in this respect.” Warner has since poured fuel on the fire, backing Broad. “I couldn’t agree more and that’s hard for me to say!” he responded on X on Wednesday. Lehmann declined to comment when contacted.

World.title: We were beset by bogongs. Is a beetle invasion next?
World.content:
Associate Professor Tanya Latty is on the forefront of discovering what’s really going on with Christmas beetles.

Every spring, people ask where the Christmas beetles have gone. We’re on the precipice of an answer.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

You may have noticed by now that Christmas beetles are disappearing. The thing is, despite a decade of headlines asking where all the iridescent insects have gone, we still don’t know know if they’re actually declining. You know? That’s because it takes years of grit, data and determination to convert anecdotal evidence into the hard, published, sciencey kind. Especially when it comes to insect research. Many of the beetles are iridescent thanks to the microscopic structure of their exoskeletons. Wolter Peeters Associate Professor Tanya Latty has taken on the task of gathering this critical data. Now, after years of running a citizen science project aimed at collecting beetle sightings, she’s at the precipice of being able to answer that yearly question: Where have all the Christmas beetles gone? What’s really happening with these beautiful living baubles? After the great bogong moth bounceback of 2026, could we be in for a bumper year of beetles? The key citizen science project



“We’ve been doing the Christmas Beetle Count on an entirely unfunded basis for the last six years, and it’s been driven by community members going out, seeing a Christmas beetle and submitting that to iNaturalist,” Latty, an entomologist from the University of Sydney, says. (iNaturalist is an online database for species sightings.) “When we started, there were a few thousand sightings of Christmas beetles in Australia. As of today, we’re up to 26,497 observations of 40 species, including nine species that hadn’t been seen for decades before the count started.” “The problem is that it tells us where people are seeing a beetle. It doesn’t tell us where people are not seeing a beetle.” So while the Christmas beetle count has built unprecedented data on where and when different types of beetles emerge each year, it can’t tell us for sure whether populations are declining. Beware the impostor: the invasive Argentinian scarab beetle is often mistaken for a Christmas beetle. Wolter Peeters That’s why Latty is taking $30,000 awarded to the project by the Australian Geographic Society to fund a long-term national monitoring network of beetle catchers.



Latty and her colleagues are recruiting and training 50 members of the public to set up UV lights against white sheets in Sydney, Cairns, Canberra, Brisbane and Darwin. Once a month, the volunteers will run the light traps and record which beetles show up. That data could change the game. Having rigorous, long-term, location-based baseline population data may finally answer the question of what’s really going on with the Christmas beetles – and what we can do to bring them back. There are more than 40 Christmas beetle species across Australia. Wolter Peeters Australia’s most popular beetle at risk Applying for research funding is tricky without proof the beetles are vanishing. “The problem with Christmas beetles has always been that technically, they’re not threatened. There’s not really any data that their numbers have decreased, even though everybody feels like their numbers have decreased,” Latty says.



“It’s a bit of a chicken-and-the-egg problem. You kind of need the funding to be able to demonstrate that there’s a decline, but you can’t demonstrate the decline until you have funding.” Christmas Beetle Count data has already helped identify at-risk species that are confined to small habitats. One of those species is the gold Christmas beetle, which is so lustrous it looks as if an 18-carat scarab pendant popped off a pharaoh’s neck and sprang to life. A golden Christmas beetle (right) beside a larger species. Wolter Peeters The public just crowned the gleaming insect as the ABC’s Insect of the Year. It lives in a very small, specific range in Far North Queensland. “If there was a significant natural disaster, then that could conceivably wipe out all the habitat for that one species because it is found in such a small area,” Latty says. A big beetle year?



After a boom comeback year for the endangered bogongs, could we see a big year for beetles amid their seeming long-term decline? It’s hard to say, given there are so many unknowns about both insects, Latty says. “But my gut feeling is it could be a good year. For a lot of insects, a warm, milder winter tends to mean they’re able to grow faster, get bigger and come out a little bit earlier, and we’ve seen that with the Christmas Beetle Count data.” The first sightings came through in September, she says, “a good month earlier than they did last year”. Specimens at the museum could be key to studying genetic bottlenecks and the effects of climate change. Wolter Peeters Dr Chris Reid says the beetles can become trapped underground when the soil hardens during drought. Wolter Peeters Dr Chris Reid, senior research scientist and beetle expert at the Australian Museum, has already spotted three species near his home in the Illawarra, including the brown campfire beetle and the hairy spotted beetle, which has traded flamboyant colour for a fine fur coat.

The Victorian Curriculum and Assessment Authority has confirmed its website was hacked on Wednesday evening, but says there is no evidence that the hacker accessed this year’s exam papers as they have claimed. At about 6pm, a message laced with profanities appeared on VCAA’s homepage, authored by someone using the alias “DaggerElite”, claiming to have hacked the site and sold VCE exams to “hundreds of students statewide”. VCAA has confirmed its homepage was hacked on Wednesday night. Joe Armao The hacker claimed they had breached the security of not only VCAA, but the authority’s external printing providers, from which they had downloaded the VCE exams. They did not name the provider in the message. The hacker then claimed to have sent the exams to the students via an email address belonging to a law firm, whose system they said they also hacked.



“The success of their campaign could not have been possible without all their help together,” they wrote with mock gratitude. The message posted on VCAA website on Wednesday evening. VCAA website The hacker also claimed the “hundreds of students statewide” who participated in the scheme this year would allow them to start selling papers for 2027 “well in advance”. In a statement, VCAA confirmed its site had been the “subject of vandalism”, but an initial investigation had shown no evidence that sensitive data or exam papers had been accessed. “There is no indication that exam papers from today or previous weeks have been accessed,” it said in a statement. It also confirmed VCE exams would continue as normal and the incident had been reported to Victoria Police.



The website remained largely blank several hours after the hack, with a message telling visitors it was “undergoing maintenance”. On Wednesday evening, GoAhead lawyers said they suspected its email address had been spoofed by a third party. Email spoofing is the creation of an email with a forged sender address. Principal lawyer Sukhwinder Singh said his firm had not authorised any emails distributing VCE papers. “Our checks so far have found no record of the reported emails in our systems, and we cannot confirm that they were sent from a Go Ahead Lawyers account,” Singh said in a statement.



Singh said he had reported the suspected spoofing to VCAA and will assist with its inquiries. Related Article Exclusive

VCE Cover sheets and additional exams uncovered in VCE bungle Several VCE students and parents contacted The Age after discovering the hacker’s message. One of them, David Charlesworth, has a daughter in her final year who was alerted to the message by her friends. Charlesworth said even if the hacker was lying about selling exams, the hack itself was reason enough to worry and said it made it hard for him to have confidence in the system. “They’ve been through this before,” he said of VCAA. “They can do a better job.”



“Students are very upset about this,” said another parent on social media. “Some still have exams to go.” The hack comes two years after the government ordered a review into the 2024 exam period after VCAA unintentionally published 56 test papers that gave thousands of students an advantage over others. VCAA’s then-chief executive Kylie White resigned after the bungle, before the board was sacked in 2025. There were also errors in papers in the 2022 and 2023 exam periods. Education Minister Gabrielle Williams was contacted for comment.



The Coalition’s education spokesperson Brad Roswell said he had sought a briefing from the department and VCAA. The 2026 VCE exam period still has a week to run, concluding with language exams on November 18. Results are set to be released on December 10. Be the first to know when major news happens.

Tony Everett’s query regarding the third jewel-themed room (after Sapphire and Emerald) at the Australia Hotel (C8) is an entanglement. Clytie Williams of Randwick remembers her dad, key figure Bill Cullip, running front-of-house operations in the late1930s. “I recall having lunch there as a very little girl of about five in the Diamond Room, the third jewel-themed room your reader was looking for. I remember feeling very grown-up being in such a splendid chandelier-encased, white table-clothed and silver-laden-table room and certainly learned my early table manners there!” A deep dive on the establishment could not uncover a Diamond Room, but a major third room is listed by a number of sources as the Amethyst Room. Clytie?

Further complicating things is Steven Maher of Forster: “In response to the query about the third jewel-themed room at the Australia Hotel, I celebrated my 18th birthday in 1966 in the Jade Room at that establishment. The resident singer was Michael Klentos. I requested he sing More from the 1962 movie Mondo Cane, and he did. Memories are made of this. Gone are the days.” In this case, the Jade Room did exist, but did so after a renovation. Room for any more?

“Recently on radio, I heard an independent MLA suggest that ‘Sydney needs more articulate buses’,” notes Colin Taylor Evans of Lane Cove. “Well said!”

As far as ginger nut biscuits (C8) go, “the results are in,” according to Gregory Nell of Tamworth: “There are 11 more ginger nuts in a Queensland variety packet than there are in a NSW variety packet of the same net weight. That would possibly make purchasing the Queensland better value, unless one ends up dunking two Queensland variety biscuits into one’s cup of tea (because they’re thinner) for every one NSW variety biscuit. So endeth the investigation.”

Lance Dover of Pretty Beach writes: “Whilst my late mother was serving at the confectionery counter of David Jones (C8), Barrack and George Street store, laughter rang out from the workroom where they made up bags of DJ’s trademark ‘Mary Pumpkin’ sweets. The reason? One of the ladies’ dentures had fallen into the bin of hundreds and thousands. I forget if she told us whether the bin was discarded or not!”

World.title: Premier, police minister subpoenaed for court appearance five days before poll
World.content:
PoliticsNSWNSW State Parliament Premier, police minister subpoenaed for court appearance five days before poll Jessica McSweeney November 11, 2026 — 8:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

NSW Premier Chris Minns and senior ministers may be forced to testify in court just days before the March state election as part of the criminal case against demonstrators at the now-infamous Town Hall protest. The defence case says it has subpoenaed Minns, Police Minister Yasmin Catley and Tourism Minister Steve Kamper to answer questions about their role in decision-making in the lead-up to and on February 9, which resulted in confrontations between protesters and police. Police face protesters at Sydney Town Hall demonstrating against Israeli President Isaac Herzog in February. Kate Geraghty More than a dozen protesters are facing charges connected to the demonstration against visiting Israeli President Isaac Herzog, including assaulting police. The rally is also the subject of a Law Enforcement Conduct Commission investigation into police conduct. A subpoena is a legal order from the court, but one that can be challenged with a valid objection in a motion to the court. That can include relevancy, or if the terms of the subpoena are oppressive, and a judge can decide to set the subpoena aside on those grounds.



A government spokesperson said it would be inappropriate to comment given the matter was before the courts. Lawyer Nick Hanna, who is representing the protesters, said: “At the hearing we will argue that the police operation was unlawful and that the unlawful nature of it stemmed right from the top of the government.” Hanna said the date given on the subpoena, March 8, is the first day of hearings in the legal argument as to the lawfulness of police conduct at the protest. Hanna argued there were “cogent and compelling reasons” requiring Minns and the senior ministers to attend court. The election is set for March 13. The defence will highlight comments Minns gave about the police watchdog inquiry into police actions on the night of the protest, Hanna said. Minns said in February: “We can’t blame the police for doing what we asked them to do, and that is to keep the people of NSW safe, protect mourners who were down at the ICC on that evening.”



Related Article Protests Commissioner’s SCG briefing, police miscommunications in spotlight at Town Hall protest inquiry Police officers were operating with powers under multiple pieces of state legislation on the night of the protest, including a Public Assembly Restriction Declaration (PARD), which was part of now-struck-out legislation passed after the Bondi terror attack. The PARD prohibited protest marches within parts of Sydney designated by the police commissioner, but was later ruled invalid by the NSW Court of Appeal for burdening the implied right to freedom of political communication. The PARD was invoked by officers on the night and cited in fact sheets used in court cases against protesters, according to court documents seen by this masthead. Police were also given powers under the Major Events Act, a law which is still valid and one rally organisers failed to overturn in a court challenge in the hours before the protest. World.title: Liberals creating a rod for their back with preference deal
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Liberals creating a rod for their back with preference deal November 11, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Photo: Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. The Victoria Coalition has made a serious strategic mistake (“Liberals to put Labor, Greens last”, 11/11). Not in terms of the election outcome with Jess Wilson, according to the polls, certain to be Victoria’s next premier. Rather, by threatening its prospects of being in government beyond a single term.

Adopting the “default position to preference One Nation”, the Opposition has almost certainly guaranteed that Pauline Hanson’s party will have lower house seats and, crucially, will hold the balance of power in the Legislative Council. Previous election outcomes, notably in the Queensland state election in 1998, show that One Nation is incapable of holding together an angry, disparate group.

The Coalition is creating a rod for its own back once in government. Goodness knows what it will have to agree to in order to govern, almost certainly ending in tears.

James Young, Mt Eliza Holding balance of power a disaster

Jess Wilson’s decision to preference One Nation will be especially problematic for Liberal urban moderates (including in her own seat of Kew). One Nation policies to scrap net zero, expand coal-fired power stations, ban renewable installations on agricultural land, revive native forest logging and end the nuclear ban (and build a nuclear reactor) are all evidence of a mindset firmly rooted in the past. Preferencing One Nation might be a fail-safe for the Liberals, but if elected, Wilson can only hope these preferences don’t result in One Nation winning (more than) enough seats in a hung parliament to acquire the balance of power. That would be an unmitigated disaster for the state of Victoria.

Neil Hudson, East Melbourne May turn to federal Labor advantage

The Coalition edges closer to a Faustian bargain that would see it in an alliance to share government in Victoria with One Nation (″⁣Liberals to put Labor, Greens last″⁣, 11/11). The only winner out of this arrangement could be federal Labor, given there will be ample time for the Victorian electorate to experience how such an arrangement could result in a chaos. The price to pay for such a partnership could mean the Coalition may have to accede to some extreme demands from their chosen governing partners to maintain the alliance. This could give the wider electorate an illustration of the dangers of putting in power such a conglomerate brought about primarily by the Coalition quest to share power at any cost.

Bill Pimm, Mentone



Political expediency over integrity

I have lost all respect for the Liberal Party since they announced that they are going to preference One Nation above other parties. It smacks of political expediency over integrity. With our voting system, preferences do have a big impact. I am astounded that after all the information about One Nation candidates and their policies have been exposed and reported in the media, the Liberals have stooped to this. Bring in the first past the post voting system.

Susan Simpson, Surrey Hills A vote gone with this announcement

I have given serious thought to voting Liberal (for the first time ever) because I am disgusted by the failure of Labor to rein in corruption on major projects, and because my local MP’s office (Matthew Guy) have been very helpful on an issue I raised with them. But Jess Wilson’s decision to preference One Nation has sent me hurtling away from them. It’s only one little vote, but they blew it. By their friends ye shall know them.

Stephen Yolland, Templestowe A recipe for chaos

To those correspondents who say such things as Victoria needs a reboot (Letters, 11/11), I say be careful what you wish for – think of the four years of inertia during the Baillieu-Napthine period, and add One Nation into the mix controlling the upper house. A recipe for chaos.

Brandon Mack, Deepdene THE FORUM Rethink school funding

Thank you Adam Voigt for your sensible appraisal of public-funded schooling as a viable choice for your child (Comment, 11/11). While state and federal governments indicate that funding will improve for Victorian public schools, currently the most poorly funded nationally, this won’t occur until 2034. Meanwhile our schooling system will continue to deteriorate while governments of all persuasions continue to fund the private sector at a higher rate per child than the public sector. Surely how and where your children are educated, and by whom, is a critical decision and one that needs more discussion and advocacy by parents. It’s not to late to recalibrate education in Australia so that it benefits everyone.

Denise Stevens, St Kilda



Follow Canada’s lead

Adam Voigt says that in Canada 92 per cent of children go to public schools and that schools function as a piece of civil infrastructure, not a market. If they can do it surely we can.

If, like many of us, your taxes are going to private schools that you couldn’t afford to send your kids to, or that have values you wouldn’t want your kids indoctrinated in, think about it when you vote.

Kym Tonkin, Preston Outsourcing’s human toll

The revolutionary “brave new world” of AI brings a two-edged sword of gain and loss to the consequent upheaval of capital and labour. Those who benefit call it “progress” and those who don’t, the human toll, call it all manner of things, none of which are favourable.

And so it is with Qantas outsourcing 850 Australian jobs to India, “modernising the technology behind our business and becoming more efficient, so we can keep investing in our customers, our people and our future”. Such rosy corporate spin doesn’t mention those who stand to gain the most – shareholders, workers in India, and Qantas CEOs. Nor does it mention those who are the human toll of others’ lucrative progress. Although Qantas chief executive Vanessa Hudson does acknowledge, “I know this is hard news for some and I’m sorry for the uncertainty it brings.” Cold comfort no doubt for the “some” losing their jobs.

Deborah Morrison, Malvern East Labor must act

The article ″⁣Bracket creep to hit lowest paid hardest″⁣ (11/11) reopens the question of reducing the reliance on income taxes and broader tax reform.

The Coalition’s tax indexation policy is a sleight of hand as it tempts voters with claims of tax cuts but is merely a steady as she goes approach while avoiding the tougher question of what do we do about burgeoning government expenditure driven by health and welfare services for an ageing population.

Increasing the GST, cutting taxes for the lowest paid, increasing pensions while indexing middle-income earners’ tax rates and reforming corporate tax has to occur. Otherwise the federal Labor government will, to paraphrase Paul Keating, ″⁣be a political carcass swingin’ in the breeze″⁣.

Pier Paolo De Carlo, Ascot Vale Dilemma of truth

While the sandpaper scandal eight years ago remains a stain on Australian cricket, reopening the investigation will not remove that stain nor will it resolve the variations in truth telling from those who were there. When a person in authority (CA in this case) attempts to find out exactly what happened, who was involved directly and indirectly, it is common to get two versions of the truth. This is the case from the rushed investigation at the time and the later statements from certain players.

Given it’s now eight years, the chance of everyone recalling the same truth is as likely as someone matching Bradman’s batting average. CA CEO Todd Greenberg ruled out reopening the investigation and was “comfortable” with its actions (Editorial, 11/11). CA should have embarked on a more thorough investigation immediately after the Test series. They seemed satisfied with a rushed one.

Sometimes finding the precise truth is not the most important thing in the time of a crisis, rather an opportunity to grow and change. That has certainly been the case for the Australian cricket team who have redefined their culture and are still winning regularly.

David Twite, East Melbourne Kids, trust the adult

The AFP’s Paula Hudson is asking young Australians who are embracing extremism ideas to turn to trusted adults rather than AI chatbots. I doubt that these young men (and it seems to be mainly males) would trust any adult. Pity hate laws have been shelved due to the Nationals and Greens objections.

Marie Nash, Balwyn



Wherefore Victoria?

Good luck to the Liberals with their preferences for the election. By choosing to preference One Nation they are clearly indicating they don’t care about the people of Victoria, only about winning. Yet the alleged corruption involving the Big Build while Labor has been in office cannot be ignored.

Victorians go to the election with a Hobson’s Choice in a few weeks. Sad that our progressive, tolerant state has come to this.

Cheryl Day, Beaumaris DJs the interloper

If, God forbid, we are faced with the demise of Myers in the future, I wonder if Sydney residents will be treated to the same feast of nostalgia that we Melburnians have been fed about the turmoil at David Jones. While its decline is regrettable, David Jones nostalgia is mainly Sydney-centric. It’s hardly been the focus of long-gone Melbourne memories. When I was growing up in Melbourne there were no David Jones Christmas windows to marvel at, only Myers. The store next to Myers in Bourke St then was Buckley and Nunn. To me David Jones, when it arrived in Melbourne, was just an over-priced import.

Mike Smith, Sandringham Consider the young

It is unfair and selfish of those living in the older established suburbs to reject high-rise developments.

High-rise housing along transport corridors is the best way to slow the sprawl that blows out the infrastructure costs of the housing our younger generations desperately need. I understand the reluctance of the green leafy suburbs to see high-rise accommodation but we need to consider the younger generations. If suburbs want to reject high rise, those who enjoy the comforts should be prepared to pay significant additional levies for the privilege and these levies should be used to support the new housing.

Michael Fewster, Adelaide Big ideas please

The ″⁣thinness″⁣ of the political debate being espoused by Jess Wilson and Warren Pickering seriously worries me. Such simple offerings disguised as solutions in no way draws the state forward. To ″⁣fix″⁣ this and to ″⁣complain″⁣ about ″⁣that″⁣ simply doesn’t cut it. Where are the big ideas, the state building ideas? Despite the fact that the Big Build may have been executed poorly and has cost us money, my sons and grandsons will be physically reaping the benefits for years to come.

Frank Flynn, Cape Paterson Fighting nonsense

Come on, Jess Wilson, with all the criticism of budget blowouts and the issues that need fixing, you want to blow millions of dollars bringing cage fighting and wrestling to Melbourne? This state has no need to emulate Donald Trump with his cage fighting on the White House lawn. Criticise the government for wasting taxes, tell us how you will fix the economy, but don’t come out with nonsense to pander to a minority.

Stuart Perry, Longford



Mental health funding

The notion that deinstitutionalisation has failed (Letters, 11/11) gives a mixed message. Closing the large institutions for marginalised and stigmatised Victorians with mental illnesses was necessary on humanitarian grounds. However, state governments of both persuasions have instead seen the action as a cost-saving measure and have failed abysmally to fund proper support services for people living in the community and provide adequate short-term acute services. What is required is not the re-establishment of large institutions but rather well-funded and staffed community-based services to support and assist people with chronic or acute mental health issues.

John Annison, Lilydale Protest vote doubts

It is disconcerting and sad that a percentage of the public seems to think that a protest vote for One Nation and against the major parties will somehow solve their grievances. One Nation likes to blame, complain and be critical of the government and opposition without offering any solutions or answers. It is a party aligning itself with oligarchs and following in the footsteps of (the now derailed) Donald Trump. I wonder if those people who are so enamoured with One Nation are actually aware of what they are doing? Do they seek simple answers to highly complex questions or problems? Are they that naive or ignorant and misinformed? Perhaps there is a sense of self-entitlement, or they have become so entwined in the ″⁣me″⁣ culture that they cannot see beyond themselves or even their hip pocket?

Tad Zagorski, Whittlesea Throttle this back

If an electric bike or e-scooter has a throttle that allows higher speeds than pedalling, why are they permitted to use shared cycle and walking paths?

Vivienne Whitehead, Paynesville Cromwell’s message

As Oliver Cromwell said to the British parliament, “You have sat too long here for any good you have done. Depart, I say, and let us have done with you.“

Sandra Torpey, Hawthorn



Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING Qantas

While Qantas shifts another 850 jobs offshore, perhaps it’s time to remove the Spirit of Australia name from its carriers.

Annie Wilson, Inverloch Jobs sent overseas. This is surely not ″⁣the Spirit of Australia″⁣, Qantas. We ″⁣Still call Australia Home″⁣.

Ron Stone. Kangaroo Flat That Qantas, “The Australian Airline”, is to move jobs to India as part of an agreement with Accenture is appalling. It makes a mockery of their theme song We still call Australia Home.

Petrushka Owen, Hawthorn



If all goes well, Qantas will soon end up providing air services in Queensland and the Northern Territory.

Dick Danckert, Torquay What’s happened to ″⁣Made in Australia″⁣?

Malcolm McDonald, Burwood Politics

The Liberals can no longer deny that a vote for them is a vote for One Nation.

Ian Taylor, Torquay Can’t wait for the Liberal-One Nation coalition. It should go down a treat in Toorak and Mount Eliza.

Tim Durbridge, Brunswick It seems the forthcoming election hinges on whether centre-right Liberals preference unhinged One Nation ahead of rusty Labor.

Greg Curtin, Nunawading



This preference alliance will give Victoria a pothole the size of an open-cut mine.

Belinda Burke, Hawthorn The LNP obviously didn’t watch last Sunday’s 60 minutes before deciding to preference One Nation.

Michael Brinkman, Ventnor The fact that the Liberals would prefer One Nation to Labor is absolutely frightening. Is there any viable way to ensure that none of them win?

Les Aisen, Elsternwick Finally

Cricket Australia seems to be very adept at playing the sweep-it-under-the-carpet shot.

John Rawson, Mernda

World.content:
NationalQueenslandBuilding Bad Former department head given contempt warning, as probe calls for new building code Matt Dennien November 11, 2026 — 7:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Queensland’s CFMEU inquiry boss has warned lawyers for a former top bureaucrat that he was at risk of being found in contempt over his professed inability to recall details of discussions at the heart of two key concessions granted to the union. It comes as the $95 million Stuart Wood-led probe issued an interim report late on Wednesday making formal recommendations for the Crisafulli government to introduce a new state building code and establish a new regulator to monitor and enforce compliance. The inquiry this week returned to a case study into regulatory capture of the workplace safety regulator by the union, focusing particularly on the pressure exerted by the CFMEU during the short-lived tenure of one of Michael De’Ath’s deputies. Former Education Department director-general Michael De’Ath giving evidence at the commission of inquiry. Commission of inquiry Former Education Department director-general De’Ath, who in that role between 2021 and 2024 also oversaw the state’s industrial relations and racing offices, returned to the stand on Wednesday for a second full day.



His evidence included early efforts by the mega-department’s deputy director-general in charge of the Office of Industrial Relations, Kym Bancroft, to remove a CFMEU-favoured figure with responsibility for managing safety inspectors, which raised the ire of the union. De’Ath, the most senior former public servant called to date, said on Tuesday he could not recall calls and texts with since-ousted CFMEU state secretary Michael Ravbar in early August 2022, after it was put to him by counsel assisting that Ravbar had expressed disdain over the decision. Commissioner Stuart Wood pictured during hearings last month. Pool - NewsWire/John Gass After this and other efforts by Bancroft to address cultural issues within the office, union figures began calling her directly with site complaints and concerns, leading to a proposal for a general 1300 number to be established to field and triage complaints.



The inquiry heard on Wednesday that the union refused to engage in early consultation on this system, which was also backed and signed off by De’Ath in mid-March 2023, and that it was simultaneously pushing for Bancroft to be removed from an executive director selection panel. Related Article Updated

Queensland government Former workplace safety boss wanted to sack ‘friend of the CFMEU’, but couldn’t Around this time, Ravbar threatened to take his concerns to then-industrial relations minister Grace Grace, and attended a meeting with De’Ath and Bancroft that the director-general cut short due to Ravbar’s aggressive and inappropriate behaviour. The inquiry was then shown an invitation for a meeting sent by Grace’s office to Ravbar and other building sector union figures the same day of his threat, set for early April. Around the end of that meeting, on April 3, call records showed De’Ath was phoned by Grace’s office, and had a meeting of his own set with Grace for the following day. De’Ath said he could not recall what the pair discussed.



The inquiry was then shown an email by Bancroft from the morning of April 5, indicating the triage system was still being pursued. By that afternoon, following a call between De’Ath and Bancroft, it was to be paused with further consultation and an independent facilitator. Related Article Queensland government Crisafulli brushes off calls for special CFMEU probe prosecutor Counsel assisting, Dimitri Ternovski, put Bancroft’s version of events – that De’Ath told her Grace had considered the triage system and it would not be going ahead until the new executive director of compliance and field services was appointed – and asked if it was the truth. De’Ath said it was not, but could not remember the detail of the call, while conceding the shift from the 1300 hotline to an interim arrangement was “another accommodation” of the union’s demands, but that he believed he and Grace would have “problem-solved” to make that shift. At this point, Commissioner Wood reminded De’Ath’s lawyer, Emma Hoiberg, of a High Court opinion that the “feigned inability to remember”, if used by a witness to deliberately evade questions, can amount to an allegation of contempt.



Asked by Hoiberg if such a finding might be made against De’Ath, Wood said: “It seems to me that we’re getting very close to that position.” Hoiberg said the questions related to phone calls and conversations from, in some cases, four years ago in the context of De’Ath’s “wide portfolio across a range of matters” and that “it’s not unexpected for Mr De’Ath to not have specific recall”. After a break to allow Hoiberg to speak with De’Ath, Wood said he was effectively giving the warning required in some jurisdictions before a formal charge could be pursued either by an inquiry or the Supreme Court, but this did not mean it would be pursued. De’Ath said he understood the frustrations of the inquiry, but that he was “sincere and genuine in saying that I just don’t remember all of those conversations” and was “not trying to be in any way evasive”. He said he was not aware of any formal record of a decision to pause the pursuit of the triage system, nor that the department was required to keep one under the Public Records Act, but he rejected the suggestion this was an effort to obscure an intervention from Grace.



De’Ath earlier told the inquiry there was no influence from Grace’s office around either the pausing of the triage system or the eventual dismissal of Bancroft later that month relating to conflict of interest concerns De’Ath took to the Crime and Corruption Commission. After the conclusion of evidence, the attorney-general tabled an interim report from Wood on a question it had posed to stakeholders about the reintroduction of a state building code and a “suitably resourced” regulator to oversee it. Both were formally recommended by Wood. Despite suggesting during a hearing last month that it might not be prudent to wait until the inquiry’s final reporting date in December 2027 to start making broader recommendations to deal with evidence heard of wrongdoing, no such measures featured in Wednesday’s report. The inquiry continues on Thursday, with further evidence from De’Ath. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Our five favourite luxury tree-change homes for sale now
World.content:
PropertyNewsLuxury property Our five favourite luxury tree-change homes for sale now Shona Hendley November 11, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 Gift this free article Share full article with anyone — no subscription needed to read it.
