With health benefits and a slower pace of life, a tree change can offer a whole host of advantages. Property options are another, often with larger land sizes and houses costing far less than those in the city, many rich in history and of luxurious quality. Here are five luxury tree change homes for sale now. 205 Wahring-Murchison East Road, Wahring VIC



Noorilim Estate sits along the Goulburn River and features an Italianate mansion of luxurious proportions. Designed in the gold rush era, around 1879, by architect James Gall for parliamentarian William Winter-Irving, the building features a majestic tower, elaborately arched verandahs, grand columns and ornate balustrades. This high standard continues throughout the home’s 20 rooms and 10 bedrooms. The great hall has soaring ceilings, Corinthian columns, elaborate cornices and luminous Minton tiles laid by Italian artisans. A minstrel gallery once hosted a performance by operatic soprano Dame Nellie Melba. The property has 300 established trees, including ancient Moreton Bay figs, rolling lawns, an Italian garden and a circular rose garden with a central fountain. It also features an ornamental lake and a boathouse. 11 Wagstaffe Avenue, Wagstaffe NSW



With its own private tidal beach, this waterfront property designed by architect Darren Tye was completed only recently. The approximately 891 square-metre property also includes a deep-water jetty and boathouse. The home features a pavilion form, clean lines and lots of natural light. The floorplan, high ceilings and wide stacker doors create an indoor-outdoor flow that makes the most of its setting. Upstairs, a separate retreat with a bedroom and wet bar can be used as guest accommodation or for flexible family living.



Outside, there is a central deck and pool. 760 White Hill Road, Red Hill VIC Tumbywood is a 17-hectare property on a high vantage point in Red Hill. Inarc Architects designed it to capture the Mornington Peninsula’s landscape and to suit its lifestyle.



The home features a sculpted Corten steel facade, while inside, substantial glazing offers views across Port Phillip Bay to the You Yangs, Port Arlington, Swan Bay and Mud Island. There are polished concrete floors with underfloor hydronic heating, rich grey ironbark walls, four distinct living spaces and integrated technology including Sonos sound, and a dedicated communications room. The property includes a separate double-storey residence, The Cottage, which has its own gate and three bedrooms. There are also established gardens, paddocks, a separate wellness retreat, an inviting in-ground pool and spa and manicured lawns. 355 Centennial Road, Bowral NSW



Perfect for the equestrian lover or cattle farmer, Cardington Park spans almost 60 hectares, featuring manicured gardens, mostly cleared blocks of land, fenced paddocks and a dam. The home sits at the end of a tree-lined driveway and includes an open-plan layout that captures views of the surrounding scenery. There is an additional separate cottage, a detached garage and workshop, and a large shed. Located less than six kilometres from the Bowral town centre, the location is another highlight. 20 Byrne Lane, Maleny QLD



Located in the Sunshine Coast Hinterland, this property blends a rich history with extensive contemporary renovations. Exquisite period features include original leadlight glass windows and doors sourced from Brisbane’s historic Petrie Mansions, as well as solid timber internal doors with period detailing. Updates include a modern kitchen with LED-illuminated granite benchtops, a steam oven, a pyrolytic oven and a speed oven, plus bifold doors that open to the surrounding verandah and entertaining areas. The garden is another highlight, with fruit trees and established magnolias, camellias, azaleas, agapanthus, bromeliads, poinciana trees, Australian natives and privacy hedges.

World.title: Victorian election hot seats: ‘You sweating?’ In Shepparton, One Nation and the Nationals face a grilling
World.content:
A notorious pothole in Melbourne’s east has been filled overnight after becoming a social media star in the run-up to the state election.

Sitting at the intersection of Mahoneys and Canterbury roads in Forest Hill and straddling the electorates of Glen Waverley and Ringwood, the pothole had been there since at least December, according to Google Street View images. Liberal candidate for Ringwood Nick McGowan says it dated back to at least mid-2025.

One local resident, whose identity The Age has not been able to confirm, created an Instagram page drawing attention to the problem on November 1, with the bio “just a pothole living my best life”. Since then, the account has gathered more than 550 followers and posted daily updates on the gaping hole.

World.title: ‘Absolutely false’: Another former coach denies knowledge of sandpaper plot
World.content:
Exclusive SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘Absolutely false’: Another former coach denies knowledge of sandpaper plot Andrew Wu and Christy Doran Updated November 11, 2026 — 7:39pm ,first published 1:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A member of Darren Lehmann’s coaching staff from the 2018 South Africa tour has denied having any knowledge of the sandpaper plot, slamming Usman Khawaja’s assertion it was known by all members of the touring party as “absolutely false”. As David Warner hit back at Lehmann for downplaying his knowledge of the scandal, Australia’s former batting coach Graeme Hick said he was not aware of the use of sandpaper until footage emerged of Cameron Bancroft on the big screen. Australia’s former batting coach Graeme Hick with Steve Smith during the 2019 Ashes series. PA The revelation came on a day when Khawaja pulled out of television and radio interviews to promote his memoir Sabr after his grilling from multiple Walkley winner Sarah Ferguson on the ABC’s 7.30 program, during which he failed to answer key questions about Sandpapergate. Test captain Pat Cummins is expected to speak publicly for the first time since Khawaja’s explosive claims on Friday, though Cricket Australia said that was yet to be confirmed.



Australia’s stand-in ODI captain Mitch Marsh is due to speak at his pre-game press conference on Thursday ahead of the first game against England, where he is likely to be quizzed on his knowledge of the events from eight years ago. Australia’s former batting coach Graeme Hick in 2018. Getty Images A close friend of Cummins and a former state teammate of Bancroft, Marsh has told national teammates he is nervous about how he will address the matter, according to a source with knowledge of the matter. The all-rounder was in the attack at the time South African broadcaster SuperSport aired footage of Bancroft hiding a piece of sandpaper down his trousers. Cameron Bancroft slid a yellow strip of sandpaper into his pants in Cape Town. Getty Images



Hick, Australia’s batting coach from 2016-2020, denied any involvement or knowledge of the plan to use sandpaper in Cape Town and, as claimed by Khawaja, in Port Elizabeth. Lehmann also denied knowledge of the plan and questioned Khawaja’s claim that all members of the team knew. Khawaja has said the entire squad was complicit in the use of sandpaper and should share the blame instead of allowing his close friend Warner, Bancroft and former captain Steve Smith, who all copped lengthy bans from Cricket Australia, to carry the burden. Loading Khawaja also claimed a member of the coaching staff had encouraged Bancroft to use sandpaper during an interval of the Cape Town Test. “I have seen the various statements around the coaches and I’m very disappointed with the broad nature of them,” Hick told this masthead.



“Khawaja puts it simply: ‘It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us.’ To me what Khawaja is implying here is absolutely false. “In regard to any discussions around the ball tampering in Port Elizabeth or Cape Town that took place, I will say in true honesty that I did not hear or know anything!! “My first knowledge of all this was, like many, when it appeared on the big screen in Cape Town as I was sat on the outside balcony at the time.” “I have seen the various statements around the coaches and I’m very disappointed with the broad nature of them. “Khawaja puts it simply: ‘It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us.’ To me what Khawaja is implying here is absolutely false.” Graeme Hick Victoria captain Peter Handscomb, who was on a walkie-talkie to Lehmann in Cape Town after vision emerged of Bancroft on the big screen in Cape Town, said he did not want to speak about the affair.



“I appreciate you have to ask these questions,” Handscomb said after making an unbeaten 131 against Western Australia at the MCG. “I’ve had a nice day today, it’s not really something that I want to comment on right now. I’ll sort of just let the powers of be do their thing.” Warner took to social media on Wednesday morning and agreed with former International Cricket Council match referee Chris Broad – the father of England great Stuart – that Lehmann should not have been Australia’s coach if he had no idea that sandpaper was being used in Newlands. Loading “Darren Lehmann surely knew all about it,” said Broad on Talk Radio, after Lehmann denied that “everyone” knew that sandpaper was being used during the infamous third Test between Australia and South Africa in Cape Town in 2018 on ABC radio. “And if he didn’t, he shouldn’t have been the coach at the time.



“I think he’s got away lightly … OK, he left his job a few months later, but he didn’t get any sanctions.” View post on X Broad, who played 25 Tests for England, also said Lehmann had double standards during his term as Australia’s coach, saying he was “very angry” at his response to his son’s decision not to walk during a controversial Ashes Test in 2013. “And there he was in 2013, taking the moral high ground against my son, where he played the Australian game of nicking the ball and waiting for the umpire to give him out, and he got given not out on that occasion, and then [Lehmann] came out in the media saying ‘we’re going to make him cry when he comes to Australia next,’” Broad continued. Former Australia coach Darren Lehmann (right) with batsman Dave Warner. Getty Images



“And here he is, the coach of the Australian cricket team that brought sandpaper out onto the field of play and denied any knowledge of this happening. “I’m very angry at Darren Lehmann in this respect.” Warner has since poured fuel on the fire, backing Broad. “I couldn’t agree more and that’s hard for me to say!” he responded on X on Wednesday. Lehmann declined to comment when contacted.

World.title: Crimson Education founder Jamie Beaton named Entrepreneur Of The Year
World.content:
The founder of global university advisory business Crimson Education has been named EY Entrepreneur Of The Year.

Crimson founder and chief executive Jamie Beaton also accepted the Technology and Emerging Industries Entrepreneur award at last night's gala event in Auckland.

He was previously honoured with the Young Entrepreneur award in 2023.

The independent judging panel was made up of past award winners with nominees assessed on four core criteria, including entrepreneurial spirit, impact, growth and purpose.

Chair of judges and last year's overall winner Phil Thomson said Beaton's growth as an entrepreneur impressed the judging panel.

"Jamie Beaton really impressed all the judges around his bold vision in championing education, not just for New Zealanders and everyone across the world, but for anyone. And then secondly, the scale of what he's built over the last decade or so, from a very young age initially," Thomson said.

Crimson Education was established in 2013 and offered online schooling, tutoring, mentoring and academic enrichment.

Its business portfolio included Crimson Education, Crimson Global Academy, NumberWorks'nWords and Revision Village.

Beaton also established the Te Ara a Kupe Beaton Scholarship, which provided educational support for Māori and Pasifika students pursuing international study opportunities.

Thomson - who was also the co-founder of retail crime intelligence platform Auror - said the calibre of the candidates for the top award were outstanding.

Other winners:

Patrick Moynahan (Echo Tech), Young Entrepreneur

Sarah Kennedy (Calocurb), Product Entrepreneur

Peter Shenoda (Bargain Chemist), Services Entrepreneur

Lindsay Faithfull (McKay), Master Entrepreneur

The judges earlier recognised Pic Picot of Pic's Peanut Butter with an Award for Outstanding Contribution to Entrepreneurship and Community, acknowledging his impact on the Nelson community and his broader contribution to innovation within New Zealand's food sector.

World.title: Police say person who fired gun at officers still at large
World.content:
Police say a person who fired a gun at officers in Napier is still at large.

Eastern District Commander Superintendent Joel Lamb said Police tried to stop a vehicle in the Pirimai Area at about 10pm on Tuesday.

He said someone in the back seat pointed what was presumed to be a firearm at officers pursuing the vehicle.

"Staff have then heard two distinct gunshots as the firearm was discharged.

"Fortunately, neither of our officers were injured, and the patrol vehicle did not sustain any damage."

He said hours later, the vehicle was seen travelling north on the Waikato Expressway towards Auckland.

Police seized the vehicle at an address in Manurewa, but they had not found the alleged offender.

Lamb said people who lived at the Manurewa address were engaging with Police.

He said Eastern District and Counties Manukau Police were making enquiries.

"Presenting a firearm at a Police officer is a serious escalation that puts our staff and the wider community at risk. This behaviour is entirely unacceptable.

"We are taking this incident extremely seriously and will be pursuing all lines of enquiry to locate the offender and hold them accountable."

Police asked anyone who witnessed the incident to contact Police on 105 or online using the reference number 261111/3764.

World.title: Severe weather hits North Island prompting flood rescues
World.content:
Severe weather hit parts of the North Island on Wednesday after multiple red weather warnings were issued throughout the afternoon.

Several people had to be rescued after attempting to drive through floodwater in the Waikato, amid thunderstorm warnings.

Fire and Emergency said one person who drove into floodwater at the intersection of Old Taupo Road and Wiltsdown Road on Tuesday afternoon was assisted by a truck driver, who towed the car out.

Both Police and Fire and Emergency New Zealand were called to the area at about 3:30pm but had since left.

Police said they had received reports of vehicles becoming stuck and closed Old Taupo Road because of severe flooding.

World.title: Two arrested after firearm brandished following assault at Dargaville shop
World.content:
A 29-year-old man and a 63-year-old woman have been charged after an assault at a Dargaville shop.

Whangārei-Kaipara area investigations manager Detective Senior Sergeant Shane Pilmer said Police were called to a store on Victoria Road just before 11am on Tuesday.

"An assault has occurred inside the store involving parties known to each other."

"The alleged offender in the assault then left the store, before getting into a vehicle and leaving the area."

He said a man in the vehicle allegedly pointed a firearm and made verbal threats towards a person at a bus stop.

The man has been charged with commission of a crime with a firearm, presenting a pistol, and threatening to kill; while an older woman has been charged with two counts of assault.

World.title: Sports club loses $40,000 of gear in suspected fireworks related blaze
World.content:
A sports club says it has taken years of fundraising to afford gear that has now been burnt in a fire they believe was caused by fireworks.

Police are investigating after a fire at a Hamilton park destroyed thousands of dollars of football gear for junior players.

Witnesess says people were aiming firecrackers at each other at Discovery Park shortly before the blaze. Police ask anyone who saw this to come forward.

Mark Oliphant from Northern United Sports Club said the park was a second home for hundreds of kids during the football season.

"When we all learnt about it (the fire) on the Friday morning, we were despondent really," he told Checkpoint.

He said it would cost the club $40,000 to replace the gear.

Burnt gear included football goals, uniforms, balls, first aid kits, and a pitch line marker.

Oliphant said some of the gear was insured, but not all.

He said the response from the community, as well as neighbouring sports clubs, had been incredible.

"It's been quite heartwarming."

World.title: Private school apologises after 'computer systems issue' halts NCEA English exam
World.content:
A Christchurch private school has apologised after a "computer systems issue" prevented Year 13 English students from completing their NCEA exam on Wednesday morning.

In a letter to parents, St Andrew's College rector Mark Wilson said there had been a significant disruption to the Level 3 English exam.

"The examination commenced as scheduled at 9.30am but was stopped part-way through following a computer systems issue," he said.

"This was very distressing and disappointing for the approximately 120 students affected, particularly given the preparation they had undertaken for this important examination."

The college would not explain what the issue was or answer further questions from RNZ.

Students would receive the grade from their internal examination results instead, Wilson said.

"For external examinations, where a student is unable to complete an examination because of circumstances outside their control, the established process is for a derived grade to be used. As a college, we recognise that some students have been significantly impacted by today's disruption and we are committed to supporting them through this process."

NZQA did not provide schools with sufficient paper-based copies for all students when exams were to be completed digitally, meaning there was not a paper-based exam available for all affected students to move to, Wilson said.

"Having spoken with NZQA today, we understand that digital examination incidents are not unusual and that NZQA receives multiple reports of issues during each examination season," he said.

"St Andrew's College has a robust digital environment with students well supported by devices and network infrastructure. However, as we have experienced today, no digital system is completely immune from disruption."

The problem was addressed and remaining exams would continue as planned, Wilson said.

The college would have sufficient paper copies on hand for future exams in case of any further issues.

World.title: New Zealand's only David Jones store to close
World.content:
The sole David Jones store in New Zealand is to close.

The shop at Newmarket in Auckland is one of 19 stores of the iconic Australian department store that will shut.

The receivers, FTI Consulting, said the stores would remain open for now as consultation with staff is done, but they were expected to shut by the end of the year.

They said the closures were regrettable but unavoidable.

"The Receivers have made the difficult decision to proceed with an urgent restructure of the business, in line with management's plan for the future of David Jones that was being worked on prior to the appointment," the receivers said in a statement.

"Whilst the impacts are highly regrettable, the receivers believe the steps are unavoidable if David Jones is to continue as a viable business and these measures will help give David Jones the best chance for a sustainable future."

The group was put into receivership and administration a week ago after the company could not negotiate a deal with its major landlord, the Westfield mall owners.

The Newmarket store, in the Westfield mall, made a loss of $4.4 million in 2024/25, which included a significant write down involving its lease. The parent group made a loss of $95.5m in the same year, which followed a $74m loss in the preceding year.

World.title: Past, present and future health champions honour MAPAS pioneer Professor Colin Mantell
World.content:
Generations of Māori and Pacific health professionals have gathered at Waipapa Marae to honour the legacy of the man who helped shape the future of Māori and Pacific medical education.

Emeritus Professor Colin Mantell (Ngāi Tahu) died peacefully on 3 October 2026, leaving behind a remarkable legacy in medicine, medical education, and Māori and Pacific health.

Over a career spanning more than six decades, Mantell helped transform the pathways available to Māori and Pacific students entering medicine. An internationally recognised researcher and specialist in obstetrics and gynaecology, he went on to become the University of Auckland's inaugural Professor of Māori and Pacific Health.

Among his many contributions to the health sector was his role as the founding chair of the Māori and Pacific Admission Scheme (MAPAS), which sought to grow a health workforce that better reflected and served Māori and Pacific communities.

"He leaves behind generations of doctors he inspired, a grateful community, and a family who loved him fiercely," Mantell's obituary states.

Over a career spanning more than six decades, Professor Colin Mantell (Ngāi Tahu) helped transform the pathways available to Māori and Pacific students entering medicine. Supplied / Wanaka App

Throughout the kawe mate, held on Wednesday at Waipapa Taumata Rau, Auckland University, generations of colleagues and health leaders reflected on Mantell's commitment to creating a fairer health system.

In the late 1990s, Mantell became a driving force behind Vision 20:20, a kaupapa aimed at growing the number of Māori and Pacific people working across Aotearoa's health system.

As part of that vision, the university established a foundation programme for Māori and Pacific students preparing for health professional study, which later became Hikitia Te Ora, the Certificate in Health Sciences.

RNZ/ Layla Bailey-McDowell

Reflecting on the programme, Mantell said at the time, it was important that students did not feel they were "always on the outer, always at risk of failure", and instead received support that recognised their individual needs and potential.

Professor Papaarangi Reid, Tumuaki of Te Kupenga Hauora Māori, said Mantell recognised early that meaningful change in health required a different approach to medical education.

"Generations of students have walked through doors that Colin helped open. His legacy lives in us, in the communities we serve and in the continuing work of MAPAS. We owe him an enormous debt of gratitude."

RNZ / Coco Lance

Among those paying tribute at the kawe mate was Professor David Tipene-Leach, who was involved in the programme's early development.

"Colin Mantell was a visionary," Tipene-Leach told RNZ.

An obstetrician by training, Mantell became concerned by the differences in health outcomes between Māori and Pacific babies and those of non-Māori and non-Pacific backgrounds.

Tipene-Leach (Pōrangahau, Ngāti Kere and Ngāti Manuhiri) said Mantell recognised the need to address those inequities and used his position within the medical school to help grow a pathway for Māori and Pacific students into health professions.

"He grew the MAPAS scheme from two, three entries a year up to the huge number of entries that they have now."

That legacy was echoed throughout the kawe mate, as speakers reflected on Mantell's lifelong commitment to addressing inequities in Māori and Pacific health.

Professor David Tipene-Leach (Pōrangahau, Ngāti Kere and Ngāti Manuhiri). RNZ / Coco Lance

Tipene-Leach said Mantell took responsibility for nurturing MAPA's vision and expanding its reach.

At the time Tipene-Leach began medical school in 1974, there were just three Māori students in his year, and one in the year before.

Today, MAPAS has produced more than 1,000 graduates from the University of Auckland, with dozens of students entering the programme each year.

The tribute comes as MAPAS faces renewed political scrutiny, with debate over the future of targeted admission schemes for Māori and Pacific students.

Tipene-Leach said the programme's value could be demonstrated through the outcomes of its graduates.

A kawe mate was held at Waipapa Taumata Rau, honouring the legacy of Emeritus Professor Colin Mantell (Ngāi Tahu). RNZ/ Layla Bailey-McDowell

"We've heard from the present controversy that's going on around whether we should or shouldn't have a MAPAS scheme," he said.

"We've found that these MAPAS graduates, they pass at the same rates, they stay in New Zealand, they don't go overseas, they are more likely to become general practitioners. And we know there's a shortage of that. They're more likely to go into the regions, into rural medicine, and we know there's a shortage there.

"These are exactly the doctors that we should be training in New Zealand."

After five decades in medical practice, Tipene-Leach said his vision was for a Māori health workforce equipped to serve its own communities.

A Tino Rangatiratanga Flag flies at Waipapa Marae. RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

"I've been in practice for 50 years now, and it's always been that we have a Māori workforce that is able to service our community and be the front line of service in our community. But the truth is that what we need is we need allies who are there with us in the battle for good health for Māori people, for Pacific people, in fact, for everybody in Aotearoa New Zealand who at the moment don't get a fair deal."

World.title: Want to win an AFLW flag? Club culture matters, data shows
World.content:
AFLW sides are more likely to finish down the bottom of the ladder when their players rate their workplace culture low, the players' association says.

Data collected from the union around the middle of the season suggests a strong correlation between workplace culture and on-field performance.

"If we look at AFLW, what we're seeing is there is a bit of a widening gap between the best of our workplace culture data and that which is more at the bottom," AFL Players Association chief executive James Gallagher told ABC Sport.

"We're seeing some of the highest scores ever reported at the top end, so that's fantastic. That's what we want to see, but we are seeing a gap between the best and the bottom end."

Collingwood's woeful AFLW season Former AFLW player and coach Lauren Arnell has criticised the standard of Collingwood, while emphasising the responsibility of coaches to "put on a show" to grow the game.

This year, four teams were assessed as having the best workplace culture on record and four teams the worst.

This was evaluated according to club care, mental breaks, off-field expectations, relationships, schedule flexibility and study/work support.

Five of this year's finals teams were in the top seven for "overall workplace culture". Non-finalist teams overwhelmingly rated on the lower end for workplace culture scores.

It comes after widespread media scrutiny on struggling clubs, particularly Collingwood.

James Gallagher says there is a correlation between successful AFLW sides and workplace culture ratings. (Getty: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

The Magpies, along with St Kilda, finished with one win each this season, while GWS and Essendon had just two victories out of their 12 games.

Of those four bottom-ladder clubs, all but the Giants parted ways with their head coaches.

The Magpies and Saints are now set to undertake external reviews of their women's programs,. Essendon has opted to conduct an expanded internal review.

North Melbourne, Geelong, Melbourne, Carlton, Gold Coast, Sydney, Western Bulldogs and Hawthorn finished in the top eight this year.

Sydney and the Western Bulldogs featured in the finals series this year. (Getty: Darrian Traynor)

The Kangaroos have lost one game in three years and the Demons have regularly finished in the finals.

The data also showed some players as having rated respect for the men's AFL club head of performance and head coach as low to extremely low.

Furthermore, men's players being embroiled in off-field news, such as the Sydney Swans saga involving allegations of sexual assault or GWS' "controversial couples" night leading to player sanctions, can impact the women's programs.

"There's no doubt they are extraordinarily challenging for all to navigate. I mean, do they have an impact on AFLW playing groups? In some cases, they do for sure," Mr Gallagher said.

"Making sure there's an opportunity for those players' views to be heard and considered is a really important part of how footy clubs in 2026 now operate."

Pies launch AFLW review As a tough season nears its end, Collingwood announces a strategic review into the struggling AFLW program, with the club's president admitting the Pies had not "got it right".

Crucially, with the seasons overlapping more every year, men's and women's programs require access to the same facilities, including the gym and communal areas.

Just half of all players said they felt their men's and women's programs were aligned.

"Those clubs that report the strongest workplace environments are much more likely to be successful, and that's reflected in the final series in front of us," Mr Gallagher said.

"The game is a high-performance game and to enable that to be successful you do need people who are fronting up, comfortable, confident, feeling like they're really well supported, and we're seeing that reflected in the wins and losses column now, for sure."

Women's teams with strong workplace culture are more likely to make the finals, according to the AFLPA. (Getty: Kelly Defina)

Workplace culture includes club support for players outside football commitments, including work and study.

While players have seen huge strides in increased contact hours since season one, more than half of all players still work outside football.

Sixty-four per cent engage in casual work, 32 per cent work part-time and 4 per cent full-time. None of the 45 Irish players can work due to their visas.

The players' association expects next year's AFLW season to accommodate more double-headers. The start date is yet to be announced.

World.title: The rebuild is on as Labuschagne makes shaky return to Shield cricket
World.content:
Marnus Labuschagne's return to first-class cricket following his axing from the Test team lasted 36 balls for Queensland in the Sheffield Shield on Wednesday.

Labuschagne made 12 runs before nicking off to Tasmania's Jake Doran off the bowling of Riley Meredith.

The 32-year-old's dismissal looked similar to so many of his recent failings at Test level, prodding on fourth stump without a hint of foot movement.

Ordinarily Sheffield Shield games retain some semblance of importance for Test players searching for form ahead of The Summer of Cricket.

Uniquely for Queensland's captain, this match means nothing — at least in the short-term.

He's already been flung on the Test scrap heap, a dire run of form eventually hastening his demise from an Australian Test team that crushed England in last year's Ashes, but has won just two of its last five Tests against Bangladesh and South Africa, without claiming a series victory.

Spectators didn't mind that though, and more than a handful had turned out to show support to their beleaguered skipper.

Those who arrived on time had to wait an hour and 20 minutes before Labuschagne came to the crease after Angus Lovell (18 off 60 balls) edged Beau Webster into the slips. The opener furiously smacked his bat after doing so much of the hard work on a pitch that offered plenty of zip.

Labuschagne's arrival was greeted with warm applause, the clapping briefly drowning out the incessant jackhammering of the building sites around the Gabba.

"Come on Marnus," one punter among the hundred or so faithful called out as he took his mark.

Marnus Labuschagne lasted 36 balls in his first return to the crease since South Africa. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Labuschagne wasted no time in getting into the thick of the action, crushing a square drive for four off the very first ball he faced from former Test teammate Webster.

A streaky edge past third slip off the bowling of Jackson Bird though, reiterated that Labuschagne's rebuild could be a process as drawn out as the redevelopment around the ground.

As good as his opening salvo was, the idiosyncrasies that all too often verged towards idiocies during his faltering stays in the middle during Test matches, were still there.

There was a wave of his hands here, a period of shadow-batting there that were as prevalent at the Gabba as they were in Gqeberha, where he scored 14 and 39 in Australia's innings defeat.

As Bell got closer to the off-stump, Labuschagne's leaves became ever more flamboyant, a batting matador daring the bull to crash into his stumps.

He lasted until lunch, walking off with eight runs to his name.

His demise came soon after the break when edged a delivery he didn't need to play at into the gloves of the keeper.

Labuschagne waited a moment at the crease, miffed at his dismissal, before trudging off.

Fortunately for him, it was far from a bumper day of scores around the country.

Sam Konstas scored 24 and Kurtis Patterson a duck for New South Wales as they were bundled out for 204 against South Australia, while Marcus Harris managed just 15 on an MCG pitch that looked good for batting, given Peter Handscomb's century for Victoria.

It is far too soon after his return from South Africa to rectify any wrongs in his technique or banish the demons residing within his head.

As much as the hammering taking place outside the Gabba, the work to build Labuschagne back into a principle Test batter will take time.

World.title: How a small scrap of sandpaper shed light on cricket's so-called dark arts
World.content:
Eight years after then-prime minister Malcolm Turnbull felt the need to weigh in on Australia's ball tampering in the Cape Town Test, sandpaper and cricket are back in the headlines together.

Usman Khawaja's book, featuring revelations, allusions and confirmations of what most everyone already believed, has reignited conversations about the Australian team's conduct during that 2018 tour of South Africa.

But whatever the team did, who did it and who knew about it, one thing is for sure: they weren't the first to fiddle with the ball.

So why did they do it and why was the reaction so extreme?

'A beautiful art'

Reverse swing can make even the best batters look silly. (Getty Images: Tom Shaw)

In the wake of Khawaja's exclusive interview with Nine Newspapers on the weekend, outspoken former Australia fast bowler Geoff Lawson added to the conversation with a brilliantly headlined article.

" I don't know a bowler who hasn't licked, flicked, scratched or slobbered on a cricket ball. "

Thanks for those mental images, Geoff.

Evocative wording or not, the 46-Test veteran is right. But why?

Explaining the mysteries of swing bowling It is one of the most devastating weapons a fast bowler can own — but the art of swing is steeped in mystery and myths that only science can explain.

The science of conventionally swinging a cricket ball through the air is relatively simple and adheres to some basic rules of drag, air pressure and laminar flow (a lot of the same stuff that keeps an aeroplane in the air).

When a cricket ball is new, its stitched seam is standing at its tallest, allowing a bowler to angle that seam towards or away from the batter and the air will get caught on the seam, dragging the ball in that direction.

But the proud seam on a dark red ball is clearly visible to a batter, and the best ones can see what's happening and account for it.

Reverse swing is a little more complicated and prized due to it being more difficult to deliver, predict and face.

Conventional swing (left) vs reverse swing (right). (ABC News: Gabrielle Flood and Nina Maile Gordon)

"As a batter it's the hardest thing to face. It's a beautiful art," former Proteas captain Faf du Plessis told The Grade Cricketer podcast on the eve of Australia's return to Cape Town last month.

The ball swings towards the side of the ball that looks smoother due to small abrasions on that "shiny" side of the ball, more of which is facing the batter and therefore offering more surface area and turbulent airflow, this time dragging the ball in the opposite direction to the way the seam is facing.

It also happens later in the ball's flight, often too late for the batter to react.

It only comes after the ball has been bowled for a few dozen overs and whacked around the field a bit; once the seam has flattened out, and the leather has been, crucially, roughed up and dried out.

Weather conditions have to be perfect, the bowlers have to be incredibly skilled and the care for the ball has to be spot-on, to the point that former England captain Alastair Cook was prized as a ball shiner because he barely sweats.

Of course, there are other ways to help this along.

Spit, sunscreen and swing

There are plenty of legal ways to shine the ball. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Once a cricket pitch has flattened out from the start of a game, the new ball has lost its shine and proud seam, and before it becomes a spinner's paradise on days four and five (although this is becoming more and more rare), reverse swing is one of the few tools in fast bowler's arsenal.

For decades, cricket teams have worked on the ball feverishly to try to work on conventional and reverse swing.

Often players will shine the ball on their groin or hip, or some sweat from their forehead (or spit in pre-COVID times).

In those processes, there are some grey areas.

Any sensible cricketer will be wearing sunscreen, some will be wearing hair products, many will be chewing gum or chomping on a lolly.

Sweat can be used to shine the ball but keeping it dry is key to reverse swing. (Getty Images: Stu Forster)

All of that gives a little extra viscosity to the sweat or saliva used on the ball, but match referees couldn't very well force players to spit their gum into a hanky on the boundary line or force them to have a shower before entering the field of play, so there is not much they can do.

Then there's the flip side, where players try to create a rougher surface to generate that turbulent airflow, which can include simple things like picking at the seam of a ball or fielders intentionally throwing the ball in short to ensure it bounces on the coarse pitch block.

Ironically enough, du Plessis, South Africa's captain on that fateful 2018 tour, twice stumbled from lightish grey into gun-metal territory earlier in his career.

In 2013, after a failed attempt with his fingernails, du Plessis was caught on camera blatantly scratching the ball on the zip of his pants pocket, mere centimetres from legal territory.

Teams work hard on the ball to create the conditions for conventional and reverse swing bowling. (Getty Images: Santanu Banik/MB Media)

A few years later, as he skippered the team during a 2016 tour of Australia, he was again seen on the field opening his mouth, touching his fingers to a massive white mint on the middle of his tongue, then applying that sugary saliva directly to the ball.

Had he simply sucked the mint, popped it into his cheek and then touched his tongue, he could have avoided his own chase through the airport and a hefty fine.

Du Plessis described the fallout from his 2013 zipper incident as "a week of hell", so it's no wonder he expressed so much sympathy for Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith (curiously no mention of David Warner) as the world closed in on them.

After massive bans and public disgrace, you would think the world would have moved on, but between the long-awaited Test return to South Africa and now Khawaja's book, the controversy seems never-ending.

Why the sandpaper saga?

One part absolutely boils to down to Australian cricket's sense of exceptionalism and perception of itself as arbiter of what is and isn't acceptable on a cricket field.

But the brazen nature of the ball tampering is perhaps the biggest reason that this was and remains such a big story.

Sandpapergate continues to wound Australia Usman Khawaja and David Warner's Sandpapergate revelations may have set the scene for civil war in Australian cricket as the 2018 ball-tampering scandal continues to captivate and damage.

England skipper Michael Atherton was caught rubbing dirt into the ball and his reputation remains pristine but, like the various fructose or lotion-enhanced bodily fluids, that's the sort of thing one could use on the ball opportunistically or even inadvertently.

Perhaps that's why Bancroft's first feeble attempt at deflection was claiming he "saw an opportunity to potentially use some tape [and] get some granules from the rough patches on the wicket", rather than bringing some 300 grit onto the field where its only purpose could be ball tampering.

There are legendary tales of bottle caps being used to help out reverse swing kings like Wasim Akram and Waqar Younis in Test matches way back when, and Khawaja wrote about some of the methods he had seen or heard of in Sheffield Shield cricket.

But in a high-profile Test series, to be so obvious when the team knew they already had heat on them betrayed a sense that they thought they were untouchable or that winning was worth the risk.

Alas, the SuperSport cameras caught him in high definition and super slow-mo and put the so-called dark arts very much under a spotlight.

After du Plessis's minty moment, Dirk Nannes said in commentary at the time for ABC Sport: "It's an art and some of the art is doing it and not getting caught."

If that is the case, consider Cameron Bancroft less Gauguin and more Gallagher.

World.title: ACL battles haven't halted these AFL draft hopefuls
World.content:
In just the second game of this year's footy season, Gus White did not realise he had suffered an ACL injury when he hurt his knee.

"I landed a bit funny and hyperextended my knee … it didn't hurt that bad," he said.

" I went and got scans a couple of days later, the result came back with the ACL, which was really devastating. "

The 18-year-old is one of many teenage footballers vying for a chance in the AFL draft later this month — and is hopeful he will be in contention, despite only playing one full game of football this year.

"I'm obviously really nervous, not having much control over my playing this year," he said.

For months, White has been firmly focused on recovery. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

White said he initially sat in the emotions of the injury but quickly shifted his focus.

"I just gave myself 24 to 48 hours to sit in my thoughts and really feel it and from then move on and accept that it's happened," he said.

" 'Control the controllables' was the main goal — and [to] just stay as positive as I could. "

The South Adelaide product just hit the six-month milestone of recovery, a significant halfway mark of an injury that sidelines most players for about a year.

'Every journey's different'

When the injury first happened, White spoke to someone who had trodden the same path a year earlier.

North Adelaide's Memphis Webb injured his ACL last year. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

It was round 2 of the 2025 SANFL season when North Adelaide's Memphis Webb injured his ACL.

"The 12 months was long, but I made strategies and figured out ways to get through it," he said.

Webb decided to step away from football for the year as he recovered.

"I learnt a lot about myself, because before that my life had pretty much just been football," he said.

" Obviously it wasn't great not playing footy for a year, but it was almost a blessing as well. "

Webb stepped away from football for a year. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

The 18-year-old said the recovery process had given him a lot of time to reflect, and had reignited his love for football when finally returned to playing in round 4 this year.

"I was like a little kid again, playing footy for the first time," Webb said.

The midfielder said he was at the match, but not yet back playing, when White did his ACL against North Adelaide in round 2.

"We had a good chat about things to expect for him — I just said, 'Every journey's different, don't try and compare to other people'," he said.

Webb returned to the field earlier this year. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

White said Webb was one of the first people he went to about his injury.

"I asked him how he dealt with things and what worked for him, what didn't," White said.

White, who is also a midfielder, said seeing someone else experience the same injury and return to the field after such a hard time was motivating.

"It sort of opens that light at the end of the tunnel," he said.

White says discussion with Webb helped boost confidence in recovery. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

'Dream to play AFL footy'

White was invited to the AFL Draft Combine, where top junior prospects undergo physical testing and interviews, but was unable to be involved.

He was hopeful his junior years of footy had been enough to show prospective AFL clubs what he could achieve.

"Ever since I was four years old, it's been the dream to play AFL footy, so if my name were to be called out on draft night, I'll be over the moon," he said.

Webb is prepared for all eventualities. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

Webb was also invited to the national combine but instead featured at the state event due to sickness.

While feeling nervous ahead of the draft, he was grateful for the experience so far.

"Not many people my age get to experience this journey that I've been on," he said.

" I'm just looking forward to it, whatever happens will happen. "

The AFL draft will be held over two nights on November 19 and 20.

World.title: Minjee Lee set to end horror 2026 season with Tour Championship absence
World.content:
Minjee Lee will miss the LPGA's rich and prestigious Tour Championship for the first time in more than a decade after calling an end to her deflating 2026 season.

Australia's triple major champion has opted out of The ANNIKA, the all-important penultimate event of the year starting on Thursday, rendering Lee no chance of scraping into next week's $US11 million ($16 million) showpiece in Florida.

Lee hasn't missed the season-ending championship since 2014.

But after slumping from third in the world rankings last October to 24th, her equal-lowest standing in 11 years, the WA superstar has opted for a reset following her last-place finish at the Japan Classic on Sunday.

Battling swing issues, the 30-year-old has slumped to 79th in the season-long point standings, with only the top 60 to qualify for the Tour Championship in Naples from November 19-22.

The 11-times LPGA Tour winner tied for 13th last year, with her best result in the event being a share of seventh on debut as a teenager in 2015.

While Lee will be absent this week, four Australians will be striving to punch their tickets to the Tour Championship at Pelican Golf Club in Belleair.

Perched safely in 11th place in the points race, Hannah Green is also sitting out The ANNIKA tournament.

But Cassie Porter (47th), Grace Kim (51st), Karis Davidson (54th) and Robyn Choi (61st) are all teeing it up.

Currently one spot outside the qualification zone, Choi likely needs a top-30 finish to clinch a maiden berth at the Tour Championship after enjoying a fruitful Asian swing.

Having become the first woman ever to clinch player-of-the-year honours before the Tour Championship, world No.1 Nelly Korda is chasing more history this week.

The American can become the first LPGA professional to win the same event for the fourth time since The ANNIKA tournament namesake Annika Sorenstam in 2005.

Korda also has a chance to become the fifth player in LPGA Tour history to win the same tournament at least four times and the first since Se Ri Pak at the Jamie Farr Kroger Classic in 2003.

AAP

World.title: Warner jabs former Australian coach Lehmann over Sandpapergate sanctions
World.content:
David Warner has fired an indirect jab at Darren Lehmann, suggesting the ex-Australian coach knew of the use of sandpaper in the 2018 ball-tampering scandal.

Warner agreed with former International Cricket Council match referee Chris Broad, who said that Lehmann must have known of Australia's use of sandpaper on the ball, and if he did not, then he should not have been coach.

"Darren Lehmann surely knew all about it," Broad told Track Radio.

"And if he didn't, he shouldn't have been the coach at the time.

"He has got away lightly because he, OK, he left his job a few months later, but he didn't get any sanctions."

Warner replied to Track Radio's social media post of Broad's comments, writing on X: "I couldn't agree more and that's hard for me to say!"

Lehmann, who stepped down as Australia's coach in the aftermath of the 2018 scandal in South Africa, has denied personal knowledge of the Test team using sandpaper on the ball.

"I don't think everyone would have known [about the use of sandpaper]. You do know ball tampering is going on because it's been happening for 150 years," Lehmann, who will co-host the ABC's cricket podcast this season, told Summer Grandstand on the weekend.

"It's just how it's being done, and how you would know to that extent? That's an individual case-by-case, to be fair.

"I can only speak to what I know, and I know ball tampering was a big part of the game of cricket. Now it is obsolete.

Loading...

"That doesn't make it right either, but that's the case, and we paid a heavy price for that."

Lehmann's comments are at odds with Usman Khawaja's claims the whole team knew of the sandpaper plans, and the illegal tactic was also used in the match prior to being uncovered by television cameras at the infamous 2018 Test in Cape Town.

Cricket Australia (CA) has ruled out reopening its investigation into the scandal.

Warner on Monday night backed Khawaja's claims, labelling CA's investigation as "rushed and botched" after it found only he, Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith knew of the plan.

CA banned Smith and Warner from playing any cricket for one year and also suspended Bancroft for nine months. Smith and Warner were also stripped of their respective captain and vice-captain roles.

Paceman Mitchell Starc repeated his denial of the sandpaper plot when he became the first player from the match to front media, citing a statement he and his fellow bowlers made in 2021.

Usman Khawaja's (left) claims that everyone knew about the use of sandpaper has been backed by David Warner (second from left), denied by Darren Lehmann (right), while Steve Smith (second from right) is yet to comment. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

"We [bowlers] weren't aware anything was taken on to the field to be tampered with," Starc said on Tuesday.

"We saw [the sandpaper] on the big screen in Cape Town."

Asked why he and Khawaja had differing views, Starc responded: "That's a question for him."

"I'll stick to what I said … at the time, eight years ago. Clearly, there's different versions from different people."

Australian Cricketers Association chief executive Paul Marsh said on Tuesday it was understandable players' versions of events could differ.

Loading...

"Players and staff at the heart of the issue are entitled to share their experiences, just as others are entitled to put such a challenging period in their life behind them," Marsh said in a statement.

"There are no winners in this issue, and nothing can undo what happened.

"But we must recognise that there are humans in the centre of this and we are calling for the ongoing vitriol directed at those involved to come to an end."

Marsh's statement attracted the ire of former Test batsman Damien Martyn, who posted on X: "This statement from our players union does not reflect all ex players' opinions."

Meanwhile, the author of a review into Australia's cricket culture said he may have been lied to by players.

Simon Longstaff led an Ethics Centre team tasked with examining the sport's culture, but not the sandpaper scandal itself.

"Those matters had been investigated by Cricket Australia, and the findings were concluded," Longstaff wrote in the Australian Financial Review on Wednesday.

"Even so, we picked up whispers — few and very faint — that, perhaps, the public record did not tell the full story.

"All I can say is that if what Khawaja alleges turns out to be true, then I was also lied to.

"It is easy enough to understand how a group of players might perpetuate — either by act or omission — what could turn out to be a lie."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Usman Khawaja makes changes to book tour after tense 7.30 interview
World.content:
Usman Khawaja's publisher Penguin has confirmed that "adjustments" have been made to his book tour following a tense TV interview.

Khawaja's book, Sabr, released on Tuesday, contains an entire chapter titled "Sandpaper" dedicated to Australia's infamous 2018 tour of South Africa, which resulted in Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft being suspended for ball-tampering.

The 37-year-old appeared uncomfortable during an appearance on the ABC's 7.30 on Tuesday night, when he dodged questions from host Sarah Ferguson about the aforementioned chapter.

Khawaja denies starting 'witch-hunt' over Sandpapergate claims Usman Khawaja rejects claims he has reopened some of Australian crickets biggest wounds just to sell copies of his new book as he admits concerns it may have damaged friendships.

In a written statement to ABC Sport, Penguin pushed back on reports suggesting Khawaja's book tour had been cancelled altogether.

The publisher would not confirm what specific interviews had been cancelled, but that "adjustments" had been made.

"The book tour is 100 [per cent] still going ahead, we've just had to make some adjustments this week but no major cancellation of the tour at all," the statement read.

Penguin also confirmed Khawaja will be doing further interviews regarding his new book.

In the 7.30 interview, Khawaja was adamant that he did not want a "witch-hunt" to take place as a result of his claim that the entire Australian team was aware of the plan to tamper with the ball against South Africa.

Khawaja's account has been backed by Warner, who described it as being "100 per cent accurate" in his own statement on Monday night.

Bancroft refused to speak in depth on Khawaja's claims in a short interview with reporters as he arrived at Melbourne Airport prior to a Sheffield Shield clash between Western Australia and Victoria at the MCG this week, while Smith is yet to speak publicly regarding the new book.

Australian paceman Mitchell Starc denied suggestions the bowlers were in on the sandpaper ploy in a media appearance on Tuesday afternoon.

World.title: 'Discrimination' claim as AFLW player delisted weeks out from giving birth
World.content:
The AFLW pregnancy policy has been called into question as Gold Coast Suns player Georgia Clayden was delisted this week, just weeks before she is due to give birth.

Clayden spent this season on the inactive list with "injury (pregnancy)". The club announced on Tuesday that Clayden and fellow player Sienna McMullen were informed they would not be offered contracts for the 2027 season.

Former AFLW All-Australian-turned-commentator Kate McCarthy said more needed to be done to protect and support AFLW players and female athletes who choose to become mothers during their playing careers.

"A player should be able to make the incredible life decision to start a family without fearing it could come at the expense of their football career," McCarthy wrote on Instagram

Loading Instagram content

"There needs to be greater security and a genuine opportunity for players to return to the game after giving birth."

North Melbourne premiership player Eilish Sheerin responded publicly to McCarthy's post: "So well said. In other industries this would be viewed as discrimination."

Last December, former Carlton captain Kerryn Peterson was told by Carlton that she would not be offered a contract for 2026, just months after she gave birth to her first child.

Peterson was placed on the inactive list for this season after welcoming her newborn son, Max, in August, and had planned to return to the Blues the following season.

Essendon welcomed Bess Keaney back onto its list after she had a baby last season. (Getty Images: Daniel Carson)

Alternatively, Essendon's Bess Keaney rejoined her club's primary list this season after having a baby last year. She was placed on the club's inactive list with "injury" (pregnancy).

Rules within the Collective Bargaining Agreement allow for players returning from pregnancy to come off the inactive list at any point.

Replacement players signed in the meantime are then able to see out the entirety of their one-season contract, with the team in question allowed to have a squad of 31 for the remainder of that season.

In order for a player to return from the inactive list after pregnancy, they must be assessed as medically fit by the club doctor or an AFL medical officer.

McCarthy said it was not simply on clubs to offer this, as they needed greater support in this area too and called for policy change.

"With such limited spots in the AFLW, clubs are already forced to make incredibly difficult list management decisions. The current systems put both players and clubs in an unfair position," McCarthy said.

"Clubs should have the ability to retain a player returning from maternity leave without that player occupying one of their limited list spots. This would give the athlete the time and security to work towards returning to the level required, while allowing clubs the flexibility to manage their lists if that player isn't ready to return.

"Becoming a mother should not mean putting your football career at risk. And clubs shouldn't be forced into a position where supporting a player's return comes at the expense of another list spot. We should be creating a system that supports both. Right now, we're not."

Tech.title: Microsoft’s DLSS competitor is out for the Xbox Ally X and works in handheld mode
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Microsoft is now rolling out Automatic Super Resolution (Auto SR), an upscaling technology that competes with Nvidia’s DLSS, for the Xbox Ally X, Xbox Ally X20, and select Windows Copilot Plus PCs, the company announced today. Auto SR is also getting some new features alongside this official release.

In April, Microsoft started testing Auto SR on the Xbox Ally X, but you could only use it while docked. The full release of Auto SR announced today now works while you’re playing handheld and running on battery, and it also supports games running at 1080p. Microsoft does note that playing in handheld and at 1080p might lead to performance that “may not be as optimal as other configurations,” but says you’ll see visual improvements “especially in older games.”

Previously, Auto SR was also limited to framerates of “around” 60 to 75fps, but support for a new Auto SR Performance mode will allow you to hit framerates of up to 120fps. The Performance mode, and new compatibility with Auto HDR, will be available through Windows updates.

Tech.title: The VR Disney Plus app on Meta Quest now has 3D movies
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Disney is bringing more than 60 3D movies to the Disney Plus app on Meta Quest. The movies will be available to Disney Plus subscribers as part of an updated Disney Plus app that’s rolling out today.

The 3D movies you can check out include The Avengers and Black Panther, Meta says. But the updated Quest app doesn’t just offer 3D movies; you’ll also be able to see some films in themed, immersive virtual environments, like a Tatooine environment when watching Star Wars: A New Hope or a Scare Floor one for Monsters, Inc. I got to see an Avengers-themed immersive environment for myself while trying Meta’s forthcoming VR Glasses in September, and while it was novel for the few minutes I tried it, I wasn’t sure if it would be good during an entire movie.

The Disney Plus app on the VR Glasses, which are set to release sometime in spring 2027, will also let you watch IMAX Enhanced movies, including Avengers: Endgame, Lightyear, and Tron: Ares. The VR Glasses will also be a place to watch 3D movies from Lionsgate.

Tech.title: Oura is acquiring medical AI chatbot startup Counsel Health
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Oura announced its quarterly earnings today and said it agreed to acquire Counsel Health for $625 million, after adding the company’s AI chatbot to its app earlier this year. Counsel Health calls itself an “AI-native primary care company,” using the app to deliver AI-generated responses and insights based on users’ health data reported from their wearables that can then proceed to a conversation with one of its in-house physicians.

Oura says it expects the deal to close before the end of the year.

Oura CEO Tom Hale said in an interview with Bloomberg that the acquisition is part of a plan to connect wearables, clinical AI, and access to doctors based on insights from biometric data to answer questions or monitor ongoing conditions. Counsel Health’s AI chatbot can connect Oura users to a real doctor directly from the app and draw on users’ biometric data from their wearables in its answers to medical questions. The plan they describe in the press release is to focus on three areas, including preventative care, acute care for episodic health concerns, and specialty and chronic care for things like reproductive and cardiometabolic health.

According to Bloomberg, Counsel Health’s CEO Muthu Alagappan says it’s also planning to expand its network of on-demand physicians, which is currently “made up of about 50 people.” Counsel’s 70 employees will join Oura as part of the deal, with Alagappan becoming Oura’s chief clinical AI officer. Oura says in its announcement that Counsel will also continue offering its medical AI platform outside of Oura’s user base through new and existing enterprise partners, including “health plans, health systems, consumer health organizations, and employers.”

Tech.title: Sony cancels live-service shooter Fairgames
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The Fairgames cancellation won’t result in job cuts, and developer Haven Studios will now support other PlayStation studios, Bloomberg reports. The game was canceled following a recent test where “player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set,” according to part of an executive memo published by Bloomberg, which also cited “challenging market conditions in the PVP shooter genre.” Sony acquired Haven Studios in 2022.

Sony’s live service efforts have seen some success with Helldivers 2, which is also available on Xbox. Bungie’s Marathon, which launched this year, has had a rough start, but today the studio showed off some new features coming in a December update, including a new co-op PvE roguelite mode and a PvP deathmatch mode. Sony is also working on a live service Horizon spinoff, but recently rebooted it.

Tech.title: The PlayStation Plus PC app is shutting down next month
Tech.content: With a very small number of eligible PlayStation Plus Premium members (less than 0.4%) using the PlayStation Plus app on PC, making this change allows us to focus on enhancing high-quality experiences that more of our members want to use. As a result, the PlayStation Plus cloud streaming app on PC will no longer be available.

Tech.title: Starlink Mini 2 adds a swappable battery
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

SpaceX announced a new version of its all-in-one satellite internet terminal that integrates a dish, Wi-Fi router, and now a battery into a single device about the size of a laptop. According to some users on X who shared screenshots of invitations to order Starlink Mini 2, the dish is priced at $999, which includes a full year of Roam Unlimited service that SpaceX values at $2,100.

The Starlink Mini 2 will run for up to 4.5 hours on a full charge, SpaceX claims, but that can be expanded by hot-swapping in additional batteries that will be sold separately, or by connecting the dish to a 60W power source over USB-C.

Despite the addition of an integrated battery, the Starlink Mini 2 dish is thinner than the original Mini. SpaceX has managed to slim it down to 23.1mm thick, while the previous version of the Mini was 38.5mm. The Starlink Mini 2 is slightly heavier at around 3.5 pounds as a result of the added battery weight, but carries forward an IP67 dust- and waterproof rating so it’s still safe to use outdoors.

Preorders are now open “by invitation for select US customers,” according to the Starlink website, but “coming soon” to more customers and countries.

Tech.title: The US is winning the AI race. Jensen Huang could have blown it
Tech.content:
is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes.

As espionage targets go, Jensen Huang is perhaps one of the least surprising on Earth. The Nvidia CEO runs one of the world’s most valuable companies, controls the in-demand technology fueling the AI boom, and is cozy with presidents, CEOs, and all manner of important people. He also wears a cool leather jacket.

Which makes Huang’s admission that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy — reportedly while her spying was known to US intelligence and even President Donald Trump — all the more shocking. The fallout goes well beyond his marriage, his reputation, or Nvidia itself. Experts tell The Verge the incident threatens to disrupt the entire US AI industry, potentially jeopardize national security, and could undermine America’s efforts to maintain its fragile technological lead over China in AI.

“With those chips, the US lead could vanish in a matter of weeks or months.”

Nvidia is the undisputed leader in advanced computer chips, among the AI industry’s scarcest resources. While many ingredients go into building AI models — including talent, energy, capital, and data — top-tier chips are one of the most important, and Nvidia is one of a handful of companies with the expertise to design or manufacture them at the cutting edge. That makes it a gatekeeper to hardware that has become a key bottleneck in global AI development. US companies — including Meta, Anthropic, and OpenAI — are racing to develop chips of their own, in part to reduce their dependence on Nvidia, even as they spend billions securing ever more compute.

For China, the US’s main rival at the frontier of AI, that bottleneck is even tighter. To maintain its technological lead, the US has restricted the sale of the most advanced AI chips to the country in the hopes of slowing its progress in the sector, which has been impressive and is thought to trail the US by a matter of months. In response, China has made developing domestic alternatives a strategic national priority, though its leaders still lag Nvidia at the bleeding edge. At the same time, a thriving black market for restricted Nvidia chips has emerged.

Experts tell The Verge that China could exploit access to Nvidia to accelerate its own development, or to impede the US development of AI.

Getting its hands on more Nvidia chips is the most obvious win for Beijing, says Emily Kilcrease, a senior fellow and director of the energy, economics, and security program at the Center for a New American Security (CNAS) think tank. China has advantages in other parts of the AI race — including abundant energy and a solid ecosystem of open weight models — but without the latest Nvidia chips, it “cannot close the gap with US frontier capabilities,” Kilcrease tells The Verge. “With those chips, the US lead could vanish in a matter of weeks or months.”

It is not clear how successful the alleged spying operation has been on that front. There is no public evidence indicating that Huang himself has helped direct restricted Nvidia chips toward China or that sensitive information about them was obtained from him. But companies linked to the alleged spy, Alice Huang — no relation to Jensen — have reportedly enabled at least $7 billion of Nvidia chip sales to China.

Brookings fellow Kyle Chan tells The Verge that a concern for US industry could be that companies with alleged ties to China may have had priority access to Nvidia’s latest GPUs. “In a time of chip scarcity,” that would make it much harder for American companies to access them, Chan says.

Huang is also a prominent critic of American restrictions on chip sales, and Nvidia spends a formidable amount lobbying in Washington. Last year, he successfully secured White House approval to start exporting Nvidia’s H200 AI GPU chips to “approved customers” in China and other countries. Crucially, Huang also has the ear of President Trump as well as other world leaders, giving him great influence over policy decisions.

Hardware is not the only thing of value China could get from close access to Huang, Sunny Cheung, a fellow for China studies at the Jamestown Foundation think tank, tells The Verge. “I actually think too many people are focused on whether somebody managed to steal Nvidia’s trade secrets,” Cheung says, calling it a “very narrow way” of looking at espionage. “I would hope Jensen Huang isn’t foolish enough to hand over the blueprints for Nvidia’s next-generation chips to a suspected Chinese intelligence operative.”

The Nvidia CEO’s relationships with other tech executives, senior policymakers, and Trump himself give him an unusually intimate view into how some of the most powerful people in the US are thinking and planning. Beijing could use information on how American companies are planning major infrastructure expansions, their compute requirements, or broad industry trends to inform its own investments and industrial strategy, Cheung says.

Huang’s intelligence value could extend well beyond AI, too. “That information alone could be extremely valuable,” says Cheung, pointing to insights Beijing could glean into White House thinking about export controls or the private views of Silicon Valley executives on China and Taiwan.

“When so much of America’s AI infrastructure depends on one company, any significant security or governance problem at Nvidia can create uncertainty across the industry.”

But helping China advance is only one side of this equation. Disrupting Nvidia — as this scandal clearly has — could destabilize America’s entire AI industry. More than most companies, Nvidia is remarkably closely tied to the identity and reputation of its rockstar CEO. Huang cofounded the company more than three decades ago, and ever since then he has served as its president, chief executive, and a member of the board of directors. Despite holding a relatively small stake in the company, in many ways Nvidia is Jensen Huang. Nvidia shares have slumped since news of the affair broke.

“When so much of America’s AI infrastructure depends on one company, any significant security or governance problem at Nvidia can create uncertainty across the industry,” Cheung says.

Kilcrease echoes those concerns, warning that the scandal could “destabilize” the company. At the very least, she says the various investigations already underway “will consume an immense amount of bandwidth within the company,” creating a very real risk of weighing down Nvidia’s day-to-day operations. If those distractions begin to affect Nvidia’s ability to execute — slowing decisions, product rollouts, or the allocation of already scarce chips — the consequences could quickly reach customers. The AI labs and hyperscalers such as OpenAI and Anthropic “could have a real issue accessing the vast amounts of compute they need,” Kilcrease says, adding that switching to other hardware “takes time.”

In a race to build increasingly powerful AI, time is a precious resource. Experts say China trails the US closely, meaning that even modest delays for American companies can help Chinese rivals catch up. Nvidia is almost certain to face further disruption as investigations continue, though the extent to which the turmoil will roil the rest of the industry may be difficult to measure.

For China, however, the scandal could be about to backfire spectacularly now everything is out in the open. “The odds of AI chip control legislation being passed in Congress just went through the roof,” Kilcrease says.

Correction, Tuesday November 10th: A sentence in this article misstated that Anthropic is the leader in advanced computer chips. It is Nvidia.

Tech.title: Google’s Pixel Tag tracker is now available
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

At 0.4 ounces, the Pixel Tag is slightly lighter than the AirTag 2 and while its oblong design is longer than Apple’s tracker, Google’s is a bit thinner. It doesn’t include a hole to attach it to keys, luggage, or other items you want to track, but you can pair it with accessories that make it easy to tether to objects. Unlike Apple’s AirTags, the Pixel Tag has a button that can be pressed to trigger a sound should your phone get misplaced instead of the tracker.

Google says the Pixel Tag will run for over a year on a single CR2032 coin battery, and it has an IP67 rating so it’s dustproof and can survive a shallow dunking. The tracker also features ultra wideband (UWB) support and Channel Sounding through Bluetooth 6.0. Android phones with a UWB chip can display the exact distance and direction to the Pixel Tag in the Find Hub app once you’re close to it, while Bluetooth Channel Sounding is limited to just distance.

The Pixel Tag is compatible with smartphones running Android 9 or later, but you’ll need devices that specifically include a UWB chip or support Bluetooth 6.0 to take advantage of Find Hub’s precise locating features.

Tech.title: Nvidia’s crisis has corporate governance experts reaching for the popcorn
Tech.content:
Nvidia’s stock sank 5.47% on Tuesday, following a 4% drop on Monday, a loss of about 9.5% in two days, even though there wasn’t much news out of the company. CEO Jensen Huang has reportedly been trying to conduct business as usual after admitting to an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence agencies believe was spying for China. The biggest development: the board hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an internal investigation.

What comes next is mostly a guessing game, even for the people who study how boards are supposed to handle crises. Two corporate governance professors, Ann Lipton of the University of Colorado and Todd Henderson of the University of Chicago, say there is no real precedent for a CEO caught up in a suspected honeypot. And while they have views on what the investigation should ask, like everyone else, they’re watching to see how it plays out.

“There have actually been affair cases and sexual harassment cases,” Lipton said, but was quick to add that she doesn’t know of previous cases that also involve potential national security compromises. Henderson, whose research interests include corporations, securities regulation, and law and economics, said much depends on facts few people have yet, including, most importantly, what, if anything, Alice Huang got out of Jensen Huang. (Secrets about Nvidia’s fabs or chip designs would matter to the Justice Department. Ordinary corporate information probably would not.)

Lipton described the investigation led by Nvidia’s independent board members, with their own outside counsel, as perhaps the most “standard” aspect of the whole affair so far. She also observed that an investigation will be “exactly as thorough” as the directors running it want it to be, which is also standard. Henderson made a related point about incentives, saying that Washington law firms that conduct internal investigations “know who pays their bills.” He didn’t suggest that’s happening here.

Lipton said she sees three lines of inquiry, including whether the law was broken, whether Huang violated Nvidia’s internal policies, and whether the board was misled, including how forthcoming he was and when he was on notice. It’s notable, as Wired reported Monday, that Huang hired a PR crisis firm known for handling sex scandals a full year ago. Of course, the driver could have been about the affair alone. It’s unclear when Huang learned Alice Huang was a suspected spy. The board said in a Sunday statement about the matter that Nvidia has “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.”

Henderson similarly stressed the importance of what Huang knew and when. He described two scenarios. In one, Huang hires a PR firm because an extramarital affair is embarrassing, without knowing who the woman is. In the other, he knows she is a suspected Chinese spy. “I think that’s very different,” he said. “If I were a board member and the CEO of a company with very sensitive technology was in that situation, I would be furious if they didn’t tell me.” Not telling the board that you have cancer “or that you’ve been sleeping with a Chinese spy,” said Henderson, “seems to me to be a fireable offense.”

Either way, Lipton expects shareholder suits, and she said two kinds are possible. Securities fraud, which she said is “only about lying,” is the most obvious, and as we reported yesterday, Nvidia is already facing a proposed class action lawsuit that alleges Nvidia and Huang misled investors by concealing Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang while describing dealings with her former employer as routine. “You can have as many affairs with Chinese spies as you like,” Lipton said. “You just can’t lie about it under the federal securities laws.”

A mismanagement claim under Delaware law, where Nvidia is incorporated, is much harder.
